Setup. Consider a compound-nucleus resonance described by a statistical model with the following ingredients:

(i) A set of N reduced partial neutron width amplitudes {γ_n^(i)} (i = 1,…,N) attached to N resonances of fixed spin and parity at excitation energies near the neutron separation threshold. In the standard Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) random-matrix description, these amplitudes are independent zero-mean Gaussian random variables, so that the reduced neutron widths Γ_n^(i) ∝ (γ_n^(i))^2 are distributed according to the Porter–Thomas distribution

   P(x) dx = (1/√(2π x)) exp(−x/2) dx,   x = Γ_n^(i)/⟨Γ_n⟩,

i.e. a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom.

(ii) A set of gamma decay channels c = 1,…,M from each resonance to lower-lying final states, with partial gamma widths Γ_{γ,c}^(i) and total gamma width Γ_γ^(i) = Σ_c Γ_{γ,c}^(i). In the standard picture the partial-width amplitudes γ_{γ,c}^(i) are also independent zero-mean Gaussian random variables, so each Γ_{γ,c}^(i) is Porter–Thomas distributed and, by the central limit theorem, the total widths Γ_γ^(i) have a relative variance that scales as 1/M_eff and is therefore strongly peaked about its mean for large effective channel number M_eff.

Hypothesis. Suppose now that a small subset S ⊂ {1,…,M} of gamma decay channels (with |S| ≪ M, e.g. transitions to a few low-lying final states) is anomalously strongly coupled, in the sense that the variances ⟨(γ_{γ,c}^(i))^2⟩ for c ∈ S are much larger than the variances for c ∉ S. Assume |S| is small enough that the central-limit-theorem narrowing of the distribution of Γ_γ^(i) is evaded (so the distribution of total gamma widths is broadened toward experimental values), yet large enough in coupling strength to shift the average Γ_γ^(i) toward the experimentally observed values.

Within a unified random-matrix / shell-model statistical framework where neutron and gamma channels are treated on the same footing (e.g. via a non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian H_eff = H_GOE − (i/2) Σ_c V_c V_c^T with channel-coupling vectors V_c), the strong gamma channels in S contribute rank-|S| anti-Hermitian terms that break orthogonal invariance and mix the resonances.

Question. Does the presence of such a small number |S| of strongly coupled gamma decay channels — sufficient to broaden the distribution of total gamma decay widths Γ_γ^(i) and shift its mean toward experiment — necessarily induce a measurable deviation of the distribution of normalized reduced neutron widths Γ_n^(i)/⟨Γ_n⟩ from the Porter–Thomas (chi-squared, one degree of freedom) distribution? Quantify the deviation, for instance by computing the effective number of degrees of freedom ν in a fit to a chi-squared distribution of ν degrees of freedom, as a function of |S| and of the coupling strengths of the strong gamma channels.

Subsequent work has shown that channel coupling can in principle modify the Porter–Thomas distribution: rank-one and few-channel anti-Hermitian perturbations to a GOE Hamiltonian provably alter the chi-squared(1) law for partial widths, and realistic estimates of nonstatistical gamma decay yield significant modifications of the PTD for neutron widths. The Hoyle state is the second 0⁺ excited state of the ¹²C nucleus, located near the 3α breakup threshold and known to decay predominantly through the sequential channel ¹²C* → ⁸Be(g.s.) + α → 3α. A direct three-body breakup channel ¹²C* → 3α (in which the three α particles are emitted simultaneously, not via an intermediate ⁸Be ground state) is also kinematically allowed and is regarded as a sensitive probe of an underlying α-cluster (in particular, dilute α-condensate-like) structure of the Hoyle state.

Let Γ_{3α,direct} denote the partial width for the direct three-α decay of the Hoyle state and let Γ denote its total width (equivalently, let Γ_{8Be+α} be the partial width of the sequential channel). Define the direct branching ratio
    B_direct = Γ_{3α,direct} / Γ   (or, equivalently, Γ_{3α,direct} / Γ_{8Be+α} to leading order).

Existing experimental searches have, at the time of formulation, established only upper bounds B_direct ≲ 10⁻⁴ relative to the sequential ⁸Be + α channel, with no positive observation.

Problem. Determine whether a nonzero direct three-α decay branch of the Hoyle state can be experimentally observed (i.e., whether B_direct > 0 can be established at a statistically significant level), and assess whether such an observation, together with the kinematical correlations of the three outgoing α particles, provides a quantitative discriminator of the internal α-cluster structure of the Hoyle state.

In a microscopic α-cluster description of light self-conjugate nuclei, the second 0⁺ state of ¹²C (the Hoyle state, near 7.65 MeV) is interpreted as a dilute, weakly interacting gas of three α particles essentially condensed into an S-wave 0s orbital. Building on this picture, consider the following two linked questions:

(a) Is the first 1⁻ state of ¹²C (the lowest J^π = 1⁻ excited state, at roughly 10.84 MeV) an "α-gas" state obtained from the Hoyle state by promoting exactly one of the three α particles from the 0s orbital into a 0p (P-shell) orbital, so that the resulting state has an anomalously large root-mean-square radius characteristic of a dilute α-condensate? Provide a theoretical demonstration (e.g., via a THSR-type α-condensate wave function, RGM/GCM, or equivalent microscopic α-cluster calculation) and/or experimental confirmation (e.g., from the matter/charge radius, monopole/dipole transition strengths, and α-decay branching) that establishes or refutes this interpretation.

(b) The fifth 0⁺ state of ¹⁶O has been interpreted as a structure consisting of an α particle orbiting the 1⁻ state of ¹²C. Assuming the interpretation in (a) is confirmed, determine how this structural assignment for the fifth 0⁺ state of ¹⁶O must be revised, and exhibit a corresponding microscopic four-α (or α + ¹²C*) cluster wave function, together with predicted observables (excitation energy, radius, decay widths, and electromagnetic transition strengths) consistent with the revised interpretation.

$$w = -\frac{L(f^3)}{3\,L(f^2)^2}\, t, \qquad t \geq 0.$$

For each integer $n \geq 2$, consider the coefficient functional $\Lambda_n(f) = a_n$, the $n$-th Taylor coefficient of $f$. Prove that for every extremal function $f \in S$ for $\operatorname{Re}\,\Lambda_n$, the associated asymptotic half-line is radial, i.e.
$$\frac{\Lambda_n(f^3)}{\Lambda_n(f^2)^2} \in \mathbb{R}.$$

(It is known that this holds for $n = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$; the problem is to establish it for all $n \geq 2$.)

Let $S\subset H(\mathbb{D})$ be the class of normalised univalent functions, i.e. functions $f$ that are analytic and one-to-one on $\mathbb{D}$ with $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=1$. The Koebe function is $k(z)=z/(1-z)^2$, and a rotation of the Koebe function is any function of the form $k_\theta(z)=e^{-i\theta}k(e^{i\theta}z)$ for $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$.

Suppose $L_1,L_2:H(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{C}$ are continuous complex-linear functionals, each of which is non-constant on $S$, and suppose that $L_1\neq tL_2$ for every real $t>0$. Assume that there exists $f\in S$ such that
$$\operatorname{Re} L_1(f)=\sup_{g\in S}\operatorname{Re} L_1(g)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{Re} L_2(f)=\sup_{g\in S}\operatorname{Re} L_2(g).$$

Must $f$ be a rotation of the Koebe function?

Consider a self-conjugate light nucleus modeled as a dilute system of bosonic constituents in which the lowest 0⁺ state lying near the four-α breakup threshold of ¹⁶O is interpreted as a Hoyle-analog state. Two competing condensation pictures are proposed for this 0⁺ state:

(i) a Bose–Einstein-like condensate of four α particles, in which all four α clusters occupy a common 0S single-particle orbital (a Tohsaki–Horiuchi–Schuck–Röpke (THSR) type wave function built from four α's);

(ii) a Bose–Einstein-like condensate of two ⁸Be-like bosonic "molecules," in which the four α's are first paired into two ⁸Be subunits, and the two ⁸Be bosons then occupy a common 0S orbital.

Both trial wave functions are fully antisymmetrized in the underlying nucleons, and numerical experience suggests that, as with the Hoyle state of ¹²C (where the THSR wave function and the Kamimura-type 3α wave function have approximately 100% squared overlap), the two ¹⁶O wave functions may have a very large mutual overlap.

Problem. Determine, on the theoretical level, whether the Hoyle-analog 0⁺ state of ¹⁶O is best described as a condensate of four individual α particles or as a condensate of two ⁸Be-like bosonic molecules, and devise observables or mathematical criteria (e.g., occupation numbers of the one-α and one-⁸Be density matrices, intrinsic-density structure, momentum distributions, or decay-channel branching ratios) capable of unambiguously distinguishing these two condensation pictures even when their many-body wave functions have nearly unit squared overlap.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk. Suppose $f(z)=z+a_2 z^2+a_3 z^3+\cdots$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{D}$ and maps $\mathbb{D}$ univalently onto a simply connected domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}$. Let $F:\Omega\to\mathbb{D}$ denote the inverse map of $f$, so that $F$ is conformal on $\Omega$ with $F'$ its complex derivative. Consider the intersection of $\Omega$ with the real axis $\mathbb{R}$, which is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$, and the integral
$$ I_p(\Omega) \;=\; \int_{\Omega\cap\mathbb{R}} |F'(x)|^p\, dx. $$
It is known that $I_1(\Omega)$ is finite, with a bound independent of $f$ (Hayman–Wu theorem), and that $I_2(\Omega)$ can be infinite (for instance for slit disks of suitable radius).

Question: Is it true that for every such univalent $f$ and every $p$ with $1\le p<2$,
$$ \int_{\Omega\cap\mathbb{R}} |F'(x)|^p\, dx \;<\; \infty\, ? $$

representations.normalized:
In nuclear cluster physics, the Hoyle state is the second 0⁺ excited state of ¹²C near 7.65 MeV above the ground state, and is interpreted as a dilute, weakly interacting gas-like (Bose–Einstein-condensate-like) configuration of three α particles. Such configurations have so far been studied principally in self-conjugate nuclei with equal neutron and proton numbers N = Z (e.g., ⁸Be, ¹²C, ¹⁶O, ²⁰Ne, …), where they are conjectured to appear near the Nα breakup threshold.

Consider neutron-rich nuclei that can be modeled as an α-cluster core surrounded by additional valence neutrons, in particular the carbon isotopes ¹³C (3α + n) and ¹⁴C (3α + 2n), and the beryllium isotopes (e.g., 2α + xn systems such as ⁹Be, ¹⁰Be, ¹¹Be, ¹²Be).

Problem:

(a) Determine which of these neutron-rich nuclei support Hoyle-like α-cluster gas states, i.e., low-density excited 0⁺ (or analogous Jᵖ) states near the multi-α + xn breakup threshold whose intrinsic structure is well approximated by a dilute condensate of α particles together with valence neutrons in single-particle (molecular-orbital or covalent) configurations.

(b) Quantify how the presence of the extra valence neutrons modifies the α-cluster structure relative to the corresponding N = Z Hoyle-like state, addressing the binding energy and excitation energy of such states relative to the multi-α threshold, the spatial extent and density profile of the α-cluster core, the rotational/vibrational band structure built upon these states, and the role of the valence neutrons (covalent "molecular" binding versus mean-field-like delocalization) in stabilizing or destabilizing the α gas configuration.

Provide a theoretical characterization of these Hoyle-like states with valence neutrons and identify experimental signatures that would distinguish them from non-clusterized excited states.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk. For a conformal (i.e. holomorphic and injective) map $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{D}$ and a real number $p\in(-\infty,+\infty)$, define the integral means spectrum of $f$ by
$$\beta_f(p)=\limsup_{r\to 1^-}\frac{\log\!\left(\int_{|\zeta|=1}|f'(r\zeta)|^p\,|d\zeta|\right)}{\log\!\dfrac{1}{1-r}}.$$
Define the universal integral means spectrum (restricted to conformal self-maps of $\mathbb{D}$) by
$$B(p)=\sup\bigl\{\beta_f(p):f\text{ a conformal map of }\mathbb{D}\text{ into }\mathbb{D}\bigr\}.$$
Prove or disprove the following conjectured exact formula:
$$B(p)=\begin{cases}-p-1, & p\le -2,\\[2pt] p^2/4, & -2\le p\le 2,\\[2pt] p-1, & p\ge 2.\end{cases}$$
In particular, establish the equality $B(p)=|p|-1$ at $p=\pm 2$ (the Brennan-type endpoint values) and the equality $B(p)=p^2/4$ for $|p|\le 2$.

The conjectured exact formula for the universal integral means spectrum B(p) (combining the Brennan, Carleson–Jones, and Kraetzer conjectures) remains open. The Brennan conjecture B(p)=|p|-1 at p=±2 has been verified only in special cases (e.g., for univalent rational functions and for semigroups of holomorphic functions in recent works), and Carleson–Jones proved an asymptotic expansion near p=2. Kraetzer's conjecture B(p)=p²/4 for |p|≤2 is supported by numerical evidence but unproven; it is known that B(p)≥p²/4 in this range.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk. A function $f$ holomorphic in $\mathbb{D}$ is called $p$-valent in $\mathbb{D}$ (where $p$ is a positive integer) if $f$ takes no value more than $p$ times in $\mathbb{D}$ and takes some value exactly $p$ times.

Fix positive integers $p$ and $q$ with $1\le q\le p$, and let
$$f(z)=z^{q}+\sum_{n=q+1}^{\infty}a_{n}z^{n}$$
be $p$-valent in $\mathbb{D}$. Suppose $f$ has exactly $s$ zeros (counted with multiplicity) $\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\dots,\beta_{s}$ in $\mathbb{D}\setminus\{0\}$, so that $0<|\beta_k|<1$ for each $k$, and assume $t:=p-q-s\ge 0$.

Define the comparison function
$$F(z)=\frac{z^{q}}{(1-z)^{2q+2s}}\Big(1+\frac{z}{1-z}\Big)^{2t}\prod_{k=1}^{s}\bigl(1+|\beta_{k}|z\bigr)\bigl(1+|\beta_{k}|^{-1}z\bigr)\cdot\prod_{k=1}^{s}|\beta_k|,$$
written so that
$$F(z)=z+\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}A_{n}z^{n}.$$

Prove or disprove: under the above hypotheses,
$$|a_{n}|\le |A_{n}|\quad\text{for every } n\ge q+1.$$

Consider the verification of an automated-driving system whose safety claim requires statistically significant evidence of correct behavior across the operational domain. Direct field operational testing (FOT), in which the system is driven on public roads to accumulate exposure to real traffic, is estimated to require on the order of 10^5 to 10^11 miles to attain such statistical significance, which is infeasible within realistic project time-frames. A central source of difficulty is the existence of "corner-case" scenarios — situations whose probability of occurrence on actual roads is extremely low, so that they are essentially never sampled by FOT, yet whose correct handling is critical to the system's safety case.

Develop a verification methodology that replaces, or substantially reduces reliance on, infeasible FOT by combining:
(a) simulation-based testing, in which scenarios are generated and executed in a virtual environment, and
(b) short-mileage reproduction of rare corner-case scenarios on physical test courses.

The methodology must specify:
1. A formal definition of the operational domain and of the class of corner-case scenarios to be covered.
2. A procedure for systematically generating, sampling, or enumerating corner-case scenarios with extremely low natural occurrence probability so that statistically meaningful coverage is achieved.
3. A quantitative argument relating performance measured under simulation and short test-course mileage to the safety performance that would have been measured by full-scale FOT, including a treatment of the reality gap between simulated/test-course conditions and real-road conditions.
4. Criteria under which the combined simulation plus short-mileage test-course evidence is sufficient to substitute for FOT of the order required for statistical significance.

Provide such a methodology, or prove that no methodology meeting all four requirements can exist under stated assumptions.

Let $S$ denote the usual class of analytic univalent functions $f$ on the unit disk $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ normalized by $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=1$. For $f,g\in S$ and parameters $\alpha,\beta\in(0,1)$ with $\alpha+\beta=1$, define the arithmetic and geometric mean functions
$$F(z)=\alpha f(z)+\beta g(z),\qquad G(z)=z\left(\frac{f(z)}{z}\right)^{\!\alpha}\!\left(\frac{g(z)}{z}\right)^{\!\beta},$$
where the principal branch of the powers is used (so $G$ is analytic on $\mathbb{D}$ with $G(0)=0$, $G'(0)=1$). For an analytic function $h$ on $\mathbb{D}$, let its valence be $\sup_{w\in\mathbb{C}}\#\{z\in\mathbb{D}:h(z)=w\}\in\{1,2,\dots,\infty\}$.

It is known that whenever
$$\frac{1}{1+e^{\pi}}<\alpha,\beta<\frac{e^{\pi}}{1+e^{\pi}},$$
there exist $f,g\in S$ for which both $F$ and $G$ have infinite valence in $\mathbb{D}$.

Investigate the behavior at the "fringes" of the interval $(0,1)$: for $0<\alpha\le \frac{1}{1+e^{\pi}}$ (with $\beta=1-\alpha$), is there a finite upper bound, depending only on $\alpha$, on the valence of $F$ and on the valence of $G$ as $f,g$ range over $S$? If so, determine such a bound as a function of $\alpha$.

Consider a safety-critical system S that is decomposed into subsystems, some of which contain one or more machine-learning (ML) models. Classical (deductive) engineering produces components whose behavior is specified and verified against explicit requirements, while ML components are obtained inductively from data and therefore carry residual uncertainty. Suppose S has a set of system-level safety requirements R_S. For each subsystem U ⊆ S that contains ML models M_1, ..., M_k, one wishes to derive a set of ML-model-level requirements R_{M_i} such that:

(i) Satisfaction of R_{M_1}, ..., R_{M_k}, together with the requirements assigned to the non-ML parts of U, formally entails the subsystem-level requirements R_U allocated from R_S.
(ii) The derivation simultaneously accommodates the deductive development process used for non-ML components and the inductive development process used for the ML models.
(iii) The derivation is compatible with, and exploits, the following safety-analysis mechanisms: (a) black-box verification of trained ML models; (b) encapsulation of ML models by rule-based safeguards that constrain their outputs; (c) redundant and diverse architectures that mitigate and absorb the uncertainty of ML models; (d) system-modification patterns that allow new requirements to be satisfied without retraining or altering the ML model, so as to limit the "Change Anything Change Everything" (CACE) effect by which any change to an ML model can affect any of its outputs.

Provide a rigorous methodology — i.e., a formal framework, a set of decomposition rules, and an associated proof obligation discharge procedure — for performing the breakdown R_U ↦ {R_{M_i}} satisfying (i)–(iii), and demonstrate its soundness.

Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk. For a function $g$ analytic in $\mathbb{D}$, the valence of $g$ is defined as
$$v(g) = \sup_{w \in \mathbb{C}} \#\{z \in \mathbb{D} : g(z) = w\} \in \{1, 2, 3, \dots\} \cup \{\infty\}.$$
A sequence $\{v_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ of positive integers (allowing the value $\infty$) is called a valence sequence if there exists a function $f$ analytic in $\mathbb{D}$ such that, for every $n \geq 1$, the $n$-th derivative $f^{(n)}$ has valence $v_n$ in $\mathbb{D}$, i.e. $v(f^{(n)}) = v_n$ for all $n \geq 1$.

Problem: Find non-trivial necessary conditions on a sequence $\{v_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ for it to be a valence sequence, and find non-trivial sufficient conditions on $\{v_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ that guarantee it is a valence sequence. Ideally, characterize valence sequences completely.

Consider two system-level safety assurance frameworks used for engineering safety-critical systems:

1. STAMP/STPA (Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes / System-Theoretic Process Analysis): a hazard analysis technique that models a system as a hierarchical control structure of controllers, actuators, sensors, and controlled processes, and identifies unsafe control actions and their causal scenarios.

2. Goal Structuring Notation (GSN): a graphical argumentation notation for safety cases, in which top-level safety goals are decomposed via strategies into subgoals, supported by context, assumptions, justifications, and evidence (solutions).

Now consider safety-critical systems that contain subsystems implemented by machine-learning models, i.e., functions f: X → Y obtained by training on data, whose behavior carries intrinsic uncertainty (epistemic uncertainty about the learned hypothesis, aleatoric uncertainty in the data and operating environment, distributional shift between training and deployment, and quantifiable confidence/calibration of predictions).

Problem. Propose a principled extension of STAMP/STPA and of GSN such that:
(a) STAMP/STPA control-structure models and unsafe-control-action / causal-scenario analyses can explicitly represent and reason about machine-learning–induced uncertainty (e.g., model confidence, input-distribution coverage, training-data assumptions, and failure modes specific to learned components);
(b) GSN safety-case arguments can express claims, strategies, contexts, assumptions, and evidence types that capture and discharge machine-learning uncertainty in a sound, auditable manner;
(c) The extensions admit a formal semantics or notational discipline that supports compositional reasoning when learned components are integrated into the broader control system.

Provide such extensions, including their syntax, semantics, and demonstration that they faithfully capture the uncertainty associated with ML components in safety-critical subsystems.

Let $\mathcal{S}_H$ denote the class of complex-valued harmonic functions $f = h + \overline{g}$ on the unit disk $\mathbb{D} = \{z\in\mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ that are univalent and sense-preserving, normalized so that $h(0) = g(0) = 0$ and $h'(0) = 1$. Let $\mathcal{S}_H^{\,0}$ denote the subclass of $\mathcal{S}_H$ consisting of those $f$ with the additional normalization $g'(0) = 0$. Write each $f\in\mathcal{S}_H$ as
$$h(z) = z + \sum_{n\ge 2} a_n z^n, \qquad g(z) = \sum_{n\ge 1} b_n z^n.$$

It is known that for every $f\in\mathcal{S}_H^{\,0}$ one has $\{w : |w| < 1/16\} \subset f(\mathbb{D})$, and that the function
$$k_0(z) = \mathrm{Re}\!\left(\frac{z + \tfrac{1}{3}z^3}{(1-z)^3}\right) + i\,\mathrm{Im}\!\left(\frac{z}{(1-z)^2}\right)$$
belongs to $\mathcal{S}_H^{\,0}$ and maps $\mathbb{D}$ onto the plane slit along the real axis from $-1/6$ to $-\infty$.

(a) Prove that the Koebe constant for the class $\mathcal{S}_H^{\,0}$ — that is, $\inf\{\mathrm{dist}(0, \partial f(\mathbb{D})) : f\in\mathcal{S}_H^{\,0}\}$ — equals $1/6$.

(b) Determine the value of
$$\alpha := \sup\{|a_2| : f \in \mathcal{S}_H\}.$$

(It is known that the Koebe constant $d$ for $\mathcal{S}_H$ satisfies $d \ge 1/(2\alpha)$, and the best known bound is $\alpha < 57.05$.)

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The Clunie–Sheil-Small conjecture that the Koebe constant for $\mathcal{S}_H^{\,0}$ equals $1/6$ (with the harmonic Koebe function as extremal) remains open in general; it has been verified only for special subclasses (starlike, typically real, convex in one direction, close-to-convex). The exact value of $\sup\{|a_2| : f\in\mathcal{S}_H\}$ is also still unknown, with only numerical upper bounds available. Recent (2024–2025) arXiv work continues to attack these problems but does not resolve them.

Consider a machine-learning model M (for example, a trained classifier or regressor) that is to be deployed as a component of a safety-critical system. Beyond classical predictive accuracy (e.g., confusion-matrix-based metrics), identify and rigorously define a complete set of quality characteristics that should be specified, measured, and evaluated to certify M for safety-critical use. In particular, provide precise mathematical or operational definitions, together with concrete evaluation procedures (metrics, test protocols, and acceptance criteria), for at least the following candidate characteristics:

1. Resource behavior: quantitative measures of the memory footprint required for inference (and, if relevant, training).
2. Time behavior: quantitative measures of inference latency and throughput, including worst-case execution time bounds.
3. Robustness against adversarial examples: given an input space X with a metric d and a perturbation budget ε > 0, define and evaluate the model's resistance to inputs x' with d(x, x') ≤ ε that change the model's output in an unsafe way; specify both empirical attack-based metrics and certified/provable robustness metrics.
4. Analyzability / interpretability: formal notions of the ease with which the internal computations of M can be inspected, visualized, or explained, together with quantitative measures of explanation quality.
5. Testability for formal verification: structural properties of M (e.g., architectural simplicity, piecewise-linearity, bounded depth) that enable tractable application of formal verification methods, together with measures of verification cost and coverage.

Propose a coherent quality model that integrates these characteristics, demonstrate that the proposed definitions are mutually consistent and measurable, and discuss any trade-offs (e.g., between accuracy, robustness, interpretability, and verification cost) that arise when optimizing M with respect to all of them simultaneously.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ and let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the class of analytic functions $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ of the form $f(z)=z+\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}a_k z^k$. For $f\in\mathcal{A}$ and $\delta\geq 0$, define the $\delta$-neighbourhood of $f$ by
$$N_\delta(f)=\Big\{g\in\mathcal{A}: g(z)=z+\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}b_k z^k,\ \sum_{k=2}^{\infty}k\,|a_k-b_k|\le\delta\Big\}.$$
Let $\mathcal{S}$ denote the class of normalised univalent functions on $\mathbb{D}$, let $\mathcal{S}t\subset\mathcal{S}$ denote the subclass of starlike functions, and let $\prec$ denote subordination. For real numbers $A,B$ with $-1\le B<A\le 1$, define the Janowski class
$$K[A,B]=\Big\{f\in\mathcal{S}: 1+\frac{zf''(z)}{f'(z)}\prec\frac{1+Az}{1+Bz},\ z\in\mathbb{D}\Big\}.$$
Define
$$\delta(A,B)=\begin{cases}(1-B)(A-B)/B,& B\ne 0,\\ e^{-A},& B=0.\end{cases}$$
It is known that for every $f\in K[A,B]$, the inclusion $N_{\delta(A,B)}(f)\subset \mathcal{S}t$ holds (with $\delta(A,B)$ best possible) provided either
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $-(\sqrt{3}+2)^{-1}\le B<A\le 1$, or
\item[(b)] $-1\le -A\le B<A\le 1$.
\end{enumerate}
Determine whether the inclusion $N_{\delta(A,B)}(f)\subset \mathcal{S}t$ holds for every $f\in K[A,B]$ and every pair $(A,B)$ with $-1\le B<A\le 1$, without the additional hypotheses (a) or (b).

representations.normalized:
Consider a supervised machine-learning system deployed in a safety-critical setting. During development, the model is trained and validated on data drawn from a fixed but unknown distribution P_test on an input–output space X × Y. After deployment, the system observes a stream of operational inputs (and, possibly delayed or partially observed, corresponding outputs) (x_t, y_t)_{t≥1} drawn from a time-varying operational distribution P_op,t that may drift away from P_test as t grows.

Develop a principled methodology for the operation and maintenance phase that simultaneously:

1. (Consistency monitoring) Provides a statistical procedure that, at each time t, tests the null hypothesis H_0: P_op,t = P_test against the alternative of drift, with controlled false-alarm rate and quantifiable detection delay, using only the streaming operational data and a finite reference sample from P_test.

2. (Adaptation) Specifies a continuous update rule that modifies the deployed model f_t whenever significant drift is detected (or continuously), in such a way that
   (a) the updated model's risk under P_op,t is bounded above by a prescribed safety threshold,
   (b) safety-relevant performance guarantees established at development time are preserved or re-established under the updated distribution, and
   (c) the procedure is robust to label scarcity, label delay, and adversarial or rare-event inputs.

Formulate precise sufficient conditions on P_test, the family {P_op,t}, the model class, and the available feedback under which such a monitoring-and-adaptation scheme exists, and characterize fundamental limits (in terms of detection delay, sample complexity, and post-update risk) on any scheme satisfying the above safety requirements.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Concept/data drift detection and safe continual adaptation for deployed ML systems remain active research areas. While many algorithms exist (e.g., ADWIN, DDM, MMD-based two-sample tests, conformal change detection, online learning under covariate shift), no general methodology provides certified safety guarantees for arbitrary safety-critical ML systems under non-stationary operational data. Recent surveys on concept drift, distribution-shift monitoring, and assurance of safety-critical ML continue to list this as an open challenge.

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{C}$ be a rectifiable curve, and let $E\subset\Gamma$ be a Borel subset with one-dimensional Hausdorff measure (length) zero. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}$ be any simply connected domain (with $E$ contained in the boundary or in $\overline{\Omega}$ in the relevant boundary sense), and let $z\in\Omega$. Denote by $\omega(z,\,\cdot\,,\Omega)$ the harmonic measure on $\partial\Omega$ from the point $z$. Is it always true that
$$\omega(z,E,\Omega)=0?$$
Equivalently: is harmonic measure on a simply connected domain absolutely continuous with respect to arclength on every rectifiable curve meeting its boundary?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The conjecture (due to Øksendal) was established affirmatively for simply connected planar domains by Bishop, Carleson, Garnett, and Jones in "Harmonic measures supported on curves" (Pacific J. Math., 1989), and is also presented in C. Bishop's "Harmonic measure and arclength" (Annals of Math., 1990): for a rectifiable curve $\Gamma$ and a simply connected domain $\Omega$, harmonic measure restricted to $\Gamma$ is absolutely continuous with respect to arclength, so subsets of zero length have zero harmonic measure.

Consider a safety-critical system whose decisions depend on a trained neural network classifier f: X -> Y, where X is a space of input signals (e.g., images) and Y a finite set of labels. Two standard neural-network visualization techniques are available:

(i) Occlusion-based saliency: for an input x in X, define a region-of-interest map S_occ(x) by masking subregions of x with a baseline value and recording where f's output probability for the predicted class changes most sharply.

(ii) Activation back-propagation: starting from highly activated nodes in deeper feature-extraction layers of f, back-propagate activation values to the input space to obtain a region-of-interest map S_bp(x).

Formulate and exhibit concrete, well-defined use cases in which the maps S_occ and S_bp can be employed as actionable tools for (a) debugging the network during training and (b) validating the behavior of the trained network, in such a way that the visualizations provide verifiable interpretability and transparency guarantees suitable for safety-critical deployment. Specifically, describe operational procedures, acceptance criteria, and quantitative metrics under which these visualization methods yield decisions about model correctness that can be incorporated into a safety assurance argument.

Let $G \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a domain containing the origin $0$ that is axially symmetric with respect to the real axis: whenever $z \in G$, the closed line segment from $z$ to its complex conjugate $\bar z$ also lies in $G$ (in particular, $G$ is simply connected). For each $t > 0$, define
- $G_t$ to be the connected component containing $0$ of $\{z \in G : \operatorname{Im} z < t\}$,
- $G'_t$ to be the connected component containing $0$ of $\{z \in G : \operatorname{Re} z < t\}$.

Let $\omega_t(G)$ denote the harmonic measure, evaluated at $0$, of $\partial G_t \cap \{\operatorname{Im} z = t\}$ relative to the domain $G_t$, and let $\omega'_t(G)$ denote the harmonic measure, evaluated at $0$, of $\partial G'_t \cap \{\operatorname{Re} z = t\}$ relative to the domain $G'_t$.

Now suppose $D_1$ and $D_2$ are two such axially symmetric domains. Investigate the following:

(a) If $\omega_t(D_1) = \omega_t(D_2)$ for every $t > 0$, must $D_1 = D_2$?

(b) If $\omega'_t(D_1) = \omega'_t(D_2)$ for every $t > 0$, must $D_1 = D_2$?

(c) If neither (a) nor (b) holds, does $D_1 = D_2$ follow when both $\omega_t(D_1) = \omega_t(D_2)$ and $\omega'_t(D_1) = \omega'_t(D_2)$ hold for all $t > 0$?

In addition: if (a) or (b) is affirmative, identify the smallest sets of values of $t$ (e.g., a sequence of $t$'s such that $\{\operatorname{Im} z = t\}$ or $\{\operatorname{Re} z = t\}$ meets the domains, or only a dense set of such $t$'s) for which the corresponding conclusion still holds. Finally, in any affirmative case, determine whether the axial-symmetry hypothesis can be weakened to mere simple connectivity, or omitted entirely.

Consider the family of asymptotically conical (AC) 7-dimensional Riemannian manifolds $(X,g)$ with holonomy contained in the exceptional Lie group $G_2$ that arise as cohomogeneity-one manifolds for an isometric action of $SU(2)\times SU(2)\times U(1)$ with a single singular orbit. (Here a complete Riemannian $G_2$-manifold $(X,g)$ is asymptotically conical if outside a compact set it is diffeomorphic to a cone $C(\Sigma)=(R_0,\infty)\times\Sigma$ over a smooth compact 6-manifold $\Sigma$, with the metric $g$ converging at a polynomial rate to the conical metric $dr^2+r^2 g_\Sigma$ where $g_\Sigma$ is a nearly Kähler metric on $\Sigma$.) Among the families of such metrics constructed via cohomogeneity-one methods, distinguish in particular the family denoted $D_7$.

A $G_2$-instanton on $X$ is a connection $A$ on a principal $G$-bundle $P\to X$ (for $G$ a compact Lie group, e.g. $SU(2)$) whose curvature $F_A\in\Omega^2(X;\mathrm{ad}\,P)$ satisfies $F_A\wedge\psi=0$, where $\psi=*\varphi$ is the Hodge dual of the defining $G_2$ 3-form $\varphi$ on $X$. An $SU(2)\times SU(2)\times U(1)$-invariant $G_2$-instanton is one for which the action lifts to $P$ and preserves $A$.

Local existence of invariant $G_2$-instantons in a neighborhood of the singular orbit is known; equivariantly, near the singular orbit the equations reduce to an ODE system whose solutions are parameterized by a finite-dimensional moduli of initial data compatible with the isotropy representation.

Problems:
(a) For each of these AC $G_2$-manifolds $X$ (and especially for the $D_7$ family), determine which of the locally defined $SU(2)\times SU(2)\times U(1)$-invariant $G_2$-instantons defined in a neighborhood of the singular orbit extend to globally defined smooth $G_2$-instantons on all of $X$ with finite Yang–Mills energy and an appropriate decay rate at infinity.
(b) Classify all such global invariant $G_2$-instantons, and, when a nontrivial family exists, describe the global properties of the resulting moduli space (dimension, smoothness, compactness, behavior at the boundary corresponding to bubbling or to limits along the asymptotic cone).

Let $D$ be a simply-connected domain in the complex plane (with at least two boundary points), and let $\{P_n(z)\}_{n=0}^{\infty}$ denote the associated sequence of Faber polynomials of $D$ (defined via the conformal map of the exterior of $D$ onto the exterior of a disk). Every function $f$ analytic in $D$ admits a unique expansion
$$f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n P_n(z), \qquad z \in D.$$
Let $\mathcal{P}(D)$ denote the family of all functions $f$ analytic in $D$ with $\operatorname{Re} f(z) > 0$ for all $z \in D$. For each fixed integer $n \ge 0$, determine the coefficient body
$$V_n \;=\; \bigl\{\, a_n \in \mathbb{C} \,:\, a_n \text{ is the } n\text{-th Faber coefficient of some } f \in \mathcal{P}(D)\,\bigr\}.$$
It is known that when $D$ is a disk, $V_n$ is a closed disk, and when $D$ is an ellipse, $V_n$ is a closed elliptical region. Determine $V_n$ for general simply-connected $D$.

representations.normalized:
Let $(M^7, \varphi, g)$ be an asymptotically conical $G_2$-manifold; that is, a complete 7-manifold equipped with a torsion-free $G_2$-structure $\varphi$ (with associated metric $g$) which, outside a compact set, is asymptotic at a polynomial rate to the Riemannian cone $C(\Sigma) = (\mathbb{R}_{>0} \times \Sigma, dr^2 + r^2 g_\Sigma)$ over a nearly Kähler 6-manifold $(\Sigma, g_\Sigma)$. Let $P \to M$ be a principal $G$-bundle with compact structure group $G$. A $G_2$-instanton on $P$ is a connection $A$ whose curvature $F_A$ satisfies $F_A \wedge \psi = 0$, where $\psi = *\varphi$. Asymptotic to a fixed dilation-invariant $G_2$-instanton on $C(\Sigma)$ (equivalently, a pseudo-Hermitian–Yang–Mills/$SU(3)$-instanton on $\Sigma$), one obtains a moduli space $\mathcal{M}(M)$ of asymptotically conical $G_2$-instantons on $M$ and a moduli space $\mathcal{M}(\Sigma)$ of nearly Kähler instantons on $\Sigma$, together with a natural restriction-to-link projection $\pi:\mathcal{M}(M) \to \mathcal{M}(\Sigma)$.

Address the following:

(a) Describe the local structure of $\mathcal{M}(M)$ near a given asymptotically conical $G_2$-instanton (its expected dimension, obstruction theory, and smoothness conditions).

(b) Prove a uniqueness statement for the "basic" $G_2$-instanton on $\mathbb{R}^7$ with gauge group $G_2$ (the canonical $G_2$-instanton built from the spin connection / octonionic structure on flat $\mathbb{R}^7$): show that, within an appropriate class of asymptotically conical $G_2$-instantons on $\mathbb{R}^7$ with gauge group $G_2$, the basic instanton is the unique solution.

(c) Suppose $H$ is a Lie group acting on $(M, \varphi)$ by $G_2$-automorphisms preserving a given $H$-invariant $G_2$-instanton $A_0$. Show, or determine the obstructions to showing, that every sufficiently small deformation of $A_0$ within $\mathcal{M}(M)$ is gauge-equivalent to an $H$-invariant connection.

(d) Determine geometric and analytic properties of the projection $\pi:\mathcal{M}(M) \to \mathcal{M}(\Sigma)$; in particular, decide whether $\pi$ is surjective.

Joe Driscoll's 2020 PhD thesis (University of Leeds) "Deformations of Asymptotically Conical G2-Instantons" develops the local deformation theory addressing part (a), relating deformations to the kernel of a twisted Dirac operator on M and to eigenvalues on the nearly Kähler link. Subsequent work (e.g., Driscoll's paper on G2-instantons on the spinor bundle of S^3, J. Geom. Anal. 2024) builds on this. The full uniqueness of the basic G2-instanton on R^7, the symmetry-preservation question for general H, and surjectivity of the projection to the nearly Kähler instanton moduli space do not appear settled in the literature, so the overall problem is partially solved.

Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a sequence of independent random signs (each $\varepsilon_n=\pm 1$ with probability $1/2$), and let $(a_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a fixed sequence of complex (or real) numbers with
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |a_n|^2 = \infty.$$
Define the random analytic function on the open unit disk $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ by
$$F(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \varepsilon_n a_n z^n.$$
(It is known that $F$ is almost surely an analytic function on $\mathbb{D}$ that is unbounded.) Determine, in terms of the sequence $(a_n)$, whether the following hold:

(a) With probability one, the image $F(\mathbb{D})$ is dense in $\mathbb{C}$.

(b) With probability one, $F(\mathbb{D}) = \mathbb{C}$.

(c) For each fixed $w_0 \in \mathbb{C}$, with probability one $w_0 \in F(\mathbb{D})$.

In particular, characterize the sequences $(a_n)$ for which (a), (b), and (c) hold. (As a benchmark, when $a_n = n^{\lambda}$, statement (b) holds for $\lambda > 1/2$ and statement (a) holds for $-1/2 < \lambda < 1/2$.)

The problem has seen substantial progress. Offord (1987, Annals of Probability) proved that a Gaussian Taylor series with $\sum|a_n|^2=\infty$ almost surely takes every complex value with at most one exception, addressing Kahane's question in the Gaussian case. More recently (arXiv:2403.19380, 2024), it was shown via a branching-process method that any unbounded random Taylor series with rotationally invariant coefficients has a.s. dense image, and that for complex Gaussian coefficients with sufficiently regular variances the image is a.s. all of $\mathbb{C}$. The full characterization for the Rademacher (random sign) case as posed remains not completely resolved.

Let $(M,\varphi)$ denote the Bryant–Salamon $G_2$-holonomy manifold $M = \mathbb{R}^4 \times S^3$, regarded as the spinor bundle of $S^3$ equipped with its complete torsion-free $G_2$-structure $\varphi$ of cohomogeneity one under the natural action of $SU(2)^2 \times U(1)$, with singular orbit the associative $3$-sphere $S^3 \subset M$. Over the principal stratum, the isotropy of a point is the diagonal $U(1)$ and one has the principal $SO(4)$-bundle of frames; restrict attention to the $SU(2)$-bundle $P_{\mathrm{id}} \to M$ corresponding to the identity homomorphism $U(1) \hookrightarrow SU(2)$ (so that $P_{\mathrm{id}}$ extends smoothly across the singular orbit $S^3$).

A connection $A$ on $P_{\mathrm{id}}$ with curvature $F_A$ is a $G_2$-instanton if $F_A \wedge \psi = 0$, where $\psi = *\varphi$ is the coassociative $4$-form of $\varphi$.

Suppose it is known that there exists a smooth one-parameter family $\{A_{y_0}\}_{y_0 \in \mathbb{R}}$ of $SU(2)^2 \times U(1)$-invariant $G_2$-instantons on $P_{\mathrm{id}}$, each defined on an open neighbourhood of $S^3$ in $M$ and extending smoothly across $S^3$, and that the distinguished member $A_0$ corresponding to $y_0 = 0$ extends to a globally defined $SU(2)^3$-invariant $G_2$-instanton on all of $M$.

Determine:
(a) whether there exists any $y_0 \neq 0$ for which the locally defined $G_2$-instanton $A_{y_0}$ extends to a smooth $G_2$-instanton on the whole of $M = \mathbb{R}^4 \times S^3$;
(b) for every such $y_0 \neq 0$ for which a global extension exists, whether the pointwise norm $|F_{A_{y_0}}|$ of the curvature, measured with respect to the Bryant–Salamon metric, is necessarily unbounded as one tends to infinity in $M$.

Let $K \geq 1$. A homeomorphism $f \colon \Omega \to \Omega'$ between domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is called $K$-quasiconformal if $f$ belongs to the Sobolev space $W^{1,n}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and its dilatation
$$ K(x,f) = \frac{\max_{|h|=1}|Df(x)h|^n}{|\det Df(x)|} $$
satisfies $K(x,f) \leq K$ for almost every $x \in \Omega$ (equivalently, the maximal dilatation of $f$ is at most $K$). The composition of a $K_1$-quasiconformal map and a $K_2$-quasiconformal map is $K_1 K_2$-quasiconformal.

It is known that in dimension $n=2$, every $K$-quasiconformal map of a planar domain can be written as the composition $f = g \circ h$ of two quasiconformal maps $g$ and $h$ whose maximal dilatations are both strictly less than $K$.

Question: Does the analogous statement hold in dimension $n=3$? That is, can every $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphism between domains in $\mathbb{R}^3$ be expressed as a composition of two quasiconformal homeomorphisms each having maximal dilatation strictly less than $K$?

A web search did not yield a definitive resolution of Gehring's question on factoring a K-quasiconformal map in 3-space as a composition of two quasiconformal maps each with maximal dilatation strictly less than K. Standard references on quasiconformal mappings in space (Gehring, Väisälä, Heinonen) discuss the multiplicativity of dilatation under composition and the planar case, but no source found confirms a positive or negative answer in dimension three.

Setup. Let $(C,g_C)$ be a Calabi-Yau cone of complex dimension $3$, and let $(M,\varphi,g)$ be a complete asymptotically locally conical (ALC) $G_2$-manifold of dimension $7$, meaning that outside a compact set $M$ is diffeomorphic to a circle bundle over the link of $C$ whose $G_2$-structure $\varphi$ approaches, with suitable decay, the product of $g_C$ with the standard metric on a circle of fixed asymptotic length. Assume $M$ lies in a one-parameter family of ALC $G_2$-manifolds that collapses, as the asymptotic circle length tends to $0$, to the Calabi-Yau cone $C$ in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense (the "degenerate Calabi-Yau cone limit"); in particular such $M$ may have only a $U(1)$ symmetry (acting by rotation of the asymptotic circle fibers).

A $G_2$-instanton on a principal $G$-bundle $P \to M$ is a connection $A$ whose curvature $F_A$ satisfies $F_A \wedge \psi = 0$, where $\psi = *\varphi$ is the coassociative $4$-form. A Calabi-Yau monopole on $C$ is a pair $(B,\Phi)$ consisting of a connection $B$ and a Higgs field $\Phi$ on a principal $G$-bundle over $C$ satisfying $F_B \wedge \tfrac{1}{2}\omega^2 = *_{C}\, d_B\Phi$, where $\omega$ is the Kähler form of the Calabi-Yau structure on $C$.

Problem. For ALC $G_2$-manifolds $M$ close to the degenerate Calabi-Yau cone limit (and in particular for examples that are only $U(1)$-invariant rather than enjoying larger continuous symmetry), construct $G_2$-instantons on $M$ that, in the collapsing limit, converge in an appropriate gauge-theoretic sense to a prescribed Calabi-Yau monopole $(B,\Phi)$ on the cone $C$. More precisely, given a Calabi-Yau monopole $(B,\Phi)$ on $C$, produce a family of $G_2$-instantons $A_\epsilon$ on the corresponding ALC $G_2$-manifolds $M_\epsilon$ (parameterized by the asymptotic circle length $\epsilon$) such that $A_\epsilon$ converges to $(B,\Phi)$ as $\epsilon \to 0$, with $\Phi$ recovered from the component of $A_\epsilon$ along the collapsing circle.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent work (e.g., the 2025 study of the large-mass limit of G2 and Calabi-Yau monopoles, and related works on invariant gauge theory on asymptotically conical Calabi-Yau 3-folds) develops structural results in the Donaldson-Segal programme connecting Calabi-Yau monopoles to G2-instantons via collapse, and constructs explicit invariant G2-instantons in highly symmetric examples (e.g., SU(2)^2-invariant settings on the spinor bundle of S^3). However, no general construction of G2-instantons on the merely U(1)-invariant ALC G2-manifolds close to a degenerate Calabi-Yau cone limit, converging to Calabi-Yau monopoles on the cone, appears to have been carried out. The problem appears to remain open.

representations.normalized:
Let $K \geq 1$. A homeomorphism $f: \Omega \to \Omega'$ between planar domains $\Omega, \Omega' \subset \mathbb{C}$ is called $K$-quasiconformal if $f$ belongs to the Sobolev space $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and its complex partial derivatives satisfy the Beltrami inequality
$$|\partial_{\bar z} f(z)| \leq \frac{K-1}{K+1}\, |\partial_z f(z)| \quad \text{for almost every } z \in \Omega.$$
It is known (Bojarski) that there exists a constant $c = c(K) > 0$ such that the partial derivatives $\partial_z f$ and $\partial_{\bar z} f$ belong to $L^p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ for every $p$ with $2 \leq p < 2 + c$.

Prove that one may take
$$c(K) = \frac{2}{K-1},$$
i.e., that for every $K$-quasiconformal mapping $f$ defined on a planar domain $\Omega$, the partial derivatives of $f$ belong to $L^p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ for every $p$ with
$$2 \leq p < \frac{2K}{K-1}.$$
The example $f(z) = z\, |z|^{1/K - 1}$ shows that the exponent $\frac{2K}{K-1}$ cannot in general be replaced by anything larger, so such a result would be sharp.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

This is Gehring's sharp higher integrability conjecture for planar K-quasiconformal mappings. It was solved by Kari Astala in his 1994 Acta Mathematica paper "Area distortion of quasiconformal mappings", which established the sharp local integrability exponent p(K) = 2K/(K-1) for the derivatives of planar K-quasiconformal maps.

Setup. Let $M = \mathbb{R}^4 \times S^3$ equipped with the Brandhuber–Gauntlett–Gibbons–Gukov (BGGG) complete $G_2$-holonomy metric, viewed as a cohomogeneity-one manifold under the action of $\mathrm{SU}(2)^2 \times \mathrm{U}(1)$, with principal orbit $\mathrm{SU}(2)^2 \times \mathrm{U}(1)/\Delta\mathrm{U}(1) \cong S^3 \times S^3$ and singular orbit $S^3$. Let $P_1 \to M$ be the principal $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-bundle whose connections extend smoothly across the singular orbit in the standard way considered for this cohomogeneity-one reduction, and consider $\mathrm{SU}(2)^2 \times \mathrm{U}(1)$-invariant $G_2$-instantons $A$ on $P_1$.

Such invariant connections on the principal orbit are described by an ODE system in two real-valued radial functions $f_1(t), g_1(t)$ (the standard parameters appearing in the cohomogeneity-one ansatz for $\mathrm{SU}(2)^2 \times \mathrm{U}(1)$-invariant $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-connections). Smooth extension across the singular orbit determines initial data $(f_1^+, g_1^+) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, namely the values of $(f_1, g_1)$ at the singular orbit.

Known results for this setup state:
(i) If $f_1^+ \le 1/2$, or if $g_1^+ \ge 0$ with $g_1^+ \ge f_1^+$, then any $G_2$-instanton $A$ extending globally to $M$ with bounded curvature must have abelian gauge group $\mathrm{U}(1)$.
(ii) If $f_1^+ \ge 1/2 + g_1^+ > 1/2$, then $A$ is irreducible and extends globally to $M$ with bounded curvature.

These leave open the parameter region
$$\mathcal{R} = \{(f_1^+, g_1^+) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : 0 < f_1^+ - \tfrac{1}{2} < g_1^+ < f_1^+\}.$$

Problem.
(a) Determine, for each $(f_1^+, g_1^+) \in \mathcal{R}$, whether the corresponding irreducible $\mathrm{SU}(2)^2 \times \mathrm{U}(1)$-invariant $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ $G_2$-instanton on $P_1$ extends to a globally defined $G_2$-instanton on $M$ with bounded curvature, or fails to do so. In particular, identify the subset of $\mathcal{R}$ giving rise to globally defined bounded-curvature instantons and the complementary subset on which global extension or curvature boundedness fails, thereby completing the description of the moduli space $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{BGGG}}_{P_1}$.
(b) Extend the analogous existence/non-existence picture to the full Bogoyavlenskaya family of complete cohomogeneity-one $G_2$-metrics on $\mathbb{R}^4 \times S^3$ (which interpolates with the BGGG metric and which contains it), specifying precisely how the dichotomy in (a) deforms across this family.

Let $n\ge 2$ and $K\ge 1$. A continuous mapping $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n$, defined on a domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, is called $K$-quasiregular if $f$ belongs to the Sobolev space $W^{1,n}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^n)$ and its (a.e. defined) differential $Df(x)$ satisfies
$$|Df(x)|^n \le K\, J_f(x) \qquad \text{for almost every } x\in\Omega,$$
where $|Df(x)|$ is the operator norm and $J_f(x)=\det Df(x)$ is the Jacobian determinant. (When $f$ is in addition injective it is called $K$-quasiconformal.)

Prove that there exists a constant $c=c(K,n)>0$ such that for every $K$-quasiregular mapping $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n$ the partial derivatives $\partial f_i/\partial x_j$ belong to $L^p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ for every exponent $p$ with
$$n \le p \le n+c.$$
(The corresponding statement under the additional assumption that $f$ is injective—i.e., for $K$-quasiconformal mappings—is known.)

The higher integrability of the derivatives of $K$-quasiregular mappings (the non-injective extension of Gehring's theorem for quasiconformal maps) was established for general quasiregular mappings via the Gehring lemma / reverse Hölder inequality technique, with contributions by Bojarski, Iwaniec, and Martin; it is now a standard part of the $L^p$-theory of quasiregular mappings (e.g., Iwaniec, "$L^p$-theory of quasiregular mappings", 1992; Iwaniec–Martin, "Geometric Function Theory and Non-linear Analysis").

Let M = ℝ⁴ × S³ be equipped with the BGGG (Brandhuber–Gauntlett–Gibbons–Gubser) complete G₂-holonomy metric, which admits an isometric action of SU(2) × SU(2) × U(1). It is known that the moduli space M^{BGGG}_{P₁} of irreducible such G₂-instantons (with gauge group SU(2)) contains a nonempty unbounded open subset parametrized by an open set U ⊂ ℝ², with two real parameters f₁⁺ and g₁⁺ that may tend to infinity.

(a) Construct a natural compactification of the moduli space M^{BGGG}_{P₁}.

(b) Describe the bubbling behaviour of the family of G₂-instantons as one or both of the parameters f₁⁺ and g₁⁺ tend to infinity. In particular, determine whether the limiting bubbles correspond to anti-self-dual instantons on the Taub-NUT space (analogous to the bubbling phenomenon established for the Bryant–Salamon G₂-metric, where bubbles are ASD instantons on ℝ⁴).

representations.normalized:
Let V = (V⁺, V⁻) be a Jordan pair, and let L(V) denote its Tits–Kantor–Koecher Lie algebra. The projective elementary group PE(V) is defined as the subgroup of Aut(L(V)) generated by the one-parameter subgroups exp(ad x) for x ∈ V⁺ and x ∈ V⁻. A Jordan pair V is called simple if it has no nonzero proper ideals and its product is nonzero; the simple factors of V are the simple Jordan pairs occurring in a decomposition of V. Distinguish three "exceptional" simple Jordan pairs: (F₂, F₂), (F₃, F₃), and (H₂(F₂), H₂(F₂)) (where Hₙ(F) denotes the Jordan pair of n×n hermitian matrices over F).

Two known theorems for finite-dimensional Jordan pairs over a field state:
(T1) PE(V) is a perfect group if and only if V has no simple factor isomorphic to (F₂, F₂), (F₃, F₃), or (H₂(F₂), H₂(F₂));
(T2) PE(V) is a simple group if and only if V is simple and not isomorphic to any of those three exceptional Jordan pairs.

Problem: Determine whether (T1) and (T2) extend to broader classes of Jordan pairs (for instance, infinite-dimensional Jordan pairs, or Jordan pairs over arbitrary commutative rings). Specifically, prove or disprove that for the broader class under consideration:
(a) PE(V) is perfect ⇔ V has no simple factor isomorphic to (F₂, F₂), (F₃, F₃), or (H₂(F₂), H₂(F₂));
(b) Assuming V is simple, PE(V) is simple ⇔ V is not isomorphic to any of (F₂, F₂), (F₃, F₃), or (H₂(F₂), H₂(F₂)).

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{C}$ be a Jordan curve (the homeomorphic image of a circle) such that the origin $z=0$ lies in the bounded component of $\mathbb{C}\setminus\Gamma$. Let $C(\Gamma)$ denote the Banach space of continuous complex-valued functions on $\Gamma$ with the supremum norm. A set $S\subset\mathbb{Z}$ is said to give a spanning family of monomials if the closed linear span in $C(\Gamma)$ of the functions $\{z^{n}\mid n\in S\}$ equals $C(\Gamma)$.

It is known that:
(i) If $\Gamma$ has infinite length, then $\{z^{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}\}$ spans $C(\Gamma)$.
(ii) Under suitable conditions on $\Gamma$, for any finite set of integers $\{n_{1},\dots,n_{k}\}$, the family $\{z^{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{n_{1},\dots,n_{k}\}\}$ spans $C(\Gamma)$.

Determine necessary and/or sufficient geometric or analytic conditions on the Jordan curve $\Gamma$ under which there exists an infinite set $E\subset\mathbb{Z}$ such that the family $\{z^{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus E\}$ still spans $C(\Gamma)$. Equivalently, characterize for which Jordan curves $\Gamma$ (containing $0$ in their interior) one can omit an infinite set of integer powers of $z$ and retain a spanning set in $C(\Gamma)$.

representations.normalized:
Setup. Let F be a field and let V = (V^+, V^-) be a Jordan pair over F equipped with a quadratic operator Q: V^σ → Hom(V^{-σ}, V^σ). Suppose V carries a root grading R, that is, a decomposition V^σ = ⨁_{α ∈ R_1} V^σ_α indexed by the set R_1 of "one-roots" of a (possibly non-reduced) finite root system R, satisfying the standard compatibility axioms with the Jordan pair structure. Assume:

(i) The grading R is fully idempotent (every root space contains a non-degenerate idempotent giving the expected Peirce decomposition consistent with R).

(ii) The grading R is a division grading: for every root α ∈ R_1 and every nonzero x ∈ V_α, the operator Q(x) restricts to an invertible F-linear map from the opposite root space V_{-α} onto V_α.

Let St(V, R) denote the Steinberg group associated to (V, R), defined by generators x_α(v) for α ∈ R_1, v ∈ V_α subject to the standard Steinberg relations attached to the root grading. Recall that St(V, R) is said to be centrally closed if its canonical central extension (the universal central extension in the appropriate category) is trivial, i.e. the kernel of the natural projection from a universal central extension to St(V, R) is trivial.

A finite list T of "exceptional small-field restrictions" is fixed in advance, consisting of pairs (R, F) where R is a root system of rank between 2 and 4 and F is a field belonging to a small finite list of small fields (e.g. small finite fields such as F_2, F_3, F_4, depending on the type of R).

Question. Is the following statement true? For every Jordan pair V over F with fully idempotent division root grading R of rank r with 2 ≤ r ≤ 4, if the Steinberg group St(V, R) is not centrally closed, then:

(a) dim_F V_α = 1 for every α ∈ R_1, and

(b) the pair (R, F) lies in the prescribed exceptional list T.

(ii) the Steinberg group $\mathrm{St}(V, R)$, defined by generators $x_\alpha(v)$ for $\alpha \in R$ and $v \in V_\alpha$, subject to the additivity relations in each $V_\alpha$ and the standard Steinberg-type commutator relations modeled on those satisfied in $\mathrm{PE}(V)$.

There is a canonical surjective group homomorphism

sending each generator $x_\alpha(v)$ to the corresponding elementary automorphism of $V$.

Determine sufficient conditions on the pair $(V, \Gamma)$ (and on the irreducible finite-rank root system $R$) under which the kernel $\ker(\pi)$ is contained in the center of $\mathrm{St}(V, R)$, i.e., conditions guaranteeing that $\pi$ is a central extension.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The Erdős–Ulam question of whether a dense rational distance set exists in the plane remains open. Conditional negative answers are known: Shaffaf and Tao independently showed the Bombieri–Lang conjecture implies no such set exists, and Pasten showed the abc conjecture also implies a negative answer. Solymosi–de Zeeuw proved related results restricting infinite rational-distance subsets of algebraic curves to lines and circles.

representations.normalized:
An ordinary differential equation is said to have the Painlevé property if every movable singularity of every solution (i.e., a singularity whose location depends on the initial conditions) is a pole. The six Painlevé equations P_I, ..., P_VI are the canonical second-order ODEs with the Painlevé property whose general solutions define new transcendental functions (the Painlevé transcendents); to each Painlevé equation P_J there is also an associated Hamiltonian "sigma-equation" (the Painlevé sigma-equation) satisfied by an auxiliary Hamiltonian function.

Problem. Devise an algorithmic procedure (taking as input an ordinary differential equation that is known to have the Painlevé property) which decides, in finitely many effective steps, whether the given equation can be solved in closed form in terms of one of the Painlevé equations P_I,...,P_VI or one of the associated Painlevé sigma-equations, and, when it can, produces an explicit transformation reducing the given equation to that Painlevé (or sigma-) equation.

The Painlevé equivalence problem remains an active area of research with no fully general algorithm known. Recent work using algebro-geometric methods (Okamoto's spaces of initial conditions, iterative blow-up regularisation) has produced essentially algorithmic step-by-step identification procedures that work for specific classes of systems (e.g., Bureau–Guillot systems, certain constrained 3D systems, identifications with Painlevé VI), so the problem is partially solved in those settings but a complete general algorithm has not been established.

Let $N\ge 2$ be an integer and let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_N$ be pairwise distinct real numbers. Define the trigonometric exponential sum
$$P(\theta)=\sum_{n=1}^{N} e^{i\lambda_n \theta},\qquad \theta\in\mathbb{R},$$
and set
$$\mu(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N)=\inf_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}}|P(\theta)|.$$
A direct computation gives $|P(\theta)|^2=N+2\sum_{m\ne n}\cos((\lambda_m-\lambda_n)\theta)$, and an averaging argument (using that the mean value of $\cos((\lambda_m-\lambda_n)\theta)$ is $0$) yields the bound
$$\mu(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N)\le (N-1)^{1/2}.$$
Determine the best possible upper bound for $\mu(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N)$ as $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N$ range over all $N$-tuples of distinct real numbers; that is, find
$$M(N)=\sup\bigl\{\mu(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N):\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N\in\mathbb{R}\text{ distinct}\bigr\},$$
and in particular decide whether $M(N)=(N-1)^{1/2}$ or whether a smaller upper bound holds. The corresponding question when all $\lambda_n$ are rational reduces to bounding $\inf_\theta|Q(\theta)|$ for trigonometric polynomials $Q$ with $0/1$ coefficients.

representations.normalized:
The six Painlevé equations P_I, P_II, ..., P_VI are a distinguished family of second-order nonlinear ordinary differential equations in the complex plane whose solutions (the Painlevé transcendents) define new transcendental functions and possess a rich integrable structure: each admits an isomonodromic Lax-pair representation, a Riemann–Hilbert problem characterization, Bäcklund transformations, tau-function descriptions, and (for special parameter values) hierarchies of rational and special-function solutions.

Standard initial-value solvers (e.g., explicit and embedded Runge–Kutta methods such as RK4, Dormand–Prince, and related adaptive ODE schemes) treat these equations as generic stiff or non-stiff nonlinear ODEs and do not make use of any of the integrable structure listed above.

Problem. Design and analyze numerical methods for computing solutions of the Painlevé equations along real or complex paths that explicitly exploit their integrable structure (for example, by basing the computation on the associated isomonodromic Riemann–Hilbert problem, on the Lax-pair / isomonodromic deformation, on Bäcklund transformations, on tau-function identities, or on Hamiltonian/symplectic structure preserving discretizations), and prove that such methods can achieve strictly better performance — in accuracy, stability across movable singularities, global validity in the complex plane, or computational cost — than what is attainable by Runge–Kutta methods and other generic ODE solvers. Equivalently: do there exist integrability-aware algorithms that demonstrably outperform generic Runge–Kutta-type ODE solvers for the Painlevé transcendents?

Standard initial-value solvers (e.g., explicit and embedded Runge–Kutta methods such as RK4, Dormand–Prince, and related adaptive ODE schemes) treat these equations as generic stiff or non-stiff nonlinear ODEs and do not make use of any of the integrable structure listed above.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

There exist published Riemann–Hilbert / isomonodromic numerical methods (e.g., Olver, Trogdon, Bornemann and collaborators) that compute Painlevé transcendents accurately throughout the complex plane, including across the Stokes lines and near movable poles, where standard Runge–Kutta solvers degrade or fail. These works demonstrate concrete advantages of integrability-based algorithms. However, the broader question of systematically characterizing when and by how much integrable-structure-aware methods outperform generic ODE solvers across all six Painlevé equations and regimes remains an active research direction rather than a closed problem, so the question is best classified as partially solved.

For a compact set $K \subset \mathbb{C}$, the analytic capacity of $K$ is defined by
$$\gamma(K) = \sup\{|f'(\infty)| : f : \mathbb{C}_\infty \setminus K \to \mathbb{C} \text{ is holomorphic, } \|f\|_\infty \le 1\},$$
where $f'(\infty) = \lim_{z\to\infty} z(f(z) - f(\infty))$.

Determine whether there exists an absolute constant $M > 0$ such that
$$\gamma(K_1 \cup K_2) \le M\bigl(\gamma(K_1) + \gamma(K_2)\bigr)$$
for every pair of compact sets $K_1, K_2 \subset \mathbb{C}$ (semiadditivity of analytic capacity). The special case in which $\gamma(K_2) = 0$ should also be addressed.

Determine whether there exists an absolute constant $M > 0$ such that
$$\gamma(K_1 \cup K_2) \le M\bigl(\gamma(K_1) + \gamma(K_2)\bigr)$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The semiadditivity of analytic capacity was proved by Xavier Tolsa (Acta Math. 190 (2003), 105–149), establishing the existence of an absolute constant M such that γ(K₁ ∪ K₂) ≤ M(γ(K₁) + γ(K₂)) for all compact K₁, K₂ ⊂ ℂ. The special case γ(K₂)=0 (countable semiadditivity / Painlevé's problem) is also a consequence of Tolsa's work.

Determine whether numerical computation of solutions to the continuous Painlevé equations should be carried out via integrable discretizations (i.e., discrete Painlevé equations admitting the prescribed continuum limit to the target Painlevé equation) rather than via generic discretizations of the differential equations. Let $D \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a bounded simply-connected domain. Call $D$ **conformally rigid** if there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every conformal (i.e. holomorphic and injective) self-map $f \colon D \to D$ satisfying $\sup_{z \in D} |f(z) - z| < \varepsilon$ must be the identity, $f(z) \equiv z$.

Recall the notion of prime ends in the sense of Carathéodory: if $\varphi \colon \mathbb{D} \to D$ is a Riemann map from the open unit disk onto $D$, the prime ends of $D$ are equivalence classes of chains of cross-cuts and correspond bijectively to points of $\partial \mathbb{D}$. The **impression** of a prime end $p$ is the set of all limit points in $\overline{D}$ of $\varphi(z_n)$ for sequences $z_n \in \mathbb{D}$ converging to the corresponding boundary point. We say a prime end is a *singleton* when its impression consists of a single point.

It is known that if every prime end of $D$ has singleton impression, then $D$ is not conformally rigid. Prove the converse: if $D$ has at least one prime end whose impression is not a singleton, then $D$ is conformally rigid; equivalently, $D$ is conformally rigid if and only if not every prime end of $D$ is a singleton.

Fix an integer $p\ge 1$ and a length $\ell\in(0,1)$. For each choice of angles $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_p\in[0,2\pi)$, let
$$D=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^{p}\{re^{i\theta_k}:1-\ell\le r\le 1\},$$
i.e. the open unit disc with $p$ radial slits of common length $\ell$ removed, each emanating inward from the outer boundary $\{|z|=1\}$. Let $u$ be the bounded harmonic function on $D$ with boundary values $1$ on the part of $\partial D$ lying on $\{|z|=1\}$ (the "outer" arcs not removed) and $0$ on the two sides of every radial slit; equivalently, $u(z)=\omega(z,\{|\zeta|=1\}\cap\partial D,D)$ is the harmonic measure of the circular boundary arcs from the point $z$.

Determine the configuration $(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_p)$ that minimizes $u(0)$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem, posed by Gonchar, was resolved by V. N. Dubinin using his method of dissymmetrization: among all configurations of $p$ radial slits of equal length emanating from the unit circle, the symmetric (equally spaced) configuration minimizes the harmonic measure of the circle at the origin. Baernstein later extended this to general compact radial sets.

Consider ten-dimensional type II supergravity (type IIA or type IIB) compactified on a compact six-dimensional group manifold M_6 (a quotient of a six-dimensional Lie group by a discrete subgroup), with the following standard "smeared" ansatz:

(i) The ten-dimensional spacetime is a warped product dS_4 × M_6 of four-dimensional de Sitter space and M_6, in the regime where warping is dropped and the metric on M_6 is left-invariant.

(ii) The bosonic content includes the dilaton φ (assumed constant on M_6), the NSNS three-form H, and the RR field strengths F_q. All form fluxes are taken to be left-invariant (constant) on M_6.

(iii) Sources are present in the form of Op-planes and/or Dp-branes (for some fixed p ∈ {3,4,5,6,7,8}) wrapping calibrated cycles, smeared over their transverse directions, with their localized contributions to the Bianchi identities replaced by their integrated charges.

For such a solution, define:
 • The internal volume V = vol(M_6) measured in string units ℓ_s = √α′.
 • The string coupling g_s = e^{φ}.
 • The orientifold number N_O = total number of Op-planes appearing in the source content (counted with multiplicity in the relevant homology class).
 • Quantized fluxes: the periods of H/(2π α′) and of the F_q/(2π α′)^{(q)} over integral cycles of M_6 are required to take integer values.

Question: Does there exist any classical de Sitter solution of the above kind that simultaneously satisfies all four of the following conditions?

 (a) Large internal volume: V can be made arbitrarily large (V → ∞);
 (b) Weak string coupling: g_s can be made arbitrarily small (g_s → 0);
 (c) Bounded orientifold number: N_O remains bounded by a fixed constant independent of the limits in (a), (b);
 (d) Properly quantized fluxes as defined above.

Equivalently: prove or disprove that no solution in this class can realize (a)–(d) simultaneously.

A domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (with $n \geq 2$) is called linearly accessible if for every point $y \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus D$ there exists a ray emanating from $y$ and going to $\infty$ that does not meet $D$. Fix $x_0 \in D$ and let $g(\,\cdot\,, x_0)$ denote the Green's function of $D$ with pole at $x_0$ (i.e., the function harmonic in $D \setminus \{x_0\}$ that vanishes on $\partial D$ in the appropriate sense, with the standard fundamental-solution singularity at $x_0$).

Assume $D$ is a linearly accessible domain. Prove or disprove: for every $t \in (0, \infty)$, the superlevel set
$$\{x \in D : g(x, x_0) > t\}$$
is itself a linearly accessible domain. (The conclusion is known to hold when $n = 2$; the question concerns general $n \geq 3$.)

Two large ground-based ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray observatories independently measure the all-particle differential energy spectrum J(E) of cosmic rays at energies E ≳ 10^19 eV. One observatory is located in the Southern Hemisphere and views the sky in the declination band roughly −90° ≤ δ ≲ +45°; the other is located in the Northern Hemisphere and views roughly −16° ≲ δ ≤ +90°. Each observatory reconstructs primary energies via its own calibration chain (combining surface-detector signals with fluorescence-detector calorimetric measurements) and reports its spectrum with associated systematic uncertainties on the absolute energy scale.

When the two reported spectra J_A(E) and J_T(E) are compared above approximately E* = 10^19.4 eV, statistically significant differences remain even after applying any single global rescaling E → (1+α)E of one observatory's energy scale relative to the other (i.e., no energy-independent shift α can simultaneously reconcile the spectra in this regime, in particular reconciling the inferred flux-suppression energies).

Determine which of the following is the dominant cause of these residual differences above ~10^19.4 eV:

(a) experiment-specific systematic effects in energy reconstruction and calibration that depend on energy (so that the effective miscalibration grows with E and cannot be captured by a constant rescaling), or

(b) genuine astrophysical anisotropy of the ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray sky, so that the two observatories sample intrinsically different flux distributions because their fields of view (declination bands) cover different regions of the celestial sphere.

Equivalently, decide whether the residual discrepancy is removed once one allows for an energy-dependent (but isotropic) inter-observatory energy-scale correction, or whether it persists when the comparison is restricted to the common declination band accessible to both instruments and therefore must be attributed to a declination-dependent astrophysical flux.

Recent joint Auger–Telescope Array working-group analyses (2024–2025) provide strong evidence that an energy-independent rescaling cannot eliminate the discrepancy above ~10^19.4 eV: the inferred suppression energies differ by ~42% (Auger ~48 EeV vs TA ~68 EeV, >3σ). Telescope Array has reported a declination-dependent feature in its spectrum, and updated comparisons indicate the tension is largely accounted for by a combination of an energy-dependent energy-scale mismatch and astrophysical (declination-dependent) effects, with proposed source-based explanations also under discussion. A definitive single-cause resolution has not yet been established, so the question is partially solved.

Ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) are charged particles (atomic nuclei) of astrophysical origin observed with energies exceeding roughly 10^18 eV. Their primary mass is inferred indirectly from extensive air showers, principally via the depth of shower maximum X_max, whose first two moments (mean and standard deviation) are interpreted through hadronic-interaction Monte Carlo models to estimate the fractional abundances of light, intermediate, and heavy nuclear species as functions of primary energy E.

Existing measurements indicate that the mean primary mass decreases with E up to about 10^18.3 eV (the "ankle" of the energy spectrum) and then increases (composition becomes heavier) as E approaches 10^20 eV; however, no composition fractions have been established at and above E ≈ 10^20 eV due to limited event statistics and uncertainties in hadronic-interaction models.

Problem. With substantially increased exposure and improved hadronic-interaction modeling:

(a) Determine the mass composition (the fractional abundances of proton, helium, nitrogen/CNO, and iron-like primary nuclei) of UHECRs at energies E ≥ 10^20 eV.

(b) Decide whether the observed trend of increasing mean primary mass with energy in the range 10^18.3 eV ≲ E ≲ 10^20 eV continues monotonically toward heavier primaries above 10^20 eV, flattens to an approximately constant heavy composition, or changes character (for example, by re-emergence of a light component) at the highest energies.

Provide quantitative composition fractions with uncertainties at E ≥ 10^20 eV and a determination of the qualitative behavior in (b).

For a bounded measurable set $A\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, let $|A|$ denote its $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

(i) (One-dimensional version.) Let $E\subset\mathbb{R}$ be a compact set, and for each $x\in E$ let a positive number $\delta_x>0$ be given. Define $I_x=(x-\delta_x,\,x+\delta_x)$. Determine the supremum of all constants $c\ge 0$ with the following property: for every such $E$ and every assignment $x\mapsto\delta_x$, there exists a (countable) pairwise disjoint subcollection $\{I_{x_j}\}_{j}$ of $\{I_x:x\in E\}$ satisfying
$$\sum_{j}|I_{x_j}|\;\ge\;c\,|E|.$$
It is known that $c=	frac12$ is always achievable and that no $c>	frac23$ works in general; determine the exact best constant.

(ii) ($n$-dimensional version.) Let $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be an open, bounded, centrally symmetric, convex set. Let $E\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be compact, and for each $x\in E$ let $\delta_x>0$ be given; set $K_x=x+\delta_x K$. Define
$$c(K)=\sup\{c\ge 0:	ext{ for every such }E	ext{ and every choice of }\{\delta_x\},	ext{ there exists a pairwise}\	ext{disjoint subcollection }\{K_{x_j}\}	ext{ with }\sum_{j}|K_{x_j}|\ge c|E|\}.$$
It is known that $2^{-n}\le c(K)<1$. Determine $c(K)$, and in particular determine the asymptotic behavior as $n	o\infty$ of $c(Q_n)$, where $Q_n=(-1,1)^n$ is the open unit $n$-cube, and of $c(S_n)$, where $S_n$ is the open unit Euclidean $n$-ball.

The problem is connected to optimal constants in weak-type inequalities for the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function associated with the family $\{K_x\}$.

Ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays are charged nuclei with energies E ≳ 10^18 eV arriving at Earth from astrophysical sources. For a nucleus of charge number Z and energy E, define its magnetic rigidity by R = E/Z. The typical angular deflection of such a particle traveling a distance L through a (turbulent or coherent) magnetic field of characteristic strength B scales inversely with rigidity, so that small deflections—and hence the feasibility of identifying point sources or large-scale anisotropies pointing back to astrophysical accelerators—require sufficiently large R.

Let ⟨ln A⟩(E) denote the energy-dependent mean of the logarithm of the cosmic-ray mass number, and let ⟨ln Z⟩(E) denote the corresponding mean of ln Z, both inferred from air-shower observables (such as depth of shower maximum X_max and its fluctuations) under a chosen hadronic interaction model. Define the average (logarithmic) rigidity by

  ⟨ln R⟩(E) = ln E − ⟨ln Z⟩(E).

Determine the function ⟨ln R⟩(E) (equivalently, the energy dependence of the mean rigidity ⟨R⟩(E) = ⟨E/Z⟩) of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays across the range roughly 10^18 eV ≤ E ≤ 10^20.5 eV, and decide whether ⟨R⟩(E) grows fast enough with E that, given realistic Galactic and extragalactic magnetic-field models, the typical magnetic deflection at the highest observed energies becomes small enough (e.g., on the order of a few degrees or less) to permit meaningful anisotropy and source-correlation studies, despite the simultaneous observed trend of increasing average mass ⟨A⟩(E) with E.

Let $n \ge 2$ and let $B^n = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : |x| < 1\}$ be the open unit ball, with boundary $\partial B^n = S^{n-1}$. Let $D \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a Jordan domain (a domain whose boundary $\partial D$ is homeomorphic to $S^{n-1}$). Suppose $f : B^n \to D$ is a quasi-conformal homeomorphism; it is known that $f$ extends to a homeomorphism $\overline{B^n} \to \overline{D}$, still denoted $f$. Let $\Lambda^{n-1}$ denote $(n-1)$-dimensional Hausdorff measure, and let $|\cdot|$ denote the surface measure on $\partial B^n$. Assume that $\partial D$ is rectifiable in the sense that $\Lambda^{n-1}(\partial D) < \infty$.

(a) Is $f|_{\partial B^n}$ absolutely continuous, in the sense that $\Lambda^{n-1}(f(E)) = 0$ for every set $E \subset \partial B^n$ with $|E| = 0$?

(b) Is $f^{-1}|_{\partial D}$ absolutely continuous, in the analogous sense?

(c) For $n = 3$, suppose in addition that $f$ admits a quasi-conformal extension to all of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Is $f^{-1}|_{\partial D}$ absolutely continuous in this case?

Determine the answers to (a), (b), and (c).

Heinonen ("The boundary absolute continuity of quasiconformal mappings (II)", Rev. Mat. Iberoamericana 12 (1996), 697–725) constructed, for each n ≥ 3, examples of quasi-conformal maps of B^n onto Jordan domains with (n−1)-rectifiable boundary whose boundary values are not absolutely continuous, settling parts (a) and (b) negatively in general. For n = 3 with a global quasi-conformal extension, Gehring's result gives absolute continuity of f|_{∂B^n}, but the question whether f^{-1}|_{∂D} is absolutely continuous in this setting does not appear to be definitively resolved in the literature located.
