Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, with $N > 4$. Consider the Kirchhoff-type problem
$$
(P_\lambda)\quad -\Bigl(a + b\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,dx\Bigr)\Delta u \;=\; \lambda\bigl(|u|^{2^*-2}u + g(x,u)\bigr) + h(x,v(x)) \quad\text{in }\Omega,\qquad u = 0 \text{ on }\partial\Omega,
$$
where $a\ge 0$, $b>0$ are positive parameters, $\lambda>0$, $2^* = 2N/(N-2)$ is the critical Sobolev exponent, and $g,h$ are suitable subcritical Carathéodory perturbations (with $v$ a fixed function entering as a parameter through $h$). The associated energy functional on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is
$$
J_\lambda(u) \;=\; \tfrac{a}{2}\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,dx \;+\; \tfrac{b}{4}\Bigl(\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,dx\Bigr)^2 \;-\; \tfrac{\lambda}{2^*}\int_\Omega |u|^{2^*}\,dx \;-\; \lambda\!\int_\Omega G(x,u)\,dx \;-\; \int_\Omega H(x,v(x))u\,dx,
$$
with $G,H$ the antiderivatives of $g,h$ in the second variable.

There exist explicit dimensional constants $0 < C_1(N) \le C_2(N)$ such that the following multiplicity result is known: if
$$
a^{(N-4)/2}\,b \;>\; C_2(N),
$$
then for every sufficiently large $\lambda>0$ and every convex set $\mathcal{C}\subset L^2(\Omega)$ whose closure in $L^2(\Omega)$ contains $H^1_0(\Omega)$, there exists $v^*\in\mathcal{C}$ such that problem $(P_\lambda)$ admits at least three weak solutions, two of which are global minima in $H^1_0(\Omega)$ of the energy functional $J_\lambda$.

Question. When $N>4$, does the same conclusion remain valid for all $a\ge 0$, $b>0$ satisfying the below-threshold condition
$$
a^{(N-4)/2}\,b \;<\; C_1(N)\,?
$$
That is, under this condition, prove or disprove that for every sufficiently large $\lambda>0$ and every convex set $\mathcal{C}\subset L^2(\Omega)$ whose closure in $L^2(\Omega)$ contains $H^1_0(\Omega)$, there exists $v^*\in\mathcal{C}$ such that $(P_\lambda)$ has at least three weak solutions, two of which are global minima of $J_\lambda$ in $H^1_0(\Omega)$.

Let $n\ge 1$. Fix an invertible matrix $A\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ and a full-rank lattice $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ (i.e., $\Gamma = P\mathbb{Z}^n$ for some $P\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$). A finite collection $\Psi=\{\psi^1,\ldots,\psi^L\}\subset L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is called an orthonormal wavelet associated with $(A,\Gamma)$ if the system
$$\{|\det A|^{j/2}\,\psi^\ell(A^j x-\gamma) : j\in\mathbb{Z},\ \gamma\in\Gamma,\ \ell=1,\ldots,L\}$$
is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$. (We restrict to the case $L=1$ of single-generator orthonormal wavelets.)

A measurable set $W\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is called an $(A,\Gamma)$-wavelet set if
\begin{itemize}
\item[(t)] $\{W+\gamma\}_{\gamma\in\Gamma^*}$ partitions $\mathbb{R}^n$ modulo null sets, where $\Gamma^*$ is the dual lattice, and
\item[(d)] $\{(A^T)^j W\}_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}$ partitions $\mathbb{R}^n$ modulo null sets.
\end{itemize}
A function $\psi\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is called a minimally supported frequency (MSF) wavelet associated with $(A,\Gamma)$ if $|\widehat{\psi}|=\mathbf{1}_W$ (up to normalization) for some $(A,\Gamma)$-wavelet set $W$; equivalently, $\psi$ is an orthonormal wavelet whose Fourier transform has minimal possible support.

Question: Suppose there exists a single-generator orthonormal wavelet associated with $(A,\Gamma)$. Must there exist a minimally supported frequency wavelet associated with $(A,\Gamma)$?

Let $n \geq 1$, let $A \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ be an invertible real $n \times n$ matrix, and let $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a full-rank lattice. For $\psi \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ define the associated wavelet system
$$\{ \psi_{j,k}(x) := |\det A|^{j/2}\, \psi(A^j x - k) : j \in \mathbb{Z},\; k \in \Gamma \}.$$
Call $\psi$ an orthonormal wavelet associated with $(A,\Gamma)$ if this system is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and a Parseval wavelet if the system is a Parseval (normalized tight) frame for $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$, i.e.
$$\|f\|_2^2 = \sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}} \sum_{k \in \Gamma} |\langle f, \psi_{j,k}\rangle|^2 \quad \text{for all } f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^n).$$
Let $\widehat{\psi}$ denote the Fourier transform of $\psi$.

Question: Does the Calderón formula
$$\sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}} |\widehat{\psi}((A^T)^j \xi)|^2 = 1 \quad \text{for almost every } \xi \in \mathbb{R}^n$$
hold for every orthonormal wavelet (or, more generally, every Parseval wavelet) $\psi$ associated with $(A, \Gamma)$, with no further assumption on $A$ or $\Gamma$?

Setup. Consider a compound nucleus formed by s-wave neutron capture on a target nucleus, producing neutron resonances at excitation energies near the neutron separation energy S_n. Each resonance λ has a total radiative (gamma) decay width Γ_γ(λ) = Σ_f Γ_γ(λ → f), where the sum runs over all energetically accessible final states f.

In the statistical model of nuclear reactions, the partial gamma decay widths from a resonance λ at excitation energy E_λ to a final state f at energy E_f are computed using a gamma-ray strength function f_XL(E_γ) (for multipolarity XL and gamma-ray energy E_γ = E_λ − E_f) together with a level density ρ(E_f, J_f, π_f). The Brink–Axel hypothesis asserts that the gamma-ray strength function f_XL(E_γ) depends only on the gamma-ray energy E_γ and is independent of the properties (excitation energy, spin, parity) of the initial and final nuclear states involved in the transition. Under this hypothesis one obtains theoretical mean total gamma decay widths ⟨Γ_γ⟩_theory.

Empirical observation. The mean total gamma decay widths ⟨Γ_γ⟩_exp measured for ensembles of neutron resonances are systematically larger than the predictions ⟨Γ_γ⟩_theory of the statistical model based on the Brink–Axel hypothesis, indicating missing gamma strength in the model.

Problem. Determine whether the Brink–Axel hypothesis (in its generalized form, asserting independence of f_XL(E_γ) from initial- and final-state properties) holds for all gamma transitions that contribute significantly to the gamma decay of neutron resonances. Specifically, identify whether a violation of the Brink–Axel hypothesis for the dominant contributing transitions (for instance through dependence of the strength function on excitation energy, spin, parity, or temperature, or through additional structure such as low-energy enhancements, scissors modes, or pygmy resonances built on excited states) can quantitatively account for the observed underprediction of ⟨Γ_γ⟩ by the statistical model.

Recent experimental and theoretical work gives a mixed, nucleus- and energy-dependent picture. Several Oslo-method studies (e.g., on Sn isotopes and on 238Np) report that the generalized Brink–Axel hypothesis holds reasonably well for dipole strength below the neutron separation energy, supporting its use in statistical-model calculations. However, clear violations have been documented at low gamma-ray energies (low-energy enhancement/upbend, scissors-mode discrepancies between decay and absorption) and in finite-temperature regimes, and a comprehensive 2021 test in the pygmy dipole region as well as 2025 work on the upbend resonance demonstrate that the hypothesis cannot be assumed universally. Whether such violations are sufficient to fully explain the underpredicted mean total gamma decay widths of neutron resonances remains unresolved.

Let $\Gamma = \mathbb{Z}^n$ act on $\mathbb{R}^n$ by translations, and let $A \in GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ be an expansive matrix, i.e., every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$ satisfies $|\lambda| > 1$. For a finite collection $\Psi = \{\psi^1, \dots, \psi^L\} \subset L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$, the associated wavelet system is
$$\{ |\det A|^{j/2}\, \psi^l(A^j x - k) : 1 \le l \le L,\ j \in \mathbb{Z},\ k \in \mathbb{Z}^n \}.$$
We call $\Psi$ an orthonormal wavelet associated with $(A, \mathbb{Z}^n)$ if this system is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$. A function $\psi \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is said to be well-localized if there exists $N > 0$ such that
$$\psi(x) = O(|x|^{-N})\ \text{as}\ |x| \to \infty, \qquad \widehat{\psi}(\xi) = O(|\xi|^{-N})\ \text{as}\ |\xi| \to \infty.$$
A wavelet $\Psi$ is well-localized if every $\psi^l$ is well-localized.

Characterize precisely the expansive matrices $A \in GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ for which there exists a well-localized orthonormal wavelet (with possibly multiple generators) associated with $(A, \mathbb{Z}^n)$.

representations.normalized:
Consider a self-conjugate even-even nucleus consisting of N alpha particles (each alpha treated as a four-nucleon cluster of two protons and two neutrons in its internal 0s ground state). An "alpha-gas" (alpha-condensate) trial state is the fully antisymmetrized N-alpha product wave function in which the center-of-mass coordinate of each alpha occupies the same lowest harmonic-oscillator-type single-alpha orbit, denoted 0S. Given a microscopic many-body wave function Psi for such a state, define the bosonic single-alpha density matrix
  rho(r, r') = <Psi | a_alpha^dagger(r) a_alpha(r') | Psi>,
where a_alpha^dagger(r) creates a (properly antisymmetrized) alpha cluster centered at r, and let {n_i} denote its eigenvalues (the bosonic occupation numbers of the natural alpha orbits phi_i), normalized so that sum_i n_i = N. The "0S occupation fraction" is f_{0S} = n_{0S}/N, the fraction of alpha particles occupying the lowest natural alpha orbit.

Problem. Develop and carry out microscopic calculations of the bosonic alpha occupation numbers {n_i}, and in particular of the 0S occupation fraction f_{0S}, for candidate N-alpha gas states in self-conjugate even-even nuclei. As the principal benchmark, compute f_{0S} for the second 0+ (Hoyle) state of 12C (N = 3) and decide whether it attains a value (typically reported to be of order 70–80%) consistent with an alpha-condensate interpretation. Extend the analysis to heavier candidate alpha-gas states (e.g., N = 4 in 16O, N = 5 in 20Ne, and beyond) to test how broadly the alpha-condensate character, as quantified by a dominant 0S bosonic occupation, persists.

$$\{|\det A|^{j/2}\,\psi^\ell(A^j x - k) : j\in\mathbb{Z},\ k\in\mathbb{Z}^n,\ \ell=1,\dots,L\}$$

The problem is known to be solved affirmatively in dimension $n\le 2$: for every expansive $2\times 2$ integer dilation, there exists an orthonormal wavelet consisting of $|\det A|-1$ band-limited Schwartz-class functions. Recent work (2025) extends Schwartz-class wavelet constructions to rational expansive dilations via MRA-based Meyer-type constructions. However, for general integer expansive dilations in dimensions $n\ge 3$, the existence of Schwartz-class wavelets remains open.

Let $\psi \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$. We say that $\psi$ is an orthonormal wavelet (with respect to the dyadic dilation) if the family
$$\psi_{j,k}(x) := 2^{j/2}\psi(2^j x - k), \qquad j,k \in \mathbb{Z},$$
forms an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.

Recall that the Schwartz class $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$ is the space of all $C^\infty$ functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ such that for every pair of nonnegative integers $m,n$,
$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}} |x|^m \,|f^{(n)}(x)| < \infty.$$

The Fourier transform is normalized by $\widehat{f}(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x) e^{-2\pi i x \xi}\,dx$.

Question: Suppose $\psi$ is an orthonormal wavelet such that $\psi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$. Must the Fourier transform $\widehat{\psi}$ necessarily be compactly supported?

Consider the carbon-12 nucleus as a system of three α particles (each α being a tightly bound 4-nucleon cluster treated as a structureless boson). The Hoyle state is the second 0⁺ excited state of ¹²C, located at about 7.65 MeV above the ground state, and is interpreted as a dilute Bose-condensate-like configuration in which all three α particles occupy the same lowest (0S) relative orbital.

Let the third 0⁺ state of ¹²C, denoted 0₃⁺, be the 0⁺ resonance observed near 10.08 MeV excitation energy.

(a) Determine whether the 0₃⁺ state can be characterized as a higher-nodal "breathing-mode" excitation of the Hoyle condensate, in the precise sense that all three α particles occupy a common relative 1S orbital (one radial node) so that the state still qualifies as an α-particle Bose condensate but with a higher-nodal single-particle wave function than the Hoyle state.

(b) Determine the branching pattern of the three-α decay of this 0₃⁺ resonance: in particular, quantify the probability of direct (democratic) breakup into three α particles versus the sequential decay through the ⁸Be(0⁺) + α channel, and identify any qualitative differences between the direct three-α decay of the breathing 0₃⁺ state and that of the Hoyle state.

Consider a permissionless distributed payment system that issues a stablecoin (a token whose nominal value is pegged to some external reference). The system is permissionless in the sense that any participant may, at zero or negligible cost, create an arbitrary number of fresh pseudonymous identities (a Sybil capability), and there is no mechanism that binds an identity to a real-world entity, to off-chain wealth, or to verifiable future income.

The system offers collateralized loans: a borrower locks collateral of value C (denominated in the stablecoin's reference unit) and receives a loan of L stablecoins, subject to a smart contract that may enforce repayment schedules, interest, and liquidation of the collateral. A loan is called under-collateralized if C < L at the time of issuance, and fully collateralized if C ≥ L.

Assume borrowers are rational utility maximizers who may, at any time, abandon any identity (and any associated debt obligations not secured by on-chain collateral) and continue participating under a new identity at no cost.

Question: Is there any incentive-compatible loan-issuance mechanism implementable in this setting that allows under-collateralized loans (C < L) without enabling unbounded arbitrage by borrowers who create fresh Sybil identities, take out loans, and abandon the debt? Equivalently, must every such system in the permissionless, Sybil-vulnerable setting reduce to offering only fully collateralized loans (C ≥ L)?

Provide a proof that no such under-collateralized mechanism can exist, or exhibit a mechanism that achieves under-collateralization while remaining robust to Sybil exit-scam strategies.

Consider a permissionless distributed payment system that issues a stablecoin (a token whose nominal value is pegged to some external reference). The system is permissionless in the sense that any participant may, at zero or negligible cost, create an arbitrary number of fresh pseudonymous identities (a Sybil capability), and there is no mechanism that binds an identity to a real-world entity, to off-chain wealth, or to verifiable future income.

The system offers collateralized loans: a borrower locks collateral of value C (denominated in the stablecoin's reference unit) and receives a loan of L stablecoins, subject to a smart contract that may enforce repayment schedules, interest, and liquidation of the collateral. A loan is called under-collateralized if C < L at the time of issuance, and fully collateralized if C ≥ L.

Assume borrowers are rational utility maximizers who may, at any time, abandon any identity (and any associated debt obligations not secured by on-chain collateral) and continue participating under a new identity at no cost.

Question: Is there any incentive-compatible loan-issuance mechanism implementable in this setting that allows under-collateralized loans (C < L) without enabling unbounded arbitrage by borrowers who create fresh Sybil identities, take out loans, and abandon the debt? Equivalently, must every such system in the permissionless, Sybil-vulnerable setting reduce to offering only fully collateralized loans (C ≥ L)?

Provide a proof that no such under-collateralized mechanism can exist, or exhibit a mechanism that achieves under-collateralization while remaining robust to Sybil exit-scam strategies.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

The question is posed as an informal claim/theorem about permissionless stablecoins. While it is widely repeated in the cryptocurrency literature that Sybil attacks force on-chain loans to be over- or fully collateralized in the absence of strong identities, there is no universally accepted formal impossibility result; ongoing work on decentralized identity, reputation, soulbound tokens, and zero-knowledge KYC continues to explore partial workarounds. The status of a fully formal, model-independent impossibility theorem is best classified as unknown.

Consider a stablecoin system that maintains a peg of its token against a reference asset by means of currency interventions: a monetary authority holds a reserve of the reference asset and commits to a publicly known rule under which it buys or sells stablecoins against the reserve whenever the market price deviates from the peg. Suppose the system is fully transparent, in the sense that (i) the intervention rule (the mapping from observed market state to buy/sell volume and price), (ii) the current size and composition of the reserves, and (iii) every past on-chain action of the authority are common knowledge to all market participants in real time.

Model the market as a game between the monetary authority, whose objective is to keep the exchange rate within a tolerance band around the peg subject to a finite reserve constraint, and a set of strategic speculators who observe the full state and the rule and choose trading strategies to maximize expected profit, possibly coordinating to mount speculative attacks that deplete the reserve.

Formulate and analyze the following questions in this setting:

1. Under what conditions on the intervention rule, the reserve size, the distribution of exogenous demand shocks, and the speculators' information and coordination capabilities does a fully transparent intervention policy admit a profitable speculative strategy that forces the peg to break with positive probability?

2. Quantify the loss in effectiveness (e.g., expected time to peg failure, expected reserve depletion, or maximum sustainable shock) of an optimal transparent intervention policy relative to an analogous policy that can be kept partially or fully opaque.

3. Determine whether there exists a transparent intervention rule that is incentive-compatible in the sense that no coalition of speculators with bounded capital has a strictly profitable deviation from non-attacking behavior, and characterize such rules if they exist.

The nucleus carbon-12 ($^{12}$C), consisting of six protons and six neutrons, is often modeled as a system of three $\alpha$-particle clusters. Two phenomenological pictures of its low-energy spectrum are:

(a) a ground-state rotational band built on the $0^+_1$ ground state, interpreted as a rigid, permanently spinning equilateral triangular $\alpha$-cluster configuration with $D_{3h}$ symmetry;

(b) a so-called "Hoyle band," a rotational band built on the second $0^+$ state (the Hoyle state, $0^+_2$ at $\approx 7.65$ MeV), with the $0^+_2$ acting as the band head.

Settle the following questions about the structure of $^{12}$C:

1. Is the ground-state band of $^{12}$C correctly described as a permanent (rigid) spinning triangular three-$\alpha$ configuration? In particular, mean-field (Hartree–Fock or Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov) calculations without angular-momentum or parity projection produce only a perfectly round oblate intrinsic shape rather than a triangular one; reconcile this with, or refute, the rigid spinning-triangle interpretation.

2. Does the "Hoyle band" constitute a genuine rotational band with a well-defined band head at the $0^+_2$ state? In particular, the measured electromagnetic transition strengths $B(E2)$ from the second $2^+$ state to the $0^+_2$ and to the $0^+_3$ states are comparable in magnitude, which is in tension with the existence of a unique band-head assignment for the $2^+_2$ within the Hoyle band.

Provide a definitive theoretical and/or experimental determination of (1) and (2).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The structure of low-lying $^{12}$C states remains under active debate. Experimental work (e.g., Marín-Lámbarri et al., 2014) has been interpreted as evidence for a $D_{3h}$ spinning-triangle ground-state band, while recent ab-initio lattice and no-core shell model calculations (e.g., Shen et al., Nature Commun. 2023) support an emergent triangular/obtuse-triangle geometry but reinterpret the Hoyle state as a "bent-arm" or breathing mode rather than a rigidly spinning triangle. Whether the Hoyle band is a genuine rotational band with a well-defined band head is still disputed, with the $B(E2)$ ratios from $2^+_2$ being a key piece of conflicting evidence. The questions are therefore not definitively settled.

Consider a stablecoin system that targets a fixed peg (e.g., 1 unit of stablecoin = 1 USD) and that contracts its circulating money supply via a "self-tokenizing" open market operation defined as follows. When the stablecoin price falls below the peg, the system issues special-purpose internal tokens (distinct from the stablecoin) and auctions them for stablecoins; the stablecoins received are then destroyed (burned). Holders of the special-purpose tokens are entitled to a future payoff, paid only when the stablecoin returns to and remains at the peg, in one of two forms:

(a) a promised absolute quantity of newly minted future stablecoins (debt-like claim), or
(b) a relative share of all future money-supply growth (equity-like claim).

Let demand for the stablecoin follow a stochastic process subject to negative shocks and to repeated speculative attacks against the peg. Each contraction round increases the outstanding stock of unredeemed special-purpose token claims, which in turn dilutes the per-token expected payoff (under scheme (b)) or expands the contingent future supply obligation (under scheme (a)).

Formulate and analyze a model of this mechanism that answers the following:

1. Derive conditions on the demand process, attack frequency, and risk-adjusted discount factor of speculators under which there exists a market-clearing price for the special-purpose tokens that allows the system to absorb a given contraction in stablecoin supply.

2. Determine whether, under repeated speculative attacks, the sequence of clearing prices for special-purpose tokens converges to zero in finite time (mechanism failure) or remains bounded away from zero (mechanism resilience), and characterize the threshold separating these regimes for both compensation schemes (a) and (b).

3. Compare schemes (a) and (b): show whether one is strictly more resilient than the other, or identify parameter regions in which each dominates.

Provide either an existence/stability theorem for the peg-defense mechanism or a proof that no such mechanism can sustain the peg almost surely against an adversary capable of arbitrarily many attack rounds.

The question of whether self-tokenizing (seigniorage-share / bond-style) stablecoin contractions are robust to repeated speculative attacks and prolonged demand declines remains an open and actively debated research question. Empirical failures of such designs (e.g., the collapse of Basis Cash and the May 2022 collapse of Terra/UST, which used a related two-token absorption mechanism) are widely cited as evidence that the mechanism is fragile, and several theoretical analyses (e.g., on "death spirals" of algorithmic stablecoins) provide partial negative results, but no general resilience theorem or full characterization is established.

Consider a stablecoin system that issues a digital currency whose circulating supply S(t) evolves over time. The system has access to a set of monetary mechanisms capable of permanently reducing S(t), namely: (i) charging interest rates on collateralized loans of the currency, (ii) currency interventions in which the issuer buys back currency on secondary markets using reserve assets, (iii) standard open market operations (OMO), in which the issuer sells interest-bearing debt instruments denominated in the currency in exchange for currency, retiring the proceeds, and (iv) proxy open market operations, in which a separate "share" or governance token is auctioned in exchange for currency that is then destroyed.

Assume the currency targets a fixed peg p* (e.g., one unit of fiat). Let demand shocks be modeled by a stochastic process D(t), and let the market price p(t) be determined by an inverse demand relation p(t) = f(D(t), S(t)) with ∂f/∂S < 0 and ∂f/∂D > 0.

Formulate and analyze the following:

1. Construct quantitative models of mechanisms (i)–(iv) describing how each contracts S(t) as a function of policy parameters (interest rate r, intervention budget B, OMO bond yield y, share auction parameters), and derive the resulting closed-loop dynamics of p(t) under a generic demand-shock process.

2. Identify the practical risks of each mechanism, including but not limited to: insufficient reserves to fund interventions, insolvency of the bond issuer in standard OMO, dilution spirals or "death spirals" in proxy OMO when share prices collapse, and adverse selection in lending markets.

3. Determine, for each mechanism, sufficient conditions on policy parameters and on the demand-shock process under which the peg p(t) ≡ p* is maintained with high probability over a fixed horizon T, and compare the stabilizing potential of mechanisms (i)–(iv) under identical shock environments.

4. Assess whether any of the four mechanisms can, in isolation or in combination, guarantee long-run peg stability, or provide counterexamples (shock scenarios) under which stability provably fails.

In nuclear cluster physics, the Hoyle state of carbon-12 is the second 0+ state at approximately 7.65 MeV, lying just above the three-α breakup threshold, and it is interpreted as a dilute three-α "gas-like" condensate; its α-condensate character is supported by precise measurement of the (e,e') inelastic form factor, whose magnitude and shape are sensitive to the spatial extension of the state.

For oxygen-16, an analogous picture predicts a four-α gas-like 0+ state lying close to the four-α breakup threshold (≈14.4 MeV). The sixth 0+ state of 16O, located at about 15.1 MeV (roughly 700 keV above the four-α threshold), has been proposed as such a Hoyle-analog state, and a peak observed near 15.2 MeV in the inverse-kinematics reaction 20Ne + α has been suggested as a candidate for the four-α gas state.

Problem. Establish whether either (a) the 0+ state of 16O at ≈15.1 MeV, or (b) the resonance observed near 15.2 MeV in 20Ne + α, can be confirmed as the four-α Hoyle-analog (α-condensate) gas state. Specifically:

1. Determine the inelastic electron-scattering form factor F(q) from the 16O ground state to the 0+ state at 15.1 MeV, and compare its magnitude and momentum-transfer dependence with the prediction of a four-α condensate (THSR-type) wave function representing a dilute, spatially extended four-α gas, to decide whether the 15.1 MeV state has the large radius and condensate character expected for the Hoyle analog.

2. Assign the spin and parity of the 15.2 MeV resonance observed in 20Ne + α and determine whether it is the same state as, or distinct from, the 0+ state at 15.1 MeV, thereby confirming or refuting its identification as the four-α gas state.

Recent experimental work has searched for the Hoyle analogue in 16O using inelastic α scattering with complete-kinematics detection of the four-α breakup. These measurements did not confirm the giant radius predicted by the α-particle condensate model for the 0+_6 state near 15.1 MeV, suggesting the state may not have a rarefied four-α gas structure. However, the precise (e,e') inelastic form factor — the most direct probe analogous to the Hoyle-state measurement — has not been reported, and a definitive spin assignment for the 15.2 MeV peak in 20Ne + α has not been firmly established. The question is therefore only partially resolved.

Consider a cryptocurrency that maintains a soft peg to a reference asset (i.e., a fixed target exchange rate that the issuer defends, but which may be abandoned or adjusted, as opposed to a hard peg enforced by an irrevocable mechanism). A speculative attack on such a peg is a coordinated action by market participants who short or redeem the pegged currency in sufficient volume to exhaust the issuer's defensive reserves and force a devaluation.

Distinguish the following collateralization regimes for a stablecoin of total outstanding money stock M (denominated in units of the peg target):

(a) Full proxy-collateralization: the issuer holds, in custody, reserves of the peg target (or assets denominated in it) of value at least M at all times, and these reserves are unconditionally available to redeem the currency at the pegged rate.

(b) Full self-collateralization: every unit of the stablecoin is backed by collateral, denominated in another crypto-asset, whose market value is maintained at or above M through on-chain over-collateralization and liquidation rules, and which can be liquidated to buy back the entire money stock at the pegged rate at any moment.

(c) Partial or fractional collateralization: reserves strictly less than M.

Formulate precise conditions on the collateral, redemption mechanism, and market microstructure under which such immunity holds, or exhibit a speculative-attack strategy that succeeds against any soft peg even under full proxy- or self-collateralization.

In the cluster description of light nuclei, the Tohsaki–Horiuchi–Schuck–Röpke (THSR) wave function is a fully antisymmetrized product ansatz in which α particles are placed in a common deformed Gaussian orbital, designed to capture nonlocalized, gas-like α-clustering. In its standard "extended" form for $^{16}$O, the nucleus is described as a $^{12}$C core plus an α particle, where the $^{12}$C subsystem is restricted to positive-parity intrinsic configurations (notably the ground state and the Hoyle-like $0^+_2$ state of $^{12}$C).

Comparison of the resulting $^{16}$O spectrum with experiment and with other microscopic calculations indicates that one $0^+$ state of $^{16}$O is absent from the extended THSR spectrum, namely the state naturally interpreted as an α particle orbiting the first $1^-$ excited state of $^{12}$C.

Problem. Construct an enlargement of the extended THSR framework for $^{16}$O that incorporates negative-parity intrinsic configurations of the $^{12}$C subsystem (in particular, the $1^-_1$ state of $^{12}$C coupled with relative orbital angular momentum yielding a $0^+$ total state), and demonstrate, by explicit microscopic calculation with full antisymmetrization, that the resulting $^{16}$O spectrum contains the missing $0^+$ state describable as an α particle orbiting the $1^-_1$ state of $^{12}$C. Determine its excitation energy and structure (in particular, whether it has the character of an α-gas state).

Consider a cryptocurrency C whose monetary authority (or protocol) wishes to implement an inflation-targeting regime. Inflation is to be measured by tracking the price, denominated in units of C, of a representative basket B = {(g_i, w_i)} of goods and services (with weights w_i ≥ 0 summing to 1). Assume that for each good g_i there is a price p_i^N(t) quoted in some national fiat currency N_i, and let e_{N_i,C}(t) denote the exchange rate from N_i to C at time t. Then the C-denominated price of the basket is

  P_B^C(t) = Σ_i w_i · p_i^N(t) · e_{N_i,C}(t),

and the measured inflation rate is π_C(t) = d/dt log P_B^C(t).

(a) Formulate a precise definition of an "adequate" basket B for the purpose of cryptocurrency inflation targeting, including criteria (e.g., representativeness of cryptocurrency-denominated economic activity, observability of prices, robustness to manipulation) under which π_C(t) measures intrinsic purchasing-power changes of C rather than mere exchange-rate variability against the fiat currencies N_i.

(b) Prove or disprove the following claim: if essentially all goods in B are quoted in a single fiat currency N, then inflation targeting (stabilizing π_C(t)) for C is functionally equivalent to exchange-rate targeting of e_{N,C}(t), in the sense that any monetary policy rule stabilizing one stabilizes the other up to bounded error.

(c) Propose and analyze a construction of a basket B (or a family of baskets) and an associated price index for which inflation targeting is provably distinct from exchange-rate targeting against any single fiat currency, and characterize the conditions on the joint dynamics of (p_i^N, e_{N_i,C}) under which this distinction is meaningful.

Consider a cryptocurrency system whose protocol controls the money supply through programmable issuance and possibly through interventions in secondary markets. Define the purchasing power of one unit of the cryptocurrency at time t as 1/P(t), where P(t) is the price level of a reference consumption basket denominated in units of the cryptocurrency. Consider three classes of monetary policy regimes that the protocol may commit to:

(R1) Fixed exchange-rate targeting: the protocol commits to maintaining a one-to-one (or otherwise fixed) exchange rate E(t) = E* between the cryptocurrency and a reference fiat currency (e.g., USD), by issuing or absorbing supply against reserves.

(R2) Monetary targeting: the protocol commits to a rule-based path for the money supply M(t) (for example, a constant growth rule, a Taylor-type rule, or a nominal-income targeting rule) without targeting any exchange rate.

(R3) Monetary targeting combined with managed floating / short-term exchange-rate smoothing: the protocol follows a rule for M(t) as in (R2) but additionally intervenes to dampen high-frequency fluctuations of E(t), without committing to any long-run exchange-rate level.

Let Var_T[1/P(t)] denote the long-run (T → ∞) variance of purchasing power induced by a regime, and let Pr[collapse] denote the probability that the regime fails (e.g., reserves are exhausted or the peg is broken) under stochastic demand and supply shocks.

Problem. Formulate a model in which the demand for the cryptocurrency, the reference fiat price level, and the basket prices follow stochastic processes, and determine whether there exists a rule-based monetary-targeting regime of type (R3) — monetary targeting together with short-term smoothing of E(t) — that achieves both

(a) strictly lower long-run variance of purchasing power Var_T[1/P(t)] than every feasible regime of type (R1), and
(b) strictly lower probability of regime collapse Pr[collapse] than every feasible regime of type (R1),

or else prove that no such regime exists. In particular, identify sufficient conditions on the shock processes and on the protocol's reserve constraints under which (R3) dominates (R1) in the sense above, and compare (R3) with the pure monetary-targeting regime (R2).

Consider the α-decay system $^{212}\mathrm{Po} \to {}^{208}\mathrm{Pb} + \alpha$, viewed as a four-nucleon (two protons and two neutrons) cluster moving in the mean field of a doubly-magic $^{208}\mathrm{Pb}$ core. Two complementary descriptions of this system are:

(i) A quartetting/THSR-type wave-function approach in which the α-cluster is described by a Tohsaki–Horiuchi–Schuck–Röpke product ansatz for four nucleons, combined with a local-density approximation. In this picture the four nucleons form an identifiable bound α cluster at low matter density (the nuclear surface), but at a critical core density the four-body intrinsic bound state dissolves and the nucleons must be described as four independent shell-model quasiparticles. This yields an effective potential pocket for the α coordinate.

(ii) A double-folding procedure in which a phenomenological effective nucleon–nucleon interaction (e.g.\ M3Y) is folded with the density distribution of the α particle and that of the $^{208}\mathrm{Pb}$ core, again producing an α–core potential exhibiting a pocket that supports a quasibound resonance whose width gives the α-decay width.

Develop a fully microscopic, quantum-mechanical description of α preformation in $^{212}\mathrm{Po}$ that:

(a) treats consistently the transition, as a function of the local nuclear density, of the four-nucleon wave function from a bound α cluster at the surface to four uncorrelated shell-model nucleons in the high-density interior;

(b) reproduces the measured α-decay width of $^{212}\mathrm{Po}$;

(c) establishes a quantitative correspondence between the THSR/local-density-approximation pocket potential of approach (i) and the double-folding pocket potential of approach (ii), explaining under what assumptions the two approaches give equivalent α–core potentials and decay widths.

Consider a distributed cryptocurrency protocol operating in a fully permissionless setting, defined as a system in which no prior assumptions can be made about the identifiability, reputation, or trustworthiness of participants: any party may join or leave the protocol at any time under arbitrary (possibly Sybil) identities, and there is no designated set of trusted actors. Call such a cryptocurrency "effectively price-stable" if its protocol guarantees, with high probability and against a rational/adversarial subset of participants, that the exchange rate of one unit of the cryptocurrency, measured against some specified external reference asset (e.g., a fiat currency or a basket of goods), remains within a bounded neighborhood of a target value over arbitrarily long time horizons, despite fluctuations in demand and adversarial behavior.

Question: Does there exist a protocol for a cryptocurrency that is simultaneously (i) fully permissionless in the above sense and (ii) effectively price-stable in the above sense? Equivalently, prove either the existence of such a protocol (by construction together with a security/stability analysis) or an impossibility theorem showing that no such protocol can exist under standard cryptographic and economic assumptions.

Consider a cryptocurrency protocol operating on a permissionless distributed ledger that aims to maintain a stable nominal value relative to a chosen external anchor (for example, a fiat currency or a basket of goods). Implementing a monetary policy that targets such an anchor requires the protocol to have access, on-chain, to external information such as the current exchange rate or price of the cryptocurrency relative to the anchor. A component that supplies such external information to the ledger is called an oracle. An oracle is said to be permissionless if its operation does not rely on any fixed, globally trusted party or fixed group of trusted parties (whether identified by signing keys, identities, or otherwise) whose honesty must be assumed for the correctness of the reported data; instead, any party should be able to participate in or verify the data-supply process under the protocol's open-membership rules.

Question: Does there exist a mechanism by which a stablecoin protocol on a permissionless ledger can obtain external price or exchange-rate information for its nominal anchor, with provable security guarantees against manipulation, without reintroducing a globally trusted party or trusted committee whose honesty must be assumed? Equivalently, is it possible to design a secure permissionless price-feed oracle suitable for informing on-chain monetary policy decisions, and if so, characterize the assumptions (economic, cryptographic, or game-theoretic) under which such security can be established; if not, prove an impossibility result delineating the obstruction.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of designing secure permissionless price-feed oracles for stablecoins remains an active research area. Existing systems (Chainlink, Witnet, Tellor, DIA, UMA) provide decentralized oracle networks using staking, reputation, aggregation of node reports, or optimistic dispute mechanisms, but each still relies on assumptions about a sufficiently honest set of participants, economic incentives, or fallback governance, and price-oracle manipulations remain a documented attack surface in DeFi. No solution has been established as fully secure under purely permissionless assumptions without some trusted-set or economic-honesty assumption, so the question as posed appears to remain open.

Consider a safety-critical automated driving system that must operate within a specified operational design domain (ODD), defined as the set of environmental, geographical, temporal, and traffic conditions under which the system is designed to function safely. Suppose one has access to large logs of real-world driving data obtained from past field operational tests and from customer vehicles, where each log can be segmented into discrete "driving scenarios" (each scenario being a tuple consisting of road geometry, surrounding agents and their trajectories, weather and lighting conditions, ego-vehicle state, and triggering events).

(a) Propose a methodology for efficiently collecting and curating, from such large-scale logs, a finite scenario set S that adequately represents the ODD, including a formal model of the scenario space and a sampling/selection procedure that is tractable on industrial-scale datasets.

(b) Define a quantitative evaluation criterion (a notion of "test coverage") C(S) for any such finite collection S, together with a threshold or sufficiency condition under which one may certify that S is adequate to provide safety and security assurance for the system within its declared ODD. The coverage notion must be well-defined on the scenario model from (a) and must support an argument linking C(S) ≥ threshold to a bound on residual risk.

The problem is to provide such a methodology and coverage definition, or to prove that no such procedure can simultaneously satisfy tractability of collection and a meaningful residual-risk guarantee.

Consider a permissionless proof-of-work blockchain that supports a stablecoin protocol. A stablecoin requires a nominal anchor — a reference signal (typically tied to an external price level) that the protocol can use to adjust supply or collateral parameters so that the coin's value remains stable. Suppose that secure permissionless oracles for arbitrary off-chain data (such as exchange rates) are unavailable, so the protocol may only use information that is verifiable on-chain (purely endogenous quantities such as the sequence of block timestamps, block headers, transaction data, the current mining difficulty target, and the inferred mining hash rate).

Define an on-chain proxy variable to be a function P: (chain history up to height h) → ℝ computable by any full node. Call such a proxy a viable nominal-anchor proxy if it satisfies all of the following:

(i) Informativeness: P is statistically correlated with an external nominal anchor (e.g. the purchasing power or fiat price of the native coin) strongly enough that a control rule based on P can keep the stablecoin's market value within a bounded band around its target with high probability under normal economic conditions.

(ii) Incentive compatibility: in the game where miners and users choose strategies to maximize expected profit, honest participation (truthful block production at the natural difficulty) remains a (sub-game-perfect) equilibrium when the stablecoin protocol consumes P.

(iii) Non-gameability: there is no coalition of miners and/or users controlling less than some threshold α < 1/2 of hash power and bounded capital that can profitably manipulate P away from its honest value by more than ε, for specified small ε > 0.

(iv) Security: the protocol built on P does not introduce new attack vectors that reduce the consensus security of the underlying blockchain.

Question: Does there exist an on-chain proxy variable P — for instance one constructed from the mining hash rate, inter-block timing, or the mining difficulty — that is a viable nominal-anchor proxy in the sense above? Equivalently, exhibit such a P together with a proof that it satisfies (i)–(iv), or prove that no function of purely on-chain data can simultaneously satisfy (i)–(iv).

Let $(M, \eta_0, \xi_0, \Phi_0, g_0)$ be a compact connected Sasaki manifold of dimension $2n+1$, where $\eta_0$ is the contact 1-form, $\xi_0$ the Reeb vector field, $\Phi_0$ an endomorphism of $TM$, and $g_0$ the Sasaki metric. Let $D = \ker \eta_0$ be the contact distribution, and let $J = \Phi_0|_D$ be the induced complex structure on $D$, so that $(D, J)$ is the underlying contact CR structure.

The Sasaki cone $\kappa(D, J)$ is defined as the moduli space of Sasaki structures $(\eta, \xi, \Phi, g)$ on $M$ that are compatible with the fixed CR structure $(D, J)$ (equivalently, the space of Reeb vector fields in the Lie algebra of a maximal torus in the CR automorphism group, modulo the action of that automorphism group). Each ray in $\kappa(D, J)$ corresponds to the family obtained by transverse homothety (rescaling the Reeb vector field by positive constants).

A ray in $\kappa(D, J)$ is called a constant scalar curvature (CSC) ray if it contains a Sasaki metric whose scalar curvature is constant on $M$.

Question: Is it true that for every compact connected Sasaki manifold with fixed underlying contact CR structure $(D, J)$, the CSC rays in the Sasaki cone $\kappa(D, J)$ are isolated points of the set of CSC rays — that is, no CSC ray lies in a continuous (non-isolated) family of CSC rays inside $\kappa(D, J)$?

The problem appears to remain open in general. Partial results exist: in three-dimensional Sasaki cones the CSC rays are known to be isolated, and isolation has been established in various special constructions (e.g., Sasaki joins). Recent work has produced examples of multiple (but still isolated) CSC rays within a single Sasaki cone, sometimes separated by regions devoid of extremal rays, but no example of a non-isolated continuous family of CSC rays is known, and no general proof of isolation has been published.

Consider a safety-critical system that contains one or more subsystems whose behavior is determined by a trained machine-learning model f: X -> Y (e.g., a classifier or regressor) obtained from a finite training sample drawn from an unknown data-generating distribution D over X x Y. Because f is learned from finite data and operates in possibly shifted environments at deployment, its predictions carry uncertainty arising from (i) aleatoric noise inherent in D, (ii) epistemic uncertainty due to limited training data and model class mis-specification, and (iii) distributional shift between training and operational distributions.

Develop a principled framework that, for such a learned subsystem, expresses the predictive uncertainty as explicit statistical measures (e.g., calibrated probability distributions over outputs, prediction intervals with guaranteed coverage, conditional risk bounds, false-positive/false-negative rates, or distributionally robust performance bounds) such that:

1. The measures admit precise mathematical definitions and estimable quantities from data.
2. The measures can be incorporated as quantitative requirements (e.g., "Pr[ loss(f(X), Y) > tau ] <= epsilon under operational distribution D'") that are verifiable during design and assurance.
3. The framework provides composition rules for propagating these uncertainty measures through a larger system containing both ML and non-ML components, yielding system-level statistical guarantees.

Formally specify such a set of statistical measures, the assumptions on D and f under which they are well-defined and estimable with finite-sample guarantees, and the propagation rules through system composition.

Let $(M, D, J)$ be a compact connected Sasaki manifold with fixed underlying contact CR structure, where $D \subset TM$ is the contact distribution and $J$ is an integrable complex structure on $D$. The Sasaki cone $\kappa(D,J)$ is the moduli space of Sasaki metrics compatible with $(D,J)$, parametrized by Reeb vector fields; it has a natural ray structure (the Reeb field can be rescaled by positive constants, giving rise to "rays" in the cone). A Sasaki metric is called extremal if its Reeb field is a critical point of the squared $L^2$-norm of the scalar curvature restricted to a fixed Sasaki cone (equivalently, the $(1,0)$-gradient of the transverse scalar curvature is transversely holomorphic), and a ray of Sasaki metrics is called extremal (respectively, constant scalar curvature, CSC) if it consists of extremal (respectively, CSC) Sasaki metrics.

Question: Suppose $\kappa(D,J)$ contains at least one extremal ray. Must $\kappa(D,J)$ then contain at least one constant scalar curvature ray?

The question has been answered in the negative. A subsequent work ("Existence and Non-Existence of Constant Scalar Curvature and Extremal Sasaki Metrics," arXiv:2210.12203, published in Mathematische Zeitschrift) gives explicit examples showing that a non-empty extremal Sasaki–Reeb cone need not contain any constant scalar curvature Sasaki metric. Let Σ_2 be a closed Riemann surface of genus 2, and let M_3 denote the total space of the primitive circle bundle over Σ_2 endowed with its standard Sasaki structure of constant transverse sectional curvature −1 (so that the Reeb foliation has Kähler quotient the hyperbolic metric on Σ_2). Let S^3_{3,2} denote the 3-sphere equipped with the weighted Sasaki structure of weights (3,2). Form the Sasaki join

   M = M_3 ⋆_{1,101} S^3_{3,2},

which is a 5-dimensional compact Sasaki manifold; topologically, M is a lens space bundle over Σ_2. The join construction endows M with a distinguished Sasaki structure (S, J̄), and one may consider its Sasaki cone (the space of compatible Sasaki structures obtained by deforming the Reeb vector field within the appropriate cone). Inside this Sasaki cone, the so-called admissible Sasaki metrics are those constructed by the standard admissible (join-type) ansatz compatible with the bundle structure.

A Sasaki metric is called extremal if the (1,0)-gradient of its transverse scalar curvature is a transversely holomorphic vector field (the Sasaki analogue of Calabi's notion of extremal Kähler metrics).

Question: Do there exist extremal Sasaki metrics in the Sasaki class (S, J̄) on M that are not admissible?

Consider a system S composed of n component modules M_1, ..., M_n arranged in a redundant architecture described by a directed acyclic graph G = (V, E), where each component M_i is intended to implement a (yet-to-be-trained) machine-learning model. Suppose that for each component M_i a probabilistic uncertainty model is given a priori in the form of a conditional output distribution P_i(y_i | x_i, theta_i), where theta_i parameterizes a stochastic error model (for example, a bound on the misclassification probability, a noise distribution on outputs, or a confidence-calibrated error rate). The redundant architecture specifies a deterministic combination rule F that maps the joint outputs (y_1, ..., y_n) to a system output Y = F(y_1, ..., y_n) (e.g., majority voting, weighted ensembling, or a safety monitor with fallback).

Given a system-level safety specification phi (for instance, "Pr[Y is incorrect on input X] <= epsilon" for a stipulated input distribution D over X), develop a verification procedure that, using only the per-component uncertainty models {P_i} and the architecture (G, F) — and without training any of the actual machine-learning models — decides whether the redundant architecture absorbs or mitigates the per-component uncertainty so that the system satisfies phi. Formally:

(a) Define a precise mathematical framework (composition semantics) under which the joint distribution of (y_1, ..., y_n) given X is determined by the {P_i} and a specified dependence structure (e.g., conditional independence given X, or a copula constraint).

(b) Provide an algorithm that, given (G, F, {P_i}, D, phi), outputs YES if the induced distribution of Y satisfies phi, and otherwise outputs NO together with a witness assignment of component behaviors consistent with {P_i} that violates phi.

(c) Establish soundness, completeness, and computational complexity of the procedure, and characterize the class of redundant architectures (G, F) for which uncertainty absorption can be certified in polynomial time before training.

Given a system-level safety specification phi (for instance, "Pr[Y is incorrect on input X] <= epsilon" for a stipulated input distribution D over X), develop a verification procedure that, using only the per-component uncertainty models {P_i} and the architecture (G, F) — and without training any of the actual machine-learning models — decides whether the redundant architecture absorbs or mitigates the per-component uncertainty so that the system satisfies phi. (a) Define a precise mathematical framework (composition semantics) under which the joint distribution of (y_1, ..., y_n) given X is determined by the {P_i} and a specified dependence structure (e.g., conditional independence given X, or a copula constraint).

(b) Provide an algorithm that, given (G, F, {P_i}, D, phi), outputs YES if the induced distribution of Y satisfies phi, and otherwise outputs NO together with a witness assignment of component behaviors consistent with {P_i} that violates phi.

(c) Establish soundness, completeness, and computational complexity of the procedure, and characterize the class of redundant architectures (G, F) for which uncertainty absorption can be certified in polynomial time before training.

Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$, $L, B > 0$, and $\varepsilon > 0$. Let $\mathcal{F}^d_{L,B}$ denote the class of convex, $L$-Lipschitz functions $F:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ that attain their minimum over the Euclidean ball $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \|x\| \le B\}$ at some point $x^*$ with $\|x^*\| \le B$.

A memory-bounded first-order optimization algorithm with $T$ queries and $M$ bits of memory is specified as follows: at each round $t = 1, \dots, T$, the algorithm chooses a query point $x_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ as a (possibly randomized) function of its current memory state $S_{t-1} \in \{0,1\}^M$; it then receives from an exact first-order oracle the pair $(F(x_t), g_t)$ where $g_t \in \partial F(x_t)$; finally it updates the memory state to $S_t \in \{0,1\}^M$ as a (possibly randomized) function of $S_{t-1}$ and $(F(x_t), g_t)$. After $T$ rounds the algorithm outputs a point $A(F) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ as a function of $S_T$. Let $\mathcal{A}_{M,T}$ denote the class of all such algorithms.

Define the minimax memory-bounded first-order oracle complexity
$$T_{L,B}(d, M, \varepsilon) \;=\; \inf\Big\{ T \in \mathbb{N} \;:\; \inf_{A \in \mathcal{A}_{M,T}} \sup_{F \in \mathcal{F}^d_{L,B}} \mathbb{E}\big[F(A(F))\big] - \min_{\|x\|\le B} F(x) \;\le\; \varepsilon \Big\}.$$

Provide a complete characterization of $T_{L,B}(d, M, \varepsilon)$ and of the set of achievable pairs $(T,M)$, preferably up to constant factors and at worst up to factors poly-logarithmic in $T$ and $M$.

The problem has been partially resolved but not fully characterized. Marsden, Sharan, Sidford, and Valiant (2022) proved the first nontrivial lower bound, showing that any first-order algorithm using at most $d^{1.25-\delta}$ bits of memory needs $\Omega(d^{1+(4/3)\delta})$ queries to minimize 1-Lipschitz convex functions over the unit ball to $1/\mathrm{poly}(d)$ accuracy. Let $B \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be the Euclidean unit ball and let $\mathcal{F}_{L,B}$ denote the class of convex, $L$-Lipschitz functions $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$. A first-order optimization algorithm interacts with an oracle that, given a query point $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, returns the pair $(f(x), g)$ for some subgradient $g \in \partial f(x)$. The algorithm is constrained so that, between consecutive oracle queries, it may store at most $M$ bits of working memory (the query point itself is recomputed from this state).

Define $T(d, M, \varepsilon)$ to be the smallest integer $T$ such that there exists a (possibly randomized) first-order algorithm using at most $M$ bits of memory between queries which, for every $f\in\mathcal{F}_{L,B}$, after at most $T$ oracle queries outputs a point $\hat x \in B$ satisfying
$$ \mathbb{E}[f(\hat x)] - \min_{x\in B} f(x) \le \varepsilon. $$

Consider the regime in which the dimension scales with the accuracy as
$$ d = \Omega(\log^c(1/\varepsilon)) \quad\text{for every constant } c>0, \qquad d = O((1/\varepsilon)^c) \quad\text{for every constant } c>0, $$
i.e. $d$ grows faster than any polylogarithm in $1/\varepsilon$ but slower than any polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$.

Question: With memory budget $M = \widetilde{O}(d)$ (in particular $M = \Theta(d \cdot \mathrm{polylog}(LB/\varepsilon))$, where $B$ is the radius bound), is it possible to achieve
$$ T(d, M, \varepsilon) = \mathrm{poly}(d)\,? $$
That is, characterize $T(d,\Theta(d\,\mathrm{polylog}(LB/\varepsilon)),1/\varepsilon)$ in this intermediate scaling regime, and determine whether a query complexity polynomial in $d$ is achievable with essentially linear memory.

The original open problem asks whether linear-memory first-order algorithms can solve convex Lipschitz optimization with poly(d) queries. Marsden, Sharan, Sidford and Valiant (2022) proved that any first-order algorithm using at most d^{1.25-δ} bits of memory must make Ω̃(d^{1+(4/3)δ}) queries to achieve 1/poly(d) accuracy, showing that linear-memory algorithms cannot match the Õ(d) cutting-plane query complexity and giving the first super-linear lower bound. Subsequent works (Blanchard–Zhang–Jaillet 2023; Chen–Peng 2023) gave further memory-query tradeoffs and recursive cutting-plane upper bounds. However, the precise question of whether T(d, Õ(d), ε) = poly(d) in the stated intermediate regime is not fully resolved: known lower bounds rule out this for low accuracy regimes but a tight characterization across the full intermediate scaling remains open.

Let M be a machine-learning model intended to be deployed in a safety-critical operational environment. Model the operational environment as a measurable space (X, Σ) of inputs together with a family E = {E_i} of mutually exclusive operating conditions (each E_i ⊆ X measurable, with associated conditional input distribution P_i on (X, Σ)) representing the situations in which M will be used. Suppose that for each operating condition E_i a required performance specification R_i is given (for instance, in a classification setting, a required confusion matrix C_i = (c^{(i)}_{jk}) whose entries lower-bound the conditional probabilities P_i(M predicts class k | true class j)).

Develop a methodology that, given E and {R_i}, deductively produces a set of test-data requirements with the following properties:

1. (Distributional reflection) The methodology specifies a target test-data distribution Q on (X, Σ) (or a family of conditional test distributions Q_i) such that Q faithfully reflects the operating conditions encoded by E and {P_i}, in a precisely defined sense (e.g., Q = Σ_i w_i P_i for explicit weights w_i tied to operational exposure, or Q_i ≈ P_i in a chosen statistical divergence with a stated tolerance).

2. (Explicit property description) The methodology yields an explicit, machine-checkable description of the properties that test data must satisfy, specifying for each E_i the qualitative features, attribute coverage, and quantitative coverage criteria that test samples drawn for E_i must fulfill.

3. (Condition–performance association) The methodology produces a formal association ϕ: E_i ↦ R_i linking each assumed operating condition to its required performance specification, together with a statistical acceptance procedure that, on test data conforming to (1) and (2), decides whether M satisfies R_i for every i with prescribed confidence.

Question: Construct such a methodology — i.e., give a formal framework (language, semantics, and procedures) for describing assumed operational environments of machine-learning models, for specifying required-performance functions on those environments (such as condition-specific confusion matrices), and for deriving from these specifications test-data distributional and property requirements that admit sound statistical verification — or prove that no single framework can simultaneously achieve (1), (2), and (3) under stated minimal assumptions.

For an algorithm A interacting with such an oracle, let M(A) denote the number of bits of memory it may retain between consecutive oracle calls, and let T(d, M, ε) denote the minimum number of oracle queries needed by any (possibly randomized) algorithm with memory budget M to output, with constant probability, a point x̂ ∈ [-1,1]^d satisfying f(x̂) − min f ≤ ε.

   T(d, M, ε) = Õ(d · polylog(1/ε))
while using only M = O(d^{2−δ}) bits of memory between oracle calls? Equivalently, is strictly subquadratic memory compatible with near-optimal (Õ(d)) query complexity for convex Lipschitz optimization in this regime?

Consider the problem of minimizing a convex 1-Lipschitz function f: B → ℝ on the unit ball B ⊂ ℝ^d (with respect to the Euclidean norm), to additive accuracy ε, using a first-order oracle that on query x ∈ B returns the pair (f(x), g) with g a subgradient of f at x. Two known regimes for (T, M) are:
(i) Gradient descent, achieving T = O(1/ε²) queries with M = O(d · log(LB/ε)) bits of memory (where L = 1 is the Lipschitz constant and B = 1 is the radius of the domain, kept symbolic to indicate scaling).
(ii) Center-of-mass / cutting-plane methods, achieving T = O(d · log(1/ε)) queries with M = O(d² · log²(LB/ε)) bits of memory.

Question: Does there exist any algorithm whose query-memory pair (T, M) lies polynomially strictly between these two extremes — that is, with T = poly(d, 1/ε) strictly larger (in the relevant scaling) than O(d log(1/ε)) and strictly smaller than O(1/ε²), and M correspondingly strictly between O(d log(LB/ε)) and O(d² log²(LB/ε)) — or, conversely, is every such intermediate tradeoff ruled out by an unconditional lower bound?

A signed graph is a pair $\Gamma=(G,\sigma)$, where $G=(V,E)$ is a simple graph and $\sigma:E\to\{+1,-1\}$ is a sign function on its edges. The adjacency matrix $A(\Gamma)$ is the $|V|\times|V|$ matrix whose $(u,v)$-entry equals $\sigma(uv)$ if $uv\in E$ and $0$ otherwise; the spectrum of $\Gamma$ is the multiset of eigenvalues of $A(\Gamma)$. The negation of $\Gamma$ is $-\Gamma=(G,-\sigma)$. A switching at a vertex set $U\subseteq V$ replaces $\sigma(uv)$ by $-\sigma(uv)$ for every edge $uv$ with exactly one endpoint in $U$; two signed graphs on the same underlying graph are switching isomorphic if one can be obtained from the other by a vertex permutation followed by a switching. The signed graph $\Gamma$ is called sign-symmetric if $\Gamma$ is switching isomorphic to $-\Gamma$. (Sign-symmetry implies that the spectrum of $\Gamma$ is symmetric with respect to the origin.)

Question: Does there exist a connected signed graph $\Gamma=(G,\sigma)$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G$ is not a complete graph,
\item the spectrum of $\Gamma$ is symmetric with respect to the origin, and
\item $\Gamma$ is not sign-symmetric (equivalently, $\Gamma$ is not switching isomorphic to $-\Gamma$)?
\end{enumerate}

This is a well-known open question, often attributed to de Caen. Connected graphs with four or five distinct adjacency eigenvalues can have arbitrarily many distinct vertex degrees (constructions by van Dam and collaborators), but no example is known of a graph with three distinct eigenvalues having more than three distinct degrees, and the question remains unresolved in recent surveys and research articles on graphs with three distinct eigenvalues.

Let $K_1, K_2, K_3$ be three pairwise disjoint closed subsets of the extended complex plane $\widehat{\mathbb{C}} = \mathbb{C} \cup \{\infty\}$, and let $C_1, C_2, C_3$ be three complex constants. Define the function $f$ on $K := K_1 \cup K_2 \cup K_3$ by $f(z) = C_i$ for $z \in K_i$, $i = 1, 2, 3$. For each positive integer $n$, let $R_n$ denote the class of rational functions of degree at most $n$, and define the best uniform rational approximation error
$$\rho_n(f) = \inf_{g \in R_n} \, \max_{z \in K} |f(z) - g(z)|.$$
Provide a geometric characterization (in terms of the configuration of the sets $K_1, K_2, K_3$, e.g.\ in terms of capacities, condenser problems, or potential-theoretic quantities) of the limit
$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \rho_n(f)^{1/n}.$$
(The case of two sets was settled by Gonchar, who showed that the analogous limit equals $e^{-1/\mathrm{cap}(K_1,K_2)}$, where $\mathrm{cap}(K_1,K_2)$ is the capacity of the condenser with plates $K_1$ and $K_2$.)

Let $f : \mathcal{X} 	o \mathcal{Y}$ be a classifier on an input space $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ equipped with a norm $\|\cdot\|$, and let $D = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathcal{X} 	imes \mathcal{Y}$ be a finite labelled test set on which $f$ is correct, i.e.\ $f(x_i) = y_i$ for all $i$. For each test point $x_i$ define the pointwise robustness radius
$$ r_i(f) \;=\; \inf igl\{\, \|\delta\| \;:\; \delta \in \mathbb{R}^d,\ x_i + \delta \in \mathcal{X},\ f(x_i + \delta) 
eq y_i \, igr\}, $$
with $r_i(f) = +\infty$ if no such $\delta$ exists. An \emph{adversarial robustness measure} is any functional $R(f, D)$ aggregating the radii $\{r_i(f)\}_{i=1}^n$ (for instance the minimum, an empirical quantile, or the mean) intended to quantify the resistance of $f$ to small input perturbations beyond what ordinary test accuracy on $D$ can reveal.

The problem has two parts.

(a) Design and justify a measurement procedure that, given oracle access to $f$ and the test set $D$, produces an estimate $\widehat{R}(f, D)$ of the adversarial robustness of $f$ which (i) provides provable guarantees relating $\widehat{R}$ to the true radii $r_i(f)$, and (ii) is computationally tractable for high-dimensional models such as deep neural networks where exact computation of $r_i(f)$ is intractable.

(b) For a general quality characteristic $Q$ of a learned model (for example fairness, calibration, stability under distribution shift, monotonicity, or interpretability), formulate an analogous measurement framework: specify a pointwise quantity $q_i(f)$ associated with each test instance, an aggregation $R_Q(f, D)$, and a tractable estimation procedure together with guarantees relating the estimate to $R_Q(f, D)$, such that $R_Q$ captures aspects of $Q$ that cannot be assessed from ordinary test accuracy on $D$ alone.

Develop a framework for automatic coverage verification of machine-learning models using formal verification technology, suitable for use in quality assurance of safety-critical machine-learning systems. Concretely:

1. Define a rigorous notion of "coverage" for a trained machine-learning model f : X → Y (for example, a neural network classifier or regressor), analogous to code or structural coverage criteria in classical software testing. The coverage notion should refer to measurable structural or behavioral aspects of f, such as activation patterns of internal units, partitions of the input domain X induced by decision regions, or specification-based criteria over a set Φ of logical properties expressed in a formal language (e.g., linear real arithmetic over inputs and outputs).

2. Provide an algorithmic procedure that, given f and a coverage criterion C together with a (possibly infinite) input domain X with a specified distribution or constraint set, automatically decides or quantifies the extent to which f satisfies C, using sound formal verification techniques (e.g., SMT solving, abstract interpretation, mixed-integer linear programming, or interval bound propagation), as opposed to statistical testing on finite samples.

3. Prove soundness and, where possible, completeness of the procedure, and analyze its computational complexity in terms of the size of f (number of parameters, layers, or activations) and the complexity of the specification class Φ.

4. Demonstrate how the resulting coverage verification fits into a quality assurance process for safety-critical ML systems, in particular how the produced coverage guarantees can be combined with property-based formal verification (e.g., robustness, monotonicity, or safety envelopes) to yield assurance claims about the deployed model.

The problem is to design such a coverage criterion, the corresponding verification algorithm, and the supporting theoretical guarantees, or to establish theoretical limits (hardness or undecidability) showing why such a framework cannot exist in full generality.

This is a broad research/engineering challenge rather than a single mathematical conjecture. The conjecture remains open in full generality. Partial results are known: it has been proved that there is a constant K such that every connected graph with smallest eigenvalue at least -3 and minimum degree at least K is 2-integrable, and integrability has been established for various subclasses (e.g., strongly regular and sesqui-regular graphs with smallest eigenvalue at least -3 under valency bounds). Background and definitions.

(a) A nearly Kähler 6-manifold is a Riemannian 6-manifold $(N,g,J)$ with an almost complex structure $J$ compatible with $g$ such that $(\nabla_X J)X = 0$ for all vector fields $X$, where $\nabla$ is the Levi–Civita connection. The known simply connected homogeneous nearly Kähler 6-manifolds are $S^6 = G_2/\mathrm{SU}(3)$, $\mathbb{CP}^3 = \mathrm{Sp}(2)/(\mathrm{Sp}(1)\cdot \mathrm{U}(1))$, $S^3\times S^3 = (\mathrm{SU}(2)^3)/\mathrm{SU}(2)$, and the flag manifold $F_{1,2} = \mathrm{SU}(3)/T^2$.

(b) A nearly Kähler instanton (or pseudo-Hermitian–Yang–Mills connection) on a nearly Kähler 6-manifold $(N,\omega)$ is a connection $A$ on a principal $G$-bundle over $N$ whose curvature $F_A$ satisfies $F_A \wedge \omega^2 = 0$ and $F_A \lrcorner \, \Omega = 0$, where $\Omega$ is the $(3,0)$-form defining the nearly Kähler structure.

(c) An asymptotically conical (AC) $G_2$-manifold is a complete 7-manifold $(M,\varphi)$ with torsion-free $G_2$-structure $\varphi$ that is asymptotic, outside a compact set, to the Riemannian cone $C(N) = (0,\infty)\times N$ over a nearly Kähler 6-manifold $(N,\omega,\Omega)$, with cone metric $g_C = dr^2 + r^2 g_N$ and $G_2$-form $\varphi_C = r^2\,dr\wedge \omega + r^3\,\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$.

(d) A $G_2$-instanton on $(M,\varphi)$ is a connection $A$ on a principal $G$-bundle over $M$ whose curvature satisfies $F_A \wedge \psi = 0$, where $\psi = *\varphi$. For an AC $G_2$-manifold, suitable $G_2$-instantons admit a limit at infinity that is a nearly Kähler instanton on the asymptotic link $N$.

Problem. For each of the nearly Kähler 6-manifolds $S^6$, $\mathbb{CP}^3$, $S^3\times S^3$ (and finite quotients thereof), and $F_{1,2}$:

(1) Construct explicit examples of nearly Kähler instantons (i.e., pseudo-Hermitian–Yang–Mills connections) on nontrivial principal bundles over $N$, beyond the canonical connection.

(2) For each such nearly Kähler instanton $A_\infty$ on $N$, determine whether there exists an AC $G_2$-manifold $(M,\varphi)$ with asymptotic link $N$ and a $G_2$-instanton $A$ on $M$ whose limit at infinity equals $A_\infty$.

(3) When such $G_2$-instantons exist, determine the cardinality (or moduli) of the set of $G_2$-instantons on AC $G_2$-manifolds asymptotic to $C(N)$ that have $A_\infty$ as their prescribed limit at infinity.

Examples of nearly Kähler instantons on the homogeneous nearly Kähler 6-manifolds remain scarce; deformation theory has been developed (e.g., Charbonneau–Harland) showing canonical connections are rigid as $H$-instantons but have rich deformations as $\mathrm{SU}(3)$-instantons. representations.normalized:
A signed graph is a pair $\Sigma = (G, \sigma)$ consisting of a simple graph $G = (V, E)$ together with a sign function $\sigma: E \to \{+1, -1\}$. Its adjacency matrix $A(\Sigma)$ is the symmetric $|V| \times |V|$ matrix whose $(u,v)$-entry equals $\sigma(uv)$ if $uv \in E$ and $0$ otherwise; the eigenvalues of $\Sigma$ are the eigenvalues of $A(\Sigma)$, and the smallest eigenvalue is denoted $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)$. Two signed graphs are switching equivalent if one is obtained from the other by selecting a vertex subset $U \subseteq V$ and negating the signs of all edges with exactly one endpoint in $U$; switching equivalence preserves the spectrum.

Call a signed graph $\Sigma$ on vertex set $V$ maximal with smallest eigenvalue at least $-3$ if $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma) \ge -3$ and no signed graph $\Sigma'$ on the same vertex set $V$ that strictly contains $\Sigma$ as a signed subgraph (i.e., $E(\Sigma) \subsetneq E(\Sigma')$ and the signs of $\Sigma$ are inherited) satisfies $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma') \ge -3$.

Problem: Construct, up to switching equivalence and isomorphism, all maximal signed graphs whose smallest adjacency eigenvalue is at least $-3$.

representations.normalized:
A signed graph is a pair $(G,\sigma)$ where $G=(V,E)$ is a finite simple graph and $\sigma:E\to\{+1,-1\}$ is a sign function on the edges. The adjacency matrix $A(G,\sigma)$ is the $V\times V$ matrix whose $(u,v)$-entry is $\sigma(uv)$ if $uv\in E$ and $0$ otherwise; its smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\min}(G,\sigma)$ is a basic spectral invariant.

For unsigned graphs, a Hoffman graph is a triple $\mathfrak h=(H,\mu)$ where $H$ is an undirected graph with vertex set partitioned into a set of "slim" vertices $V_s(\mathfrak h)$ and a set of "fat" vertices $V_f(\mathfrak h)$, such that every fat vertex is adjacent only to slim vertices and no two fat vertices share a slim neighbour. The special matrix of $\mathfrak h$ is $A(\mathfrak h)=A_s-N N^{\top}$, where $A_s$ is the adjacency matrix of the slim subgraph and $N$ is the slim–fat incidence matrix; the smallest eigenvalue of $\mathfrak h$ is $\lambda_{\min}(\mathfrak h):=\lambda_{\min}(A(\mathfrak h))$. One says that an (unsigned) graph $G$ is represented by a family $\mathcal F$ of Hoffman graphs if $G$ admits an "$\mathcal F$-decomposition"; this machinery yields structural classifications and lower bounds for $\lambda_{\min}(G)$, in particular underlying the description of graphs with smallest eigenvalue $\geq -1-\sqrt 2$.

Problem. Develop an analogous theory of signed Hoffman graphs for signed graphs. Concretely, define a notion of a signed Hoffman graph (with slim and fat parts and a sign function on its slim–slim and possibly slim–fat edges), define an associated special matrix and smallest eigenvalue, define a notion of $\mathcal F$-decomposition (or representation) of a signed graph by a family of signed Hoffman graphs, and establish the corresponding structure and reduction theorems. The theory should specialise to the classical Hoffman-graph theory when all signs are $+1$, and should be powerful enough to yield structural classifications and sharp lower bounds for $\lambda_{\min}(G,\sigma)$ for natural classes of signed graphs (for example, those with $\lambda_{\min}(G,\sigma)\geq -1-\sqrt 2$ or $\geq -2$).

Substantial progress has been made toward a Hoffman-graph theory for signed graphs. Greaves classified edge-signed graphs with smallest eigenvalue greater than -2; Abiad–Greaves–Koolen and others introduced signed analogues of line graphs; and a 2026 preprint develops a structure theory for signed graphs with fixed smallest eigenvalue (e.g. greater than -1-sqrt(2)). A signed graph is a pair (Γ, σ) consisting of a simple connected unsigned graph Γ = (V, E) together with a signature σ : E → {+1, −1}. The adjacency matrix A(Γ, σ) is the symmetric |V| × |V| matrix whose (u, v)-entry equals σ(uv) if uv ∈ E and 0 otherwise. The spectral radius ρ(Γ, σ) is the largest absolute value among the eigenvalues of A(Γ, σ).

Two signatures σ and σ' on Γ are switching-equivalent if there exists a function θ : V → {+1, −1} such that σ'(uv) = θ(u) σ(uv) θ(v) for every edge uv; switching-equivalent signatures yield similar adjacency matrices and hence the same spectrum.

Problem. Let Γ be an arbitrary simple connected unsigned graph. Characterize, up to switching equivalence, the signature(s) σ̄ on Γ that minimize the spectral radius, i.e. that satisfy
   ρ(Γ, σ̄) ≤ ρ(Γ, σ)
for every signature σ of Γ. In particular, give a structural or combinatorial description of such minimizing signatures for general Γ.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected $d$-regular graph on $n$ vertices, with $d\ge 2$. A signature of $G$ is a function $\sigma:E\to\{+1,-1\}$. The signed adjacency matrix $A_\sigma$ is the $n\times n$ symmetric matrix whose $(u,v)$-entry equals $\sigma(\{u,v\})$ if $\{u,v\}\in E$ and $0$ otherwise. Its spectral radius is $\rho(A_\sigma)=\max_i |\lambda_i(A_\sigma)|$.

Prove or disprove: for every connected $d$-regular graph $G$, there exists a signature $\sigma:E\to\{+1,-1\}$ such that
$$\rho(A_\sigma)\;\le\; 2\sqrt{d-1}.$$

The Bilu–Linial conjecture is still open in full generality. Bilu and Linial (2006) proved a weaker bound of order $\sqrt{d\log^3 d}$. Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava (2015) established the bipartite case via interlacing families, yielding bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree, but the non-bipartite case remains unresolved.

Let $(C,g_C,\omega,\Omega)$ be a Calabi–Yau cone of complex dimension $3$, i.e. $C=(0,\infty)\times\Gamma$ with cone metric $g_C=dr^2+r^2 g_\Gamma$, Kähler form $\omega$, and holomorphic volume form $\Omega$ satisfying the Calabi–Yau conditions $d\omega=0$, $d\Omega=0$, and $\omega^3/6=(i/8)\Omega\wedge\bar\Omega$. A Calabi–Yau monopole on $C$ (with structure group a compact Lie group $G$) is a pair $(a,\Phi)$, where $a$ is a connection on a principal $G$-bundle $P\to C$ and $\Phi$ is a section of the adjoint bundle $\mathrm{ad}(P)$, satisfying
$$F_a\wedge\omega^2=0,\qquad F_a\wedge\Omega=0,\qquad F_a\wedge\omega^2 \;=\; *\,d_a\Phi$$
(equivalently, $F_a$ is of type $(1,1)$ and primitive, and $d_a\Phi=*(F_a\wedge\omega^2/2)$, so that $(a,\Phi)$ is the dimensional reduction of a $G_2$-instanton on $\mathbb{R}\times C$ with cylindrical $G_2$-structure built from $(\omega,\Omega)$).

Analogously, define a Calabi–Yau monopole on an asymptotically conical Calabi–Yau $3$-fold $(Y,g,\omega,\Omega)$ with asymptotic cone $C$ as a pair $(a,\Phi)$ on a $G$-bundle over $Y$ satisfying the same equations, with $|F_a|$ and $|\nabla\Phi|$ decaying suitably at infinity (for instance with quadratically decaying curvature) and $\Phi$ tending to a limit Higgs field along the radial direction.

Problem. Develop a general existence theory for Calabi–Yau monopoles on Calabi–Yau cones $C$ of complex dimension $3$ and on asymptotically conical Calabi–Yau $3$-folds $Y$. In particular, construct new families of nontrivial Calabi–Yau monopoles (beyond the SU(2)$\times$SU(2)-invariant examples on the Stenzel metric on $T^*S^3$, on the small resolution of the conifold, and on the canonical bundle of $\mathbb{CP}^1\times\mathbb{CP}^1$), and identify those that arise as bubbling/rescaled limits of $G_2$-instantons on asymptotically locally conical (ALC) $G_2$-manifolds.
