Let Γ = (V, E) be a finite simple connected graph. A signature of Γ is a function σ : E → {+1, −1}; the signed adjacency matrix Aσ is the symmetric {0, +1, −1}-matrix indexed by V whose (u,v)-entry equals σ(uv) if uv ∈ E and 0 otherwise. Let ρ(Γ, σ) denote the spectral radius of Aσ (the largest absolute value of its eigenvalues). A symmetric weighing matrix of weight k and order n is a symmetric n×n matrix W with entries in {0, +1, −1} satisfying W W^T = k I_n.

It is known that for every signature σ of Γ,
   ρ(Γ, σ) ≥ √(d̄),
where d̄ is the average degree of Γ, with equality if and only if Γ is k-regular (so d̄ = k) and Aσ is a symmetric weighing matrix of weight k.

Question: Determine all 5-regular graphs Γ that admit a signature σ such that Aσ is a symmetric weighing matrix of weight 5 (equivalently, ρ(Γ, σ) = √5). In particular, do there exist 5-regular graphs with this property other than those obtainable from the standard known constructions (e.g. derived from symmetric conference-type or Hadamard-type weighing matrices)?

Let (M, φ, g) be a complete non-compact 7-manifold with a torsion-free G2-structure φ which is asymptotically locally conical (ALC): outside a compact set, M fibers as a circle bundle over an asymptotically conical (AC) Calabi-Yau 3-fold (X, ω, Ω) with cone (C(Σ), ω_C, Ω_C) over a Sasaki-Einstein 5-manifold Σ, and the G2-metric g asymptotes to a circle-invariant G2-metric whose collapse along the circle fibers recovers the AC Calabi-Yau metric on X. A G2-instanton on M is a connection A on a principal G-bundle P → M (G a compact Lie group) whose curvature F_A satisfies F_A ∧ ψ = 0, where ψ = *φ. A Calabi-Yau monopole on an AC Calabi-Yau 3-fold (X, ω, Ω) is a pair (B, Φ), where B is a connection on a G-bundle Q → X and Φ ∈ Ω^0(X, ad Q), satisfying the Bogomolny-type equations F_B ∧ ω^2 = 0 and F_B ∧ Ω = d_B Φ ∧ ½ ω^2 (equivalently, F_B ∧ ω^2 = *d_B Φ).

Solve the following:

(a) Develop the deformation theory of G2-instantons A on the ALC G2-manifold M with prescribed asymptotic behaviour at the ALC end: identify the linearized operator, compute its index in suitable weighted Sobolev spaces, describe the obstruction space, and give conditions under which the moduli space M_{G_2}^{ALC}(M) is smooth of the predicted dimension.

(b) Develop in parallel the deformation theory of Calabi-Yau monopoles (B, Φ) on the AC Calabi-Yau 3-fold (X, ω, Ω) with prescribed conical asymptotics: identify the linearized monopole operator, compute its index, describe the obstructions, and give a transversality criterion that makes the monopole moduli space M_{CY-mon}(X) a smooth manifold of the predicted dimension.

(c) Define the natural asymptotic projection π: M_{G_2}^{ALC}(M) → M_{CY-mon}(X) sending a G2-instanton on M to its limiting Calabi-Yau monopole on the asymptotic AC Calabi-Yau cone X. Determine the image of π: characterize, in terms of cohomological/topological invariants and analytic conditions on (B, Φ), exactly which Calabi-Yau monopoles on X arise as asymptotic limits of G2-instantons on M.

Background and definitions. A signed graph is a pair $\Gamma=(G,\sigma)$ where $G=(V,E)$ is a finite simple graph and $\sigma:E\to\{+1,-1\}$ is a signature. The (signed) adjacency matrix $A_\sigma$ of $\Gamma$ has $(A_\sigma)_{uv}=\sigma(uv)$ if $uv\in E$ and $0$ otherwise. The spectral radius of $\Gamma$ is $\rho(\Gamma)=\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }A_\sigma\}$. The sign of a cycle $C$ in $\Gamma$ is $\sigma(C)=\prod_{e\in E(C)}\sigma(e)\in\{+1,-1\}$; the cycle is called positive (resp. negative) accordingly. Two signatures $\sigma,\sigma'$ on $G$ are switching-equivalent if there exists $\theta:V\to\{+1,-1\}$ such that $\sigma'(uv)=\theta(u)\sigma(uv)\theta(v)$ for every edge $uv$; switching-equivalent signatures yield similar adjacency matrices and hence the same spectrum.

Setup. Fix an integer $k\ge 1$ and an odd integer $\ell\ge 3$. Let $G$ be the graph obtained from $2k$ vertex-disjoint cycles of common length $\ell$ by identifying one vertex of each cycle to a single common vertex (so $G$ is a bouquet of $2k$ odd cycles of equal length sharing a single vertex). On $G$ consider the signature $\sigma^\star$ in which exactly $k$ of the $2k$ cycles are positive and the remaining $k$ are negative (this signature, up to switching equivalence, depends only on which cycles are positive and which are negative, and any two such signatures with the same partition of cycles into $k$ positive and $k$ negative are switching-equivalent). It is known that the resulting signed graph $\Gamma^\star=(G,\sigma^\star)$ satisfies $\rho(\Gamma^\star)<2\sqrt{4k-1}$.

Question. Among all signatures $\sigma$ on the underlying graph $G$, does $\sigma^\star$ achieve the minimum value of the spectral radius $\rho((G,\sigma))$? Equivalently, prove or disprove that $\rho((G,\sigma))\ge\rho(\Gamma^\star)$ for every signature $\sigma$ of $G$.

Let $\{(M_s, g_s, \varphi_s)\}_{s>0}$ denote the one-parameter family of complete asymptotically locally conical (ALC) $G_2$-holonomy manifolds constructed by Bogoyavlenskaya, where each $M_s$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^4 \times S^3$, the metric $g_s$ has cohomogeneity one under an $SU(2)^2$-action, and the parameter $s>0$ controls the asymptotic radius of the circle fiber at infinity (so that the link at infinity is a circle bundle over a Calabi-Yau cone — the cone over $S^2 \times S^3$ — with circle of length proportional to $s$). A $G_2$-instanton on a principal $G$-bundle $P \to (M, \varphi)$ is a connection $A$ whose curvature $F_A$ satisfies $F_A \wedge \psi = 0$, where $\psi = *_g \varphi$.

Suppose $\{A_s\}_{s>0}$ is a smooth family of $SU(2)^2$-invariant $G_2$-instantons, one on each $(M_s, \varphi_s)$, on a fixed underlying bundle (e.g.\ the natural $SU(2)$-bundle).

(a) (Large-circle limit.) As $s \to \infty$, does $(M_s, g_s)$ converge (in the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff / smooth Cheeger–Gromov sense) to the Bryant–Salamon asymptotically conical $G_2$-metric on $\mathbb{R}^4 \times S^3$, and do the connections $A_s$ converge to a $G_2$-instanton for the Bryant–Salamon metric? Identify the limit instanton explicitly.

(b) (Small-circle / collapsing limit.) As $s \to 0$, the family $(M_s, g_s)$ collapses with bounded curvature to the asymptotically conical Calabi–Yau metric on the deformed conifold $T^*S^3$. Determine the precise relation between the collapsing family $A_s$ and Calabi–Yau monopoles on the deformed conifold (i.e.\ pairs $(B, \Phi)$ on a bundle over $T^*S^3$ where $B$ is a connection, $\Phi$ a Higgs field, satisfying $F_B \wedge \omega^2 = 0$ and $F_B = *(d_B \Phi \wedge \omega)$ with respect to the Calabi–Yau structure $(\omega, \Omega)$). In particular, show that the dimensional reduction along the collapsing $S^1$ produces such a Calabi–Yau monopole, and characterize which monopoles arise.

A signed graph is a pair Γ = (G, σ), where G = (V, E) is a simple finite undirected graph and σ : E → {+1, −1} is a signature on its edges. The adjacency matrix A(Γ) is the symmetric matrix with entries A(Γ)_{uv} = σ(uv) if uv ∈ E and 0 otherwise; the spectrum of Γ is the multiset of eigenvalues of A(Γ). Two signed graphs on the same vertex set are switching equivalent if one is obtained from the other by, for some U ⊆ V, negating the signs of all edges with exactly one endpoint in U; switching equivalent signed graphs are cospectral.

For a signed graph Γ = (G, σ) on vertex set V, let Ḡ = (V, Ē) denote the usual graph-theoretic complement of G (so Ē consists of all unordered pairs of distinct vertices of V that are non-adjacent in G). The signed union Γ ∪ Γ̄ is the signed graph on V whose underlying graph is the complete graph K_{|V|} and whose signature restricts to σ on E(G) and to σ̄ on Ē.

Problem. Define a signature σ̄ : Ē → {+1, −1} on the complement Ḡ, depending only on (G, σ), so that the resulting "complement signed graph" Γ̄ = (Ḡ, σ̄) and the associated signed complete graph Γ ∪ Γ̄ exhibit good spectral behavior — for instance, so that Γ ∪ Γ̄ is well-defined up to switching equivalence and the spectra of Γ and Γ̄ are related to the spectrum of Γ ∪ Γ̄ in a manner analogous to the Laplacian-spectrum relation A(G) + A(Ḡ) = J − I that holds for unsigned graphs.

A set of lines through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is called equiangular with common angle $\arccos(\alpha)$ (where $0<\alpha<1$) if the angle between any two distinct lines in the set equals $\arccos(\alpha)$. For each dimension $d\ge 1$ and each $\alpha\in(0,1)$, let $N_\alpha(d)$ denote the maximum cardinality of such a set of equiangular lines in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with common angle $\arccos(\alpha)$.

Prove or disprove the following two statements about the case $\alpha=1/5$:
1. For every integer $d$ with $23 \le d \le 185$, one has $N_{1/5}(d) = 276$.
2. For every integer $d \ge 185$, one has $N_{1/5}(d) = \lfloor 3(d-1)/2 \rfloor$.

Consider the periodic Cauchy problem for the Korteweg–de Vries equation
  u_t + u u_x + u_{xxx} = 0,    x ∈ T = R/2πZ, t ∈ R,
  u(x,0) = φ(x),
where φ ∈ H^s(T) and H^s(T) denotes the L^2-based Sobolev space of order s on the circle. Say that the problem is well-posed in H^s(T) if for every φ ∈ H^s(T) there exists a unique distributional solution u ∈ C(R; H^s(T)) and the data-to-solution map φ ↦ u is continuous from H^s(T) to C([−T,T]; H^s(T)) for every T > 0.

It is known that the problem is well-posed in H^s(T) for every s ≥ −1. Determine whether the problem is well-posed in H^s(T) for some (equivalently, any) s < −1.

Let $V = (V^+, V^-)$ be a Jordan pair, that is, a pair of modules over a commutative unital ring equipped with trilinear "quadratic" products $Q_\sigma : V^\sigma \times V^{-\sigma} \times V^\sigma \to V^\sigma$ (for $\sigma = \pm$) satisfying the standard Jordan pair identities. Associated with $V$ are the one-parameter exponential subgroups $\exp_\sigma(x)$, $x \in V^\sigma$, acting on $V$, and the projective elementary group is defined as
$$\mathrm{PE}(V) := \langle \exp_+(x), \exp_-(y) : x \in V^+,\ y \in V^- \rangle,$$
viewed as a subgroup of the automorphism group of $V$ (modulo the appropriate centre, when relevant).

Problem: For an arbitrary Jordan pair $V$, describe the complete normal subgroup structure of $\mathrm{PE}(V)$; that is, classify all normal subgroups of $\mathrm{PE}(V)$.

The simplicity of $\mathrm{PE}(V)$ has been established for large classes of Jordan pairs (in particular, those graded by a 3-graded root system, with three small exceptions over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and $\mathbb{F}_3$), via Iwasawa's criterion applied to a Steinberg-type cover. Let $\Gamma$ be a simple undirected graph on $n$ vertices with adjacency matrix $A(\Gamma)$. The Seidel matrix of $\Gamma$ is the symmetric $n\times n$ matrix
$$S(\Gamma) = J_n - I_n - 2A(\Gamma),$$
where $J_n$ is the all-ones matrix and $I_n$ is the identity matrix. Equivalently, $S(\Gamma)$ has $0$ on the diagonal, $-1$ in entry $(i,j)$ when $i\sim j$ in $\Gamma$, and $+1$ when $i\neq j$ and $i\not\sim j$. Two graphs on the same vertex set are called Seidel-switching equivalent if their Seidel matrices are conjugate by a diagonal $\pm 1$ matrix; the Seidel spectrum is an invariant of the switching class.

Provide a combinatorial interpretation (in terms of the structure of the graph, its switching class, or associated combinatorial/geometric objects such as equiangular line systems, two-graphs, designs, or regular structures) characterizing exactly those Seidel matrices $S(\Gamma)$ that have exactly three distinct eigenvalues.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No general combinatorial characterization is known. Partial progress has been made: Seidel matrices with three distinct eigenvalues are closely connected to systems of equiangular lines and to regular two-graphs, and complete enumerations have been carried out for small orders (n ≤ 23). Recent work (e.g., on determinants of Seidel matrices, regular graphs in the switching class, and split graphs with few Laplacian eigenvalues) addresses related subcases, but a full combinatorial interpretation remains open.

Let $S$ be a symmetric $n\times n$ matrix with zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries in $\{-1,+1\}$; such a matrix is called a Seidel matrix. To every simple graph $\Gamma$ on $n$ vertices one associates the Seidel matrix $S(\Gamma)$ whose $(i,j)$-entry (for $i\neq j$) equals $-1$ if $i$ and $j$ are adjacent in $\Gamma$ and $+1$ otherwise. Two graphs $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ on the same vertex set are called Seidel-switching equivalent if there exists a subset $U$ of the vertex set such that $\Gamma'$ is obtained from $\Gamma$ by complementing all edges between $U$ and its complement (and leaving all other adjacencies unchanged). The switching class of $\Gamma$ is the equivalence class under this relation; equivalently, it corresponds to the equivalence class of $S(\Gamma)$ under conjugation by signed diagonal $\pm 1$ matrices.

Question: Does there exist an integer $n \ge 14$ and a Seidel matrix $S$ of order $n$ such that $S$ has exactly three distinct eigenvalues and the switching class of (any graph corresponding to) $S$ contains no regular graph?

Question: Does there exist an integer $n \ge 14$ and a Seidel matrix $S$ of order $n$ such that $S$ has exactly three distinct eigenvalues and the switching class of (any graph corresponding to) $S$ contains no regular graph?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Known partial results: every Seidel matrix of odd order with precisely three distinct eigenvalues contains a regular (in fact strongly regular) graph in its switching class, and the same holds for all such matrices of order at most 12. Some sources indicate that examples (even an infinite family) of Seidel matrices with exactly three distinct eigenvalues whose switching class contains no regular graph have been pointed out in subsequent work (e.g. enumeration/classification work by Szöllősi and Östergård up to order 23, with a candidate at order 18), but the search did not yield a definitive, citable confirmation that the existence question for orders $\ge 14$ has been fully resolved. The status is therefore reported as unknown.

Setup. A Jordan division algebra is a unital Jordan algebra $J$ in which every nonzero element is invertible. Associated to such a $J$ one has a rank-one Steinberg group $\mathrm{St}(J)$, defined by generators and relations as follows. Take two copies $\{x_+(a) : a \in J\}$ and $\{x_-(b) : b \in J\}$ of the additive group $(J,+)$, and impose:
(i) $x_\sigma(a)x_\sigma(a') = x_\sigma(a+a')$ for $\sigma \in \{+,-\}$ and $a,a' \in J$;
(ii) for every invertible $a \in J$, the element $w(a) := x_-(-a^{-1})\, x_+(a)\, x_-(-a^{-1})$ satisfies the Weyl-type relation $w(a)\, x_+(b)\, w(a)^{-1} = x_-(-U_{a^{-1}}\, b)$ for all $b \in J$, where $U$ denotes the quadratic representation of $J$.

A group $G$ is called centrally closed if its universal central extension is $G$ itself, equivalently if the Schur multiplier $H_2(G,\mathbb{Z})$ vanishes and $G$ is perfect (so that the identity map $G\to G$ is a universal central extension).

Question. Let $J$ be a Jordan division algebra. Is $\mathrm{St}(J)$ centrally closed in every case, with the only possible exceptions being $J = \mathbb{F}_q$ (the field with $q$ elements regarded as a Jordan algebra) for $q \in \{2,3,4,9\}$?

Let $B^n = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : |x| \le 1\}$ denote the closed Euclidean unit ball, with boundary $\partial B^n = S^{n-1}$. Let $\Sigma$ be a smooth $k$-dimensional manifold with boundary $\partial\Sigma$, and let $\phi : \Sigma \to B^n$ be a smooth immersion (respectively, embedding) such that $\phi(\partial\Sigma) \subset \partial B^n$ and $\phi(\mathrm{int}\,\Sigma) \subset \mathrm{int}\,B^n$. Call $\phi$ an immersed (resp. embedded) free boundary minimal submanifold if:
(i) $\phi(\Sigma)$ is a minimal submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (its mean curvature vector vanishes identically); and
(ii) $\phi(\Sigma)$ meets $\partial B^n$ orthogonally along $\phi(\partial\Sigma)$, i.e., at each boundary point the position vector (the outward unit normal to $\partial B^n$) lies in the tangent space of $\phi(\Sigma)$.

Determine all topological restrictions (if any) that the underlying manifold $\Sigma$ must satisfy in order for such an immersion (resp. embedding) into $B^n$ to exist. In particular, decide whether the set of admissible topological types of $\Sigma$ depends on whether one requires $\phi$ to be merely immersed or to be embedded.

Let $V = (V^+, V^-)$ be a Jordan pair over a commutative unital ring $k$, and suppose that $V$ is split root graded by a 3-graded locally finite root system $(R, R_1)$; that is, $V^\sigma = \bigoplus_{\alpha \in R_1} V^\sigma_\alpha$ for $\sigma = \pm$, with grading compatibilities under the quadratic operators $Q_x$ and trilinear products $\{x,y,z\}$, and the grading is split in the sense that each homogeneous component $V^\sigma_\alpha$ contains a distinguished invertible element giving rise to a Jordan pair isomorphism with the "split" model attached to $\alpha$.

Associated with $V$ one defines the Steinberg group $\mathrm{St}(V)$ by generators $x_\sigma(v)$ for $\sigma \in \{+,-\}$ and $v \in V^\sigma$, subject to a small set of relations (additivity in each root-homogeneous component, and commutator/Weyl-type relations indexed by the 3-graded root system $R$) that abstract the relations holding among the elementary unipotent elements in the projective elementary group $\mathrm{PE}(V)$.

For comparison, recall the basis-free presentation method of van der Kallen, originally developed for the linear Steinberg groups $\mathrm{St}_n(R)$ and their analogues, which produces a presentation of the Steinberg group purely in terms of the underlying module structure, without choosing a basis and without splitting into separate cases according to the type of the root system.

Question: Can van der Kallen's basis-free presentation method be extended so as to give, in a uniform and case-free manner (i.e. without separate arguments for each Jordan-pair type, in particular without excluding the exceptional types), a presentation of the Steinberg group $\mathrm{St}(V)$ for every split root graded Jordan pair $V$?

Let Σ be a smooth compact surface with non-empty boundary, of a fixed topological type (specified by its orientability, genus γ, and number of boundary components b). For a smooth Riemannian metric g on Σ, the Steklov eigenvalue problem consists in finding all real numbers σ such that there exists a non-zero function u ∈ C^∞(Σ) satisfying

  Δ_g u = 0 in Σ,    ∂u/∂ν = σ u on ∂Σ,

where ν is the outward unit conormal to ∂Σ. The eigenvalues form a discrete sequence

  0 = σ_0(g) < σ_1(g) ≤ σ_2(g) ≤ ⋯ → ∞.

Let |∂Σ|_g denote the length of ∂Σ in the metric g. For each positive integer k, define

  Σ_k^*(Σ) := sup_{g} σ_k(g) · |∂Σ|_g,

where the supremum is taken over all smooth Riemannian metrics g on Σ.

(a) Determine the exact value of Σ_k^*(Σ) in terms of the topological type of Σ and of k.

(b) Decide whether the supremum Σ_k^*(Σ) is attained by some smooth Riemannian metric g on Σ, or whether it is realized only as a limit (e.g. by a degenerating sequence of metrics).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The general problem remains open. Sharp values are known only in a few special cases: for the disk (γ=0, b=1), Σ_k^* = 2πk (Hersch–Payne–Schiffer / Girouard–Polterovich); for the annulus (γ=0, b=2) and k=1, the sharp bound is realized by the critical catenoid (Fraser–Schoen). representations.normalized:
Let $n \geq 3$ and let $B^n \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ denote the closed Euclidean unit ball. A smooth properly embedded hypersurface $\Sigma \subset B^n$ is called a free boundary minimal hypersurface if it has zero mean curvature and meets $\partial B^n$ orthogonally along $\partial \Sigma$. For each positive integer $p$, the $p$-width $\omega_p(B^n)$ is defined via Almgren–Pitts min–max theory as
$$\omega_p(B^n) = \inf_{\Phi} \sup_{x \in \mathrm{dmn}(\Phi)} \mathbf{M}(\Phi(x)),$$
where the infimum is taken over all $p$-sweepouts $\Phi$ (continuous maps from a simplicial complex into the space of mod-$2$ flat $(n-1)$-cycles in $B^n$ with boundary in $\partial B^n$, having $p$-nontrivial cohomology class), and $\mathbf{M}$ denotes mass.

It is known that for each $p \in \mathbb{N}$ there exist a smooth embedded free boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma_p \subset B^n$ and a positive integer $n_p$ such that
$$\omega_p(B^n) = n_p \, |\Sigma_p|,$$
where $|\Sigma_p|$ denotes the $(n-1)$-dimensional Hausdorff measure of $\Sigma_p$.

Prove or disprove:
(a) The collection $\{\Sigma_p\}_{p \in \mathbb{N}}$ contains infinitely many pairwise non-congruent (or otherwise geometrically distinct) hypersurfaces.
(b) If (a) holds, then $|\Sigma_p| \to +\infty$ as $p \to \infty$.

Let $B^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the closed Euclidean unit ball. A properly embedded surface $\Sigma \subset B^3$ with $\partial\Sigma \subset \partial B^3 = S^2$ is called a free boundary minimal surface if it has zero mean curvature in $B^3$ and meets $S^2$ orthogonally along $\partial\Sigma$.

Two known constructions produce, for every sufficiently large integer $g$, an embedded free boundary minimal surface in $B^3$ of genus $g$ with exactly three boundary components and invariant under the dihedral group $D_{g+1}$ (acting by rotations about a fixed axis through angles that are multiples of $2\pi/(g+1)$ together with a reflection):

(a) A desingularization construction $\Sigma_g^{\mathrm{KL}}$, obtained by desingularizing the union of the critical catenoid and the equatorial disk (which intersect orthogonally inside $B^3$) along their circle of intersection by gluing in scaled Scherk-type singly periodic minimal surfaces, producing for all sufficiently large $g$ an embedded free boundary minimal surface of genus $g$ with three boundary components and the above dihedral symmetry.

(b) An equivariant min-max construction $\Sigma_g^{K}$, obtained as a min-max critical point of the area functional in the class of $D_{g+1}$-equivariant sweepouts of $B^3$, yielding for each sufficiently large $g$ an embedded free boundary minimal surface of genus $g$ with three boundary components and the same dihedral symmetry.

Question: Is it true that for all sufficiently large $g$, the surfaces $\Sigma_g^{\mathrm{KL}}$ and $\Sigma_g^K$ are congruent, i.e., they coincide up to a rigid motion of $B^3$?

Let $B^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the closed unit ball. A free boundary minimal surface in $B^3$ is a (smooth) immersed surface $\Sigma \looparrowright B^3$ whose mean curvature vanishes identically and whose boundary $\partial\Sigma$ lies on $\partial B^3 = S^2$ and meets $S^2$ orthogonally. The Morse index of such a surface is the number of negative eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity) of the second variation (Jacobi) quadratic form for the area functional under variations whose boundary is free to move along $S^2$.

The critical catenoid $K \subset B^3$ is the unique (up to rotation) piece of a Euclidean catenoid that meets $\partial B^3$ orthogonally; it is rotationally symmetric, embedded, and has Morse index equal to $4$.

Question: Is $K$, up to rigid motions of $B^3$, the only immersed free boundary minimal surface in $B^3$ whose Morse index is equal to $4$?

Let $B^n \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ denote the closed Euclidean unit ball with boundary $S^{n-1}$. A smooth, properly embedded hypersurface $\Sigma \subset B^n$ with boundary $\partial\Sigma \subset S^{n-1}$ is called a free boundary minimal hypersurface if $\Sigma$ has zero mean curvature in $B^n$ and meets $S^{n-1}$ orthogonally along $\partial\Sigma$. For such $\Sigma$, the Dirichlet-to-Neumann (Steklov) operator on $\partial\Sigma$ is defined by $u \mapsto \partial_\nu \hat u\big|_{\partial\Sigma}$, where $\hat u$ is the harmonic extension of $u\in C^\infty(\partial\Sigma)$ to $\Sigma$ (i.e., $\Delta_\Sigma \hat u=0$ with $\hat u|_{\partial\Sigma}=u$) and $\nu$ is the outward unit conormal of $\partial\Sigma$ in $\Sigma$. Let $\sigma_1(\Sigma)$ denote the first nonzero eigenvalue of this Steklov operator. Because the coordinate functions of $\mathbb{R}^n$ restricted to $\Sigma$ are Steklov eigenfunctions with eigenvalue $1$, one has $\sigma_1(\Sigma) \le 1$.

Prove or disprove: for every embedded free boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma \subset B^n$, $\sigma_1(\Sigma) = 1$.

Let $S$ denote the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and let $(\varphi,	heta,r)$ be spherical coordinates. Fix real constants $\alpha, eta$ such that $\alpha- eta(k+1)
eq 0$ for every integer $k\ge 0$. For each $h\in L^2(S)$, consider the exterior Robin problem: find a function $w(\varphi,	heta,r)$, twice continuously differentiable for $r>1$, $2\pi$-periodic in $	heta$, harmonic on $\{r>1\}$, and satisfying
$$\lim_{r	o 1^+} igl\|\alpha\,w(\varphi,	heta,r)+ eta\,\partial_r w(\varphi,	heta,r)-h(\varphi,	heta) igr\|_{L^2(S)}=0,\qquad \lim_{r	o\infty}w(\varphi,	heta,r)=0.$$
For $r\ge 1$ define a family of operators $T(r):L^2(S)	o L^2(S)$ by $T(r)h:=w(\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,,r)$. It is known that $\{T(r)\}_{r\ge 1}$ is a one-parameter semigroup if and only if $ eta=0$ (Dirichlet case) or $\alpha=0$ (Neumann case).

In the Dirichlet and Neumann cases, where $T(r)=e^{(r-1)A}$ for an infinitesimal generator $A$, the central tool linking the resolvents of $A$ and of its inverse $A^{-1}$ is the interconnection identity
$$\lambda R(\lambda;A^{-1})f \;=\; f-\lambda^{-1}R(\lambda^{-1};A)f$$
valid for suitable $f\in L^2(S)$ and admissible $\lambda$. This identity is the key step in establishing equivalences between approximation-theoretic and ergodic-theoretic statements about the boundary behavior of $w$.

Problem. Determine whether there exists an analogue of the above interconnection identity applicable to the Robin family $\{T(r)\}_{r\ge 1}$ (which fails to be a semigroup outside the Dirichlet and Neumann cases), or more generally to a closed linear operator $A$ on a Banach space that is not the infinitesimal generator of a $C_0$-semigroup, in such a way that it can play the role of the classical interconnection identity in deriving equivalences between resolvent estimates and inverse/ergodic assertions for the Robin boundary value problem on the unit sphere.

Let $B^n = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : |x| \le 1\}$ be the closed Euclidean unit ball, and let $\Sigma^k \subset B^n$ be a (smoothly) immersed $k$-dimensional free boundary minimal submanifold; that is, $\Sigma$ has zero mean curvature in $B^n$, its boundary $\partial \Sigma$ lies in $\partial B^n = S^{n-1}$, and $\Sigma$ meets $S^{n-1}$ orthogonally along $\partial \Sigma$. Let $f : B^n \to B^n$ be a conformal diffeomorphism of the ball (equivalently, the restriction to $B^n$ of a Möbius transformation of $\mathbb{R}^n \cup \{\infty\}$ that preserves $B^n$). Denote by $|\,\cdot\,|$ the $k$-dimensional Hausdorff (volume) measure.

Let $B^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the closed unit ball. A free boundary minimal surface in $B^3$ is an immersed surface $\Sigma \subset B^3$ that is minimal (zero mean curvature) and meets the boundary sphere $S^2 = \partial B^3$ orthogonally along $\partial \Sigma \subset S^2$. Two basic examples are: (i) the equatorial disk $D$, obtained as the intersection of $B^3$ with a plane through the origin, which has area $|D| = \pi$; and (ii) the critical catenoid $K$, the unique (up to ambient rotation) piece of a suitably rescaled catenoid that meets $S^2$ orthogonally, whose area $|K|$ is a specific constant strictly greater than $\pi$.

Question: Let $\Sigma^2$ be an immersed free boundary minimal surface in $B^3$, and assume $\Sigma$ is not an equatorial disk. Must
$$|\Sigma| \geq |K|\,?$$

Equivalently, is the critical catenoid the next smallest-area example, after the equatorial disk, among immersed free boundary minimal surfaces in $B^3$?

Fix an integer n ≥ 1 and let F denote the normalized n×n discrete Fourier transform matrix, i.e. the unitary matrix with entries F_{jk} = (1/√n) exp(2πi jk/n) for 0 ≤ j,k ≤ n−1. Let F* denote its conjugate transpose. Define the 2n×2n unitary block matrix

   G = [[0, F], [−F*, 0]],

and, for a real parameter α, the 2n×2n unitary matrix

   X_α = (cos α) I_{2n} + (sin α) G.

Consider the following linear computational model. An "algorithm" computing a 2n×2n unitary U is a factorization U = R_T R_{T−1} ⋯ R_1, where each R_t is a 2n×2n unitary that is, up to permutation of coordinates, block-diagonal with one nontrivial 2×2 unitary block acting on two coordinates and the identity on the remaining 2n−2 coordinates. The cost of the algorithm is T, the number of such two-coordinate steps. Let c(U) denote the minimum cost over all such factorizations of U.

It is known that c(F) = Ω(n log n), and that c(X_α) ≥ Ω(α² n log n) and c(X_α) ≥ Ω(α n log n) can be established for small α > 0.

Determine the true asymptotic behavior of c(X_α) as α → 0 (with n → ∞). In particular, prove or disprove the conjecture that

   c(X_α) = Ω( (n log n) / log(1/α) ),

and decide whether c(X_α) = Ω(n log n) holds, i.e. whether the dependence on α can be eliminated entirely from the lower bound.

Obtaining tight super-linear lower bounds for computing Fourier-type unitaries in the 2×2 unitary gate linear model is a longstanding open problem. The six Painlevé equations are nonlinear second-order ordinary differential equations whose general solutions (the Painlevé transcendents) define nonlinear special functions playing a role in nonlinear mathematical physics analogous to that of Airy, Bessel, and hypergeometric functions in linear physics. Each Painlevé equation is integrable in the sense of the isomonodromy method: its solutions are encoded by the monodromy data of an associated linear system, and recovering a particular solution w(z) from prescribed monodromy data is equivalent to solving an associated matrix Riemann–Hilbert problem (RHP) on a contour in the complex plane with prescribed jump matrices.

Develop a general framework, suitable for implementation as numerical software, that exploits this Riemann–Hilbert structure to compute Painlevé transcendents w(z) at arbitrary finite values of the independent variable z to high accuracy. Specifically, the framework should:

1. Take as input the monodromy / Stokes data that uniquely determine a particular Painlevé solution.
2. Produce, for any prescribed z in the relevant domain, a numerically deformed RHP whose contour and jump matrices are tailored to z (e.g., via steepest-descent–type contour deformations) so that direct numerical solution of the RHP is uniformly well-conditioned in z, including in asymptotic regimes |z| → ∞.
3. Combine the analytically known asymptotic information about w(z) extracted from the RHP (connection formulas, large-|z| expansions, pole distributions) with efficient numerical solvers for singular integral equations on contours, so that the same code yields accurate values at small, moderate, and large |z|.
4. Provide rigorous or empirically validated error bounds for the computed values of w(z) and its derivative.

Construct such a framework, prove its convergence, and demonstrate that it yields a practical numerical code applicable, in principle, to all six Painlevé equations and to general choices of monodromy data.

Substantial progress has been made: Olver and Trogdon developed a numerical framework for Riemann–Hilbert problems applied to Painlevé II (Hastings–McLeod solution), including automatic deformation of contours, and the methodology has been extended to other integrable systems (e.g., KdV via Deconinck–Olver–Trogdon). Setup. Fix an integer n ≥ 2. Consider the computational model in which a linear operator on ℂ^n is built by composing a sequence of "two-coordinate unitary steps": each step is a unitary U_t ∈ U(n) that acts as the identity on all but two coordinates i_t, j_t, and acts as an arbitrary 2×2 unitary on the (i_t, j_t)-block. The complexity of computing a target unitary X ∈ U(n) is the minimum number T of such steps needed so that the composition U_T ⋯ U_1 equals X (or, in approximate versions, lies within a prescribed neighborhood of X).

For a unitary U ∈ U(n), define the matrix-entropy potential
   Φ(U) = − Σ_{i,j} |U_{i,j}|^2 · log |U_{i,j}|^2 ,
with the convention 0·log 0 = 0. A single two-coordinate step can change Φ by at most O(1), and this is the key ingredient that yields the known lower bound Ω(α n log n) for computing a family of target unitaries {X_α}_{α∈(0,1]} associated with the (suitably normalized) discrete Fourier transform on ℂ^n, where α encodes a quality/precision parameter (so that α = 1 corresponds to exact computation of the Fourier transform).

Representation-theoretic approach. Let Ψ : U(n) → U(n′) be any (continuous) unitary representation of U(n). Then the composed potential Φ ∘ Ψ : U(n) → ℝ is also a candidate progress measure for the same two-coordinate model. A natural example is the order-k determinant representation Ψ_{det}^{k} : U(n) → U( C(n,k) ), whose rows and columns are indexed by k-subsets I, J ⊆ {1,…,n} and whose (I, J) entry is det U_{I,J}, the determinant of the k×k submatrix of U with rows I and columns J.

Problem. Prove a lower bound on the number of two-coordinate unitary steps required to compute X_α (in the model above) that is asymptotically stronger than Ω(α n log n). In particular, decide whether choosing a non-trivial unitary representation Ψ of U(n) — for instance Ψ = Ψ_{det}^{k} for some 1 < k < n — and using the composed potential Φ ∘ Ψ as a progress measure can be made to yield such an improved lower bound.

Setup. Let n be a positive even integer. Consider the "two-coordinate unitary-step" computational model for n×n unitary matrices: an algorithm is a finite sequence of elementary steps U_1, U_2, …, U_T, where each U_t is an n×n unitary matrix that acts non-trivially on at most two coordinates (i.e., its restriction to some pair of coordinates {i,j} is an arbitrary 2×2 unitary, and it is the identity on the remaining n−2 coordinates). The algorithm computes the unitary U_T U_{T−1} ⋯ U_1, and its cost is the number of steps T. For an n×n unitary M, let C(M) denote the minimum cost over all algorithms computing M exactly.

For a real angle α, let R(α) = [[cos α, −sin α],[sin α, cos α]] denote the 2×2 rotation, and define the n×n unitary
   X_α = R(α) ⊕ R(α) ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ R(α)   (n/2 blocks on the diagonal).

Define the entropy potential Φ on n×n unitaries by
   Φ(U) = ∑_{i,j=1}^{n} h(|U_{ij}|^2),   where h(x) = −x log_2 x   (with h(0)=0).
A standard estimate shows that any single two-coordinate unitary step changes Φ by at most a bounded amount, and using only this potential one can derive the lower bound
   C(X_{π/4}) ≥ (1/(2√2)) · n log_2 n.

Question. Prove or disprove: there exists a constant c > 1/(2√2) such that, for all sufficiently large even n,
   C(X_{π/4}) ≥ c · n log_2 n.
Equivalently, can one establish a lower bound on the two-coordinate unitary-step complexity of X_{π/4} that strictly improves the constant 1/(2√2) obtained from the vanilla entropy potential Φ?

The six Painlevé equations $P_I, P_{II}, \ldots, P_{VI}$ are the canonical second-order ordinary differential equations of the form $w'' = F(z, w, w')$, with $F$ rational in $w$, $w'$ and locally analytic in $z$, whose solutions have the Painlevé property: all movable singularities of all solutions are poles. They are known to possess a rich collection of special structural properties, including:

(i) Hamiltonian representations: each Painlevé equation can be written as a non-autonomous Hamiltonian system $q' = \partial H/\partial p$, $p' = -\partial H/\partial q$ for an explicit polynomial Hamiltonian $H(q,p,z)$.

(ii) Exact special solutions: for special values of the parameters, rational solutions, algebraic solutions, and solutions expressible in terms of classical special functions (Airy, Bessel, Weber–Hermite, Whittaker, Kummer, hypergeometric/Gauss) exist.

(iii) Bäcklund transformations: birational maps that send a solution of a Painlevé equation with one set of parameters to a solution of the same equation with shifted parameters; these generate affine Weyl group symmetries acting on the parameter space.

(iv) Isomonodromic Lax pair representations: each equation arises as the compatibility condition of an overdetermined linear system whose monodromy data is preserved under deformation in $z$.

(v) Asymptotic expansions in the complex plane near fixed singular points (typically $z=0$, $z=\infty$) and along Stokes rays, together with connection formulae relating the asymptotic behaviour in different sectors via the monodromy/Stokes data.

Problem. Provide a complete classification of these properties across the family of Painlevé equations $P_I$–$P_{VI}$ (including their degenerations and discrete analogues), and exhibit a single unifying mathematical structure from which all of (i)–(v) can be derived in a uniform manner, replacing the current fragmentary, equation-by-equation treatment by a systematic theory.

Let $\mathbb{F}_2$ be the field with two elements and let $\mathcal{A}_2$ denote the mod-2 Steenrod algebra. For an integer $d \geq 1$, let $P_d = \mathbb{F}_2[x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d]$ be the polynomial algebra in $d$ variables, graded by total degree (each $x_i$ in degree 1). The Steenrod algebra $\mathcal{A}_2$ acts on $P_d$ in the standard way: the Steenrod squares $Sq^k$ are determined by $Sq^0 = \mathrm{id}$, $Sq^k(x_i) = x_i^2$ if $k=1$ and $0$ if $k \geq 2$, together with the Cartan formula $Sq^k(fg) = \sum_{i+j=k} Sq^i(f)\,Sq^j(g)$, making $P_d$ a graded left $\mathcal{A}_2$-module.

Let $\mathcal{A}_2^+ \subset \mathcal{A}_2$ denote the augmentation ideal (the two-sided ideal generated by all $Sq^k$ with $k \geq 1$). Define the graded $\mathbb{F}_2$-vector space
$$QP_d \;=\; \mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{\mathcal{A}_2} P_d \;\cong\; P_d \,/\, \mathcal{A}_2^+ P_d.$$
A polynomial $f \in P_d$ is called "hit" if $f \in \mathcal{A}_2^+ P_d$. The Peterson hit problem asks, for each $d$, to determine an explicit minimal set of homogeneous generators of $P_d$ as an $\mathcal{A}_2$-module, equivalently to determine an explicit homogeneous $\mathbb{F}_2$-basis of $QP_d$ in every degree.

Problem: For every $d \geq 5$, exhibit such an explicit minimal generating set of $P_d$ as a left $\mathcal{A}_2$-module (equivalently, an explicit basis of $QP_d$ in every degree $n \geq 0$).

Let $\mathbb{F}_2$ denote the field of two elements and let $A = A_2$ be the mod-2 Steenrod algebra. For a positive integer $d$, let $V_d = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^d$ and consider its classifying space $BV_d$. The mod-2 homology $H_*(BV_d;\mathbb{F}_2)$ carries a natural left action of $A$, and the general linear group $GL_d := GL_d(\mathbb{F}_2)$ acts on $H_*(BV_d;\mathbb{F}_2)$ by permuting/transforming the generators.

Let $P_A H_*(BV_d;\mathbb{F}_2)$ denote the subspace of $A$-annihilated elements (the primitives under the action of positive-degree Steenrod operations), and let
$$\bigl(\mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{GL_d} P_A H_*(BV_d;\mathbb{F}_2)\bigr)_n$$
denote its $GL_d$-coinvariants in internal degree $n$.

Singer's algebraic transfer is a homomorphism
$$Tr_d : \bigl(\mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{GL_d} P_A H_*(BV_d;\mathbb{F}_2)\bigr)_n \;\longrightarrow\; \mathrm{Ext}_{A}^{d,\,d+n}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2),$$
defined for every $d \geq 1$ and every $n \geq 0$.

Question: Is $Tr_d$ a monomorphism for every integer $d > 4$ and every $n \geq 0$?

The conjecture is trivial for d ≤ 3 and was confirmed for d = 4. For d > 4, it had remained open in general; however, recent work (2025) claims a counterexample disproving Singer's conjecture in rank 6 at bidegree (6, 6+36). Consider 10-dimensional type II supergravity (type IIA or type IIB) compactified to 4 dimensions on a compact 6-dimensional group manifold M_6, with the following standard "smeared" ansatz:

- The 10d spacetime is a warped product of a 4d maximally symmetric Lorentzian space with M_6, where the warp factor and dilaton are taken constant.
- The Ramond–Ramond and NSNS field strengths are constant on M_6 (i.e. they are left-invariant forms of the group manifold with constant coefficients in the Maurer–Cartan basis).
- The orientifold and D-brane sources (Op-planes and Dp-branes for some fixed p ∈ {3,4,5,6,7,8}) are smeared, so that their contribution to the equations of motion is captured by a constant source density that enters the Bianchi identities and energy-momentum tensor; the localized source action is replaced by its smeared analogue.
- The internal source configurations are "intersecting": there exist at least two distinct Op/Dp source sets whose internal wrapped cycles intersect in a sub-cycle of strictly lower dimension than each of them (equivalently, the calibration forms of the different source sets are not all parallel).

Assume the resulting 4d effective theory yields a positive cosmological constant (a classical de Sitter solution), i.e. all 10d equations of motion and Bianchi identities are satisfied with 4d geometry of constant positive curvature.

Let V denote the 4d scalar potential as a function of the (closed-string) moduli that parametrize the smeared compactification ansatz, and let the de Sitter solution correspond to a critical point m_0 of V with V(m_0) > 0. Define the slow-roll-style parameter
  η_V(m_0) = (minimum eigenvalue of the canonically normalized Hessian of V at m_0) / V(m_0).

Prove or disprove the following statement: For every classical de Sitter solution of the above form with intersecting Op/Dp source sets, one has η_V(m_0) < 0; equivalently, the spectrum of 4d scalar mass-squareds at m_0 contains at least one strictly negative (tachyonic) mode, so that the solution is perturbatively unstable.

Let $A_2$ denote the mod-2 Steenrod algebra and let $\mathrm{Ext}^{s,t}_{A_2}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2)$ denote the bigraded Ext groups appearing as the $E_2$-page of the classical Adams spectral sequence converging to the 2-local stable homotopy groups of spheres. For each integer $i\ge 0$, let $h_i \in \mathrm{Ext}^{1,2^i}_{A_2}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2)$ be the standard generator, and consider the class $h_i^2 \in \mathrm{Ext}^{2,2^{i+1}}_{A_2}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2)$.

By a theorem of Browder, a smooth framed manifold of Kervaire invariant one can exist only in dimensions of the form $2^{i+1}-2$, and such a manifold exists in dimension $2^{i+1}-2$ if and only if the class $h_i^2$ is a permanent cycle in the Adams spectral sequence, i.e. detects an element $\theta_i : S^{2^{i+1}-2} \to S^0$ in the stable stems.

It is known that $\theta_i$ exists for $0 \le i \le 5$ (dimensions $2,6,14,30,62$) and that $\theta_i$ does not exist for $i \ge 7$.

Question: Does there exist a smooth framed manifold of Kervaire invariant one in dimension $2^7 - 2 = 126$? Equivalently, does $h_6^2 \in \mathrm{Ext}^{2,128}_{A_2}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2)$ represent an element $\theta_6 : S^{126} \to S^0$ in the stable homotopy groups of spheres?

In December 2024, Weinan Lin, Guozhen Wang, and Zhouli Xu posted a preprint proving that $h_6^2$ is a permanent cycle in the Adams spectral sequence, establishing the existence of $\theta_6$ and hence of a framed manifold of Kervaire invariant one in dimension 126. Let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the mod-2 Steenrod algebra and let $P_h = \mathbb{F}_2[x_1,\dots,x_h]$ be the polynomial algebra on $h$ generators of degree 1, regarded as a left $\mathcal{A}$-module. Let $\mathcal{A}_2^+ \subset \mathcal{A}$ denote the augmentation ideal, and define the "hit quotient"
$$QP_h \;=\; P_h/\mathcal{A}_2^+ P_h \;=\; \mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{\mathcal{A}} P_h.$$
The general linear group $GL_h = GL_h(\mathbb{F}_2)$ acts on $P_h$ by linear substitution and this action descends to $QP_h$; write $(QP_h)^{GL_h}_d$ for the subspace of $GL_h$-invariants in internal degree $d$. Singer's algebraic transfer is a homomorphism
$$Tr_h : (\mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{GL_h} (QP_h)^*)_d \longrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}^{\mathcal{A}}_{h, h+d}(\mathbb{F}_2, \mathbb{F}_2),$$
defined for each rank $h \geq 1$ and each internal degree $d \geq 0$. Let $Sq^0_*$ denote the classical squaring (Kameko) operation acting on $QP_h$ in the relevant degrees, and let $\bigl(\operatorname{Ker}(Sq^0_*)\bigr)(h, d)$ be its kernel in bidegree $(h,d)$.

Question. For every integer $t \geq 2$, is the rank-5 Singer transfer
$$Tr_5 : \bigl(\mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{GL_5} (QP_5)^*\bigr)_{13\cdot 2^t - 5} \longrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}^{\mathcal{A}}_{5,\, 5 + (13\cdot 2^t - 5)}(\mathbb{F}_2, \mathbb{F}_2)$$
an isomorphism? Equivalently, determine the $GL_5$-invariants $(QP_5)^{GL_5}_{13\cdot 2^2 - 5} = (QP_5)^{GL_5}_{47}$, and in particular decide whether
$$\bigl(\operatorname{Ker}(Sq^0_*)(5, 47)\bigr)^{GL_5} \;=\; 0,$$
in which case $Tr_5$ is an isomorphism in bidegree $(5,\, 5+(13\cdot 2^t - 5))$ for every $t \geq 2$. Alternatively, exhibit the more interesting situation in which this kernel of $GL_5$-invariants is nontrivial and $\dim (QP_5)^{GL_5}_{47} \neq 1$.

$$QP_h \;=\; P_h/\mathcal{A}_2^+ P_h \;=\; \mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{\mathcal{A}} P_h.$$
The general linear group $GL_h = GL_h(\mathbb{F}_2)$ acts on $P_h$ by linear substitution and this action descends to $QP_h$; write $(QP_h)^{GL_h}_d$ for the subspace of $GL_h$-invariants in internal degree $d$. Singer's algebraic transfer is a homomorphism
$$Tr_h : (\mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{GL_h} (QP_h)^*)_d \longrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}^{\mathcal{A}}_{h, h+d}(\mathbb{F}_2, \mathbb{F}_2),$$
defined for each rank $h \geq 1$ and each internal degree $d \geq 0$. Let $Sq^0_*$ denote the classical squaring (Kameko) operation acting on $QP_h$ in the relevant degrees, and let $\bigl(\operatorname{Ker}(Sq^0_*)\bigr)(h, d)$ be its kernel in bidegree $(h,d)$.

Question. For every integer $t \geq 2$, is the rank-5 Singer transfer
$$Tr_5 : \bigl(\mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{GL_5} (QP_5)^*\bigr)_{13\cdot 2^t - 5} \longrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}^{\mathcal{A}}_{5,\, 5 + (13\cdot 2^t - 5)}(\mathbb{F}_2, \mathbb{F}_2)$$
an isomorphism? Equivalently, determine the $GL_5$-invariants $(QP_5)^{GL_5}_{13\cdot 2^2 - 5} = (QP_5)^{GL_5}_{47}$, and in particular decide whether
$$\bigl(\operatorname{Ker}(Sq^0_*)(5, 47)\bigr)^{GL_5} \;=\; 0,$$
in which case $Tr_5$ is an isomorphism in bidegree $(5,\, 5+(13\cdot 2^t - 5))$ for every $t \geq 2$. Alternatively, exhibit the more interesting situation in which this kernel of $GL_5$-invariants is nontrivial and $\dim (QP_5)^{GL_5}_{47} \neq 1$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Web searches turned up many recent works on Singer's conjecture for the algebraic transfer (rank 4 confirmed, rank 5 known to fail in internal degree 108, rank 6 negation results), but none of the located sources explicitly settle whether $Tr_5$ is an isomorphism in bidegree $(5,\,5+(13\cdot 2^t-5))$ for all $t\geq 2$, nor whether $(\operatorname{Ker}(Sq^0_*)(5,47))^{GL_5}=0$. The status of this specific family of bidegrees could not be confirmed from the search.

Ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) are cosmic-ray particles with energies E > 10^18 eV. Their observed properties include: (i) a diffuse all-sky energy flux extending up to about 10^20 eV; (ii) a measured mass composition that, at the highest energies, appears to shift toward heavier nuclei; (iii) limited small-scale anisotropy/clustering on the sky. Identify the astrophysical source population(s) that produce the bulk of UHECRs by determining whether any known candidate class of sources (e.g., active galactic nuclei, gamma-ray bursts, starburst galaxies, tidal disruption events, magnetars, radio galaxies, galaxy clusters, etc.) can simultaneously satisfy all of the following requirements:

(a) Acceleration capability: the source class must satisfy the Hillas condition E_max ≳ Z e B R β_s c, allowing acceleration of nuclei of charge Z up to E ≈ 10^20 eV, given the source's characteristic magnetic field B, size R, and shock/outflow velocity β_s c.

(b) Energy budget: the integrated cosmological energy injection rate of the source population in UHECRs must be sufficient to reproduce the observed diffuse UHECR flux above 10^18 eV (typically of order 10^44 erg Mpc^{-3} yr^{-1}).

(c) Source density: the local volumetric number density n_s of sources must be high enough that the predicted small-scale arrival-direction clustering of UHECRs (after accounting for energy losses, magnetic deflections, and the GZK horizon) is consistent with the observed limits on clustering.

(d) Composition consistency: the predicted UHECR mass composition emerging from the sources, after propagation through intergalactic space (including photodisintegration, pair production, and adiabatic losses), must match the composition inferred from air-shower observations.

Provide such a source class together with the parameter region in which (a)–(d) hold, or prove that no presently known astrophysical class can simultaneously satisfy all four conditions.

Setup. Let R be an Ore domain (an associative ring with no zero divisors in which every pair of nonzero elements has a common nonzero left and right multiple). A skew PBW extension of R is a ring A containing R together with finitely many indeterminates x_1,...,x_n such that:
(i) A is a free left R-module with basis the standard monomials x_1^{α_1}···x_n^{α_n}, α_i ∈ ℕ;
(ii) for every r ∈ R\{0} and every i, there exists c_{i,r} ∈ R\{0} with x_i r − c_{i,r} x_i ∈ R;
(iii) for every 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n, there exists c_{i,j} ∈ R\{0} with x_j x_i − c_{i,j} x_i x_j ∈ R + Rx_1 + ··· + Rx_n.
The extension A is called bijective if each map r ↦ c_{i,r} is bijective and each c_{i,j} is invertible in R.

Under these hypotheses A is known to be an Ore domain, so its total (two-sided) ring of fractions Q(A) exists. Let Z(A) denote the center of A, and Q(Z(A)) its field of fractions, and Z(Q(A)) the center of Q(A).

Problem. For every bijective skew PBW extension A of an Ore domain R:
(a) Establish a Gelfand–Kirillov-type description of Q(A), i.e., realize Q(A) as a skew field of fractions of an iterated Ore extension of a purely transcendental extension of an appropriate base division ring.
(b) Prove (or disprove) that the natural embedding Q(Z(A)) ↪ Z(Q(A)) is an isomorphism, i.e.,
   Q(Z(A)) ≅ Z(Q(A)).

representations.normalized:
Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) are charged particles (protons and atomic nuclei) arriving at Earth from extragalactic sources with energies exceeding roughly 10^18 eV. The measured all-particle energy spectrum of cosmic rays exhibits a pronounced suppression (a steep decrease in differential flux) at energies above approximately 4 × 10^19 eV. Two principal mechanisms have been proposed to explain this high-energy cut-off:

(i) Propagation losses: as UHECRs travel through intergalactic space they interact with cosmic background photons (the cosmic microwave background and the extragalactic background light). For protons, photopion production above the threshold for p + γ_CMB → N + π gives rise to the Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin (GZK) effect, while heavier nuclei lose energy mainly through photodisintegration and pair production. These processes impose a horizon beyond which particles above a given energy cannot reach Earth without substantial energy loss.

(ii) Source-limited maximum energy: astrophysical accelerators can impart only a finite maximum rigidity E_max/Z to nuclei of charge Z, so the spectrum injected by sources is itself truncated, producing a cut-off independent of propagation losses.

Determine which of the following best accounts for the observed flux suppression at the highest energies:
(a) propagation energy losses on cosmic background photons (GZK-type effect) alone;
(b) a maximum acceleration energy imposed by the (predominantly nearby) sources alone;
(c) a combination of propagation effects and a source-limited maximum energy.

Provide quantitative criteria, in terms of the measured energy spectrum and the inferred mass composition (mean and dispersion of ln A) at and above the suppression, that would discriminate between scenarios (a), (b), and (c).

The origin of the UHECR flux suppression remains debated. Recent analyses combining the Pierre Auger spectrum and mass-composition measurements favor a mixed composition with a relatively low maximum rigidity of a few EV at the sources, suggesting the cut-off is at least partly source-limited rather than purely a GZK effect. Let $K$ be a field and let $\sigma$ be an automorphism of $K$ of finite order. Consider the iterated skew polynomial ring
$$A := K[x_1, \ldots, x_n; \sigma],$$
defined as the $K$-algebra generated by $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ subject to the relations
- $x_i x_j = x_j x_i$ for all $1 \le i, j \le n$, and
- $x_i r = \sigma(r) x_i$ for every $r \in K$ and every $1 \le i \le n$.

It is known (a noncommutative analogue of the Quillen–Suslin theorem) that every finitely generated projective left $A$-module is free. The task is the following:

Provide a matrix-constructive proof of this fact. More precisely, give an explicit algorithm which, on input a finitely generated projective left $A$-module $M$ (presented, e.g., by an idempotent matrix over $A$ or by generators and relations), outputs a finite free basis of $M$ as a left $A$-module, together with the explicit unimodular transformation matrices over $A$ realizing the isomorphism $M \cong A^r$.

Let $B$ be an associative $\mathbb{K}$-algebra over a field $\mathbb{K}$. We say $B$ is left semi-graded if there exists an ascending filtration $\{B_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ of $\mathbb{K}$-subspaces with $B_0 = \mathbb{K}$, $B = \bigcup_{n\geq 0} B_n$, $B_m \cdot B_n \subseteq B_{m+n}$, and each $B_n$ finite-dimensional, where the associated graded structure need not be connected graded in the classical sense (so the multiplication of homogeneous components $B_n^{sg} := B_n/B_{n-1}$ may include lower-degree contributions). Define the Gelfand–Kirillov (GK) dimension of $B$ in the usual way via $\mathrm{GKdim}(B) = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \log_n \dim_{\mathbb{K}} B_n$.

A left semi-graded algebra $B$ is called left semi-graded Artin–Schelter regular (left SAS regular) if:
(i) $B$ has finite left global dimension $d$;
(ii) $\mathrm{Ext}^i_B(\mathbb{K}, B) = 0$ for $i \neq d$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^d_B(\mathbb{K}, B) \cong \mathbb{K}$ (Gorenstein-type condition adapted to the semi-graded setting), where $\mathbb{K}$ denotes the trivial left $B$-module $B/B_{>0}$.

Question: If $B$ is a left SAS regular algebra with $\mathrm{GKdim}(B) < \infty$, must $B$ be a left noetherian domain?

Ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) are charged nuclei observed at Earth with energies above roughly 10^18 eV. Air-shower experiments infer, as a function of primary energy E, the relative abundances of mass groups (e.g., protons, helium, CNO, Si-like, Fe-like). Observations indicate an energy-dependent sequence in which the dominant mass group becomes heavier with increasing energy, with successive "groups" of elements appearing in an alternating pattern.

Two competing physical mechanisms have been proposed to explain this behavior:

(a) A "Peters cycle" at the sources: cosmic-ray accelerators have a maximum energy per particle that scales with magnetic rigidity R = E/Z, where Z is the nuclear charge. (b) Photonuclear spallation: during propagation through cosmic photon backgrounds (or inside the source environment), nuclei of mass number A photodisintegrate, with the relevant kinematic scale being energy per nucleon E/A. Heavier nuclei survive only at correspondingly larger total energies, producing an apparent mass-energy ordering controlled by E/A rather than E/Z.

The problem is the following:

(i) Determine, from the energy-dependent mass composition of UHECRs, whether the observed sequence of mass groups is governed by a rigidity-based Peters cycle (E/Z scaling), by photonuclear spallation (E/A scaling), or by a combination of both mechanisms (and in what proportion).

Work over a field $K$ of characteristic $0$. A $K$-algebra $B$ is called semi-graded if $B = \bigoplus_{n\geq 0} B_n$ as a $K$-vector space with $1 \in B_0$, $B_n B_m \subseteq \bigoplus_{k\leq n+m} B_k$, and each $B_n$ finite-dimensional over $K$. Such $B$ is said to be semi-graded Artin–Schelter (SAS) regular if it has finite global dimension $d$, finite Gelfand–Kirillov dimension, and satisfies the Gorenstein-type condition $\mathrm{Ext}^i_B(K,B) = 0$ for $i \neq d$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^d_B(K,B) \cong K$ (with analogous condition on the right). Say $B$ is cancellative if, for every $K$-algebra $C$, an isomorphism of $K$-algebras $B[t] \cong C[t]$ (polynomial rings in one central indeterminate) implies $B \cong C$ as $K$-algebras.

Question: Let $B$ be a SAS regular $K$-algebra that is left and right noetherian, generated as a $K$-algebra in degree $1$, and has global dimension $3$. Must $B$ be cancellative?

Let $k$ be a field and let $A=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0} A_n$ be a connected graded $k$-algebra (so $A_0=k$ and $A$ is finitely generated in degree $\geq 1$). Recall that $A$ is called Artin–Schelter regular if:

(1) $A$ has finite global dimension $d<\infty$;
(2) $A$ has finite Gelfand–Kirillov dimension; and
(3) $A$ is Artin–Schelter Gorenstein, meaning that
$$\operatorname{Ext}^{i}_{A}(k,A)=\begin{cases} 0 & i\neq d,\\ k(\ell) & i=d,\end{cases}$$
for some integer $\ell$ (the AS index), where $k=A/A_{\geq 1}$ is the trivial module.

Question: Must every Artin–Schelter regular algebra $A$ (in the sense above) be a domain, i.e., have no nonzero zero-divisors?

Positive answers are known in restricted cases: every AS-regular algebra of global dimension at most 3 is a domain; every noetherian AS-regular algebra of dimension at most 4 is a domain; and every noetherian PI Artin–Schelter regular algebra is a domain (and a maximal order in its quotient division ring). Let Ω ⊂ R_+ be a measurable set parametrizing a one-dimensional epigenetic state x. Consider the nonnegative density Q(t,x) of resting-phase stem cells governed by the delay-free heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration equation

  ∂Q(t,x)/∂t = −Q(t,x)(β(Q̂(t),x) + κ(x)) + 2 ∫_Ω β(Q̂(t),y) Q(t,y) e^{−μ(y)} p(x,y) dy,

where:
 • Q̂(t) = ∫_Ω Q(t,x) ζ(x) dx is the effective cytokine signal,
 • β: R_+ × Ω → R_+ is a proliferation rate (in general depending on both Q̂ and the epigenetic state x),
 • κ: Ω → R_+ is a death/clearance rate,
 • μ: Ω → R_+ is a mitotic loss rate (e^{−μ(y)} ∈ (0,1]),
 • ζ: Ω → R_+ is a nonnegative weighting function,
 • p(x,y) is a transition (inheritance) kernel with 0 ≤ p(x,y) ≤ 1 and ∫_Ω p(x,y) dx = 1 for each mother state y ∈ Ω.

A steady state is a nonnegative function Q(x) on Ω together with a scalar Q̂ ≥ 0 satisfying the coupled system

  L_{Q̂}[Q](x) := 2 ∫_Ω β(Q̂,y) e^{−μ(y)} p(x,y) Q(y) dy − (β(Q̂,x) + κ(x)) Q(x) = 0,
  Q̂ = ∫_Ω Q(x) ζ(x) dx.

Equivalently, one seeks a positive scalar Q̂ such that the linear operator L_{Q̂} has 0 as an eigenvalue with a corresponding nonnegative eigenfunction Q(x), normalized by ∫_Ω Q(x) ζ(x) dx = Q̂.

Questions, in the general setting where β genuinely depends on x and the kernel p(x,y) genuinely depends on the mother state y:

(i) Determine sufficient conditions on β, κ, μ, ζ, p ensuring the existence of a positive Q̂ admitting a nonnegative eigenfunction Q(x) of L_{Q̂}.
(ii) Determine sufficient conditions guaranteeing uniqueness of such a steady state.
(iii) Determine sufficient conditions under which a steady state is (locally or globally) asymptotically stable for the time-dependent evolution.

(The special case in which p(x,y) = p(x) is independent of the mother state y has been treated previously; the question concerns the general mother-state-dependent case.)

Available literature on the heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration framework treats the homogeneous G0 case and the special case p(x,y)=p(x) (mother-independent inheritance), where existence, uniqueness and stability of positive steady states have been established. Let Ω ⊂ ℝ^d be a measurable space of epigenetic states. Consider a heterogeneous cell population whose density Q(t,x) ≥ 0 over states x ∈ Ω evolves according to a delay-free stem-cell regeneration model of the form

   ∂_t Q(t,x) = -(β(x) + μ(x)) Q(t,x) + 2 ∫_Ω β(y) p(x,y) Q(t,y) dy,

where β(x) ≥ 0 is the proliferation rate, μ(x) ≥ 0 is the apoptosis/removal rate, and p(x,y) ≥ 0 is a nonlocal epigenetic transition kernel satisfying ∫_Ω p(x,y) dx = 1 for every y ∈ Ω (so that each dividing cell at state y produces two daughters whose epigenetic states are distributed according to p(·,y)).

Define the total cell number
   Q(t) = ∫_Ω Q(t,x) dx,
the epigenetic-state fraction
   f(t,x) = Q(t,x) / Q(t),
and the multicellular Gibbs–Shannon entropy
   E(t) = - ∫_Ω f(t,x) log f(t,x) dx.

Derive the induced evolution equation for f(t,x), and address the following questions.

(a) Can the time derivative dE/dt be decomposed as
   dE/dt = epr(t) - edr(t),
where epr(t) ≥ 0 (entropy production rate) and edr(t) ≥ 0 (entropy dissipation rate) are functionals of f, β, μ, p that are pointwise (in t) nonnegative for every admissible state f?

(b) Provide explicit formulas for epr and edr in this decomposition, and characterize the conditions on the rate functions β, μ and on the nonlocal transition kernel p(x,y) under which the developmental process is entropy-increasing, i.e. dE/dt ≥ 0 for all t ≥ 0.

Consider a heterogeneous cell population model in which each cell is characterized by an epigenetic state x belonging to a state space Ω ⊂ ℝ^d. Let Q(t) > 0 denote the total population size (e.g., tumor volume) at time t, and let f(t,x) ≥ 0 denote the fraction of cells in state x at time t, so that ∫_Ω f(t,x) dx = 1. The dynamics are governed by four nonnegative rate functions on Ω:
  • β(x): proliferation rate,
  • κ(x): differentiation/death/senescence (exit) rate,
  • μ(x): apoptosis rate,
  • ζ(x): cytokine-secretion rate,
and by a transition kernel p(x, y) ≥ 0, where p(x, y) is the conditional probability density that a daughter cell has state x given that the mother cell had state y, satisfying ∫_Ω p(x,y) dx = 1 for every y ∈ Ω.

The pair (Q(t), f(t,x)) evolves according to a structured population equation in which new cells of state x are produced at rate ∫_Ω β(y) p(x,y) f(t,y) dy · Q(t), and cells of state x are removed at rate (κ(x) + μ(x)) f(t,x) Q(t), with cytokine production proportional to ∫_Ω ζ(x) f(t,x) dx · Q(t).

Assume one is given (possibly noisy, partial, multimodal) longitudinal observations of the population: for example, total volume measurements Q(t_i), empirical state distributions sampled from f(t_i, ·) via single-cell sequencing, biomarker concentrations, imaging-derived spatial information, and liquid-biopsy data, collected at finitely many times t_1 < t_2 < ⋯ < t_N.

Problem. Develop a mathematically rigorous inverse-problem framework that, from such observational data, identifies (or estimates with quantified uncertainty) the rate functions β(x), κ(x), μ(x), ζ(x) and the transition kernel p(x, y). Specifically:
  (a) Determine conditions on the observation operators and data under which the parameters (β, κ, μ, ζ, p) are uniquely identifiable from the observed data.
  (b) Construct a stable reconstruction procedure (e.g., regularized variational, Bayesian, or learning-based) that recovers (β, κ, μ, ζ, p) and provide convergence and stability estimates as data resolution increases.
  (c) Establish error bounds on predictions of (Q(t), f(t,x)) for t beyond the observation window, sufficient to support personalized predictive modeling and optimal treatment-decision problems.

Consider a heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration model without delay in which cells are indexed by an epigenetic state x in a bounded domain Ω ⊂ ℝ. Let f(x) ≥ 0 denote a normalized steady-state cell distribution with ∫_Ω f(x) dx = 1. Given are:

• a proliferation rate β(q,x) depending on a feedback variable q and on x,
• an apoptosis/removal rate κ(x),
• a per-division epigenetic noise function μ(x),
• a feedback weight ζ(x) ≥ 0 and a constant Q* > 0,
• the net production rate γ(q,x) = β(q,x)(2 e^{−μ(x)} − 1) − κ(x).

Assume that the epigenetic-state transition kernel during division is local: p(x,y) = φ(y − x), where φ(r) ≥ 0, φ(r) > 0 only for |r| < ε ≪ 1, ∫ φ(r) dr = 1, and define the moments
   a = ∫ r φ(r) dr,    D = ∫ r² φ(r) dr.

Substituting this local kernel into the steady-state form of the normalized regeneration model and expanding to second order in ε yields a second-order differential equation for f involving the terms β(λ,x) e^{−μ(x)} f(x) and γ(λ,x) f(x) (with first- and second-order spatial derivatives weighted by a and D/2 respectively), together with the constraints
   f(x) ≥ 0,    ∫_Ω f(x) dx = 1,
and the nonlinear eigenvalue / self-consistency relation
   λ = Q* ∫_Ω f(x) ζ(x) dx = Q̂.

For this local-transition limit, formulate and solve:
(i) the steady-state problem: existence, uniqueness, and dynamical stability of (f, λ) satisfying the second-order differential-integral system together with the nonlinear eigenvalue condition;
(ii) the entropy-decomposition problem: identify a Lyapunov / entropy functional for the time-dependent local-transition equation whose decomposition characterizes convergence to the steady state;
(iii) the inverse-estimation problem: from observable functionals of f (such as moments or the feedback functional ∫ f ζ dx), reconstruct the unknown rate functions β, κ, μ and the kernel parameters a, D.

Consider a LoRa (Long Range) wireless network architecture consisting of: (i) battery-powered end-devices that periodically transmit short uplink packets, (ii) a set of gateways that receive these packets and forward them to (iii) a network server / application server backbone. Each gateway has a finite reception capacity, a propagation-dependent coverage region (parameterized by spreading factor, transmit power, bandwidth, and channel model), and known hardware constraints (e.g., number of demodulator chains, antenna gain, deployment cost). Each end-device is characterized by its location, traffic pattern (arrival rate, payload size), required quality-of-service (delivery ratio, latency, lifetime), and energy budget.

Given a deployment region with a spatial distribution of end-devices and an application category C (e.g., smart agriculture, smart city, industrial monitoring, asset tracking) specifying the QoS targets and hardware constraint set H_C, design a generic algorithmic method that, taking (C, H_C, the end-device distribution, and the propagation environment) as input, outputs:

  (a) the number N of gateways to deploy, and
  (b) the physical placement {x_1, ..., x_N} of these gateways within the region,

such that the resulting deployment simultaneously:
  1. maximizes scalability (number of supported end-devices),
  2. minimizes inter-device and inter-gateway interference / collision rate,
  3. maximizes coverage of the end-device population,
  4. minimizes end-device energy consumption (extending battery lifetime),
  5. optimizes overall network performance metrics such as packet delivery ratio and throughput.

The required method must be generic in the sense that the same procedure, instantiated with the parameters of any application category C and hardware-constraint set H_C, yields a Pareto-optimal (or provably near-optimal) (N, {x_i}) configuration. Formulate such a method and establish its optimality guarantees.

Multiple recent works address specific instances of LoRa multi-gateway placement using bio-inspired/evolutionary algorithms (EPSO), clustering-based models (DPLACE using Gap-statistics), ray-tracing channel models, and PDR/CAPEX-OPEX multi-objective optimization. Consider a low-power wide-area network operating under the LoRaWAN Class A protocol. Each end-device, after transmitting a confirmed uplink frame, opens exactly two short receive windows (at fixed delays T1 and T2 after the end of the uplink) during which it can receive a downlink acknowledgment (ACK) from the network server, relayed through a gateway. Outside these two windows the device cannot receive. The gateway is half-duplex (it cannot transmit while receiving), it serves many devices on a small set of shared sub-GHz channels subject to duty-cycle regulations, and it has no a priori optimal rule for choosing the data rate (spreading factor) of the downlink ACK. As a consequence, an ACK may (i) be delayed because the relevant channel is busy with another scheduled transmission during the interval T1, (ii) be lost or corrupted due to overlapping frames or poor link budget at the chosen data rate, or (iii) miss both receive windows because of limited downlink opportunities. When this happens, the end-device either retransmits an already correctly delivered uplink or is blocked from sending subsequent uplinks until the confirmation procedure terminates, degrading network throughput and energy efficiency.

Design a dynamic acknowledgment mechanism for LoRaWAN Class A — specifying when the gateway should listen on the channel during T1, how it should schedule and prioritize ACK transmissions among contending devices, how it should select the downlink data rate and receive window (RX1 vs. RX2), and how the end-device should interpret missing or late ACKs — that provably prevents delayed or corrupted downlink acknowledgments from blocking later uplink packets or triggering unnecessary retransmissions, while remaining compliant with duty-cycle constraints and the single-gateway, multi-device, multi-channel setting described above.

The LoRaWAN Class A specification still mandates fixed RX1/RX2 receive windows after a confirmed uplink, with no standardized adaptive scheme for downlink ACK scheduling or data-rate selection. Consider a low-power wide-area network in which end-devices transmit uplink messages to a gateway over a lossy wireless channel and expect downlink acknowledgments (ACKs) within a retransmission timer T. If an ACK is not received before T expires, the device retransmits the message; this wastes energy and channel time when the original message was in fact received correctly but its ACK was delayed beyond T or corrupted in transit. Each end-device has tight constraints on memory, computation, and energy, and the channel exhibits highly variable delay distributions across different deployment scenarios (e.g., urban, rural, indoor, mobile).

Design a dynamic retransmission-timer policy T = T(state) — where 'state' may include locally observable quantities such as past ACK round-trip times, recent loss/duplicate-ACK events, spreading factor, duty-cycle constraints, and coarse load indicators — with the following requirements:

1. Trigger awareness: the policy must explicitly mitigate retransmissions whose triggering cause is a delayed or corrupted ACK rather than a lost uplink message, using empirically identifiable retransmission triggers.
2. Hardware feasibility: the policy must be implementable on resource-constrained end-device hardware (limited RAM, no floating-point unit, limited energy budget) and produce decisions in real time.
3. Modularity: the policy must function as a stand-alone retransmission mechanism, without requiring joint operation with channel coding or payload compression.
4. Cross-scenario robustness: the policy must achieve, across heterogeneous deployment scenarios, a provable or empirically demonstrated improvement over any static choice of T in terms of expected number of redundant retransmissions per successfully delivered message, while keeping the message delivery probability and end-to-end latency at least as good as a tuned static baseline.

Provide such a policy together with an analysis (or testbed-validated evaluation) establishing properties (1)–(4).

Consider the LoRa (Long Range) wireless communication system, in which low-power end devices transmit Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) modulated packets to gateways over distances of several kilometers. A LoRa gateway equipped with a commercially available LoRa transceiver chip can detect the presence of an incoming chirp packet whose received signal strength lies above its detection threshold but below the threshold needed to correctly demodulate and decode the payload; such packets are normally discarded.

Design a reliable communication scheme that extends the effective decoding range of LoRa uplinks under the following constraints:

1. End devices use unmodified, commercially available LoRa radio chips and standard CSS-modulated transmissions (no custom backscatter hardware, no replacement of the chip's PHY-layer signal generation, and no use of software-defined radios such as USRPs at the end-device side).
2. Gateways may be augmented only by lightweight, well-specified auxiliary processing (for example, additional digital signal processing in firmware/cloud, multi-antenna combining, or coordinated multi-gateway reception), but must not require replacing the commercial LoRa chip itself or rely on implementation paths whose realizability on commercial chips is unclear.
3. The scheme must enable the recovery of payload bits from packets whose per-gateway SNR is below the standard LoRa decoding threshold, by exploiting weak-but-detectable signals (e.g., through joint/coherent combining across multiple gateways or antennas, denoising, or comparable techniques).

Specify the signal-processing and networking algorithm, prove or empirically establish that it strictly enlarges the decodable range compared with a single standard LoRa gateway, and quantify the achievable range gain and energy/battery-life impact while preserving compatibility with unmodified commercial LoRa end devices.

Several systems have substantially advanced this problem since it was posed. Charm performs coherent combining of weak signals across multiple gateways; MALoRa uses gateway antenna diversity to combine signals before standard LoRa demodulation; and SRLoRa applies neural super-resolution-style denoising across multiple gateways to decode signals well below the single-gateway SNR threshold. These approaches keep commercial LoRa end devices unmodified and report multi-fold range and battery improvements. Consider a LoRaWAN-style low-power wide-area network consisting of: (i) a set of end devices D, (ii) one or more gateways, (iii) a Network Server (NS) operated by a network service provider, and (iv) an Application Server (AS) operated by an application service provider, where NS and AS may belong to distinct administrative organizations. Each end device d ∈ D shares two symmetric session keys: a Network Session Key NwkSKey_d (used for MAC-layer integrity/authentication between d and NS) and an Application Session Key AppSKey_d (used for end-to-end payload confidentiality between d and AS). In current deployments these keys are derived once (e.g., from a root key during a Join procedure) and are never refreshed, and both NS and AS are structurally able to compute, or have access to, both keys.

Design a security architecture and key-management protocol for such a network that simultaneously satisfies all of the following requirements:

1. Key separation and confidentiality across organizations: AppSKey_d must remain unknown to the NS, and NwkSKey_d must remain unknown to the AS, even though both servers participate in delivering each uplink/downlink frame.
2. Key generation and periodic key update: provide explicit mechanisms by which NwkSKey_d and AppSKey_d (and any underlying root keys) are generated at session establishment and rotated during the lifetime of a device, including rekeying triggers and synchronization between d, NS, and AS.
3. Optional trusted third-party authorization: specify how a trusted Key Management Server, distinct from NS and AS, can mediate join, key derivation, and key update so that neither NS nor AS learns the other's session key.
4. Resistance to the following attack classes, each of which must be formally characterized by an adversary model and against which the protocol must be proven (or argued) secure:
   (a) node impersonation, (b) passive eavesdropping, (c) black-hole attacks, (d) wormhole attacks, (e) jamming, (f) replay attacks, (g) beacon-synchronization attacks, (h) traffic analysis, (i) man-in-the-middle attacks, and (j) compromise of one or more session keys (forward and backward secrecy under key compromise).
5. Per-application differentiation: provide a methodology for tailoring the above mechanisms to the heterogeneous security requirements of distinct LoRa application classes (e.g., metering, healthcare, industrial control, smart agriculture), including how requirements such as confidentiality, integrity, availability, and privacy are quantified and mapped to concrete protocol parameters.

Produce such an architecture together with a security proof (or rigorous justification) of the claimed properties under standard cryptographic assumptions, and analyze its overhead in terms of the constrained energy, bandwidth, and duty-cycle budget characteristic of LoRa end devices.

Consider a LoRa (Long Range, Chirp Spread Spectrum based) wireless network in which a single gateway must receive uplink transmissions from a very large population of end-devices (on the order of thousands) that may transmit simultaneously on the same frequency band, producing colliding signals at the gateway. Assume the standard LoRa physical layer: each end-device modulates data using up-chirp symbols parameterized by a spreading factor SF (so each symbol carries SF bits and lasts 2^SF / BW seconds for bandwidth BW), and the gateway demodulates by dechirping followed by an FFT. Channel coding (e.g., Hamming codes used in LoRaWAN) cannot in general guarantee recovery of payload bits from collided symbols, and known distributed-coding / backscatter-style schemes based on chirp spread spectrum can demonstrably resolve at most on the order of 256 concurrent transmissions in a single FFT operation.

Design and analyze an interference-cancellation scheme for the LoRa physical layer that, given the superposition signal received at one gateway from N end-devices transmitting concurrently (with possibly different starting times, carrier frequency offsets, and received powers, and possibly with some signals below the noise floor), recovers each device's payload with high probability for N scaling to the thousands. Specifically, exhibit a decoding algorithm together with rigorous performance guarantees (in terms of bit/packet error rate as a function of N, SF, SNR distribution, and timing/frequency offset distribution) that strictly improves the achievable concurrency beyond the 256-user regime, or prove an information-theoretic upper bound showing that no such scheme can scale to thousands of concurrent LoRa transmissions on a single gateway under realistic channel conditions.

Subsequent work has substantially advanced LoRa concurrent decoding beyond the 256-transmission benchmark of NetScatter. Concurrent Interference Cancellation (CIC, SIGCOMM 2021) reportedly increases capacity up to 10x over standard LoRa and 4x over prior art; PCube (ACM TOSN 2022) uses multi-antenna reception diversity to scale concurrent transmissions; and more recent systems (e.g., Canas, and large-scale parallel decoding work in IEEE TMC 2024) push concurrency further by orthogonalizing many logical channels. However, no scheme has been proven to provably and reliably decode thousands of simultaneous LoRa transmissions at a single gateway under general conditions, so the underlying problem of fully scalable LoRa interference cancellation remains only partially solved.
