Consider a low-power wide-area wireless network in which end devices transmit short packets to a gateway over a noisy channel that exhibits both random bit errors and bursty packet losses (entire packets dropped in consecutive bursts). Each device is severely constrained in memory, computation, energy, and tolerable latency, and any retransmission contributes to channel interference and collisions.

A baseline application-layer redundancy scheme works as follows. To transmit an information sequence of packets x_1, x_2, ..., x_n, each transmitted packet y_k carries x_k together with a linear combination over GF(2) of a window of the W previous information packets {x_{k-1}, ..., x_{k-W}} (with coefficients chosen by some generator). The receiver recovers lost packets by Gaussian elimination on the resulting banded generator matrix. This scheme has the following drawbacks: (i) it requires buffering the previous W packets at the encoder, (ii) the banded structure of the generator matrix prevents constructing an LT-code-like degree distribution, (iii) Gaussian-elimination decoding has high complexity, (iv) it does not effectively recover bursty losses, and (v) any added redundancy or retransmission increases collisions.

Problem. Design a channel/erasure coding scheme for such a network, together with an encoding and decoding algorithm, that simultaneously satisfies the following requirements:

1. Recovers from both isolated bit corruption and bursty packet erasures of length up to B with probability at least 1 − ε, for prescribed B and ε.
2. Uses encoder memory o(W) and per-packet encoding work O(1) (or at most polylogarithmic in n).
3. Admits a decoding algorithm whose time and space complexity are strictly lower than Gaussian elimination on a banded n × n matrix (e.g., near-linear in n).
4. Achieves end-to-end latency bounded by a constant number of packet intervals, without requiring feedback-driven retransmission.
5. Adds asymptotically less redundancy overhead than the baseline window scheme while matching or exceeding its packet-recovery rate, so that the offered traffic load (and hence collision probability) is not increased.

Provide such a code construction and prove the above properties, or prove that no scheme can simultaneously achieve (1)–(5) under the stated resource constraints.

The problem of designing a channel-coding scheme for LoRa that overcomes the limitations of redundancy-based application-layer codes (e.g., DaRe) — bursty-loss vulnerability, memory and decoding complexity, latency, and increased collisions — remains an active research area. Surveys and recent works continue to list it as an open issue, and proposed schemes (e.g., variants of fountain/LT codes, network coding, and FEC for LoRa) address subsets of the requirements but no single solution is established as fully satisfactory.

Consider a LoRa (Long Range) wireless network consisting of a set of end-devices E = {e_1, ..., e_N} communicating with one or more gateways. Each end-device e_i must, at every transmission instant t, choose a vector of communication parameters

  p_i(t) = (SF_i, TP_i, BW_i, CH_i, DR_i, FR_i),

where SF_i ∈ {7,8,9,10,11,12} is the spreading factor, TP_i ∈ [TP_min, TP_max] is the transmission power, BW_i ∈ {125, 250, 500} kHz is the bandwidth, CH_i is the channel index from a finite set of available channels, DR_i is the data rate, and FR_i ∈ ℕ is the frame repetition rate.

The deployment environment is described by an environmental state vector ε(t) which may include ambient temperature T(t), indoor/outdoor classification, ambient RF noise level, multipath/shadowing, and node mobility. The received signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio at the gateway and the corresponding packet reception probability depend on p_i(t), ε(t), and the joint choices {p_j(t)}_{j ≠ i} of other devices via standard LoRa link and capture models, with the additional realistic constraint that increasing T(t) decreases received signal strength, and that increasing SF does not monotonically improve link quality once interference and time-on-air are taken into account.

Define network-level objectives:
 (S) scalability: maximum number of end-devices supportable while keeping packet delivery ratio above a threshold;
 (P) packet reception ratio averaged over devices and time;
 (Q) average energy consumption per successfully delivered packet;
 (R) reliability, measured as the probability that each device achieves its target delivery ratio over a window.

Problem. Design a (possibly distributed) policy π: (history of local observations and feedback, ε(t)) → p_i(t), per end-device, such that for every environment trajectory ε(·) drawn from a class encompassing indoor, outdoor, high-noise, and temperature-varying conditions, the policy simultaneously improves S, P, Q, and R relative to any static or environment-agnostic parameter assignment, while

 (i) explicitly incorporating environmental covariates (in particular ambient temperature) into the parameter choice,
 (ii) not relying on the assumption that larger SF always yields better communication performance, and
 (iii) producing a personalized parameter vector p_i for each device rather than a network-wide uniform setting.

Characterize the existence, structure, and optimality guarantees of such a policy, and quantify the achievable trade-off region among (S, P, Q, R) as a function of the environmental class.

Consider a weakly collisional, magnetized plasma such as the solar wind, modeled by the Vlasov–Maxwell system for ion and electron distribution functions f_s(x,v,t) (s ∈ {i,e}) coupled to electromagnetic fields (E,B). Assume a turbulent state in which energy injected at large (magnetohydrodynamic) scales cascades to smaller scales, crossing the ion kinetic scales (ion gyroradius ρ_i and ion inertial length d_i) and continuing down to the electron kinetic scales (ρ_e, d_e), where it is ultimately converted into particle internal energy (heating) by collisionless mechanisms.

Candidate collisionless dissipation/cascade mechanisms that may operate simultaneously include: (i) linear and nonlinear Landau damping on ions and electrons; (ii) cyclotron (ion or electron) resonant damping; (iii) stochastic ion heating by low-frequency, large-amplitude fluctuations; (iv) magnetic reconnection in current sheets formed by the cascade; (v) dissipation in coherent structures such as current sheets and vortices; (vi) wave–particle interactions associated with kinetic Alfvén waves, whistler waves, and ion-Bernstein modes.

Problem. Develop a predictive theory of the kinetic-scale turbulent cascade in such a plasma that:

Consider three-dimensional, three-velocity (3D3V) kinetic simulations of magnetized collisionless plasma turbulence in a periodic cubic domain, in which the plasma is driven at large scales and the turbulent cascade extends down to and below the ion kinetic scales (the ion gyroradius and ion inertial length). Different simulations may use different numerical models, including (i) fully kinetic Vlasov–Maxwell or particle-in-cell descriptions of both ions and electrons, and (ii) hybrid-kinetic descriptions in which ions are treated kinetically and electrons are treated as a (possibly massless) neutralizing fluid. Simulations may also differ in their large-scale driving mechanism, in box size, in spectral or hyper-dissipative filtering choices, and, in the fully kinetic case, in the (often artificially reduced) ion-to-electron mass ratio.

Define a "universal kinetic-scale turbulence feature" as a statistical property of the turbulent fluctuations at scales near and below the ion kinetic scales—such as the slope and shape of the magnetic, electric, and density power spectra, the spectral anisotropy with respect to the local mean magnetic field, intermittency exponents and structure functions, the distribution and morphology of current sheets and reconnection sites, the partitioning of energy dissipation between ions and electrons, and ion and electron velocity-space structures—whose value, up to controlled corrections, is independent of the choice of numerical model and of the above simulation parameters.

Problem. Determine whether such universal kinetic-scale turbulence features exist. More precisely:

(a) Identify a (possibly empty) set of statistical observables of 3D3V collisionless plasma turbulence whose values at sub-ion scales agree, within quantifiable error bars, across independently performed hybrid-kinetic and fully kinetic 3D3V simulations after suitable normalization (e.g., to the ion gyroradius, ion inertial length, and rms turbulent amplitude).

(b) For each such observable, separate the contribution that is robust under variation of the driving prescription, box size, filtering/dissipation, mass ratio, and hybrid-versus-fully-kinetic treatment from contributions that depend on these choices, and provide explicit scalings or bounds for the dependence on each parameter.

(c) Identify the underlying physical mechanism(s) (for example, magnetic reconnection in a sea of intermittent current sheets, kinetic Alfvén wave turbulence, stochastic heating, or Landau/cyclotron damping) responsible for the universal features identified in (a), and derive their statistical predictions from first principles in a way that reproduces the measured universal observables.

Consider a magnetized, weakly collisional plasma exhibiting a turbulent cascade that extends below the ion gyroradius and ion inertial scales (the "sub-ion" range). At these scales, linear Vlasov–Maxwell theory admits several wave branches, including:

(i) kinetic Alfvén waves (KAW), characterized by predicted ratios among electric, magnetic, density, and velocity fluctuations,
(ii) whistler waves,
(iii) ion-cyclotron waves, and
(iv) ion Bernstein waves.

For each linear branch one can compute predicted "spectral ratios" — e.g. the ratio of magnetic compressibility |δB_∥|²/|δB|², the density-magnetic ratio (n_e/n_0)²/(δB_∥/B_0)², and the Alfvén ratio |δu|²/|δB|² in appropriate units — as functions of the perpendicular wavenumber k_⊥ρ_i.

Suppose that in fully kinetic 3D-3V simulations (and in spacecraft observations) of sub-ion-range turbulence the measured spectral ratios are broadly close to the linear KAW predictions but do not match them exactly.

Question. Determine whether the sub-ion-scale electromagnetic and density polarizations of the turbulent fluctuations are genuinely dominated by KAW-like modes, or whether the observed deviations from linear KAW spectral ratios are produced by:
(a) an admixture of other linear wave branches (whistler, ion-cyclotron, and/or ion-Bernstein fluctuations) coexisting with KAWs in the cascade, and/or
(b) intrinsically nonlinear dynamics that drive the polarizations away from any asymptotic linear-mode prediction.

Quantify the relative contributions of (a) and (b) and identify a diagnostic, computable from the field correlation tensor of the turbulence, that unambiguously distinguishes a single-mode KAW cascade from a multi-mode and/or strongly nonlinear sub-ion cascade producing the same approximate spectral ratios.

Consider a weakly collisional, magnetized plasma (such as the solar wind) modeled by the 3D-3V Vlasov–Maxwell system, in which a turbulent cascade transfers electromagnetic and kinetic-fluctuation energy from large MHD scales through the ion-Larmor scale (k ρ_i ~ 1) into the sub-ion range (k ρ_i ≫ 1, with k ρ_e ≲ 1). For a fluctuating field f (e.g., a magnetic-field component), define the scale-dependent increment δf(ℓ) = f(x+ℓ) − f(x) and the scale-dependent kurtosis

  K(ℓ) = ⟨δf(ℓ)^4⟩ / ⟨δf(ℓ)^2⟩^2,

which measures intermittency (Gaussian statistics give K=3).

Empirically, in-situ solar-wind measurements indicate that K(ℓ) grows through the inertial range, reaches a maximum near the ion scale, and then becomes approximately scale-independent (saturates) throughout the sub-ion range. By contrast, fully kinetic 3D-3V simulations of driven plasma turbulence show K(ℓ) continuing to grow monotonically through the sub-ion range, with no such saturation.

Problem. Identify and justify the physical mechanism that produces the observed sub-ion-scale saturation of K(ℓ) in the solar wind but is either absent or insufficiently active in current 3D-3V kinetic simulations. In particular, decide between the following hypotheses (or formulate an alternative):

(a) Collisionless magnetic reconnection: sub-ion-scale intermittent structures are sufficiently sheet-like (large aspect ratio) to be tearing-unstable, and reconnection disrupts them before they reach smaller scales, thereby capping K(ℓ).

(b) Collisionless damping (e.g., Landau damping, cyclotron damping, stochastic heating) of fluctuations preferentially removes the most intermittent contributions to δf and saturates K(ℓ).

(c) A different mechanism, to be specified, with quantitative criteria for when it dominates.

A complete solution should provide a quantitative criterion (e.g., a threshold aspect ratio or damping rate compared with the nonlinear cascade rate) that determines saturation, and should explain why presently feasible 3D-3V simulations fail to reproduce it.

Consider a weakly collisional, magnetized plasma composed of multiple charged species (e.g., protons, electrons, and possibly heavier ions) immersed in a mean magnetic field, and driven into a statistically steady state of broadband electromagnetic turbulence whose cascade extends from magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) scales down through and below the ion kinetic scales (the ion Larmor radius ρ_i and the ion inertial length d_i). At kinetic scales, candidate collisionless dissipation channels for the turbulent fluctuations include: (i) ion and electron Landau damping, (ii) ion and electron transit-time (Barnes) damping, (iii) ion cyclotron damping, (iv) ion stochastic heating by low-frequency, large-amplitude perpendicular electric-field fluctuations, (v) collisionless magnetic reconnection in current sheets formed by the cascade, and (vi) kinetic "viscous" (pressure–strain) heating quantified via the scale-filtered Vlasov–Maxwell pressure–strain interaction Π_s = −(P_s · ∇) · u_s. The relevant plasma parameters include the ion plasma beta β_i = 8πn_i T_i / B^2, the electron-to-ion temperature ratio T_e/T_i, the fluctuation amplitude δB/B_0 at the ion gyroscale, and the propagation-angle/anisotropy of the cascade.

Problem. Determine, as a function of the plasma parameters (β_i, T_e/T_i, δB/B_0, anisotropy, and species composition), which of the above collisionless dissipation mechanisms dominate the removal of energy from turbulent fluctuations in the kinetic range, and derive the resulting partition of dissipated turbulent energy among the constituent plasma species (and between their parallel and perpendicular degrees of freedom). The answer must specify, for each region of parameter space, (a) the operative dissipation pathway(s), (b) the fractional heating rates Q_s / Σ_s' Q_s' for each species s, and (c) the consistency of (a)–(b) with the scale-by-scale energy balance dictated by the Vlasov–Maxwell equations.

Consider a collisionless or weakly collisional magnetized plasma whose dynamics are governed by the Vlasov–Maxwell system

  ∂_t f_s + v·∇_x f_s + (q_s/m_s)(E + v×B/c)·∇_v f_s = 0,    s ∈ {ions, electrons},
  ∇×B = (4π/c) J + (1/c) ∂_t E,    ∇×E = −(1/c) ∂_t B,
  ∇·E = 4π ρ,    ∇·B = 0,

with current and charge densities J = Σ_s q_s ∫ v f_s dv and ρ = Σ_s q_s ∫ f_s dv. Suppose the system is driven into a statistically stationary, fully developed turbulent state on a triply periodic three-dimensional spatial domain with three-dimensional velocity space (3D3V), with a mean magnetic field B_0 and turbulent fluctuations spanning scales from the magnetohydrodynamic range through the ion and electron kinetic ranges.

Define the local fluctuation energy density

  ε(x,t) = (|δB(x,t)|² + |δE(x,t)|²)/(8π) + Σ_s ∫ (m_s |v − u_s|² / 2) δf_s(x,v,t) dv,

and its space–time correlation/spectral structure via the four-dimensional Fourier transform ε̂(k,ω) of ε(x,t) (or, equivalently, of the underlying electromagnetic and particle-fluctuation fields).

Problem. Characterize quantitatively how turbulent energy is distributed jointly in physical space x and in time t (equivalently, in wavenumber k and frequency ω) in such a kinetic plasma turbulence state. In particular:

(a) Determine the joint (k,ω) energy distribution across the inertial, ion-kinetic, and electron-kinetic ranges, identifying which fraction of energy lies on linear wave dispersion surfaces ω = ω_α(k) (e.g. Alfvén, slow, kinetic Alfvén, whistler, ion-cyclotron branches) versus in non-wavelike, advected or coherent structures.

(b) Quantify the degree of spatial intermittency (volume-filling factor, multifractal scaling exponents of structure functions, and statistics of energy-dissipation surrogates) and the temporal intermittency (waiting-time and burst-duration distributions) of the energy density ε(x,t).

(c) Provide a predictive theory linking (a) and (b) to the driving parameters (plasma beta, ion-to-electron mass and temperature ratios, Alfvén Mach number, system size in units of ρ_i and d_i).

Give either a rigorous derivation, a closed phenomenological model with verified scaling laws, or a definitive numerical/observational characterization.

representations.normalized:
Consider a magnetized collisionless plasma described by the Vlasov–Maxwell system in three spatial and three velocity dimensions, in a statistically homogeneous turbulent state with a mean magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$. In such a system energy injected at large (fluid) scales is transferred through a nonlinear cascade down to kinetic scales (ion and electron gyroradii and inertial lengths), where it is ultimately converted into particle heat.

Define the scale-dependent energy transfer rate using a generalized third-order (Yaglom-type / Kolmogorov-Hill) structure-function flux $\Pi(\boldsymbol{\ell})$, expressed as a function of the three-dimensional separation vector $\boldsymbol{\ell}$. Decompose $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ into:
- a component $\ell_\parallel$ parallel to the local mean magnetic field,
- a component $\ell_{\perp,1}$ perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}_0$ but aligned with the local fluctuation direction (e.g., the local perpendicular magnetic-field perturbation),
- a component $\ell_{\perp,2}$ perpendicular to both.

Problem. Determine the full three-dimensional anisotropic structure of the energy transfer rate $\Pi(\ell_\parallel,\ell_{\perp,1},\ell_{\perp,2})$ across the inertial, ion-kinetic, and sub-ion-kinetic ranges of a turbulent collisionless plasma. Specifically, characterize:
1. how the magnitude and direction of energy flux depend on the orientation of $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ with respect to both the local mean magnetic field and the local turbulent structure,
2. the scaling of $\Pi$ along each of the three axes as scales cross the ion gyroradius,
3. whether the cascade exhibits a single dominant transfer direction (e.g., predominantly perpendicular) or a non-trivial three-dimensional flux pattern, and
4. the relative role of the three symmetry axes in setting spectral slopes and dissipation channels.

Consider a fully ionized, weakly collisional, magnetized plasma in three spatial and three velocity dimensions, modeled by the Vlasov–Maxwell system

  ∂_t f_s + v·∇_x f_s + (q_s/m_s)(E + v×B/c)·∇_v f_s = 0,   s = i, e,
  ∂_t B = −c∇×E,    ∇×B = (4π/c) Σ_s q_s ∫ v f_s d^3v + (1/c) ∂_t E,
  ∇·B = 0,    ∇·E = 4π Σ_s q_s ∫ f_s d^3v,

driven into a statistically steady, strongly turbulent state with a mean magnetic field B_0 and characteristic ion gyroradius ρ_i and inertial length d_i. Let δψ_ℓ(x) = ψ(x+ℓ) − ψ(x) denote the spatial increment of a fluctuating field ψ ∈ {B, E, u_s, n_s, …} over a separation ℓ, and define the structure functions

  S_p^ψ(ℓ) = ⟨ |δψ_ℓ|^p ⟩,    p ≥ 1,

together with the scale-dependent kurtosis

  K^ψ(ℓ) = S_4^ψ(ℓ) / [S_2^ψ(ℓ)]^2,

and the standardized probability density functions P(δψ_ℓ / σ_ℓ).

Determine the high-order statistical structure of the turbulent fluctuations across the kinetic range ℓ ≲ ρ_i, d_i. Specifically:

(a) Characterize, for each field ψ, the scaling exponents ζ_p^ψ defined by S_p^ψ(ℓ) ∼ ℓ^{ζ_p^ψ} and the resulting multifractal spectrum, including any departure from a linear (self-similar) dependence ζ_p^ψ = p·ζ_1^ψ.

(b) Determine the scale dependence of K^ψ(ℓ) and of the full PDF P(δψ_ℓ/σ_ℓ) at sub-ion scales, including whether intermittency increases, saturates, or decreases as ℓ crosses ρ_i and d_i down to electron scales.

(c) Identify which fields (magnetic field components, electric field, ion and electron bulk velocities, densities) display the strongest non-Gaussian, intermittent behavior, and relate the observed higher-order statistics to the coherent structures (current sheets, vortices, reconnection sites) that produce them.

The high-order statistical structure of fluctuations at kinetic (sub-ion to electron) scales in collisionless plasma turbulence remains an active and unresolved area. Recent observational and numerical studies (MMS observations, 3D3V Vlasov simulations, hybrid PIC, HelioSwarm forecasts) report partial and sometimes conflicting results: some find a transition from intermittent to globally self-similar non-Gaussian statistics below ρ_i, while others report sustained intermittency tied to current sheets and reconnection, and electron-scale statistics are still poorly constrained. No complete theory of the multifractal spectrum and PDFs across the kinetic range exists.

Consider a magnetized, weakly collisional plasma exhibiting kinetic turbulence (e.g., a stellar/solar wind) advected past a stationary probe with bulk flow velocity $\mathbf{U}_0$. Taylor's hypothesis is the assumption that temporal fluctuations $\delta f(t)$ measured by the stationary probe at a fixed spatial point are dominated by the rigid advection of spatial structures past the probe, so that an observed angular frequency $\omega_{\rm sc}$ is related to a wavevector $\mathbf{k}$ in the plasma frame by $\omega_{\rm sc} = \mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{U}_0$, allowing the conversion of time series into spatial spectra via $k = \omega_{\rm sc}/U_0$.

Let $L$ denote the energy-containing (outer) scale of the turbulence, $\rho_i$ the ion gyroradius, $d_i = c/\omega_{pi}$ the ion inertial length, $\rho_e$ the electron gyroradius, and let $V_A$ be the Alfvén speed and $\delta V$ the rms turbulent velocity fluctuation amplitude at scale $\ell$. In the magnetohydrodynamic inertial range ($\ell \gg \rho_i$), the standard sufficient condition $\delta V \ll U_0$ (and, when relevant, $V_A \ll U_0$, i.e., super-Alfvénic flow) is known to render Taylor's hypothesis reliable. At sub-ion (kinetic) scales ($\ell \lesssim \rho_i$), however, dispersive wave modes (e.g., kinetic Alfvén waves, whistlers) can have intrinsic frequencies $\omega(\mathbf{k})$ comparable to or exceeding $\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{U}_0$, potentially violating the hypothesis.

Determine the precise range of temporal frequencies $\omega_{\rm sc}$ and spatial scales $\ell$ (spanning from $L$ down through $\rho_i$, $d_i$, and into the sub-electron scales $\ell \lesssim \rho_e$) over which Taylor's hypothesis $\omega_{\rm sc} = \mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{U}_0$ remains a quantitatively reliable conversion between single-point temporal measurements and spatial structure for fully developed three-dimensional kinetic plasma turbulence. Equivalently, characterize, in terms of the dimensionless parameters $\delta V/U_0$, $V_A/U_0$, $k\rho_i$, $k d_i$, $k\rho_e$, and the angle between $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{U}_0$, the regime in which the hypothesis holds and the regime in which it fails.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Several studies have analyzed the validity of Taylor's hypothesis at kinetic scales: Howes et al. (2014, arXiv:1405.5460) showed it holds for kinetic Alfvén waves but can fail for whistler-supported dissipation ranges; subsequent works (Chhiber et al. 2019; Bourouaine & Perez 2018; Perez et al. 2021 for Parker Solar Probe; Zank et al. 2022 for the heliosheath) refined the conditions in terms of $\delta V/(V_A+U_0)$, dispersion, and obliquity. A complete, scale-resolved characterization spanning the full MHD-to-sub-electron range remains an active research problem with no single closed-form answer, so the question is best classified as partially solved.

Consider datasets of the form $\mathcal{D}=\{(m_i, x_i)\}_{i=1}^N$, where each sample consists of fixed-dimensional metadata $m_i \in \mathcal{M}$ (categorical and/or continuous attributes) and an associated multivariate time series $x_i = (x_i^{(1)}, \dots, x_i^{(T_i)})$ with $x_i^{(t)} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and possibly variable length $T_i$. Such datasets arise in networking contexts (e.g., traffic measurements, system telemetry, user session traces) and exhibit features such as heterogeneous metadata distributions, long-range temporal correlations, multi-scale behavior, and strong coupling between metadata and time-series dynamics.

A generative model $G_\theta$ is said to produce a synthetic dataset $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}$ that is "high-fidelity and task-generalizable" if, for a broad family $\mathcal{T}$ of downstream predictive or analytic tasks (each specified by a loss $\ell_T$ and an algorithm $A_T$ trained on a dataset), the performance gap
$$\Delta(T) = \big| \mathbb{E}[\ell_T(A_T(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}))] - \mathbb{E}[\ell_T(A_T(\mathcal{D}))] \big|$$
is uniformly small over $T \in \mathcal{T}$, and if standard distributional fidelity metrics (marginal distributions of metadata, autocorrelation functions of time series, joint metadata–time-series statistics) on $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}$ closely match those of $\mathcal{D}$.

Question: Does there exist a generative-adversarial-network–based procedure $G_\theta$, trained on $\mathcal{D}$ without task-specific supervision and without dataset-specific feature engineering or hand-crafted workload assumptions, such that for arbitrary networking datasets of the above form the resulting synthetic dataset $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}$ is high-fidelity and task-generalizable in the sense above? Equivalently, characterize the conditions on $\mathcal{D}$, on the GAN architecture, and on the training procedure under which such universal high-fidelity, task-agnostic synthetic data generation is achievable.

The question of building GAN-based synthetic data generators for networked time series that are high-fidelity and generalize across downstream tasks without manual feature engineering remains an active and open research area.   - the intended downstream analytical tasks,
  - the assumed adversarial capabilities and auxiliary information, and
  - the utility requirements,
selects or constructs a privacy definition that is (a) semantically meaningful for the stated threat model, (b) composable under repeated releases, (c) achievable simultaneously with acceptable utility on the stated tasks, and (d) interpretable to data custodians.

Consider the problem of releasing a synthetic version of a networked time-series dataset using a generative adversarial network (GAN). Formally, let $\mathcal{D} = \{(m_i, x_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ be a dataset where each record consists of a vector of metadata $m_i \in \mathcal{M}$ (e.g., per-object attributes) and an associated time series $x_i = (x_i^{(1)}, \dots, x_i^{(T)}) \in \mathcal{X}^T$. A GAN consists of a generator $G_\theta: \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{X}^T$ trained against a discriminator $D_\phi$ so that the induced distribution $P_{G_\theta}$ approximates the empirical distribution of $\mathcal{D}$.

A "flexible notion of privacy" refers to a family $\mathcal{P} = \{\Pi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ of privacy specifications, where each $\Pi_\alpha$ may, for example, prescribe (i) a differential-privacy guarantee at level $(\varepsilon_\alpha, \delta_\alpha)$ for releasing $G_\theta$ or its samples, (ii) protection against membership inference for a specified subset of records, (iii) hiding of designated metadata attributes, or (iv) bounded leakage of designated time-series features, while preserving the joint distribution of the remaining attributes.

Determine whether there exist training procedures (loss functions, optimizers, noise-injection mechanisms, architectures) and sampling/generation configurations for $G_\theta$ such that, for a given specification $\Pi_\alpha \in \mathcal{P}$, the generator simultaneously (a) provably satisfies $\Pi_\alpha$ and (b) produces synthetic networked time-series samples whose statistical fidelity (in terms of marginal, temporal, and cross-record correlation metrics) is comparable to that of a non-private GAN trained on $\mathcal{D}$. Characterize the set of specifications $\Pi_\alpha$ for which such configurations exist, and describe explicit training/generation configurations achieving them.

Let $\mathcal{D} = \{x^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ be a dataset of networked time series, where each $x^{(i)} = (m^{(i)}, s^{(i)}_1, s^{(i)}_2, \ldots, s^{(i)}_T)$ consists of a vector $m^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_m}$ of static metadata features and a sequence $s^{(i)}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_s}$, $t=1,\ldots,T$, of measurements. Such datasets typically exhibit (i) long-range temporal correlations within each series, (ii) heterogeneous and high-dimensional joint distributions over metadata, and (iii) strong cross-feature dependencies between metadata and the temporal signal.

A generative model $G_\theta$ trained on $\mathcal{D}$ produces synthetic samples $\tilde{x} \sim G_\theta$. Define:

1. A fidelity functional $F(G_\theta, \mathcal{D}) \in \mathbb{R}$ that measures how well synthetic samples reproduce marginal distributions of metadata, autocorrelation and spectral structure of the time series, and joint metadata–measurement statistics (for example, via a weighted sum of Wasserstein or Jensen–Shannon distances between empirical distributions of these quantities under $\mathcal{D}$ and under $G_\theta$).

2. A privacy guarantee parameterized, e.g., by $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy: the training procedure $\mathcal{A}: \mathcal{D} \mapsto \theta$ satisfies, for every pair of datasets $\mathcal{D}, \mathcal{D}'$ differing in one record and every measurable set $S$,
$$\Pr[\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}') \in S] + \delta.$$

The question is the following. Fix thresholds $\varepsilon^* > 0$, $\delta^* \in (0,1)$ regarded as "meaningful" privacy levels (e.g., $\varepsilon^* \le 10$, $\delta^* \le 1/N$), and a fidelity threshold $F^*$ regarded as "practical" for downstream networking tasks (such as preserving rank orderings of flow durations, packet-count autocorrelations, and conditional metadata–measurement statistics within a prescribed tolerance).

Does there exist a training algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ producing a generator $G_\theta$ for networked time-series data such that simultaneously
$$\mathcal{A} \text{ is } (\varepsilon, \delta)\text{-differentially private with } \varepsilon \le \varepsilon^*, \ \delta \le \delta^*, \quad \text{and} \quad F(G_\theta, \mathcal{D}) \le F^*?$$

Equivalently, characterize the achievable Pareto frontier of $(\varepsilon, F)$ pairs for differentially private GAN-style training on the class of networked time-series distributions described above, and determine whether this frontier admits points that are practical for typical networking datasets.

Consider the problem of evaluating the fidelity of a generative adversarial network (GAN) trained on networked-systems data, where each sample is a pair $(M, X)$ consisting of a metadata vector $M \in \mathcal{M}$ (a mixture of categorical and continuous attributes) and a multivariate time series $X = (x_1, \ldots, x_T) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times T}$ of variable or fixed length $T$. Let $P_{\text{real}}$ denote the (unknown) joint distribution over $(M, X)$ from which a finite training set is drawn, and let $P_{\text{gen}}$ denote the distribution induced by a trained generator $G$.

The most widely adopted GAN fidelity metrics (such as Inception Score and Fréchet Inception Distance) rely on features extracted by classifiers pretrained on large labeled image corpora and therefore do not apply to $(M, X)$ samples of this form.

Problem. Design a principled, general-purpose methodology for evaluating the fidelity of $P_{\text{gen}}$ relative to $P_{\text{real}}$ in this setting. Specifically:

(a) Propose a quantitative metric, or a finite collection of metrics, $\{\mu_i(P_{\text{real}}, P_{\text{gen}})\}_{i=1}^k$, that
  (i) is well-defined for joint distributions over (metadata, time series) pairs of the form above,
  (ii) captures both marginal statistical properties (e.g., distributions of metadata attributes, marginal value distributions of the time series, autocorrelation structure) and joint properties (e.g., dependence between metadata and temporal dynamics, and long-range temporal correlations),
  (iii) admits consistent finite-sample estimators with quantifiable error,
  (iv) does not depend on a domain-specific pretrained feature extractor.

(b) Provide criteria under which low values of the proposed metrics imply that $P_{\text{gen}}$ is suitable as a substitute for $P_{\text{real}}$ in downstream networked-systems tasks (e.g., classification, anomaly detection, simulation), and conversely identify failure modes that the metrics provably detect.

(c) Compare the proposed metrics, in terms of statistical power and computational cost, against existing alternatives such as classifier two-sample tests, predictive-score gaps (train-on-synthetic / test-on-real), and discrepancies of empirical autocorrelation or attribute distributions.

No universally accepted fidelity metric exists for GANs over (metadata, time series) data. Recent surveys and benchmarks (ACM Computing Surveys 2023; DeepIntoStreams evaluation pipeline; SeriesGAN 2024) note that GAN evaluation for time series still lags computer vision and relies on ad-hoc combinations of microbenchmarks (marginal/autocorrelation distances, Jensen–Shannon divergence), classifier two-sample tests (e.g., LSTM discriminator), and downstream predictive-score gaps. The problem of a principled, general fidelity metric remains open.

Let $\mathcal{D} = \{(a_i, x_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ be a dataset where each sample consists of an attribute vector $a_i \in \mathcal{A}$ (e.g., categorical or numerical metadata) and an associated time-series record $x_i \in \mathcal{X} = \mathbb{R}^{T \times d}$. Suppose a generative model has been trained to produce joint synthetic samples $(A, X)$ approximating the joint distribution $P(A, X) = P(A)\,P(X \mid A)$ of real data, where $P(A)$ is the marginal attribute distribution and $P(X \mid A)$ is the conditional distribution of time series given attributes.

A data publisher wishes to release synthetic data whose marginal attribute distribution matches a chosen target distribution $Q(A)$ (which may differ from the empirical $P(A)$, for instance to anonymize, rebalance rare categories, or correct sampling bias), while preserving the learned conditional behavior $P(X \mid A)$ between attributes and records.

Design and analyze a principled procedure that, given:
(i) a generator $G$ producing samples from $P(A, X)$,
(ii) a desired target attribute distribution $Q(A)$,

outputs a synthetic dataset $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}$ whose attribute marginal converges (in a specified statistical sense, e.g., total variation or Wasserstein distance) to $Q(A)$ and whose conditional law $\widetilde{P}(X \mid A)$ remains close to the original $P(X \mid A)$. Specifically:

1. Formulate sufficient conditions on $G$, on $Q(A)$, and on the relationship between $Q(A)$ and the support of $P(A)$ under which such a procedure is well-defined and statistically consistent.
2. Provide quantitative bounds relating any divergence $D(Q \| P)$ on attributes to the achievable fidelity of the conditional $\widetilde{P}(X \mid A)$ versus $P(X \mid A)$.
3. Characterize fundamental obstructions (e.g., when $Q$ places mass on attribute regions poorly covered by training data) and propose diagnostics that detect when realistic tuning is infeasible.

Let $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ denote the space of feasible trajectories of a networked system (for example, sequences of packet arrivals, throughput measurements, or system-resource time series). Suppose there is a deterministic or stochastic simulator $S:\mathcal{U}	o\mathcal{X}$ that, given control inputs $u\in\mathcal{U}$, produces outputs respecting hard physical or protocol-level constraints encoded by a constraint set $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{X}$ (e.g., causality, conservation of bytes, queueing dynamics, link-capacity limits), so that $S(u)\in\mathcal{C}$ for all $u$. Let $\mu^*$ be an unknown distribution over $\mathcal{C}$ from which a finite sample of real networked time series is drawn.

Design a generative-adversarial framework consisting of a generator $G_	heta$, a discriminator $D_\phi$, and a coupling with the simulator $S$, together with a training objective
$$\min_	heta \max_\phi \; \mathcal{L}(G_	heta, D_\phi, S),$$
such that the induced distribution $\mu_	heta$ of generated samples satisfies the following simultaneously:

1. (Hard-constraint satisfaction) $\mathrm{supp}(\mu_	heta)\subseteq\mathcal{C}$, i.e., every generated trajectory is physically/protocol-feasible.
2. (Statistical fidelity) $\mu_	heta$ converges, in an appropriate metric (e.g., Wasserstein distance or Jensen–Shannon divergence) restricted to $\mathcal{C}$, to $\mu^*$ as the sample size and capacity grow.
3. (Strict improvement) On at least one realistic networked time-series benchmark, the framework strictly improves over both (a) a pure GAN trained without the simulator and (b) the simulator $S$ alone, with respect to a fixed downstream utility metric.

Provide such a construction together with a proof (or principled empirical demonstration) that conditions 1–3 can be met, or show that no GAN-with-simulator coupling can simultaneously achieve all three.

Suppose there is a deterministic or stochastic simulator $S:\mathcal{U}	o\mathcal{X}$ that, given control inputs $u\in\mathcal{U}$, produces outputs respecting hard physical or protocol-level constraints encoded by a constraint set $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{X}$ (e.g., causality, conservation of bytes, queueing dynamics, link-capacity limits), so that $S(u)\in\mathcal{C}$ for all $u$. Let $\mu^*$ be an unknown distribution over $\mathcal{C}$ from which a finite sample of real networked time series is drawn.

Design a generative-adversarial framework consisting of a generator $G_	heta$, a discriminator $D_\phi$, and a coupling with the simulator $S$, together with a training objective
$$\min_	heta \max_\phi \; \mathcal{L}(G_	heta, D_\phi, S),$$
such that the induced distribution $\mu_	heta$ of generated samples satisfies the following simultaneously:

1. (Hard-constraint satisfaction) $\mathrm{supp}(\mu_	heta)\subseteq\mathcal{C}$, i.e., every generated trajectory is physically/protocol-feasible.
2. (Statistical fidelity) $\mu_	heta$ converges, in an appropriate metric (e.g., Wasserstein distance or Jensen–Shannon divergence) restricted to $\mathcal{C}$, to $\mu^*$ as the sample size and capacity grow.
3. (Strict improvement) On at least one realistic networked time-series benchmark, the framework strictly improves over both (a) a pure GAN trained without the simulator and (b) the simulator $S$ alone, with respect to a fixed downstream utility metric.

Provide such a construction together with a proof (or principled empirical demonstration) that conditions 1–3 can be met, or show that no GAN-with-simulator coupling can simultaneously achieve all three.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is a forward-looking research direction about combining GAN training with physics/protocol-aware simulators for networked time-series data generation. Subsequent work on simulator-in-the-loop and physics-informed GANs (e.g., physics-informed GANs, Sim2Real GANs, hybrid model-based generative models) has explored related ideas, but no definitive, general framework specifically resolving the combination for networked-systems data with guaranteed constraint satisfaction and statistical fidelity has been established. The problem appears to remain an open research direction.

Setting. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a distribution over multivariate time series $x = (x_1,\dots,x_T) \in \mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ optionally accompanied by metadata $m \in \mathcal{M}$. A generator is a (possibly randomized) map $G_\theta$ taking a noise seed $z$ (and optionally metadata) to a synthetic sample. A training mechanism $\mathcal{A}$ takes a dataset $S = \{(x^{(i)}, m^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^n \sim \mathcal{D}^n$ and outputs trained parameters $\theta = \mathcal{A}(S)$.

Differential privacy. The mechanism $\mathcal{A}$ is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if, for any two datasets $S, S'$ differing in a single record and every measurable set $E$ of parameter outputs,
$$\Pr[\mathcal{A}(S) \in E] \le e^{\varepsilon}\, \Pr[\mathcal{A}(S') \in E] + \delta.$$

Fidelity. Fix a finite collection of statistics $\mathcal{T} = \{T_1,\dots,T_K\}$ where each $T_k$ maps a dataset of time series to a value in a metric space $(\mathcal{Y}_k, \rho_k)$ (e.g.\ marginal distributions, autocorrelation functions, cross-feature joint distributions, downstream classifier accuracy). For a real dataset $S$ and synthetic dataset $\tilde S$ generated by $G_\theta$, define the fidelity gap
$$\mathrm{Fid}(\theta; S) = \max_{1\le k\le K} \rho_k\!\big(T_k(S),\, T_k(\tilde S)\big).$$

Question. Does there exist a training mechanism $\mathcal{A}$ for time-series generative adversarial networks that is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private with meaningful parameters (say $\varepsilon = O(1)$ and $\delta = o(1/n)$), and such that for natural classes of networked time-series distributions $\mathcal{D}$ the expected fidelity gap $\mathbb{E}_{S\sim \mathcal{D}^n}[\mathrm{Fid}(\mathcal{A}(S); S)]$ converges to that of a comparable non-private GAN as $n \to \infty$?

Equivalently: can differentially private GAN mechanisms for time-series generation be improved enough to provide meaningful privacy guarantees without collapsing the fidelity of the generated data on standard fidelity metrics?

Consider the problem of releasing a synthetic version of a networked time-series dataset $D = \{X^{(1)}, X^{(2)}, \ldots, X^{(n)}\}$, where each sample $X^{(i)} = (x^{(i)}_1, \ldots, x^{(i)}_T)$ is a multivariate time series (together with optional categorical metadata) that may aggregate or summarize the activity of many distinct users, devices, or entities, rather than corresponding to a single individual. Recall that a randomized mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ acting on databases is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if for every pair of databases $D, D'$ that differ in a single record and every measurable set $S$ in the output space,
$$\Pr[\mathcal{M}(D) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\, \Pr[\mathcal{M}(D') \in S] + \delta.$$
The standard "single-record" granularity of differential privacy implicitly assumes that one record corresponds to one individual whose privacy is to be protected.

Question: For networked time-series datasets of the type above, in which a single released sample $X^{(i)}$ can encode behavior of many users or entities simultaneously, formulate and decide whether differential privacy (in any of its standard variants: record-level, user-level, group, Rényi, or local DP) is an appropriate privacy metric for the data-sharing problem. Specifically, either
(a) exhibit a precise formal threat model on networked time-series data and a corresponding granularity of DP that provably captures the desired notion of "no individual entity's data is leaked," together with achievability and utility guarantees; or
(b) prove an impossibility / inadequacy result showing that no standard DP variant (with reasonable parameters and granularity) simultaneously protects all entities summarized within a single record while preserving sufficient utility for typical downstream tasks (e.g., distributional fidelity of inter-arrival times, flow sizes, or correlations across the network).

This is a conceptual/methodological open question about the appropriateness of differential privacy for aggregated networked time-series data. The literature on DP for time-series and network data continues to grow (e.g., user-level DP, event-level DP, pan-privacy, and recent work on DP for synthetic time-series via GANs and diffusion models), but no consensus has emerged that DP, in any standard granularity, is the "right" metric when a single record summarizes many entities. The question remains open as a research direction.

Consider the setting in which a data holder possesses a dataset of networked time series, i.e., a collection of multivariate sequences {X_i = (X_i^{(1)}, X_i^{(2)}, ..., X_i^{(T_i)})}_{i=1}^N indexed by entities in a network (each X_i^{(t)} ∈ R^d, possibly accompanied by static attributes A_i ∈ R^k). The holder wishes to release a synthetic dataset {Ŷ_j}_{j=1}^M produced by a generative adversarial network (GAN) trained on {X_i, A_i} so that downstream parties may perform analyses (e.g., distributional fidelity of marginals, autocorrelations, cross-series correlations, and rare-event statistics) without compromising the privacy of contributing entities.

Recall that a randomized release mechanism M satisfies (ε, δ)-differential privacy if for every pair of datasets D, D' differing in a single entity's record and every measurable set S of outputs, Pr[M(D) ∈ S] ≤ e^ε · Pr[M(D') ∈ S] + δ. Empirically, training GANs under (ε, δ)-DP with practically meaningful (ε, δ) typically degrades fidelity of long, high-dimensional networked time series substantially.

Problem. Propose and rigorously formalize a privacy metric P (a functional on pairs (training distribution, release mechanism)) suitable for evaluating GAN-based releases of networked time-series data, satisfying all of the following desiderata:
(a) P admits a precise mathematical definition with explicit adversarial threat model (specifying adversary knowledge, queries, and success criterion).
(b) P composes under repeated or sequential releases in a quantifiable way.
(c) P is post-processing robust: applying any data-independent function to the release does not decrease privacy as measured by P.
(d) P captures protection against the principal attacks relevant to time-series releases—membership inference, attribute inference of static attributes A_i, and trace/trajectory reconstruction of X_i—via provable reductions.
(e) P is empirically estimable from a trained GAN and a finite training set with computable confidence bounds.
(f) Under P, there exist non-trivial GAN training procedures that achieve a quantitatively meaningful privacy level while preserving utility (measured by a stated set of statistical functionals of the time series) strictly better than what is achievable under (ε, δ)-differential privacy at comparable utility.

Provide such a metric P, prove items (a)–(d), give an estimator with finite-sample guarantees for (e), and exhibit a training algorithm with a theorem establishing (f), or prove that no metric can simultaneously satisfy (a)–(f).

The question is a broad open research direction concerning alternative privacy notions for GAN-generated networked time series. Subsequent literature has proposed candidate metrics (e.g., membership-inference-based audits, attribute-inference resistance, plausible deniability, Rényi DP, f-DP, and similarity-based heuristics), but no single metric has been established as a definitive replacement for differential privacy with the stated combination of properties for time-series GANs. The general problem remains open.

Consider a system of $N$ stateful agents indexed by $i \in \{1,\dots,N\}$, each evolving in discrete time $t = 1,\dots,T$. Each agent $i$ has a hidden state $s^{(i)}_t \in \mathcal{S}$, an observable measurement $x^{(i)}_t \in \mathcal{X}$, and an associated time-invariant attribute $a^{(i)} \in \mathcal{A}$. The agents are coupled through a (possibly time-varying) interaction graph $G_t = (V, E_t)$ on $V = \{1,\dots,N\}$, and the joint dynamics satisfy a causal update rule of the form
$$ s^{(i)}_{t+1} = f\!\left(s^{(i)}_t,\; \{x^{(j)}_t : (j,i) \in E_t\},\; a^{(i)},\; \xi^{(i)}_t\right), \qquad x^{(i)}_t = g\!\left(s^{(i)}_t,\; \eta^{(i)}_t\right), $$
for some unknown stochastic functions $f, g$ and independent noise variables $\xi^{(i)}_t, \eta^{(i)}_t$. A dataset $\mathcal{D}$ consists of i.i.d. realizations of the full collection $\bigl(\{a^{(i)}\}_i, \{x^{(i)}_t\}_{i,t}\bigr)$.

Design a generative model — extending the architecture of generative adversarial networks for mixed attribute/time-series data (in which a generator first produces per-agent attributes from noise and then unrolls a per-agent recurrent network to emit a measurement sequence, trained against a pair of discriminators on attributes and on full trajectories) — that takes $\mathcal{D}$ as training data and produces synthetic samples whose joint distribution over $\bigl(\{a^{(i)}\}_i, \{x^{(i)}_t\}_{i,t}\bigr)$ faithfully reproduces:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the marginal per-agent attribute and trajectory distributions,
\item the cross-agent dependencies induced by the latent interaction graph $\{G_t\}$, and
\item the causal temporal dependencies in which agent $i$'s behavior at time $t+1$ depends on the behaviors of its neighbors at times $\leq t$.
\end{enumerate}
Provide an explicit architecture and training objective, together with theoretical guarantees (e.g., consistency, identifiability of the interaction structure, or fidelity bounds on multi-agent statistics) under stated assumptions on $f, g$ and the graph process. In particular, determine whether such guarantees are achievable when the graph $\{G_t\}$ is unobserved and must be inferred from the data alone.

The problem of extending DoppelGANger-style synthetic data generation to multi-agent networking datasets with causal inter-agent dependencies is described as an open challenge. Subsequent work has explored related directions (e.g., graph-based or multi-agent time-series GANs), but no published method to date provides a comprehensive, theoretically-grounded extension that handles causal interactions among stateful agents in networking traces. The problem appears to remain open.

Consider a networked system that produces multivariate time series data, where each trace records the temporal behavior of agents (e.g., flows, users, devices) interacting through shared infrastructure. Suppose a generative model G (such as a GAN) has been trained on observed traces drawn from a joint distribution P(X, C), where X denotes the time series and C denotes auxiliary system parameters or conditions (e.g., topology, link capacities, traffic mix, protocol settings). Standard conditional generation can produce samples X ~ G(· | C) for values of C represented in the training data.

Now suppose a practitioner wishes to perform "what-if" analysis: predict and synthesize plausible time series for a modified system specified by a new condition C' that represents an intervention (for example, changing routing, introducing a new protocol, scaling the user population, or altering link capacities). When the intervention is small, one might hope that the learned conditional distribution P(X | C) extrapolates to C'; however, when the intervention is large, the original conditional distributions become invalid because the underlying physical/networking dynamics are themselves altered.

Formulate and solve the following problem:

(a) Provide a principled framework that combines a learned generative model of agent-level or fine-grained behavior with an explicit mechanistic / physical-system simulator of the network so that, given an intervention C' outside the training distribution, the framework produces synthetic time series whose joint distribution faithfully approximates the true post-intervention distribution P*(X | do(C')).

(b) Specify identifiability conditions on the decomposition (which aspects of behavior are modeled by G versus by the simulator) under which the resulting hybrid generator is consistent as the amount of pre-intervention training data grows.

(c) Develop quantitative evaluation criteria — beyond marginal or conditional fidelity on observed C — for assessing the accuracy of synthetic data produced under counterfactual interventions C', and demonstrate the framework on a concrete networked time-series setting.

Let $X$ be a Banach space (the state space) and $U$ a normed space of input values, and let $\mathcal{U}$ be a space of admissible input functions $u:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to U$. Consider a control system $\Sigma$ with state trajectories $x(\cdot;x_0,u)\in X$ defined for initial state $x_0\in X$ and input $u\in\mathcal{U}$. Recall the comparison-function classes $\mathcal{K}$, $\mathcal{K}_\infty$, and $\mathcal{KL}$.

A continuous functional $V:X\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ that is locally Lipschitz on $X\setminus\{0\}$ and satisfies
$$\psi_1(\|x\|_X)\leq V(x)\leq \psi_2(\|x\|_X),\qquad \forall x\in X,$$
for some $\psi_1,\psi_2\in\mathcal{K}_\infty$, is called:

(a) an ISS Lyapunov function in dissipative form for $\Sigma$ if there exist $\alpha\in\mathcal{K}_\infty$ and $\sigma\in\mathcal{K}$ such that for almost every $t\geq 0$, along every trajectory,
$$\dot V(x(t))\leq -\alpha(\|x(t)\|_X)+\sigma(\|u(t)\|_U);$$

(b) an ISS Lyapunov function in implication form for $\Sigma$ if there exist $\chi\in\mathcal{K}$ and $\alpha\in\mathcal{K}_\infty$ such that
$$\|x\|_X\geq \chi(\|u(t)\|_U)\;\Longrightarrow\;\dot V(x(t))\leq -\alpha(\|x(t)\|_X).$$

It is straightforward that (a) implies (b). For finite-dimensional ODE systems with sufficient regularity, the converse also holds (the two notions are equivalent).

Question: Is it true, for every infinite-dimensional control system $\Sigma$ on a Banach space $X$ (in a suitable general class encompassing well-posed evolution equations), that the existence of an ISS Lyapunov function in implication form implies the existence of an ISS Lyapunov function in dissipative form, without imposing restrictive additional regularity or structural assumptions on $\Sigma$ or $V$?

Setting. Let $X$ be a Banach space (the state space) with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $U$ be a normed space of input values, and let $\mathcal{U}$ be a space of admissible input functions $u:\mathbb{R}_+\to U$ equipped with a norm $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{U}}$. Consider a (generally nonlinear, infinite-dimensional) control system $\Sigma=(X,\mathcal{U},\phi)$, where $\phi(t,x,u)\in X$ denotes the state at time $t\ge 0$ starting from $x\in X$ under input $u\in\mathcal{U}$, and $\phi$ satisfies the standard axioms of a control system (identity, causality, cocycle property, continuity).

Comparison-function classes. $\mathcal{K}$ is the set of continuous strictly increasing functions $\alpha:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{R}_+$ with $\alpha(0)=0$; $\mathcal{K}_\infty$ consists of unbounded $\mathcal{K}$-functions; $\mathcal{KL}$ is the set of functions $\beta(\cdot,\cdot)$ that are $\mathcal{K}$ in the first argument and decreasing to $0$ in the second.

Local input-to-state stability (LISS). $\Sigma$ is called LISS if there exist $r>0$, $\beta\in\mathcal{KL}$, and $\gamma\in\mathcal{K}$ such that for all $x\in X$ with $\|x\|_X\le r$ and all $u\in\mathcal{U}$ with $\|u\|_{\mathcal{U}}\le r$,
$$\|\phi(t,x,u)\|_X\le \beta(\|x\|_X,t)+\gamma(\|u\|_{\mathcal{U}}),\qquad t\ge 0.$$

Non-coercive ISS Lyapunov functions. A continuous functional $V:D\to\mathbb{R}_+$, defined on an open neighborhood $D\subset X$ of $0$, is called a non-coercive Lyapunov function if there exist $\psi_2\in\mathcal{K}_\infty$ such that
$$0\le V(x)\le \psi_2(\|x\|_X)\qquad\text{for all }x\in D,$$
(no lower bound $\psi_1(\|x\|_X)\le V(x)$ is required; coercive Lyapunov functions are those that additionally satisfy such a lower bound).

Two forms of the infinitesimal decay condition (with Dini derivative $\dot V_u(x):=\limsup_{t\to 0^+}\tfrac{1}{t}(V(\phi(t,x,u))-V(x))$):
- Dissipative form: there exist $\alpha\in\mathcal{K}_\infty$ and $\sigma\in\mathcal{K}$ such that $\dot V_u(x)\le -\alpha(\|x\|_X)+\sigma(\|u\|_{\mathcal{U}})$.
- Implication form: there exist $\rho,\alpha\in\mathcal{K}_\infty$ such that $\|x\|_X\ge \rho(\|u\|_{\mathcal{U}})\ \Rightarrow\ \dot V_u(x)\le -\alpha(\|x\|_X)$.

Problem. Develop non-coercive Lyapunov criteria for LISS of infinite-dimensional control systems. Specifically:

(a) Prove that the existence of a non-coercive Lyapunov function $V$ on a neighborhood $D$ of $0$ satisfying the dissipative-form decay only locally (for $\|x\|_X,\|u\|_{\mathcal{U}}$ small) implies that $\Sigma$ is LISS.

(b) Establish an analogous LISS criterion when the non-coercive Lyapunov function is given in implication form.

(c) In the global case, prove that the existence of a non-coercive ISS Lyapunov function in implication form implies that $\Sigma$ is ISS.

Identify natural regularity/admissibility hypotheses on $\Sigma$ (e.g., the BRS, CEP, or robust-equilibrium properties used in infinite-dimensional ISS theory) under which the implications above hold, or exhibit counterexamples showing that without such hypotheses they fail.

Setup. Let $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ be a Banach space (the state space) and $(U,\|\cdot\|_U)$ a normed space of admissible input values; let $\mathcal{U}$ be a normed space of admissible input functions $u:\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\to U$ (e.g. $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0},U)$) endowed with norm $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{U}}$. Consider a forward complete control system $\Sigma$ on $X$ with input space $\mathcal{U}$, whose solution starting from $x\in X$ under input $u\in\mathcal{U}$ is denoted $\phi(t,x,u)$, defined for all $t\ge 0$ on the relevant domain.

Recall that a function $\gamma:\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ is of class $\mathcal{K}$ if it is continuous, strictly increasing, and $\gamma(0)=0$; it is of class $\mathcal{K}_\infty$ if additionally $\gamma(r)\to\infty$ as $r\to\infty$. A function $\beta:\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ is of class $\mathcal{KL}$ if $\beta(\cdot,t)\in\mathcal{K}$ for each fixed $t\ge 0$ and $\beta(r,t)\downarrow 0$ as $t\to\infty$ for each fixed $r\ge 0$.

The system $\Sigma$ is called locally input-to-state stable (LISS) if there exist $\beta\in\mathcal{KL}$, $\gamma\in\mathcal{K}$, and constants $\rho_x,\rho_u>0$ such that for all $x\in X$ with $\|x\|_X\le \rho_x$ and all $u\in\mathcal{U}$ with $\|u\|_{\mathcal{U}}\le \rho_u$, the trajectory $\phi(\cdot,x,u)$ exists for all $t\ge 0$ and satisfies
$$\|\phi(t,x,u)\|_X \;\le\; \beta(\|x\|_X,t) + \gamma(\|u\|_{\mathcal{U}}), \qquad t\ge 0. \tag{$\ast$}$$

More generally, given $\beta\in\mathcal{KL}$ and $\gamma\in\mathcal{K}$, define the validity region
$$R(\beta,\gamma)\;:=\;\bigl\{(x,u)\in X\times\mathcal{U} : \phi(\cdot,x,u)\text{ is global and }(\ast)\text{ holds for all }t\ge 0\bigr\}.$$

Problem. Develop a method that, beyond merely asserting the existence of some neighborhood of $(0,0)\in X\times\mathcal{U}$ contained in $R(\beta,\gamma)$, yields explicit, usable lower bounds on $R(\beta,\gamma)$ for a given LISS infinite-dimensional system $\Sigma$ and given comparison functions $\beta,\gamma$. In particular, produce constructive estimates (for instance via Lyapunov-type or other functional-analytic techniques) of the largest sublevel-style set $\{(x,u)\in X\times\mathcal{U} : \|x\|_X\le r_x,\ \|u\|_{\mathcal{U}}\le r_u\}\subset R(\beta,\gamma)$, and more generally describe quantitatively the shape of $R(\beta,\gamma)$ in $X\times\mathcal{U}$.

Setup. Consider control systems of the form
  ẋ(t) = Ax(t) + f(x(t), u(t)),    x(t) ∈ X,  u ∈ U_c,
where X is a Banach space (the state space), U_c is a space of admissible input functions u: [0, ∞) → U taking values in a Banach space U (typically L^∞ or piecewise continuous functions), and the dynamics are given either by

(a) a general nonlinear evolution equation, where A generates a strongly continuous semigroup on X and f: X × U → X (or, more generally, into an extrapolation space) is a nonlinear term ensuring well-posedness of mild solutions, or

(b) a general linear boundary control system, written abstractly as
  ẋ(t) = 𝔄 x(t),    𝔅 x(t) = u(t),
where 𝔄: D(𝔄) ⊂ X → X is a closed linear operator, 𝔅: D(𝔄) → U is a boundary operator, and (𝔄, 𝔅) generates a well-posed boundary control system in the sense of Salamon–Weiss.

Definitions. Let 𝒦 = { γ: ℝ_{≥0} → ℝ_{≥0} : continuous, strictly increasing, γ(0)=0 }, 𝒦_∞ the subclass of unbounded such functions, and 𝒦𝓛 the class of functions β(r,t) that are 𝒦 in r and decay to 0 in t. The system is called input-to-state stable (ISS) if there exist β ∈ 𝒦𝓛 and γ ∈ 𝒦_∞ such that, for every initial state x_0 ∈ X and every admissible input u,
  ‖x(t; x_0, u)‖_X ≤ β(‖x_0‖_X, t) + γ(‖u‖_{[0,t]})    for all t ≥ 0.

A continuous function V: X → ℝ_{≥0} is called an ISS Lyapunov function if there exist ψ_1, ψ_2 ∈ 𝒦_∞, α ∈ 𝒦_∞, and χ ∈ 𝒦 such that
  ψ_1(‖x‖) ≤ V(x) ≤ ψ_2(‖x‖)    for all x ∈ X,
and along solutions
  ‖x‖ ≥ χ(‖u‖)   ⟹   V̇(x, u) ≤ −α(‖x‖),
where V̇ is the appropriate (Dini or Lie) derivative along the system.

Problem. Prove (or disprove) the following converse ISS Lyapunov theorems:

(1) For the general nonlinear class (a): if the system is ISS, then there exists a (coercive, possibly Lipschitz continuous) ISS Lyapunov function V: X → ℝ_{≥0}.

(2) For general linear boundary control systems (b): if the system is ISS (with respect to a suitable norm on the input space), then there exists an ISS Lyapunov function V on X.

Determine, in each case, the strongest regularity (continuity, local Lipschitz continuity, smoothness) and the structural form (coercive vs. non-coercive, quadratic when applicable) of the ISS Lyapunov function that can be guaranteed.

Setup. Let $X$ and $U$ be Banach spaces, and consider a linear control system
$$\dot x(t) = A x(t) + B u(t), \qquad x(0) = x_0 \in X, \qquad t \geq 0,$$
where $A : D(A) \subset X \to X$ generates a strongly continuous semigroup $(T(t))_{t\ge 0}$ on $X$ and $B \in \mathcal{L}(U, X_{-1})$ is a (possibly) unbounded admissible control operator, with $X_{-1}$ the usual extrapolation space associated with $A$. For an admissible input space $\mathcal{U} = L^\infty(\mathbb{R}_+, U)$, the mild solution is
$$x(t; x_0, u) = T(t) x_0 + \int_0^t T_{-1}(t-s) B u(s)\, ds \in X.$$

Definitions.
1. The system is input-to-state stable (ISS) with respect to $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}_+, U)$ if there exist $\beta \in \mathcal{KL}$ and $\gamma \in \mathcal{K}_\infty$ such that for every $x_0 \in X$ and every $u \in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}_+, U)$,
$$\|x(t; x_0, u)\|_X \leq \beta(\|x_0\|_X, t) + \gamma(\|u\|_{L^\infty(0,t;U)}), \qquad t \ge 0.$$
2. The system is integral input-to-state stable (iISS) with respect to $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}_+, U)$ if there exist $\beta \in \mathcal{KL}$ and $\theta, \mu \in \mathcal{K}_\infty$ such that for every $x_0 \in X$ and every $u \in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}_+, U)$,
$$\|x(t; x_0, u)\|_X \leq \beta(\|x_0\|_X, t) + \theta\!\left(\int_0^t \mu(\|u(s)\|_U)\, ds\right), \qquad t \ge 0.$$

It is known that, in this setting, iISS with respect to $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}_+, U)$ implies ISS with respect to $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}_+, U)$.

Question. For linear infinite-dimensional systems of the above form with possibly unbounded admissible control operator $B$, does ISS with respect to $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}_+, U)$ imply iISS with respect to $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}_+, U)$?

Consider a linear infinite-dimensional control system of the form
  ẋ(t) = A x(t) + B u(t),  x(0) = x₀ ∈ X,
where X is a Banach space, A: D(A) ⊂ X → X generates a strongly continuous semigroup (T(t))_{t≥0} on X, and B: U → X_{-1} is a (possibly unbounded) linear input operator with values in the extrapolation space X_{-1}, U being a Banach space of input values. Inputs u are taken from L^∞(0,∞;U) (or another suitable input space).

The system is called input-to-state stable (ISS) if there exist β ∈ KL and γ ∈ K such that for every initial state x₀ ∈ X and every admissible input u,
  ‖x(t; x₀, u)‖_X ≤ β(‖x₀‖_X, t) + γ(‖u‖_∞)   for all t ≥ 0.

A continuous functional V: X → [0,∞) is called a non-coercive ISS Lyapunov function if there exist α ∈ K_∞, ψ_2 ∈ K_∞, ρ ∈ K, and α_3 > 0 (or a positive definite α_3) such that
  ψ_1(‖x‖) ≤ V(x) ≤ ψ_2(‖x‖)   with ψ_1 only positive definite (not necessarily of class K_∞),
and the Dini derivative along trajectories satisfies V̇(x,u) ≤ −α_3(‖x‖) + ρ(‖u‖). It is called a coercive ISS Lyapunov function if additionally ψ_1 ∈ K_∞.

The operator B is called admissible (for (T(t))) if there exist t > 0 and c > 0 such that ∫₀^t T(t−s) B u(s) ds ∈ X with norm ≤ c‖u‖_{L^p(0,t;U)} for all u.

Address the following questions, providing proofs or counterexamples:
(a) Does ISS of the system always imply the existence of a (coercive or at least non-coercive) ISS Lyapunov function?
(b) Does the heat equation
  x_t = x_{xx} on (0,1), x(t,0) = u(t), x(t,1) = 0,
viewed as an ISS system in X = L^2(0,1) with Dirichlet boundary input, admit a coercive ISS Lyapunov function? More generally, do systems governed by analytic semigroups whose generators have unbounded spectrum admit coercive ISS Lyapunov functions?
(c) Do there exist linear ISS control systems with unbounded admissible input operators that admit non-coercive ISS Lyapunov functions but no coercive ISS Lyapunov function?
(d) Can admissibility of the input operator B (relative to an exponentially stable semigroup) be characterized in terms of existence of an appropriate Lyapunov-type functional?

Substantial progress has been made on each sub-question but the program is not fully complete. Non-coercive ISS Lyapunov functions for linear systems with unbounded admissible input operators (including the Dirichlet heat equation) were constructed by Jacob, Mironchenko, Partington, Wirth (SICON, 2020). Recent work on quadratic ISS Lyapunov functions for linear analytic systems (2023) and on coercive ISS-Lyapunov functionals via the regular-systems framework (MCSS, 2025), as well as generalized Lyapunov functionals (Automatica, 2024), give positive answers for several classes including the Dirichlet heat equation, but a complete general Lyapunov theory and a Lyapunov characterization of admissibility remain not fully settled.

Consider the viscous Burgers equation on the spatial interval $(0,1)$ with boundary control:
$$x_t(t,z) = \mu\, x_{zz}(t,z) - \nu\, x(t,z)\, x_z(t,z), \qquad t>0,\ z\in(0,1),$$
$$x(t,0) = 0, \qquad x(t,1) = u(t), \qquad t \ge 0,$$
with constants $\mu>0$, $\nu>0$, initial condition $x(0,\cdot)\in L^2(0,1)$, and input $u$ in the space $PC_b(\mathbb{R}_+,\mathbb{R})$ of bounded piecewise-continuous real-valued functions on $\mathbb{R}_+$, equipped with the supremum norm.

The system is called input-to-state stable (ISS) with respect to the state space $X := L^2(0,1)$ and the input space $\mathcal{U} := PC_b(\mathbb{R}_+,\mathbb{R})$ if there exist functions $\beta \in \mathcal{KL}$ and $\gamma \in \mathcal{K}$ such that for every initial state $x_0 \in L^2(0,1)$ and every input $u \in \mathcal{U}$ the corresponding (mild) solution satisfies
$$\|x(t,\cdot)\|_{L^2(0,1)} \le \beta\bigl(\|x_0\|_{L^2(0,1)},\, t\bigr) + \gamma\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty}\bigr) \qquad \text{for all } t \ge 0,$$
with no a priori restriction on the magnitude of $\|x_0\|_{L^2(0,1)}$ or $\|u\|_{\infty}$.

Question: Prove or disprove that the above boundary-controlled viscous Burgers equation is input-to-state stable in this sense, without any restriction on the magnitude of inputs (or, more generally, decide ISS for some other natural input space in place of $PC_b(\mathbb{R}_+,\mathbb{R})$).

Consider an infinite network of interconnected control systems indexed by a countable set $I$. Each subsystem $\Sigma_i$ has state $x_i$ in some Banach space, an external input $u_i$, and is interconnected with the other subsystems through nonlinear gains $\gamma_{ij}\in\mathcal{K}_\infty\cup\{0\}$ that quantify the influence of $x_j$ on $x_i$. Assume each $\Sigma_i$ is input-to-state stable (ISS) with respect to its inputs and to the states of its neighbors, with gains $\gamma_{ij}$.

Form the (in general infinite-dimensional) nonlinear monotone gain operator
$$\Gamma:\ell_+^\infty(I)	o \ell_+^\infty(I),\qquad \Gamma(s)_i=\sup_{j\in I}\gamma_{ij}(s_j),$$
and consider the following candidate small-gain conditions on $\Gamma$:

(a) Spectral small-gain condition: $r(\Gamma)<1$ in an appropriate spectral-radius sense for monotone (sub-)linear maps.

(b) Robust strong small-gain condition: there exists $ho\in\mathcal{K}_\infty$ such that $D_ho\circ\Gamma$ has a suitable global stability property, where $D_ho(s)=((\mathrm{id}+ho)(s_i))_i$.

(c) Existence of an $\Omega$-path: a continuous, componentwise strictly increasing path $\sigma:[0,\infty)	o\ell_+^\infty(I)$ with $\sigma(0)=0$, $\sigma(r)	o\infty$ as $r	o\infty$, such that $\Gamma(\sigma(r))<\sigma(r)$ componentwise for all $r>0$.

(d) Monotone invertibility of $\mathrm{id}-\Gamma$: for every $w\in\ell_+^\infty(I)$, the inequality $v\le \Gamma(v)+w$ implies $v\le\chi(\|w\|)\mathbf{1}$ for some $\chi\in\mathcal{K}_\infty$ (equivalently a monotone bounded invertibility property of $\mathrm{id}-\Gamma$).

Problem. (i) Determine the precise logical relationships (implications, equivalences, and counterexamples) among conditions (a)–(d) for infinite networks (it is known that for finite networks under standard assumptions they are essentially equivalent). (ii) Using these relationships, formulate and prove ISS small-gain theorems for infinite networks of interconnected ISS systems with general nonlinear gains $\gamma_{ij}$, giving conditions on $\Gamma$ that guarantee ISS of the whole interconnection (in trajectory and/or Lyapunov form).

Substantial progress has been made since the question was posed. Kawan, Mironchenko, Noroozi, Schwenninger, Zamani and collaborators (e.g., "Nonlinear small-gain theorems for ISS of infinite interconnections", MCSS 2021/2022; "A Lyapunov-based ISS small-gain theorem for infinite networks of nonlinear systems", arXiv:2103.07439; "ISS small-gain criteria for infinite networks with linear gains", 2021; and "The small-gain condition for infinite networks modeled on $\ell^\infty$-spaces", arXiv:2503.03925) have clarified key relationships: the monotone limit property, uniform small-gain condition, and monotone bounded invertibility of $\mathrm{id}-\Gamma$ are equivalent in broad settings, and existence of a path of strict decay (Ω-path) yields trajectory- and Lyapunov-based ISS small-gain theorems for countable networks. Consider time-delay control systems regarded as infinite-dimensional dynamical systems. Fix a finite delay r>0 and a state space X of functions on [-r,0] (e.g. C([-r,0];R^n) or L^∞([-r,0];R^n)), and consider systems of the form
    ẋ(t) = f(x_t, u(t)),    t ≥ 0,
where x_t(θ) := x(t+θ) for θ ∈ [-r,0], u: [0,∞) → R^m is a measurable essentially bounded input, and f satisfies standard regularity assumptions ensuring local existence and uniqueness of solutions.

Define the following properties:
  (FC) Forward completeness: for every initial state x_0 ∈ X and every admissible input u, the solution exists for all t ≥ 0.
  (BRS) Bounded reachability sets: for every T > 0 and every R > 0, the set {x_t : t ∈ [0,T], ‖x_0‖_X ≤ R, ‖u‖_∞ ≤ R} is bounded in X.
  (LIM) Limit property: there exists γ ∈ K_∞ such that for every x_0 ∈ X and every input u, liminf_{t→∞} ‖x(t)‖ ≤ γ(‖u‖_∞).
  (ULIM) Uniform limit property: there exists γ ∈ K_∞ such that for every ε > 0 and every R > 0 there is τ = τ(ε,R) with the property that for every ‖x_0‖_X ≤ R and every input u, there exists t ≤ τ with ‖x(t)‖ ≤ γ(‖u‖_∞) + ε.

Questions:
(a) For time-delay systems on a given state space X, is (FC) equivalent to (BRS)?
(b) For time-delay systems, is (LIM) equivalent to (ULIM)?
(c) More generally, do time-delay systems admit strictly tighter input-to-state stability (ISS) characterizations than those provided by the general infinite-dimensional ISS superposition theorem?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent research has partially resolved part (a). On the state space C([-r,0];R^n) of continuous functions, forward completeness has been shown NOT to imply boundedness of reachability sets, with explicit counterexamples (Chaillet, Pepe, Mironchenko, Wirth, 2023). On the state space L^∞([-r,0];R^n) of essentially bounded measurable functions, forward completeness DOES imply bounded reachability sets (Mironchenko, Chaillet, Pepe, Wirth, 2024, IEEE TAC). Parts (b) and (c) regarding LIM vs ULIM equivalence and the existence of tighter ISS characterizations for time-delay systems beyond the general superposition theorem remain, to our knowledge, open.

Consider a retarded nonlinear time-delay system of the form
    ẋ(t) = f(x_t, u(t)),    t ≥ 0,
where, for some maximum delay r > 0, the state history is x_t ∈ C([−r,0]; ℝ^n) defined by x_t(θ) = x(t+θ), the input u: [0,∞) → U takes values in a normed input space (U, |·|_U) and is locally essentially bounded, and f: C([−r,0]; ℝ^n) × U → ℝ^n is locally Lipschitz and ensures forward completeness of solutions. The system is called input-to-state stable (ISS) if there exist β ∈ KL and γ ∈ K_∞ such that
    |x(t)| ≤ β(‖x_0‖_C, t) + γ(‖u‖_{L^∞(0,t;U)})
for every initial condition x_0 ∈ C([−r,0]; ℝ^n), every admissible input u, and every t ≥ 0.

Let V: C([−r,0]; ℝ^n) → ℝ_{≥0} be a continuous Lyapunov–Krasovskii functional that is locally Lipschitz on bounded sets, and assume there exist ψ_1, ψ_2 ∈ K_∞ with
    ψ_1(|φ(0)|) ≤ V(φ) ≤ ψ_2(‖φ‖_C)    for all φ ∈ C([−r,0]; ℝ^n).
For an absolutely continuous solution x(·) corresponding to input u, denote by V̇_u(x_t) the upper-right Dini derivative of t ↦ V(x_t) along trajectories.

Question. Do there exist α, χ ∈ K_∞ such that the pointwise dissipation implication
    |x(0)| ≥ χ(‖u‖_U)    ⟹    V̇_u(x_t) ≤ −α(|x(0)|)
(where |x(0)| denotes the magnitude of the current state value x_t(0) and ‖u‖_U denotes the essential supremum norm of the input) is by itself sufficient to imply that the system is ISS? Equivalently, can the standard Lyapunov–Krasovskii sufficient condition
    V(x_t) ≥ χ(|u(t)|)    ⟹    V̇_u(x_t) ≤ −α(|x(0)|)
be weakened to the above condition, which depends only on the current state magnitude and the full input norm?

The question is generally regarded as still open in full generality. Partial results exist: the analogous statement for integral ISS (iISS) has been answered positively, and recent work shows that if the Lyapunov–Krasovskii functional with pointwise dissipation also yields uniform global stability, then ISS follows. A 2026 superposition-based approach gives further partial progress, but no complete proof or counterexample for the full conjecture has been published.

Setting. Consider an abstract control system $\Sigma=(X,\mathcal{U},\phi)$, where:
- $X$ is a Banach space (the state space) with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$ and zero element $0$;
- $\mathcal{U}$ is a normed vector space of admissible input functions $u:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to U$ (where $U$ is a Banach space of input values), closed under concatenation and time-shifts;
- $\phi:D_\phi\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times X\times\mathcal{U}\to X$ is a transition map satisfying the standard cocycle/causality axioms (identity, causality, cocycle property, continuity in time on its maximal interval of existence).

Comparison function classes. $\mathcal{K}$ denotes continuous strictly increasing functions $\alpha:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ with $\alpha(0)=0$; $\mathcal{K}_\infty\subset\mathcal{K}$ are unbounded; $\mathcal{L}$ denotes continuous decreasing functions tending to $0$; $\mathcal{KL}=\{\beta:\beta(\cdot,t)\in\mathcal{K},\,\beta(r,\cdot)\in\mathcal{L}\}$.

Definition (iISS). $\Sigma$ is called integral input-to-state stable (iISS) if it is forward complete and there exist $\beta\in\mathcal{KL}$ and $\alpha,\gamma\in\mathcal{K}_\infty$ such that for every $x\in X$, every $u\in\mathcal{U}$, and every $t\geq 0$,
$$\alpha(\|\phi(t,x,u)\|_X)\;\leq\;\beta(\|x\|_X,t)\;+\;\int_0^t \gamma(\|u(s)\|_U)\,ds.$$

Background fact (ISS superposition theorem). For $\Sigma$ as above, input-to-state stability (ISS) is known to be equivalent to the conjunction of two strictly weaker properties: uniform local stability together with a suitable asymptotic gain / limit property (e.g., the bounded-input/uniform-limit property or the ULIM property), generalizing the Sontag–Wang superposition theorem from finite-dimensional ODEs to Banach-space systems. For finite-dimensional ODE systems, an analogous superposition-type non-Lyapunov characterization of iISS is known: iISS is equivalent to forward completeness combined with the global asymptotic stability of the zero-input system and a bounded-energy/converging-input bounded-state property.

Problem. Establish a superposition-type theorem for iISS in the infinite-dimensional setting. Specifically, identify a finite list of qualitative trajectory-based properties $(P_1),\dots,(P_k)$ — none of which involves the construction of a Lyapunov function — such that for every abstract control system $\Sigma=(X,\mathcal{U},\phi)$ on a Banach space $X$,
$$\Sigma\text{ is iISS}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (P_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge (P_k).$$
The characterization should reduce, in the special case $X=\mathbb{R}^n$ with ordinary differential equation dynamics, to the known finite-dimensional non-Lyapunov characterization of iISS, and should play the role for iISS that the ISS superposition theorem plays for ISS.

Superposition theorems for ISS and, more recently, for input-to-output stability (IOS) of infinite-dimensional systems have been established, and iISS has been characterized in various restricted settings (e.g., 1-D parabolic PDEs, time-varying systems, bilinear systems). However, a general non-Lyapunov superposition-style characterization of iISS for abstract control systems on Banach spaces, analogous to the ISS superposition theorem and matching the finite-dimensional ODE iISS theory, does not appear in the literature; recent surveys (2024) still discuss iISS characterizations as an active and partially developed research direction. Status appears open.
