In perturbative QCD applied to deep inelastic scattering (DIS), an observable such as a structure function is computed as a truncated expansion in the strong coupling $\alpha_s(\mu_R)$ together with parton distribution functions evolved at a factorization scale $\mu_F$, plus power-suppressed higher-twist corrections of the form $\mathcal{O}(\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}^2/Q^2)$ that are not captured by the perturbative series. The standard prescription for assigning a "theoretical uncertainty" to a fixed-order prediction is to take the envelope of results obtained as $(\mu_R,\mu_F)$ vary over the conventional brackets
$$\mu_R/2 \le \mu_F \le 2\mu_R, \qquad \mu_F/2 \le \mu_R \le 2\mu_F,$$
about a central choice $\mu_R=\mu_F=Q$. This procedure has no rigorous statistical interpretation, ignores higher-twist contributions, and depends on an arbitrary factor of two.

Problem. Devise a principled, quantitatively reliable method for estimating the theoretical uncertainty of a perturbative DIS prediction that improves upon the standard scale-variation envelope. Specifically, formulate a scheme that
(i) provides an estimator of the uncertainty due to missing higher orders in $\alpha_s$ with a defensible probabilistic or otherwise rigorous interpretation,
(ii) accounts in a controlled way for unknown higher-twist (power-suppressed) corrections to the structure functions, and
(iii) yields uncertainty bands that, in the limit of arbitrarily many computed perturbative orders, converge to the true theoretical error.
Either construct such a method and prove it satisfies (i)–(iii), or demonstrate that no such improvement over the conventional bracket prescription is possible without additional nonperturbative input.

Consider Drell-Yan-like inclusive hard-scattering processes (e.g., $h_1 h_2 \to \gamma^*/Z/W + X$ with the lepton-pair invariant mass $Q$ large). The standard collinear factorization formula expresses the cross section as a convolution of perturbative partonic coefficient functions with leading-twist (twist-2) parton distribution functions, modulo power-suppressed corrections of order $(\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}/Q)^n$ associated with higher-twist matrix elements.

It is known that for these Drell-Yan-like processes the infrared (collinear/soft) divergences appearing in the higher-twist (in particular, next-to-leading-twist, twist-3 and twist-4) contributions to the partonic cross sections do not cancel beyond the one-loop level against the corresponding ultraviolet renormalization of higher-twist operator matrix elements; equivalently, no all-order collinear factorization theorem for next-to-leading-twist contributions is currently established for Drell-Yan.

Problem. Formulate a consistent and predictive framework for incorporating next-to-leading-twist (power-suppressed, $\mathcal{O}(\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}^2/Q^2)$) contributions into the theoretical description of Drell-Yan-like processes that:

(a) provides a well-defined operator basis of higher-twist distributions and their evolution equations;
(b) yields finite, infrared-safe partonic coefficient functions at two-loop order and beyond, by either proving cancellation of the residual infrared divergences against suitable redefinitions of higher-twist matrix elements, or by establishing a generalized factorization theorem in which such divergences are systematically absorbed; and
(c) is compatible with the precision of NNLO (and higher) perturbative calculations for the leading-twist part, so that combined leading-plus-next-to-leading-twist predictions can be confronted with high-precision Drell-Yan data.

Either prove such a factorization/subtraction scheme exists at all orders (or to a specified order) for Drell-Yan-like processes, or demonstrate an obstruction to its existence.

In the framework of lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the theory of an SU(3) gauge field coupled to quark fields with a Lagrangian (current) quark mass m_q, address the following two questions.

(a) Devise a gauge-invariant construction on the lattice of a propagator G(p) for a confined quark inside a hadron such that:
  (i) G(p) is invariant under local SU(3) gauge transformations of the quark and gluon fields;
  (ii) G(p) is well-defined and computable in pure lattice QCD (without recourse to model assumptions);
  (iii) the resulting spectral function or pole-like structure of G(p) exhibits a peak at an effective "constituent" mass M_c that exceeds the Lagrangian mass m_q (or the small chiral-model mass) by approximately 300 MeV for the light quarks (u, d).

(b) Using only first-principles lattice QCD computations, determine whether the mass splittings between baryons composed of the same quark flavor content but with different total spin or different internal quark-spin alignments (for example the N(939)–Δ(1232) splitting, or the Σ–Λ splitting) are dominantly accounted for by a single perturbative one-gluon-exchange interaction between constituent quarks (in the spirit of the De Rújula–Georgi–Glashow chromomagnetic hyperfine interaction proportional to (λ_i·λ_j)(σ_i·σ_j)/(m_i m_j)), as opposed to receiving comparable contributions from other non-perturbative or multi-gluon mechanisms.

Provide either an explicit construction and lattice measurement establishing both (a) and (b), or a proof that no such gauge-invariant constituent-quark propagator with the stated property exists, or that one-gluon-exchange dominance fails for these baryon mass splittings.

representations.normalized:
Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) is the non-abelian gauge theory with gauge group SU(3) describing the strong interaction of quarks and gluons, with Lagrangian
  L = -(1/4) G^a_{μν} G^{a μν} + Σ_f \bar{ψ}_f (i γ^μ D_μ - m_f) ψ_f,
where D_μ = ∂_μ - i g_s t^a A^a_μ and G^a_{μν} is the non-abelian field strength. In high-energy hadronic collisions, observable cross sections receive contributions from (i) a perturbatively calculable hard partonic scattering, (ii) a perturbative parton shower describing collinear/soft radiation, (iii) hadronization, the non-perturbative transition from colored partons to color-singlet hadrons, and (iv) the underlying event, the additional soft activity associated with spectator partons of the colliding hadrons. In current practice, components (iii) and (iv) are modeled by phenomenological prescriptions such as the Lund string model or cluster hadronization model, with parameters fixed by tuning to data (possibly using machine learning), and the validity of factorization theorems—the statement that the cross section can be written as a convolution of process-independent non-perturbative functions (parton distributions, fragmentation functions) with perturbatively computable hard kernels—is in this full realistic setting effectively assumed as an ansatz beyond the regimes where it has been rigorously proved.

Problem. Provide a first-principles derivation, directly from the QCD Lagrangian above, that:
(a) gives a quantitatively predictive description of hadronization, i.e. computes from QCD alone (without recourse to tuned phenomenological string or cluster models) the probability distributions for a system of colored partons to evolve into a definite final state of hadrons, in agreement with experimental data;
(b) gives a first-principles description of the underlying event in hadron–hadron collisions; and
(c) establishes factorization of inclusive and semi-inclusive hadronic cross sections in this realistic full setting, including the contributions of (a) and (b), as a theorem derived from QCD rather than as an assumed ansatz.

Hadronization, the underlying event, and a fully general proof of factorization remain widely acknowledged open problems in QCD. Consider quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the non-abelian gauge theory with gauge group SU(3) coupled to quark fields in the fundamental representation, defined (formally) by the Yang-Mills Lagrangian with quarks. Numerical lattice gauge theory computations indicate that the static potential V(r) between an infinitely heavy quark-antiquark pair separated by a distance r satisfies, at large r, the asymptotic behavior

   V(r) ~ sigma * r + c/r   as r -> infinity,

where sigma > 0 is the string tension and c is a constant (the so-called Lüscher term). This linear rise is the conventional indicator of color confinement: isolated colored states do not appear in the physical spectrum.

Problem. Provide a mathematically rigorous derivation, from first principles of the (continuum) SU(3) Yang-Mills theory with quarks, of color confinement. Concretely:

(a) Construct the quantum SU(3) Yang-Mills theory on R^4 (in a Wightman/Osterwalder-Schrader or equivalent rigorous sense) and prove that it has a positive mass gap.

(b) Prove that the physical Hilbert space contains no asymptotic states transforming nontrivially under the global color SU(3): all finite-energy states are color singlets.

(c) Prove the area law for large Wilson loops in the pure gauge theory, equivalently establish that the static quark-antiquark potential V(r) is confining, and in particular satisfies V(r) -> infinity as r -> infinity (ideally with linear leading behavior V(r) ~ sigma r with sigma > 0).

Give a complete mathematical proof, or otherwise determine the correct mechanism and analytic description of confinement in QCD.

representations.normalized:
Let $d\ge 1$ and, for $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, define the centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal function
$$Mf(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{m(B(x,r))}\int_{B(x,r)}|f(y)|\,dy,$$
where $B(x,r)$ is the open Euclidean ball of center $x$ and radius $r$ and $m$ denotes $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Define the uncentered Hardy–Littlewood maximal function $\widetilde{M}f(x)$ analogously, taking the supremum of averages $\frac{1}{m(B)}\int_B|f(y)|\,dy$ over all open balls $B\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ that contain $x$. Let $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ denote the Sobolev space of integrable functions whose distributional gradient lies in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)$.

Prove or disprove: for every $f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, the function $Mf$ is weakly differentiable, and there exists a constant $C=C(d)$, independent of $f$, such that
$$\|\nabla Mf\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le C\,\|\nabla f\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)}.$$
Equivalently, decide whether the sublinear map $f\mapsto |\nabla Mf|$ is bounded from $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ to $L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$. The same question is posed with $M$ replaced by the uncentered maximal operator $\widetilde{M}$.

The problem is known in dimension one: Tanaka (and Aldaz–Pérez Lázaro with sharp constant 1) settled the uncentered case, and Kurka established the centered case in $d=1$. Partial results are known in higher dimensions for special classes (e.g., radial functions, block-decreasing functions, Hardy–Sobolev variants), but the full endpoint $W^{1,1}\to L^1$ gradient bound for both the centered and uncentered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator in $\mathbb{R}^d$, $d\ge 2$, remains open.

Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function of bounded variation, and let
\[
(Mf)(x) \;=\; \sup_{r>0} \frac{1}{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r} |f(y)|\,dy
\]
denote the one-dimensional centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator. The total variation of a function $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is
\[

Let $d\ge 2$ and let $M$ denote the centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator on $\mathbb{R}^d$, defined for locally integrable $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$$Mf(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{|B(x,r)|}\int_{B(x,r)}|f(y)|\,dy,$$
where $B(x,r)$ is the open Euclidean ball of radius $r$ centered at $x$ and $|B(x,r)|$ its Lebesgue measure. A function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ is called radial if $f(x)=f(y)$ whenever $|x|=|y|$. Let $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ denote the Sobolev space of $L^1$ functions whose distributional gradient lies in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)$, equipped with $\|\nabla f\|_{L^1}$.

It is known that the analogous statement holds for the uncentered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator $\widetilde{M}$ (defined as the supremum over averages on balls containing $x$, not necessarily centered at $x$): if $f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is radial, then $\widetilde{M}f$ is weakly differentiable and
$$\|\nabla \widetilde{M}f\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le C(d)\,\|\nabla f\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)}.$$

Question: Does this result remain true for the centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator $M$? That is, is it the case that for every radial $f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, the function $Mf$ is weakly differentiable and there exists a constant $C=C(d)$ such that
$$\|\nabla Mf\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le C(d)\,\|\nabla f\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)}\,?$$

For an integer $d\ge 2$, let $S^{d-1}(x,r)=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d:|z-x|=r\}$ denote the $(d-1)$-dimensional sphere of center $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and radius $r>0$, equipped with its surface measure $\sigma$, and let $\omega_{d-1}$ denote the surface area of the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The spherical maximal operator $M_S$ is defined for locally integrable $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$$M_S f(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{\omega_{d-1} r^{d-1}}\int_{S^{d-1}(x,r)}|f(z)|\,d\sigma(z).$$
For $1<p<\infty$, the Sobolev space $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ consists of those $f\in L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$ whose distributional gradient $\nabla f$ also lies in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$, with norm $\|f\|_{W^{1,p}}=\|f\|_{L^p}+\|\nabla f\|_{L^p}$.

Question: For every $d\ge 2$ and every $p$ with $1<p\le d/(d-1)$, is $M_S$ a bounded operator from $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$?

Let $S^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^4$ denote the unit round $3$-sphere with its standard Riemannian metric. A geodesic net on $S^3$ is a pair $(V,E)$ consisting of a finite set $V$ of points of $S^3$ (vertices) and a finite set $E$ of non-constant, pairwise distinct geodesic arcs (edges), each joining two vertices in $V$, such that at every vertex $v \in V$ the sum of the outgoing unit tangent vectors of all edges incident to $v$ equals $0 \in T_v S^3$. The geodesic net is called embedded if no edge has a self-intersection and any two distinct edges meet only at common endpoints in $V$; it is called connected if the underlying graph is connected.

Given a finite connected $3$-regular (i.e., every vertex has degree exactly $3$) graph $G$, we say that $S^3$ admits a closed embedded geodesic net modelled on $G$ if there exists an embedded geodesic net $(V,E)$ on $S^3$ whose underlying graph is isomorphic to $G$.

Problem: Determine, with proof, exactly which finite connected $3$-regular graphs $G$ have the property that $S^3$ admits a connected embedded closed geodesic net modelled on $G$.

where $m$ denotes Lebesgue measure and $B(x,r)$ is the open Euclidean ball of radius $r$ centered at $x$. Define the uncentered fractional maximal function $\widetilde{M}_\beta f(x)$ analogously, with the supremum taken over all open balls $B$ that contain $x$ (not necessarily centered at $x$):
$$\widetilde{M}_\beta f(x)=\sup_{B\ni x}\frac{1}{m(B)^{1-\beta/d}}\int_{B}|f(y)|\,dy.$$

$$f\;\longmapsto\;|\nabla M_\beta f|$$

$$\bigl\||\nabla M_\beta f|\bigr\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le C\,\|f\|_{W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)}\qquad\text{for all }f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d),$$
and answer the analogous question with $M_\beta$ replaced by the uncentered fractional maximal operator $\widetilde{M}_\beta$.

Z., 2022; arXiv:2010.05561) establish that for all $0<\alpha<d$ and $1\le p<d/\alpha$, both the centered and uncentered Hardy–Littlewood fractional maximal operators $\mathcal{M}_\alpha f$ are weakly differentiable on $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with $\|\nabla\mathcal{M}_\alpha f\|_{p^*}\le C_{d,\alpha,p}\|\nabla f\|_p$, where $p^*=(p^{-1}-\alpha/d)^{-1}$, explicitly covering the previously unknown endpoint $p=1$ for $0<\alpha<1$ (with $W^{1,1}$ replaceable by BV). This affirmatively answers both the centered and uncentered versions of the question.

Let $d\geq 2$ and $0<\beta<1$. For a locally integrable function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$, define the centered fractional Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator by
$$M_\beta f(x) \;=\; \sup_{r>0}\, r^{\beta}\, \frac{1}{|B(x,r)|}\int_{B(x,r)} |f(y)|\,dy,$$
where $B(x,r)$ is the open Euclidean ball of radius $r$ centered at $x$. A function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ is called radial if $f(x)$ depends only on $|x|$. Set $q=d/(d-\beta)$.

Prove or disprove: there exists a constant $C=C(d,\beta)$ such that, for every radial function $f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, the function $M_\beta f$ is weakly differentiable on $\mathbb{R}^d$ and satisfies
$$\|\nabla M_\beta f\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R}^d)} \;\leq\; C\,\|\nabla f\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)}.$$

Fix a parameter $0<\beta<1$ and set $q=1/(1-\beta)$. For a function $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$, define the one-dimensional discrete centered fractional maximal operator by
$$M_\beta f(n)\;=\;\sup_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}}\;\frac{1}{(2r+1)^{1-\beta}}\sum_{k=-r}^{r}|f(n+k)|,\qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}.$$
For a function $g:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ and $1\le p<\infty$, define its $p$-variation by
$$\operatorname{Var}_p(g)\;=\;\Big(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}|g(n+1)-g(n)|^{p}\Big)^{1/p},$$
and write $\operatorname{Var}(g)=\operatorname{Var}_1(g)$ for the (total) variation.

Question: Does there exist a universal constant $C=C(\beta)>0$ (independent of $f$) such that, for every $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ of bounded variation for which $M_\beta f$ is not identically $+\infty$,
$$\operatorname{Var}_q(M_\beta f)\;\le\;C\,\operatorname{Var}(f)?$$

The question is posed as an open problem in the discrete fractional maximal operator regularity literature. While related results exist for one-sided/uncentered discrete fractional maximal operators (with $\ell^1\to\mathrm{BV}$-type bounds), no resolution of this $\operatorname{Var}_q$ inequality for the centered discrete fractional maximal operator was located in the search. Status appears to remain open.

Let $d\ge 1$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded open convex set with Lipschitz boundary that contains the origin in its interior. For $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $r\ge 0$ set $\Omega(x,r)=x+r\,\Omega$, and let $N(x,r)=\#(\Omega(x,r)\cap\mathbb{Z}^d)$ denote the number of lattice points in $\Omega(x,r)$.

For $0\le \beta<d$ and $f:\mathbb{Z}^d\to\mathbb{R}$, define the discrete centered fractional maximal operator associated to $\Omega$ by
$$M_{\Omega,\beta} f(n)=\sup_{r\ge 0}\frac{1}{N(0,r)^{1-\beta/d}}\sum_{m\in\Omega(0,r)\cap\mathbb{Z}^d}|f(n+m)|, \qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}^d.$$
Define the uncentered version $\widetilde{M}_{\Omega,\beta}f(n)$ analogously, taking the supremum over all $\Omega$-balls $\Omega(x,r)$ containing $n$.

For $g:\mathbb{Z}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ let $\nabla g$ denote the discrete gradient $(\nabla g)(n)=\bigl(g(n+e_i)-g(n)\bigr)_{i=1}^d$, and for $1\le q<\infty$ write $\|\nabla g\|_{\ell^q(\mathbb{Z}^d)}=\bigl(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^d}|\nabla g(n)|^q\bigr)^{1/q}$.

(a) Let $0\le\beta<1$ and $q=d/(d-\beta)$. Does there exist a constant $C=C(d,\Omega,\beta)$ such that for every $f:\mathbb{Z}^d\to\mathbb{R}$,
$$\|\nabla M_{\Omega,\beta}f\|_{\ell^q(\mathbb{Z}^d)}\le C\,\|\nabla f\|_{\ell^1(\mathbb{Z}^d)}\,?$$

(b) More generally, given $0\le\alpha\le\beta<1$ and $q=d/(d-\beta+\alpha)$, does the inequality
$$\|\nabla M_{\Omega,\beta}f\|_{\ell^q(\mathbb{Z}^d)}\le C(d,\Omega,\beta,\alpha)\,\|\nabla f\|_{\ell^{d/(d-\alpha)}(\mathbb{Z}^d)}$$
hold for all $f:\mathbb{Z}^d\to\mathbb{R}$?

(c) Do the analogous inequalities hold with $M_{\Omega,\beta}$ replaced by the uncentered operator $\widetilde{M}_{\Omega,\beta}$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Endpoint Sobolev bounds for fractional maximal operators in the continuous setting were established by Beltran–Madrid (arXiv:2010.05561, Math. Z. 2022). For the discrete setting on general convex Ω-balls in Z^d as posed here, no resolution appears in the literature; partial results exist only for specific cases (e.g., ℓ¹-balls and multisublinear variants). The problem as stated for general convex Ω with Lipschitz boundary appears to remain open.

Let $M$ denote the one-dimensional centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator, defined for $f\in L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R})$ by
$$Mf(x) = \sup_{r>0} \frac{1}{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r} |f(y)|\,dy.$$
It is known that if $f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$ then $Mf$ is weakly differentiable with $(Mf)'\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, so the map $T: f \mapsto (Mf)'$ is well-defined from $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$ into $L^1(\mathbb{R})$.

Determine whether $T$ is continuous: that is, whether for every sequence $\{f_j\}\subset W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$ with $f_j \to f$ in $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$, one has $(Mf_j)' \to (Mf)'$ in $L^1(\mathbb{R})$.

Let $\mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R})$ denote the Banach space of functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ of bounded total variation, equipped with the norm
$$\|f\|_{\mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R})} = |f(-\infty)| + \mathrm{Var}(f),$$
where $f(-\infty) = \lim_{x\to-\infty} f(x)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(f)$ is the total variation of $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $\widetilde{M}$ denote the one-dimensional uncentered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator, defined for a locally integrable function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$$\widetilde{M}f(x) = \sup_{I\ni x} \frac{1}{|I|}\int_I |f(y)|\,dy,$$
where the supremum is taken over all bounded open intervals $I\subset\mathbb{R}$ containing $x$.

It is known that $\widetilde{M}$ maps $\mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R})$ into itself boundedly. Determine whether the map
$$\widetilde{M} : \mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R})$$
is continuous.

Consider the federated learning setting in which a population of clients (data-holding parties) collaboratively trains a shared statistical model under the coordination of a central server, without exchanging raw local data. Two principal deployment regimes are distinguished:

(a) Cross-device federated learning: the client population consists of a very large number (potentially millions) of unreliable, resource-constrained devices (e.g., mobile phones), each holding a small, non-IID local dataset; only a small random subset participates in any round, and clients may drop out.

(b) Cross-silo federated learning: the client population consists of a small number (typically 2–100) of reliable organizational participants (e.g., hospitals, banks), each holding a large local dataset, with stable availability across rounds.

Design a principled framework for the empirical evaluation of federated learning algorithms by accomplishing the following:

1. Specify a set of standard quantitative evaluation metrics that jointly capture (i) model utility (e.g., predictive accuracy, calibration, fairness across clients), (ii) communication cost (uplink/downlink bytes per round and to convergence), (iii) on-device computation and memory cost, (iv) client participation efficiency (rounds-to-accuracy under realistic availability and dropout models), (v) robustness to heterogeneity in data distributions and system characteristics, (vi) privacy guarantees (e.g., differential-privacy budget (ε, δ)), and (vii) robustness to adversarial or Byzantine clients.

2. Construct standard benchmark datasets and accompanying client-partitioning schemes that faithfully reflect the statistical and systems heterogeneity of each regime, with explicit, reproducible protocols for client sampling, data non-IID-ness, availability patterns, and dropout, separately tailored to (a) and (b).

3. Provide a precise comparison protocol under which any two proposed federated learning methods can be ranked on the above metrics in a manner that is realistic, reproducible, and broadly accepted, replacing ad hoc simulation choices.

State criteria a proposed metric set and benchmark suite must satisfy to be deemed adequate for each regime, and exhibit such metrics, datasets, and a protocol meeting these criteria.

Consider a cross-silo federated learning setting in which a finite collection of silos (institutions) S_1, ..., S_K jointly train a model by exchanging messages with a coordinator (or with each other) according to some protocol M. Each silo S_k holds a private dataset D_k = {x_{k,1}, ..., x_{k,n_k}} corresponding to n_k distinct end users. Two threat models are of particular interest:

(a) Inter-silo threat: other participating silos S_j (j ≠ k) are considered potential adversaries who observe all messages sent by S_k during the protocol and may collude.

(b) User-level threat: an adversary (which may include other silos and/or the coordinator) attempts to infer information about an individual end user whose data may comprise an arbitrary subset of records within a single silo, rather than a single record.

Recall the standard definitions:
• A randomized mechanism M is (ε, δ)-centrally differentially private if for all neighboring datasets D, D' differing in one record and all measurable sets E, Pr[M(D) ∈ E] ≤ e^ε Pr[M(D') ∈ E] + δ.
• M is (ε, δ)-locally differentially private if each user's data is randomized before release, i.e. for all x, x' and measurable E, Pr[M(x) ∈ E] ≤ e^ε Pr[M(x') ∈ E] + δ.
• User-level differential privacy strengthens the neighboring relation so that D and D' differ in the entire collection of records belonging to a single user.

Problem. Formulate and justify a formal privacy notion P (together with its quantitative parameters) for cross-silo federated learning that simultaneously:
   1. provides a meaningful guarantee against an adversary consisting of an arbitrary coalition of the other K−1 silos (and possibly the coordinator),
   2. provides a guarantee at the user level when each silo holds data from many end users (so that all records contributed by any single user are protected as a group), and
   3. is achievable by a concrete protocol M with utility (e.g., excess empirical or population risk for a learning task) comparable, up to explicit factors depending on K, n_k, ε, δ, to the best known bounds under standard central differential privacy.

Provide the definition of P, prove its composition and post-processing properties, exhibit a protocol achieving P with quantified utility, and prove matching or near-matching lower bounds showing the privacy/utility trade-off is essentially tight. Systematically compare P to local, central, shuffle, and distributed differential privacy in the cross-silo setting.

Consider a federated learning setting in which a neural network model M with L layers is trained collaboratively by a central server S and a collection of N resource-constrained edge devices D_1,...,D_N (each device having limited compute, memory, and bandwidth, and holding a private local dataset). In split learning, the model M is partitioned at a designated cut layer ℓ into a client-side sub-model M_c (layers 1,...,ℓ) executed on each edge device and a server-side sub-model M_s (layers ℓ+1,...,L) executed on S, with forward activations at layer ℓ and backward gradients exchanged between device and server. In its standard formulation, devices interact with the server sequentially, so that the centralized training time scales roughly linearly with N.

Design a parallelized variant of split learning satisfying all of the following requirements, or prove that no such variant exists:

(a) Multiple devices D_i may execute their forward and backward passes on M_c concurrently and the server may process the corresponding server-side computations on M_s in parallel, so that the total wall-clock training time per global epoch is sublinear in N (ideally O(1) up to communication and aggregation costs).

(b) The per-device computation, memory footprint, and communication volume per round remain within the budget of resource-constrained edge devices, independent of N.

(c) The trained global model achieves accuracy comparable (within a specified tolerance ε > 0) to that obtained by sequential split learning on the same data and architecture.

(d) The privacy properties of split learning (i.e., raw data never leaves any device D_i) are preserved.

Specify the protocol explicitly, including how client-side sub-model weights are synchronized across devices, how the server schedules and aggregates parallel activations and gradients, and provide a convergence analysis together with bounds on the centralized training time, communication cost, and accuracy gap relative to the sequential baseline.

Multiple subsequent works have proposed parallelized split-learning frameworks for resource-constrained edge devices, including SplitFed/SFL, CPSL (cluster-based parallel SL), EdgeSplit, HSFL, and ParallelSFL. These frameworks demonstrate empirically that parallelization is feasible and reduces wall-clock training time while preserving privacy and approximate accuracy. However, fully general theoretical guarantees on convergence, optimal cut-layer selection, and tight communication/computation/accuracy trade-offs under arbitrary device heterogeneity remain active research directions, so the broad open question is best characterized as partially solved.

Sevenfold star construction. Place seven equally spaced "outer vertices" on a circle of center O in the Euclidean plane (vertices of a regular heptagon). Fix the algebraic angle α₀ = 88/21 radians and a small real parameter φ. Define the zeroth layer V₀ of inner vertices by attaching, at each outer vertex, a pair of edges making angles α₀ ± φ with prescribed reference directions, in the standard way for this seven-pointed star construction. Recursively construct layers V₁, V₂, … as follows. Each new layer is obtained from the previous one by "winging" each vertex (locally extending the net so that the new vertex is balanced, i.e. the unit tangent vectors at it sum to zero). When such winging fails to balance, one performs a "suspension": an odd-indexed layer is suspended from a single nearest outer "hook" P, and an even-indexed layer is suspended from the two nearest outer hooks P, Q.

For each layer V_i define a suspension-angle function φ_i(φ) as follows:
• For odd i, with v the suspended vertex and P the (single) outer hook, set φ_i(φ) = ∠O P v.
• For even i ≥ 2, let X be the third vertex of the equilateral triangle built on the two hooks P, Q (on the side containing v) and set φ_i(φ) = ∠O X v.
• For i = 0, set φ_0(φ) = φ.

The construction depends smoothly on φ in a neighborhood of 0, and φ_i(0) = 0 for every i ≥ 0. Consider the sequence of derivatives
   a_i := φ_i'(0),  i = 0, 1, 2, …

Question: Is the sequence (a_i)_{i≥0} pairwise nonrepeating, i.e. a_i ≠ a_j whenever i ≠ j?

representations.normalized:
Split learning is a distributed machine learning protocol in which a neural network f = f_server ∘ f_client is partitioned at a designated "cut layer" between a client and a server. The client holds private input data x (and possibly labels y) and computes the forward pass up to the cut layer, transmitting the intermediate activations a = f_client(x; θ_client) (the "smashed data") to the server. The server completes the forward pass, computes the loss, and sends gradients back through the cut layer so the client can update θ_client. Training and/or inference proceeds over many rounds, during which the server observes the sequence of smashed activations (and, in training, receives gradients on them) for every client input.

Problem. Develop a rigorous privacy analysis of split learning. Specifically:

1. Define a precise threat model for split learning that specifies (a) the adversary's role (honest-but-curious or malicious server, colluding clients, or external eavesdroppers), (b) the adversary's auxiliary knowledge (architecture, parameters, public data distribution), and (c) the observable transcript, including the smashed activations a_t = f_client(x_t; θ_client^{(t)}) sent from clients across all training and inference rounds, together with any gradient signals returned to the client.

2. Under this threat model, prove formal privacy guarantees for the client's raw inputs (and labels, where relevant) against the server. The guarantees should be expressible in a standard cryptographic or statistical privacy framework — for example, (ε, δ)-differential privacy, Rényi differential privacy, mutual-information bounds I(x ; transcript) ≤ β, or simulation-based / indistinguishability guarantees — and must explicitly account for the information leaked by the communicated activations (smashed data) and any associated gradients, not merely the leakage from the final trained model.

3. Quantify the privacy/utility tradeoff: state and prove how the privacy parameters depend on the choice of cut layer, the dimensionality and statistics of the smashed data, the number of communication rounds, and any randomization mechanism (e.g. additive noise, clipping, or cryptographic protocol) applied to the activations, and exhibit matching upper and lower bounds whenever possible.

Provide such a formal privacy guarantee, or prove an impossibility result showing that no nontrivial guarantee of the specified form can hold for vanilla split learning.

Consider the following "finite sevenfold star" construction in the Euclidean plane. For a small real parameter ϕ in some interval (−ε, ε), one builds a planar graph G_n(ϕ) organized into n+1 layers V_0, V_1, …, V_n of vertices, obtained inductively by attaching to each existing "hook" vertex either a one-hook or two-hook suspension that emanates from it along geodesic (straight) segments. Each layer V_i carries an associated "suspension-angle" function ϕ_i(ϕ), defined as the angle that the corresponding suspension edge in V_i makes with a fixed reference direction; ϕ_0(ϕ), ϕ_1(ϕ), …, ϕ_n(ϕ) are real-analytic functions of ϕ with ϕ_i(0) = 0.

A geodesic net is a finite graph embedded in the plane whose edges are straight segments, in which every interior ("balanced") vertex has the property that the sum of the unit tangent vectors of the edges incident to it is zero, and where each edge has weight one (i.e. edges intersect only transversally, never overlapping in segments). If overlapping edges are allowed and counted with multiplicity, the structure is called a geodesic multinet.

Prove or disprove the following two statements:

(1) For all sufficiently small nonzero ϕ ∈ (−ε, ε), the finite sequence ϕ_0(ϕ), ϕ_1(ϕ), …, ϕ_n(ϕ) consists of pairwise distinct values.

(2) Whenever (1) holds, G_n(ϕ) is a genuine geodesic net (not merely a geodesic multinet) such that every edge has weight one, G_n(ϕ) has exactly 14 unbalanced vertices, and by choosing n large one can make the number of balanced vertices of G_n(ϕ) arbitrarily large.

(1) For all sufficiently small nonzero ϕ ∈ (−ε, ε), the finite sequence ϕ_0(ϕ), ϕ_1(ϕ), …, ϕ_n(ϕ) consists of pairwise distinct values.

(2) Whenever (1) holds, G_n(ϕ) is a genuine geodesic net (not merely a geodesic multinet) such that every edge has weight one, G_n(ϕ) has exactly 14 unbalanced vertices, and by choosing n large one can make the number of balanced vertices of G_n(ϕ) arbitrarily large.

Consider the federated learning setting in which a population of clients $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ each hold a local data distribution $P_i$ over an input-output space $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$, and the global learning task concerns the mixture $P = \sum_{i=1}^N w_i P_i$ for client weights $w_i \ge 0$ with $\sum_i w_i = 1$. Cross-client heterogeneity (non-IID-ness) can arise from several distinct mechanisms, including: (i) feature distribution skew, where the marginals $P_i(x)$ differ but $P_i(y \mid x)$ is shared; (ii) label distribution skew, where $P_i(y)$ differs but $P_i(x \mid y)$ is shared; (iii) concept drift, where $P_i(y \mid x)$ differs across clients while $P_i(x)$ is shared; (iv) concept shift, where $P_i(x \mid y)$ differs while $P_i(y)$ is shared; and (v) quantity skew, where the local sample sizes $n_i$ differ substantially.

Develop a quantitative framework that:

1. Defines measurable statistics $\{T_k(P_1, \dots, P_N)\}$ that decompose the heterogeneity present in a real-world federated dataset into contributions from the mechanisms (i)–(v) above (and possibly others, such as temporal drift within a client).

2. Estimates these statistics from samples and applies the framework to representative real-world partitioned datasets (e.g., user-keyed text, image, or sensor data) to characterize the actual mixture of effects observed in deployment.

3. Specifies a generative procedure $\mathcal{G}(\theta)$ — parameterized by a vector $\theta$ controlling the magnitudes of mechanisms (i)–(v) — that produces synthetic federated benchmarks whose statistics $\{T_k\}$ provably match (in expectation, up to a prescribed tolerance) those measured on real datasets, while also allowing controlled interpolation between IID and extreme heterogeneity regimes.

4. Demonstrates that the resulting controlled benchmarks are predictive: i.e., the relative performance of federated optimization algorithms on $\mathcal{G}(\theta_{\text{real}})$ correlates (in a precise, reported sense) with their performance on the corresponding real-world federated datasets, for a representative class of algorithms such as FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, and personalized variants.

The problem is to provide such a characterization and benchmark-construction methodology, together with the analyses establishing properties (1)–(4).

representations.normalized: Let (R^2, g) be a smooth complete Riemannian metric on the plane with Gaussian curvature K. A geodesic net in (R^2, g) is a finite graph whose vertices are points of R^2 and whose edges are geodesic segments joining them; each vertex v is classified as balanced if the sum of the unit tangent vectors at v of the edges incident to v is zero, and otherwise unbalanced. It is known that if K ≤ 0 everywhere, then any geodesic net having exactly three unbalanced vertices A_1, A_2, A_3 must consist of exactly one balanced vertex O, located at the Fermat point of A_1, A_2, A_3, together with the three edges OA_1, OA_2, OA_3. Question: does there exist a constant ε > 0 such that the same rigidity conclusion (exactly one balanced vertex O, the Fermat point of {A_1, A_2, A_3}, with the three edges OA_1, OA_2, OA_3 and no others) holds for every smooth complete Riemannian metric g on R^2 satisfying ∫_{R^2} max(K, 0) dA_g < ε, for every geodesic net in (R^2, g) with exactly three unbalanced vertices?

Consider a distributed optimization problem in which a central server seeks to minimize a global objective F(w) = (1/N) Σ_{i=1}^N F_i(w), where each F_i: R^d → R is a local objective held by client i, accessible only through stochastic gradient queries. Training proceeds in synchronous rounds: in round t the server broadcasts a model w_t to a subset S_t of clients; each client i ∈ S_t initializes w_{t,0}^{(i)} = w_t and performs K local stochastic gradient steps w_{t,k+1}^{(i)} = w_{t,k}^{(i)} − η ∇̂F_i(w_{t,k}^{(i)}); the server then aggregates the resulting local iterates via an aggregation rule A to form w_{t+1} = A({w_{t,K}^{(i)} : i ∈ S_t}). Each round incurs a wall-clock cost τ_round(K) = τ_compute · K + τ_communication, where τ_compute and τ_communication are positive constants modeling per-step local computation time and per-round communication time, respectively. Increasing K reduces the number of communication rounds but increases the divergence between local iterates before aggregation, while decreasing K incurs more communication overhead.

Problem: Determine the choice of the local-step count K (possibly varying with t) and of the aggregation rule A that minimizes the expected wall-clock time required to reach a target sub-optimality E[F(w_T)] − inf F ≤ ε, as opposed to merely minimizing the number of rounds T or the iteration complexity. In particular, characterize, under standard assumptions (e.g., L-smoothness of each F_i, bounded stochastic gradient variance, and a measure of client heterogeneity), the optimal K* = K*(τ_compute, τ_communication, ε, L, σ², heterogeneity) and identify whether simple averaging A(w^{(1)},…,w^{(n)}) = (1/n) Σ w^{(i)} is wall-clock optimal, or whether some other aggregation rule yields strictly faster wall-clock convergence.

Consider the federated learning setting in which a central coordinator collaborates with a population of clients i = 1, ..., N, each holding a local data distribution D_i, to learn personalized predictive models f_i without centralizing raw data. A multi-task / learning-to-learn (LTL) viewpoint regards each client's task as drawn from a meta-distribution over tasks, and seeks shared representations or meta-parameters that transfer across clients. Concept drift refers to the phenomenon in which a client's data distribution D_i(t) changes over time t, so that the optimal predictor f_i(t) is non-stationary. Lifelong learning algorithms aim to continually learn a sequence of tasks while retaining performance on earlier ones; among them, parameter-transfer methods (e.g., MAML-style approaches) share weights across tasks, while non-parameter-transfer methods such as Prototypical Networks (ProtoNets) operate by computing class prototypes in an embedding space and classifying new points by nearest-prototype rules, without transferring task-specific parameters.

Address the following two questions:

(a) Formulate concept drift in federated learning as a lifelong-learning problem within the multi-task / LTL framework. Specifically, design an algorithmic framework and provide a theoretical analysis (e.g., generalization or regret bounds) for federated learning under client-side concept drift, treating the temporal sequence of distributions {D_i(t)} on each client as a stream of related tasks to be learned in a lifelong-learning sense.

(b) Design and analyze a federated learning algorithm based on a non-parameter-transfer lifelong-learning method such as Prototypical Networks. Determine whether such non-parameter-transfer schemes can be made useful in federated learning, and characterize conditions under which they yield provable benefits (in accuracy, communication cost, privacy, or robustness to heterogeneity) over parameter-transfer-based federated meta-learning approaches.

Setting. Consider a federated learning environment with $K$ clients. Each client $k \in \{1,\dots,K\}$ has access to an i.i.d. sample $S_k = \{z^{(k)}_1,\dots,z^{(k)}_{m_k}\}$ of size $m_k$ drawn from a client-specific distribution $\mathcal{D}_k$ over a common instance space $\mathcal{Z}$. Fix a hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ and a loss function $\ell:\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{Z}\to[0,1]$. For a hypothesis $h\in\mathcal{H}$ define the local population risk $L_k(h) = \mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{D}_k}[\ell(h,z)]$.

Consider three classes of estimators:
1. The purely local baseline $h_k$, obtained by training only on $S_k$ (e.g.\ empirical risk minimization on $S_k$).
2. The shared global baseline $h_{\mathrm{FL}}$, obtained by federated learning on $\bigcup_k S_k$ (e.g.\ ERM with respect to $\sum_k (m_k/M) L_k$ where $M=\sum_k m_k$, or the output of FedAvg).
3. A personalized estimator $h^{\mathrm{pers}}_k$ that may use both the global aggregated information and the local sample $S_k$.

Let $\rho$ be a chosen notion of dissimilarity between distributions $\{\mathcal{D}_k\}$ (e.g.\ total variation, Wasserstein, or a discrepancy tailored to $\ell$ and $\mathcal{H}$).

Questions. Provide rigorous answers to all three of the following.

(a) Identify explicit, quantitative conditions on $(\rho,\{\mathcal{D}_k\},\{m_k\},\mathcal{H})$ under which, for every client $k$, $\mathbb{E}[L_k(h_{\mathrm{FL}})] \le \mathbb{E}[L_k(h_k)]$, i.e.\ the global federated model is no worse than the purely local model on each client.

(b) Under such conditions, derive a tight (matching upper and lower) bound on the expected improvement $\mathbb{E}[L_k(h_k) - L_k(h_{\mathrm{FL}})]$ in terms of $m_k$, $M$, the complexity of $\mathcal{H}$, and the dissimilarity $\rho$.

(c) Construct a personalization scheme $h^{\mathrm{pers}}_k$ together with a proof that, for every client $k$ and every configuration of $(\{\mathcal{D}_k\},\{m_k\})$,
$$\mathbb{E}[L_k(h^{\mathrm{pers}}_k)] \le \min\bigl(\mathbb{E}[L_k(h_k)],\ \mathbb{E}[L_k(h_{\mathrm{FL}})]\bigr) + o(1)$$
as $m_k,M\to\infty$, with explicit non-asymptotic rates.

Substantial partial progress exists. Fallah, Mokhtari, and Ozdaglar (NeurIPS 2020) develop a MAML-based Per-FedAvg with convergence guarantees in non-convex settings, quantifying performance via TV and Wasserstein distances between client distributions. Subsequent work (e.g., ICLR 2023 personalized FL papers, PeFLL 2023, and many follow-ups) gives further guarantees, but a complete theory giving sharp matching upper and lower bounds and personalization estimators that provably dominate both the local and global baselines uniformly across all heterogeneity regimes remains incomplete.

Setting. Let a population of $N$ clients each hold a private local dataset $D_i$ drawn from an unknown distribution $\mathcal{P}_i$ over a common data domain $\mathcal{X}$. A central server may interact with the clients only through a federated protocol: in each round it broadcasts a message, each participating client computes a local update from its own data, and the aggregated client messages are released to the server through a mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ that is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private at the user (client) level, i.e. for every pair of neighboring client populations differing in the data of a single user and every measurable event $S$,
$$\Pr[\mathcal{M}(\text{population}) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\Pr[\mathcal{M}(\text{neighbor}) \in S] + \delta.$$
Raw examples in any $D_i$ may never be transmitted to the server or to a human analyst.

Practical workflow questions. A machine-learning practitioner training a model $f_\theta:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ on the federation needs to perform standard debugging and interpretability tasks on the union $\bigcup_i D_i$, including:
(a) inspecting representative failure cases on which $f_\theta$ errs;
(b) detecting and characterizing outliers or distribution shift between subpopulations of clients;
(c) auditing the model and the data for bias with respect to a sensitive attribute $A$;
(d) producing human-interpretable summaries or example-level explanations of model behavior.

Problem.
1. Design a family of $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-user-level differentially private federated procedures $\{\mathcal{A}_q\}$, one for each workflow question $q$ in (a)–(d), that produce releases $\mathcal{A}_q(D_1,\dots,D_N)$ enabling the practitioner to faithfully answer $q$, and prove formal utility guarantees relating the answers obtained from $\mathcal{A}_q$ to the answers that would be obtained from direct inspection of $\bigcup_i D_i$.

2. Consider the special case where $\mathcal{A}_q$ is implemented by training a generative model $G_\phi$ over $\mathcal{X}$ via a federated, user-level $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP optimization procedure, and then answering workflow questions by drawing synthetic samples from $G_\phi$. Define a fidelity measure $\mathrm{Fid}(G_\phi,\mathcal{P})$ (for example, the total variation or Wasserstein distance to the underlying mixture $\mathcal{P} = \tfrac{1}{N}\sum_i \mathcal{P}_i$, or the gap between expectations of a chosen test class of statistics under $G_\phi$ and under $\mathcal{P}$). Develop training algorithms and theoretical analyses showing how $\mathrm{Fid}(G_\phi,\mathcal{P})$ can be made small enough — as a function of $\varepsilon$, $\delta$, $N$, the per-client sample size, the model class, and the data dimension — that synthetic samples from $G_\phi$ faithfully support the debugging and interpretability tasks (a)–(d), in the sense that decisions made by the practitioner from $G_\phi$-samples agree with decisions that would be made from the true data with high probability.

The goal is both to identify which workflow questions admit such privacy-preserving answers and to quantitatively improve the achievable fidelity of differentially private federated generative models to the level required by these uses.

Recent work (e.g., DP federated diffusion models for tabular data such as DP-Fed-FinDiff, federated synthetic data generation with DP, and explainable DP-FL frameworks like FedHDPrivacy) has produced partial advances on training higher-fidelity DP federated generative models and on using them as proxies for inspecting private decentralized data. However, the literature explicitly frames raising the fidelity of DP federated generative models to the level required for faithful debugging, outlier and bias inspection on decentralized user data as an active and unresolved research direction. No general solution with formal utility guarantees covering the full range of debugging and interpretability workflows is established.

Consider the federated learning setting in which a central server coordinates the training of a global model with parameters $w \in \mathbb{R}^d$ across $N$ clients, where client $i$ holds a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ and a local loss $F_i(w) = \mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{D}_i}[\ell(w;z)]$. The goal is to (approximately) minimize the global objective $F(w) = \sum_{i=1}^N p_i F_i(w)$ for given weights $p_i \ge 0$ with $\sum_i p_i = 1$, by an iterative protocol consisting of $T$ rounds in which, on each round, a subset of clients receive the current model from the server, perform local computation, and transmit a message back; the total number of bits sent on the uplink (and downlink) channels is the communication cost $C$, and the accuracy of the resulting model $\hat w$ is measured by the optimization error $F(\hat w) - \min_w F(w)$ or by the test accuracy on held-out data.

Existing communication-reduction techniques include (i) gradient/model quantization, (ii) sparsification (top-$k$ or random-$k$), (iii) low-rank or sketched updates, (iv) reducing the number of communication rounds via multiple local SGD steps (e.g., FedAvg), and combinations thereof. Restricting attention to algorithms that solve federated optimization problems of the above form under standard assumptions (e.g., $L$-smooth, possibly non-convex local losses, bounded heterogeneity, stochastic gradient access at each client):

(a) Determine whether the total communication cost $C$ required to achieve a target optimization (or generalization) accuracy $\varepsilon$ can be reduced substantially below what is achieved by current methods such as quantized/sparsified FedAvg and its variants.

(b) Characterize the optimal trade-off curve between communication cost $C$ and achievable accuracy $\varepsilon$ for federated optimization, taking the underlying optimization algorithm (its convergence rate, local computation, and client sampling) as an integral part of the problem rather than abstracting it away as in pure information-theoretic distributed estimation lower bounds. In particular, exhibit matching algorithmic upper bounds and lower bounds on $C$ as a function of $\varepsilon$, $d$, $N$, the number of participating clients per round, and the heterogeneity of $\{F_i\}$.

This is a broadly stated open research direction in federated learning. Substantial progress has been made on individual compression methods (quantization, sparsification, error feedback, local SGD analysis) and on distributed estimation lower bounds, but a tight characterization of the practical optimal communication–accuracy trade-off that incorporates the optimization algorithm remains an active and unresolved area as of 2026.

Substantial progress has been made since the question was posed. Schemes such as the Skellam mechanism, distributed discrete Gaussian, and Johnson–Lindenstrauss-based linear compressors have been shown to be jointly compatible with secure aggregation and differential privacy, and Chen et al. (ICML 2022) established fundamental price-of-secure-aggregation lower bounds for DP mean estimation. Recent works (e.g., Fed-DPRoC, 2025) extend this to robustness as well. However, tight upper/lower bounds across the full (communication, privacy, accuracy) trade-off region remain incomplete, so the broader design problem is best characterized as partially solved.

Numerous follow-up works propose threshold and multi-key HE schemes for federated aggregation (e.g., tMK-CKKS, distributed threshold additive HE with dropout resiliency, FedML-HE), distributing the decryption key among clients via secret sharing so that no single party (including the server) can decrypt individual updates. These address the trust issue under specific corruption thresholds and online/dropout assumptions, but no single solution has emerged that simultaneously handles cross-device churn, key rotation, and minimal trust assumptions optimally; recent critical analyses highlight remaining limitations. The broad open question of the right trust structure thus remains an active research area, with substantial partial progress.

Consider the federated learning setting in which a central server coordinates the training of a shared model with many clients. Each client holds private local data and computes a local update (e.g., a gradient or model delta), which is sent to the server, which aggregates the updates to produce the next global model.

Recall that an interactive zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) system allows a prover holding a secret witness w for a statement x in a language L to convince a verifier that x ∈ L through a multi-round interactive protocol, while leaking no information about w beyond this fact. A non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (NIZK) achieves the same guarantee with a single message from prover to verifier (typically in a common reference string or random oracle model). Standard requirements are completeness, computational (or statistical) soundness, and the zero-knowledge property; efficiency is measured by prover time, verifier time, proof size, and any setup/CRS cost.

Design ZKP or NIZK protocols that are simultaneously practical for the following two federated-learning tasks, and prove the corresponding completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge properties together with concrete asymptotic and concrete efficiency bounds:

1. Server-directed proofs of input properties. For a fixed predicate P on client local inputs/updates (for example: norm bounds on a gradient, correctness of the local training procedure with respect to a published model and a committed dataset, validity of dataset format, or honest sampling from a committed local distribution), construct a NIZK such that each client can prove to the server that its submitted update u satisfies P(u) = 1 with respect to a public commitment to the client's data, while revealing nothing about the client's data or update beyond P(u) = 1. The protocol must scale to model sizes and client populations typical of federated learning, with prover cost achievable on resource-constrained client devices and aggregate verifier cost on the server sublinear or efficient in the number of clients.

2. Client-directed verification of multi-party-dependent statements. Construct a (possibly interactive) ZKP or NIZK that allows the server (or another designated prover) to convince an individual client that a statement S depending on the joint inputs of many clients holds — for instance, that the published global model was correctly aggregated from valid client updates, that a claimed differential-privacy noise was added correctly, or that a particular client's contribution was included — without revealing the other clients' inputs and while producing a statement that the verifying client can meaningfully trust given that it has no direct access to the other clients' data.

The problem is to determine whether such protocols can be instantiated with end-to-end efficiency (prover time, verifier time, proof size, setup) suitable for deployment in federated learning at realistic scales, and to provide concrete constructions together with security proofs, or alternatively to establish lower bounds ruling out such efficient constructions.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Recent works (2023–2025), including zkFL, ProxyZKP, VPFL, and various verifiable-FL surveys, give NIZK/zk-SNARK constructions for proving properties of client updates and for verifying aggregation, with reported speedups over generic zk-SNARKs and Bulletproofs. However, no construction is known that simultaneously delivers practical prover cost on resource-constrained clients, sublinear server verification at federated scale, and full coverage of multi-party-dependent client-side verification statements; the general question of efficient ZKP/NIZK for federated learning remains an active open research direction.

Consider a federated learning setting in which a population of users $u = 1, \ldots, n$ each hold local datasets $D_u$ of possibly very different sizes $|D_u|$, and a central server iteratively trains a model $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ by aggregating per-user updates $\Delta_u(\theta)$. The training procedure is required to satisfy user-level $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy, meaning that the distribution over the released model (or sequence of models) is $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-indistinguishable when an arbitrary single user's entire dataset $D_u$ is replaced. A standard mechanism enforces this by clipping each per-user update to have $\ell_2$-norm at most $C$ and adding Gaussian noise calibrated to $C$.

(a) Determine the fundamental information-theoretic trade-offs between accuracy and user-level differential privacy in this setting when the data-per-user distribution $\{|D_u|\}_{u=1}^n$ is highly heterogeneous. Specifically, for canonical learning and estimation tasks (e.g., mean estimation of a bounded random variable, stochastic convex optimization, and empirical risk minimization on Lipschitz losses), characterize tight upper and lower bounds on the achievable excess risk (or estimation error) as a function of $n$, $\varepsilon$, $\delta$, and the empirical distribution of $\{|D_u|\}$.

(b) Design and analyze a procedure that adaptively chooses, for each user $u$ and each round $t$, a clipping bound $C_{u,t}$ (and corresponding model-parameter or update bound) so as to:
  (i) satisfy user-level $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy for the entire training procedure, and
  (ii) achieve excess risk matching the lower bounds from (a) up to constants or polylogarithmic factors,
without requiring a priori knowledge of the per-user update-norm distribution or the data-size distribution.

The question concerns a research direction rather than a single sharp conjecture. While there is substantial recent work proposing adaptive clipping heuristics (e.g., quantile-based adaptive clipping by Andrew et al., ULDP-AVG/SGD for cross-silo user-level DP, and various adaptive-clipping FL schemes from 2023–2025), tight characterizations of the fundamental privacy–accuracy trade-offs for user-level DP under highly unequal user contributions, and provably optimal adaptive clipping schemes matching such bounds, are not established. The broad direction therefore remains open.

Setting. Consider a federated learning system with a central server and a set of clients $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$. The global model is partitioned into $M$ disjoint sub-models $\theta = (\theta_1,\dots,\theta_M)$, where $\theta_m \in \mathbb{R}^{d_m}$. Each client $i$ holds local data $\mathcal{D}_i$ that is relevant to exactly one sub-model index $s(i) \in \{1,\dots,M\}$, known only to that client. In each round, client $i$ wishes to (a) download the current value of $\theta_{s(i)}$ from the server, (b) compute a local update $\Delta_{s(i)}^{(i)}$ from $\mathcal{D}_i$, and (c) contribute this update so that the server can form an aggregated update to $\theta_{s(i)}$, without ever revealing $s(i)$ or $\Delta_{s(i)}^{(i)}$ in the clear.

Define a federated sub-model training protocol $\Pi$ to be a multi-round interactive protocol between the server and clients that, at the end of training, produces an updated global model $\hat\theta$. Let $\mathrm{Acc}(\Pi)$ denote the expected utility (e.g., test accuracy) of $\hat\theta$ on the underlying task, and let $\mathrm{Comm}(\Pi)$ denote the total expected per-client communication (uplink plus downlink) per round, measured in bits. Say that $\Pi$ is:
- communication-efficient if $\mathrm{Comm}(\Pi) = o\!\left(\sum_{m=1}^M d_m\right)$ in the relevant asymptotic regime, ideally scaling polynomially in $\max_m d_m$ rather than in the full model dimension;
- index-private if for every pair of clients $i,j$ and every adversary modeled as the server colluding with any subset $T \subset \{1,\dots,N\}\setminus\{i,j\}$ of size at most $t$, the protocol transcript reveals (in either an information-theoretic or a cryptographic sense) no more about $s(i)$ than is implied by aggregate statistics released by the protocol;
- update-private if, in addition, the individual update vector $\Delta_{s(i)}^{(i)}$ is hidden from the same adversary, except through its contribution to the aggregated sums on each sub-model.

Problem. Determine whether there exists a federated sub-model training protocol $\Pi$ that is simultaneously communication-efficient, index-private, and update-private, and that achieves utility $\mathrm{Acc}(\Pi)$ matching (up to a vanishing additive error) the utility of the non-private baseline in which each client sends $\Delta_{s(i)}^{(i)}$ in the clear together with its index $s(i)$. Specifically:

(i) Identify sparsity regimes on $(N, M, d_1,\dots,d_M)$ and on the distribution of indices $\{s(i)\}_{i=1}^N$ (e.g., heavy-tailed versus near-uniform popularity of sub-models) under which such a protocol exists.

(ii) Construct, or prove the impossibility of, a protocol combining a private information retrieval (PIR) or oblivious-RAM-style download mechanism for $\theta_{s(i)}$ with a secure aggregation scheme tolerating up to $t$ colluding parties for the upload of $\Delta_{s(i)}^{(i)}$, whose total communication is sublinear in $\sum_m d_m$.

(iii) Quantify the optimal trade-off, as a function of the sparsity parameters, the collusion threshold $t$, and the desired privacy level, between $\mathrm{Comm}(\Pi)$ and the achievable utility $\mathrm{Acc}(\Pi)$.

The question has stimulated an active research line. Several works (e.g., information-theoretically private federated submodel learning with multiple non-colluding databases, secure-aggregation-based private submodel updates, and hierarchical submodel training) propose protocols that target communication efficiency together with privacy of the submodel index and updates. However, no single protocol is known to simultaneously achieve sublinear communication, full index- and update-privacy under realistic single-server collusion models, and baseline utility across general sparsity regimes; trade-offs are still being mapped, so the broad question remains only partially resolved.

Formulate a rigorous trust and threat model for federated learning under a "trusted-but-verified" server paradigm, and analyze its feasibility. Specifically, consider the following setting:

- A central server $S$ coordinates the training of a global model with a population of $N$ client devices $\{C_1, \dots, C_N\}$. In each round, $S$ selects a subset of clients, distributes the current model, receives client updates, and aggregates them into a new global model.
- An adversary $\mathcal{A}$ may statically or adaptively corrupt up to a fraction $\beta \in [0,1]$ of the clients, and/or corrupt the server $S$. Corrupted parties may deviate arbitrarily from the protocol (Byzantine behavior). Honest clients hold private local data and require that no party learn more about their data than what is implied by the final model.
- A "trusted-but-verified" server is a server whose actions during training (client selection, aggregation, model update application, randomness usage, etc.) are accompanied by cryptographic or statistical evidence (e.g., commitments, transparency logs, zero-knowledge proofs, secure enclaves with remote attestation, or audit transcripts) that any honest client (or external auditor) can check in order to detect deviation from the prescribed protocol.

Provide answers, with proofs or impossibility results, to the following:

1. Define formally what it means for a federated learning protocol $\Pi$ to realize a trusted-but-verified server under simultaneous corruption of at most a $\beta$-fraction of clients and a possibly distinct corruption status of the server. Specify the privacy, integrity, and verifiability guarantees as ideal-functionality requirements.

2. Determine, as a function of $\beta$, the largest fraction of compromised clients under which there exists an efficient protocol $\Pi$ achieving the definition in (1) with: (a) an honest server, (b) a malicious server but honest client majority, and (c) simultaneously malicious server and a fraction $\beta$ of malicious clients.

3. Decide whether case (c) is achievable at all, or prove that simultaneous compromise of the server and a large fraction of clients makes the trusted-but-verified guarantee impossible without additional trust assumptions (e.g., trusted hardware, a public bulletin board, or a trusted setup).

4. Identify the minimal additional assumptions (cryptographic primitives, hardware, or infrastructure) sufficient to realize the trusted-but-verified server model in regime (c), and quantify the resulting communication, computation, and round complexity overhead relative to the baseline non-verified protocol.

This is a broad open research direction in federated learning. Subsequent surveys (Kairouz et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2021 and later) continue to list realistic trust modeling and verifiable-server designs as unresolved. While individual building blocks (secure aggregation, ZK proofs of training, trusted execution environments) have advanced, no comprehensive formalization with tight feasibility/impossibility results for the trusted-but-verified server under joint server/client corruption has been established.

Consider a federated learning setting in which a central server coordinates the training of a global model with parameters $	heta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ across $N$ clients. In each round $t$, the server broadcasts the current model $	heta_t$, a subset $S_t \subseteq \{1,\dots,N\}$ of clients each compute an update $\Delta_i^{(t)}$ from their private local dataset $D_i$, and the server aggregates these updates to obtain $	heta_{t+1} = 	heta_t + \mathrm{Agg} igl(\{\Delta_i^{(t)}\}_{i \in S_t} igr)$. The server cannot observe the client data $D_i$ nor any data drawn from the same distribution.

Two classes of adversarial behavior are considered for a fraction $ho$ of compromised clients:
(i) Data poisoning: the adversary alters the local dataset $D_i$ but the client otherwise follows the prescribed local training protocol, producing $\Delta_i^{(t)}$ honestly from the corrupted data.
(ii) Model-update poisoning: the adversary may submit any vector $\Delta_i^{(t)} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ subject to specified constraints (e.g., norm bounds or stealth constraints), without regard to any underlying dataset.

Two standard centralized defenses are:
- Data sanitization: filter or relabel training points by detecting outliers in the training data using a reference (clean) dataset.
- Network pruning: identify and remove neurons or weights that activate primarily on backdoored or anomalous inputs, using clean validation data to detect such neurons.

Both defenses, in their classical forms, require direct access to (a sample of) clean training data resembling the clients' data.

Resolve the following:

(A) Design and analyze data-sanitization-style and network-pruning-style defenses that operate in the federated setting under the constraint that the server has no access to clients' private data and no auxiliary dataset drawn from their distribution, while preserving formally stated privacy guarantees (e.g., $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy with respect to each $D_i$). Provide either (a) provable robustness guarantees—bounds on the deviation $\|	heta_T - 	heta_T^{\mathrm{clean}}\|$ or on the test risk under a specified poisoning model—matching those of the centralized analogues, or (b) impossibility results showing that the centralized guarantees cannot be achieved by any defense satisfying the stated privacy constraint, thereby establishing whether genuinely new federated-specific defenses against data poisoning are required.

(B) Formulate a quantitative measure $G(\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{data}}, \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{model}})$ of the gap between the worst-case attack success achievable by a data-poisoning adversary $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{data}}$ and a model-update-poisoning adversary $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{model}}$ operating under matched, realistic capability budgets (fraction $ho$ of corrupted clients, bounds on per-client update norm, knowledge of other clients' data and of the aggregation rule, computational budget). Prove upper and lower bounds on $G$ as a function of these capability parameters and the aggregation rule $\mathrm{Agg}$, and relate $G$ to a precise notion of relative adversarial strength between the two threat models.

The problem remains broadly open. Although since 2020 numerous federated defenses have appeared (FoolsGold, robust aggregation rules, anomaly-detection-based filtering, federated data sanitization variants such as FDSD, pruning-style backdoor mitigation), there is no defense that simultaneously matches centralized data-sanitization/network-pruning guarantees while provably respecting client privacy, and recent work continues to break state-of-the-art defenses with optimization-based attacks. No widely accepted quantitative theory of the data-poisoning vs. model-update-poisoning gap under matched federated capabilities has been established.

Consider a federated learning system in which a central server seeks to compute, in each round, the sum (or average) of model updates contributed by a large population of clients, while ensuring that no individual client's update is revealed to the server or to other clients. A secure aggregation protocol (SecAgg) is a cryptographic protocol that allows the server to learn only the aggregate of the clients' vectors, using pairwise masks (e.g., based on Diffie–Hellman key agreement and secret sharing) that cancel when summed. In standard SecAgg, all participating clients must remain online and respond within a fixed time window of a single synchronous round; clients who are slow ("stragglers") or who disconnect ("dropouts") force the protocol either to wait, to abort, or to reconstruct shared secrets, which scales poorly and limits robustness.

Address the following two open design questions:

(1) Design a secure aggregation protocol that tolerates stragglers and dropouts more gracefully than synchronous SecAgg. Concretely, either:
   (a) construct an asynchronous variant of SecAgg in which clients are not required to participate during a single fixed time window, while still guaranteeing that the server learns only the aggregate of contributed updates and nothing about individual updates; or
   (b) construct a SecAgg variant that aggregates client contributions across multiple computation rounds (so that masks introduced in one round can be canceled by contributions in later rounds), with formal privacy and correctness guarantees against a specified threat model that includes a curious server and a bounded fraction of colluding or dropping clients.
Specify the communication, computation, and round complexity, and prove privacy guarantees that remain meaningful under arbitrary client dropout patterns.

(2) Design general-purpose debugging methods for machine learning training pipelines in the federated setting that can diagnose data-pipeline failures (e.g., malformed features, label corruption, distribution shift, preprocessing bugs) without the debugger or server ever directly inspecting raw user data on individual devices. Formalize what diagnostic information may be released, prove that the released information satisfies a stated privacy notion (e.g., differential privacy or secure aggregation–based release), and demonstrate that the method suffices to localize a class of realistic pipeline bugs.

   (a) construct an asynchronous variant of SecAgg in which clients are not required to participate during a single fixed time window, while still guaranteeing that the server learns only the aggregate of contributed updates and nothing about individual updates; or
   (b) construct a SecAgg variant that aggregates client contributions across multiple computation rounds (so that masks introduced in one round can be canceled by contributions in later rounds), with formal privacy and correctness guarantees against a specified threat model that includes a curious server and a bounded fraction of colluding or dropping clients.
Specify the communication, computation, and round complexity, and prove privacy guarantees that remain meaningful under arbitrary client dropout patterns.

(2) Design general-purpose debugging methods for machine learning training pipelines in the federated setting that can diagnose data-pipeline failures (e.g., malformed features, label corruption, distribution shift, preprocessing bugs) without the debugger or server ever directly inspecting raw user data on individual devices. Formalize what diagnostic information may be released, prove that the released information satisfies a stated privacy notion (e.g., differential privacy or secure aggregation–based release), and demonstrate that the method suffices to localize a class of realistic pipeline bugs.

Buffered asynchronous secure aggregation protocols such as FedBuff (with TEE-based buffering), BASecAgg (which designs masks that cancel across different rounds without TEEs), Owl, and Buffalo all address stragglers and dropouts in asynchronous or multi-round settings, indicating that the SecAgg-resilience question is partially resolved with multiple constructions, though no single protocol is universally optimal. Consider a federated learning setting in which a set of clients $\{C_1, \ldots, C_K\}$ each holds a local dataset $D_k = \{(x_{k,i}, y_{k,i})\}_{i=1}^{n_k}$ drawn from a (possibly client-specific) distribution $\mathcal{P}_k$ over an input space $\mathcal{X}$ and label space $\mathcal{Y}$, together with a sensitive attribute $a_{k,i} \in \mathcal{A}$. A global model $f_\theta : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is trained collaboratively (without centralizing the raw data) by minimizing some federated objective such as $\sum_k \tfrac{n_k}{N} \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim \mathcal{P}_k}[\ell(f_\theta(x), y)]$. Assume that the data-generating processes $\mathcal{P}_k$ may themselves be biased, in the sense that there exist measurable disparities in conditional distributions across values of the sensitive attribute (e.g., $\mathcal{P}_k(y \mid a = a_0) \neq \mathcal{P}_k(y \mid a = a_1)$) arising from the collection or interaction mechanism rather than from sampling noise.

(a) Develop a rigorous framework, compatible with the federated constraints (clients do not share raw data, communication is limited, and individual data may be subject to privacy mechanisms such as differential privacy), under which one can detect biases that originate in the data-generating processes $\{\mathcal{P}_k\}$. Specifically, give procedures and provable guarantees for identifying when observed disparities in the trained model $f_\theta$ are attributable to bias in $\{\mathcal{P}_k\}$ rather than to optimization, heterogeneity, or finite-sample effects.

(b) Develop federated training algorithms that provably mitigate such data-generation bias under standard fairness criteria (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds, calibration), with quantitative trade-offs between fairness, accuracy, communication, and privacy.

(c) Develop post-hoc correction methods that, given an already-trained federated model $f_\theta$ and limited (possibly decentralized and privacy-protected) access to client data or summary statistics, produce a corrected predictor $\tilde f$ satisfying a prescribed fairness criterion, with guarantees on the deviation from $f_\theta$ in predictive performance.

Provide methods for (a), (b), and (c), or establish impossibility results delineating the limits of bias detection and mitigation under federated, decentralized interaction-data settings.

Consider a federated learning setting in which a global model is trained collaboratively across a large number of clients, each holding private local data, without sharing raw data with a central server or with other clients. Suppose that for every data point, the value of any "sensitive" attribute (such as race, gender, age, or other protected group membership) is unavailable to all parties — neither clients nor the server may observe or store such attributes. The trained global (or personalized) model is then deployed to make predictions on data drawn from the union of client distributions.

Formalize and resolve the following three intertwined questions in this setting:

1. (Measurement) Define a quantitative notion of "unfairness" of a predictor f : X → Y that (a) does not require access to sensitive group labels at training or audit time, (b) is well-defined when data are partitioned across many clients with heterogeneous, non-IID local distributions, and (c) reduces to a meaningful classical group-fairness criterion (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds, or calibration across groups) when sensitive attributes happen to be observable. Provide an estimator of this quantity that can be computed under the communication and privacy constraints of federated learning, together with finite-sample guarantees.

2. (Correction / algorithms) Design federated training algorithms that provably reduce the unfairness measure from (1). In particular, develop scalable federated counterparts of distributionally robust optimization (DRO) — i.e., algorithms that minimize the worst-case loss over an appropriately chosen ambiguity set of subpopulations — and of multicalibration — i.e., algorithms that guarantee calibration of f simultaneously over a rich family C of subsets of X — such that the per-round communication, per-client computation, and total sample complexity scale at most polylogarithmically (or otherwise tractably) in the dimension d of the feature space, the number of clients n, and the complexity (e.g., VC dimension) of C. Prove convergence and fairness guarantees for these algorithms under standard federated assumptions (partial participation, client heterogeneity, local SGD updates, and differential privacy).

3. (Theory of fairness without sensitive attributes) Develop a theoretical framework for defining and reasoning about fairness when sensitive attributes are not available even in principle. Specifically, identify axiomatic conditions a notion of "fairness without sensitive attributes" should satisfy, characterize the family of all such notions, prove impossibility or possibility theorems analogous to those known for classical group fairness, and clarify the relationship between such attribute-free notions and DRO-, multicalibration-, and individual-fairness-based formulations.
