Consider a federated learning system consisting of a central server and a population of clients $\mathcal{C} = \{1,2,\dots,N\}$. Each client $i \in \mathcal{C}$ holds a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ over an input-label-attribute space $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{A}$, where $\mathcal{A}$ encodes a protected attribute (e.g. demographic group). At each round $t$, a (possibly biased) sampling mechanism selects a subset $S_t \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ of clients according to a distribution $q_t$ that may depend on availability constraints, device characteristics, network connectivity, time zone, or other systematic factors that cause $q_t$ to deviate from the uniform distribution. The server then aggregates locally trained updates from clients in $S_t$ to produce a global model $h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$.

Fix a fairness criterion $\mathcal{F}(h)$ for centralized learning (e.g. demographic parity, equalized odds, calibration, or individual fairness with respect to a metric on $\mathcal{X}$), defined as a functional of $h$ and a global data distribution $\mathcal{D}^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{D}_i$. Suppose that in the centralized setting (where a learner has direct sample access to $\mathcal{D}^*$) there exists a known algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\text{cen}}$ that produces a model $h$ achieving $\mathcal{F}(h) \le \varepsilon$ while attaining utility within $\delta$ of the unconstrained optimum.

Address the following:

1. Quantify, as a function of the divergence between $q_t$ and the uniform distribution and of the heterogeneity among the $\mathcal{D}_i$, how client-sampling bias and decentralized data collection degrade $\mathcal{F}(h)$ for the model produced by standard federated aggregation (e.g. FedAvg).

2. Identify minimal assumptions on (a) the sampling distributions $\{q_t\}$, (b) the inter-client heterogeneity (e.g. bounded $\chi^2$ or KL divergence between $\mathcal{D}_i$ and $\mathcal{D}^*$), (c) the availability of protected-attribute information at clients or server, and (d) the communication and privacy constraints (such as differential privacy or secure aggregation), under which $\mathcal{A}_{\text{cen}}$ can be adapted into a federated algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\text{fed}}$ that, with high probability, returns a global model $h$ satisfying $\mathcal{F}(h) \le \varepsilon + o(1)$ while preserving utility within $\delta + o(1)$ of the federated optimum.

3. Either construct such an adaptation $\mathcal{A}_{\text{fed}}$ for a representative class of fairness criteria, or prove an impossibility result showing that under the stated constraints no federated algorithm can simultaneously achieve approximate fairness, approximate utility, and the required privacy/communication guarantees.

Consider a federated learning system in which a global model is trained by repeatedly selecting a subset of client devices from a population $\mathcal{D}=\{1,\dots,N\}$, having each selected device $i$ compute a local update from its private data distribution $P_i$, and aggregating the updates on a coordinating server. In realistic deployments, devices differ in hardware capability, network connectivity, battery level, availability schedule, and dataset size, so the probability $q_i$ that device $i$ successfully participates in any given training round is not uniform. Let the resulting trained model be denoted $\hat{\theta}$, and let the population-fair target be the model $\theta^\star$ that would be obtained if every device contributed equally. Define the system-induced bias as any systematic deviation between $\hat{\theta}$ and $\theta^\star$ (or between their downstream performance on subgroups of $\mathcal{D}$) that arises from heterogeneity in $\{q_i\}$ rather than from differences in $\{P_i\}$ themselves.

Develop a rigorous framework that:

(a) defines and quantifies system-induced bias in federated learning, including useful proxy metrics such as the expected rate of contribution $q_i$ of each device and its relationship to per-subgroup model performance;

(b) provides a root-cause decomposition that attributes observed bias to identifiable system factors (e.g., device class, connectivity, time zone, battery policy, dropout during training);

(c) gives stratification strategies for partitioning $\mathcal{D}$ into meaningful subgroups along which bias should be measured and audited; and

(d) designs client-selection (scheduling) and update-weighting policies $\pi$ such that the trained model $\hat{\theta}_\pi$ provably reduces system-induced bias under realistic constraints (limited per-round participation, intermittent availability, privacy, communication budget), while maintaining convergence and utility guarantees.

Establish quantitative guarantees relating the chosen proxy metrics, the scheduling/weighting policy, and the resulting bias of $\hat{\theta}_\pi$.

Consider a federated learning system in which a central coordinator orchestrates training of a shared model across a large population of distributed clients. The performance of such a system can be characterized by multiple, often competing, criteria, including: (i) model quality Q (e.g., validation accuracy or loss), (ii) throughput T (e.g., updates processed per unit time), (iii) convergence speed C (e.g., wall-clock time or rounds to reach a target quality), (iv) fairness F across clients (e.g., variance of per-client performance, or worst-client utility), (v) a privacy guarantee P (e.g., the (ε, δ) parameters of a differential-privacy mechanism, or a bound on information leakage), (vi) robustness R against adversarial or Byzantine clients and against client drift, and (vii) resource use U (communication bandwidth, on-device compute, energy). Each of these is itself a function of a vector θ of tunable system parameters (number of clients sampled per round, local epochs, learning rates, batch sizes, compression and quantization levels, noise multipliers, aggregation rules, secure-aggregation thresholds, dropout-tolerance settings, etc.).

Formalize and solve the following:

1. Design a family of composite objective functions Φ(θ) = Φ(Q(θ), T(θ), C(θ), F(θ), P(θ), R(θ), U(θ)) suitable for use as optimization targets when tuning a federated learning system, such that Φ encodes principled trade-offs among the seven criteria above and admits meaningful Pareto analysis.

2. Provide algorithms that, given only black-box (and noisy) access to the criteria via system runs or simulations, automatically select θ to optimize Φ — replacing manual tuning — and prove guarantees on their sample complexity, regret, or convergence to (approximate) Pareto-optimal configurations under appropriate assumptions on the criteria as functions of θ.

The task is to produce both the principled construction of Φ and the accompanying automatic-tuning algorithms with formal guarantees.

For c < 1/4, Fox and Loh (2012) showed that f(n;c) = n^{O(1/log log n)}, refuting the conjecture that f(n;c) > n^ε for some ε>0. A clique covering of $G$ is a collection $\mathcal{C}$ of cliques of $G$ whose union of edge sets covers some subset of the edges of $G$; an edge of $G$ is said to be covered by $\mathcal{C}$ if it is contained in at least one clique of $\mathcal{C}$. (i) $\max_{v} d_{\mathcal{C}}(v) = o(n)$, and

(ii) all but $o(n^2)$ edges of $G$ are covered by $\mathcal{C}$.

Moreover, determine whether one can sharpen (i) to $\max_{v} d_{\mathcal{C}}(v) = O(n/\log n)$, while still satisfying (ii).

Let $P$ be a fixed convex polygon with $n \ge 8$ vertices. A triangulation of $P$ is a maximal set of pairwise non-crossing diagonals of $P$, which subdivides $P$ into triangles. Two triangulations $T$ and $T'$ are said to be adjacent if there exist a diagonal $d \in T$ and a diagonal $d' \in T'$ such that $T' = (T \setminus \{d\}) \cup \{d'\}$; equivalently, $d$ and $d'$ are the two diagonals of some convex quadrilateral formed by two adjacent triangles of $T$, and replacing $d$ by $d'$ is called a diagonal flip. This adjacency relation defines the flip graph $\mathcal{F}_n$, whose vertices are the triangulations of $P$. Let $f(n)$ denote the diameter of $\mathcal{F}_n$, that is, the maximum, over all pairs of triangulations $T, T'$ of $P$, of the minimum number of flips needed to transform $T$ into $T'$.

It is known that $f(n) \le 2n - 10$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Determine whether this upper bound is tight: is it true that $f(n) = 2n - 10$ for all sufficiently large $n$ (and, more strongly, asymptotically optimal in the sense $f(n)/n \to 2$)?

The conjecture was settled by Lionel Pournin (2014), who gave a combinatorial proof that the diameter of the associahedron — equivalently, the maximum flip distance between two triangulations of a convex $n$-gon — equals $2n-10$ for all $n \ge 13$. This resolves the question posed originally by Sleator, Tarjan, and Thurston, who established the upper bound and proved tightness only for sufficiently large $n$ via hyperbolic geometry without an explicit threshold.

A threshold graph is a graph that can be constructed from a single vertex by repeatedly adding either an isolated vertex or a dominating vertex (one adjacent to all existing vertices). Equivalently, threshold graphs are exactly the graphs containing no induced subgraph isomorphic to 2K_2, P_4, or C_4.

Consider the following two extremal questions about threshold graphs.

(i) Cover vs. partition. Suppose there exists a family of graphs {G_n} such that, for every n, the edge set E(G_n) can be covered by the edge sets of 2n threshold subgraphs of G_n (these threshold subgraphs may overlap), but any partition of E(G_n) into edge-disjoint threshold subgraphs requires at least 3n parts. Determine whether the ratio 3n/2n = 3/2 is the largest possible separation. More precisely, find the supremum of constants c such that there exists a graph family in which the minimum size of a threshold edge-cover is m_n while the minimum size of a threshold edge-partition is at least c·m_n + o(m_n).

(ii) Large threshold subgraphs in dense graphs. Determine the largest constant c with the following property: every graph on 2n vertices with at least n^2 + 1 edges contains a threshold subgraph with at least cn edges. Equivalently, find
   c* = lim inf_{n→∞} (1/n) · min { t(G) : |V(G)| = 2n, |E(G)| ≥ n^2 + 1 },
where t(G) denotes the maximum number of edges in a threshold subgraph of G.

Let $k, m \ge 1$ be integers. Suppose the unit interval $[0,1]$ is partitioned into $k$ measurable subsets $C_1, \dots, C_k$ (the "color classes"), each of positive Lebesgue measure $|C_i|$. An $m$-partition of $[0,1]$ consists of $m$ pairwise disjoint subsets $A_1, \dots, A_m$ whose union is $[0,1]$, where each $A_j$ is a finite union of subintervals of $[0,1]$, and such that for every color $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$ and every part $j \in \{1,\dots,m\}$,
$$|A_j \cap C_i| = \frac{1}{m} |C_i|.$$
The number of cuts of such an $m$-partition is the number of interior endpoints of the constituent subintervals (equivalently, the minimum number of points in $(0,1)$ at which $[0,1]$ must be cut so that the resulting open intervals can be reassembled into the parts $A_1,\dots,A_m$).

Let $k, m \ge 1$ be integers. Suppose the unit interval $[0,1]$ is partitioned into $k$ measurable subsets $C_1, \dots, C_k$ (the "color classes"), each of positive Lebesgue measure $|C_i|$. $$|A_j \cap C_i| = \frac{1}{m} |C_i|.$$

Define $c(m,k)$ to be the smallest integer $N$ such that, for every choice of $k$ measurable color classes $C_1,\dots,C_k$ partitioning $[0,1]$, there exists an $m$-partition using at most $N$ cuts.

Prove or disprove: $c(m,k) = (m-1)k$ for all positive integers $m$ and $k$.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite graph on $n=|V|$ vertices and $m=|E|$ edges. The distance $d_G(u,v)$ between two vertices $u,v\in V$ is the number of edges in a shortest path from $u$ to $v$ (or $+\infty$ if no such path exists). The diameter of $G$ is
$$\mathrm{diam}(G) \;=\; \max_{u,v\in V} d_G(u,v).$$

It is known that $\mathrm{diam}(G)$ can be computed by first solving all-pairs shortest paths, which via fast (Boolean/min-plus) matrix multiplication can be done in time $O(n^{\omega})$ for unweighted graphs, where $\omega<2.373$ is the matrix-multiplication exponent.

Problem. Design an algorithm that computes the exact diameter $\mathrm{diam}(G)$ of an arbitrary (say unweighted, undirected) graph $G$ in time asymptotically faster than the matrix-multiplication-based $O(n^{\omega})$ bound; equivalently, determine whether exact diameter computation is strictly easier than all-pairs shortest paths, or prove that no such speed-up is possible.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The exact complexity of computing graph diameter remains open. The fastest exact algorithm still runs in $O(n^{\omega})$ time via fast matrix multiplication, and it is a well-known open question whether exact diameter requires solving all-pairs shortest paths. Conditional lower bounds under SETH rule out truly subquadratic $O((n+m)^{2-\varepsilon})$ algorithms for sparse graphs, but no unconditional improvement over the matrix-multiplication bound is known, and approximation/directed/dynamic variants remain active research areas.

This is a conjecture commonly attributed to Thomassen. It remains open in general. Recent work (e.g., a 2024 Electronic Journal of Combinatorics paper, "Highly Connected Graphs Have Highly Connected Spanning Bipartite Subgraphs") establishes that every t-connected graph has a k-connected spanning bipartite subgraph for some t = t(k,n) bounded above by a function such as O(k^2 log n), but the linear bound 2k-1 (independent of n) is not known. The existence of SIC-POVMs in all finite dimensions (Zauner's conjecture) remains open. Exact solutions are known in many specific dimensions (e.g., 2–24, 28, 30, 31, 35, 37, 39, 43, 48, 124, and additional sporadic cases extended through 2024–2025), and conjectural infinite-family constructions exist (e.g., Kopp's construction for odd primes $d\equiv 2\pmod 3$ contingent on a Stark-type conjecture about real units in ray class fields). A collection of orthonormal bases $\{|\psi^{(1)}_i\rangle\}_{i=1}^N,\dots,\{|\psi^{(M)}_i\rangle\}_{i=1}^N$ of $\mathcal{H}_N$ is called a set of mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) if, for every pair of distinct bases $m\neq n$ and all indices $i,j\in\{1,\dots,N\}$,
$$|\langle \psi^{(m)}_i\,|\,\psi^{(n)}_j\rangle|^2=\frac{1}{N}.$$
It is known that any set of MUBs in $\mathcal{H}_N$ has cardinality at most $N+1$, and that this bound is attained whenever $N$ is a prime power.

Determine, for every dimension $N$ that is not a prime power, the maximum cardinality $M(N)$ of a set of mutually unbiased bases in $\mathbb{C}^N$. In particular, decide whether $M(6)=3$ or whether four mutually unbiased bases can exist in $\mathbb{C}^6$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem remains open. Dimension 6 is the smallest non-prime-power case and it is still unknown whether more than 3 mutually unbiased bases exist in C^6 (the conjectured maximum is 3, and no set of 4 MUBs has ever been found, despite extensive analytical and numerical searches). Recent work in 2025 reformulates the question as a polynomial optimization problem and shows the algorithm would in principle resolve dimension 6 but remains computationally intractable. A 2025 note also invalidated some structural theorems previously claimed about hypothetical sets of 4 MUBs in C^6.

representations.normalized:
A Latin square of order N is an N×N array filled with N symbols such that each symbol occurs exactly once in every row and exactly once in every column. Two Latin squares L = (l_{ij}) and M = (m_{ij}) of order N are said to be orthogonal if the N^2 ordered pairs (l_{ij}, m_{ij}), as (i,j) ranges over all positions, are all distinct. A set of Latin squares of order N is called mutually orthogonal (MOLS) if every two of them are orthogonal. Let N(n) denote the maximum size of a set of MOLS of order n. It is classical that N(n) ≤ n−1 for all n ≥ 2, with equality whenever n is a prime power.

Determine N(n) for arbitrary n. In particular, give a formula or characterization of the maximal number of mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order n for every positive integer n that is not a prime power.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Determining the maximum number N(n) of mutually orthogonal Latin squares for general (non prime-power) order n is a long-standing open problem in combinatorial design theory. Only the upper bound N(n) ≤ n−1 (attained for prime powers), partial values for small n, and asymptotic lower bounds such as N(n) ≥ n^{1/17} − 2 for large n are known. The exact value remains unknown even for n = 10, 12, and many other small composite orders.

Background and definitions.

(a) Discrete setting. For a Hilbert space of dimension N, two orthonormal bases {|e_i⟩} and {|f_j⟩} are called mutually unbiased if |⟨e_i|f_j⟩|^2 = 1/N for all i,j. Let M(N) denote the maximum number of pairwise mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) in dimension N. It is known that M(N) ≤ N+1, with equality when N is a prime power. The value of M(6) is unknown; only M(6) ≥ 3 has been established, and it is widely conjectured but unproven that M(6) = 3. This is the so-called "dimension-6 conundrum".

(b) Continuous-variable setting. For a single continuous-variable quantum system (e.g., position/momentum on L^2(ℝ)), the maximum number of mutually unbiased bases (suitably defined via canonical conjugacy) is exactly 3.

(c) Coarse-grained setting. Consider periodic coarse-graining of continuous-variable observables that produces effective d-dimensional measurements, leading to the notion of mutually unbiased measurements (MUMs) in the coarse-grained scenario. In this framework, every even-dimensional coarse-grained system admits at most 3 MUMs (matching the continuous-variable bound), while odd-dimensional coarse-grained systems may admit more.

Problem. Establish or refute a structural relationship between the following two phenomena:
(i) the fact that in the coarse-grained continuous-variable scenario the number of mutually unbiased measurements in even dimensions is bounded by 3 (so that, in particular, dimension 6 is not distinguished from other even dimensions), and
(ii) the open question of whether M(6) = 3 in the discrete Hilbert-space setting.

Specifically: provide a rigorous mathematical link (e.g., a limiting procedure, embedding, or no-go argument) that derives the conjectural bound M(6) ≤ 3 from the even-dimensional coarse-grained bound, or alternatively prove that no such direct connection exists.

The maximum number of mutually unbiased bases in dimension 6 remains a well-known open problem; only the bound M(6) ≥ 3 is established, with M(6) = 3 conjectured but unproven. Setup. Let $\mathcal{H}_A = \mathcal{H}_B = \mathbb{C}^d$ with $d\geq 3$, and consider bipartite quantum states, i.e. density operators $ho$ on $\mathcal{H}_A\otimes\mathcal{H}_B$ (positive semidefinite, trace one). The partial transpose of $ho$ with respect to $B$ is the operator $ho^{\Gamma}$ defined by $(|iangle\langle k|\otimes |jangle\langle l|)^{\Gamma}=|iangle\langle k|\otimes |langle\langle j|$ extended by linearity. The state $ho$ is said to have negative partial transpose (NPT) if $ho^{\Gamma}$ has at least one strictly negative eigenvalue, and positive partial transpose (PPT) otherwise. A state $ho$ is separable if it is a convex combination of product states $\sigma_A\otimes\sigma_B$, and entangled otherwise.

A bipartite state $ho$ is said to be distillable if there exist an integer $n\geq 1$, a number $K\geq 2$, and local operations with classical communication (LOCC), i.e. a trace-non-increasing completely positive map of the form $\Lambda(\cdot)=\sum_i (A_i\otimes B_i)(\cdot)(A_i\otimes B_i)^{\dagger}$ on $n$ copies, such that the output $\Lambda(ho^{\otimes n})/\mathrm{Tr}\,\Lambda(ho^{\otimes n})$ has fidelity strictly greater than $1/K$ with the maximally entangled state $|\Phi_K^+angle=	frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}\sum_{i=1}^{K}|iiangle$ on $\mathbb{C}^K\otimes\mathbb{C}^K$. A state that is entangled but not distillable is called bound entangled.

For $d\geq 2$ and $p\in[-1,1]$, the Werner state on $\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d$ is
$$W_{d,p} \;=\;  rac{1}{d^2-dp} igl(\mathbb{1} - p\,\mathbb{F} igr),$$
where $\mathbb{F}=\sum_{i,j}|ijangle\langle ji|$ is the swap operator. The state $W_{d,p}$ is NPT if and only if $p>1/d$.

Problem. Decide whether there exists a bipartite quantum state $ho$ on $\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d$ for some $d\geq 3$ that is simultaneously NPT and nondistillable. Equivalently, decide whether there exist $d\geq 3$ and $p\in(1/d,1]$ such that the Werner state $W_{d,p}$ is nondistillable.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The existence of NPT bound entangled states (equivalently, nondistillable NPT Werner states in dimension d≥3) remains a long-standing open problem in quantum information theory. Recent works from 2024–2025 (e.g., new partial-trace inequalities for distillability of Werner states and reductions of N-undistillability to repeated 1-undistillability checks) report partial progress but do not resolve the question. Sources state the problem has been open for nearly 30 years.

Let $H_d$ denote a $d$-dimensional complex Hilbert space, and let $V$ be the swap (flip) operator on $H_d \otimes H_d$ defined by $\langle ij | V | kl \rangle = \delta_{il}\delta_{jk}$. For $d \geq 2$ and $\alpha \in [-1, 1]$, define the Werner state
$$\rho(d,\alpha) = \frac{I \otimes I + \alpha V}{d^2 + \alpha d}.$$
A bipartite state $\rho$ acting on $H_A \otimes H_B$ is called $n$-copy distillable if there exist a Schmidt-rank-2 vector $|\psi\rangle \in (H_A^{\otimes n}) \otimes (H_B^{\otimes n})$ and local operators $A, B$ acting on $H_A^{\otimes n}, H_B^{\otimes n}$ respectively such that
$$\langle \psi | (A \otimes B)\, \rho^{\otimes n} (A \otimes B)^\dagger | \psi \rangle > \tfrac{1}{2} \langle \psi | (A \otimes B)(A \otimes B)^\dagger | \psi \rangle \cdot \mathrm{Tr}(\rho^{\otimes n}(A\otimes B)^\dagger(A\otimes B))/\mathrm{Tr}((A\otimes B)^\dagger(A\otimes B)\rho^{\otimes n}),$$
equivalently, such that $(A \otimes B)\,\rho^{\otimes n}(A \otimes B)^\dagger$, suitably normalized, has fidelity greater than $1/2$ with a maximally entangled two-qubit state under the projection onto the support of $|\psi\rangle$. The state $\rho$ is called distillable if it is $n$-copy distillable for some finite $n$, and completely non-distillable otherwise.

Prove or disprove: for every dimension $d \geq 2$ and every parameter $\alpha \in [-1,1]$ such that the Werner state $\rho(d,\alpha)$ is not $1$-copy distillable, $\rho(d,\alpha)$ is not $n$-copy distillable for any finite $n \geq 1$ (in particular, $1$-copy non-distillability is equivalent to complete non-distillability within the Werner family).

Let $d=4$ and let $\mathbb{F}\in M_d\otimes M_d$ denote the swap (flip) operator $\mathbb{F}|i\rangle|j\rangle=|j\rangle|i\rangle$. The two-ququart Werner state with parameter $f=-1/2$ is
$$\rho(4,-1/2)=\frac{1}{d^2-d\cdot(-1/2)\cdot 2}\bigl(I-2\cdot(-1/2)\,\mathbb{F}\bigr)\cdot c,$$
normalized to a density operator (equivalently, the unique two-ququart Werner state whose partial transpose is proportional to a unitary). A bipartite state $\rho$ on $\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d$ is called $n$-copy distillable if there exists a Schmidt-rank-2 vector $|\psi\rangle\in(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes n}\otimes(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes n}$ such that $\langle\psi|(\rho^{\otimes n})^{T_B}|\psi\rangle<0$, where $T_B$ denotes the partial transpose on the second factor.

Prove that $\rho(4,-1/2)$ is not $2$-copy distillable.

Equivalently, prove the following algebraic statement: for every pair of traceless complex $4\times 4$ matrices $A,B\in M_4(\mathbb{C})$ satisfying
$$\operatorname{Tr}(A^\dagger A)+\operatorname{Tr}(B^\dagger B)=\tfrac{1}{4},$$
the Kronecker sum $A\oplus B := A\otimes I_4 + I_4\otimes B$ has its two largest singular values $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2$ satisfying
$$\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2 \le \tfrac{1}{2}.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The two-copy distillability problem for the 4×4 Werner state ρ(4,−1/2) remains an open conjecture in quantum information theory. Partial results have been established: Chen and collaborators (2021) proved the conjecture for monomial matrices A, B, and a 2023 follow-up extended this to matrices A, B with at most four nonzero entries. No general proof is known as of 2026.

Let $\rho_{AB}$ be a bipartite density matrix on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_A\otimes\mathcal{H}_B$. The partial transpose $\rho_{AB}^{\Gamma}$ (taken on system $B$) is defined by $\langle i,k|\rho^{\Gamma}|j,l\rangle = \langle i,l|\rho|j,k\rangle$. The state $\rho_{AB}$ is said to have negative partial transpose (NPT) if $\rho_{AB}^{\Gamma}$ has at least one strictly negative eigenvalue, and is called NPT entangled when it is also entangled (which, for NPT states, follows automatically by the Peres criterion).

A private bit (pbit) is a bipartite state of the form
$$\gamma_{AA'BB'} = U\bigl(|\Phi^+\rangle\langle\Phi^+|_{AB}\otimes\sigma_{A'B'}\bigr)U^\dagger,$$
where $|\Phi^+\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)$ is the two-qubit maximally entangled state held jointly by Alice ($A$) and Bob ($B$), $\sigma_{A'B'}$ is an arbitrary state of the auxiliary "shield" systems $A'$ (held by Alice) and $B'$ (held by Bob), and $U$ is a "twisting" unitary of the form $U = \sum_{ij}|ij\rangle\langle ij|_{AB}\otimes U_{ij}^{A'B'}$ with each $U_{ij}^{A'B'}$ unitary on $A'B'$. Measuring $A$ and $B$ in the computational basis of a pbit yields a perfectly correlated and uniformly random bit that is decoupled from any purifying eavesdropper, hence the term "private bit."

Distillability of pbits is defined under the class of LOCC (local operations and classical communication): $\rho_{AB}$ is said to allow pbit distillation if for every $\epsilon>0$ and some integer $m\ge 1$ there exists an LOCC protocol mapping $\rho_{AB}^{\otimes n}$ (for some $n$) to a state $\tau$ on $AA'BB'$ with $\|\tau - \gamma_m\|_1 \le \epsilon$ for some $m$-pbit $\gamma_m$, and the asymptotic key rate is positive. The protocol is called one-way (from Alice to Bob) if all classical messages exchanged during the LOCC flow only from Alice to Bob.

(a) Every NPT entangled bipartite state $\rho_{AB}$ admits a pbit-distillation protocol with positive asymptotic key rate.

(b) If (a) holds, then for every NPT entangled $\rho_{AB}$ such a pbit-distillation protocol can be implemented using only one-way classical communication from Alice to Bob.

Let $\rho_{AB}$ be a bipartite density matrix on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_A\otimes\mathcal{H}_B$. A private bit (pbit) is a bipartite state of the form

Let T = [0,τ] ⊂ ℝ and let R^T denote the space of paths x: T → ℝ. Consider a (suitably regular) potential V: ℝ × T → ℝ, and define the Feynman state function formally as the Henstock path integral

  ψ(ξ,τ) = ∫_{R^T} exp(-i ∫_T V(x(t),t) dt) · exp((i/2) ∫_T (dx/dt)^2 dt) ∏_{t∈T} (δx(t)/√(2π i dt)),

where the integral is interpreted in the Henstock (gauge) sense on the path space R^T, and the product over t ∈ T is the standard formal Feynman normalization. Expand the interaction factor as a power series:

  exp(-i ∫_T V(x(t),t) dt) = Σ_{r=0}^∞ (-i)^r/r! · (∫_T V(x(t),t) dt)^r,

and define formally, for each r ≥ 0,

  ψ_r(ξ,τ) = ∫_{R^T} ((-i)^r/r!) (∫_T V(x(t),t) dt)^r · exp((i/2) ∫_T (dx/dt)^2 dt) ∏_{t∈T} (δx(t)/√(2π i dt)).

Question: Provide a rigorous mathematical justification — within the framework of the Henstock path integral on R^T — for the interchange of the infinite series and the path integral, i.e. establish hypotheses on V (and on ξ, τ) under which each ψ_r is a well-defined Henstock path integral and the identity

  ψ(ξ,τ) = Σ_{r=0}^∞ ψ_r(ξ,τ)

holds, thereby giving a mathematically rigorous foundation for the Feynman-diagram (perturbative) expansion. Equivalently, formulate and prove a dominated/monotone convergence type theorem for the Henstock path integral that legitimizes this term-by-term integration, or show that no such theorem can hold in this setting.

Fix a positive integer T and consider the space $\mathbb{R}^T$ of paths $x:\{1,\dots,T\}\to\mathbb{R}$. For a tagged division $(x,N,I[N])$ of $\mathbb{R}^T$ subordinate to a gauge $\gamma_0$ (a $\gamma_0$-fine associated triple in the sense of Henstock), let \[ g_0(x,N,I[N]) \] denote the free-particle Fresnel integrand used in the Henstock formulation of the Feynman path integral, and let \[ \beta(x,N,I[N]) \] be a positive integrable majorant required by the bounded convergence theorem for Henstock integration on $\mathbb{R}^T$.

Let $E$ be a Banach space equipped with a closed convex cone $P\subset E$ that induces a partial order $\le$ on $E$ via $u\le v\iff v-u\in P$. Assume that the maps $|g_0|$ and $\beta$, regarded as elements indexed by $\gamma_0$-fine associated triples, lie in $E$.

Consider the hypothesis
\[ |g_0(x,N,I[N])|-\beta(x,N,I[N])\in P \qquad\text{for every $\gamma_0$-fine }(x,N,I[N]), \]
equivalently $\beta\le|g_0|$ pointwise on the set of $\gamma_0$-fine associated triples.

Problem. Define a notion of supremum in the ordered Banach space $(E,P)$ (for instance, a least upper bound with respect to $\le$, possibly relative to a suitable subfamily) that is well adapted to the families $\{|g_0|\}$ and $\{\beta\}$, and use this supremum together with the hypothesis above to derive a contradiction with the bounded convergence requirement. Use the resulting argument to determine whether the Henstock path integral on $\mathbb{R}^T$ can be interchanged with the summation of the perturbation series defining the Feynman path integral.

Let $T = [a,b] \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a compact interval and let $\mathbb{R}^T$ denote the set of all functions $x : T \to \mathbb{R}$ (regarded as paths). Let $N(T)$ denote the collection of finite ordered partitions of $T$ (i.e. finite increasing tuples $a = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = b$), and let $I(\mathbb{R}^T)$ denote a chosen family of "interval-like" subsets of $\mathbb{R}^T$ (cylinder sets determined by finitely many coordinates). Suppose that on $\mathbb{R}^T$ one has fixed a Henstock-type integration scheme so that for a complex-valued function $h$ defined on triples $(x, P, J) \in \mathbb{R}^T \times N(T) \times I(\mathbb{R}^T)$ the symbol $\int_{\mathbb{R}^T} h$ has a precise meaning (as a Henstock limit of Riemann-type sums indexed by partitions $P$ and cylinder sets $J$).

Define the function space
$$H \;=\; \Bigl\{\, h : \mathbb{R}^T \times N(T) \times I(\mathbb{R}^T) \to \mathbb{C} \;:\; \Bigl|\int_{\mathbb{R}^T} h\Bigr| < \infty \,\Bigr\},$$
viewed as a complex vector space under pointwise operations.

Prove or disprove: the cardinality of $H$ satisfies $\mathrm{Card}(H) \le \mathfrak{c}$ (the cardinality of the continuum), and consequently the vector-space dimension of $H$ over $\mathbb{C}$ equals $\mathfrak{c}$.

Let $T$ be a (possibly uncountable) index set and consider the path space $\mathbb{R}^T$ of all functions $\gamma : T \to \mathbb{R}$. Suppose that an appropriate notion of Henstock (Henstock–Kurzweil-type) integral has been defined on $\mathbb{R}^T$, and let $\mathcal{H}$ denote the corresponding linear space of Henstock-integrable real-valued functions on $\mathbb{R}^T$ (the space used to give a rigorous Henstock-integral formulation of the Feynman path integral).

It is known that for the finite-dimensional analogue — the space $HK(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R})$ of Henstock–Kurzweil integrable functions $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ — there exists no "natural" Banach space norm; that is, $HK(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R})$ cannot be equipped with a norm, defined intrinsically from the Henstock integration structure, that makes it a Banach space.

Question: Does this non-existence result extend to the path-space setting? More precisely, prove or disprove that there is no natural Banach space norm on $\mathcal{H}$, i.e. that $\mathcal{H}$ admits no intrinsic norm under which it becomes a Banach space.

A nature-inspired (metaheuristic) optimization algorithm is an iterative stochastic procedure that, for a given objective function f : S → ℝ on a search space S ⊆ ℝ^d, generates a sequence of populations {X_t}_{t≥0} of candidate solutions in S according to update rules typically parameterized by control parameters and inspired by natural phenomena (e.g., genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, simulated annealing, differential evolution, ant colony optimization, firefly algorithm, cuckoo search, bat algorithm, etc.). For such an algorithm A, one is interested in the following analytical properties:

(i) Convergence: the existence of a (random or deterministic) limit lim_{t→∞} f(X_t^*) toward the global optimum f* = inf_{x∈S} f(x), where X_t^* denotes the best solution in population X_t, in an appropriate probabilistic sense (almost sure, in probability, in expectation).

(ii) Rate of convergence: quantitative bounds on E[f(X_t^*) − f*] or on the hitting time τ_ε = inf{t : f(X_t^*) − f* ≤ ε} as a function of t, ε, dimension d, population size, and algorithm parameters.

(iii) Stability: continuous dependence of the trajectory {X_t} (and of its limit) on initial conditions, parameter perturbations, and stochastic noise.

(iv) Robustness: preservation of (i)–(iii) under classes of perturbations of the objective function f and of the algorithmic dynamics.

Problem. Construct a single mathematical framework — for instance, a common formalism based on Markov processes, dynamical systems, stochastic approximation, mean-field limits, or operator-theoretic recursions — broad enough to encompass the principal classes of nature-inspired optimization algorithms listed above, and within which one can rigorously prove general theorems giving:

(a) sufficient conditions on the algorithmic update operators and parameters that guarantee global convergence of {f(X_t^*)} to f*;
(b) explicit, non-asymptotic rates of convergence in terms of the structural parameters of the framework;
(c) quantitative stability estimates with respect to initial population, parameter values, and stochastic perturbations;
(d) robustness guarantees under specified classes of objective and dynamical perturbations.

The framework should specialize, by appropriate choices of its ingredients, to the standard formulations of the major nature-inspired algorithms, recovering or improving known case-by-case analyses as corollaries.

Let A be a nature-inspired (meta)heuristic optimization algorithm depending on a finite vector of control parameters θ ∈ Θ ⊆ R^k (for example, population size, mutation/crossover rates, inertia weights, cooling schedules, etc.). Let F be a specified class of optimization problems f : D → R (with D a given search domain), and let P(A, θ, f, t) denote a chosen scalar performance measure of A applied to problem f with parameters θ over a computational budget t (for instance, expected best-so-far objective value, success rate of reaching an ε-optimum, or expected runtime to a target).

(a) Static tuning. Determine, for the class F, a parameter setting
   θ* ∈ arg max_{θ ∈ Θ}  E_{f ∼ F} [ P(A, θ, f, t) ],
and provide a constructive, theoretically justified procedure for finding θ* (or a provably near-optimal surrogate) that does not rely solely on exhaustive empirical search.

(b) Dynamic control. Allow the parameters to be a function θ(s) of the algorithm's internal state s (iteration counter, population statistics, search history, etc.). Determine a control policy
   π* : S → Θ
that maximizes E_{f ∼ F} [ P(A, π, f, t) ] over admissible policies π, and characterize structural properties (monotonicity, schedules, feedback rules) of optimal or near-optimal policies for natural classes F.

Provide either explicit optimal/near-optimal tuning rules and control policies for meaningful classes F, or rigorous performance guarantees (upper and lower bounds) for the resulting tuned algorithm.

representations.normalized:
Consider the setting of black-box optimization, where an algorithm A is a (possibly randomized) procedure that, given access to an objective function f : X → Y from some class F of functions on a finite search space X with values in a finite ordered set Y, sequentially queries points x_1, x_2, … ∈ X, observes values f(x_1), f(x_2), …, and outputs a trace T_m(A,f) = ((x_1,f(x_1)),…,(x_m,f(x_m))) of length m without revisiting points. A performance measure is a function Φ(T_m(A,f)) ∈ ℝ (e.g. best-so-far value), and the average performance of A on a probability distribution P over F is E_{f∼P}[Φ(T_m(A,f))].

The classical No Free Lunch (NFL) theorem states: if P is uniform over the set Y^X of all functions f : X → Y (or, more generally, if P is closed under permutation of X), then for every performance measure Φ depending only on the multiset of observed values, all non-revisiting algorithms A have identical average performance E_{f∼P}[Φ(T_m(A,f))].

Address the following two linked questions for nature-inspired (metaheuristic) optimization algorithms:

(a) Benchmarking. Formulate criteria characterizing which benchmark suites B ⊂ F (finite collections of test functions, possibly with associated distributions and performance measures) yield comparisons of algorithms that are genuinely informative — in the sense of being predictive of performance on unseen problems of practical interest, robust under reasonable transformations (translations, rotations, rescalings, irrelevant variables), and not artificially favoring any particular algorithmic bias. Provide a precise mathematical framework in which such "useful benchmarking" can be defined and verified.

(b) Free lunches. Determine conditions on the function class F, the prior distribution P, the algorithm class 𝒜, and the performance measure Φ under which strict free lunches exist, i.e., there exist algorithms A, A' ∈ 𝒜 with
   E_{f∼P}[Φ(T_m(A,f))] > E_{f∼P}[Φ(T_m(A',f))].
Characterize as completely as possible the structural properties of (F, P) — for instance, non-closure under permutation, restrictions to functions with bounded description length / Kolmogorov complexity, smoothness or Lipschitz constraints, co-evolutionary settings, multi-objective settings, or restrictions on 𝒜 — that admit free lunches, and quantify the maximal achievable gap.

The original NFL theorems (Wolpert–Macready, 1997) are proved, but follow-up "free lunch" results are still actively investigated: known results include free lunches for co-evolution (Wolpert–Macready 2005), for sets of functions not closed under permutation (Schumacher–Vose–Whitley 2001; Igel–Toussaint 2004), for restricted-complexity function classes (Lattimore–Hutter 2013), and for multi-objective optimization (Corne–Knowles 2003). However, a comprehensive characterization of "useful benchmarking" for nature-inspired algorithms and a complete classification of conditions under which free lunches exist remains an open research direction, frequently cited as an open problem in metaheuristics surveys.

Consider the class N of nature-inspired (meta)heuristic optimization algorithms, i.e., iterative stochastic procedures A that, given a black-box objective function f : X → R on a search space X (typically X ⊆ R^n or a discrete combinatorial domain), produce a sequence of candidate solutions x_1, x_2, … ∈ X aimed at approximating arg min_{x ∈ X} f(x). Examples include genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution, simulated annealing, ant colony optimization, cuckoo search, firefly algorithm, and similar population-based or trajectory-based heuristics.

A performance metric is a functional M that, given an algorithm A ∈ N, a benchmark distribution or set of test problems F = {f_1, …, f_K}, a computational budget B (e.g., maximum number of function evaluations), and a probabilistic model of A's randomness, assigns a real number M(A; F, B) measuring quality (e.g., expected best-so-far value, success rate to reach a target, expected runtime, anytime performance, convergence rate, robustness across problem instances, or computational complexity per iteration).

A comparison framework is a tuple (F, B, M, S) consisting of a benchmark family F, a budget specification B, one or more metrics M, and a statistical decision procedure S that, on the basis of finitely many independent runs of each algorithm, outputs a (possibly partial) ranking of any finite subset of N.

Problems:
(1) Identify performance metrics M that are most suitable for fairly comparing arbitrary algorithms A, A' ∈ N, where 'fair' requires at minimum that M be invariant under cosmetic reformulations of an algorithm (renaming, trivial reparameterizations), account for per-iteration computational cost, control for tuning effort and the No-Free-Lunch constraint that average performance over all functions is identical for all algorithms, and provide statistically rigorous (e.g., distribution-free) guarantees from a finite number of runs.
(2) Determine whether there exists a single unified comparison framework (F, B, M, S) that, applied to every pair A, A' ∈ N, yields rankings that are fair in the above sense and rigorous in the sense of admitting provable statistical or complexity-theoretic guarantees; or, alternatively, prove that no such unified framework can exist (e.g., by an impossibility theorem analogous to No-Free-Lunch or to Arrow-type results).

The question is posed as an open problem about benchmarking methodology for nature-inspired optimization algorithms. While benchmarking suites (BBOB/COCO, CEC, IOHprofiler) and statistical comparison protocols (Demšar-style nonparametric tests, fixed-budget vs. fixed-target analyses) are widely used and continue to be refined, no unified, universally accepted "fair and rigorous" framework comparing all metaheuristics has been established; the metaheuristics community continues to debate fairness of comparisons, novelty of "new" nature-inspired methods, and No-Free-Lunch implications. The problem appears to remain open as a methodological/foundational question.

Consider the class of nature-inspired metaheuristic optimization algorithms (for example, evolutionary algorithms, particle swarm optimization, ant colony optimization, differential evolution, firefly algorithm, cuckoo search, and similar population-based stochastic search methods) designed to approximately solve optimization problems of the form

  minimize f(x)  subject to  x ∈ Ω ⊆ R^n,

where f : Ω → R may be nonlinear, nonconvex, multimodal, noisy, or only available as a black-box oracle, and Ω may be defined by complicated (possibly nonlinear or combinatorial) constraints.

It is empirically established that many such algorithms perform well on small-scale instances (with n at most a few tens of variables and modest numbers of constraints). Develop a systematic methodology — including algorithmic modifications, theoretical analysis of convergence and complexity, and guidelines for parameter tuning, decomposition, parallelization, dimensionality reduction, surrogate modelling, and constraint handling — that allows such algorithms to be scaled up so that they solve truly large-scale real-world optimization problems (with n on the order of 10^4 to 10^6 or more variables, and large numbers of constraints) efficiently, in the sense of producing high-quality solutions within practically acceptable computational budgets. Specifically: identify general principles that govern when and how a small-scale nature-inspired algorithm can be extended to the large-scale regime while preserving solution quality, and provide quantitative performance guarantees as functions of problem dimension, structure, and computational resources.

Consider a population-based stochastic optimization algorithm intended to minimize an objective function f : S → R over a (possibly high-dimensional, non-convex) search space S. At each iteration t, the algorithm maintains a population X_t ⊂ S and generates new candidate solutions by combining two kinds of moves:

• Exploitation moves, which generate candidates close to the current best-known solutions in X_t (intensifying the search around promising regions).
• Exploration moves, which generate candidates far from the current population, sampling previously unvisited regions of S (diversifying the search).

Let p_t ∈ [0,1] denote the probability (or, more generally, the fractional weight) that a given candidate at iteration t is generated by an exploration move rather than an exploitation move, and let the remaining 1 − p_t weight be assigned to exploitation. The schedule {p_t}_{t≥0} controls the exploration–exploitation tradeoff of the algorithm.

Problem. Provide a principled, general framework that prescribes the schedule {p_t} (possibly adaptive, depending on observed values of f, on diversity measures of X_t, and on the iteration budget T) so as to optimally balance exploitation and exploration. Specifically:

1. Formulate a precise notion of an "optimal" exploration–exploitation tradeoff for such a population-based algorithm — for example, a schedule that minimizes the expected optimality gap E[f(x_T^*) − min_{x ∈ S} f(x)] after a fixed budget of T function evaluations, uniformly over a meaningful class F of objective functions f.

2. Determine, under that formulation, an explicit optimal or asymptotically optimal schedule {p_t}, or prove rigorous lower and upper bounds on the achievable expected optimality gap as a function of the schedule.

3. Identify conditions on f and on the algorithm's exploitation/exploration operators under which the proposed schedule provably outperforms any fixed-ratio schedule p_t ≡ p.

In short: rigorously characterize how a nature-inspired (population-based stochastic) optimization algorithm should allocate its effort between exploitation of currently promising regions and exploration of new regions in order to make this tradeoff as effective as possible.

Consider a constrained nonlinear optimization problem of the form

    minimize    f(x),    x ∈ D ⊆ R^n,
    subject to  g_i(x) ≤ 0,   i = 1, …, m,
                h_j(x) = 0,   j = 1, …, p,

where f, g_1, …, g_m, h_1, …, h_p : R^n → R are (possibly non-convex, non-differentiable) nonlinear functions and the feasible set
F = { x ∈ D : g_i(x) ≤ 0 ∀ i, h_j(x) = 0 ∀ j }
may be disconnected, of measure zero (due to equality constraints), or otherwise hard to sample.

A nature-inspired (population-based) optimization algorithm maintains a population {x^(t)_1, …, x^(t)_N} ⊂ D at iteration t and updates it via stochastic, derivative-free rules inspired by natural processes (e.g. genetic algorithms, particle swarm, differential evolution, firefly, cuckoo search, bat algorithm, etc.). Such algorithms in their unconstrained form do not directly account for constraints, and standard remedies include static/dynamic/adaptive penalty functions, feasibility rules, ε-constrained methods, repair operators, stochastic ranking, and multi-objective reformulations.

Problem. Design a constraint-handling framework, applicable to a generic population-based nature-inspired metaheuristic, with the following provable properties:

(a) Convergence: For any instance of the above constrained problem satisfying mild regularity conditions (e.g. continuity of f, g_i, h_j and nonempty F), the sequence of best feasible iterates produced by the algorithm converges in probability to a global minimizer of f over F.

(b) Feasibility: The probability that the incumbent solution is feasible tends to 1 as t → ∞, and equality constraints h_j(x) = 0 are handled without requiring a priori transformation into inequalities.

(c) Tunability-free behavior: The framework does not rely on problem-specific penalty parameters that must be hand-tuned per instance; any internal parameters are either self-adaptive or admit guarantees uniform over a broad class of constraint geometries.

(d) Balance of exploration and exploitation: The framework preserves the exploration capability of the underlying metaheuristic while concentrating samples near F, in a quantifiable sense (e.g. a bound on the expected distance from the population to F as a function of t).

Either exhibit such a framework together with a rigorous proof of (a)–(d), or prove that no constraint-handling scheme satisfying (a)–(d) simultaneously can exist for the full class of nonlinear constrained problems described above.

where f, g_1, …, g_m, h_1, …, h_p : R^n → R are (possibly non-convex, non-differentiable) nonlinear functions and the feasible set
F = { x ∈ D : g_i(x) ≤ 0 ∀ i, h_j(x) = 0 ∀ j }
may be disconnected, of measure zero (due to equality constraints), or otherwise hard to sample.

A nature-inspired (population-based) optimization algorithm maintains a population {x^(t)_1, …, x^(t)_N} ⊂ D at iteration t and updates it via stochastic, derivative-free rules inspired by natural processes (e.g. genetic algorithms, particle swarm, differential evolution, firefly, cuckoo search, bat algorithm, etc.). Such algorithms in their unconstrained form do not directly account for constraints, and standard remedies include static/dynamic/adaptive penalty functions, feasibility rules, ε-constrained methods, repair operators, stochastic ranking, and multi-objective reformulations.

Problem. Design a constraint-handling framework, applicable to a generic population-based nature-inspired metaheuristic, with the following provable properties:

(a) Convergence: For any instance of the above constrained problem satisfying mild regularity conditions (e.g. continuity of f, g_i, h_j and nonempty F), the sequence of best feasible iterates produced by the algorithm converges in probability to a global minimizer of f over F.

(b) Feasibility: The probability that the incumbent solution is feasible tends to 1 as t → ∞, and equality constraints h_j(x) = 0 are handled without requiring a priori transformation into inequalities.

(c) Tunability-free behavior: The framework does not rely on problem-specific penalty parameters that must be hand-tuned per instance; any internal parameters are either self-adaptive or admit guarantees uniform over a broad class of constraint geometries.

(d) Balance of exploration and exploitation: The framework preserves the exploration capability of the underlying metaheuristic while concentrating samples near F, in a quantifiable sense (e.g. a bound on the expected distance from the population to F as a function of t).

Either exhibit such a framework together with a rigorous proof of (a)–(d), or prove that no constraint-handling scheme satisfying (a)–(d) simultaneously can exist for the full class of nonlinear constrained problems described above.

Constraint handling in nature-inspired metaheuristics is widely recognized as an open research area. Surveys from 2016 onward (e.g., Mezura-Montes & Coello, Coello Coello's reviews, and recent surveys through 2024) consistently list effective handling of nonlinear—especially equality—constraints among unresolved challenges, with no universal scheme satisfying provable convergence, feasibility, and parameter-free properties for general nonlinear constrained problems.

A nature-inspired (metaheuristic) optimization algorithm is an iterative population-based stochastic search procedure that, given an objective function f : X → R on a search space X, maintains a population P_t ⊂ X of candidate solutions and updates it via stochastic operators inspired by natural processes (e.g., evolution, swarm dynamics, physical annealing) so as to approximately minimize f. Examples include genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution, simulated annealing, the firefly algorithm, cuckoo search, and the bat algorithm.

In machine learning and deep learning, typical optimization tasks include:
(i) training: given a parametric model h_θ with θ ∈ R^d (e.g., the weights of a deep neural network) and a training set, minimize an empirical loss L(θ) = (1/N) Σ_i ℓ(h_θ(x_i), y_i), where L is generally non-convex, high-dimensional, and only accessible through (mini-batch) stochastic evaluations of L and possibly its gradient;
(ii) hyperparameter and architecture optimization: minimize a validation loss V(λ) with respect to discrete and/or continuous hyperparameters λ (including neural architecture choices), where each evaluation of V(λ) requires training a model;
(iii) feature selection: choose a subset S ⊆ {1,…,p} of input features minimizing a generalization error criterion.

Develop a principled framework for using nature-inspired optimization algorithms in tasks (i)–(iii). Specifically, address the following:

1. Identify conditions on the loss landscape L (e.g., dimensionality d, smoothness, noise level, separability) and on the algorithmic operators under which a chosen nature-inspired algorithm provably converges, in expectation or with high probability, to an ε-approximate stationary point or global minimizer of L, and provide non-asymptotic complexity bounds (number of function evaluations as a function of d and ε).

2. Design hybrid schemes combining nature-inspired global search with gradient-based local search (e.g., SGD, Adam) for training deep neural networks, and prove that such hybrids match or improve the convergence guarantees of pure gradient methods on standard non-convex training objectives while improving exploration of the loss landscape.

3. For hyperparameter optimization and neural architecture search, characterize the regret of nature-inspired population strategies relative to Bayesian optimization and bandit-based baselines on a defined class of black-box objectives.

4. Determine to what extent and in what regimes nature-inspired algorithms can outperform stochastic gradient methods for problems (i)–(iii), supported by both theoretical guarantees and reproducible empirical benchmarks on standard datasets.

Provide either rigorous theorems answering (1)–(4) or precise impossibility/lower-bound results.

Let $1 < p < \infty$ and let $n \geq 2$. Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a connected open set, and let $u \in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ be a weak solution of the $p$-Laplace equation
$$\operatorname{div}\bigl(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u\bigr) = 0 \quad \text{in } \Omega,$$
i.e., $\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u\cdot\nabla\varphi\, dx = 0$ for every $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. We say that $u$ vanishes of infinite order at an interior point $x_0 \in \Omega$ if for every integer $N \geq 1$,
$$\lim_{r \to 0^+} r^{-N} \int_{B_r(x_0)} |u|^p\, dx = 0,$$
where $B_r(x_0) \subset \Omega$ is the Euclidean ball of radius $r$ centered at $x_0$.

Question: If $u$ vanishes of infinite order at some interior point $x_0 \in \Omega$, must $u \equiv 0$ on all of $\Omega$?

The strong unique continuation property for weak solutions of the p-Laplace equation is known in the plane (n=2) and in the linear case p=2 (classical Aronszajn-type results). For n≥3 and p≠2 the problem remains open; surveys and recent works on unique continuation for the p-Laplacian (e.g., partial results via Almgren-type frequency functions, including on the Heisenberg group under boundedness assumptions) continue to treat it as an open question.

Let $n\geq 3$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Consider the elliptic eigenvalue problem
$$\operatorname{div}(A\,\nabla u) - q\,u + \lambda\,\rho\,u = 0 \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial\Omega,$$
where $A:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is symmetric and uniformly elliptic (i.e., there exists $K>0$ with $K^{-1}|\xi|^2\leq A(x)\xi\cdot\xi\leq K|\xi|^2$ for all $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and a.e. $x\in\Omega$), the entries of $A$ are merely Hölder continuous (and not necessarily Lipschitz), $q,\rho\in L^\infty(\Omega)$, and $\rho\geq K^{-1}>0$ a.e.

Recall Courant's Nodal Domain Theorem: if $\{\lambda_k\}_{k\geq 1}$ are the Dirichlet eigenvalues listed in nondecreasing order with multiplicity, and $u_k$ is an eigenfunction associated to $\lambda_k$, then the number of connected components (nodal domains) of $\{x\in\Omega: u_k(x)\neq 0\}$ is at most $k$.

It is known that for Lipschitz $A$ this conclusion follows from the strong unique continuation property. Determine: under which conditions on $A$ (with $A$ only Hölder continuous and such that the unique continuation property for the equation above is not implied) does Courant's Nodal Domain Theorem remain valid?

Consider connected complex manifolds in the noncompact setting, and the following two notions of a deformation of a connected complex n-manifold X:

(A) A C^∞ map f : 𝒳 → Y between C^∞ manifolds, with Y connected, such that there exists a distinguished point 0 ∈ Y with f^{-1}(0) biholomorphic to X, and such that each fiber X_y := f^{-1}(y) carries the structure of a connected complex n-manifold induced by a system of local "fiberwise complex coordinates" on 𝒳: that is, each point of 𝒳 has an open neighborhood U with C^∞ coordinates (z_1,…,z_n, t_1,…,t_m) such that (t_1,…,t_m) are pulled back from C^∞ coordinates on Y and (z_1,…,z_n) restrict to holomorphic coordinates on each fiber. No properness of f and no C^∞ local triviality of f are assumed.

(B) A holomorphic surjective submersion π : 𝒳̃ → D, where D ⊂ ℂ is an open disc centered at 0, such that π^{-1}(0) is biholomorphic to X and π is locally trivial in the C^∞ category (i.e. for every point of D there exists an open neighborhood V ⊂ D and a C^∞ diffeomorphism π^{-1}(V) ≅ V × X over V).

Determine hypotheses on X, on the base, and/or on the map under which a deformation in sense (A) gives rise to a deformation in sense (B), and conversely. In particular, identify natural sufficient conditions under which the two notions coincide.

Two compact complex manifolds $X_0$ and $X_1$ of the same complex dimension are said to be deformation equivalent if there exist a connected complex manifold $\mathcal{X}$ and a proper holomorphic submersion $\pi:\mathcal{X}\to B$ over a connected complex base $B$ such that $X_0$ and $X_1$ both occur as fibers $\pi^{-1}(b_0)$ and $\pi^{-1}(b_1)$. Two compact (stably) complex manifolds are said to be (complex) cobordant if their disjoint union bounds a compact (stably) complex manifold with boundary.

Develop a precise comparison between the equivalence relation of deformation and the equivalence relation of (complex) cobordism on the class of compact complex manifolds. In particular:

(a) Determine whether deformation equivalence implies complex cobordism, and conversely whether complex cobordism (with appropriate stably complex structure) implies deformation equivalence, providing proofs or explicit counterexamples in each direction.

(b) Identify intermediate equivalence relations or refined invariants (for example, those built from Chern numbers, Hodge numbers, or holomorphic Euler characteristics) that are simultaneously cobordism invariants and deformation invariants, and characterize the discrepancy between the two relations in terms of such invariants.

(c) Formulate and prove a structural statement describing how the deformation equivalence classes of compact complex manifolds sit inside the complex cobordism classes.

Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer, and let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional complex manifold with (nonempty) boundary $\partial M$, where $\partial M$ is a smooth real hypersurface decomposing into a disjoint union of connected components. Suppose that $M$ admits a nontrivial deformation. Determine what kind of cobordism (in the smooth or appropriate geometric category) must exist between the connected components of $\partial M$. In other words, characterize the cobordism class, or the type of cobordism (e.g. smooth, complex, contact, h-cobordism, etc.), that necessarily relates the connected components of $\partial M$ whenever $M$ has nontrivial deformations.

A compact manifold with boundary $M$ (with interior $\mathring M$) is said to be rigid if every continuous deformation of its smooth/topological structure (precisely: every one-parameter family of compactifiable manifold structures on $\mathring M$ extending $M$) is, up to an appropriate equivalence, trivial — i.e. $M$ admits no nontrivial deformations as a compactifiable manifold. Recall that the s-cobordism theorem provides a complete numerical/algebraic obstruction to triviality of h-cobordisms: an h-cobordism $(W;M_0,M_1)$ of dimension $\geq 6$ is diffeomorphic to the cylinder $M_0 \times [0,1]$ if and only if its Whitehead torsion $\tau(W,M_0) \in \mathrm{Wh}(\pi_1 M_0)$ vanishes.

Question: Does there exist an analogous invariant — a function $\rho$ assigning to each compact manifold with boundary $M$ an element $\rho(M)$ of some explicitly defined abelian group (or set with distinguished element $0$) — such that $M$ is rigid (in the sense above) if and only if $\rho(M) = 0$? In other words, produce such a "rigidity invariant" for compact manifolds with boundary, or prove that no such invariant exists.

A deformation of a complex space $Y$ is a flat proper holomorphic map $\mathcal{Y} \to S$ of complex spaces with a distinguished point $0 \in S$ and an isomorphism of the fiber $\mathcal{Y}_0$ with $Y$ (in the non-compact case, one uses the appropriate notion of deformation of a complex space, e.g. as in the Grauert–Kerner–Forster–Knorr theory). Given a deformation $\mathcal{X}' \to S$ of $X'$ together with a compatible deformation $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{X}'$ of the analytic subset $D$, one obtains a deformation of $X$ by setting $\mathcal{X} := \mathcal{X}' \setminus \mathcal{D}$.

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the pair $(X', D)$ (or equivalently on $X$ together with the choice of compactification) under which every deformation of $X$ is, up to isomorphism, induced in this way from a deformation of $X'$ together with a deformation of the analytic boundary $D \subset X'$.

Let $k \geq 1$ be an integer and let
$$X = W_k := \mathrm{Tot}\bigl(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(-k) \oplus \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(k-2)\bigr)$$
denote the total space of the rank-2 holomorphic vector bundle $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(-k) \oplus \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(k-2)$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$. The natural projection $X \to \mathbb{P}^1$ endows $X$ with the structure of a rank-2 affine bundle over $\mathbb{P}^1$.

By a compactifiable (resp. projectivizable) deformation of $X$ we mean a tuple $(\mathcal{X}, D, Y, f, o, j)$ where:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $\mathcal{X}$ is a complex manifold (resp. smooth complex projective variety),
  \item $D \subset \mathcal{X}$ is a smooth divisor (the boundary at infinity), set $\mathcal{X}^\circ := \mathcal{X} \setminus D$,
  \item $Y$ is a complex manifold (resp. variety) with a distinguished base point $o \in Y$,
  \item $f : \mathcal{X} \to Y$ is a proper holomorphic submersion (resp. smooth projective morphism) such that $f|_D : D \to Y$ is also a submersion,
  \item $j : X \hookrightarrow \mathcal{X}^\circ$ is a biholomorphism onto the central fiber $\mathcal{X}^\circ_o = f^{-1}(o) \setminus D$.
\end{itemize}
For $t \in Y$, write $\mathcal{X}_t := f^{-1}(t)$ and $\mathcal{X}^\circ_t := \mathcal{X}_t \setminus D$.

Determine, in terms of the deformation data:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[(a)] the locus of $t \in Y$ for which there exists a surjective morphism $\mathcal{X}_t \twoheadrightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$ whose restriction to $\mathcal{X}^\circ_t$ extends the affine bundle structure $X \to \mathbb{P}^1$ inherited via $j$ at $t = o$;
  \item[(b)] the (possibly larger) locus of $t \in Y$ for which $\mathcal{X}_t$ is covered by codimension-1 projective subspaces (i.e. through every point of $\mathcal{X}_t$ passes a closed subvariety isomorphic to $\mathbb{P}^{\dim \mathcal{X}_t - 1}$).
\end{enumerate}

(1) n ≥ 3, and for every x ∈ X there exists an integer t > 0 and global sections f_1, …, f_t ∈ H^0(X, ω_X^{⊗ t}) which give local holomorphic coordinates at x; or

(2) for every x ∈ X there exists an integer t > 0 and global sections f_1, …, f_n ∈ H^0(X, ω_X^{⊗ t}) which give local holomorphic coordinates at x, and in addition for every pair of distinct points x, y ∈ X there exist an integer m > 0 and a section f ∈ H^0(X, ω_X^{⊗ m}) with f(x) = 0 and f(y) ≠ 0.

Question: Does there exist a compact complex analytic space X̄ together with a holomorphic open embedding X ↪ X̄ realizing X as an open subset of X̄ (a "completion" of X)? Equivalently, can every such pseudoconcave manifold X be holomorphically completed to a compact complex space?

A Calabi–Yau threefold is a smooth complex three-dimensional manifold X with trivial canonical bundle K_X ≅ O_X and (in the noncompact setting) which is not required to be projective or compact. A deformation of X is a flat family π : 𝒳 → B over a connected complex base B with a distinguished point 0 ∈ B such that π^{-1}(0) ≅ X; two deformations are said to give nonisomorphic threefolds if their general fibers are not biholomorphic to each other.

Problem. Identify geometric conditions on a noncompact Calabi–Yau threefold X that guarantee the existence of infinitely many pairwise nonisomorphic complex deformations of X. More precisely, find natural hypotheses on X (for example, on its topology, its asymptotic/end structure, the existence and configuration of compact or noncompact divisors and curves, the behavior of its holomorphic volume form, or the dimension of its deformation space H^1(X, T_X)) that imply the set of isomorphism classes of small deformations of X is infinite.

Let $X$ be a noncompact complex manifold. In the classical Kodaira–Spencer theory of deformations of compact complex manifolds, infinitesimal deformations of the complex structure are parametrized by $H^1(X, T_X)$, and the vanishing $H^1(X, T_X) = 0$ implies rigidity (every small deformation is trivial). For noncompact $X$, this correspondence fails in general: $H^1(X, T_X)$ need not parametrize deformations correctly, and its vanishing need not force triviality of deformations (especially when one allows the underlying smooth type to vary in the family).

Identify (or construct) a cohomology theory $\mathcal{H}^*(X)$ — defined naturally for noncompact complex manifolds $X$, possibly taking into account behavior at infinity (e.g., on a chosen compactification $\overline{X}$ with boundary divisor $D = \overline{X} \setminus X$) — with the following two properties:

1. (Parametrization) The first group $\mathcal{H}^1(X)$ is in natural bijection with isomorphism classes of (suitably defined) infinitesimal deformations of the complex structure of $X$.

2. (Rigidity) The vanishing $\mathcal{H}^1(X) = 0$ implies that every deformation of $X$ in the appropriate category is trivial.

Determine such a cohomology theory and prove that it satisfies both properties.

Let L be a complete lattice. An element p ∈ L is called co-prime (or meet-irreducible in the dual sense) if p ≠ ⊤ and whenever p ≥ a ∧ b for a, b ∈ L, one has p ≥ a or p ≥ b (equivalently, taking the dual formulation: x is co-prime if x ≤ a ∨ b implies x ≤ a or x ≤ b). Say that L has enough co-primes if every element of L is the infimum (meet) of co-primes lying above it. It is known that a complete lattice has enough co-primes if and only if it is isomorphic to the lattice C(X) of all closed subsets of some topological space X, ordered by inclusion.

The Scott topology σ(L) on L has as open sets those U ⊆ L which are upper sets (x ∈ U and x ≤ y imply y ∈ U) and inaccessible by directed suprema (whenever D ⊆ L is a directed set with sup D ∈ U, then D ∩ U ≠ ∅). A topological space (Y, τ) is sober if every nonempty irreducible closed set (a closed set that is not the union of two proper closed subsets) is the closure of a unique point.

Question: Does there exist a complete lattice L with enough co-primes — equivalently, a complete lattice isomorphic to the lattice of all closed subsets of some topological space — such that the Scott topology σ(L) on L is not sober?

Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the real line with its usual topology. A subset $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is called regular open if $U = \mathrm{int}(\overline{U})$, where $\overline{U}$ is the closure and $\mathrm{int}$ the interior in $\mathbb{R}$. Let $B$ denote the collection of all regular open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. It is well known that $B$, ordered by set inclusion, is a complete Boolean algebra (in particular a complete lattice, and hence a directed-complete partially ordered set).

For a dcpo $(P,\le)$, the Scott topology $\sigma(P)$ on $P$ has as its open sets those subsets $U \subseteq P$ which are upper sets (i.e. $x \in U$ and $x \le y$ imply $y \in U$) and which are inaccessible by directed suprema (i.e. for every directed set $D \subseteq P$ with $\sup D \in U$ one has $D \cap U \neq \emptyset$). The resulting topological space is denoted $\Sigma P$.

A topological space $X$ is sober if every nonempty irreducible closed subset of $X$ (a nonempty closed set that cannot be written as the union of two proper closed subsets) is the closure of a unique point of $X$.

Question: Is the Scott space $\Sigma B$ sober?

Recall the following definitions. Let $(P,\le)$ be a poset. A topology $\tau$ on $P$ is said to be compatible with the order $\le$ if the specialization order of $\tau$ — namely $x \le_\tau y$ iff $x \in \overline{\{y\}}^\tau$ — coincides with $\le$. A topological space $(X,\tau)$ is called well-filtered if for every filtered family $\{K_i : i \in I\}$ of compact saturated subsets of $X$ (saturated meaning equal to the intersection of its open neighborhoods) and every open set $U \subseteq X$ with $\bigcap_{i\in I} K_i \subseteq U$, there exists some $i_0 \in I$ with $K_{i_0} \subseteq U$.

Call a poset $P$ a well-filtered poset if there exists a well-filtered topology $\tau$ on $P$ that is compatible with the original order of $P$.

Background and definitions.

Let $P$ be a poset. A nonempty subset $D \subseteq P$ is directed if every pair of elements of $D$ has an upper bound in $D$. A poset $P$ is a directed-complete partial order (dcpo) if every directed subset $D \subseteq P$ has a least upper bound $\bigvee D$ in $P$.

A subset $U$ of a dcpo $P$ is Scott open if (i) $U$ is an upper set, i.e. $x \in U$ and $x \leq y$ imply $y \in U$, and (ii) for every directed $D \subseteq P$ with $\bigvee D \in U$, there exists $d \in D$ with $d \in U$. The collection of Scott-open sets forms a topology on $P$, called the Scott topology; the resulting topological space is denoted $\Sigma P$.

A subset $K$ of a topological space $X$ is saturated if it equals the intersection of its open neighborhoods (equivalently, $K$ is an upper set in the specialization preorder). A topological space $X$ is well-filtered if for every filtered family $\{K_i\}_{i \in I}$ of nonempty compact saturated subsets of $X$ (filtered meaning that for any $i, j \in I$ there exists $k \in I$ with $K_k \subseteq K_i \cap K_j$) and every open set $U \subseteq X$ such that $\bigcap_{i \in I} K_i \subseteq U$, there exists some $i_0 \in I$ with $K_{i_0} \subseteq U$.

A dcpo $P$ is called Scott well-filtered if its Scott space $\Sigma P$ is a well-filtered topological space.

Problem.

Provide a purely order-theoretic characterization of Scott well-filtered dcpos: namely, formulate a condition on a dcpo $P$, expressed only in terms of the order $\leq$ on $P$ (without reference to the Scott topology, compact saturated sets, or other topological notions), that is equivalent to $\Sigma P$ being well-filtered.

Recall the following definitions. A topological space $X$ is $T_0$ if for any two distinct points there is an open set containing exactly one of them. A nonempty closed subset $C \subseteq X$ is irreducible if whenever $C \subseteq C_1 \cup C_2$ with $C_1, C_2$ closed, then $C \subseteq C_1$ or $C \subseteq C_2$. A $T_0$ space $X$ is sober if every irreducible closed subset of $X$ is the closure $\overline{\{x\}}$ of a unique point $x \in X$.

A directed complete partially ordered set (dcpo) is a poset $(P, \le)$ in which every directed subset has a supremum. The Scott topology on a dcpo $P$ has as its open sets those upper sets $U \subseteq P$ (i.e., $x \in U$ and $x \le y$ imply $y \in U$) such that whenever $D \subseteq P$ is a directed set with $\sup D \in U$, then $D \cap U \ne \emptyset$. The resulting topological space is called the Scott space of $P$.

Question. Does there exist a topological property $\mathcal{P}$ of $T_0$ spaces such that:

(i) $\mathcal{P}$ is strictly weaker than sobriety in the class of all $T_0$ topological spaces (every sober $T_0$ space has property $\mathcal{P}$, but there exists a $T_0$ space with property $\mathcal{P}$ that is not sober); and

(ii) for every dcpo $P$, the Scott space of $P$ has property $\mathcal{P}$ if and only if it is sober?

Let $\mathbf{Top}_0$ denote the category of $T_0$ topological spaces with continuous maps, and let $\mathbf{Sob}$ denote its full subcategory of sober spaces. Let $\mathbf{K}$ be a full subcategory of $\mathbf{Top}_0$ that contains $\mathbf{Sob}$ and is closed under homeomorphisms (a typical example being a Keimel–Lawson category, i.e., a full subcategory of $\mathbf{Top}_0$ containing $\mathbf{Sob}$ that is closed under finite products and equalizers in $\mathbf{Top}_0$, closed under formation of arbitrary subspaces of homeomorphic copies of its members, and closed under topological sums).

For a $T_0$ space $X$, write $\mathcal{O}(X)$ for its lattice of open sets. Define the canonical map
$$\eta_X : X \longrightarrow \prod_{Y\in\mathbf{K},\, f \in \mathbf{Top}_0(X,Y)} Y, \qquad \eta_X(x) = (f(x))_{Y,f},$$
and call $X$ a $\mathbf{K}$-\emph{determined space} if $\eta_X$ is a topological embedding onto a subspace whose image is determined (in the appropriate categorical sense) by $\mathbf{K}$; equivalently, $X$ is $\mathbf{K}$-determined if it is homeomorphic to a subspace of a product of objects of $\mathbf{K}$, i.e., it lies in the epireflective hull of $\mathbf{K}$ in $\mathbf{Top}_0$.

Question: Is the product (in $\mathbf{Top}_0$) of an arbitrary family of $\mathbf{K}$-determined spaces again a $\mathbf{K}$-determined space?

Let $X$ be a $T_0$ topological space. Denote by $\mathcal{O}(X)$ the lattice of open subsets of $X$, and by $K(X)$ the family of nonempty compact saturated subsets of $X$ (a subset is saturated if it equals the intersection of all open sets containing it). The Smyth power space $P_S(X)$ is the set $K(X)$ equipped with the upper Vietoris topology, namely the topology generated by the base
$$\{\,\Box U : U \in \mathcal{O}(X)\,\}, \qquad \Box U = \{K \in K(X) : K \subseteq U\}.$$
A $T_0$ space $Y$ is called well-filtered if for every filtered family $\{K_i\}_{i\in I} \subseteq K(Y)$ (filtered under reverse inclusion) and every open set $U$ with $\bigcap_{i\in I} K_i \subseteq U$, there exists $i_0 \in I$ with $K_{i_0} \subseteq U$.

A continuous map $f : Y \to Z$ from a $T_0$ space $Y$ to a well-filtered $T_0$ space $Z$ is said to extend uniquely along the well-filtered reflection if it factors uniquely through the well-filtered reflection of $Y$. A $T_0$ space $Y$ is called well-filtered determined (WD) if for every continuous map $f : Y \to Z$ into a well-filtered $T_0$ space $Z$, $f$ extends uniquely to a continuous map from the well-filtered reflection of $Y$; equivalently, $Y$ admits a well-filtered reflection in the standard categorical sense in the category of $T_0$ spaces.

Question: If $X$ is a well-filtered determined $T_0$ space, must its Smyth power space $P_S(X)$ also be well-filtered determined?

Let $X$ be a topological space. Recall the following definitions.

(i) For a topological space $Y$, let $\mathcal{O}(Y)$ denote its lattice of open sets. The upper Kuratowski topology on $\mathcal{O}(Y)$ is the topology obtained as the supremum of all topologies for which the closure $\mathrm{cl}(\{U\}) = \{V \in \mathcal{O}(Y) : V \subseteq U\}$ holds. Equivalently, it has subbasic closed sets of the form $\{V \in \mathcal{O}(Y) : V \subseteq U\}$ for $U \in \mathcal{O}(Y)$. The co-compact topology on $\mathcal{O}(Y)$ has subbasic open sets $\Box K = \{V \in \mathcal{O}(Y) : K \subseteq V\}$ for $K \subseteq Y$ compact saturated. The space $Y$ is called consonant if these two topologies coincide on $\mathcal{O}(Y)$.

(ii) Let $\Gamma(X)$ denote the set of all closed subsets of $X$. The Hoare power space (or lower space) of $X$ is
$$P_H(X) = \Gamma(X) \setminus \{\emptyset\}$$
equipped with the lower Vietoris topology, generated by the subbasic open sets
$$\Diamond U = \{F \in \Gamma(X) \setminus \{\emptyset\} : F \cap U \neq \emptyset\}, \qquad U \in \mathcal{O}(X).$$

Question. Suppose $X$ is a $T_0$ space that is consonant. Must its Hoare power space $P_H(X)$ also be consonant?

Background and definitions.

All spaces below are $T_0$ topological spaces. For a $T_0$ space $X$, the specialization order is defined by $x \le y$ iff $x \in \overline{\{y\}}$. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is saturated if $A$ equals the intersection of its open neighborhoods (equivalently, $A$ is an upper set in the specialization order). Let $K(X)$ denote the set of nonempty compact saturated subsets of $X$. The Smyth power space $P_S(X)$ is the set $K(X)$ equipped with the upper Vietoris topology, generated by the basic open sets
$$\Box U = \{ Q \in K(X) : Q \subseteq U \}, \qquad U \subseteq X \text{ open}.$$

A class $\mathcal{K}$ of $T_0$ spaces is called a Smyth category if it is closed under homeomorphisms and is closed under the formation of Smyth power spaces, i.e. $X \in \mathcal{K}$ implies $P_S(X) \in \mathcal{K}$. A Smyth category $\mathcal{K}$ is called adequate if, in addition, for every $T_0$ space $X$ that lies in $\mathcal{K}$, every closed subspace of $X$ also lies in $\mathcal{K}$ and the canonical $T_0$ reflection maps and the Smyth power-space construction interact suitably with $\mathcal{K}$ (in particular, $\mathcal{K}$ contains all sober spaces and is closed under arbitrary topological products and under taking suprema of closed subsets).

For a class $\mathcal{K}$ of $T_0$ spaces, a $T_0$ space $X$ is called $\mathcal{K}$-determined if for every continuous map $f \colon X \to Y$ into a member $Y \in \mathcal{K}$, there is a unique extension to a continuous map from the $\mathcal{K}$-reflection (the free $\mathcal{K}$-space generated by $X$) into $Y$; equivalently, $X$ has the same continuous-map behaviour towards spaces in $\mathcal{K}$ as its $\mathcal{K}$-reflection.

Question. Let $\mathcal{K}$ be an adequate Smyth category, and let $X$ be a $\mathcal{K}$-determined $T_0$ space. Is the Smyth power space $P_S(X)$ also $\mathcal{K}$-determined?

Let $X$ be a $T_0$ topological space. For $x \in X$, write $\uparrow x = \{y \in X : x \le y\}$, where $\le$ is the specialization order of $X$ (i.e., $x \le y$ iff $x \in \overline{\{y\}}$). Call $X$ a strong $d$-space if for every $D \in \mathcal{D}(X)$, every $x \in X$, and every $U \in \mathcal{O}(X)$,
$$\bigcap_{d \in D} (\uparrow d \cap \uparrow x) \subseteq U \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \uparrow d \cap \uparrow x \subseteq U \text{ for some } d \in D.$$
