representations.normalized:
Consider the open one-dimensional symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP) on a lattice of L sites, in which each particle attempts to hop to each nearest-neighbor empty site at rate 1, and the boundary sites 1 and L are coupled to particle reservoirs of densities ρ_a and ρ_b respectively (so particles are injected/removed at the two ends at rates compatible with these reservoir densities). Let A_t denote the dynamical activity up to time t, defined as the total number of particle jumps (in either direction, across any bond, including boundary exchanges) performed by the process during the time interval [0, t]. For a real parameter λ, define the tilted (activity-conditioned) generating function

  Z_L(λ, t) = E[ exp(λ A_t) ],

and consider the diffusive scaling λ = s L² with s held fixed as L → ∞.

Take the symmetric reservoir choice ρ_a = ρ_b = 1/2. A formal mapping of the activity-tilted SSEP to a weakly asymmetric exclusion process (WASEP) yields a quantitative criterion for spontaneous breaking of particle–hole symmetry that, in the SSEP limit (asymmetry parameter ν₁ = 0), predicts no symmetry-breaking interval for any value of λ.

Question: In this setting, does the activity-conditioned open SSEP nevertheless exhibit critical behavior in a neighborhood of the value λ = −π²/2 (equivalently, of the rescaled value s = −π²/2 in the diffusive scaling, after replacing L by 1)? In particular, do power-law spatial correlations of the conditioned density profile emerge as λ approaches −π²/2, even though no particle–hole symmetry breaking occurs?

(ii) every two non-parallel lines of L intersect in a (unique) point that belongs to P.

Determine sharp lower and upper bounds for the number of construction lines |L| as a function of the number of registration marks k; that is, determine f(k) and F(k) for every k ≥ 0 for which arrangements exist.

Work in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. Define an *arrangement* to be an ordered pair $(L,P)$ where:
- $L$ is a finite set of straight lines (called *construction lines*),
- $P$ is a finite set of points (called *registration marks*),
satisfying the two conditions:
1. every point of $P$ is the intersection of at least two distinct lines of $L$, and
2. every two non-parallel lines of $L$ meet in a point that belongs to $P$ (so all pairwise intersections of lines of $L$ are recorded in $P$).

Two arrangements $(L,P)$ and $(L',P')$ are considered equivalent if they have the same combinatorial (equivalently, projective) incidence type, i.e. there is a bijection between the lines and a bijection between the registration marks preserving the line–point incidence relation (up to the chosen equivalence: combinatorial isomorphism of the incidence structure, or projective equivalence of the underlying configuration).

For each integer $k\ge 0$, let $N(k)$ denote the number of equivalence classes of arrangements $(L,P)$ for which $|P|=k$ (i.e. the lines of $L$ meet in exactly $k$ registration marks).

Determine $N(k)$ as a function of $k$, or give a closed-form / generating-function description of the sequence $\{N(k)\}_{k\ge 0}$.

Let L be a finite collection of distinct lines in the Euclidean plane and let P be a finite set of points in the plane satisfying the following two incidence axioms:

(i) every point of P is the intersection of at least two lines belonging to L;
(ii) any two non-parallel lines in L meet in a (unique) point that lies in P.

Such a pair (L, P) will be called an arrangement.

Recall that a finite linear space is a pair (P, L) consisting of a finite point set P and a family L of subsets of P (called lines), each of size at least two, such that every pair of distinct points of P is contained in exactly one line of L.

Problem: Characterize all arrangements (L, P) in the above sense with the additional property that every pair of distinct points of P lies on some line of L. Equivalently, determine which arrangements (L, P) of construction lines and registration marks (in the sense of (i)–(ii)) yield a finite linear space when each line ℓ ∈ L is identified with its set of incident points ℓ ∩ P.

$$S = \Bigl\{ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} x_j : x_j \in K_j \text{ for every } j \Bigr\},$$
and for each integer $z \geq 0$ define the tail set
$$R_z = \Bigl\{ \sum_{i=z+1}^{\infty} x_i : x_i \in K_i \text{ for every } i > z \Bigr\}.$$
Note that $S$ is a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$ containing $0$, and that $S = R_0$.

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions, expressed in terms of the tail sets $R_z$, under which $S$ is a (closed) interval, and conditions under which $S$ is a finite union of (nondegenerate) closed intervals.

Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of positive real numbers with $a_n \to 0$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n < \infty$. Define the achievement set (or subsum set)
$$S = S(a) = \Big\{ \sum_{n \in A} a_n : A \subseteq \mathbb{N} \Big\} \subseteq \mathbb{R},$$
and for each integer $z \ge 0$ define the tail set
$$R_z = \Big\{ \sum_{n \in A} a_n : A \subseteq \{z+1, z+2, \dots\} \Big\}.$$
A nonempty perfect compact subset $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is called a Cantorval if it is the closure of its interior and yet both endpoints of every nontrivial component interval are accumulation points of trivial components (singletons). More specifically:
- $C$ is an $M$-Cantorval if every gap (i.e., bounded connected component of the complement of $C$ inside the convex hull of $C$) is accumulated on both sides by infinitely many component intervals of $C$ and by infinitely many gaps.
- $C$ is an $L$-Cantorval if every gap has a component interval of $C$ adjacent to it on the right while being accumulated on the left by infinitely many component intervals and infinitely many gaps.
- $C$ is an $R$-Cantorval if it is the mirror image (under $x \mapsto -x$) of an $L$-Cantorval.

It is known that $S$ is always either a finite union of closed intervals, a Cantor set, or a Cantorval (of one of the three types above).

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the family of tail sets $\{R_z\}_{z\ge 0}$ that characterize when $S$ is an $M$-Cantorval, an $L$-Cantorval, and an $R$-Cantorval, respectively.

- $C$ is an $L$-Cantorval if every gap has a component interval of $C$ adjacent to it on the right while being accumulated on the left by infinitely many component intervals and infinitely many gaps.
- $C$ is an $R$-Cantorval if it is the mirror image (under $x \mapsto -x$) of an $L$-Cantorval.

It is known that $S$ is always either a finite union of closed intervals, a Cantor set, or a Cantorval (of one of the three types above). 

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the family of tail sets $\{R_z\}_{z\ge 0}$ that characterize when $S$ is an $M$-Cantorval, an $L$-Cantorval, and an $R$-Cantorval, respectively.

The question is posed as an open problem in surveys on subsums of null sequences, and recent papers (e.g., on multigeometric Cantorvals, 2022–2025) continue to address only special cases.

$$S \;=\; \Big\{ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} x_j \;:\; x_j \in K_j \text{ for each } j \ge 1 \Big\},$$
which converges since the diameters tend to $0$. For each $z \in S$, define the tail set
$$R_z \;=\; \Big\{ \sum_{j=n+1}^{\infty} x_j \;:\; n \ge 0,\; x_j \in K_j,\; z - \sum_{j=n+1}^{\infty} x_j \in S \Big\},$$

$$z \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} x_j, \qquad x_j \in K_j.$$

representations.normalized:
Consider the planar polynomial differential system
\[
\dot{x} = -y + x\,F(x,y), \qquad \dot{y} = x + y\,F(x,y),
\]
where $F(x,y)$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $3$. Such systems are called rigid because in polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ they satisfy $\dot{\theta} = 1$. After a standard reduction that removes the constant term and one further coefficient (so that the discriminant reduction is performed), one may assume that
\[
F(x,y) = a + b x + c y + d x^{2} + e x y,
\]
with $(a,b,c,d,e)\in\mathbb{R}^{5}$. A limit cycle of the system is an isolated periodic orbit in the phase plane.

Question: Is the maximum number of limit cycles that the system
\[
\dot{x} = -y + x\bigl(a + b x + c y + d x^{2} + e x y\bigr), \qquad \dot{y} = x + y\bigl(a + b x + c y + d x^{2} + e x y\bigr)
\]
can possess, as $(a,b,c,d,e)$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}^{5}$, equal to $2$?

representations.normalized:
Consider the polynomial Liénard system in the plane
$$x' = y - F(x), \qquad y' = -x,$$
where $F(x)$ is a real polynomial of degree $n$ with $F(0)=0$. For an integer $n\ge 1$, let $\mathrm{Lie}(n)$ denote the maximum number of limit cycles that such a system can have, taken over all polynomials $F$ of degree at most $n$. It is classically known that $\mathrm{Lie}(3) = 1$ and $\mathrm{Lie}(4) = 1$.

Recall that a Dulac function for a planar vector field $X = (P,Q)$ on a simply connected region $U \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is a $C^1$ function $B: U \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the divergence
$$\operatorname{div}(BX) = \frac{\partial (BP)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial (BQ)}{\partial y}$$
does not change sign and is not identically zero on $U$; the existence of such a $B$ on an annular region precludes more than one limit cycle there (Bendixson–Dulac theorem and its annular generalization).

Problem: Produce explicit Dulac functions (or Dulac–Cherkas functions) and an accompanying argument that proves $\mathrm{Lie}(3) = 1$ and $\mathrm{Lie}(4) = 1$ for the above polynomial Liénard family.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general problem of determining the maximum number of 2π-periodic limit cycles for generalized Abel equations x' = A(t)x^p + B(t)x^q with trigonometric polynomial coefficients of given degrees remains open. Only partial results exist: lower bounds (e.g., H_{3,2}(n,m) ≥ 2(n+m)-1), exact results in special cases such as linear trigonometric coefficients (giving 3 limit cycles for the classical p=3, q=2 case), and Chebyshev-type criteria providing upper bounds in restricted settings. Recent works (2023–2026) continue to address sub-cases rather than the full question.

For a planar polynomial differential system
$$\dot x = P(x,y),\qquad \dot y = Q(x,y),$$
with $P,Q\in\mathbb{R}[x,y]$, define its number of monomials to be the total count of distinct monomial terms appearing across the two components $P\,\partial_x$ and $Q\,\partial_y$ of the associated vector field (each monomial $x^iy^j\,\partial_x$ and $x^iy^j\,\partial_y$ counted separately, only if its coefficient is nonzero). Let $\mathcal{M}_m$ denote the family of all such planar polynomial vector fields having exactly $m$ monomial terms, and define
$$HM[m] \;=\; \sup\bigl\{\, \text{(number of limit cycles of $X$)} : X\in \mathcal{M}_m\,\bigr\},$$
where a limit cycle is an isolated periodic orbit of the system in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

(i) Determine nontrivial upper and lower bounds for $HM[m]$ as a function of $m\in\mathbb{N}$.

(ii) Determine the smallest integer $m$ for which there exists a planar polynomial differential system in $\mathcal{M}_m$ possessing at least $m+1$ limit cycles, i.e., the simplest planar polynomial vector field (in terms of monomial count) whose number of limit cycles strictly exceeds its number of monomials.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is a variant of Hilbert's 16th problem in which one bounds limit cycles by the number of monomials rather than the degree. Only partial results are known: HM[m]=0 for m≤3, and for m≥4 one has HM[m]≥m−3 via Liénard-type constructions, with stronger lower bounds along certain subsequences of m. Sharp upper and lower bounds and the minimal m with a system having more limit cycles than monomials remain open.

A planar polynomial differential system of degree $n$ is a system of ordinary differential equations of the form
$$\dot x = P(x,y), \qquad \dot y = Q(x,y),$$
where $P, Q \in \mathbb{R}[x,y]$ and $\max\{\deg P, \deg Q\} = n$. A singular point $p_0 = (x_0,y_0)$ (i.e., $P(p_0)=Q(p_0)=0$) is called a center if there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $p_0$ such that $U \setminus \{p_0\}$ is entirely filled with periodic orbits of the system.

For each integer $n \ge 4$, let
$$C_n = \sup\bigl\{\,\#\{\text{centers of }(P,Q)\} : (P,Q)\text{ is a planar polynomial system of degree }n\,\bigr\}.$$

Determine the value of $C_n$ for every $n \ge 4$.

Determine the value of $C_n$ for every $n \ge 4$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general problem of determining the maximum number of centers $C_n$ for planar polynomial differential systems of degree $n \ge 4$ appears to remain open. Partial results exist for restricted subclasses (e.g., quartic Kolmogorov systems, where the maximum is seven, and certain cubic Kolmogorov classes), and constructions of families with many centers are known (e.g., new families of centers in arbitrary even degree), but no closed-form value of $C_n$ for general $n \ge 4$ has been established.

Consider rational difference equations of the form
   x_{n+k} = (A_0 + A_1 x_n + A_2 x_{n+1} + ... + A_k x_{n+k-1}) / (B_0 + B_1 x_n + B_2 x_{n+1} + ... + B_k x_{n+k-1}),
where k ≥ 1 is an integer and the coefficients A_0,...,A_k, B_0,...,B_k are nonnegative real numbers, with the positivity conditions ensuring that, for any positive initial conditions x_0, x_1, ..., x_{k-1} > 0, the recurrence is well-defined and produces a sequence of positive real numbers. Such an equation is called globally periodic if there exists a positive integer p such that x_{n+p} = x_n for all n ≥ 0 and for every choice of positive initial conditions.

Two equations of this form are called equivalent if one can be transformed into the other by a change of variables of the form y_n = α x_{n+s}^{±1} (with α > 0 and s ∈ ℤ), or more generally by Möbius-type transformations preserving the form of the family.

The following five equations are globally periodic examples within this family:
   (i)   x_{n+1} = x_n              (period 1),
   (ii)  x_{n+1} = 1/x_n            (period 2),
   (iii) x_{n+2} = x_{n+1}/x_n      (period 6),
   (iv)  x_{n+2} = (1 + x_{n+1})/x_n   (period 5),
   (v)   x_{n+3} = (1 + x_{n+1} + x_{n+2})/x_n   (period 8).

Question: Does there exist a globally periodic rational difference equation of the above form that is not equivalent to any of the five equations (i)–(v)?

The global periodicity problem for rational difference equations is a long-standing open problem. Surveys (e.g., Cima–Gasull–Mañosas, "Different approaches to the global periodicity problem", 2012) discuss the classification and note that no further globally periodic examples beyond the classical short list have been found, but a complete classification has not been established. No source found that resolves the question for the full family with positive coefficients.

Let $H_{2n}(x,y)$ and $H_m(x,y)$ be real homogeneous polynomials of degrees $2n$ and $m$, respectively, with $m > 2n \geq 2$, and consider the planar Hamiltonian system
$$\dot x = \frac{\partial H}{\partial y}, \qquad \dot y = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x},$$
with Hamiltonian $H(x,y) = H_{2n}(x,y) + H_m(x,y)$. Assume that the origin is a center of this system, and let $\mathcal{P}$ be its period annulus, i.e., the maximal punctured neighborhood of the origin foliated by periodic orbits. For each periodic orbit $\gamma_h \subset \mathcal{P}$ on the energy level $\{H = h\}$, let $T(h)$ denote its minimal period. A value $h_0$ is called a critical period if $T'(h_0) = 0$.

Prove or disprove: the period function $T$ on $\mathcal{P}$ has at most one critical period.

Consider planar polynomial differential systems of the form
\[
\dot x = P_{2k+1}(x,y), \qquad \dot y = Q_{2l+1}(x,y),
\]
where $P_{2k+1}(x,y)$ and $Q_{2l+1}(x,y)$ are real homogeneous polynomials in $(x,y)$ of odd degrees $2k+1$ and $2l+1$ respectively, with $k,l\ge 0$ integers. Recall that a singular point $p$ of such a system is called a center if it has a punctured neighborhood entirely filled with periodic orbits surrounding $p$. The period function $T(\rho)$ assigns to each periodic orbit (parametrized by some transverse parameter $\rho$ on the period annulus) its minimal period; an oscillation of the period function is a (simple) critical point of $T$, and the number of oscillations is the number of such critical points.

(i) Characterize all systems in the above family that possess a center.

(ii) For the centers occurring in this family, determine the maximum possible number of oscillations of the period function.

A web search returned no source giving a complete characterization of centers nor a determination of the maximum number of period-function oscillations for general planar systems with homogeneous nonlinearities of arbitrary odd degrees $2k+1$ and $2l+1$. Consider planar polynomial differential systems of the form
  dx/dt = P(x, y),  dy/dt = Q(x, y),
where P and Q are real polynomials with max(deg P, deg Q) = n. A center is an isolated equilibrium point surrounded by a punctured neighborhood entirely foliated by periodic orbits. For such a center, the period function assigns to each periodic orbit in the period annulus its minimal period, viewed as a smooth function of a transverse parameter. A critical period is a critical point of this period function (excluding the value at the center itself).

Let T(n) denote the maximum number of critical periods that the period function of a center of a planar polynomial system of degree n can have, taken over all such systems and all centers.

Question: Does there exist a constant C > 0 such that
  T(n) ≥ C · n² · log(n)
for all sufficiently large n?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Recent work on planar polynomial centers near a maximum number of cusps establishes the lower bound T(n) ≥ C n² log n by constructing Hamiltonian planar polynomial vector fields (of both odd and even degree n) whose period function has at least on the order of n² log n critical periods, via a perturbation method using vector fields with many cusp equilibria. This appears to affirmatively resolve the question, although the optimality of the bound remains unclear.

Consider the two-parameter family of planar polynomial differential systems
\[
\dot x = -y + x y, \qquad \dot y = x + D\,x^2 + F\,y^2,
\]
with $(D,F)\in\mathbb{R}^2$. For each such parameter, the origin is a reversible quadratic center, and it is surrounded by a punctured neighborhood (its period annulus) foliated by periodic orbits. The period function assigns to each periodic orbit in the period annulus its minimal period; a critical period is an isolated critical point of this function.

Determine whether $2$ is the maximum number of critical periods that the period function of this family can have, i.e., whether for every $(D,F)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ the period function of the center at the origin has at most two critical periods, and whether this bound is attained.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is part of Chicone's long-standing conjecture that reversible quadratic centers have at most two critical periods. Recent work (Mañosas–Rojas–Villadelprat, JDE 2022, arXiv:2203.12966) proves that the criticality of the period function at the outer boundary is at most 2 for parameters outside certain segments, providing strong partial progress but not a full resolution. No source confirms a complete proof of the bound for the full family.

$$\dot z \;=\; i\,z \;+\; (z ar z)^{n}\, ar z^{\,k+1},\qquad z\in\mathbb{C},$$

A 2025 paper by A. Gasull and D. Rojas, "Monotonous Period Function for Equivariant Differential Equations with Homogeneous Nonlinearities" (Mediterranean Journal of Mathematics), proves that the period function of the center at the origin of the $\mathbb{Z}_k$-equivariant equation $\dot z = iz + a(z\bar z)^n z^{k+1}$ is monotonically decreasing for all positive integers $n,k$ (and any $a\neq 0$). representations.normalized:
Consider two classes of planar polynomial differential systems on $\mathbb{R}^2$:

(A) Quadratic polynomial systems
$$\dot{x}=P(x,y),\qquad \dot{y}=Q(x,y),$$
where $P,Q\in\mathbb{R}[x,y]$ have $\max(\deg P,\deg Q)=2$.

(B) Piecewise linear differential systems with two zones separated by a straight line: after an affine change of coordinates the separation line is $\Sigma=\{x=0\}$, and the system is given by
$$(\dot{x},\dot{y})=\begin{cases} (a_1 x+b_1 y+c_1,\ d_1 x+e_1 y+f_1), & x>0,\\ (a_2 x+b_2 y+c_2,\ d_2 x+e_2 y+f_2), & x<0,\end{cases}$$
with Filippov convention on $\Sigma$.

A limit cycle is an isolated periodic orbit of the system (in case (B), an isolated closed trajectory in the Filippov sense which may cross $\Sigma$). An algebraic limit cycle is a limit cycle contained in the zero set of an irreducible real polynomial that is invariant under the flow (in case (B), invariant in each zone). An algebraic limit cycle $\gamma$ given by $\{f(x,y)=0\}$ is hyperbolic if its associated cofactor does not vanish identically along $\gamma$ in the appropriate sense; otherwise it is non-hyperbolic. A critical period of a center is a critical point of the period function on the punctured period annulus.

For each class (A) and (B), determine the sharp (best possible) values of the following five quantities:

1. The maximum number of limit cycles.
2. The maximum number of algebraic limit cycles.
3. The maximum number of non-hyperbolic algebraic limit cycles.
4. Whether algebraic and non-algebraic limit cycles can coexist in the same system (yes/no).
5. The maximum number of critical periods.

The currently conjectured values to be improved are: for (A), $4$, $1$, $0$, no, $2$; for (B), $3$, $2$, $1$, no, unknown.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

All five quantities, in both the quadratic polynomial and the piecewise linear (one straight separation line) settings, remain open. Even the maximum number of limit cycles is unsettled: for piecewise linear systems with one straight line of separation, the longstanding conjectured upper bound is 3 (with examples reaching 3) but no proof of sharpness exists; for quadratic systems the Hilbert number $H(2)$ is famously unknown (at least 4). Recent works continue to improve bounds and constructions, but the precise sharp values for algebraic limit cycles, non-hyperbolic algebraic limit cycles, coexistence, and critical periods are not established.

For each integer n ≥ 1, define the following two Hilbert-type numbers.

(a) Polynomial Hilbert number H(n): the supremum, over all planar polynomial vector fields
    x' = P(x,y),   y' = Q(x,y)
with deg P, deg Q ≤ n, of the number of isolated periodic orbits (limit cycles) of the system.

(b) Piecewise linear number L(n): the supremum, over all planar discontinuous piecewise linear vector fields of the form
    (x',y') = A^+(x,y) + b^+   if  Φ(x,y) > 0,
    (x',y') = A^-(x,y) + b^-   if  Φ(x,y) < 0,
where A^± are 2×2 real matrices, b^± ∈ ℝ², and the discontinuity set {Φ = 0} is a single irreducible branch of a real algebraic curve of degree n, of the number of crossing limit cycles of the system.

The currently known unconditional lower bounds are
    H(2) ≥ 4,    H(3) ≥ 13,    H(n) ≥ K · n² / log n  for some absolute constant K > 0,
    L(1) ≥ 3,    L(2) ≥ 4,     L(n) ≥ ⌊n/2⌋.

Problem. Improve any of these six lower bounds: produce explicit families of polynomial (respectively, piecewise linear) systems exhibiting strictly more limit cycles than the bounds above guarantee, for the corresponding value(s) of n.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The polynomial bounds H(2) ≥ 4, H(3) ≥ 13, and H(n) ≥ K n²/log n remain the best known unconditional lower bounds in the literature. For the piecewise linear case with algebraic curve separation, recent work (e.g., on systems separated by y = x^n and related classes) has established improved lower bounds for L(n) for specific small n and specific separation curves, but a complete improvement of all six listed bounds has not been achieved. The general problem is still open.

Recall the Markus–Yamabe hypothesis on a smooth vector field $F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$: $F$ has a (unique) equilibrium and, for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, all eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix $DF(x)$ have negative real part. The classical Markus–Yamabe conjecture asserts that under this hypothesis the equilibrium is a global attractor; this is true in dimension $n=2$ but is known to fail for $n\geq 3$.

Question: Does there exist a smooth vector field $F:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ satisfying the Markus–Yamabe hypothesis (i.e., all eigenvalues of $DF(x)$ have strictly negative real part for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^3$) whose associated dynamical system $\dot x = F(x)$ admits at least one periodic orbit?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is listed as an open problem in a 2020 collection of open problems in low-dimensional dynamical systems. Known counterexamples to the Markus–Yamabe conjecture in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (e.g., polynomial families) provide trajectories escaping to infinity but, to current knowledge, no smooth example with a genuine periodic orbit under the full Markus–Yamabe spectral hypothesis has been exhibited. No subsequent resolution was found in the search.

Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth map possessing a fixed point $p\in\mathbb{R}^2$ (i.e., $F(p)=p$). For each $x\in\mathbb{R}^2$, let $DF(x)$ denote the Jacobian matrix of $F$ at $x$, let $|DF(x)|$ denote the $2\times 2$ matrix obtained from $DF(x)$ by replacing each entry by its absolute value, and let $\rho(\cdot)$ denote the spectral radius (the maximum modulus of eigenvalues) of a square matrix. Assume that
$$\rho(|DF(x)|) < 1 \qquad \text{for every } x\in\mathbb{R}^2.$$
Question: Must the fixed point $p$ be globally asymptotically stable for the discrete dynamical system $x_{n+1}=F(x_n)$? That is, must $p$ be a Lyapunov-stable fixed point such that $\lim_{n\to\infty}F^n(x)=p$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^2$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is a planar discrete global asymptotic stability problem of Markus–Yamabe / LaSalle type, using the entry-wise absolute-value Jacobian and its spectral radius. It appears in lists of open problems on low-dimensional dynamical systems and on LaSalle's problems; while related discrete Markus–Yamabe results are known (the discrete Markus–Yamabe conjecture holds for planar polynomial maps but fails in higher dimensions), no resolution of this specific entry-wise variant in dimension two has been located.

Let $A_0, A_1, \dots, A_n$ be independent identically distributed standard normal random variables, and consider the random $n$-th order linear homogeneous differential equation
$$A_n x^{(n)}(t) + A_{n-1} x^{(n-1)}(t) + \cdots + A_1 x'(t) + A_0 x(t) = 0.$$
The zero solution of this equation is said to be globally asymptotically stable if every solution $x(t)$ tends to $0$ as $t \to \infty$; equivalently, the (random) characteristic polynomial $A_n z^n + A_{n-1} z^{n-1} + \cdots + A_0$ is a Hurwitz polynomial (i.e., all of its complex roots have strictly negative real part). Let
$$p_n = \mathbb{P}\bigl(\text{the zero solution of the above equation is globally asymptotically stable}\bigr).$$

(a) Determine a complete asymptotic expansion of $p_n$ as $n \to \infty$.

(b) Decide whether the sequence $(p_n)_{n \ge 1}$ is strictly decreasing.

Let $C_1, C_2 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be two irreducible real algebraic curves of degrees $n$ and $m$ respectively, with $n+m > 4$, and assume that each of $C_1$ and $C_2$ contains an oval (a smooth, connected, bounded, simple closed component of its real locus). Define the Poncelet map $P$ associated with the pair $(C_1, C_2)$ as follows: given a point $x$ on the oval of $C_1$, draw a tangent line $\ell$ to the oval of $C_2$ through $x$; the line $\ell$ meets the oval of $C_1$ in (generically) one other point $x'$, and one sets $P(x) = x'$. Assume the construction can be made consistent so that $P$ is a well-defined homeomorphism of the oval of $C_1$ to itself (homeomorphic to a circle $S^1$).

Question: Do there exist such curves $C_1, C_2$ (with $n+m>4$) for which the Poncelet map $P$ is well defined and is topologically conjugate to a rotation of the circle?

A targeted web search did not surface a published resolution of this generalized Poncelet question for pairs of irreducible algebraic curves of degrees $n,m$ with $n+m>4$ each carrying an oval. The classical Poncelet closure theorem covers the conic case ($n=m=2$); extensions to higher-degree curves remain a topic of active investigation, but no source was found that confirms or refutes the existence of such a pair conjugating the Poncelet map to a rotation. Status is therefore taken as unknown.

Let $\gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be the unit circle defined by $x^2 + y^2 - 1 = 0$. Let $p_2(x,y)$ be a real polynomial of degree $2$ such that the conic $\Gamma_0 = \{p_2(x,y) = 0\}$ is an ellipse strictly surrounding $\gamma$, and let $p_m(x,y)$ be a real polynomial of degree $m \ge 3$. For a small real parameter $\varepsilon$, set
$$\Gamma_\varepsilon = \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : p_2(x,y) + \varepsilon\, p_m(x,y) = 0\},$$
and assume that the curve $p_2 + \varepsilon p_m = 0$ is irreducible and that $\Gamma_\varepsilon$ is a smooth oval surrounding $\gamma$. The Poncelet map $P_\varepsilon : \Gamma_\varepsilon \to \Gamma_\varepsilon$ associated with the pair of ovals $(\gamma, \Gamma_\varepsilon)$ is defined as follows: from a point $q \in \Gamma_\varepsilon$, draw one of the two tangent lines from $q$ to $\gamma$ (chosen consistently by orientation); this line meets $\Gamma_\varepsilon$ in a second point $q'$, and one sets $P_\varepsilon(q) = q'$.

Prove or disprove: the Poncelet map $P_\varepsilon$ is topologically conjugate to a rigid rotation of the circle if and only if $\varepsilon = 0$.

Let $f:U\to\mathbb{C}$ be a complex-valued function that is real-analytic in a neighborhood $U\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ of the origin, where points are written as $(x,y)$ and $z=x+iy$, $\bar z=x-iy$. For a fixed positive integer $n$, define the planar vector field $X_n=(P,Q)$ on $U$ by
$$P(x,y)=2^n\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left(\frac{\partial^n f}{\partial \bar z^{\,n}}(x,y)\right),\qquad Q(x,y)=2^n\,\mathrm{Im}\!\left(\frac{\partial^n f}{\partial \bar z^{\,n}}(x,y)\right),$$
where $\partial/\partial\bar z=\tfrac12(\partial/\partial x+i\,\partial/\partial y)$. Suppose that the origin is an isolated zero of $X_n$ (i.e., an isolated equilibrium of the differential equation $(x',y')=(P,Q)$). Let $\mathrm{ind}_0(X_n)\in\mathbb{Z}$ denote the Poincaré–Hopf index of $X_n$ at the origin.

Prove or disprove: $\mathrm{ind}_0(X_n)\le n$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Loewner's conjecture in this general $n$ form remains open. The case $n=2$ would imply Carathéodory's conjecture on umbilic points of convex surfaces; while several proofs of the $n=2$/Carathéodory case have been announced (e.g., Ivanov 2002, Guilfoyle–Klingenberg), they are not universally accepted, and the conjecture for general $n$ is widely regarded as open. Recent work (e.g., bounds on the index of an umbilic point, 2024) continues to investigate partial results.

The question of finite moment determinacy for sparse (k-monomial) polynomials, in the form of finding a bound N(k) that forces vanishing of f from the first N(k) moments of f^n on [0,1], is discussed in work of Françoise–Pakovich–Yomdin–Zhao and related literature on the polynomial moment vanishing problem. Consider a system of two real polynomial equations in two real variables
$$f_1(x,y)=0,\qquad f_2(x,y)=0,$$
where each $f_i\in\mathbb{R}[x,y]$ is a (Laurent) polynomial having exactly $m_i$ distinct monomial terms (i.e., $f_i$ is an $m_i$-nomial), $i=1,2$. A solution $(x_0,y_0)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ is called positive if $x_0>0$ and $y_0>0$, and is called simple (nondegenerate) if the Jacobian $\det\!\bigl(\partial(f_1,f_2)/\partial(x,y)\bigr)$ is nonzero at $(x_0,y_0)$.

Let $N(m_1,m_2)$ denote the maximum, over all such pairs $(f_1,f_2)$, of the number of simple positive solutions of the system. Determine a reasonable (or sharp) upper bound for $N(m_1,m_2)$ as a function of $m_1$ and $m_2$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general problem of finding sharp fewnomial upper bounds for the number of positive solutions of a bivariate system in terms of the numbers of monomials $m_1, m_2$ remains open. Sharp results are known only in very small cases: for $m_1+m_2=5$ the sharp bound 6 has been established (Bihan and others, with constructions via tropical geometry), and general upper bounds (e.g., of the form $(e^2+3)/4 \cdot 2^{\binom{k}{2}} n^k$ specialized to $n=k=2$) are known but not sharp.

The Casas-Alvero conjecture has been verified for many families of degrees (e.g., prime powers and certain composite cases) for years. A January 2025 arXiv preprint by Soham Ghosh ("Proof of the Casas-Alvero conjecture", arXiv:2501.09272) claims a complete proof in characteristic zero using Koszul homology, but as of May 2026 this proof has not yet been confirmed as published/refereed in a journal of record, so the conjecture's full resolution remains not universally accepted. Other 2023–2025 works (Schaub–Spivakovsky, etc.) provide further partial results.

For a natural number $n$ written in base 10, let $\mathrm{rev}(n)$ denote the natural number obtained by reversing the order of the decimal digits of $n$. Define the reverse-and-add map $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ by $f(n)=n+\mathrm{rev}(n)$, and let $f^k$ denote the $k$-fold iterate of $f$ (with $f^0(n)=n$). A natural number $m$ is called a palindrome if $\mathrm{rev}(m)=m$. Call $n\in\mathbb{N}$ a Lychrel number if $f^k(n)$ is not a palindrome for any integer $k\ge 0$.

Prove or disprove the following statements:
(a) There exist infinitely many Lychrel numbers.
(b) The smallest Lychrel number is $196$.

Let α be an irrational number and let a_n = {nα} denote the fractional part of nα. For a positive integer N, consider the N distinct points a_1, a_2, …, a_N ∈ [0,1). Construct a 4-regular graph G_N on the vertex set {1, 2, …, N} as follows:

1. Connect i to i+1 for every 1 ≤ i ≤ N−1, and also connect N to 1 (cyclic order edges in the original index ordering).
2. Let π be the permutation of {1, …, N} such that a_{π(1)} < a_{π(2)} < ⋯ < a_{π(N)}. Connect π(i) to π(i+1) for every 1 ≤ i ≤ N−1, and also connect π(N) to π(1) (cyclic order edges in the value-sorted ordering).

The resulting multigraph is 4-regular. Numerical experiments show that, when drawn with vertices placed so as to reflect their structure, G_N appears to approximate a two-dimensional surface embedded in three-space resembling a torus with an additional twist, and that the qualitative geometric features of these graphs depend on the Diophantine approximation properties of α (e.g. its continued fraction expansion).

Problem. Prove rigorously what large-scale geometric/combinatorial structure the family {G_N}_{N ≥ 1} possesses (for instance, identify G_N as a circulant graph or a graph that admits a canonical embedding into a torus), and quantify how this structure (in particular the embedding, the genus, gap statistics, or graph-metric asymptotics) depends on the continued fraction expansion / irrationality measure of α.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Follow-up work has made substantial progress. Using the Three-Gap Theorem, the Kronecker sequence graph G_N is known to be (for appropriate N) a circulant graph, and connected circulant graphs of this form embed into the torus, providing a combinatorial explanation of the observed torus-like shape. Further regularity results on the induced "Kronecker permutations" have appeared (e.g., Clément 2025, arXiv:2509.03782), showing that for quadratic irrationals there are infinitely many N for which the sorting permutation has cycles of length at most 4. However, a complete and quantitative rigorous description of the large-scale structure with full dependence on the Diophantine properties of α does not appear to be fully settled.

Graph construction. Given a finite sequence a_1, a_2, ..., a_N of pairwise distinct real numbers, build an undirected graph G = (V,E) with vertex set V = {1, 2, ..., N} as follows. For each index i with 2 ≤ i ≤ N, let

  L(i) = argmax { a_j : 1 ≤ j < i and a_j < a_i },
  U(i) = argmin { a_j : 1 ≤ j < i and a_j > a_i }

(when these sets are non‑empty), i.e. L(i) is the index of the largest value strictly less than a_i among the predecessors, and U(i) is the index of the smallest value strictly greater than a_i among the predecessors. Place an edge between i and L(i) and an edge between i and U(i) whenever the corresponding index exists. (Apart from low‑index boundary effects every vertex has degree at most 4, and most vertices have degree exactly 4.)

Two integer sequences. Define two sequences of positive integers (a_n)_{n≥1} as follows.

Sequence S_1 ("multiplicative" Erdős–Freud–Hegyvári rule). Set a_1 = 1, a_2 = 2. For n ≥ 1, let a_{2n+2} be the smallest positive integer that has not yet appeared in the sequence, and set
  a_{2n+1} = a_{2n} · a_{2n+2}.

Sequence S_2 ("doubling" rule). Set a_1 = 1. For n ≥ 1, let a_{2n} be the smallest positive integer that has not yet appeared in the sequence, and set
  a_{2n+1} = 2 · a_{2n}.

Problem. For each of the two sequences S_1 and S_2, build the graph G_N from its initial segment a_1, ..., a_N as described above, and analyse the limiting structure of G_N as N → ∞. Specifically:

(a) Prove that the graphs associated with S_1 and S_2 admit a non-trivial asymptotic geometric/combinatorial structure (for example, a description as a near‑regular planar lattice‑like graph, an explicit decomposition into long paths or cycles, or a bounded‑bandwidth ordering of the vertices).

(b) Identify the combinatorial mechanism within the recursive definitions of S_1 and S_2 — i.e. the interaction between the "smallest missing integer" rule and the multiplicative/doubling rule — that forces this structure, and quantify how the rank of a_n inside the sorted set {a_1, ..., a_n} behaves as n → ∞.

Fix an integer base $b\ge 2$. For each nonnegative integer $n$, write its standard base-$b$ expansion $n=\sum_{k\ge 0} d_k\, b^k$ with digits $d_k\in\{0,1,\dots,b-1\}$, and define
$$a_n \;=\; \sum_{k\ge 0} d_k\,(-b)^k.$$
Equivalently, $a_n$ satisfies the recurrence
$$a_{bk+m} \;=\; -b\,a_k + m \qquad (k\ge 0,\; 0\le m\le b-1),\qquad a_0=0.$$

Fix a positive integer $N$ and form a graph $G_{b,N}$ on the vertex set $\{a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{N-1}\}\subset\mathbb{Z}$ as follows: for each $0\le n\le N-2$, place an edge between $a_n$ and $a_{n+1}$ (the "consecutive" edges), and for each $n$ in this range place an edge between $a_n$ and the vertex $a_m$ where $m$ is the index such that $a_m$ is the integer immediately succeeding $a_n$ in the sorted order of $\{a_0,\dots,a_{N-1}\}$ (the "value-order" edges). The resulting graph is $4$-regular (away from boundary vertices).

Problem. Give a rigorous explanation of the global structural features of the family of graphs $\{G_{b,N}\}_{N\ge 1}$ (for example, the appearance of nested cycles, self-similar clustering, and large-scale geometric patterns observed as $N\to\infty$). In particular, determine whether all such structural features can be derived from iterated application of the recurrence $a_{bk+m}=-b\,a_k+m$, or whether additional principles are required.

Define the EKG sequence $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ by $a_1 = 1$, $a_2 = 2$, and for every $n \ge 3$, $a_n$ is the smallest positive integer not already appearing among $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$ such that $\gcd(a_n, a_{n-1}) \ge 2$. (It is known that this sequence is a permutation of the positive integers.)

For each integer $N \ge 1$, construct a graph $G_N$ as follows. The vertex set is $\{1, 2, \dots, N\}$. Draw an edge between distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ whenever
$$\gcd(a_i, a_j) \ge 2 \quad\text{and}\quad |i - j| \le 2,$$
or, more generally, define $G_N$ to be the natural $4$-regular graph (away from boundary vertices) associated with the EKG sequence in which each vertex $i$ is connected to the indices of the two nearest preceding and two nearest following terms sharing a nontrivial common factor with $a_i$. Embed $G_N$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ using a standard spectral embedding via the eigenvectors corresponding to the smallest nonzero eigenvalues of its (combinatorial) Laplacian.

Let $\lambda_1(G_N) = 4 \ge \lambda_2(G_N) \ge \cdots$ denote the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of $G_N$.

(a) Determine the limiting geometric structure of the spectral embedding of $G_N$ as $N \to \infty$. In particular, prove or disprove that the embedded vertices asymptotically concentrate on a cone or paraboloid-type surface.

(b) Determine $\lim_{N\to\infty} \lambda_2(G_N)$, and explain rigorously why $\lambda_2(G_N)$ remains extremely close to $4$ for all large $N$ (i.e., bound the spectral gap $4 - \lambda_2(G_N)$ asymptotically).

Define the Recamán sequence $(a_n)_{n\ge 0}$ by $a_0 = 0$ and, for $n \ge 1$,
\[ a_n = \begin{cases} a_{n-1} - n & \text{if } a_{n-1} - n > 0 \text{ and } a_{n-1}-n \notin \{a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}\}, \\ a_{n-1} + n & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]
For each $N \ge 1$, let $S_N$ be the multiset $\{a_0,a_1,\dots,a_N\}$ and let $T_N \subseteq S_N$ be the set obtained by deleting every element of $S_N$ that occurs more than once (i.e., keeping only those values that appear exactly once in the segment). Re-index the retained values in their original order of appearance as $b_0,b_1,\dots,b_{M(N)}$, and form the 4-regular circulant-like graph $G_N$ on vertex set $\{0,1,\dots,M(N)\}$ in which each index $i$ is joined to $i\pm 1$ and $i\pm 2$ (mod $M(N)+1$), with the vertex $i$ embedded in the plane at the point $(i, b_i)$.

Give a precise mathematical description of the large-scale structure exhibited by the family of graphs $\{G_N\}_{N\to\infty}$ (for instance, asymptotic density of retained terms, the distribution of gaps $b_{i+1}-b_i$, recurring geometric patterns of the planar embedding, or any provable self-similarity), formulated as a rigorous statement and proof.

For a nonnegative integer $n$ with binary expansion $n = \sum_{i\ge 0} b_i 2^i$ (with $b_i \in \{0,1\}$ and only finitely many nonzero), define its binary derivative to be the infinite string $d(n) = (c_0, c_1, c_2, \ldots)$ where $c_i = b_i \oplus b_{i+1}$ (XOR). Order the nonnegative integers $n_0, n_1, n_2, \ldots$ so that the sequence of strings $d(n_0), d(n_1), d(n_2), \ldots$ is in lexicographic order; the resulting permutation $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $a(k) = n_k$, agrees with the OEIS sequence A006068 (the inverse Gray code).

Now form the following family of 4-regular graphs $G_N$ for each integer $N \ge 5$: take vertex set $V_N = \{0, 1, \ldots, N-1\}$ and, for each index $k$, connect $k$ to its two nearest neighbors on each side in the sequence $a$, i.e. join $k$ to $k\pm 1$ and $k\pm 2$ modulo $N$ in the ordering induced by $a$ (equivalently, take the 4-regular circulant-like graph defined by the consecutive 4-window structure of the sequence $(a(0), a(1), \ldots, a(N-1))$ when this list is reinterpreted as vertices via $a$).

Prove rigorously that the graphs $G_N$ exhibit the highly structured (non-random) macroscopic geometric pattern empirically observed when they are drawn with a force-directed (spring) layout: namely, identify and prove the precise combinatorial / geometric structure (e.g., number and shape of large-scale "lobes" or self-similar nested clusters, automorphism group, and growth rate of graph-theoretic diameter and bandwidth) of $G_N$ as $N \to \infty$.

Construction. Given a finite list of n distinct real numbers x_1, x_2, ..., x_n (an "ordered sequence"), associate to it a 4-regular graph G = (V, E) on n vertices labeled 1, ..., n as follows: connect vertex i (for 2 ≤ i ≤ n−1) to its two left neighbors and two right neighbors in the list when ranked by value, in the natural cyclic manner used to build the so-called "horizontal/vertical-visibility-style" 4-regular graph; equivalently, for each index i let p(i) and q(i) be the indices of the largest j < i with x_j < x_i and with x_j > x_i (respectively), and let r(i), s(i) be the analogous indices on the right side, and connect i to {p(i), q(i), r(i), s(i)} (with boundary conventions making the graph 4-regular).

Empirically, certain input sequences produce drawings of G that look like a "spiral": a long curve that winds around itself in a regular pattern. One source of such examples comes from triangular arrays: given a function a(n,k) defined for 1 ≤ k ≤ n, list the values a(1,1), a(2,1), a(2,2), a(3,1), a(3,2), a(3,3), ... by rows, then delete duplicates while preserving order, and feed the resulting sequence into the construction. In particular, the model a(n,k) = exp(k (f(n) − f(k))) for various functions f produces spiral graphs.

Problem.
(a) Give a precise characterization of which input sequences (x_1, ..., x_n) give rise to a spiral 4-regular graph under this construction.
(b) In particular, formalize and prove (or refute) the heuristic that spiral graphs arise exactly from sequences that decompose into consecutive blocks of increasing subsequences (specifying the block-length growth required).
(c) Determine the full class of triangular arrays a(n,k) whose row-by-row, duplicate-removed reading produces a spiral graph, and decide to what extent this class is captured by the family a(n,k) = exp(k (f(n) − f(k))) as f ranges over a natural class of functions.

Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space of analytic functions on the unit disk $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ in which the monomials $\{z^n\}_{n\ge 0}$ form an orthogonal basis (for example, the Hardy space $H^2$, the Bergman space $A^2$, or a weighted Dirichlet-type space $D_\alpha$ with norm $\|\sum a_n z^n\|_\alpha^2 = \sum_{n\ge 0}(n+1)^\alpha |a_n|^2$). For a function $f\in\mathcal{H}$ that does not vanish identically and a nonnegative integer $n$, the optimal polynomial approximant (opa) of degree $n$ to $1/f$ in $\mathcal{H}$ is the unique polynomial $p_n$ of degree at most $n$ that minimizes
$$\|p f - 1\|_{\mathcal{H}}$$
over all polynomials $p$ of degree at most $n$. Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ be the spatial domain and fix a particle number $N \in \mathbb{N}$. Consider the Banach space
$$X = L^1(\mathbb{R}^3) \cap L^3(\mathbb{R}^3),$$
equipped with the norm $\|n\|_X = \|n\|_{L^1} + \|n\|_{L^3}$, and the admissible set of $N$-particle densities
$$S = \Big\{ n \in X : n \ge 0 \text{ a.e.}, \ \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} n = N, \ \sqrt{n} \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^3) \Big\}.$$
For an electron–electron interaction $\hat{W}$, define the interacting Lieb (constrained-search) functional
$$F_L[n] = \inf\Big\{ \mathrm{Tr}\big(\hat{\Gamma}(\hat{T}+\hat{W})\big) : \hat{\Gamma} \text{ is an } N\text{-particle ensemble density matrix yielding } n \Big\},$$
where $\hat{T}$ denotes the kinetic-energy operator. Let
$$B \subset S$$
be the subset of densities that are interacting ensemble $v$-representable, i.e., densities $n \in S$ that arise as the ground-state density of $\hat{T}+\hat{W}+\sum_i v(x_i)$ for some external potential $v$ in a suitable dual class.

It is known that $F_L$ is convex on $S$ but is nowhere Gâteaux differentiable on $X$ in the usual sense.

Question. Does $F_L$ admit a derivative in some restricted (weak) sense at every $n \in B$? More precisely, does there exist a class $\mathcal{D}_n \subset X$ of admissible perturbation directions $\delta n$ such that:
(i) each $\delta n \in \mathcal{D}_n$ satisfies $\int \delta n = 0$ (particle-number preserving) and $n + t\,\delta n \in S$ for all sufficiently small $t > 0$;
(ii) the one-sided directional derivative
$$D_{\delta n} F_L[n] := \lim_{t \downarrow 0} \frac{F_L[n + t\,\delta n] - F_L[n]}{t}$$
exists and is finite for every $\delta n \in \mathcal{D}_n$;
(iii) the map $\delta n \mapsto D_{\delta n} F_L[n]$ is linear on $\mathcal{D}_n$ and represented by a (Kohn–Sham) potential $v_n$, in the sense that $D_{\delta n} F_L[n] = -\int v_n\, \delta n$ for all $\delta n \in \mathcal{D}_n$;
(iv) the class $\mathcal{D}_n$ is large enough to recover the conclusions normally drawn from Gâteaux differentiability of $F_L$ at $n$ (in particular, applicability to the Kohn–Sham scheme), without imposing further restrictions on $n$ beyond $n \in B$?

The question of whether the Lieb functional admits a derivative in a restricted/weak sense at every interacting ensemble v-representable density remains open in general. Lammert (2007) showed the standard proof of Gâteaux differentiability is flawed and that $F_L$ is neither Gâteaux nor Fréchet differentiable in the usual sense; positive results exist only under extra restrictions (e.g. densities bounded away from zero with $L^2$ derivatives), or in special settings such as spinless fermions in one dimension (2025 work by Sutter et al.). No general result removing all restrictions on $B$ has been established.

Setting. Consider the Kohn–Sham (KS) framework of density functional theory in which one considers N-electron systems described by single-particle densities ρ on R^3 with ρ ≥ 0 and ∫ρ = N. A density n_s is said to be non-interacting (pure-state or ensemble) v-representable if there exists a one-body local potential v_s such that n_s arises as the ground-state density of a non-interacting N-electron Hamiltonian H_s = -½Δ + v_s (acting on a Slater determinant or an ensemble of degenerate ground-state determinants). Let B_s denote the set of non-interacting ensemble v-representable densities. By the Hohenberg–Kohn theorem applied to non-interacting systems, the assignment n_s ↦ v_s[n_s] is well defined (up to an additive constant) on B_s, giving the KS potential functional v_s : B_s → (potentials modulo constants).

Let χ_s[v_s[n_s]] denote the static non-interacting density–density linear response operator at the potential v_s[n_s], i.e. the operator giving δn_s in terms of an infinitesimal perturbation δv_s of the KS potential at fixed particle number; let χ_s^{-1}[v_s[n_s]] denote its (formal) inverse on the space of density variations summing to zero.

We say that v_s admits a "derivative in a restricted sense" at n_s ∈ B_s if there exists a linear operator D[n_s], acting on an admissible class of density variations δn (those tangent to B_s, i.e. preserving total particle number and remaining inside B_s to first order), such that
   v_s[n_s + δn] - v_s[n_s] = D[n_s] · δn + o(‖δn‖)
in a suitable norm, modulo additive constants. The operator D[n_s] is said to be bounded if it extends to a bounded linear operator on the relevant Banach space of density variations.

Question. Does the KS potential functional v_s : B_s → potentials admit, at every density n_s ∈ B_s (including degenerate ground-state cases), a derivative in the above restricted sense, and is this derivative bounded? Equivalently, can one rigorously establish such a bounded restricted derivative of v_s[n_s] on B_s, in a way that would imply the non-interacting v-representability conjecture (the statement that every "reasonable" N-electron density is non-interacting ensemble v-representable)?

Note that the natural candidate D[n_s] = -χ_s^{-1}[v_s[n_s]] is in general unbounded, since the eigenvalues α_j of χ_s can approach 0, so a separate argument or alternative construction is required.

The general non-interacting v-representability problem and the existence of a (bounded) derivative of the KS potential functional in a restricted sense remain open. Partial progress has been obtained in restricted settings: a 2025 work treats non-interacting Schrödinger operators with distributional potentials on the one-dimensional torus, showing Hohenberg–Kohn and that the non-interacting Lieb functional is differentiable on the v-representable densities in that setting. No general resolution of the conjecture (covering degenerate cases in R^3) appears in the literature.

Setup. A br-graph is a graph in which each vertex is labeled either black or red (so V(H) is partitioned into B(H) ∪ R(H)). A homomorphism between br-graphs preserves both edges and vertex colors. For a br-graph H, define its switching graph S_H as the br-graph with vertex set V(H) × {0,1}, where the edges and color labels are determined by H according to the standard switching construction (so that homomorphisms G → S_H correspond to "switchings" of homomorphisms into H).

Polymorphisms. For k ≥ 1, a k-ary polymorphism of a br-graph G is a homomorphism φ : G^k → G (where G^k is the categorical product in the category of br-graphs). It is idempotent if φ(x, x, …, x) = x for every x ∈ V(G). For k ≥ 3, an idempotent polymorphism φ is a weak near unanimity (WNU) polymorphism if, for all x, y ∈ V(G),
   φ(y, x, x, …, x) = φ(x, y, x, …, x) = ⋯ = φ(x, x, …, x, y).
A polymorphism φ is conservative if φ(v_1, …, v_k) ∈ {v_1, …, v_k} for all choices of v_i.

For the switching graph S_H, a list on S_H is a subset L ⊆ V(S_H) = V(H) × {0,1}. Such a list L is called symmetric if (v, 0) ∈ L ⇔ (v, 1) ∈ L for every v ∈ V(H). A polymorphism φ of S_H is semi-conservative if for every symmetric list L and every (v_1, …, v_k) ∈ L^k one has φ(v_1, …, v_k) ∈ L (equivalently, φ preserves all symmetric lists).

Question. Is it true that, for every br-graph H, the switching graph S_H admits a semi-conservative weak near unanimity polymorphism if and only if S_H admits a conservative weak near unanimity polymorphism?

Let n be a positive integer with n ≥ 3, and consider an arrangement of n straight lines in the Euclidean plane R^2. Such an arrangement partitions the plane into open polygonal regions (cells). Call a triangle T admissible for the arrangement if:
(i) the three sides of T lie on three of the n lines, and
(ii) the open interior of T is one of the cells of the arrangement (equivalently, no other line of the arrangement crosses the interior of T, and the interiors of any two such triangles are disjoint).

Define K(n) to be the maximum, over all arrangements of n lines in the plane, of the number of admissible triangles. Determine K(n) as an explicit function of n (or, for each n, determine its exact value).

Known facts that should be respected: Tamura's upper bound K(n) ≤ ⌊n(n−2)/3⌋, and the Clément–Bader strengthening that this bound cannot be attained when n ≡ 0 or 2 (mod 6). The problem is to determine the exact value of K(n) for all n.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The Kobon triangle problem is a long-standing open problem in combinatorial geometry. Tamura's upper bound ⌊n(n−2)/3⌋ is known, and Clément–Bader showed it is not achieved for n ≡ 0, 2 (mod 6). Exact values of K(n) are known for several small n (e.g., n = 3–9, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, ...), with recent SAT-based work (Savchuk, 2025) confirming the optimum for n = 11. The general formula for K(n) remains unresolved.

Let H ⊂ ℝ² be the L-shaped hallway of unit width formed by the union
  H = {(x,y) : x ≤ 0, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1} ∪ {(x,y) : 0 ≤ x, -x ≤ y ≤ 1 - … }
more precisely, H = ((-∞, 1] × [0,1]) ∪ ([0,1] × (-∞, 1]), i.e., two perpendicular corridors of width 1 meeting at a right-angled corner.

A "sofa" is any connected planar region S ⊂ ℝ² (not required to be convex) for which there exists a closed interval I ⊂ ℝ and a continuous one-parameter family {Φ_t}_{t ∈ I} of rigid motions of the plane (each Φ_t an orientation-preserving isometry, with t ↦ Φ_t continuous in the usual topology on the group of rigid motions) such that:
  (i) for every t ∈ I, Φ_t(S) ⊂ H;
  (ii) for sufficiently early t the region Φ_t(S) lies entirely in the horizontal corridor (-∞, 1] × [0,1], and for sufficiently late t it lies entirely in the vertical corridor [0,1] × (-∞, 1].

Determine the supremum of the area of S over all such sofas, and exhibit a region attaining it. In particular, decide whether the maximum is achieved by Gerver's region (a specific shape composed of 18 analytic arc pieces with area approximately 2.2195).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

For the special case of equilateral triangles, optimal packings of n unit circles are proved only for small n (roughly n ≤ 15), with conjectured optima for n up to about 34; the problem is open in general. For arbitrary triangles the question remains unresolved for general n, with only partial results, bounds, and constant-factor approximation methods (e.g., split packing) known.

Let F ⊂ ℝ² be a fixed, known plane region (the "forest"). A parametrized curve C: [0, L] → ℝ² is said to guarantee escape from F if, for every starting point P ∈ F and every rigid motion (translation and rotation) sending the initial point C(0) to P, the resulting congruent image C̃ of C is not entirely contained in F (i.e. C̃ exits F at some parameter value).

Among all parametrized curves C that guarantee escape from F in this sense, determine one that minimizes the arc length L (equivalently, the worst-case time/distance until escape, assuming unit speed). That is, find

  inf { length(C) : C guarantees escape from F },

and exhibit an optimal curve achieving (or approaching) this infimum, for a given forest shape F — and, more ambitiously, give a procedure that produces such an optimal curve for an arbitrary plane region F.

Bellman's lost-in-a-forest problem, posed in 1955–1956, remains open in general. Optimal escape paths are known for a handful of special forest shapes (e.g. infinite strips, half-planes, circles, certain rectangles and some convex regions), but no general solution for arbitrary plane regions has been verified. A 2024 arXiv preprint by Z. Deng proposes a general framework, but it is not established as a community-accepted solution and the problem is still listed as open (e.g. on Wikipedia and related surveys).

Question: Does every Jordan curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$ inscribe a square?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general inscribed square (Toeplitz) conjecture remains open. Many special cases are known: convex curves, piecewise analytic/smooth curves (Emch and others), and recent work by Greene–Lobb (2020–2024) establishing inscribed rectangles and cyclic quadrilaterals for smooth Jordan curves and progress for Lipschitz curves. The problem for arbitrary continuous Jordan curves has not been resolved.

representations.normalized:
Let $(L, \wedge, \vee)$ be a complete lattice (e.g., the lattice of grayscale images $L = \mathbb{R}^{H\times W}$ with pointwise order). A *morphological operator* on $L$ is a mapping built from the lattice-theoretic primitives of erosion $\varepsilon_B(f)(x) = \inf_{b\in B} f(x+b)$ and dilation $\delta_B(f)(x) = \sup_{b\in B} f(x+b)$ with structuring element $B$, together with their compositions (opening, closing, etc.). A *Max-Min Basis-Based (MMBB) network* is a feed-forward parametric model whose layers are finite sup-inf (equivalently, max-min) combinations of such morphological primitives, with the structuring elements (and possibly the basis weights) treated as learnable parameters.

A *standard deep-learning layer* refers to one of: a linear convolution layer, a downsampling (strided) layer, an upsampling (e.g., transposed convolution or nearest-neighbor) layer, a max-pooling layer, or a ReLU activation $x \mapsto \max(x,0)$.

Problem. Construct hybrid feed-forward architectures that interleave MMBB layers with standard deep-learning layers (convolution, down/upsampling, max-pooling, ReLU) so that the resulting models:
(i) are end-to-end trainable by gradient-based optimization (with a well-defined notion of subgradient through the sup/inf primitives);
(ii) are universal in some precise approximation-theoretic sense on a class of image-to-image or image-to-label mappings of interest; and
(iii) on at least one standard learning task (e.g., image classification or semantic segmentation) demonstrate a quantifiable advantage—either in parameter efficiency, interpretability, or performance—over a purely convolutional baseline of comparable size.

Formalize the notion of "relevant learnable pipeline," exhibit such a construction, and prove the corresponding approximation and trainability guarantees.

Background. Mathematical morphology on grayscale images is built from two basic nonlinear operators acting on a function f : R^d → R with respect to a structuring function b : R^d → R ∪ {−∞}: the dilation (f ⊕ b)(x) = sup_{y ∈ R^d} { f(x − y) + b(y) } and the erosion (f ⊖ b)(x) = inf_{y ∈ R^d} { f(x + y) − b(y) }. A flat structuring element on a compact set B ⊂ R^d corresponds to b = 0 on B and −∞ elsewhere, recovering the local sup/inf operators. A map T between normed function spaces is L-Lipschitz if ||T(f) − T(g)|| ≤ L · ||f − g|| for all f, g.

A feed-forward neural network is a composition F = L_n ∘ σ_{n−1} ∘ L_{n−1} ∘ ··· ∘ σ_1 ∘ L_1, where each L_k is an affine (or convolutional) operator and each σ_k is a pointwise nonlinearity (e.g. ReLU x ↦ max(x,0)) possibly followed by a pooling operator (e.g. max-pooling). The Lipschitz constant of F (with respect to specified input/output norms) is bounded above by the product of the Lipschitz constants of its layers, and controls the regularity, robustness and generalization of the network.

Define a "morphological layer" to be any layer M whose action on its input feature maps is given by a finite composition of dilations, erosions, openings (f ↦ (f ⊖ b) ⊕ b), closings (f ↦ (f ⊕ b) ⊖ b), or supremal/infimal convolutions with learnable structuring functions, possibly followed by an affine combination across channels.

Problem.
(a) Characterize the families of morphological layers M as above for which one can give an explicit, sharp, computable upper bound on the Lipschitz constant Lip(M) (with respect to the L^∞ and L^2 norms on inputs and outputs), in terms of the parameters of the structuring functions; describe in particular which choices of structuring functions and channel-mixing rules guarantee Lip(M) ≤ 1.

(b) Determine whether such "Lipschitz morphological layers" can be inserted into a deep neural network so as to control its overall Lipschitz constant while preserving — or improving — the network's expressive power. Concretely: exhibit, or prove the impossibility of, an architecture in which every standard nonlinearity of the form (max-pooling ∘ ReLU) is replaced by a Lipschitz morphological layer, in such a way that the resulting class of functions is at least as expressive (in a precise approximation-theoretic sense, e.g. universal approximation on compact sets of continuous functions) as the original architecture.

Setting. Let $E$ denote a discrete workspace, e.g. $E=\mathbb{Z}^d$, and let $\mathcal{P}(E)$ denote its power set, whose elements are called shapes. Fix a transitive group $G$ acting on $E$ (for instance the translation group, the motion group, or an affine group). For a shape $X\in\mathcal{P}(E)$ and $g\in G$, write $g\cdot X = \{g\cdot x : x\in X\}$.

Given a finite collection of shapes $\mathcal{T}=\{T_1,\dots,T_k\}\subset \mathcal{P}(E)$, called templates, and a target shape $S\in\mathcal{P}(E)$, the Generalized Tailor Problem asks whether $S$ admits a decomposition
$$ S \;=\; \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{N} g_i \cdot T_{j_i}, $$
where $g_1,\dots,g_N\in G$ and $j_1,\dots,j_N\in\{1,\dots,k\}$, and the union is disjoint (a tiling of $S$ by transformed copies of templates from $\mathcal{T}$). The optimization version asks for a decomposition minimizing $N$ or another prescribed cost.

A morphological iterative network is a feed-forward neural architecture whose elementary layers are the standard operators of mathematical morphology — erosion $X\ominus B = \{x : B+x\subseteq X\}$, dilation $X\oplus B = \bigcup_{b\in B}(X+b)$, opening, closing, hit-or-miss transforms — together with their group-morphology generalizations relative to $G$ (where translation is replaced by the action of $G$), and pointwise lattice operations $\cup,\cap$. The depth of such a network is the number of sequential morphological layers, and its size is the total number of structuring elements used.

Question. Determine the optimal asymptotic complexity, in terms of network depth and size, of solving the Generalized Tailor Problem for a family of templates $\mathcal{T}$ and group $G$ by morphological iterative networks. Concretely: provide upper and lower bounds on the minimal depth $D(\mathcal{T},G,n)$ and size $S(\mathcal{T},G,n)$ of a morphological iterative network that, given any input shape $S\subseteq E$ contained in a window of $n$ points, outputs a valid decomposition of $S$ into $G$-transformed copies of templates from $\mathcal{T}$ whenever such a decomposition exists, and reports infeasibility otherwise.

representations.normalized:
Background. In mathematical morphology, given a grayscale image $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ (with $\Omega\subset\mathbb{Z}^2$) and a marker image $g\le f$, the morphological reconstruction by dilation $R_f(g)$ is defined as the limit of the iteration $g_0=g$, $g_{k+1}=(\delta_B(g_k))\wedge f$, where $\delta_B$ is the elementary dilation by a structuring element $B$ and $\wedge$ denotes pointwise minimum; this iteration converges in a finite number of steps to the smallest image $h$ with $g\le h\le f$ that is invariant under $\delta_B(\cdot)\wedge f$. Reconstruction by erosion is defined dually. Using such reconstruction operators one can compute, for every regional maximum (or minimum) $M$ of $f$, its extinction value $\mathrm{ext}(M)$ associated with a measure (volume, dynamics, area), which quantifies the persistence of $M$ under successive morphological filterings; extinction values are closely related to persistent homology of the sublevel/superlevel filtration of $f$ in dimension $0$.

Problem. Design and analyze a trainable deep neural architecture $\mathcal{N}_\theta$, with parameters $\theta$, whose internal computation realizes (or approximates) the iterative morphological reconstruction process $g_{k+1}=(\delta_B(g_k))\wedge f$ with learnable structuring elements / nonlinearities, and whose output produces, for each pixel of an input image $f$, a feature vector encoding the extinction values (equivalently, the $0$-dimensional persistence) of the regional extrema to which it belongs. Specifically:

(a) Prove or disprove that there exists such an architecture for which the learned features are provably consistent estimators of the true extinction values associated with a chosen extinction measure (volume, dynamics, or area), in the sense that as the network depth (number of unrolled reconstruction iterations) tends to infinity the output converges, uniformly on a suitable class of images, to the exact extinction map.

(b) Determine which class of architectures is best suited to implement the unbounded-iteration reconstruction fixed point: a feed-forward residual network of the form $g_{k+1}=g_k+F_\theta(g_k,f)$, a recurrent network sharing weights across iterations, or another design; in particular, characterize necessary and sufficient conditions on $F_\theta$ for the discrete dynamics to converge to $R_f(g)$.

(c) Demonstrate that the resulting persistence/extinction features can be end-to-end trained for topological image classification and semantic segmentation tasks, in the sense that gradients with respect to $\theta$ exist almost everywhere and that minimizing a suitable topological loss based on these features yields segmentations with prescribed Betti numbers.

Background. For a grayscale image f : Z^2 → R and a structuring function b : Z^2 → R ∪ {−∞}, the morphological dilation and erosion are defined by
  (f ⊕ b)(x) = sup_{y} { f(x − y) + b(y) },   (f ⊖ b)(x) = inf_{y} { f(x + y) − b(y) }.
Compositions of dilations and erosions at multiple scales (e.g. openings, closings, top-hats, alternating sequential filters) yield morphological multiscale operators. A multiscale architecture is built by stacking such operators, possibly with linear/pointwise layers, where the structuring functions b = b_θ are taken from a parametric family with learnable parameters θ.

Two parametric families of particular interest are:
  (i) Quadratic structuring functions b_Σ(y) = −(1/2) y^T Σ^{−1} y, where Σ is a positive-definite "shape covariance" matrix (so the level sets of b are ellipses);
  (ii) Convex piecewise-linear structuring functions obtained as the Minkowski sum b = s_1 ⊕ ... ⊕ s_k of oriented line segments s_i of given lengths and orientations (so the level sets are zonotopes).

Problem. Design a deep architecture whose layers are parametric morphological multiscale operators of the above type, and address the following:
  1. Provide a training scheme (e.g., suitable smooth surrogates, gradient computations, or initialization strategies) such that the parameters θ of the structuring functions can be learned efficiently from data, with provable or empirically demonstrable convergence and stability.
  2. Determine which of the parametric families (i)–(ii), or other parametric families of structuring functions, lead to the best performance and the most informative parameters (e.g., explicit shape or orientation descriptors) on shape-recognition and texture-recognition tasks, in a way that yields better interpretability than standard convolutional networks.

Specifically: do there exist parametric morphological multiscale architectures that can be trained efficiently and that achieve, on shape- or texture-classification benchmarks, competitive accuracy together with quantifiably improved interpretability of the learned filters as geometric primitives?

Recent literature on morphological neural networks (e.g., works on learnable structuring elements, PConv/Pdilation layers, and deep morphological networks 2021–2025) has explored parametric structuring functions including quadratic/elliptic and convex/zonotopal forms, with progress on differentiable training via smooth approximations. The question is best classified as an open research direction.

An ultrametric space is a metric space (X, d) in which the distance d satisfies the strong triangle inequality d(x, z) ≤ max{d(x, y), d(y, z)} for all x, y, z ∈ X. Finite ultrametric spaces are in bijection with rooted trees (dendrograms) whose leaves are the points of X, where the distance between two leaves equals the height of their lowest common ancestor.

Consider data represented as points in a finite ultrametric space, equivalently as leaves of a rooted tree (dendrogram) endowed with a height function on internal nodes. A convolutional neural network operating on such data is called an ultrametric convolutional neural network: each layer takes as input a function f : X → ℝ^c on the leaves (or more generally on the nodes) of an ultrametric/dendrogram structure and outputs another such function, in a way compatible with the hierarchical/ultrametric geometry.

Address the following:

(a) Define a notion of convolution operator on functions over a finite ultrametric space (or its associated dendrogram) which (i) respects the ultrametric/hierarchical structure, (ii) has a finite parameterization that can be learned by gradient-based optimization, and (iii) admits an efficient algorithm (specify its computational complexity in terms of the number of leaves and the depth of the tree).

(b) Define max-pooling and unpooling layers for such networks, in a way consistent with the ultrametric structure: max-pooling should aggregate values along subtrees (e.g., children of an internal node) to produce a function on a coarsened dendrogram, and unpooling should provide a corresponding inverse-like operation suitable for encoder–decoder architectures. State precise definitions and prove that the resulting operators are equivariant or invariant under the appropriate isomorphisms of dendrograms.

(c) Identify additional layer types that are specifically meaningful for ultrametric convolutional neural networks (for example, layers exploiting the lattice of internal nodes, the partial order of subtrees, or non-Archimedean arithmetic) and motivate their usefulness either theoretically or by an explicit construction.

Let $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a real-valued signal and let $b:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a structuring function. The flat/grey-level morphological dilation and erosion of $f$ by $b$ are defined by
\[
(f\oplus b)(x)=\sup_{y}\bigl(f(x-y)+b(y)\bigr),\qquad (f\ominus b)(x)=\inf_{y}\bigl(f(x+y)-b(y)\bigr),
\]
so that the basic morphological operators are governed by pointwise maxima and minima. Two well-known smooth (differentiable) families of approximations to these max/min operations are:

1. The counter-harmonic mean (CHM) of order $P\in\mathbb{R}$: for a positive weight kernel $w$ and a positive function $f$,
\[
\mathrm{CHM}_P(f;w)(x)=\frac{(w\ast f^{P+1})(x)}{(w\ast f^{P})(x)},
\]
which tends to a dilation as $P\to+\infty$, to an erosion as $P\to-\infty$, and to a standard linear convolution at $P=0$.

2. The Log-Sum-Exp (LSE) approximation with temperature $\beta>0$:
\[
\mathrm{LSE}_\beta(g)(x)=\frac{1}{\beta}\log\!\int e^{\beta\,g(x,y)}\,dy,
\]
which approximates $\sup_y g(x,y)$ as $\beta\to+\infty$ and $\inf_y g(x,y)$ as $\beta\to-\infty$.

Consider hybrid trainable layers in a deep neural network in which a learnable parameter (such as $P$ in CHM, or $\beta$ together with sign parameters in LSE) interpolates between linear convolution and a max-/min-based morphological operator, so that the layer can learn to behave either as a convolution or as a dilation/erosion (or some intermediate operator) depending on the data.

Problem. Determine which of these smooth approximations to max-min-based morphological operators (counter-harmonic means, Log-Sum-Exp, or another candidate family) is most appropriate for training such hybrid deep networks. Specifically, identify a smooth approximation family $\{T_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of morphological operators that simultaneously:
(a) recovers exact dilation, erosion, and ordinary linear convolution as limiting or special values of the parameter $\theta$;
(b) admits gradients with respect to $\theta$ and the input that are numerically stable and well-behaved across these limits;
(c) provably allows gradient-based optimization to converge to genuinely morphological (max/min) regimes when these are optimal for a given learning task;
and prove or rigorously justify the optimality of the chosen family among reasonable alternatives, or show that no such family is uniformly best and characterize the trade-offs.

Background. In mathematical morphology, the basic operators of flat dilation and erosion of a scalar image $u_0:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ by a structuring element associated with a convex function admit a partial differential equation (PDE) formulation. For example, dilation/erosion by balls of radius $t$ correspond to the Hamilton–Jacobi PDEs
$$\partial_t u = \pm\|\nabla u\|,\qquad u(\cdot,0)=u_0,$$
whose viscosity solutions $u(\cdot,t)$ realize the morphological operator at scale $t$. Solving such PDEs numerically requires specialized upwind, Rouy–Tourin, Osher–Sethian, or high-accuracy predictor–corrector schemes, and the schemes have been extended to fields of symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices $U_0:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathrm{Sym}^+(d)$ by exploiting the eigenstructure of symmetric matrices to define matrix-valued dilation/erosion.

In a deep-learning pipeline, a layer $L_\theta$ is a (typically differentiable) parametric mapping between feature tensors. A morphological layer is one whose forward pass approximates a dilation, erosion, or related nonlinear morphological operator (with learnable structuring function or shape parameters), so that gradients with respect to the parameters can be computed via backpropagation through the discretized PDE solver.

Problem. Address the following three questions.

(a) Identify which numerical schemes for the scalar morphological PDEs (upwind finite-difference, Rouy–Tourin, Engquist–Osher, semi-Lagrangian, predictor–corrector, etc.) are best suited to be embedded as layers $L_\theta$ in a deep network so that:
 (i) the forward pass faithfully approximates a parametric dilation/erosion or other nonlinear morphological operator, and
 (ii) the discrete scheme is differentiable (or admits a tractable subgradient) with respect to both the input feature tensor and the learnable parameters $\theta$ of the structuring function.

(b) Each such scheme is iterative: a target scale $t$ is reached by composing $K=t/\Delta t$ explicit time steps under a CFL-type constraint. Determine how this iterative structure should be handled inside a learnable layer—e.g., by fixing $K$, by using implicit/unrolled iterations, by adaptive time stepping, by deep-equilibrium-style fixed points, or by training-time vs. inference-time scheme switching—so that training is stable and the layer remains expressive.

(c) Let $U:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathrm{Sym}^+(d)$ be an SPD-matrix field and consider matrix-valued morphological PDEs of the form
$$\partial_t U = \pm\,\mathcal{F}(\nabla U),$$
where $\mathcal{F}$ is built from the spectral decomposition of the matrix gradient so as to preserve positive definiteness. Decide whether existing numerical schemes for such matrix-field morphological PDEs can be turned into layers of a Riemannian deep network operating on SPD-valued data (or other structured matrix-valued data) so as to provide nonlinear activations that respect the SPD geometry, and characterize what theoretical guarantees (preservation of positive definiteness, equivariance, stability under the chosen Riemannian metric) such layers can offer.

Background. Double Field Theory (DFT) is a T-duality covariant reformulation of the supergravity limit of string theory in which the target space is locally doubled: each d-dimensional patch is replaced by a 2d-dimensional "doubled" patch with coordinates (x^i, \tilde x_i), equipped with an O(d,d) invariant pairing and subject to the strong constraint \eta^{MN}\partial_M\otimes\partial_N = 0. A higher Kaluza-Klein (HKK) global formulation of DFT realises the doubled space as the total space of a higher principal bundle for the abelian gerbe (2-group) associated to the Kalb–Ramond B-field: the doubled manifold is glued via a higher group of symmetries in an (∞,1)-category of smooth higher stacks, the strong constraint is recovered as invariance under the higher principal action, and the local 2d-dimensional model is patched coherently so as to encompass T-folds and non-geometric backgrounds.

Heterotic DFT is the extension of DFT appropriate to the heterotic string, in which the doubled tangent bundle is enlarged by a non-abelian gauge bundle with structure group G (typically E_8 × E_8 or Spin(32)/Z_2), so that the local model has signature O(d, d+\dim G) and the strong constraint and generalised Lie bracket are modified to incorporate the non-abelian gauge connection and its curvature.

Problem. Construct a global geometric formulation of Heterotic Double Field Theory within the higher Kaluza-Klein framework. Concretely:

(1) Identify the appropriate higher (smooth) group H — combining the abelian gerbe of the B-field with the non-abelian gauge group G — and the class of higher principal H-bundles whose total spaces realise the heterotic doubled space.

(2) Show that the heterotic strong constraint and the heterotic generalised Lie derivative arise globally as, respectively, invariance under the higher principal H-action and the bracket of H-invariant vector fields on the total space.

(3) Demonstrate that the resulting globally defined objects reproduce, in a local trivialisation, the standard local Heterotic DFT (with its O(d, d+\dim G) structure and Green–Schwarz-type modified Bianchi identity for the B-field), and that the patching data correctly encode heterotic T-duality, including non-geometric heterotic backgrounds (heterotic T-folds).
