For a periodic point n₀, write Ω(n₀) for the cycle containing it, and let G(n₀) denote the basin of Ω(n₀), i.e. the set of all positive integers whose forward orbit under T eventually enters Ω(n₀). Let G(∞) denote the set of positive integers whose forward orbits are unbounded.

Three known cycles are:
  Ω(1) = (1 → 1),
  Ω(5) = (5 → 7 → 10 → 5),
  Ω(17) = (17 → 25 → 37 → 55 → 82 → 41 → 61 → 91 → 136 → 68 → 34 → 17).

Prove or disprove the following two statements:
(a) These are the only cycles of T on the positive integers.
(b) Every positive integer belongs to G(1) ∪ G(5) ∪ G(17); equivalently, G(∞) = ∅.

Bellman's lost-in-a-forest problem. Let F be a closed convex region in the plane (the "forest"). A "hiker" starts at an unknown point p in the interior of F facing an unknown direction θ ∈ [0, 2π). The hiker travels along a planar curve γ (a rectifiable path beginning at the origin in a coordinate system attached to the hiker's initial position and heading) and "escapes" once the path reaches the boundary ∂F. A curve γ is called a guaranteed-escape path for F if, for every starting point p ∈ F and every initial direction θ, the rigid motion of γ determined by (p, θ) meets ∂F at some finite arc length t(γ, p, θ); the worst-case escape length is

  L(γ, F) = sup_{p∈F, θ∈[0,2π)} t(γ, p, θ).

The problem: determine a curve γ* minimizing L(γ, F) over all guaranteed-escape paths, in the following two cases:
(a) F is an arbitrary triangle (the "triangular forest" case);
(b) F is an equilateral triangle of fixed side length.

In each case, find the optimal worst-case escape length L(γ*, F) and exhibit an optimal curve γ*.

Background. Let $(\mathcal{L}, \le)$ be a complete lattice (for instance, the lattice of grey-scale images $f:E\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ on a domain $E$, ordered pointwise). For a structuring function $g:E\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, define the flat/grey-scale operators on $\mathcal{L}$:
- dilation $\delta_g(f)(x)=\sup_{y\in E}\{f(x-y)+g(y)\}$,
- erosion $\varepsilon_g(f)(x)=\inf_{y\in E}\{f(x+y)-g(y)\}$,
- anti-dilation $\bar\delta_g(f)(x)=\inf_{y\in E}\{-f(x-y)-g(y)\}$,
- anti-erosion $\bar\varepsilon_g(f)(x)=\sup_{y\in E}\{-f(x+y)+g(y)\}$.

A classical representation theorem (Matheron–Maragos–Banon–Barrera, MMBB) asserts that every translation-invariant, increasing (or, more generally, suitably regular) nonlinear image operator $\Psi:\mathcal{L}\to\mathcal{L}$ can be expressed as a supremum of erosions (or, dually, an infimum of dilations) over a "basis" $\mathcal{B}(\Psi)$ of structuring functions, with analogous decompositions involving anti-dilations and anti-erosions for non-increasing operators. The minimal basis is the (unique, in the appropriate sense) smallest such family.

By an "MMBB neural network'' we mean a feed-forward parametric architecture whose layers compute finite combinations of the four primitive operations $\delta_{g_i}, \varepsilon_{g_i}, \bar\delta_{g_i}, \bar\varepsilon_{g_i}$ with learnable structuring functions $g_i$, together with lattice operations $\sup,\inf$.

Problem.
(a) Given a target nonlinear image operator $\Psi$ on $\mathcal{L}$, design an MMBB neural-network architecture and a training procedure that provably learn (from input–output samples $(f, \Psi f)$) a finite family of structuring functions $\{g_i\}$ approximating the minimal MMBB basis of $\Psi$ in the sense that the network's induced operator approximates $\Psi$ uniformly to within any prescribed $\varepsilon>0$. Quantify the sample and parameter complexity required.

(b) Formulate a notion of hierarchical (deep) MMBB architecture, i.e. a sensible way to stack MMBB layers so that intermediate representations correspond to learned bases of intermediate lattice operators, and determine whether such hierarchical MMBB networks can approximate operators that cannot be efficiently realized by a single MMBB layer of comparable size. In particular, identify a class of operators for which depth provably reduces the size of the learned basis.

Define the complexity class QMA (Quantum Merlin–Arthur) as the class of promise problems for which there exists a polynomial-time quantum verifier V such that: on input x of length n, V receives a quantum witness state |ψ⟩ on poly(n) qubits from an all-powerful prover (Merlin), and (i) if x is a yes-instance, there exists |ψ⟩ such that V accepts (x,|ψ⟩) with probability ≥ 2/3; (ii) if x is a no-instance, then for all |ψ⟩, V accepts with probability ≤ 1/3.

Define QMA(2) analogously, except that the witness is required to be a tensor product |ψ⟩ ⊗ |ϕ⟩ of two states on poly(n)-qubit registers supplied by two non-communicating, unentangled Merlins; completeness and soundness are defined as in QMA but quantifying over product states.

For an oracle O (which may be a classical oracle, or more generally a quantum oracle, i.e., a family of unitary transformations acting on poly(n) qubits accessible as black boxes to the verifier), let QMA^O and QMA(2)^O denote the analogous classes when the verifier is given oracle access to O.

Question: Does there exist an oracle O (possibly a quantum/unitary oracle) such that QMA^O ≠ QMA(2)^O?

Background. A standard feed-forward neural network layer is a map of the form $x \mapsto \sigma(Wx+b)$, where $W$ is a linear operator, $b$ a bias, and $\sigma$ a pointwise nonlinearity; such layers are linear-plus-nonlinearity operators on a vector space. A morphological layer, by contrast, is built from the basic operators of mathematical morphology on a complete lattice $(L,\le)$: the dilation $\delta_b(x)(p) = \sup_{q} \{x(p-q)+b(q)\}$ and the erosion $\varepsilon_b(x)(p) = \inf_{q}\{x(p+q)-b(q)\}$, which are residuated/adjoint operators preserving suprema and infima respectively. Compositions of dilations and erosions (and their min/max/plus arithmetic, called the (max,+)/(min,+) semiring) yield the class of Matheron–Maragos basis-based (MMBB) operators, i.e.\ translation-invariant increasing operators representable as suprema of erosions (or infima of dilations) over a structuring-element basis. A "deep MMBB network" is a finite composition of such MMBB layers; a "hybrid deep network" is a finite composition that mixes standard linear+activation layers with morphological layers.

Problem. Develop a single algebraic framework — for instance, over an idempotent semiring, a complete lattice with a compatible module structure, or a tropical/(max,+)-linear algebra — in which both standard deep-learning layers and morphological layers appear as morphisms of one common category, such that the following questions can be formulated and answered within this framework for an arbitrary composition $F = L_n \circ \cdots \circ L_1$ of layers:

(a) Continuity: characterize when $F$ is order-continuous (preserves directed suprema and/or filtered infima) on its input lattice.

(b) Invariance: describe the group/monoid of transformations (translations, scalings, lattice automorphisms) under which $F$ is equivariant or invariant.

(c) Fixed points: give existence, structure, and computation of the set $\mathrm{Fix}(F)=\{x : F(x)=x\}$, including least and greatest fixed points when $F$ is increasing.

(d) Decomposition: prove a canonical decomposition theorem expressing $F$ in terms of elementary atoms (e.g.\ erosions, dilations, linear maps, activations) analogous to the Matheron representation of increasing translation-invariant operators.

(e) Simplification: identify algebraic rewriting rules that reduce $F$ to a minimal equivalent representative, and determine when such a normal form exists and is unique.

(f) Expressiveness: characterize, for deep MMBB networks and for hybrid deep networks, the class of input–output maps they can realize as a function of depth and width, and compare it to the classes realized by purely linear+ReLU networks and by purely morphological networks.

Provide the algebraic framework and resolve as many of (a)–(f) as possible within it.

Let f : {0,1}^n -> {0,1} be a total Boolean function. Define the following query complexity measures, where an algorithm has access to the input x ∈ {0,1}^n only via queries of the form "what is x_i?":

- D(f): the deterministic query complexity, the minimum over deterministic decision trees computing f(x) on every input x of the worst-case number of queries.
- R(f): the bounded-error randomized query complexity, the minimum number of queries needed by a randomized algorithm that outputs f(x) with probability at least 2/3 on every input x.
- Q(f): the bounded-error quantum query complexity, the minimum number of quantum (oracle) queries needed by a quantum algorithm that outputs f(x) with probability at least 2/3 on every input x.

Determine the largest possible asymptotic gap between R(f) and Q(f) over all total Boolean functions f. More precisely, determine the supremum of all real α ≥ 1 such that there exists an infinite family of total Boolean functions {f_n} with

   R(f_n) = Ω̃( Q(f_n)^α ),

and prove a matching upper bound R(f) = O( Q(f)^α · polylog ) valid for every total Boolean function f. It is known that 3 ≤ α ≤ 4; identify the exact value.

Consider the class of deep neural networks built from standard layers (e.g., convolutional, fully connected, pooling, and normalization layers, together with the usual pointwise nonlinearities) and the class of deep neural networks that, in addition to such layers, also incorporate morphological layers. Here a morphological layer is a trainable nonlinear layer implementing operations from mathematical morphology over images, such as grey-scale dilations and erosions with learnable flat or non-flat structuring elements, defined respectively by

  (f ⊕ b)(x) = sup_{y} { f(x − y) + b(y) },   (f ⊖ b)(x) = inf_{y} { f(x + y) − b(y) },

and compositions thereof (openings, closings, top-hats, etc.), where b is the learnable structuring function.

Fix a family T of supervised visual learning tasks inspired by Gestalt pattern theory, i.e., tasks whose target concepts are global perceptual organization properties such as shape category, closure, good continuation, or bilateral/rotational symmetry of binary or grey-scale patterns. For an architecture A and task t ∈ T, let N(A, t, ε) denote the minimal number of i.i.d. training samples needed for A, trained by an admissible optimization procedure, to achieve generalization error at most ε on t.

Question: Is it the case that, for every Gestalt-inspired task t ∈ T and every sufficiently small ε > 0, there exists a morphology-augmented architecture A_morph and a standard architecture A_std (of comparable capacity) such that

  N(A_morph, t, ε)  <  N(A_std, t, ε),

with the gap being non-negligible? Equivalently, do deep networks that integrate morphological layers require strictly fewer training examples than purely standard deep architectures when learning Gestalt-pattern-theory-inspired visual concepts such as shape or symmetry?

Let BQP^A denote the class of problems (and more generally, transformations) implementable by a polynomial-time quantum Turing machine with oracle access to a Boolean function A:{0,1}*→{0,1}. The Unitary Synthesis Problem asks:

Does there exist, for every positive integer n and every n-qubit unitary transformation U acting on (C^2)^{⊗n}, a Boolean oracle A:{0,1}*→{0,1} such that a BQP^A machine, on input n and a description of the desired precision ε>0, implements U (to within error ε in operator norm) using time polynomial in n and 1/ε?

Equivalently: can the task of implementing an arbitrary n-qubit unitary be efficiently reduced, via an oracle quantum polynomial-time algorithm, to the task of computing some classical Boolean function?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The full problem remains open. Lombardi, Ma, and Wright (STOC 2024, arXiv:2310.08870) proved a one-query lower bound: there exist unitaries that cannot be implemented (even approximately) by any polynomial-time quantum algorithm making a single query to a Boolean oracle. A 2025 follow-up (arXiv:2508.13215) extends this to a 1.5-query lower bound. No general lower bound for arbitrarily many queries is known, so the original Aaronson–Kuperberg question is still unresolved.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ denote a class of compact subsets (or finite point sets, or graphs viewed via their vertex sets in some embedding) of $\mathbb{R}^d$. For $X \in \mathcal{S}$, consider the following morphological descriptors:

(i) The skeleton $\mathrm{Sk}(X)$, defined as the set of centers of maximal inscribed balls of $X$, together with the radius function on $\mathrm{Sk}(X)$.

(ii) The signed distance function $d_X : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$, with $d_X(z) = \mathrm{dist}(z, \partial X)$ for $z \in X$ and $d_X(z) = -\mathrm{dist}(z, \partial X)$ for $z \notin X$, together with its local extrema.

(iii) The granulometric (shape–size) distribution $G_X(r) = \mu(X \setminus (X \circ B_r))$, where $B_r$ is the closed Euclidean ball of radius $r$, $\circ$ is morphological opening, and $\mu$ is Lebesgue measure.

These descriptors are by construction invariant under permutations of any underlying point-cloud parametrization of $X$.

Address the following:

(a) Construct an encoder $\Phi : \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{R}^k$ built from descriptors (i)–(iii) (or combinations thereof) and prove that, on a specified class of inputs, $\Phi$ is more "efficient" than standard permutation-invariant set encoders (e.g. Deep Sets-type aggregators) in a precise quantitative sense — for instance, achieving universal approximation of continuous permutation-invariant functions on $\mathcal{S}$ with strictly smaller embedding dimension $k$ or with provably lower sample complexity for a chosen learning task.

(b) Exhibit a loss function $L(X, Y)$ on $\mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{S}$, defined purely in terms of the morphological descriptors above, that satisfies simultaneously:
 - permutation invariance: $L(X, Y) = L(\sigma(X), \tau(Y))$ for any reorderings $\sigma, \tau$ of any chosen parametrization;
 - scale invariance: $L(\lambda X, \lambda Y) = L(X, Y)$ for all $\lambda > 0$;
 - the metric (or at least pseudometric) axioms on the quotient of $\mathcal{S}$ by the group generated by permutations and positive scalings.

Either provide such an encoder and loss with proofs of the stated properties and efficiency gains, or prove that no such construction can outperform existing permutation-invariant set representations in the prescribed sense.

Background and definitions:

- BPP is the class of languages decided by polynomial-time probabilistic Turing machines with two-sided bounded error.
- BQP is the class of languages decided by polynomial-time quantum Turing machines with two-sided bounded error.
- For an oracle O, BPP^O and BQP^O denote the corresponding classes when both verifier and prover have access to the oracle O.
- Define IP_BQP to be the subclass of BQP consisting of all languages L such that there exists a polynomial-round interactive protocol with purely classical communication between a BQP prover P and a BPP verifier V satisfying:
  (Completeness) For every x ∈ L, V interacting with P accepts with probability at least 2/3.
  (Soundness) For every x ∉ L and every (computationally unbounded) prover P*, V interacting with P* accepts with probability at most 1/3.
  Here the number of rounds is bounded by a polynomial in |x|, and all messages exchanged are classical bit strings of polynomial length.
- The relativized class IP_BQP^O is defined analogously, with both the verifier and the prover having oracle access to O.

Question: Does there exist an oracle O such that BQP^O ≠ IP_BQP^O? Equivalently, exhibit (or prove the existence of) an oracle O and a language L ∈ BQP^O for which no BQP^O prover can convince a BPP^O verifier of membership in L through any polynomial-round classical interactive protocol satisfying the above completeness and soundness conditions.

Background. Let E be a discrete domain (e.g. E = Z^2) and let F(E, T) denote the set of functions f : E -> T with T an ordered set (e.g. T = R or T = {0,1}). For a structuring element B subset of E and f : E -> T, define the erosion (epsilon_B f)(x) = inf_{b in B} f(x+b) and the dilation (delta_B f)(x) = sup_{b in B} f(x+b). Given an ordered pair of disjoint structuring elements (B_fg, B_bg) (foreground and background templates), the classical (binary or grey-level) hit-or-miss transform of f is
   HMT_{(B_fg, B_bg)}(f)(x) = (epsilon_{B_fg} f)(x) - (delta_{B_bg} f)(x),
returning a measure of how well the pair (B_fg, B_bg) matches the local pattern of f near x. A hit-or-miss layer is a trainable parametrization (theta -> (B_fg(theta), B_bg(theta))) inserted into a deep neural network so that the templates (B_fg, B_bg) are learned end-to-end by gradient-based optimization.

For a topological group G acting on E, an operator Psi : F(E,T) -> F(E,T) is called G-equivariant if Psi(f circ g^{-1}) = Psi(f) circ g^{-1} for all g in G. Group-morphology-based hit-or-miss transforms are generalizations of HMT in which structuring elements and inf/sup operations are taken over orbits of G, so as to produce G-equivariant template-extraction operators.

Problem. Establish a theoretical and algorithmic framework for interpretable, learnable template-extraction layers based on the hit-or-miss transform. Specifically:
(1) Formulate the hit-or-miss transform (or a suitable relaxation/smoothing thereof) so that the resulting layer is differentiable with respect to the templates (B_fg, B_bg), robust to noise and small geometric perturbations of the input, and admits stable gradient-based training. Prove convergence and approximation guarantees for the proposed formulation.
(2) Determine the computational and statistical efficiency of integrating such hit-or-miss layers into deep architectures composed of standard linear, nonlinear, and pooling layers, and characterize whether their use is most effective only at early layers or also at intermediate/deep layers.
(3) For a given group G of geometric transformations of E (e.g. translations, rotations, scalings), construct group-morphology-based hit-or-miss transforms that are provably G-equivariant, and study their expressivity and trainability as deep-learning layers.
(4) Identify and analyze other morphological template-extraction operators (beyond the hit-or-miss transform) that yield interpretable trainable layers, and compare their approximation and invariance properties.

Define the glued-trees graph $G_n$ as follows. Take two complete binary trees of depth $n$, with roots called the entrance vertex $s$ and the exit vertex $t$, and connect their $2^n$ leaves by a random cycle that alternates between leaves of the two trees (so every leaf has degree 3 in $G_n$, while $s$ and $t$ have degree 2 and all internal tree vertices have degree 3). Vertices are labeled by random distinct strings, and the graph is presented via an adjacency-list oracle: given a vertex label, the oracle returns the labels of its neighbors. Only the labels of $s$ and $t$ are given for free; any other vertex can be probed only if its label has already been discovered through previous oracle queries.

It is known that a quantum walk algorithm can output the label of $t$, given the label of $s$, using $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ oracle queries with success probability at least $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$, while any classical randomized algorithm requires $2^{\Omega(n)}$ queries to do so.

Question: In the same oracle model, must any quantum algorithm that outputs an entire path (a sequence of labels of vertices forming a path in $G_n$) from $s$ to $t$ with probability at least $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ make $2^{\Omega(n)}$ queries to the adjacency-list oracle? Either prove such a $2^{\Omega(n)}$ quantum query lower bound, or give a quantum algorithm that finds an $s$–$t$ path using only $2^{o(n)}$ queries.

Let $E$ be a compact Hausdorff space (for example a finite pixel grid $E \subset \mathbb{Z}^2$) and let $\mathcal{F}(E)$ denote the collection of closed subsets of $E$. A Choquet capacity is a functional $T:\mathcal{F}(E)\to[0,1]$ that is increasing ($A\subseteq B\Rightarrow T(A)\le T(B)$), upper semicontinuous on decreasing sequences, and alternating of infinite order. By the Choquet–Matheron theorem, every Choquet capacity $T$ with $T(\emptyset)=0$ corresponds uniquely to the distribution of a random closed set $X$ in $E$ via $T(K)=\mathbb{P}(X\cap K\neq\emptyset)$ for compact $K\subset E$. Morphological random-set models (e.g. Boolean models) generate random images as $X=\bigcup_i (x_i\oplus K_i)$ where $\{x_i\}$ is a point process and $K_i$ are random compact ``grains'', with $\oplus$ denoting Minkowski addition. A morphological neural-network layer is a map built from elementary operations of dilation $(f\oplus g)(x)=\sup_y\{f(y)+g(x-y)\}$ and erosion $(f\ominus g)(x)=\inf_y\{f(y+x)-g(y)\}$ with learnable structuring functions $g$.

Consider a generative adversarial network (GAN) consisting of a generator $G_\theta:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathcal{F}(E)$ and a discriminator $D_\phi:\mathcal{F}(E)\to\mathbb{R}$, trained on samples of a target random closed set $X^\star$ with associated Choquet capacity $T^\star$.

(a) Construct a discriminator architecture in which the functional implemented by $D_\phi$ is, or contains as a component, an empirical Choquet-capacity functional $\widehat T_\phi$ on $\mathcal{F}(E)$ (i.e., a learnable map satisfying the monotonicity, upper semicontinuity and alternation-of-infinite-order axioms), and prove that minimizing the resulting adversarial loss enforces convergence of the Choquet capacity of $G_\theta$ to $T^\star$ in an appropriate metric (such as the Prokhorov-type metric on capacities).

(b) Construct a generator architecture composed of morphological layers (compositions of learnable dilations and erosions) and a stochastic point-process input such that $G_\theta$ realizes, in the limit of suitable depth/width, an arbitrary Boolean random-set model on $E$; equivalently, show that morphological-layer generators are universal approximators for random closed sets whose grain distributions lie in a prescribed class.

Determine whether both constructions (a) and (b) are achievable, and exhibit explicit architectures and training criteria for which the resulting GAN provably converges (in distribution of random closed sets) to the target morphological random-set model.

Let $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be a Boolean function, and for $z\in\{0,1\}^n$ let
$$\hat f(z) \;=\; 2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n} f(x)(-1)^{x\cdot z}$$
denote its Boolean Fourier coefficient at $z$, so that $\sum_z \hat f(z)^2 = 1$. The standard quantum Fourier-sampling procedure, given oracle access to $f$, outputs a string $s\in\{0,1\}^n$ with probability $\hat f(s)^2$ using one quantum query to $f$.

For a sequence of $k$ output strings $s_1,\dots,s_k\in\{0,1\}^n$, define the linear cross-entropy benchmark statistic
$$\chi \;:=\; \frac{2^n}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\hat f(s_i)^2.$$
It is known that, for a "generic" $f$, repeating the standard quantum Fourier-sampling algorithm $k$ times yields samples $s_1,\dots,s_k$ for which $\chi\approx 3$ (in expectation, in the regime of interest).

Determine the quantum query complexity (as a function of $n$ and $k$) of the following task: given oracle access to $f$, output samples $s_1,\dots,s_k\in\{0,1\}^n$ such that
$$\chi \;=\; \frac{2^n}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\hat f(s_i)^2 \;\approx\; 4.$$
In particular, prove non-trivial upper and lower bounds on the number of quantum queries to $f$ required to achieve $\chi\approx 4$ rather than $\chi\approx 3$.

Consider hybrid feed-forward neural networks whose layers include both classical linear/convolutional layers and morphological layers. A morphological layer is one whose neurons compute operations in the (max,+) or (min,+) semiring; concretely, a typical morphological neuron implements a dilation of the form y = max_{i}(x_i + w_i) or an erosion y = min_{i}(x_i + w_i), where w_i are trainable parameters. Such layers are naturally described in tropical algebra/tropical geometry: the function realized by a morphological (or piecewise-linear) network can be written as a tropical polynomial, and learning can in principle be formulated using tools from tropical geometry (e.g., difference-of-convex programming on max-plus expressions, Newton polytope approximations).

Address the following questions for the training of such hybrid networks:

(a) Construct an efficient training scheme that combines optimization techniques inspired by tropical geometry (for the morphological layers) with stochastic gradient descent (for the remaining layers), and analyze its convergence and empirical performance.

(b) Among standard gradient-descent–based optimizers (e.g., vanilla SGD, SGD with momentum/Nesterov, Adam, RMSProp, AdaGrad, AdamW), identify which optimizer(s) are best suited to training hybrid networks containing morphological layers, and justify the choice.

(c) Determine whether an alternating optimization strategy — in which the parameters of the convolutional/linear layers and those of the morphological layers are updated in alternation rather than jointly — improves training (in terms of convergence speed, stability, or final accuracy) compared with joint optimization of all parameters.

Background and definitions. Let $(X,\tau)$ be a topological space. The specialization order on $X$ is defined by $x \le y$ iff $x \in \overline{\{y\}}$. A space $X$ is $T_0$ if its specialization order is a partial order. A subset $D \subseteq X$ is directed if $D$ is nonempty and every pair of elements of $D$ has an upper bound in $D$ with respect to the specialization order. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called a d-set if it is closed under directed suprema that exist in $X$, i.e. for every directed subset $D \subseteq A$ such that $\sup D$ exists in $(X,\le)$, one has $\sup D \in A$.

A topological space $X$ is called a d-space if every closed subset of $X$ is a d-set, equivalently, $X$ is $T_0$ and every directed subset $D$ of $X$ has a supremum which is also a topological limit of $D$ (with respect to the specialization order).

A topological space $X$ is called a strong d-space if $X$ is $T_0$ and for every directed subset $D \subseteq X$ whose supremum $\sup D$ exists in $(X,\le)$, and for every open set $U$ containing $\sup D$, the set $D$ is eventually in $U$ (i.e. there exists $d_0 \in D$ such that $d \in U$ for all $d \in D$ with $d \ge d_0$).

Let $\mathbf{Top}_0$ denote the category whose objects are $T_0$ topological spaces and whose morphisms are continuous maps. Let $\mathbf{S\text{-}Top}_d$ denote the full subcategory of $\mathbf{Top}_0$ whose objects are the strong d-spaces. A full subcategory $\mathcal{D}$ of a category $\mathcal{C}$ is called reflective in $\mathcal{C}$ if the inclusion functor $\mathcal{D} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{C}$ has a left adjoint.

Question. Is $\mathbf{S\text{-}Top}_d$ reflective in $\mathbf{Top}_0$? Equivalently, does every $T_0$ space admit a strong d-reflection?

Consider feed-forward neural networks in which one or more layers are required to be genuinely discrete: the layer's weights, activations, and outputs all take values in a fixed finite or countable discrete set (for example, binary {-1, +1}, ternary {-1, 0, +1}, or integer-valued tensors), and the layer's operation is intrinsically defined on such discrete spaces (motivated, e.g., by discrete geometry or mathematical morphology rather than by quantization of an underlying real-valued layer). Two questions are posed about training such networks end-to-end on a supervised loss:

(1) Is it possible to design genuine discrete layers of this form and incorporate them into a deep network in such a way that the entire network can be trained effectively by gradient-descent–based optimization (possibly via surrogate gradients, relaxations, or other differentiable approximations), achieving accuracy comparable to fully real-valued networks?

(2) Alternatively, are there approaches drawn from discrete optimization (e.g., combinatorial search, integer programming, submodular methods, message passing, or related techniques) that are better suited than gradient descent to training networks composed of such genuinely discrete layers?

Provide a rigorous framework, training algorithm(s), and theoretical or empirical guarantees that resolve which paradigm—continuous gradient-based or discrete combinatorial—is appropriate for training networks with genuine discrete layers.

Background and definitions. Let $\mathbf{Top}_0$ denote the category of $T_0$ topological spaces and continuous maps. For a $T_0$ space $X$, write $\mathcal{O}(X)$ for its lattice of open sets and $\mathsf{Irr}(X)$ for the family of nonempty irreducible closed subsets (a closed set $A$ is irreducible if $A = B \cup C$ with $B,C$ closed implies $A=B$ or $A=C$).

An assignment $\mathcal{H}:\mathbf{Top}_0\to\mathbf{Set}$ is called an irreducible subset system (or $R$-subset system) if for every $T_0$ space $X$, $\mathcal{H}(X)$ is a collection of irreducible subsets of $X$ containing $\{\{x\}:x\in X\}$, and for every continuous map $f:X\to Y$ between $T_0$ spaces and every $A\in\mathcal{H}(X)$, the closure $\overline{f(A)}$ belongs to $\mathcal{H}(Y)$.

A $T_0$ space $X$ is said to be $\mathcal{H}$-sober if for every $A\in\mathcal{H}(X)$ there exists a unique point $x\in X$ such that $\overline{A}=\overline{\{x\}}$.

The Smyth power space $P_S(X)$ of a $T_0$ space $X$ is the set $\mathbf{K}(X)$ of nonempty compact saturated subsets of $X$ (a set is saturated if it is the intersection of its open neighborhoods), endowed with the upper Vietoris topology generated by the basic open sets $\Box U=\{K\in\mathbf{K}(X):K\subseteq U\}$ for $U\in\mathcal{O}(X)$.

A $T_0$ space $X$ is called super $\mathcal{H}$-sober if its Smyth power space $P_S(X)$ is $\mathcal{H}$-sober.

Question. Let $\mathcal{H}$ be an irreducible subset system, and let $\{X_i\}_{i\in I}$ be a family of super $\mathcal{H}$-sober spaces. Equipping $\prod_{i\in I} X_i$ with the product topology, must $\prod_{i\in I} X_i$ be super $\mathcal{H}$-sober?

Consider mathematical morphology, in which images are processed by operators built from a small set of primitive operations (e.g., erosion, dilation, opening, closing, geodesic reconstruction, hit-or-miss) combined with structuring elements (subsets of the underlying lattice that parameterize each operation). A "morphological program" is a finite composition (or more generally, a syntactic expression over a formal grammar) of such operators applied to structuring elements; the set of all such programs forms a formal language L whose tokens are operator symbols and structuring-element descriptors.

The goal is to develop a "morphological artificial intelligence" that learns and synthesizes morphological programs by combining natural-language-processing (NLP) techniques (token embeddings, sequence models) with combinatorial program-space search. Formalize and address the following questions:

1. Tokenization/coding: Define a coding scheme c : L → Σ* of morphological programs into a finite alphabet Σ that is best suited for NLP-style learning. In particular, decide whether structuring elements should be encoded as inflectional modifiers of operator tokens (a single token for "operator + structuring element" with morphological declensions) or as separate tokens (operator token and structuring-element token treated independently), and quantify the trade-off in expressivity vs. learnability.

2. Granularity: Determine the optimal decomposition granularity of compound operators into atomic sub-operators so that the resulting language has (a) high semantic interpretability (each token corresponds to a human-meaningful operation) and (b) is statistically learnable from finite data.

3. Corpus: Establish whether there exists a sufficiently large corpus C ⊂ L of morphological programs to train distributional embeddings (an "operator2vec" map φ : Σ → R^d) with provable approximation guarantees, and characterize the minimum corpus size as a function of vocabulary size and embedding dimension.

4. Extraction/parsing: Provide an algorithm for extracting and parsing morphological programs from heterogeneous source repositories into a normalized abstract syntax tree representation suitable for training.

5. Syntactic rewriting: Construct a confluent (or near-confluent) rewriting system R over L whose rewrite rules are semantics-preserving (i.e., for every program p, the rewritten program R(p) computes the same image transformation) and which simplifies programs in a useful normal form.

6. Hybrid search: Design an algorithm that integrates combinatorial program-space search (e.g., enumeration, SMT, genetic methods) with learned neural priors (sequence models trained on C using φ) to efficiently explore the program space and synthesize a morphological program matching a given input–output specification.

Provide constructions, theoretical guarantees, and/or impossibility results addressing each of the six points above.

Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ with $\dim X > 1$. Recall that for a line bundle $L$ on a normal projective variety $Y$, the Iitaka dimension $\kappa(L)$ is defined as the maximum dimension of the image of the rational maps $\varphi_{|L^{\otimes m}|}\colon Y \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}(H^0(Y, L^{\otimes m})^\vee)$ over $m \geq 1$ for which $h^0(Y, L^{\otimes m}) > 0$ (and as $-\infty$ if no such $m$ exists). For a vector bundle $E$ of rank $r$ on $X$, one classical extension defines the Iitaka dimension of $E$ as the Iitaka dimension of the tautological line bundle $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}(E)}(1)$ on the projectivization $\mathbb{P}(E)$.

Fix numerical invariants (rank, Chern classes) and a polarization $H$ on $X$, and let $M$ denote the moduli space of Gieseker $H$-semistable coherent sheaves on $X$ with those invariants. Because $\dim X > 1$, the properly semistable locus of $M$ contains points represented by torsion-free (or pure) coherent sheaves $\mathcal{F}$ that are not locally free; in particular the projective bundle construction $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{F})$ does not directly apply.

Problem: Formulate the optimal extension of the notion of Iitaka dimension from vector bundles to arbitrary Gieseker-semistable coherent sheaves $\mathcal{F}$ on $X$ (including non-locally-free ones), in such a way that:
(i) it agrees with the usual Iitaka dimension $\kappa(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}(E)}(1))$ when $\mathcal{F} = E$ is a vector bundle;
(ii) it behaves well in families parameterized by $M$ (e.g. semicontinuity or constancy along $S$-equivalence classes); and
(iii) it captures the asymptotic growth of global sections of symmetric powers (or a suitable replacement, such as reflexive symmetric powers $(\mathrm{Sym}^m \mathcal{F})^{\vee\vee}$) of $\mathcal{F}$.

Background and definitions.

Let $\mathbf{Top}_0$ denote the category of $T_0$ topological spaces and continuous maps, and let $\mathbf{Set}$ denote the category of sets. For a $T_0$ space $X$, write $\mathcal{P}(X)$ for the power set of $X$ and let $\mathrm{Irr}(X) \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ denote the family of nonempty irreducible closed subsets of $X$ (a closed set $C$ is irreducible if it is nonempty and cannot be written as a union of two proper closed subsets).

A subset system on $\mathbf{Top}_0$ is a functor $H : \mathbf{Top}_0 \to \mathbf{Set}$ such that for every $X \in \mathbf{Top}_0$, $H(X) \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$, and for every continuous map $f : X \to Y$, $H(f)(A) = f(A)$ for all $A \in H(X)$. An irreducible subset system is a subset system $H$ such that for every $X$, every member of $H(X)$ is an irreducible subset of $X$ (i.e., its closure is irreducible). Let $\mathbb{H}$ denote the partially ordered collection of all irreducible subset systems on $\mathbf{Top}_0$, ordered by pointwise inclusion: $H \le H'$ iff $H(X) \subseteq H'(X)$ for every $X$.

For an irreducible subset system $H$ and $X \in \mathbf{Top}_0$, a subset $A \subseteq X$ is said to have the $H$-Rudin property if for every closed set $C \subseteq X$ with $A \subseteq C$, there exists $B \in H(X)$ with $B \subseteq A$ and $\overline{B} \subseteq C$ (equivalently, $\overline{A}$ is a minimal closed set among those containing some member of $H(X)$ in a suitable sense). Define
$$H_R(X) = \{ A \subseteq X : A \text{ has the } H\text{-Rudin property} \}.$$
The assignment $X \mapsto H_R(X)$ defines a new irreducible subset system $H_R$, called the induced subset system of $H$-Rudin sets.

Define a map $R : \mathbb{H} \to \mathbb{H}$ by $R(H) = H_R$.

A map $c : P \to P$ on a poset $P$ is a closure operator if for all $x,y \in P$: (1) $x \le y \Rightarrow c(x) \le c(y)$ (monotone), (2) $x \le c(x)$ (expansive), (3) $c(c(x)) = c(x)$ (idempotent).

Property M. A subset system on $\mathbf{Top}_0$ is a functor $H : \mathbf{Top}_0 \to \mathbf{Set}$ such that for every $X \in \mathbf{Top}_0$, $H(X) \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$, and for every continuous map $f : X \to Y$, $H(f)(A) = f(A)$ for all $A \in H(X)$. An irreducible subset system is a subset system $H$ such that for every $X$, every member of $H(X)$ is an irreducible subset of $X$ (i.e., its closure is irreducible). Let $\mathbb{H}$ denote the partially ordered collection of all irreducible subset systems on $\mathbf{Top}_0$, ordered by pointwise inclusion: $H \le H'$ iff $H(X) \subseteq H'(X)$ for every $X$.

Background and definitions.

A relational language is a (here, finite or countable) set L of relation symbols, each with a fixed finite arity. An L-structure is a set together with an interpretation of each symbol of L. A class K of finite L-structures is a Fraïssé class if it is closed under isomorphism, contains structures of arbitrarily large finite cardinality, has only countably many isomorphism types, and satisfies:
 (HP) hereditary property: every substructure of a member of K is in K;
 (JEP) joint embedding property; and
 (AP) amalgamation property.
A Fraïssé class K has the strong amalgamation property (SAP) if whenever A, B, C ∈ K and f: A → B, g: A → C are embeddings, there exist D ∈ K and embeddings f′: B → D, g′: C → D with f′ ∘ f = g′ ∘ g and f′(B) ∩ g′(C) = f′(f(A)) = g′(g(A)). Every Fraïssé class K has a unique (up to isomorphism) countable homogeneous structure F = Flim(K) called its Fraïssé limit, characterized by being countable, locally K (every finitely generated substructure is in K), and ultrahomogeneous (every isomorphism between finitely generated substructures extends to an automorphism of F).

For a structure F and a finite substructure A ⊆ F, the big Ramsey degree T(A, F) is the least integer t ≥ 1 (if it exists) such that for every finite coloring of the set of copies of A in F, there is a substructure F′ ⊆ F isomorphic to F on which the copies of A take at most t colors. We say F has finite big Ramsey degrees if T(A, F) < ∞ for every finite substructure A of F.

A forbidden substructure description of a class is a specification of K = Forb(F) for some set F of finite L-structures, meaning K consists of all finite L-structures that admit no embedding from any member of F.

Problems.

(a) Characterize, in terms of intrinsic structural properties of K, exactly those Fraïssé classes K having the strong amalgamation property whose Fraïssé limit Flim(K) has finite big Ramsey degrees.

(b) Suppose K is an SAP Fraïssé class in a finite relational language defined by finitely many forbidden finite substructures, i.e., K = Forb(F) ∩ {finite L-structures} for some finite set F. Must Flim(K) have finite big Ramsey degrees?

(c) Suppose K is an SAP Fraïssé class in a relational language all of whose relation symbols have arity at most 2. Must Flim(K) have finite big Ramsey degrees?

Background and definitions.

Let $\mathcal{K}$ be a Fraïssé class of finite structures in a countable relational language and let $\mathbf{K}$ be its Fraïssé limit, a countable homogeneous structure. For finite substructures $\mathbf{A} \subseteq \mathbf{K}$, let $\binom{\mathbf{K}}{\mathbf{A}}$ denote the set of isomorphic copies of $\mathbf{A}$ in $\mathbf{K}$. The big Ramsey degree of $\mathbf{A}$ in $\mathbf{K}$ is the least integer $T(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{K}) \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ such that for every finite coloring $c : \binom{\mathbf{K}}{\mathbf{A}} \to r$ (with $r \in \mathbb{N}$) there exists a copy $\mathbf{K}' \subseteq \mathbf{K}$ of $\mathbf{K}$ on which $c$ takes at most $T(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{K})$ values. We say $\mathbf{K}$ has finite big Ramsey degrees if $T(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{K}) < \infty$ for every finite $\mathbf{A} \subseteq \mathbf{K}$.

A big Ramsey structure for $\mathbf{K}$ is an expansion $\mathbf{K}^*$ of $\mathbf{K}$ in a countable relational language extending that of $\mathbf{K}$, such that:
(i) the age of $\mathbf{K}^*$ is a Fraïssé class with finitely many expansions of each finite structure in $\mathcal{K}$;
(ii) for every finite $\mathbf{A} \subseteq \mathbf{K}$, the number of isomorphism types of expansions $\mathbf{A}^*$ realised on copies of $\mathbf{A}$ in $\mathbf{K}^*$ equals $T(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{K})$;
(iii) for every coloring of $\binom{\mathbf{K}}{\mathbf{A}}$ by isomorphism types of expansion, there is a copy of $\mathbf{K}$ in $\mathbf{K}^*$ on which all copies of $\mathbf{A}$ realise the same expansion type, and this number $T(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{K})$ cannot be reduced further.

The Kechris–Pestov–Todorčević (KPT) correspondence states that, for a Fraïssé limit $\mathbf{K}$ in a countable relational language, the class $\mathrm{Age}(\mathbf{K})$ has the Ramsey property and consists of rigid structures if and only if $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbf{K})$ is extremely amenable; more generally, finite small Ramsey degrees correspond to metrizability of the universal minimal flow $M(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbf{K}))$, and the universal minimal flow can be computed explicitly from a precompact relational expansion satisfying the expansion property and the Ramsey property.

Problem.

(a) Does every countable homogeneous structure $\mathbf{K}$ with finite big Ramsey degrees admit a big Ramsey structure in the sense above?

(b) Establish an exact analogue of the KPT correspondence linking big Ramsey structures of $\mathbf{K}$ with the topological dynamics of $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbf{K})$: identify a canonical dynamical object (for instance, a completion-type flow on the space of big Ramsey expansions) whose properties are equivalent to $\mathbf{K}$ having a big Ramsey structure, in the same way that extreme amenability and metrizability of the universal minimal flow correspond to small Ramsey-theoretic properties.

Let $X = \mathbb{P}^{n_1} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{P}^{n_k}$ be a product of complex projective spaces with $k \geq 2$, and let $T_X$ denote its holomorphic tangent bundle. A coHiggs bundle on $X$ is a pair $(E, \Phi)$ consisting of a holomorphic vector bundle $E$ on $X$ together with a Higgs field $\Phi \colon E \to E \otimes T_X$ satisfying the integrability condition $\Phi \wedge \Phi = 0 \in \mathrm{End}(E) \otimes \wedge^2 T_X$.

An ample polarization on $X$ corresponds to a tuple $\mathbf{a} = (a_1, \ldots, a_k)$ of positive integers, giving the line bundle $\mathcal{O}_X(a_1, \ldots, a_k)$; with respect to this polarization one defines slope and (semi)stability of a coHiggs bundle in the usual way (using the slope of subsheaves preserved by $\Phi$). For fixed numerical invariants (rank $r$, Chern classes) and small rank $r$, let $\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{a}}(X; r, \ldots)$ denote the moduli space of $\mathbf{a}$-semistable coHiggs bundles on $X$ with those invariants.

Describe explicitly how the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{a}}(X; r, \ldots)$ depends on the polarization $\mathbf{a}$: identify the chamber/wall structure on the ample cone of $X$, the wall-crossing transformations relating moduli spaces in adjacent chambers, and in particular compare the moduli spaces obtained for the "balanced" polarization $a_i = 1$ for all $i$ and for the anticanonical polarization $a_i = n_i + 1$ for all $i$.

Let $P$ be a rational function on the Riemann sphere of degree at least two. Call $P$ special if it is either a Lattès map (i.e., a rational function arising as a quotient of an endomorphism of an elliptic curve by a finite automorphism group), or conjugate via a Möbius transformation to $z\mapsto z^n$, $z\mapsto z^{-n}$, $z\mapsto T_n(z)$, or $z\mapsto -T_n(z)$ for some integer $n\ge 2$, where $T_n$ denotes the $n$-th Chebyshev polynomial. Otherwise, call $P$ non-special.

For a rational function $P$ of degree $\ge 2$, let
$$C(P) = \{Q\in\mathbb{C}(z) : Q\circ P = P\circ Q\}$$
be the semigroup (under composition) of rational functions commuting with $P$. Define an equivalence relation $\sim_P$ on $C(P)$ by declaring $Q_1 \sim_P Q_2$ if there exist non-negative integers $l_1, l_2$ such that
$$Q_1 \circ P^{\circ l_1} = Q_2 \circ P^{\circ l_2},$$
where $P^{\circ l}$ denotes the $l$-fold compositional iterate of $P$ (with $P^{\circ 0} = z$). When $P$ is non-special, $\sim_P$ is a congruence on $C(P)$ and the quotient $G_P := C(P)/\!\sim_P$ is a finite group.

Determine which finite groups $G$ arise as $G_P$ for some non-special rational function $P$ of degree at least two.

Let $C$ be a smooth projective complex curve of sufficiently high genus $g$. For a semistable vector bundle $E$ of rank $r$ and degree $d$ on $C$, write $h^0(E) = \dim H^0(C,E)$, and define the Brill–Noether locus
$$B(r,d,k) = \{ E \text{ semistable of rank } r, \deg E = d : h^0(E) \ge k \}$$
inside the moduli space of semistable rank-$r$ degree-$d$ bundles. The rank-$r$ Clifford index of $C$ is defined by
$$\mathrm{Cliff}_r(C) = \min\Big\{ \tfrac{1}{r}\big(\deg E - 2(h^0(E)-r)\big) : E \text{ semistable of rank } r,\ h^0(E) \ge 2r,\ \mu(E) \le g-1 \Big\},$$
and for a fixed bundle $E$ with $h^0(E) \ge 2r$ and $\mu(E)\le g-1$ one sets
$$\gamma(E) = \tfrac{1}{r}\big(\deg E - 2(h^0(E)-r)\big),$$
giving stratifications by the value of $\gamma(E)$ ("loci of fixed Clifford index").

Restrict to $r = 2$. Determine the precise relationship between the Brill–Noether loci $B(2,d,k)$ and the loci of rank-$2$ semistable bundles on $C$ with fixed value of $\gamma(E)$: describe inclusions, irreducible component structure, dimensions, and the conditions on $(d,k)$ under which these two stratifications coincide.

Fix integers $r \ge 1$ (the rank) and a tuple $\nu$ of admissible values for a chosen system of local numerical invariants. Describe explicitly the moduli space (or moduli stack)
$$\mathcal{M}_{N,\nu} \;=\; \{\,E \to N \text{ holomorphic vector bundle of rank } r \text{ with local invariants } \nu\,\}/\cong$$
of isomorphism classes of holomorphic vector bundles on $N$ whose local numerical invariants equal $\nu$. Let $A$ and $B$ be rational functions of degree at least two, viewed as self-maps of the Riemann sphere $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$. For a rational function $f$ and a point $z_0 \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$, the forward orbit of $z_0$ under $f$ is the set $\mathcal{O}_f(z_0) = \{z_0, f(z_0), f^{\circ 2}(z_0), f^{\circ 3}(z_0), \dots\}$, where $f^{\circ n}$ denotes the $n$-fold compositional iterate of $f$. Two rational functions $A$ and $B$ are said to have a common iterate if there exist positive integers $m, n$ such that $A^{\circ m} = B^{\circ n}$.

Prove or disprove: if there exist points $a, b \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$ such that the intersection $\mathcal{O}_A(a) \cap \mathcal{O}_B(b)$ is infinite, then $A$ and $B$ must have a common iterate.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The conjecture has been established in significant special cases — for nonlinear complex polynomials of equal degree (Ghioca–Tucker–Zieve, Inventiones 2008) and more generally for tame rational functions (Pakovich, JEMS), where infinite orbit intersection is shown to imply a common iterate. The full conjecture for arbitrary rational functions of degree at least two over $\mathbb{C}$ does not appear to have been resolved; in positive characteristic counterexamples exist. Thus the problem is partially solved but remains open in full generality.

Let $\mathbb{P}^1$ denote the complex projective line, and for an integer $k\ge 1$ consider one of the following rank-2 holomorphic vector bundles over $\mathbb{P}^1$:
$$W_1 := \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(-1)\oplus \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(-1),\qquad W_2 := \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(-2)\oplus \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(0),\qquad W_3 := \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(-3)\oplus \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(+1).$$
Each total space $W_k$ is a smooth non-compact Calabi–Yau threefold containing the zero section $\ell\cong \mathbb{P}^1$, and the three cases exhaust all possible normal bundles $N_{\ell/W}$ of a smooth rational curve $\ell$ that can be contracted on a Calabi–Yau threefold $W$.

Consider the moduli space $\mathcal{M}(W_k)$ of holomorphic vector bundles on $W_k$ (in the analytic topology). For a holomorphic vector bundle $E\to W_k$, one may attach local numerical invariants computed in a neighborhood of the zero section $\ell$ (for instance, the splitting type of $E|_{\ell^{(n)}}$ on infinitesimal neighborhoods, width invariants, or other holomorphic-analytic data localized near $\ell$).

Problem: Determine a complete set of local numerical invariants which stratifies $\mathcal{M}(W_k)$ into Hausdorff components in the analytic topology, for each $k\ge 1$ and for each of the three cases $W_1$, $W_2$, $W_3$.

Work over the field $\mathbb{C}$ of complex numbers. A rational function is an element of $\mathbb{C}(z)$, and for rational functions $U,V$ we write $U\circ V$ for their composition and $U^{\circ n}$ for the $n$-fold self-composition of $U$. For a non-constant rational function $U$, let $\mathbb{C}(U)\subset\mathbb{C}(z)$ denote the subfield generated by $U$ over $\mathbb{C}$. A rational function $X\in\mathbb{C}(z)$ is called a Galois covering if the field extension $\mathbb{C}(z)/\mathbb{C}(X)$ is Galois. A rational function $B$ of degree at least two is a compositional right factor of a rational function $H$ if there exists a rational function $C$ with $H=C\circ B$.

A rational function is called special if it is either a Lattès map (a rational function semiconjugate to a multiplication map on an elliptic curve via a finite-to-one holomorphic map), or, up to conjugation by a Möbius transformation, a power map $z\mapsto z^{\pm n}$ or a Chebyshev polynomial $\pm T_n$.

Let $A\in\mathbb{C}(z)$ be a non-special rational function of degree at least two. Determine whether there exist rational functions $X,F\in\mathbb{C}(z)$ with $X$ a Galois covering and
$$X\circ A \;=\; F\circ X,$$
such that for every rational function $B\in\mathbb{C}(z)$ of degree at least two the following two conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every integer $n\geq 1$, the intersection $\mathbb{C}(A^{\circ n})\cap \mathbb{C}(B)$ contains a non-constant rational function.
\item There exists an integer $\ell\geq 0$ such that $B$ is a compositional right factor of $X\circ A^{\circ \ell}$.
\end{enumerate}

A semigroup $S$ of rational functions (under composition) is called right reversible if for every $A,B\in S$ there exist $C,D\in S$ such that $A\circ C=B\circ D$ (equivalently, every two principal left ideals $S\circ A$ and $S\circ B$ intersect).

Question. Let $S$ be a semigroup of rational functions, all of degree at least two, that contains at least one non-special function. Is it true that $S$ is right reversible if and only if for every pair $A,B\in S$ there exist integers $k,l\ge 1$ such that
$$A^{\circ 2k}=A^{\circ k}\circ B^{\circ l}\qquad\text{and}\qquad B^{\circ 2l}=B^{\circ l}\circ A^{\circ k}\,?$$

Let $S$ be a smooth complex projective surface of general type. For an integer $c_2$, let $M_{c_2}(S)$ denote the moduli space of Gieseker semistable rank-$2$ torsion-free sheaves on $S$ with fixed determinant and second Chern class $c_2$, and let $\mathcal{M}_{c_2}(S)$ denote the corresponding moduli stack; write $\mathcal{M}^s_{c_2}(S)$ for the open substack parametrizing stable (or "good") objects (so that the natural morphism $\mathcal{M}^s_{c_2}(S) \to M^s_{c_2}(S)$ realizes the stable locus).

A pair of smooth projective curves $\Sigma_1, \Sigma_2$ is called Pic-independent when the Picard group of $\Sigma_1 \times \Sigma_2$ is generated by the pullbacks of line bundles from the two factors. It is known that for Pic-independent pairs $(\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2)$ and for $c_2$ sufficiently large, one has the vanishing
$$H_q\!\left(M_{c_2}(\Sigma_1\times\Sigma_2),\, \mathcal{M}^s_{c_2}(\Sigma_1\times\Sigma_2)\right) \;=\; 0 \qquad \text{for all } q < c_2.$$

Question: Does the same vanishing statement hold for every smooth complex projective surface $S$ of general type? That is, is it true that for any such $S$ there exists $C(S)$ so that for all $c_2 \geq C(S)$,
$$H_q\!\left(M_{c_2}(S),\, \mathcal{M}^s_{c_2}(S)\right) = 0 \qquad \text{for all } q < c_2?$$

It is known that for Pic-independent pairs $(\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2)$ and for $c_2$ sufficiently large, one has the vanishing
$$H_q\!\left(M_{c_2}(\Sigma_1\times\Sigma_2),\, \mathcal{M}^s_{c_2}(\Sigma_1\times\Sigma_2)\right) \;=\; 0 \qquad \text{for all } q < c_2.$$

Question: Does the same vanishing statement hold for every smooth complex projective surface $S$ of general type? That is, is it true that for any such $S$ there exists $C(S)$ so that for all $c_2 \geq C(S)$,
$$H_q\!\left(M_{c_2}(S),\, \mathcal{M}^s_{c_2}(S)\right) = 0 \qquad \text{for all } q < c_2?$$

The vanishing comparison theorem is established for products of Pic-independent curves via Kuranishi-space techniques, but no source found extends it to all surfaces of general type. The question appears to remain open.

Let $\mathbb{C}_\infty = \mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$ denote the Riemann sphere, and consider rational functions $\mathbb{C}_\infty\to\mathbb{C}_\infty$ of degree at least two under the operation of composition $\circ$. A rational function $P$ of degree at least two is called special if either $P$ is conjugate (by a Möbius transformation) to $z^{\pm n}$ or to a Chebyshev polynomial $\pm T_n$, or $P$ is a Lattès map (induced from an endomorphism of an elliptic curve). For a non-special rational function $P$ of degree at least two, define
$$E(P) = \{A : A \text{ is a rational function of degree} \ge 2 \text{ that commutes with an iterate of } P\text{ within an appropriate iterative structure}\},$$
i.e. the semigroup of rational maps $A$ for which there exist iterates with $A\circ P^{\circ n} = P^{\circ m}\circ A$ for some $n,m\ge 1$ (the "semigroup of maps semiconjugate to $P$").

A semigroup $S$ (under composition) is called right amenable if there exists a finitely additive probability measure $\mu$ on the subsets of $S$ that is invariant under right translations $s\mapsto s\circ a$ for all $a\in S$. The semigroup $S$ is called right reversible if for every $A,B\in S$ one has $S\circ A \cap S\circ B \ne \emptyset$. A free subsemigroup of rank two in $S$ is a subsemigroup isomorphic to the free semigroup on two generators.

Let $S$ be a semigroup (under composition) of rational functions of degree at least two containing at least one non-special rational function. Prove or disprove that the following five conditions are equivalent:

(1) $S$ is right amenable.
(2) $S$ is right reversible.
(3) For every $A,B\in S$ there exist integers $k,l\ge 1$ such that
$$A^{\circ 2k} = A^{\circ k}\circ B^{\circ l}\quad\text{and}\quad B^{\circ 2l} = B^{\circ l}\circ A^{\circ k}.$$
(4) $S$ contains no free subsemigroup of rank two.
(5) There exists a non-special rational function $P$ of degree at least two such that $S$ is a subsemigroup of $E(P)$.

The conjecture of equivalence of these five conditions for semigroups of rational functions containing a non-special element appears to remain open in full generality. Partial results are available: every subsemigroup of E(P) for non-special P of degree at least two is known to be amenable (and power-twisted), and analogues have been proved for polynomial semigroups and certain semigroups of formal power series, but the full equivalence (especially the implication from right amenability or absence of a rank-two free subsemigroup to membership in some E(P)) is not established in the rational case.

Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field with $q$ elements, and fix integers $n \geq 2$ and $1 \leq i \leq n-1$. For a monic polynomial $f(x) \in \mathbb{F}_q[x]$ of degree $n$, a polycyclic code of length $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ associated with $f(x)$ is, by definition, an ideal of the quotient ring $\mathbb{F}_q[x]/\langle f(x)\rangle$, viewed as an $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ via the natural identification $(c_0,c_1,\dots,c_{n-1}) \leftrightarrow c_0 + c_1 x + \cdots + c_{n-1} x^{n-1}$. Two linear codes $C, C' \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ are called equivalent if there exists a monomial transformation (a permutation of coordinates composed with multiplication of each coordinate by a nonzero scalar) that maps $C$ onto $C'$. For a polynomial $f(x) \in \mathbb{F}_q[x]$ with $f(0) \neq 0$, the order $\operatorname{Ord}(f(x))$ is the least positive integer $e$ such that $f(x) \mid x^e - 1$ in $\mathbb{F}_q[x]$.

Consider two trinomials
$$t_1(x) = x^n - a x^i - b, \qquad t_2(x) = x^n - a' x^{\,n-i} - b'$$
in $\mathbb{F}_q[x]$, with $a,b,a',b' \in \mathbb{F}_q^\times$, and assume $\operatorname{Ord}(t_1(x)) = \operatorname{Ord}(t_2(x))$. Let $\mathcal{C}_1$ denote the set of all polycyclic codes of length $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ associated with $t_1(x)$, and let $\mathcal{C}_2$ denote the analogous set for $t_2(x)$.

Prove or disprove: there always exists a bijection $\Phi : \mathcal{C}_1 \to \mathcal{C}_2$ such that for every $C \in \mathcal{C}_1$, the code $\Phi(C)$ is equivalent to $C$.

Consider the following decentralized channel-capture problem. There are n ≥ 2 users sharing a single time-slotted broadcast channel. In each slot t = 1, 2, ..., each user independently decides (using only its own past observations and possibly private randomness) whether to transmit. Let X_i[t] ∈ {0,1} indicate whether user i transmits in slot t, and let S[t] = X_1[t] + ... + X_n[t] be the number of transmitters in slot t. A slot is called a "success" if S[t] = 1 (exactly one user transmits), in which case that user is said to have captured the channel. The goal of a decentralized algorithm is to minimize the expected number of slots until the first success (equivalently, to optimize channel-capture performance), where users follow identical protocols and break symmetry only through randomization and feedback.

Under the strong feedback model, after each slot every user observes F[t] = S[t] exactly (so F[t] = 0 indicates idle, F[t] = 1 indicates success, and F[t] = k ≥ 2 indicates a collision with the exact count k of transmitters revealed).

The problem: characterize and determine optimal decentralized algorithms (in the sense of minimizing the expected time to the first success, or otherwise achieving optimal channel-capture performance) under more limited feedback models in which the exact transmitter count is not available. In particular, treat the classical ternary "idle / success / collision" feedback (F[t] ∈ {0, 1, ≥2}) and any other coarsening of S[t], and identify the optimal protocols and their performance for each such feedback model.

Let $\gamma$ be a closed smooth strictly convex plane curve bounding a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, parametrized by arc length $s$. Let $B:A \to A$ denote the standard billiard map of $\Omega$ acting on the phase cylinder $A = \mathbb{R}/L\mathbb{Z} \times (0,\pi)$ with coordinates $(s,\alpha)$, where $s$ is the arc-length coordinate of the impact point on $\gamma$ and $\alpha \in (0,\pi)$ is the angle the outgoing trajectory makes with the positively oriented tangent to $\gamma$. Fix $d > 0$ and define the shift map $S_d : A \to A$ by
$$S_d(s, \alpha) = (s + d\cot\alpha, \alpha),$$
which corresponds to geodesic travel for time $d$ along a flat cylinder of height $d$ erected over $\gamma$. Consider the composed map
$$T = S_d \circ B : A \to A,$$
which is symplectic with respect to $d s \wedge d(\cos\alpha)$.

(a) Does $T$ admit essential invariant curves (i.e., homotopically nontrivial $T$-invariant continuous curves in $A$)?

(b) In particular, do there exist KAM-type invariant curves of $T$ accumulating on, or located in any neighbourhood of, the boundary $\{\alpha = 0\} \cup \{\alpha = \pi\}$ of $A$?

Determine, as a function of the curve $\gamma$ and the height parameter $d$, the existence or nonexistence of such invariant curves.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Recent work on "coin billiards" (the same modified billiard map) has provided partial answers: when the height $d$ is sufficiently small, or when $\gamma$ is sufficiently close to a circle, KAM invariant curves are shown to exist in a region close to (but not accumulating on) the boundary of the annulus. The dual code $C^\perp$ is defined with respect to the standard Euclidean inner product on $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, and $C$ is self-dual if $C=C^\perp$.

Moreover, decide whether every such self-dual polycyclic code necessarily has minimum Hamming distance equal to $2$ and is in fact a constacyclic code (rather than a strictly more general polycyclic code).

Let γ ⊂ ℝ² be a closed smooth strictly convex plane curve bounding a billiard table Ω. Fix a real parameter h > 0, and consider the right circular cylinder C = ∂Ω × [0, h] ⊂ ℝ³, whose top and bottom bases are congruent copies of Ω. Define a map T on the space A of oriented chords of γ (equivalently, on the open annulus of unit inward-pointing vectors based on γ) as follows. Given an inward unit vector v at a point p ∈ γ, lift v to the bottom rim of C in the natural way and consider the geodesic on the lateral cylindrical surface C that starts at (p, 0) with the corresponding initial direction; this geodesic, viewed as a straight line on the unrolled cylinder, hits the top rim ∂Ω × {h} at a point (p′, h). At p′ apply the standard reflection law for billiards in Ω (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection with respect to the tangent of γ at p′), then run another geodesic on the lateral surface from (p′, h) down to a point (p″, 0) ∈ ∂Ω × {0}, and reflect again at p″ inside Ω. The composition of these two billiard reflections together with the two cylindrical-geodesic transports defines an area-preserving twist map T : A → A (the "coin billiard" map associated with γ and height h).

Question: Does there exist a closed smooth strictly convex curve γ and a height h > 0 such that the map T is ergodic with respect to its invariant (Liouville) measure on A?

At p′ apply the standard reflection law for billiards in Ω (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection with respect to the tangent of γ at p′), then run another geodesic on the lateral surface from (p′, h) down to a point (p″, 0) ∈ ∂Ω × {0}, and reflect again at p″ inside Ω. The composition of these two billiard reflections together with the two cylindrical-geodesic transports defines an area-preserving twist map T : A → A (the "coin billiard" map associated with γ and height h).

Question: Does there exist a closed smooth strictly convex curve γ and a height h > 0 such that the map T is ergodic with respect to its invariant (Liouville) measure on A?

The coin-billiard construction (introduced by Bialy and studied by Bialy–Tabachnikov and others) is known to admit KAM/invariant essential curves for small heights or near-circular tables, which precludes ergodicity in those regimes. Recent works (e.g., on existence/nonexistence of invariant curves of coin billiards, 2024) study when invariant curves disappear for large heights, but no example of an ergodic coin billiard map T over a smooth strictly convex curve appears to be known. The ergodicity question is stated as an open question in the survey of open problems on billiards and geometric optics.

Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field and let $n$ be a prime number. Consider a trinomial of the form
$$f(x) = x^n - a x^i - b \in \mathbb{F}_q[x],$$
where $a, b \in \mathbb{F}_q$ and $1 \le i \le n-1$. Let $g(x) \in \mathbb{F}_q[x]$ be a monic divisor of $f(x)$, and let $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ be the polycyclic code of length $n$ associated with $f(x)$ whose generator polynomial is $g(x)$; that is, $C$ is the image of the ideal $(g(x))/(f(x))$ in $\mathbb{F}_q[x]/(f(x))$ under the coordinate identification with $\mathbb{F}_q^n$. Let
$$C^{\perp} = \{ u \in \mathbb{F}_q^n : \langle u, c\rangle = 0 \text{ for all } c \in C\}$$
denote the Euclidean dual of $C$ with respect to the standard inner product. Prove or disprove: under the above hypotheses (in particular, $n$ prime), the code $C$ is never dual-containing, i.e. $C^{\perp} \not\subseteq C$ unless $C$ is trivial in the excluded sense.

Fix δ ∈ (0, π/2). For a smooth, closed, strictly convex curve γ in a complete simply connected surface M of constant curvature, consider the Birkhoff billiard map T inside γ: an oriented chord (a directed geodesic segment with both endpoints on γ) is mapped to its reflection at the second endpoint, where the angle of incidence with the tangent line to γ equals the angle of reflection. Identify the space of oriented chords with the open annulus parametrized by (arclength on γ, angle with the tangent), so that T is a twist map of this annulus. Call γ a δ-Gutkin curve if the set of oriented chords that meet γ at the constant angle δ is an invariant curve of T (equivalently, if a chord enters γ at angle δ then it exits γ at angle δ).

In the Euclidean plane (M = R^2), a complete description of δ-Gutkin curves is known (Gutkin's class of curves with the constant-angle invariant property).

Problem: Describe and classify the δ-Gutkin curves when M is the round 2-sphere S^2 and when M is the hyperbolic plane H^2. In particular, characterize, up to isometry, all smooth closed strictly convex curves on S^2 and on H^2 possessing the δ-Gutkin property for some δ ∈ (0, π/2), and determine for which values of δ such curves exist.

Let $G$ be a finite group. For a perfect field $k$ of positive characteristic (with $|G|$ allowed to be divisible by $\operatorname{char} k$), one can form a moduli space (more precisely, a formal stack or ind-scheme) $\Delta_G$ over $k$ whose $B$-points, for a $k$-algebra $B$, parametrize $G$-torsors over $\operatorname{Spec} B(\!(t)\!)$ (equivalently, continuous homomorphisms from the absolute Galois group of $B(\!(t)\!)$ to $G$, up to conjugation). This moduli space plays a central role in the wild McKay correspondence, where motivic integrals over $\Delta_G$ compute stringy invariants of quotient varieties $V/G$.

Problem: Construct an analogous moduli space $\Delta_G$ associated to a local field of characteristic zero, such as $\mathbb{Q}_p$, that parametrizes $G$-torsors over (families of) such local fields and that is suitable for developing a motivic integration theory and a wild McKay correspondence in mixed characteristic. Specifically, define a geometric object $\Delta_G$ over an appropriate base (e.g.\ $\operatorname{Spf} \mathbb{Z}_p$ or $\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{F}_p$) whose points classify $G$-torsors over $p$-adic local fields, establish its basic geometric properties (such as a stratification by ramification data, dimension, and a measure), and show that integration on $\Delta_G$ recovers the expected invariants of quotients in mixed characteristic.

Let $R$ be a complete discrete valuation ring of mixed characteristic (for example, the ring of $p$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_p$), with residue field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$ and fraction field $K$ of characteristic $0$. Existing theories of motivic integration provide, for a formal scheme $\mathfrak{X}$ of finite type over $R$, a measure on the arc space (or Greenberg space) of $\mathfrak{X}$ valued in a suitable Grothendieck ring of varieties, generalizing Kontsevich's motivic integration and Sebag's extension to formal schemes. Parallel work has developed motivic integration over (possibly wild) Deligne–Mumford stacks $\mathcal{X}$ in the equal-characteristic setting, i.e., over power series rings $k[[t]]$, and used it to establish motivic forms of the McKay correspondence, including for wild quotient singularities.

Problem: Develop a theory of motivic integration for Deligne–Mumford stacks $\mathcal{X}$ that are of finite type (or formal of finite type) over a complete discrete valuation ring $R$ of mixed characteristic, including:

(a) a well-defined notion of twisted arcs / jets of $\mathcal{X}$ over $R$ and an appropriate Greenberg-type space carrying a measure with values in a localized Grothendieck ring of varieties over the residue field $k$;
(b) a change-of-variables formula along proper birational (and in particular crepant) morphisms between such stacks; and
(c) using this theory, prove a motivic McKay correspondence over $R$: for a finite group $G$ acting linearly on $\mathbb{A}^n_R$ with quotient $X = \mathbb{A}^n_R/G$ and any crepant resolution (or stacky resolution) $Y \to X$, establish an equality of stringy/motivic invariants of $Y$ with a suitable orbifold/twisted-arc motivic integral on the quotient stack $[\mathbb{A}^n_R/G]$, recovering in mixed characteristic the wild McKay correspondence known in equal characteristic.

A planar projective billiard is a domain Ω ⊂ ℝℙ² (or ℝ²) bounded by a piecewise-smooth curve ∂Ω together with a smooth field of transverse lines along ∂Ω (the "projective field"). The reflection law of the projective billiard is defined as follows: an incoming oriented line ℓ hitting ∂Ω at a smooth point p reflects to the unique outgoing line ℓ' such that the four lines (ℓ, ℓ', the tangent line T_p∂Ω, and the projective line at p) form a harmonic quadruple in the pencil of lines through p. (When the projective field is the field of normals, this reduces to the usual law of optical reflection.)

A k-periodic orbit (k ≥ 2) is a closed polygonal trajectory P₁P₂…P_kP₁ with vertices on ∂Ω whose successive sides obey the projective reflection law at each P_i. The projective billiard is called k-reflective if the set of k-periodic orbits has nonempty interior in the phase space of oriented lines meeting ∂Ω (equivalently, there is an open 2-parameter family of k-periodic orbits).

Currently, the only known k-reflective planar projective billiards (for k ≥ 4) are certain polygonal constructions.

Question. Fix an integer k ≥ 4. Do there exist k-reflective planar projective billiards on domains Ω whose boundary belongs to one of the following regularity classes, beyond the known polygonal examples:
(a) polygonal domains (i.e., are there essentially new polygonal k-reflective projective billiards);
(b) piecewise-algebraic domains (boundary consisting of finitely many real-algebraic arcs);
(c) (real-)analytic domains (boundary a real-analytic curve)?

Significant progress has been made. Let $\gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n\ge 2$) be a closed, strictly convex, $C^\infty$-smooth hypersurface. Consider the space of oriented straight lines in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that intersect $\gamma$ transversally at exactly two points; this space, denoted $\Pi$ and called the phase cylinder of the billiard inside $\gamma$, is an open symplectic manifold (carrying the symplectic form induced from the standard one on the space of oriented lines in $\mathbb{R}^n$).

For any $C^\infty$ closed hypersurface $\sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ that is sufficiently close to $\gamma$, the optical reflection law from $\sigma$ defines a (partially defined) symplectomorphism $T_\sigma$ on $\Pi$: an incoming oriented line is sent to the corresponding reflected oriented line. Reflection from $\gamma$ itself is denoted $T_\gamma$.

Question: Is it true that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, every $C^\infty$ Hamiltonian symplectomorphism $\Pi \to \Pi$ can be approximated, in the $C^\infty$ topology on compact subsets of its domain, by finite compositions
$$T_{\sigma_N} \circ T_{\sigma_{N-1}} \circ \cdots \circ T_{\sigma_1},$$
where each $\sigma_j$ is either $\gamma$ itself or a closed hypersurface that is $\varepsilon$-close to $\gamma$ in the $C^k$ topology, and where only the reflection maps $T_{\sigma_j}$ themselves (and not their inverses) are allowed in the compositions?

Fix ε > 0 and consider the square lattice (ε ℤ)^2 ⊂ ℝ^2. Let γ ⊂ ℝ^2 be a smooth plane curve (for instance, a smooth simple closed curve, or a compact smooth arc), and for each translation vector v ∈ ℝ^2 let γ + v denote the translate of γ. Define the lattice-click set associated with γ to be the set of pairs

   C_ε(γ) := { (v, p) ∈ ℝ^2 × (ε ℤ)^2 : p ∈ γ + v },

equivalently, for each lattice point p ∈ (ε ℤ)^2 record the set of translations v for which the translated curve passes through p (a "click"). After projecting along a chosen direction (say, recording, as v moves along a fixed line, the sequence of times/positions at which any lattice point lies on γ + v), one obtains a "cloud of clicks" supported on a one-dimensional segment.

The geometric problem: the local density and fine structure of this click cloud encode geometric invariants of γ, in particular its curvature κ(s) as a function of arclength. However, the clicks coming from different parts of γ are superimposed on the same one-dimensional segment, obscuring this information.

Question. Is there an analogue of a Fourier transform — that is, an explicit integral transform, or a more general linear/nonlinear functional of the click cloud C_ε(γ) — which, applied to the cloud, extracts the curvature-induced patterns of γ? More precisely, construct a transform T such that T(C_ε(γ)) reveals (asymptotically as ε → 0, or in a suitable scaling limit) the curvature function κ of γ, separating contributions from different points of γ that otherwise pile up on the segment.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and let $G \subset \mathrm{GL}(V)$ be a finite subgroup whose order is divisible by $p$ (the "wild" case). Let $X = V/G$ denote the quotient variety, and let $Y \to X$ be a crepant resolution of singularities (when one exists). In characteristic zero (the tame case), the classical derived McKay correspondence asserts an equivalence of triangulated categories
$$ D^b(\mathrm{Coh}\, Y) \;\simeq\; D^b(\mathrm{Coh}^G V) $$
between the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on $Y$ and the bounded derived category of $G$-equivariant coherent sheaves on $V$ (as established for finite subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}_n$ with $n\le 3$ via the Hilbert scheme of $G$-clusters).

Problem: Formulate and prove an analogue of this derived equivalence in the wild case. Note that the naive statement above cannot hold as written, because in the wild case the category $\mathrm{Coh}^G V$ has infinite global dimension. The task is to identify the correct categorical replacement (for one or both sides) and establish a derived-categorical McKay correspondence valid when $p \mid |G|$.

The known obstruction is that the equivariant category $\mathrm{Coh}^G V$ has infinite global dimension when $p \mid |G|$, so the classical Bridgeland–King–Reid/Kapranov–Vasserot equivalence cannot hold verbatim, and an alternative formulation is required. Let $g^t$ be either a continuous-time flow ($t\in\mathbb{R}$) or a discrete cascade ($t\in\mathbb{Z}$) acting on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and preserving the planar Lebesgue measure. Define the trapped set
$$T_g = \{\, x\in\mathbb{R}^2 : \text{the forward semi-orbit } \{g^t x : t\ge 0\} \text{ is bounded, and the backward semi-orbit } \{g^t x : t\le 0\} \text{ is unbounded}\,\}.$$
For each integer $m\ge 1$, let $\mathcal{C}^m$ denote the class of such $g$ that are $C^m$-smooth (in $x$, or jointly in $x$ and $t$ in the flow case). Define
$$d(m) = \sup\{\,\dim_H T_g : g \in \mathcal{C}^m \,\},$$
where $\dim_H$ is the Hausdorff dimension. Determine the value $d(m) \in [1,2]$ as a function of the smoothness $m$, and in particular find the largest possible Hausdorff dimension of $T_g$ within each smoothness class.

Setting. Let $k$ be a number field with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_k$.

(A) Malle's conjecture. For a finite transitive subgroup $G\subset S_n$, let
$$N_k(G;X)=\#\{K/k\ \text{(in a fixed algebraic closure)}: [K:k]=n,\ \operatorname{Gal}(K^{\mathrm{gal}}/k)\simeq G\ \text{as permutation group},\ |\operatorname{Disc}(K/k)|\le X\}.$$
Malle's conjecture predicts the existence of explicit constants $a(G)\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}$ and $b(k,G)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ and a positive constant $c(k,G)$ such that
$$N_k(G;X)\sim c(k,G)\,X^{a(G)}(\log X)^{b(k,G)-1}\qquad (X\to\infty),$$
where $a(G)=1/\min_{g\in G\setminus\{1\}}\operatorname{ind}(g)$ with $\operatorname{ind}(g)=n-\#\{\text{orbits of }\langle g\rangle\text{ on }\{1,\dots,n\}\}$.

(B) Batyrev–Manin conjecture (stacky form). Let $\mathcal{X}=[V/G]$ be a smooth Deligne–Mumford quotient stack over $k$ with $V$ a faithful $G$-representation, equipped with an anticanonical-type height $H\colon \mathcal{X}(k)\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ coming from the "raised line bundle" associated to the canonical sheaf. Let $U\subset\mathcal{X}$ be a suitable open substack. The Batyrev–Manin–Peyre conjecture predicts
$$\#\{x\in U(k): H(x)\le X\}\sim c_{\mathrm{Peyre}}(\mathcal{X})\,X^{\alpha(\mathcal{X})}(\log X)^{\beta(\mathcal{X})-1}\qquad (X\to\infty),$$
for explicit exponents $\alpha(\mathcal{X}),\beta(\mathcal{X})$ defined in terms of the anticanonical class and Picard group of $\mathcal{X}$, together with an explicit Peyre-type leading constant.

Conjectural relation. The two predictions are expected to coincide when $\mathcal{X}=[\mathbb{A}^n_k/G]$ with the regular permutation representation, in the sense that $k$-points of $[\mathbb{A}^n_k/G]$ counted by the canonical height correspond to $G$-extensions $K/k$ counted by absolute discriminant, and the exponents and constants on the two sides match.

Problem. Identify a nontrivial special case (a specific group $G$ and base $k$, or a specific family of stacks $\mathcal{X}$) for which one of conjectures (A) and (B) is already established, and derive from that case a previously unknown special case of the other conjecture. Equivalently: produce a rigorous implication "(A) for $(k,G)$" $\Rightarrow$ "(B) for $[\mathbb{A}^n_k/G]$", or vice versa, and verify it on at least one example beyond what is known directly.
