Consider a patient undergoing adaptive cancer therapy, in which the dose or scheduling of treatment is dynamically modulated in response to longitudinal measurements of a disease-specific biomarker (for example, prostate-specific antigen, circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cell counts, urine markers, or quantitative imaging). Let y(t) denote the time series of such a biomarker, and suppose one wishes to use a mathematical model M (with parameter vector θ ∈ Θ ⊂ ℝ^p) of tumor–treatment dynamics to forecast the patient's future biomarker trajectory and, in particular, the time of disease progression, in real time.

Formulate and resolve the following questions:

(a) Identify general necessary conditions on the sampling frequency and noise level of y(t), on the structural and practical identifiability of θ given the observation map, on calibration and validation protocols (e.g., out-of-sample prediction error, sensitivity analysis of forecasts to θ), and on the quality of the biomarker as a surrogate for tumor burden, under which patient-specific real-time prediction of progression times is feasible with quantifiable uncertainty suitable to guide dose modulation.

(b) Provide a decision rule (a goodness-of-fit / model-adequacy criterion) that, given the calibration data of a single patient, determines when the model M may legitimately be used to issue forecasts, and when M must be rejected as unable to describe that patient's dynamics.

(c) For at least one concrete choice of biomarker and corresponding mechanistic model, demonstrate prospectively (not merely retrospectively) that the resulting predictions are sufficiently accurate and calibrated to inform clinical dose modulation.

Consider an adaptive therapy framework for treating a heterogeneous tumor composed of two cell populations: drug-sensitive cells S(t) and drug-resistant cells R(t), evolving according to competitive Lotka–Volterra-type dynamics

  dS/dt = r_S S (1 - (S + a_{SR} R)/K) - d(t) S,
  dR/dt = r_R R (1 - (R + a_{RS} S)/K),

where r_S, r_R > 0 are intrinsic growth rates, a_{SR}, a_{RS} > 0 are interspecific competition coefficients capturing frequency- and density-dependent suppression, K > 0 is a carrying capacity, and d(t) ≥ 0 is a treatment schedule that may be switched on and off. A "containment" (adaptive) strategy chooses d(t) so as to delay resuming therapy until S is large enough to strongly suppress R, thereby prolonging the period before resistance dominates.

Augment this baseline with the following clinically motivated risk components attached to maintaining a large total tumor burden N(t) = S(t) + R(t):

(i) a symptom/quality-of-life cost functional C_sym(N), increasing in N;
(ii) a biomarker model B(t) = f(S(t), R(t)) + ε(t) used (with sampling frequency Δt and measurement noise ε) to drive treatment decisions;
(iii) an additional evolutionary process generating new resistant phenotypes at a rate μ(N, d) that may depend on tumor size and on/off scheduling;
(iv) a metastatic seeding hazard λ_met(N) increasing in N, producing new lesions whose local (S_i, R_i) dynamics may differ across sites i;
(v) drug- or disease-specific safety constraints d(t) ≤ d_max and N(t) ≤ N_safe.

Problem. Within this class of models, determine whether and under what parameter regimes a containment strategy that maintains a relatively high but bounded tumor burden yields a larger expected progression-free survival (or other patient-centered objective combining survival and C_sym) than a maximum-tolerated-dose strategy that aggressively minimizes N. Specifically:

(a) Characterize the set of parameters (r_S, r_R, a_{SR}, a_{RS}, K, μ, λ_met, noise level in ε, sampling interval Δt, N_safe) for which the competitive suppression benefit of large S strictly dominates the cumulative risks (i)–(v).

(b) Derive optimal feedback controls d*(t) = d*(B observed up to time t) that balance prolonged treatment sensitivity against symptom burden, biomarker inaccuracy, ongoing somatic evolution under intermittent therapy, new metastatic seeding, and inter-lesion heterogeneity, subject to the safety constraints.

(c) Identify quantitative thresholds (e.g., on a_{RS}/a_{SR}, on μ, or on λ_met) that separate regimes in which containment is preferable from regimes in which aggressive cytoreduction is preferable, and discuss how these thresholds should inform the design of clinical trials of adaptive therapy.

Formulate a rigorous framework, and determine whether one can construct, predictive mathematical models of tumor dynamics with the following properties, sufficient to drive individualized adaptive (evolution-based) cancer therapy decisions at scale:

(a) Patient-specific state model. For each patient p, let x_p(t) ∈ R^n denote a tumor state vector (e.g., subclone burdens, biomarker levels, microenvironmental variables) evolving according to a parametric dynamical system dx_p/dt = F(x_p, u; θ_p), where u(t) is the treatment input and θ_p ∈ Θ are patient-specific parameters. Specify minimal longitudinal measurement protocols y_p(t_k) = h(x_p(t_k)) + ε_k under which θ_p and the latent state x_p(t) are practically identifiable before clinical progression occurs.

(b) Prediction under uncertainty. Given a posterior π(θ_p, x_p | y_{1:k}) obtained from sequential Bayesian inference, characterize sufficient conditions on F, h, and the observation schedule such that predicted time-to-progression and response under any admissible treatment policy u(·) have credible intervals narrow enough to discriminate among candidate policies with a prescribed error rate α.

(c) Virtual patient Phase-i comparison. Define a procedure that, for each individual patient p, generates a virtual cohort {θ_p^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N from π(θ_p | y_{1:k}), simulates outcomes under each candidate treatment policy, and outputs a ranking with guaranteed coverage (e.g., a confidence set of near-optimal policies) under model misspecification bounded in a specified metric.

(d) Decision-support guarantees. Prove or disprove the existence of such a triple (model class F, measurement protocol h, inference-and-decision algorithm A) that simultaneously: (i) is identifiable from clinically feasible data; (ii) produces calibrated predictions whose miscoverage is uniformly bounded across a heterogeneous patient population; and (iii) yields treatment recommendations whose expected clinical utility provably dominates standard-of-care policies.

State precise hypotheses on F, Θ, the noise model, and the population distribution under which (a)–(d) admit a positive solution, or exhibit fundamental obstructions (identifiability failure, uncertainty propagation lower bounds, or decision-theoretic impossibility) that prevent it.

Let $X$ be a projective variety with at worst mild singularities (e.g., smooth, or with terminal/canonical singularities). A maximal rationally connected (MRC) fibration of $X$ is a dominant rational map $\varphi : X \dashrightarrow Y$, defined up to birational equivalence of the base $Y$, whose general fibers are rationally connected and which is maximal with this property; equivalently, every rationally connected subvariety through a very general point of $X$ is contracted by $\varphi$. By a theorem of Kollár–Miyaoka–Mori (and Graber–Harris–Starr), $\varphi$ exists and can be chosen to be an almost holomorphic rational map (i.e., its general fiber is contained in the locus where $\varphi$ is defined), with $Y$ non-uniruled.

Determine general structural conditions on $X$ (and on the choice of a birational model of $Y$) under which the MRC fibration can be represented by an actual holomorphic morphism $\varphi : X \to Y'$ to some projective variety $Y'$ birational to $Y$, rather than merely by an almost holomorphic rational map. In particular, decide whether there exists a smooth (or mildly singular) projective variety $X$ admitting no holomorphic representative of its MRC fibration for any birational choice of the base.

Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold. The holomorphic sectional curvature $H$ of $X$ is the restriction of the sectional curvature to complex lines in the tangent spaces; explicitly, for a nonzero tangent vector $v$ of type $(1,0)$, $H(v) = R(v,\bar v, v, \bar v)/\|v\|^4$, where $R$ is the curvature tensor of the Kähler metric. Say that $X$ has positive holomorphic sectional curvature if $H(v) > 0$ for every nonzero $(1,0)$ tangent vector $v$ at every point of $X$. Recall that $X$ is called projective if it admits a holomorphic embedding into some complex projective space, and rationally connected if any two points of $X$ can be joined by a chain of rational curves.

Prove or disprove: every compact Kähler manifold $X$ that admits a Kähler metric of positive holomorphic sectional curvature is projective and rationally connected.

Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold. The holomorphic sectional curvature $H$ of $X$ is the restriction of the sectional curvature to complex lines in the tangent spaces; explicitly, for a nonzero tangent vector $v$ of type $(1,0)$, $H(v) = R(v,\bar v, v, \bar v)/\|v\|^4$, where $R$ is the curvature tensor of the Kähler metric. Say that $X$ has positive holomorphic sectional curvature if $H(v) > 0$ for every nonzero $(1,0)$ tangent vector $v$ at every point of $X$. Recall that $X$ is called projective if it admits a holomorphic embedding into some complex projective space, and rationally connected if any two points of $X$ can be joined by a chain of rational curves.

Prove or disprove: every compact Kähler manifold $X$ that admits a Kähler metric of positive holomorphic sectional curvature is projective and rationally connected.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The conjecture, due to Yau (Problem 47 in his 1982 problem list), was resolved affirmatively by Xiaokui Yang in 2018, who proved that a compact Kähler manifold with positive holomorphic sectional curvature is projective and rationally connected, using the notion of RC-positivity.

Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold admitting a Kähler metric of semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature (i.e., for every nonzero tangent vector $v$ of type $(1,0)$, the holomorphic sectional curvature $H(v) \ge 0$). For a smooth projective variety, the following structure theorem is known: there exists a maximal rationally connected (MRC) fibration $\varphi: X \dashrightarrow Y$ which is everywhere defined, smooth, and locally trivial (with rationally connected fiber $F$ admitting a Kähler metric of semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature), $Y$ has identically zero holomorphic sectional curvature, and the universal cover $\widetilde{X}$ splits holomorphically and isometrically as a product $\mathbb{C}^k \times \widetilde{F}$ (so in particular the MRC fibration lifts to the trivial product fibration after passing to the universal cover).

Problem: Does the same structure theorem hold for an arbitrary compact Kähler manifold $X$ (not assumed projective) carrying a Kähler metric of semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature? More precisely, must $X$ admit a smooth locally trivial MRC fibration $\varphi: X \to Y$ onto a compact Kähler manifold $Y$ of identically zero holomorphic sectional curvature, with rationally connected fiber, such that the universal cover of $X$ splits holomorphically and isometrically as $\mathbb{C}^k \times \widetilde{F}$?

The problem of extending the projective structure theorem for semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature to the compact Kähler setting appears to remain a research question being actively pursued. Recent preprints (2024–2025) by Matsumura and by Zhang–Zhang study the fundamental groups and partial semi-positivity in the Kähler case, and a related structure/splitting theorem has been obtained for compact Kähler manifolds with non-negative mixed curvature. However, no source clearly states a complete generalization of the full projective structure theorem (MRC locally trivial fibration plus universal cover splitting) to all compact Kähler manifolds. Status appears partially resolved.

Let $(X,g)$ be a compact Kähler manifold of complex dimension $n$ with semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature, i.e. $H_g(v) := R_g(v,\bar v, v,\bar v) \ge 0$ for every nonzero tangent vector $v \in T_X$. For a Kähler manifold $(Y,g_Y)$, define the "number of truly flat directions" $\mathrm{ntf}(Y,g_Y)$ at a generic point $y \in Y$ to be the maximal complex dimension of a subspace $V \subset T_{Y,y}$ such that $R_{g_Y}(v,\bar w, \cdot, \cdot) = 0$ for all $v,w \in V$ (equivalently, the maximal dimension of a "truly flat" subspace of the tangent space).

Address the following questions:

(a) Is the fundamental group $\pi_1(X)$ an extension
$$1 \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}^{2m} \longrightarrow \pi_1(X) \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow 1$$
where $G$ is a finite group and $2m = 2\dim \mathrm{Alb}(X^*)$ for some finite étale cover $X^* \to X$?

(b) Does there exist a finite étale cover $\pi: X^* \to X$ such that, denoting by $\alpha: X^* \to \mathrm{Alb}(X^*)$ the Albanese map, $\alpha$ is a surjective submersion and a general fiber $F$ admits a Kähler metric $g_F$ with $\mathrm{ntf}(F,g_F) = \dim F$?

(c) Under the conclusion of (b), is the fiber $F$ projective and rationally connected?

Let $(X,g)$ be a compact Kähler manifold. The holomorphic sectional curvature of $g$ in the direction of a nonzero tangent vector $v \in T_xX$ is $H(v) = R(v,\bar v,v,\bar v)/|v|^4$, where $R$ is the curvature tensor of the Chern (equivalently Levi-Civita) connection of $g$. Assume that $g$ has either semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature ($H(v)\ge 0$ for all $v$) or semi-negative holomorphic sectional curvature ($H(v)\le 0$ for all $v$).

Call a tangent vector $v\in T_xX$ "truly flat" (in the appropriate sense for the sign condition) if $H$ vanishes to sufficiently high order along $v$, so that $v$ lies in the zero set of the obstruction to strict positivity (respectively strict negativity) of $H$. Let $V\subset TX$ denote the set of such truly flat tangent vectors.

Answer the following:

(a) Does $V$ form an integrable holomorphic subbundle of $TX$?

(b) Does there exist a holomorphic subbundle $W\subset TX$ giving a holomorphic splitting $TX = W\oplus V$?

(c) In the semi-positive case, does there exist a maximal rationally connected (MRC) fibration $f:X\to Y$ such that $W$ coincides with the relative tangent bundle $T_{X/Y}$?

(d) In the semi-negative case, does there exist an Iitaka fibration $f:X\to Z$ associated with the canonical bundle $K_X$ such that $V$ coincides with the relative tangent bundle $T_{X/Z}$?

Background and definitions. Let $(X,\omega)$ be a compact Kähler manifold of complex dimension $n$ with Kähler metric $g$ and associated Chern (or equivalently Levi-Civita) connection on the holomorphic tangent bundle $T^{1,0}X$. For a nonzero holomorphic tangent vector $v\in T^{1,0}_pX$, the holomorphic sectional curvature is
$$H(v) \;=\; \frac{R(v,\bar v,v,\bar v)}{|v|_g^4},$$
where $R$ is the curvature tensor of $g$. One says that $(X,\omega)$ has positive (resp. semi-positive) holomorphic sectional curvature if $H(v)>0$ (resp. $H(v)\ge 0$) for every nonzero $v$ at every point of $X$. We say a complex manifold $X$ admits positive (resp. semi-positive) holomorphic sectional curvature if some Kähler metric on $X$ has this property.

Recall that the $k$-th Hirzebruch surface is $\Sigma_k=\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}\oplus \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(k))$ for $k\ge 0$. It is known that every Hirzebruch surface admits a Kähler metric of positive holomorphic sectional curvature.

Problems.
(a) Let $\tilde\Sigma_k$ denote the blow-up of a Hirzebruch surface $\Sigma_k$ at one (or finitely many) points. Does $\tilde\Sigma_k$ admit a Kähler metric of positive holomorphic sectional curvature?

(b) Classify all smooth projective varieties of complex dimension $2$ (respectively, dimension $3$) that admit a Kähler metric of positive holomorphic sectional curvature, and likewise those admitting one of semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature.

(c) Find a purely algebro-geometric notion (a property of the variety, of its tangent bundle, or of suitable cohomology classes) that is equivalent to, or serves as a natural analog of, the existence of a Kähler metric of positive (respectively semi-positive) holomorphic sectional curvature.

Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective variety whose tangent bundle $T_X$ is pseudo-effective (i.e., the tautological line bundle $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}(T_X)}(1)$ on the projectivization $\mathbb{P}(T_X)$ is a pseudo-effective line bundle). Suppose that $X$ admits a holomorphic maximal rationally connected (MRC) fibration $\varphi : X \to Y$, that is, a surjective morphism (everywhere defined) onto a smooth projective variety $Y$ whose general fibers are rationally connected and maximal with this property (so that $Y$ is not uniruled).

A surjective morphism $\varphi : X \to Y$ between smooth projective varieties is called locally trivial if for every point $y \in Y$ there exists an analytic open neighborhood $U \subset Y$ of $y$ and a biholomorphism $\varphi^{-1}(U) \cong U \times F$ over $U$, where $F$ is a fixed fiber of $\varphi$.

Question: Must such an MRC fibration $\varphi : X \to Y$ be locally trivial?

Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective manifold. Recall that:

- $X$ is called rationally connected if any two general points of $X$ can be joined by a rational curve (equivalently, by a chain of rational curves).
- A vector bundle $E$ on $X$ is called pseudo-effective if, for every ample line bundle $A$ on $X$, there exists a positive integer $m$ and a positive integer $k$ such that $S^{mk}E \otimes A^{\otimes k}$ has a non-zero global section (equivalently, the tautological line bundle $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}(E^*)}(1)$ on the projectivization $\mathbb{P}(E^*)$ is pseudo-effective).
- A Cartier divisor $D$ on $X$ is called big if its Iitaka–Kodaira dimension equals $\dim X$, i.e. $h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD))$ grows like $m^{\dim X}$.
- $K_X$ denotes the canonical divisor of $X$.

Question: Suppose $X$ is a rationally connected projective manifold whose tangent bundle $T_X$ is pseudo-effective. Must the anti-canonical divisor $-K_X$ be big?

Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective manifold. Recall that:

- $X$ is called rationally connected if any two general points of $X$ can be joined by a rational curve (equivalently, by a chain of rational curves).
- A vector bundle $E$ on $X$ is called pseudo-effective if, for every ample line bundle $A$ on $X$, there exists a positive integer $m$ and a positive integer $k$ such that $S^{mk}E \otimes A^{\otimes k}$ has a non-zero global section (equivalently, the tautological line bundle $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}(E^*)}(1)$ on the projectivization $\mathbb{P}(E^*)$ is pseudo-effective).
- A Cartier divisor $D$ on $X$ is called big if its Iitaka–Kodaira dimension equals $\dim X$, i.e. $h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD))$ grows like $m^{\dim X}$.
- $K_X$ denotes the canonical divisor of $X$.

Question: Suppose $X$ is a rationally connected projective manifold whose tangent bundle $T_X$ is pseudo-effective. Must the anti-canonical divisor $-K_X$ be big?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is posed as an open question in work on projective manifolds with pseudo-effective tangent bundle (Hosono–Iwai–Matsumura). Partial results exist: for rationally connected compact manifolds with strongly pseudo-effective tangent bundle, there is a finite cover whose universal cover has big anti-canonical bundle. Recent papers (2023–2025) on positivity of tangent sheaves and compact Kähler manifolds with nef anti-canonical bundle still treat this as an open problem in full generality.

After replacing $X$ by a suitable finite étale cover, consider the Albanese map $\alpha\colon X \to \mathrm{Alb}(X)$, and let $F$ denote a general fiber of $\alpha$.

(a) Prove or disprove: the anti-canonical divisor $-K_F$ is big, or $F$ is projective.

(b) Prove or disprove: the Albanese map $\alpha\colon X \to \mathrm{Alb}(X)$ is a maximally rationally connected (MRC) fibration of $X$ (that is, its general fibers are rationally connected and any rational curve in $X$ meeting a general fiber is contained in it).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The projective case has structure results (smooth fibration onto a flat projective manifold with rationally connected fibers), and partial results exist in the Kähler setting (e.g., for threefolds with nef anti-canonical bundle and recent work on Albanese maps for Kähler manifolds with nef anticanonical bundle). Recent work establishes that the blow-up of a Hirzebruch surface at three general points has (strongly) pseudo-effective tangent bundle, and there are characterizations of pseudo-effective tangent bundles for non-uniruled surfaces via $K_S$ nef and $c_2(S)=0$. Let $(X,\Delta)$ be a klt (Kawamata log terminal) pair such that $X$ is a smooth complex projective variety and $-(K_X+\Delta)$ is nef. Does there exist an orbifold morphism
$$\rho:(X,\Delta)\longrightarrow (R,\Delta_R)$$
satisfying all of the following:

1. $(R,\Delta_R)$ is a klt pair with $R$ smooth and $c_1(K_R+\Delta_R)=0$;
2. the general orbifold fiber $(X_r,\Delta_r)$ of $\rho$ is slope rationally connected (i.e., for a general pair of points there is an orbifold rational curve whose pullback of $T_{X_r}(-\Delta_r)$ — equivalently, the orbifold tangent sheaf — is ample, or, in the standard formulation, the orbifold fiber admits no positive-slope quotient of its orbifold cotangent sheaf with respect to any movable class);
3. the fibration $\rho$ is locally trivial with respect to pairs, meaning that locally on the base (in the analytic or étale topology), $(X,\Delta)$ is isomorphic to a product of pairs $(R,\Delta_R)\times (F,\Delta_F)$ over the base, where $(F,\Delta_F)$ is the general orbifold fiber.

Here an orbifold morphism $\rho:(X,\Delta)\to(R,\Delta_R)$ is a surjective morphism $\rho:X\to R$ compatible with the boundary divisors in the orbifold sense, and the general orbifold fiber $(X_r,\Delta_r)$ is the pair obtained by restricting $\Delta$ (minus its vertical part) to a general fiber $X_r=\rho^{-1}(r)$.

Consider rotating massive stars (initial mass roughly 15–25 solar masses with rotation) in which helium burning and subsequent carbon shell burning activate the alpha-induced reactions on $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}$, namely $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}(\alpha,n)^{25}\mathrm{Mg}$ and $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}(\alpha,\gamma)^{26}\mathrm{Mg}$. The former liberates neutrons that drive the slow neutron-capture (s) process, producing nuclei heavier than iron; its seeds are later partly photodisintegrated during the subsequent core-collapse supernova explosion to yield the proton-rich (p) nuclides.

Recent sub-Coulomb $\alpha$-transfer experiments suggest that the astrophysical reaction rate of $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}(\alpha,n)^{25}\mathrm{Mg}$ in the relevant Gamow window (corresponding to helium- and carbon-burning temperatures, roughly $T \sim 0.2$–$1$ GK) may be smaller by up to a factor of about 5 than the previously adopted reference value.

Problem: Determine the correct stellar reaction rate $N_A\langle\sigma v\rangle(T)$ of $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}(\alpha,n)^{25}\mathrm{Mg}$ (and of the competing $(\alpha,\gamma)$ channel) over the temperature range relevant to helium and carbon burning in rotating massive stars, and quantify how the resulting rate modifies (i) the efficiency of the weak s-process and the integrated production factors of s-only isotopes (e.g.\ $^{70}$Ge, $^{76}$Se, $^{80}$Kr, $^{86,87}$Sr) and (ii) the yields of the p-nuclides produced when the s-process seeds are processed by the subsequent supernova shock.

Develop a theoretical nuclear mass model capable of predicting atomic masses M(Z,N) of exotic neutron-rich nuclei (in particular near the neutron shell closures N = 126 and N = 184) with sufficient accuracy to be used in rapid neutron-capture (r-process) nucleosynthesis simulations. Concretely, construct a self-consistent mean-field (relativistic or non-relativistic, e.g. Skyrme-Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov, Gogny-HFB, or covariant density-functional) framework, augmented by beyond-mean-field corrections (such as quadrupole and octupole correlations obtained from the Generator Coordinate Method, and a proper treatment of odd-A and odd-odd nuclei including time-reversal symmetry breaking), such that:

1. The model reproduces all experimentally known atomic masses within current measurement uncertainties.
2. Predictions of unknown masses M(Z,N) for neutron-rich nuclei relevant to the r-process agree across independent parameterizations to substantially better than the current spread of approximately ±5 MeV near N = 126 and N = 184, so that the resulting (n,γ) neutron-capture rates (computed, e.g., via Hauser–Feshbach statistical theory using these masses as input) do not vary by the present 3–5 orders of magnitude between models.
3. The same model simultaneously reproduces, within accepted experimental error bars, additional nuclear (pseudo-)observables: charge radii, neutron-skin thicknesses, fission barriers and shape isomers, spectroscopic data such as 2⁺ excitation energies and moments of inertia, properties of infinite symmetric and pure neutron matter from ab initio calculations, and global neutron-star observables such as the maximum gravitational mass and the mass–radius relation.

Provide such a model (or prove its existence/non-existence under the constraints above) and quantify the residual uncertainty in r-process abundance predictions stemming from nuclear masses.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is a long-standing open challenge in nuclear astrophysics. Recent literature (2023–2025) on mass models (BSkG3, relativistic DFT, machine-learning-augmented mass tables) continues to report mass deviations of several MeV for very neutron-rich nuclei near N=126 and N=184, with corresponding order-of-magnitude spreads in (n,γ) rates, indicating the problem remains open.

Consider a cosmological model in which the spatial scale factor is replaced by a complex, branch-cut analytic continuation of the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker scale factor, so that the universe undergoes a contracting phase followed by an expanding phase joined across a horizontal branch cut (no singular Big Bang). In an anisotropic Bianchi-type generalization of this background, introduce the dimensionless ratios that measure, in units of the total energy density, the contributions of (i) spatial curvature, (ii) matter, (iii) radiation, and (iv) shear anisotropy, as functions of a thermodynamic-like dimensionless parameter ε that characterizes the equation of state of an effective fluid driving the contraction/expansion. Assume that during the final stage of contraction the curvature, matter, and radiation ratios remain "locked in" (i.e. effectively constant in their relative scaling), while the anisotropy-related ratio scales as a power of the scale factor whose sign is governed by ε, so that taking ε<0 (interpreted as a dark-matter-like component) reverses the scaling behavior of the anisotropy ratio.

Problem. Within this framework, give a fully consistent dynamical explanation of how the smoothness (near-isotropy) of the cosmic temperature fluctuations can arise: specifically, derive conditions on ε and on the locked-in ratios under which the anisotropy ratio is driven to arbitrarily small values at the end of the contracting phase and remains small throughout the subsequent expansion, and show that such conditions are compatible with the analytic structure of the branch-cut scale factor and with the observed level of CMB temperature fluctuations.

Consider the framework of "branch-cut cosmology," in which the cosmological scale factor a(t) of a Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker-type universe is analytically continued to a multi-valued complex function defined on a Riemann surface with a branch cut, so that the classical primordial singularity is replaced by a finite branch-cut transition region connecting a contracting pre-bounce sheet to an expanding post-bounce sheet. At leading order, the dynamics of the (complexified) scale factor are governed by classical Einstein-type equations of motion obtained from a Hořava–Lifshitz-style gravitational action (with higher spatial-derivative curvature terms) coupled, possibly, to a scalar inflaton field.

Provide a fully quantum-mechanical reformulation of this model. Concretely:

1. Starting from a Hořava–Lifshitz gravitational Lagrangian density coupled to matter, perform an ADM (Arnowitt–Deser–Misner) decomposition adapted to the branch-cut geometry and derive the corresponding Hamiltonian constraint H = 0 in which the dynamical variable is the complex branch-cut scale factor β(t) and its conjugate momentum π_β.

2. Promote β and π_β to operators satisfying canonical commutation relations, choose an operator-ordering prescription (with explicit ordering parameters), and obtain the resulting Wheeler–DeWitt-type equation Ĥ Ψ(β) = 0 — equivalently, a Schrödinger-type equation with a (generically non-linear) effective potential — governing the wave function Ψ of the universe on the branch-cut Riemann surface.

3. Specify boundary/matching conditions for Ψ across the branch cut connecting the contracting and expanding sheets, and demonstrate that the resulting quantum evolution describes a non-singular quantum transition (a "quantum leap") between the two phases consistent with the Bekenstein entropy bound.

4. Show that, in an appropriate semiclassical/WKB limit, the quantum description reduces to the leading-order classical branch-cut equations of motion, and analyze quantum corrections to observables in the primordial transition region.

Consider a cosmological model in which the cosmic scale factor is analytically continued to a complex variable and represented on a multi-sheeted Riemann surface obtained by introducing branch cuts in the complex plane (a "branch-cut cosmology"). In such a model, the physical evolution is parameterized by a complex time variable whose trajectory traverses successive cut-planes (sheets) connected across branch cuts, and the usual real cosmological time emerges as a projection of this trajectory.

Problem: Formulate a coherent and internally consistent prescription for mapping the temporal evolution across the cut-plane / Riemann-sheet structure of such a model. Specifically:

(a) Define precisely the complex time variable, the location and orientation of the branch cuts, and the rule by which a continuous evolution trajectory passes from one Riemann sheet to the next.

(b) Show that the resulting evolution map is single-valued and continuous in the relevant physical observables (scale factor, Hubble parameter, energy densities), and that it reduces to standard cosmological evolution in the appropriate real-time limit.

(c) Verify that the prescription is consistent with the Einstein field equations (or their analytic continuation) on each sheet and with the matching conditions across each branch cut.

Provide such a prescription, or prove that no such globally consistent evolution mapping exists under stated minimal assumptions.

Consider a cosmological model (the "branch-cut universe") whose scale factor is analytically continued across a branch cut, replacing the classical Big Bang singularity with a smooth contraction-to-expansion transition. The dynamics depend on a real parameter epsilon that controls the scaling behavior of characteristic length and density ratios near the bounce. Suppose that in the final phase of the contraction era, taking epsilon < 0 reverses the scaling behavior of one such ratio while the remaining ratios remain locked in their previous scaling.

Formulate and analyze the role of a pressureless dark matter component in this framework. Specifically:

(a) Incorporate a cold dark matter fluid (with equation of state w = 0) into the modified Friedmann equations of the branch-cut model and determine how its energy density evolves through the contraction era, the bounce, and the subsequent expansion era.

(b) Determine whether the choice epsilon < 0 (associated with the reversed scaling behavior in the contraction phase) can be consistently identified with, or sourced by, the dark matter component; in particular, derive the relation between epsilon and the dark matter density parameter at the bounce.

(c) Establish whether dark matter is necessary for the existence of the bounce in this model, and whether structure-formation observables (e.g., the matter power spectrum on linear scales) are compatible with standard late-time cosmology in the resulting solution.

Consider the branch-cut cosmology framework, a nonsingular extension of standard Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker cosmology in which the scale factor a(t) is analytically continued onto a Riemann surface so that the cosmological singularity at t = 0 is replaced by a branch cut. Concretely, the usual scale factor a(t) is replaced by a complex-valued function a_β(t) depending on a dimensionless parameter β ∈ (0, 1] such that, in the limit β → 1, one recovers the standard cosmological scale factor, while for β < 1 the function a_β(t) is everywhere nonzero and develops a branch-cut structure that removes the Big Bang singularity. Assuming the usual minimally coupled inflaton-like scalar field dynamics on this analytically extended background, with quantum fluctuations of the energy density propagating on the branch-cut geometry:

(a) Derive an explicit prediction for the primordial scalar power spectrum P_ζ(k) of energy-density fluctuations that seed cosmological structure formation in the branch-cut cosmology, expressed as a function of comoving wavenumber k and of the model parameter β, including its scalar spectral index n_s(β) and any running α_s(β) = dn_s/d ln k.

(b) Determine whether the resulting P_ζ(k), n_s(β), and α_s(β) are compatible with the Cosmic Microwave Background temperature, polarization, and lensing constraints reported by the Planck satellite mission, in particular the measured values of n_s and the upper bound on the tensor-to-scalar ratio r, and identify the range of β (if any) for which the branch-cut prediction is observationally viable.

Consider a primordial ensemble of universes (a "multiverse") that are mutually coupled through thermal contact while immersed in a common thermal bath at some initial temperature T_0. Suppose this ensemble undergoes a contracting (crunch) phase, modeled by a time-dependent scale factor a(t) with da/dt < 0 over a finite interval, during which the constituent universes exchange energy and equilibrate. At a decoupling time t_d, the universes thermally decouple and evolve independently thereafter.

Formulate and determine, within a consistent cosmological framework (for instance, a Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker model coupled to a thermal-bath energy-momentum content together with an inter-universe heat-exchange term), the temperature evolution T(t) inherited by a single member universe (taken to be "our" universe) for t > t_d. In particular:

(a) Specify the equations governing the joint thermodynamic evolution of the multiverse during the contraction phase, including the form of the inter-universe energy exchange and the equation of state of the thermal bath.

(b) Derive the decoupling condition that determines t_d and the post-decoupling initial temperature T(t_d).

(c) Obtain T(t) for t > t_d as a function of the scale factor a(t) of our universe, and identify the observable thermal imprints (if any) on its subsequent expansion history that distinguish this scenario from a universe with no prior multiverse thermal contact.

At a decoupling time t_d, the universes thermally decouple and evolve independently thereafter.

In particular:

(a) Specify the equations governing the joint thermodynamic evolution of the multiverse during the contraction phase, including the form of the inter-universe energy exchange and the equation of state of the thermal bath.

(b) Derive the decoupling condition that determines t_d and the post-decoupling initial temperature T(t_d).

(c) Obtain T(t) for t > t_d as a function of the scale factor a(t) of our universe, and identify the observable thermal imprints (if any) on its subsequent expansion history that distinguish this scenario from a universe with no prior multiverse thermal contact.

Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk in the complex plane, and let $dS$ denote normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$ (so $\int_{\mathbb{D}} dS = 1$). The Bergman space $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is the Hilbert space of analytic functions $f : \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{C}$ such that
$$\|f\|^2 = \int_{\mathbb{D}} |f(z)|^2 \, dS(z) < \infty,$$
endowed with the inner product $\langle f, g \rangle = \int_{\mathbb{D}} f(z)\overline{g(z)}\, dS(z)$. A closed subspace $J \subseteq L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is called $z$-invariant (invariant under the Bergman shift) if $zf \in J$ for every $f \in J$.

Provide a complete characterization (description / classification) of all $z$-invariant closed subspaces $J$ of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$, analogous to Beurling's theorem for the Hardy space $H^2$ of the disk.

A full characterization of the invariant subspaces of the Bergman space $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ remains a well-known open problem. A complete geometric characterization of zero sequences for the unweighted Bergman space $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ remains open. Significant partial results exist: Horowitz (1974/77) gave sufficient conditions and factorization, Luecking (1996) characterized zero sets for weighted Bergman spaces under certain conditions, and more recent work (e.g., Pau–Peláez–Perälä, 2019, and others) has extended such results to weighted settings with doubling or Bekollé–Bonami weights. The problem of finding an effective Hardy-type factorization for the Bergman space is a well-known long-standing open problem in the function theory of Bergman spaces. Significant partial progress has been made: Hedenmalm constructed canonical contractive zero-divisors playing the role of Blaschke products; Duren–Khavinson–Shapiro–Sundberg extended this to weighted Bergman spaces; Aleman–Richter–Sundberg proved a Beurling-type invariant-subspace theorem. However, no complete and effective analog of the Hardy factorization (zero-divisor / singular-type / outer-type factors with the full strength of the Hardy theory) is known, and the problem is generally regarded as still open.

representations.normalized:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk and let $dS$ denote normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. Define the Bergman space
$$L^2_a(\mathbb{D})=\Big\{f\in\mathrm{Hol}(\mathbb{D}):\|f\|^2_{L^2_a}=\int_\mathbb{D}|f(z)|^2\,dS(z)<\infty\Big\},$$
and the Hardy space $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ of holomorphic $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ with $\sup_{0<r<1}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(re^{i\theta})|^2\,\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}<\infty$.

A function $\varphi\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is called an inner divisor (in the Bergman sense) if it has unit norm and
$$\int_\mathbb{D} (|\varphi(z)|^2-1)\, q(z)\,dS(z)=0$$
for every bounded holomorphic $q$ in the invariant subspace generated by $\varphi$ (equivalently, $\varphi$ is the extremal/canonical divisor of its zero-based invariant subspace).

For such $\varphi$, let $\Phi_\varphi:\overline{\mathbb{D}}\to\mathbb{R}$ be the unique function satisfying
$$\Delta\Phi_\varphi(z)=|\varphi(z)|^2-1\quad\text{on }\mathbb{D},\qquad \Phi_\varphi\big|_{\partial\mathbb{D}}=0,$$
together with the natural boundary condition on the gradient appropriate for inner divisors (so that $\Phi_\varphi\ge 0$ on $\mathbb{D}$).

It is known that for every $f\in H^2(\mathbb{D})$,
$$\|\varphi f\|^2_{L^2_a(\mathbb{D})}=\|f\|^2_{L^2_a(\mathbb{D})}+\int_\mathbb{D}|f'(z)|^2\,\Phi_\varphi(z)\,dS(z). \qquad (\ast)$$

Determine precisely the class of inner divisors $\varphi\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ for which the identity $(\ast)$ extends to all $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$, where both sides are allowed to take the value $+\infty$.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk and let $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ denote the Bergman space of holomorphic functions on $\mathbb{D}$ that are square-integrable with respect to normalized area measure. A finite zero divisor is a function $\varphi\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ that vanishes precisely on a prescribed finite multi-set $\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}\subset\mathbb{D}$ (counted with multiplicities) and is extremal/canonical in the usual sense (the contractive divisor associated with this finite zero set).

For a positive weight $w(z)=|\varphi(z)|^2$ on $\mathbb{D}$, let $\Gamma_w(z,\zeta)$ be the Green function of the fourth-order weighted biharmonic operator
$$L_w u(z)\;=\;\Delta_z\!\bigl(w(z)^{-1}\,\Delta_z u(z)\bigr),\qquad z\in\mathbb{D},$$
with Dirichlet (clamped-plate) boundary conditions
$$\Gamma_w(z,\zeta)=0,\qquad \partial_n\Gamma_w(z,\zeta)=0,\qquad z\in\partial\mathbb{D},\ \zeta\in\mathbb{D},$$
where $\partial_n$ is the exterior unit normal derivative on the unit circle.

Question. Is it true that for every finite zero divisor $\varphi\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$, every boundary point $z\in\partial\mathbb{D}$, and every interior point $\zeta\in\mathbb{D}$,
$$\partial_n\,\Delta_z\,\Gamma_{|\varphi|^2}(z,\zeta)\;\ge\;0\ ?$$

For a finite sequence $A=(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ of points in $\mathbb{D}$ (counted with multiplicity), the associated Bergman zero divisor (canonical, or contractive, divisor) $\varphi_A$ is the unique extremal solution of the problem
$$\varphi_A(0)=\max\{\operatorname{Re} f(0):\ f\in A^2,\ \|f\|=1,\ f(a_j)=0\ \text{for all } j\},$$
normalized so $\varphi_A(0)>0$. The function $\varphi_A$ extends continuously to $\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ in the cases considered below, so $\arg\varphi_A(e^{i\theta})$ is well defined.

Suppose $A\subset B$ are two finite zero sequences in $\mathbb{D}$ (with $A$ a sub-multiset of $B$), and let $\varphi_A,\varphi_B$ be their associated Bergman zero divisors.

(a) Prove or disprove: as $z=e^{i\theta}$ traverses the unit circle once counterclockwise (i.e.\ $\theta$ increases from $0$ to $2\pi$), the argument $\arg\bigl(\varphi_B(z)/\varphi_A(z)\bigr)$ is a monotonically nondecreasing function of $\theta$.

Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk and let $dS$ denote normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. Let $\omega : \overline{\mathbb{D}} \to (0,\infty)$ be a $C^\infty$-smooth positive weight on the closed unit disk with the reproducing property at the origin for bounded harmonic functions:
$$h(0) = \int_{\mathbb{D}} h(z)\,\omega(z)\,dS(z)$$
for every bounded harmonic function $h$ on $\mathbb{D}$. Suppose moreover that $\omega$ satisfies the curvature condition
$$\Delta \log \omega(z) \;\geq\; -\frac{1}{(1-|z|^2)^2}, \qquad z \in \mathbb{D},$$
where $\Delta$ is the standard Laplacian. Let $\Gamma_\omega(z,\zeta)$ denote the Green function for the weighted biharmonic operator $\Delta\,\omega^{-1}\,\Delta$ on $\mathbb{D}$ with Dirichlet boundary conditions (so $\Gamma_\omega(\cdot,\zeta)$ and its normal derivative vanish on $\partial\mathbb{D}$, and $\Delta\,\omega^{-1}\,\Delta_z\,\Gamma_\omega(z,\zeta) = \delta_\zeta(z)$).

Prove or disprove: under the above hypotheses, $\Gamma_\omega(z,\zeta) \geq 0$ for all $(z,\zeta) \in \mathbb{D}\times\mathbb{D}$.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ be the Bergman space of holomorphic functions $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ with
$$\|f\|^2=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f(z)|^2\,dA(z)<\infty,$$
where $dA$ is the normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. A sequence $A=\{a_n\}\subset\mathbb{D}$ (with multiplicities) is called a zero sequence for $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ if there exists a nonzero $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ whose zero set (counted with multiplicity) contains $A$. Define
$$I(A)=\{f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D}):f\text{ vanishes on }A\text{ (with multiplicity)}\},$$
which is a closed subspace of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ invariant under multiplication by $z$. Let $\varphi_A\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ denote the extremal (canonical) zero divisor associated with $A$, namely the unique solution of the extremal problem
$$\sup\{\operatorname{Re} f(0_A):f\in I(A),\ \|f\|=1\},$$
where $0_A$ is the lowest-order nontrivial Taylor coefficient functional determined by $A$ (so that $\varphi_A$ has unit norm in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ and vanishes on $A$).

Question: Does $\varphi_A$ generate $I(A)$ as an invariant subspace under multiplication by $z$? Equivalently, is the linear span of $\{\varphi_A,\,z\varphi_A,\,z^2\varphi_A,\dots\}$ dense in $I(A)$?

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $dA$ be normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. For $0<p<\infty$, the Bergman space $A^p$ consists of all analytic functions $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ with $\|f\|_p^p=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f|^p\,dA<\infty$. A sequence $A=\{a_n\}\subset\mathbb{D}$ is called an $A^p$-zero sequence if there exists $f\in A^p\setminus\{0\}$ whose zero set (with multiplicities) is exactly $A$. For an $A^p$-zero sequence $A$, the (canonical / extremal) zero divisor $\varphi_A\in A^p$ is the unique solution of the extremal problem
$$\sup\{\operatorname{Re} f(0):\ f\in A^p,\ \|f\|_p\le 1,\ f\text{ vanishes on }A\}.$$
Given an $A^p$-zero sequence $A$ that does not contain the origin, let $A\cup\{0\}$ denote the sequence obtained by adjoining a simple zero at the origin, and let $\varphi_{A\cup\{0\}}$ be the corresponding extremal zero divisor.

Prove or disprove: the quotient
$$\frac{\varphi_{A\cup\{0\}}(z)}{\varphi_A(z)}$$
is a bounded analytic function on $\mathbb{D}$, for every $A^p$-zero sequence $A$.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk. Denote by $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ the Hardy space of holomorphic functions $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ with $\|f\|_{H^2}^2=\sup_{0<r<1}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(re^{i\theta})|^2\,d\theta<\infty$, and by $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ the (unweighted) Bergman space of holomorphic functions $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ with $\|f\|_{L^2_a}^2=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f(z)|^2\,dA(z)<\infty$, where $dA$ is normalized area measure. The multiplier space $M(H^2,L^2_a)$ consists of holomorphic functions $\varphi:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ such that $\varphi f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ for every $f\in H^2(\mathbb{D})$, normed by
$$\|\varphi\|_{M(H^2,L^2_a)}=\sup\{\|\varphi f\|_{L^2_a}:\|f\|_{H^2}\le 1\}.$$

It is known that any $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ which is cyclic in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is also cyclic in $A^{-\infty}$.

Question: Does the converse hold? That is, if $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is cyclic in $A^{-\infty}$, must $f$ be cyclic in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$?

$$\|f\|^2=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f(z)|^2\,dA(z)<\infty,$$
where $dA$ is normalized area measure. A closed subspace $M\subseteq L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is called $z$-invariant if $zM\subseteq M$. The index of such a subspace is defined by

Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk. Let $\mu$ be a positive Borel measure on $\mathbb{D}$ such that:

(i) point evaluation $p \mapsto p(z_0)$ is bounded on the space of holomorphic polynomials with respect to the $L^2(\mu)$-norm, for every $z_0 \in \mathbb{D}$; and

(ii) $\mu$ reproduces the origin in the sense that $\int_{\mathbb{D}} p(z)\, d\mu(z) = p(0)$ for every holomorphic polynomial $p$.

Let $P^2(\mu)$ be the closure of the holomorphic polynomials in $L^2(\mu)$; it is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of analytic functions on $\mathbb{D}$. Define the Cauchy dual of $P^2(\mu)$ to be the Hilbert space of analytic functions $g$ on $\mathbb{D}$ for which the Cauchy pairing
$$\langle f, g \rangle_C = \lim_{r \to 1^-} \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(re^{i\theta})\,\overline{g(re^{i\theta})}\, d\theta$$
(suitably interpreted via boundary behavior) extends to a bounded linear functional on $P^2(\mu)$, with norm given by the operator norm of this functional. The Cauchy dual is itself a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of analytic functions on $\mathbb{D}$.

Question: Is the reproducing kernel of the Cauchy dual of $P^2(\mu)$ always a complete Nevanlinna–Pick kernel?

(Recall: a positive definite kernel $k$ on a set $X$ is a complete Nevanlinna–Pick kernel if the matrix-valued Pick interpolation theorem holds for the multiplier algebra of the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space; equivalently, $1 - 1/k(x,y)$ has exactly one positive square after normalization at a basepoint.)

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk, and let $\omega:\mathbb{D}\to(0,\infty)$ be a logarithmically subharmonic weight (i.e., $\log\omega$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb{D}$), normalized so that the origin is a reproducing point in the sense that $\int_{\mathbb{D}} f(z)\,\omega(z)\,dA(z) = f(0)$ whenever $f$ is holomorphic and integrable against $\omega\,dA$ (here $dA$ is normalized area measure). Consider the weighted Bergman space
$$L^2_a(\mathbb{D},\omega)=\Big\{f\text{ holomorphic on }\mathbb{D}:\ \|f\|^2_\omega=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f(z)|^2\omega(z)\,dA(z)<\infty\Big\},$$
and let $k(z,\lambda)$ denote its reproducing kernel.

A reproducing kernel $k$ on $\mathbb{D}$ is said to be of McCullough–Richter (Bergman-type) form if there exist a holomorphic function $\psi:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{D}$ with $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi'(0)\neq 0$, and a positive semidefinite kernel $v:\mathbb{D}\times\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ with $v(0,0)=0$, such that
$$k(z,\lambda)=\frac{1-v(z,\lambda)}{1-\overline{\psi(\lambda)}\psi(z)},\qquad z,\lambda\in\mathbb{D}.$$

Question: For every logarithmically subharmonic weight $\omega$ as above, is the reproducing kernel of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D},\omega)$ of McCullough–Richter form?

Consider a social organization or collective modeled as a complex adaptive system, formalized as a time-dependent dynamical system whose state x(t) evolves under both endogenous interactions among its agents and exogenous shocks. Propose a precise, operational framework that distinguishes the following three notions, so that each can be quantified independently from the others on such a system:

(i) Robustness: the structural capacity of the system to withstand shocks, i.e., a property of the system's configuration (e.g., its interaction topology, redundancy, or buffering capacity) that bounds the immediate deviation of x(t) from a reference state when a shock is applied.

(ii) Stability: the dynamical property describing the system's tendency to return to, or remain near, an equilibrium or reference trajectory in the absence of further perturbations (e.g., in the sense of Lyapunov stability or asymptotic stability of x(t)).

(iii) Resilience: the systemic, time-dependent capacity of the system both to withstand shocks and to recover from them, understood as the composition of a structural component (robustness) and a dynamic component (adaptivity), where adaptivity denotes the system's ability to reorganize its internal structure or parameters in order to overcome the impact of a shock.

Specifically, define rigorous, measurable indicators R_struct(x,t) for robustness, S(x,t) for stability, and Res(x,t) for resilience on this class of models, such that:
- Res depends explicitly on time and on the shock history;
- Res can be decomposed as a function of R_struct (structural dimension) and an adaptivity indicator A(x,t) (dynamic dimension);
- The three indicators are logically independent: there exist model instances exhibiting any prescribed combination of high/low values of R_struct, S, and A.

Show that such a framework exists and is consistent across standard families of complex adaptive system models (e.g., networked agent-based models, coupled ODE systems on graphs), or otherwise identify obstructions to a unified definition.

Consider a networked system modeled as a (possibly time-varying) graph G = (V, E) in which each node i ∈ V carries an internal state x_i(t) evolving according to a prescribed dynamics, and in which interactions along edges (i, j) ∈ E permit the exchange of quantities between nodes and can propagate failures. A node is said to have "failed" at time t if its state lies in a designated failure set F_i ⊂ State_i. Let S(t) ⊂ V denote the set of failed nodes at time t.

Define:
(a) A robustness functional R(G, dynamics) that quantifies the system's ability to maintain functionality (e.g., to keep |S(t)|/|V| below a threshold, or to return to a reference state) when subjected to perturbations of either (i) exogenous type — rare external shocks applied to a subset of nodes or edges — or (ii) endogenous type — internal failure cascades triggered by individual node failures and amplified through the network topology and the inter-node dynamics.
(b) A systemic-risk measure ρ(G, dynamics) drawn from the class of measures used for interconnected systems (for example, monetary risk measures applied to aggregate losses Σ_i L_i, or CoVaR/Shapley-type allocations, or expected fraction of failed nodes under a stress scenario), which assigns a real number quantifying the risk that "large parts of the system are destroyed."

Problem. Provide a precise mathematical relationship between R and ρ within a single modeling framework that simultaneously accounts for:
1. exogenous rare-shock contributions to systemic risk, and
2. endogenous cascade contributions arising from the coupling of intra-node dynamics with inter-node exchange along the network.

Specifically: construct a class of dynamic network models for which one can prove inequalities, monotonicity relations, or functional identities linking R(G, dynamics) and ρ(G, dynamics), and identify network and dynamical conditions under which high robustness is equivalent to, implies, or is independent of low systemic risk.

Consider a dynamical system modeling a complex adaptive system (for instance an ecological community or a social organization) given by a state trajectory x(t) in some state space X, subject to perturbations. Classically, the system is called resilient at an equilibrium x* if, after a perturbation that displaces the state away from x*, the trajectory returns to x* as t tends to infinity. However, many real systems are non-stationary: their underlying dynamics evolve over time, they may possess multiple stable states, or they may lack any well-defined reference equilibrium at all (evolving systems never re-attain exactly identical states; highly volatile organizations admit no canonical reference state).

Formulate a mathematically rigorous notion of resilience that:

(a) does not require the system to return to a single fixed equilibrium x*,
(b) admits recovery to a different stable state, or to a gradually drifting reference trajectory x*(t), as a legitimate form of resilient response,
(c) reduces to the classical equilibrium-return notion in the time-invariant, single-attractor case,
(d) is operational for systems whose reference state is not a priori defined, in the sense that resilience can be detected or quantified from the observed trajectory and perturbation alone.

In particular, determine whether such a definition can be given uniformly across classes of models (deterministic ODEs, stochastic processes, agent-based models), and characterize the conditions under which it agrees with, or strictly extends, classical equilibrium-based resilience.

At the broad scale, a "society" is regarded as a system of systems: a collection S = {S_1, S_2, ..., S_k} of interacting subsystems (e.g., economic, political, cultural, technological) together with a coupling structure describing their mutual interactions. At the finer scale, a "social organization" is a formal or informal group O = (I, G, E) consisting of a set I of interrelated individuals, a collective goal G that the individuals jointly pursue, and an environment E in which the group is embedded.

Develop a principled delimitation criterion that specifies which class of social systems a quantitative model of social resilience should target. Concretely:

(a) Provide a formal definition of the class C of admissible target systems for a quantitative model of social resilience, distinguishing between system-of-systems societies and goal-directed organizations of interrelated individuals.

(b) State, with justification, which kinds of social systems must be excluded from C (for instance, aggregates lacking a shared collective goal, transient crowds, or systems without an identifiable environment), and characterize the boundary cases.

(c) For the admissible class C, specify the minimal structural ingredients (agents, interactions, goals, environment, observables) that any quantitative resilience model must incorporate, and argue why these ingredients are both necessary and sufficient to make the notion of resilience well-defined and measurable.

Consider an organization modeled as a collective system consisting of a set of agents A = {a_1, ..., a_n} together with an interaction network G = (A, E) describing their working relations, a vector of capabilities C(t) ∈ R^k that the organization possesses at time t (e.g., production, coordination, knowledge-processing capacities), and a stochastic crisis process X(t) that acts as an external stress, perturbing both the network G and the agents' states. Suppose that resilience is not a property of any individual agent but an emergent property of the collective, defined formally as a functional R[A, G, C, X] that measures the ability of the system to maintain or increase its capability vector C(t) after the onset of a crisis X(t).

(a) Propose a precise mathematical definition of the functional R[A, G, C, X] (the "focus" of organizational resilience) that captures the emergent, system-level nature of resilience rather than aggregating individual traits.

(b) Within this framework, identify structural conditions on (A, G, C) — for instance, on network topology, redundancy, modularity, feedback loops, or adaptive rules governing the evolution of G and C under X — that are necessary and/or sufficient for the organization to satisfy R[A, G, C, X] ≥ R(0), i.e., to maintain or enhance its capabilities under the crisis process.

(c) Characterize, in this formalism, why two organizations with identical initial capability vectors C(0) but different (A, G) can exhibit qualitatively different outcomes under the same crisis process X — one thriving and one failing — and produce a rigorous criterion separating the two regimes.

Consider a social organization modeled as a complex adaptive system: a collection of heterogeneous, interacting agents, each characterized by an internal state and a set of interaction rules with other agents. The macroscopic behavior of the organization is assumed to emerge from local interactions (bottom-up modeling), permitting self-organization and exhibiting path dependence, so that the trajectory of the system depends on its history and not solely on present external conditions. Suppose the organization is subjected to an exogenous shock at time t = 0 that perturbs agent states. In classical resilience analysis, one distinguishes an absorption phase (during which the system resists the shock) from a recovery phase (during which it returns toward a reference state), with two separable time scales. In the present setting, assume instead that changes in robustness (capacity to absorb perturbations) and adaptivity (capacity to reorganize) occur instantaneously and concurrently, so that absorption and recovery time scales are not cleanly separable.

Formulate a mathematical modeling framework for social resilience under these assumptions. In particular:

(a) Specify what classes of agent-based or interaction-network models are required to faithfully represent heterogeneous agent properties, explicit pairwise (or higher-order) interactions, and endogenous self-organization.

(b) Identify quantitative observables (order parameters, macroscopic indicators) that capture resilience when absorption and recovery dynamics are entangled and cannot be decomposed into two separate phases.

(c) Determine how path dependence should be encoded (e.g., via memory kernels, hysteresis, or history-dependent interaction rules) and characterize the modeling consequences—such as non-Markovianity, non-stationarity, and the failure of equilibrium-based resilience metrics—that follow from adopting a complex-adaptive-systems viewpoint.

State and justify the modeling consequences (mathematical structure, required ingredients, and qualitative predictions) that necessarily follow from these assumptions.

Consider an organization modeled as a set of agents together with relations among them. Several network representations can be used to encode such an organization:

1. Direct interaction networks: simple graphs G=(V,E) where edges represent observed interactions between pairs of agents.
2. Signed-relation networks: graphs in which each edge (i,j) carries a weight ω_{ij} ∈ ℝ whose sign indicates a positive or negative social relation (e.g., trust vs. distrust, cooperation vs. antagonism).
3. Bipartite and multi-edge networks: graphs G=(V_1∪V_2,E) with E⊆V_1×V_2 (agents linked to affiliations, events, or artifacts), possibly with multiple parallel edges between the same pair.
4. Knowledge graphs: directed labeled multigraphs whose edges are typed relations (predicates) between entities, from which one may extract one-mode projections.
5. Multilayer / multiplex networks: a family {G_α=(V,E_α)}_{α∈L} of graphs on a common (or aligned) vertex set indexed by layers α (different relation types or contexts), together with inter-layer couplings.
6. Hypergraphs: pairs H=(V,𝓔) with 𝓔⊆2^V, where each hyperedge e∈𝓔 represents a group interaction among an arbitrary subset of agents.

Problem. Identify and characterize the structural and dynamical differences between these network representations that are essential when modeling the resilience of social organizations. Specifically:

(a) For each pair of representations above, exhibit organizational features (e.g., signed balance, group-level interactions, role asymmetries, multi-relational coupling) that can be expressed in one representation but are lost or distorted under projection to the other.

(b) Determine which representation is minimally sufficient to capture (i) signed social relations ω_{ij} with positive and negative components, (ii) genuine k-body group interactions for k≥3 that are not reducible to pairwise interactions, and (iii) the coexistence of multiple relation types between the same agents.

(c) Compare how a dynamical process (e.g., a contagion, opinion, or stress-propagation model) defined on a hypergraph differs quantitatively from the same process defined on the pairwise projection of that hypergraph or on a multilayer reformulation, and identify invariants of the organization's resilience that depend on the chosen representation.

Let $\mathcal{G}_N$ denote the set of all simple (possibly signed) graphs on a fixed labeled vertex set $V=\{1,\dots,N\}$ representing agents. For each ordered pair $(i,j)$ of agents, let $p_{ij}\in[0,1]$ denote a propensity of agent $i$ to form a link with agent $j$ (a constraint encoding individual link-formation tendencies and possibly the sign $\sigma_{ij}\in\{-1,+1\}$ of the relation). A network ensemble is a probability distribution $P:\mathcal{G}_N\to[0,1]$, $\sum_{G\in\mathcal{G}_N}P(G)=1$, that is consistent with the prescribed link propensities (in the sense that the marginal probabilities of edges and signs reproduce the $p_{ij}$ and $\sigma_{ij}$).

Develop a principled construction of such an ensemble $P$ and a methodology that simultaneously addresses the following:

(a) Significance testing. Given an observed network $G^*\in\mathcal{G}_N$, provide a quantitative criterion, based on $P$, for deciding whether $G^*$ is statistically distinguishable from a typical sample of $P$, and identify which subset of constraints $\{p_{ij}\}$ is sufficient to explain $G^*$ via an iterative refinement procedure.

(b) Inference of significant interactions and signed relations. From $P$ and $G^*$, derive a procedure that infers which pairwise interactions (and their signs) are statistically significant deviations from what the constraints alone would predict.

(c) Quantification of adaptivity potential. Define and compute a diversity functional $D(P)$ — for instance, an entropy-like measure that captures not only the effective number $|\mathrm{supp}(P)|$ of attainable configurations but also their structural variety — and relate $D(P)$ to the system's adaptivity potential, i.e. the range of network configurations the system can realize while respecting the agent constraints.

Prove that the proposed ensemble $P$, the significance procedure, the inference procedure, and the diversity functional $D$ are mutually consistent, and demonstrate that this framework yields a well-defined notion of social resilience for the underlying network of agents.

Consider a social organization modeled as a time-evolving multilayer network G_t = (V, E_t, A_t, R_t), where V is a set of agents, each agent i ∈ V carries an attribute vector a_i(t) ∈ A_t (capturing internal states, resources, or roles), and each ordered pair (i,j) carries a relational attribute r_{ij}(t) ∈ R_t (capturing the type, strength, and sign of the relation). Suppose the organization is subject to a class S of exogenous and endogenous shocks s: G_t → G_{t+1} that may delete, add, or perturb agents, relations, and attributes.

Define the resilience of the organization as a scalar functional
   Res(G_t) = F( Rob(G_t), Adp(G_t) ) ∈ [0,1],
where Rob(G_t) measures robustness (the ability to retain essential structure and function under shocks from S without changing) and Adp(G_t) measures adaptivity (the ability to reorganize agents, relations, and attributes so as to recover or improve function after a shock).

The problem is to:
(a) Construct explicit proxy functionals Rob and Adp from the agent data {a_i(t)}, relational data {r_{ij}(t)}, and network data G_t that go strictly beyond purely topological summaries (e.g., they must use agent- and relation-level information, not only degree distribution, connectivity, or spectral properties of the adjacency matrix).
(b) Specify how each proxy is operationalized as a measurable quantity given partial or noisy observation of agents and relations.
(c) Determine a functional form F: [0,1] × [0,1] → [0,1] combining robustness and adaptivity into a resilience measure, with axiomatic justification (e.g., monotonicity, behavior at the boundary, response to a one-parameter family of shocks).

Provide such proxies and combining functional F, together with conditions under which Res is well-defined, computable from observable data, and not reducible to a function of the network topology alone.

The question is posed as an open modeling problem about operationalizing robustness, adaptivity, and resilience for social organizations. No general accepted resolution exists; the literature offers many domain-specific proxies (e.g., redundancy, modularity, response diversity, recovery time) but no canonical, non-topological resilience measure combining robustness and adaptivity for social systems. The problem remains open.

Consider a finite set of agents $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$, where each agent $i$ has an intrinsic importance $r_i \in \mathbb{R}$ and is connected to other agents through weighted, signed relations $w_{ij} \in \mathbb{R}$ (which may be positive, negative, or zero, representing support, opposition, or absence of influence, respectively). Define the social impact of agent $i$ as
$$I_i \;=\; \sum_{j} w_{ij}\, r_j \;=\; I_i^{p} - I_i^{n},$$
where $I_i^{p} = \sum_{j:\, w_{ij} r_j > 0} w_{ij} r_j$ aggregates supportive influences and $I_i^{n} = -\sum_{j:\, w_{ij} r_j < 0} w_{ij} r_j$ aggregates opposing influences.

Address the following:
(a) Provide a principled justification for why models of social resilience should incorporate such an individual social impact $I_i$ rather than relying solely on the intrinsic importance $r_i$.
(b) Develop a quantification scheme for $I_i$ that combines an agent's own importance with the support and opposition received from others through the weighted signed relations $w_{ij}$, and discuss how the decomposition into $I_i^{p}$ and $I_i^{n}$ captures the qualitative effects of antagonistic versus cooperative ties on collective social resilience.

Consider a social system modeled as a time-evolving multilayer network in which a set of agents A = {a_1, ..., a_n} interact over time. Assume the following data structures may be observed:

(i) Relational data: a sequence of (possibly signed) interaction graphs G_t = (A, E_t, w_t, s_t), where E_t ⊆ A × A is the set of directed dyadic interactions at time t, w_t : E_t → ℝ_{>0} assigns interaction intensities, and s_t : E_t → {+1, −1} assigns a sign (positive or negative relation).
(ii) Longitudinal data: observations of these graphs at discrete times t = 1, 2, ..., T, allowing reconstruction of trajectories of dyads and of individual agents.
(iii) Multivariate data: attribute vectors x_i(t) ∈ ℝ^d for each agent a_i recording features such as activity, role, or context, plus exogenous shock indicators ξ(t).

From such data, define operational estimators for:
 • the robustness R(t) of the system, intended as its capacity to maintain a reference structural/functional state under perturbations;
 • the adaptivity A(t), intended as its capacity to reorganize interactions in response to perturbations;
 • the resilience Res(t), combining robustness and adaptivity over a recovery window after a shock.

The problem is: determine the minimal sufficient set of relational, longitudinal, and multivariate observables — including signed relations, inferred interaction propensities p_{ij}(t) (probabilities that agents i and j interact), and temporal centrality measures C_i(t) — from which the quantities R(t), A(t), and Res(t) can be consistently estimated for a generic social system. Specify (a) which observables are required, (b) how propensities and temporal centralities are to be inferred from the raw interaction logs, and (c) how the resulting estimates of robustness, adaptivity, and resilience are to be assembled into a single resilience measure.

Call an arithmetic function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ multiplicative if $f(1)=1$ and $f(mn)=f(m)f(n)$ whenever $\gcd(m,n)=1$. Say that $f$ has property (P) if for every prime $p$ and every integer $\alpha\ge 1$ the value $f(p^\alpha)$ depends only on $\alpha$ and not on $p$; in that case write $f(p^\alpha)=g(\alpha)$ for a fixed function $g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ with $g(0)=1$.

Assume that $f$ has property (P) and that the associated function $g$ satisfies the following two conditions:
(i) $g(\alpha)$ grows like the divisor-function value $\alpha+1$, in the sense that there exist constants $0<c_1\le c_2$ with $c_1(\alpha+1)\le g(\alpha)\le c_2(\alpha+1)$ for all $\alpha\ge 1$;
(ii) the ratio $\dfrac{\log g(2)}{\log g(1)}$ is a Liouville number (i.e. an irrational $\xi$ such that for every $n\ge 1$ there exist integers $p,q$ with $q>1$ and $0<|\xi-p/q|<q^{-n}$).

Call a positive integer $N$ an $f$-champion if $f(M)<f(N)$ for every positive integer $M<N$. Let
$$Q_f(X)=\#\{N\le X : N\text{ is an }f\text{-champion}\}.$$

Must there necessarily exist a constant $c_f>0$ such that
$$Q_f(X)=O\bigl((\log X)^{c_f}\bigr)\qquad\text{as }X\to\infty\,?$$

Consider a social organization whose collaborative activity is recorded in a version-control repository (e.g., a git repository) that logs, for every change, the developer who made the change, the file(s) and code regions affected, and a timestamp. Formalize and solve the following modeling problem:

(a) Define an extraction procedure that maps the raw commit history to a time-stamped bipartite interaction record B = {(d_i, f_i, t_i, Δ_i)}, where d_i is a developer, f_i is a file (or finer code unit), t_i is a time, and Δ_i quantifies the magnitude/type of the change (e.g., number of lines added/edited, edit-distance based weights).

(b) From B, construct (i) the bipartite developer–artifact network G_B = (D ∪ F, E_B) with weighted edges encoding aggregated contributions, and (ii) its one-mode projection G_D = (D, E_D) onto developers, specifying a co-editing rule (e.g., two developers are linked when they edit overlapping code regions within a temporal window τ) and a weighting scheme on E_D.

(c) Derive from B and G_D quantitative proxies for (i) individual and collective productivity (e.g., functionals of the contribution weights Δ_i over time) and (ii) hierarchy among developers (e.g., orderings inferred from the temporal sequence of edits to shared code, such as who edits whose code).

Question: Provide such an extraction-and-construction framework, prove that the resulting networks and derived measures are well-defined (independent of irrelevant repository artifacts such as merge commits or whitespace edits), and characterize their statistical properties (degree distributions, temporal motifs, hierarchy indices) for collaborative-software repositories.

Let f: Z_{>0} → C be a multiplicative arithmetic function (i.e. f(1)=1 and f(mn)=f(m)f(n) whenever gcd(m,n)=1) with the property that the value f(p^α) at any prime power depends only on the exponent α, not on the prime p. For X ≥ 1, call a positive integer N ≤ X an f-champion (up to X) if |f(N)| ≥ |f(n)| for every positive integer n ≤ X, and let Q_f(X) denote the number of f-champions not exceeding X.

Let W be the set of positive integers N whose prime-exponent sequence is nonincreasing in the natural ordering of primes, i.e. for any primes p < q both dividing N one has v_p(N) ≥ v_q(N), where v_p(N) denotes the p-adic valuation of N. Let W(X) := #{N ∈ W : N ≤ X}.

It is known that, under the assumptions above, every f-champion belongs to W, and hence Q_f(X) ≤ W(X) for every X ≥ 1 and every f with the stated property.

Question: Does there exist a function B(X) with B(X) = o(W(X)) (or, more generally, B(X) ≤ W(X) for all large X and B(X) strictly smaller than W(X) in a quantitative sense) such that Q_f(X) ≤ B(X) holds for every X ≥ 1 and every multiplicative function f satisfying the hypothesis above? In other words, can the universal upper bound W(X) for Q_f(X) be improved?

Let $\mathcal{M}_\theta$ be a generative stochastic model of a social organization, parameterized by $\theta \in \Theta$, that produces simulated trajectories of agent-level states and interactions. Suppose one has access to a finite set of empirical observables (summary statistics) $\{s_1, \ldots, s_k\}$, each computable from either real data or model output, but no direct ground-truth labels for the latent organizational states being modeled. Assume $\theta$ has been calibrated so that for each $i$ the model-generated distribution of $s_i$ matches its empirical distribution within a chosen tolerance.

Develop a principled validation framework that:

1. Specifies a method to construct an aggregated discrepancy measure
$$D(\theta) = F(d_1(\theta), \ldots, d_k(\theta)),$$
where $d_i(\theta)$ quantifies the deviation between simulated and observed $s_i$, and $F$ is an aggregation function, such that $D$ identifies an optimal combination of the measures $\{s_i\}$ for assessing model adequacy in the absence of ground truth.

2. Provides criteria, based solely on in-sample and out-of-sample predictive performance of the model on held-out empirical observables, under which the calibrated model $\mathcal{M}_\theta$ should be considered validated.

Determine whether such a framework exists with provable guarantees (e.g., consistency, identifiability, or risk bounds) for validating $\mathcal{M}_\theta$ when ground-truth data are unavailable.

For an integer $k\geq 1$, call a positive integer $n$ a $k$-restricted highly composite number if $n$ has the form $n=2^{\alpha_1}3^{\alpha_2}\cdots p_k^{\alpha_k}$ (where $p_j$ denotes the $j$-th prime), and $d(n)>d(m)$ for every positive integer $m<n$ of the same restricted form $m=2^{\beta_1}3^{\beta_2}\cdots p_k^{\beta_k}$, where $d(\cdot)$ counts divisors. Let $Q_k(X)$ denote the number of $k$-restricted highly composite integers not exceeding $X$.

(a) For $k\geq 3$, obtain an asymptotic estimate (or sharp upper and lower bounds) for $Q_k(X)$ as $X\to\infty$.

More generally, for an integer $k\geq 2$ define the multiplicative function
$$f_k(p^\alpha)=\begin{cases}\alpha+1,& 0\le\alpha\le k,\\ 0,& \alpha>k,\end{cases}$$
and call $n$ an $f_k$-champion if $f_k(n)>f_k(m)$ for all $m<n$. Let $Q_{f_k}(X)$ be the count of $f_k$-champions up to $X$.

(b) For $k>2$, determine the limiting behavior of $\dfrac{\log Q_{f_k}(X)}{\log X}$ as $X\to\infty$, and give a sharp evaluation of this limit if it exists.

Let $\sigma(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d$ denote the sum-of-divisors function. Call a positive integer $N$ a *hyper abundant number* if there exists a real number $u$ (depending on $N$) such that
$$\frac{\sigma(M)}{M(\log M)^{u}}\;\le\;\frac{\sigma(N)}{N(\log N)^{u}}\qquad\text{for every integer }M\ge 2.$$
(That is, $N$ maximizes $M\mapsto \sigma(M)/(M(\log M)^{u})$ for some choice of $u$.)

Develop structural and counting results for the set of hyper abundant numbers, in analogy with the theory of "hyper composite" (highly composite / superabundant / colossally abundant) numbers developed by G. Robin. In particular:

(a) Describe the prime factorization structure of hyper abundant numbers (e.g., whether they are of the form $\prod_{p\le P}p^{a_p}$ with non-increasing exponents).
(b) Give an asymptotic formula, or non-trivial upper and lower bounds, for the counting function $Q(x) = \#\{N\le x : N \text{ is hyper abundant}\}$.
(c) Determine to what extent Robin-type methods (used for colossally abundant and related extremal numbers in the study of $\sigma(n)/(n\log\log n)$) can be transferred to this weighted maximization problem with $(\log M)^u$ in place of $\log\log M$.

Consider a social organization modeled as a time-evolving system whose internal state at time t is described by a (possibly high-dimensional) micro-state x(t) — for example, the configuration of agents, their interactions, and their attributes. The organization is said to be robust if it maintains its essential function under perturbations, and adaptive if it can reorganize its structure in response to perturbations while preserving function. Define:

- Adaptive capacity: the system's ability to absorb perturbations through internal reorganization without loss of function.
- Elasticity: the system's ability to return to a reference configuration (or to a new viable configuration) after a perturbation.

Problem. Identify and rigorously define a set of macro-variables M_1(t), …, M_k(t), each obtained as a (possibly nonlinear) functional of the micro-state x(t), such that:

1. The vector (M_1(t), …, M_k(t)) quantifies the adaptive capacity and elasticity of the organization.
2. The macro-variables can be empirically estimated from observable data on the organization over time.
3. Their evolution permits the monitoring of robustness and adaptivity through time.
4. Standard early-warning signal techniques — such as detection of critical slowing down, increase of variance, or increase of autocorrelation near tipping points — can be meaningfully applied to (M_1(t), …, M_k(t)) to anticipate loss of resilience.

Provide such macro-variables together with a justification that they satisfy properties (1)–(4), or prove that no such finite collection of macro-variables exists for a specified class of social-organization models.
