Consider the setting of causal supervised learning under spurious correlations. Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a set of environments (distributions) over an input-label space $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$. A predictor $f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ is said to be invariant across $\mathcal{E}$ if its conditional risk (or, in stronger formulations, its conditional distribution $P_e(Y\mid f(X))$) is identical for every $e\in\mathcal{E}$. Invariance learning methods seek to estimate such predictors from data drawn from a finite training subset $\mathcal{E}_{tr}\subset\mathcal{E}$, with the goal of robust generalization to unseen test environments $\mathcal{E}_{te}\subset\mathcal{E}$ exhibiting controlled distribution shifts (covariate shift, label shift, concept shift, anti-causal shift, etc.).

Design a standardized benchmark suite and evaluation protocol for such methods. Specifically:

(a) Specify a collection of datasets (synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real) together with explicit causal generative models or structural causal models that produce families of environments $\{P_e\}_{e\in\mathcal{E}}$ with controllable strength and type of spurious correlation between observed covariates and the label.

(b) Define quantitative evaluation metrics that measure (i) worst-case test risk over $\mathcal{E}_{te}$, (ii) gap between average and worst-environment performance, and (iii) sensitivity of the learned predictor to specified shift parameters.

(c) Provide a rigorous protocol (training/validation/test environment splits, hyperparameter-selection rules that do not use test-environment data, sample-size scaling, and statistical significance criteria) under which different invariance-learning algorithms can be compared on a common footing.

Prove or empirically establish that the proposed suite distinguishes between algorithm classes (e.g., empirical risk minimization, invariant risk minimization, distributionally robust optimization, causal feature-selection methods) in a way that toy experiments do not.

$$H(n) \;=\; \sum_{1 \le i < j \le \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_j - d_i}.$$

Prove or disprove: for every positive integer $n \ge 2$,
$$\frac{H(n)}{\tau(n)} \;\le\; \frac{H(60)}{\tau(60)},$$

For a positive integer $n$, let $1 = d_1 < d_2 < \cdots < d_{\tau(n)} = n$ be the positive divisors of $n$ in increasing order, where $\tau(n)$ denotes the number of divisors of $n$. Define
$$H(n) \;=\; \sum_{1 \le i < j \le \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_j - d_i}.$$
For $n = 60$, the divisors are $1,2,3,4,5,6,10,12,15,20,30,60$, so $\tau(60) = 12$ and one computes $H(60)/\tau(60) \approx 1.126$.

Prove or disprove: for every positive integer $n \ge 2$,
$$\frac{H(n)}{\tau(n)} \;\le\; \frac{H(60)}{\tau(60)},$$
that is, the supremum of $H(n)/\tau(n)$ over integers $n \ge 2$ is attained at $n = 60$.

The closely related Erdős problem (often catalogued as #884) asks whether $H(n)/\tau(n)$ is bounded. A 2025 manuscript by Terence Tao conditionally disproves this boundedness assuming the qualitative Hardy–Littlewood prime tuples conjecture, which would in particular falsify the proposed maximum at $n=60$. Unconditionally, however, the question (and hence the precise n=60 maximum claim) remains open.

Let $\mathcal{O} = \{(i_k, j_k, t_k)\}_{k=1}^N$ be a finite sequence of timestamped pairwise observations among a set $V$ of agents, where $(i_k, j_k, t_k)$ records an observed interaction between $i_k, j_k \in V$ at time $t_k \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. From $\mathcal{O}$ one reconstructs an interaction network in three customary ways:

1. (Window aggregation.) Given a window size $w > 0$ and an offset $s \ge 0$, form the static graph $G_{w,s} = (V, E_{w,s})$ in which $\{i,j\} \in E_{w,s}$ iff there exists at least one observation $(i,j,t) \in \mathcal{O}$ with $t \in [s, s+w]$. The edge density and all derived topological statistics (degree distribution, clustering, components, centralities) depend on $w$ and $s$.

2. (Event-time thresholding.) Given two consecutive observations involving the same pair, only those whose inter-event gap $\Delta t$ satisfies $\Delta t \le \Delta t_{\mathrm{thr}}$ are counted as a sustained interaction edge; the resulting edge set depends on the threshold $\Delta t_{\mathrm{thr}} > 0$.

3. (Temporal paths.) A temporal path of length $\ell$ from $u$ to $v$ is a sequence $(u = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_\ell = v)$ together with times $t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_\ell$ such that each $(v_{r-1}, v_r, t_r)$ is an observation. Reachability "who can potentially influence whom" is encoded by the set $R_{\ell,\tau}(u) = \{v : \exists \text{ temporal path of length } \le \ell \text{ from } u \text{ to } v \text{ with } t_\ell - t_1 \le \tau\}$.

Problem. Provide principled, data-driven rules for choosing the parameters $w$, $s$, $\Delta t_{\mathrm{thr}}$, $\ell$, and $\tau$ from $\mathcal{O}$ so that the reconstructed networks $G_{w,s}$ and the temporal reachability sets $R_{\ell,\tau}(\cdot)$ faithfully represent the underlying interaction structure. In particular: (a) determine an optimal window size $w^*$ that balances statistical stability of topological observables against temporal resolution; (b) determine an optimal inter-event threshold $\Delta t_{\mathrm{thr}}^*$ separating genuine interactions from spurious co-occurrences; (c) determine path-length and time-horizon parameters $\ell^*, \tau^*$ for meaningful potential-influence reachability. Prove or characterize the existence, uniqueness, and consistency of such optima under a stated stochastic model of the observation process.

For a positive integer $n$, let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters, and define Landau's function $g(n)$ to be the maximal order of an element of $S_n$; equivalently,
$$g(n) = \max\{\operatorname{lcm}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k) : k \ge 1,\ \lambda_i \ge 1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k = n\}.$$
Compute explicitly the values $g(10^6)$ and $g(10^9)$ (for instance, by giving the prime factorization of the corresponding optimal least common multiple), and more generally describe an algorithm that computes $g(n)$ for all $n$ up to $10^{15}$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Landau's function has been computed for large values: Jean-Pierre Massias, Jean-Louis Nicolas, and Paul Zimmermann developed algorithms in the 1980s–1990s computing $g(n)$ for $n$ up to $10^4$ and beyond, and Marc Deléglise, Nicolas, and Zimmermann (2008/2009) gave an algorithm computing $g(n)$ for $n$ up to $10^{15}$. Thus $g(10^6)$ and $g(10^9)$ have been computed.

Consider a modeling framework for the resilience of small-to-medium social organizations (collaborating teams, project groups, or working units), formalized as agent-based or network dynamical systems in which agents possess internal states (e.g., awareness, opinions, competencies), interact along a (possibly time-varying) network, and adapt via local rules that produce feedback, diversity of behaviors, and collective learning. Resilience is defined as the ability of the organization to maintain or restore its functional state after endogenous or exogenous shocks.

Within this framework, develop a principled methodology to translate model-derived insights into actionable, testable interventions for real organizations. Specifically:

1. Identify which structural and dynamical features of the model — including agent awareness, behavioral flexibility, diversity of strategies, network connectivity, decentralized (local) interventions, and mechanisms of collective learning — can be operationalized as measurable quantities in real teams.

2. Formulate intervention operators acting on the network topology, agent state distributions, or interaction rules, and derive conditions under which such operators provably increase a chosen resilience functional (e.g., basin-of-attraction size, recovery time, or persistence probability under stochastic shocks).

3. Provide guidance — restricted in scope to collaborating teams rather than whole societies — on how managers can implement these interventions, together with criteria for evaluating their effectiveness empirically.

The problem is to give such a translation and to delineate the limits of validity (scale, assumptions, data requirements) within which model-based recommendations are justified.

Let $X$ be an observed random variable taking values in a high-dimensional space $\mathcal{X}$ (e.g., images in $\mathbb{R}^d$), generated from an unknown ground-truth data-generating process. A structural causal model (SCM) $\mathcal{M} = (Z, U, \mathcal{F}, P_U)$ consists of: a tuple $Z = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_k)$ of endogenous latent causal variables; a tuple $U = (U_1, \ldots, U_k)$ of mutually independent exogenous noise variables with joint distribution $P_U$; and structural assignments $\mathcal{F} = \{Z_i := f_i(\mathrm{Pa}(Z_i), U_i)\}_{i=1}^k$ with respect to a directed acyclic graph $G$ on $\{Z_1,\ldots,Z_k\}$. A causal representation learning system additionally specifies an encoder $g: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Z}$ that maps observations to latent variables, possibly with the aid of auxiliary information (interventional data, multi-view data, temporal data, etc.).

Call a choice of latent dimension $k$ and encoder $g$ an "abstraction level." The abstraction level ranges from very fine-grained (e.g., $Z_i$ are individual pixel intensities) to very coarse-grained (e.g., $Z_i$ are high-level object- or concept-level variables).

Problem. Develop a principled, formal criterion — together with an algorithm — that, given access only to data from the observational distribution of $X$ and a specified class of admissible interventions or auxiliary signals, selects an abstraction level $(k, g)$ such that:
(i) the induced SCM $\mathcal{M}$ on $Z = g(X)$ is identifiable from the available data up to a well-defined equivalence class (e.g., permutation and elementwise reparameterization of latent variables, or graph-isomorphism equivalence of $G$);
(ii) the resulting $\mathcal{M}$ is "useful" in a quantifiable sense for downstream causal reasoning — for example, supporting sample-efficient prediction of the effects of interventions and counterfactual queries, and admitting human-interpretable variables and mechanisms.

Specifically: characterize necessary and sufficient conditions on the observation process, the auxiliary signals, and the function classes for encoder and structural assignments under which such an abstraction level exists, is unique up to the chosen equivalence class, and can be consistently estimated.

For a positive integer $N$, let $\mathcal{F}(N)$ be the set of all maps $\varepsilon\colon\{1,2,\dots,N\}\to\{-1,0,1\}$. For each $\varepsilon\in\mathcal{F}(N)$, form the rational number
\[
P(\varepsilon,N)\;=\;\prod_{n=1}^{N}\!\Bigl(\tfrac{n+1}{n}\Bigr)^{\varepsilon(n)},
\]
and write it in lowest terms as $P(\varepsilon,N)=a(\varepsilon,N)/b(\varepsilon,N)$ with $\gcd(a(\varepsilon,N),b(\varepsilon,N))=1$ and $a(\varepsilon,N)\ge 0$. Define
\[
A(N)\;=\;\max_{\varepsilon\in\mathcal{F}(N)} a(\varepsilon,N),\qquad K(N)\;=\;\frac{\log A(N)}{N\log N}.
\]
It is known that there exist constants $0<c_1\le c_2$ such that $c_1\le K(N)\le c_2$ for all sufficiently large $N$ (with current best values yielding $c_2=\tfrac{2}{3}+o(1)$ as an upper bound on $\limsup K(N)$).

Determine sharp asymptotic estimates for $A(N)$. Equivalently, determine the limiting behavior of $K(N)$ as $N\to\infty$: does $\lim_{N\to\infty} K(N)$ exist, and if so, what is its value? In particular, improve the upper bound $\limsup_{N\to\infty} K(N)\le \tfrac{2}{3}$.

Consider a satellite communication system modeled as follows. A legitimate transmitter T (a ground station or satellite) communicates with a legitimate receiver R over a wireless channel whose physical characteristics include: (i) very large propagation distances (LEO, MEO, or GEO orbits) producing severe path loss and propagation delays, (ii) high relative motion inducing Doppler shifts, (iii) limited on-board power and processing resources at the satellite, (iv) broad-beam coverage so that any geographic adversary within the footprint can receive and transmit on the same band, and (v) shared spectrum subject to atmospheric and ionospheric impairments. An adversary class A is allowed to mount two types of availability attacks:

(a) Denial-of-service flooding: A injects high-rate malicious traffic toward T or R such that the legitimate processing/queueing capacity is exceeded with probability at least p_DoS.

(b) Jamming: A emits interference signals (constant, pulsed, sweep, tone, protocol-aware, or smart/reactive jamming) of total average power up to P_J and arbitrary waveform structure within the system bandwidth W, with the goal of preventing correct decoding at R.

Design a physical-layer security (PLS) scheme—i.e., a transmission strategy specifying signal design, coding, beamforming, frequency/time hopping, power control, and/or admission control performed at the physical layer (without relying on cryptographic upper-layer mechanisms)—that achieves the following availability guarantee: for every admissible adversary strategy of types (a) and (b), the probability that R correctly decodes each transmitted message is at least 1 − ε, while the scheme remains implementable under the satellite physical constraints (i)–(v) (in particular, bounded on-board energy E, antenna aperture, and computational complexity polynomial in the block length).

The problem is: provide such a PLS construction together with a rigorous proof of its availability guarantee, or establish fundamental impossibility bounds (in terms of W, P_J, E, p_DoS, ε) showing the regimes in which no such scheme can exist.

Causal representation learning (CRL) is the task of recovering, from observed high-dimensional data X, a collection of latent variables Z = (Z_1, ..., Z_d) together with a causal structure (e.g. a directed acyclic graph G and structural assignments Z_i := f_i(Pa_G(Z_i), U_i) with exogenous noises U_i) such that X = g(Z) for some (typically unknown) mixing function g. A problem specification for CRL is a tuple consisting of: (i) assumptions on the latent causal model (graph class, functional class, noise distributions), (ii) assumptions on the mixing g (e.g. diffeomorphism, injectivity, linearity), and (iii) a supervisory signal, i.e. additional data or labels available beyond i.i.d. samples of X — for example: paired observational and interventional data with known or unknown intervention targets, multi-environment data with distribution shifts, temporal/sequential data, counterfactual pairs, weak labels on subsets of latent variables, auxiliary variables, or known group actions.

A specification is called identifiable if, given infinite data from the specified distributions, the latent variables Z and the causal graph G are recoverable up to a stated equivalence class (e.g. permutation and element-wise reparameterization).

Problem. Characterize the set of problem specifications and supervisory signals for CRL that are:
(a) sufficient for identifiability of (Z, G) up to a precisely stated equivalence;
(b) minimal, in the sense that no listed assumption or signal can be removed or weakened without losing identifiability;
(c) realistic, in the sense that the required data can plausibly be obtained in scientific or engineering settings;
(d) compatible with an algorithmic procedure that, given finite samples, provably recovers (Z, G) up to the stated equivalence with vanishing error as sample size grows.

Specifically:
1. Determine which currently used supervisory signals (e.g. single-node interventions with known targets, unknown-target interventions, multi-environment heterogeneity, temporal dependence, counterfactual pairs, weak labels) yield identifiability, and under what minimal accompanying assumptions on g and on the latent SCM.
2. Quantify the trade-offs among (strength of supervision) ↔ (strength of structural assumptions) ↔ (size of identifiability equivalence class) ↔ (statistical and computational efficiency of recovery).
3. Identify whether any specifications strictly weaker than those currently known (e.g. purely observational with only mild structural priors) are sufficient for identifiability, or prove impossibility results delimiting how far supervision can be relaxed.

Consider a satellite communication system whose uplink channel carries data from a heterogeneous population of terrestrial and aerial transmitters (e.g., handheld terminals, IoT sensors, UAVs, ground gateways) to one or more satellites in low, medium, or geostationary orbit. Each transmitter i has a finite transmit-power budget P_i, a hardware/computational complexity bound C_i, and a minimum throughput requirement R_i. The uplink is subject to (i) eavesdropping by passive adversaries, (ii) spoofing in which an adversary impersonates a legitimate transmitter, (iii) message alteration in which an adversary modifies a transmitted codeword, and (iv) denial-of-service attacks (jamming) that inject interference into the uplink band. Channel state information about the legitimate user-to-satellite link may be partial, while channel information about the adversaries is unknown beyond statistical models.

Within the framework of physical-layer security (which uses channel coding, beamforming/precoding, artificial-noise injection, cooperative jamming, secret-key generation from channel reciprocity, and authentication based on physical channel features rather than upper-layer cryptography), formulate and design a scheme that simultaneously:

1. Achieves a positive secrecy rate R_s(i) ≥ R_i^{sec} for each legitimate transmitter i against the eavesdropping model, subject to P_i and C_i.
2. Provides a physical-layer authentication test, based on measurable channel features, whose false-acceptance probability against spoofing and message-alteration attacks is at most ε_FA and whose false-rejection probability for legitimate users is at most ε_FR.
3. Maintains a guaranteed availability (probability of successful decoding) of at least 1 − δ under a specified jamming model with adversary power budget P_J.
4. Operates uniformly across the heterogeneity of devices and orbital scenarios (LEO/MEO/GEO with their associated Doppler, latency, and path-loss regimes).

Characterize the fundamental trade-off region among the tuples (R_s, ε_FA, ε_FR, δ, P_i, P_J) achievable by any such scheme, and exhibit an explicit construction (coding, precoding, and authentication procedure) that attains a point inside this region under realistic satellite channel models (Rician/shadowed-Rician fading, large Doppler shifts, long propagation delays).

Consider a satellite communication system in which a legitimate transmitter (e.g., a satellite or gateway) communicates with a legitimate receiver over a wireless main channel, while one or more eavesdroppers attempt to intercept the transmission. The classical wiretap-channel model assumes the eavesdropper is (i) passive (it does not transmit or otherwise influence the main channel), (ii) equipped with a single antenna and limited signal-processing resources, (iii) static with a known (or at least fixed) location, so that the legitimate parties can rely on channel state information (CSI) and location uncertainty to design beamforming, artificial-noise, secrecy-coding, or key-generation schemes that achieve a positive secrecy rate.

Formulate and analyze a physical-layer security framework for satellite links under a strictly stronger adversary model that simultaneously incorporates the following capabilities:

1. Active interception: the eavesdropper may transmit probing or pilot-contamination signals in order to extract (partial) CSI of the legitimate main channel, thereby degrading schemes that rely on CSI advantage at the legitimate receiver.
2. Enhanced hardware: the eavesdropper has multiple antennas and advanced signal-processing capability (e.g., MIMO combining, beam-steering, joint detection across multiple receive chains).
3. Mobility with unknown location: the eavesdropper is dynamic (for instance, a UAV-mounted receiver) with a position and trajectory that are unknown to the legitimate parties; only statistical or set-membership information about its location is available.

For this adversary model, determine:
(a) an appropriate information-theoretic secrecy metric (e.g., worst-case ergodic secrecy capacity or secrecy outage probability over the set of admissible eavesdropper states),
(b) achievable bounds on this metric for typical satellite channel models (line-of-sight dominated, shadowed-Rician, or hybrid satellite-terrestrial channels),
(c) explicit transmission strategies (beamforming, artificial noise, cooperative jamming, secret key generation, or coding) that achieve or approach these bounds, and
(d) sufficient conditions on the system parameters (transmit power, antenna numbers, location uncertainty set, pilot-contamination strength) under which a strictly positive secrecy rate is guaranteed.

Provide a redesign of physical-layer security for satellite systems that is provably robust against the combined effects of (1)–(3), or alternatively prove impossibility results identifying parameter regimes in which no positive secrecy rate is achievable.

Consider a satellite communication system consisting of a satellite transmitter and a terrestrial user (or vice versa) communicating over a wireless channel. An adversary positioned between the two legitimate parties may carry out an integrity-violation (man-in-the-middle) attack by intercepting the transmitted signal, modifying or manipulating the carried message, and retransmitting the altered signal to the intended receiver, with the goal of disrupting service or gaining unauthorized access.

Design and analyze physical-layer security (PLS) mechanisms — that is, techniques that exploit physical characteristics of the wireless transmission (such as channel state information, channel reciprocity, propagation effects, noise statistics, hardware imperfections, or signal-level fingerprints) rather than upper-layer cryptography — that provide message integrity for such satellite links. Specifically:

1. Formulate a model of the legitimate satellite-to-user (and user-to-satellite) channel and of an active man-in-the-middle adversary capable of intercepting, modifying, and retransmitting signals.
2. Propose PLS-based message-manipulation detection schemes that allow the legitimate receiver to decide, before accepting or processing the received message, whether the signal has been tampered with in transit.
3. Establish quantitative guarantees (e.g., detection probability, false-alarm probability, and the range of adversary capabilities under which detection is reliable) for the proposed schemes in the satellite setting, accounting for the long propagation distances, large path loss, Doppler effects, and atmospheric impairments characteristic of satellite links.

Consider a predictive model f : X → Y deployed in a large-scale system serving a population of N users, where N is very large (e.g., millions). For each user with feature vector x ∈ X and a (possibly undesired) prediction f(x), a causal explanation method seeks to produce an explanation E(x) — for instance, a counterfactual x' such that f(x') differs from f(x) in a desired way, or an attribution over features — that satisfies three qualitative desiderata:

1. Fidelity: the explanation must be consistent with an underlying structural causal model M = (U, V, F, P(U)) governing the data-generating process, in the sense that counterfactuals are computed via the abduction–action–prediction procedure on M (or a faithful approximation thereof), and attributions reflect causal effects rather than mere statistical associations.
2. Plausibility: the produced explanation (e.g., counterfactual instance x') must lie in regions of high density under the observational distribution P(X) and respect known feasibility constraints among variables.
3. Actionability: the explanation must correspond to interventions do(X_S = x'_S) on a subset S of variables that are admissible (mutable, non-protected) and whose downstream causal consequences on the remaining variables are accounted for.

Consider a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation in which pairs of satellites communicate over inter-satellite links (ISLs). Two link types are present: (i) radio-frequency (RF) ISLs, modeled by a time-varying channel with parameters capturing small-scale fading, large Doppler shifts due to relative orbital motion, and atmospheric/weather-induced attenuation when links graze the atmosphere; and (ii) free-space optical (FSO) ISLs, modeled by a line-of-sight channel with pointing/acquisition/tracking errors and atmospheric turbulence effects. An eavesdropper, located either on another satellite, on an aerial platform, or on the ground, attempts to intercept the legitimate transmission without active cooperation.

Within the framework of physical-layer security (PLS), where the security metric is the achievable secrecy rate
   C_s = [ log_2(1 + SNR_legit) − log_2(1 + SNR_eve) ]^+,
formulate concrete PLS strategies (e.g., beamforming, artificial noise injection, cooperative jamming, secret key generation from reciprocal channel features, or coding schemes) that explicitly exploit the distinctive physical-layer characteristics of inter-satellite links — namely the fading statistics, Doppler shift, and weather-induced effects on RF ISLs, and the narrow-beam, turbulence-affected nature of optical ISLs — to maximize C_s (or an equivalent secrecy outage / secrecy capacity metric) against eavesdropping and related passive attacks. Provide, in particular, a defense scheme for optical inter-satellite links against eavesdropping with provable secrecy guarantees.

Consider a sequence of predictive models $(f_t)_{t \ge 0}$, where each $f_t : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is a (possibly black-box) predictor deployed at time $t$, together with a sequence of input distributions $(P_t)_{t \ge 0}$ on $\mathcal{X}$ representing user/population behavior, and a sequence of utility functions $(u_t)_{t \ge 0}$ with $u_t : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{A} \to \mathbb{R}$ measuring the value an explanation $a \in \mathcal{A}$ provides to a stakeholder. An explanation method is a mapping $E : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{A}$ that, given an input $x$ and a model $f$, produces an explanation $E(x,f) \in \mathcal{A}$.

A standard validity criterion (e.g., faithfulness, sufficiency, or counterfactual correctness) can be encoded by a functional $V_t(E, x, f_t) \in \mathbb{R}$ that depends on the deployed model and on the current data-generating distribution $P_t$.

Develop a framework for explanation methods $E$ such that, when the triple $(f_t, P_t, u_t)$ varies over time (covering both gradual temporal drift and abrupt distribution shift, as well as changes in the downstream utility), the produced explanations satisfy the following:

1. (Temporal validity) There exist non-vacuous guarantees of the form
$$\mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_t}\big[V_t(E, x, f_t)\big] \ge \alpha(t)$$
for an explicit function $\alpha$, rather than guarantees that hold only under the static assumption $f_t \equiv f_0$, $P_t \equiv P_0$, $u_t \equiv u_0$.

2. (Utility consistency) The expected utility $\mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_t}[u_t(x, f_t(x), E(x, f_t))]$ remains controlled as $t$ grows.

3. (Detection and adaptation) The framework provides a procedure to detect when previously issued explanations have become invalid due to changes in $f_t$, $P_t$, or $u_t$, and to update them accordingly.

Formulate precise conditions on the dynamics of $(f_t, P_t, u_t)$ (e.g., bounded drift in some metric, an underlying causal structural model with time-varying mechanisms) under which an explanation method $E$ with the above three properties provably exists, and construct such an $E$.

Consider a satellite communication system modeled as a wiretap channel in which a legitimate transmitter T (e.g., a satellite or ground station) wishes to communicate securely with a legitimate receiver R in the presence of one or more passive eavesdroppers E. The channel model must account for satellite-specific characteristics, including: (i) long propagation distances and the resulting large free-space path loss; (ii) high relative motion and Doppler shifts; (iii) line-of-sight dominated links with rain/atmospheric attenuation (e.g., shadowed-Rician or Loo fading for LEO/MEO/GEO links); (iv) wide-area beam footprints causing potential overlap between the legitimate user's region and eavesdropper regions; (v) limited on-board processing power, energy, and storage; and (vi) restricted feedback and channel-state-information acquisition.

Physical-layer security (PLS) is quantified by the secrecy capacity
   C_s = [ log_2(1 + γ_R) − log_2(1 + γ_E) ]^+ ,
where γ_R and γ_E are the instantaneous signal-to-noise ratios at R and E, and by metrics such as secrecy outage probability P_so(R_s) = Pr[C_s < R_s] and average secrecy rate E[C_s].

Machine-learning (ML)-based PLS methods (supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement-learning approaches; e.g., for beamforming design, artificial-noise injection, power allocation, relay/jammer selection, key generation from channel reciprocity, eavesdropper detection, and resource scheduling) have been developed for terrestrial settings such as device-to-device, cognitive radio, and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) networks.

Problem. Formulate, adapt, and rigorously validate ML-based PLS schemes for the satellite wiretap setting above. Specifically:
(a) Define training data models (channel datasets, eavesdropper-location priors, mobility traces) that faithfully capture the satellite environment despite the difficulty of obtaining CSI for E.
(b) Design learning architectures and loss functions whose optimization provably (or empirically) maximizes a chosen secrecy metric (secrecy rate, secrecy outage probability, or secret-key rate) subject to on-board complexity, latency, and energy constraints.
(c) Establish performance guarantees (generalization bounds, robustness to model mismatch in shadowed-Rician parameters, Doppler, and beam geometry) showing under what satellite-specific operating conditions the ML-based scheme outperforms classical PLS baselines.
(d) Provide a methodology and benchmarks to validate applicability across LEO, MEO, and GEO scenarios, including uplink, downlink, and inter-satellite links.

Determine to what extent (a)–(d) can be achieved, identifying the regimes in which ML-based PLS is provably beneficial for satellite communication and the regimes in which it fails.

Consider a predictive model f: X -> Y together with an interactive explanation system E that, on input x in X, returns an explanation E(f, x) intended to help a user understand the prediction f(x). The explanation may take the form of feature attributions, counterfactual examples, decision-boundary information, or a causal graph describing relationships among input features. Assume an adversary may issue an adaptive sequence of queries (x_1, x_2, ...) and observes (f(x_i), E(f, x_i)) for each query. Consider four classes of attacks:

(i) Model extraction: producing a surrogate hat f such that Pr_{x ~ D}[hat f(x) = f(x)] is close to 1 for some data distribution D.
(ii) Decision-boundary reconstruction: recovering, up to small Hausdorff distance, the set { x : f(x) = c } for classes c.
(iii) Membership inference: deciding, given a candidate point z, whether z belonged to the training dataset used to fit f, with advantage non-negligibly above 1/2.
(iv) Causal-structure recovery: reconstructing the directed acyclic graph G underlying a structural causal model that f or E depends on, from the responses to interactive queries.

Design an explanation mechanism E (possibly randomized, e.g., satisfying (epsilon, delta)-differential privacy or a comparable formal guarantee) such that:

(a) For every probabilistic polynomial-time adversary issuing at most q queries, the success probability of each of the four attacks above is bounded by a specified small function alpha(q, epsilon).
(b) E retains a quantifiable notion of utility: for instance, a fidelity measure phi(E, f, x) (such as local linear-approximation error, counterfactual validity, or causal-edge recall) remains above a prescribed threshold tau on average over x ~ D.

Formally characterize the achievable trade-off region between (alpha, q, epsilon) and (tau, phi), and exhibit a construction of E achieving a non-trivial point in this region simultaneously for all four attack classes, or prove an impossibility result demonstrating that no such mechanism can satisfy (a) and (b) jointly under stated assumptions.

Recent literature (2022–2025) on privacy attacks against explainable AI shows that individual attack vectors—model extraction via gradient/LIME/SHAP explanations, membership inference from counterfactuals, and decision-boundary reconstruction—have each been demonstrated, with partial differential-privacy-based defenses proposed. However, no unified construction is known that simultaneously defends against all four classes (including causal-structure recovery) while preserving explanation utility, and no matching impossibility theorem has been established. The problem is widely regarded as open.

Consider a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) consisting of $N$ subwavelength reflecting elements arranged on a planar aperture. Each element $n$ acts as a passive scatterer whose response to an incident plane wave depends on the angle of incidence $\theta_i$, the angle of reflection $\theta_r$, the polarization, and the frequency, and is characterized by a (generally angle-dependent) reflection coefficient $\Gamma_n(\theta_i,\theta_r;\omega)$ controllable through a set of tunable parameters (e.g., bias voltages applied to varactors or PIN diodes that change the local surface impedance).

Many channel-training and channel-estimation schemes for RIS-aided wireless systems require the ability to "switch off" individual elements, meaning that the element should contribute no scattered field regardless of the directions of the incoming and outgoing waves. Formally, we say element $n$ is all-angle nulled if there exists a setting of its tunable parameters for which
$$\Gamma_n(\theta_i,\theta_r;\omega) = 0 \qquad \text{for all admissible } (\theta_i,\theta_r,\text{polarization}),$$
so that the element produces no scattered field for every incidence/reflection geometry within the operating band.

Problem. Determine whether a physically realizable RIS hardware architecture and associated control model exist that achieves all-angle nulling of an individual RIS element in the sense above. If so, describe such an architecture (specifying the unit-cell structure, the tunable mechanism, and the control rule) and prove that the resulting $\Gamma_n$ vanishes identically over all incidence and reflection angles, polarizations, and the operating frequency band. If not, characterize the fundamental electromagnetic obstructions that prevent such an all-angle null, and quantify the best achievable angular and bandwidth uniformity of the suppression $|\Gamma_n(\theta_i,\theta_r;\omega)|$ over a passive (or active) tunable unit cell.

Consider a narrowband MIMO communication link aided by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS). Let the transmitter have $M_t$ antennas, the receiver have $M_r$ antennas, and the RIS have $N$ passive reflecting elements whose phase configuration at training slot $k$ is described by a diagonal matrix $\Theta_k = \mathrm{diag}(\theta_k) \in \mathbb{C}^{N\times N}$ with unit-modulus entries. Denote by $H_1 \in \mathbb{C}^{N\times M_t}$ the transmitter-to-RIS channel and by $H_2 \in \mathbb{C}^{M_r\times N}$ the RIS-to-receiver channel, so that the end-to-end (cascaded) channel for configuration $\Theta_k$ is
$$H(\Theta_k) \;=\; H_2\,\Theta_k\,H_1.$$
Assume a mmWave/THz propagation regime in which $H_1$ and $H_2$ admit sparse geometric representations
$$H_1 = A_R(\phi_1)\,\mathrm{diag}(\alpha_1)\,A_T(\psi_1)^H, \qquad H_2 = A_R(\phi_2)\,\mathrm{diag}(\alpha_2)\,A_T(\psi_2)^H,$$
where each link has only $L \ll \min(M_t,M_r,N)$ dominant paths with angles drawn from quantized dictionaries of sizes $G, H, P$ along the relevant spatial directions, and $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ are complex gains. During training, the transmitter emits pilot symbols $\{x_k\}_{k=1}^{K}$ and the receiver observes
$$y_k = H_2\,\Theta_k\,H_1\,x_k + n_k, \qquad n_k \sim \mathcal{CN}(0,\sigma^2 I),$$
under an average pilot energy constraint $\sum_k \|x_k\|^2 \le K P_t$ and a total training budget of $K$ symbols (out of a coherence block of length $T$).

Within this model, address the following:

(a) Determine pilot signals $\{x_k\}_{k=1}^{K}$ and RIS training states $\{\Theta_k\}_{k=1}^{K}$ that are optimal (in a precise, stated sense such as minimizing worst-case or average mean-square error of the sparse-recovery estimate of $(H_1,H_2)$, or equivalently the cascaded channel, subject to the sparsity prior above) for recovery via $\ell_1$-minimization or other sparse-recovery decoders. The optimality criterion should account for the joint design of the pilot sequence and the RIS phase profiles, and should specify how restricted-isometry- or coherence-type guarantees are met with the minimum possible $K$.

(b) Derive a training-based capacity result for this RIS-aided channel in which the channel is acquired through the sparse-recovery estimator from part (a) rather than a standard linear (e.g., least-squares or LMMSE) estimator. Specifically, obtain a closed-form lower bound on the ergodic achievable rate of the form
$$R(K,P_t,T) = \frac{T-K}{T}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log_2\det\!\left(I + \rho_{\mathrm{eff}}(K,P_t)\,\widehat H \widehat H^H\right)\right],$$
where $\widehat H$ is the sparse-recovery estimate and $\rho_{\mathrm{eff}}$ accounts for residual estimation error, and optimize this bound over $K$ to characterize the optimal training length and the resulting capacity scaling in $(M_t,M_r,N,L,T,P_t)$.

Consider a predictive model f : X → Y trained on data (X, A, Y) where A denotes a sensitive attribute (e.g., race, gender) taking values in a finite set, X are covariates, and Y is the target. Existing causal fairness criteria are typically formulated in terms of equality: for example, (i) counterfactual fairness, which requires that the distribution of the prediction Ŷ(a) := f(X(a)) under the counterfactual intervention do(A = a) be invariant in a, conditional on observed features; (ii) path-specific causal fairness, which requires that the causal effect of A on Ŷ along certain "unfair" directed paths in an underlying structural causal model vanish; and (iii) demographic parity / equalized odds, expressed as marginal or conditional independence of Ŷ from A. All of these enforce strict equality of some statistical or causal quantity across groups defined by A.

Equity-based fairness, in contrast, allows for unequal treatment that is justified by relevant differences in need, baseline disadvantage, or downstream welfare, with the goal of producing equitable outcomes rather than identical procedures. The problem is to provide a rigorous formulation answering the following:

(a) Give a precise mathematical definition of an equity-based fairness criterion within a structural causal model (V, U, F, P(U)) over variables including A, X, Y, Ŷ, together with an exogenously specified "legitimate need" or "baseline disadvantage" variable D (which may be a function of (A, X, U)). The definition should specify a target equity functional E(Ŷ; D, A) that the predictor f must satisfy, in a manner that reduces to equality-based causal fairness when D is constant.

(b) Determine, for each of the equality-based criteria (i)–(iii) above, whether your equity-based criterion is (1) implied by, (2) implies, (3) is logically independent of, or (4) is incompatible with that criterion. Provide either a proof or an explicit counterexample (structural causal model and predictor) in each case.

(c) Characterize the set of joint distributions and structural causal models under which a predictor satisfying the equity-based criterion exists, and exhibit (if possible) a constructive procedure (e.g., a post-processing or constrained-optimization scheme) that produces such a predictor from an arbitrary base model.

The question is a programmatic open direction concerning how to formalize equity-based (as opposed to equality-based) fairness in causal machine learning and reconcile it with existing causal fairness definitions. The fairness literature continues to propose new equity- and need-based criteria, but no canonical operationalization within causal models has been adopted, and the relationship to counterfactual/path-specific fairness remains under active investigation. No definitive resolution was found.

Consider a wireless communication system in which a transmitter communicates with a receiver via a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) consisting of N passive reflecting elements. The cascaded channel is modeled in two time scales:

- A fast-varying component h_f ∈ C^N that changes independently in each coherence block of length T_f symbols.
- A slow-varying component h_s ∈ C^N (e.g., large-scale fading or the RIS-related geometry) that remains constant over L consecutive fast coherence blocks.

Let θ = (θ_1, …, θ_N) ∈ Θ ⊂ C^N denote the vector of RIS reflection coefficients (|θ_n| = 1), and let w denote the transmit beamforming vector with ||w||² ≤ P. The instantaneous received SNR in a fast block with fading h_f is
   γ(θ, w; h_f, h_s) = |(h_s ⊙ h_f)^H diag(θ) w|² / σ²,
and the corresponding instantaneous mutual information is C(θ, w; h_f, h_s) = log₂(1 + γ).

Suppose that the RIS reflection vector θ can be updated only on the slow time scale (once per L fast blocks), so that θ must be chosen as a function of h_s alone, while w may adapt per fast block. Assume an outer code spans many fast coherence blocks within a slow block.

Formulate and solve the following joint optimization problems:

(a) ε-Outage capacity: For a target outage probability ε ∈ (0,1), determine
   C_out(ε) = sup_{θ(h_s)} sup_{w(·)} { R : Pr_{h_f}[ C(θ(h_s), w(h_f); h_f, h_s) < R ] ≤ ε },
and characterize the optimal slow-scale RIS configuration θ*(h_s) and fast-scale beamformer w*(h_f).

(b) Throughput maximization: Determine
   T* = sup_{θ(h_s), w(·)} E_{h_f}[ C(θ(h_s), w(h_f); h_f, h_s) · 1{C ≥ R_th} ],
or, equivalently, the maximum goodput (1−ε)·R achievable under outage constraint ε.

Specifically, provide: (i) the explicit form of the optimal θ*(h_s) under standard fading distributions (e.g., Rayleigh, Rician) for h_f; (ii) conditions under which optimizing for outage capacity or throughput yields a strictly different RIS configuration than optimizing for the ergodic capacity E[C]; and (iii) quantification of the performance gap between these criteria as functions of N, L, ε, and the fading statistics.

Develop a rigorous causal-theoretic framework for the notion of "harm" in algorithmic decision-making that simultaneously addresses the following three questions, providing both formal definitions and identification/estimation procedures from data:

(1) Retrospective harm attribution. Given a structural causal model M = (U, V, F, P(U)) representing an agent and its environment, a realized action a ∈ A taken in context X = x with observed outcome Y = y, define a quantitative measure H_retro(a; x, y) of how much harm the agent's action caused, formulated in terms of counterfactual outcomes Y_{a'}(u) under alternative actions a' ∈ A. State conditions under which H_retro is identifiable from observational and/or interventional distributions, and give an estimator.

(2) Prospective expected harm. Before an action a is taken in context X = x, define E[H(a) | X = x], the expected harm of choosing a, in a way consistent with (1) under appropriate counterfactual baselines. Specify the assumptions (e.g., ignorability, monotonicity, choice of reference action) required for identification, and provide an estimation procedure.

(3) Harm–benefit decision rule. Define benefit B(a; x) as a dual quantity to harm, and formulate an optimal decision rule a*(x) ∈ argmax_{a ∈ A} { B(a; x) − λ · E[H(a) | X = x] } (or another principled aggregation) that balances expected harm against expected benefit. Characterize when such a rule is well-defined, consistent across the three questions, and learnable from finite data with statistical guarantees.

The task is to give such formal definitions, prove identification results, and provide estimation methods that coherently link (1), (2), and (3) within a single causal framework.

Consider a single-user MIMO communication system aided by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS). Let the transmitter, receiver, and RIS be equipped with $N_t$, $N_r$, and $M$ antennas/elements, respectively. The received signal is
$$ y = (H_d + H_2 \, \Phi \, H_1)\, x + n, $$
where $H_d \in \mathbb{C}^{N_r \times N_t}$ is the direct channel, $H_1 \in \mathbb{C}^{M \times N_t}$ and $H_2 \in \mathbb{C}^{N_r \times M}$ are the transmitter–RIS and RIS–receiver channels, $\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(e^{j\theta_1},\dots,e^{j\theta_M})$ is the diagonal RIS phase-shift matrix with $\theta_m \in [0,2\pi)$, $x$ is the transmit signal with covariance $Q\succeq 0$, $\mathrm{tr}(Q)\le P$, and $n\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,\sigma^2 I)$.

Assume that the channels $H_d, H_1, H_2$ are random with a known joint distribution (statistical CSI), and that the RIS configuration $\Phi$ together with the input covariance $Q$ are chosen as functions of this distribution only (i.e., they are held fixed over the coherence horizon during which the instantaneous channels vary). Define the ergodic rate
$$ R(\Phi, Q) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \log\det\!\left( I + \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}(H_d + H_2 \Phi H_1) Q (H_d + H_2 \Phi H_1)^H \right) \right], $$
with the ergodic-rate optimization problem
$$ R^\star = \sup_{\Phi,\, Q:\ \mathrm{tr}(Q)\le P} R(\Phi, Q). $$

Problem. Derive a closed-form achievable-rate inner bound $\underline{R}(\Phi,Q)$, satisfying $\underline{R}(\Phi,Q) \le R(\Phi,Q)$ for all feasible $(\Phi,Q)$, that depends only on the channel statistics (e.g., covariance matrices, line-of-sight components, Rician factors) and that can be used as a tractable surrogate objective for optimizing the long-term RIS configuration $\Phi$ and input covariance $Q$ when only statistical CSI is available. The bound should be tight enough to provide a meaningful guarantee on the achievable ergodic rate, and the resulting optimization should be amenable to practical algorithms.

A reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) is a planar array of N sub-wavelength scattering elements, each of which can be configured to impose a controllable complex reflection coefficient on an incident electromagnetic wave. Let an incident plane wave arrive at the surface from direction (θ_i, φ_i) with polarization p_i, and let the scattered field be observed in direction (θ_r, φ_r) with polarization p_r. Model the RIS as a linear two-port (or multi-port) device with a scattering operator S(θ_i, φ_i, p_i; θ_r, φ_r, p_r; Φ), where Φ = diag(e^{jϕ_1}, …, e^{jϕ_N}) encodes the per-element configuration, possibly augmented by lumped passive/active loads, magnetic biasing, or time-modulated impedances.

The RIS-induced channel is said to be reciprocal if, for every configuration Φ and every pair of directions/polarizations,
   S(θ_i, φ_i, p_i; θ_r, φ_r, p_r; Φ) = S(θ_r, φ_r, p_r; θ_i, φ_i, p_i; Φ),
and non-reciprocal otherwise.

Problem. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on
 (a) the physical realization of the unit cells (material constitutive relations, presence of magneto-optical, time-varying, or nonlinear components, active circuitry),
 (b) the angular geometry of incidence and reflection (including specular versus anomalous reflection regimes and near-field versus far-field operation), and
 (c) the surface design parameters (element spacing relative to wavelength, mutual coupling, load termination network, configuration Φ),
under which the scattering operator S satisfies the reciprocity identity above. Furthermore, for cases in which the identity fails, formulate a rigorously derived communication-channel model H_{RIS}(Φ) for a non-reciprocal RIS that is consistent with Maxwell's equations and energy-conservation constraints, and identify the experimentally measurable quantities that would distinguish reciprocal from non-reciprocal regimes.

Recent literature on reconfigurable intelligent surfaces continues to debate the conditions for channel reciprocity. Standard passive, linear, time-invariant, isotropic RIS designs are generally argued to be reciprocal by Lorentz reciprocity, but anomalous-reflection metasurfaces, space-time-modulated, magnetically biased, or actively loaded RIS designs have been proposed as non-reciprocal, with conflicting modeling assumptions in the communications literature. As of 2026 no consensus theorem or definitive experimental validation has settled the necessary and sufficient conditions, so the question remains open.

Consider an observational data setting with random variables $(X, A, Y, U)$, where $X$ denotes covariates, $A \in \{0,1\}$ a protected (sensitive) attribute, $Y$ an outcome of interest, and $U$ unobserved confounders. A structural causal model $\mathcal{M}$ over these variables induces interventional distributions $P(Y \mid do(A=a))$ and counterfactual distributions $P(Y_{A \leftarrow a} \mid X=x, A=a', Y=y)$. Causal fairness criteria (e.g., counterfactual fairness, path-specific effects, total/direct/indirect causal effects on $Y$ with respect to $A$) are functionals $\psi(\mathcal{M})$ of such quantities.

Assume that, due to hidden confounding by $U$ or to violations of standard identification assumptions (ignorability, positivity, no interference), the target functional $\psi(\mathcal{M})$ is only partially identifiable from the observational distribution $P(X,A,Y)$, i.e., the identification region
$$\Psi(P) = \{\psi(\mathcal{M}') : \mathcal{M}' \in \mathcal{F}, \; \mathcal{M}' \text{ induces } P(X,A,Y)\}$$
contains more than one value, where $\mathcal{F}$ is a class of admissible structural causal models compatible with a chosen sensitivity model (e.g., a Rosenbaum-, Tan-, or marginal-sensitivity-model-style bound on the strength of unmeasured confounding).

Develop:
(1) A general framework for computing sharp upper and lower bounds on causal fairness functionals $\psi(\mathcal{M})$ over $\mathcal{F}$, parameterized by interpretable sensitivity parameters $\Gamma$ quantifying the maximum allowable deviation from unconfoundedness or other violated assumptions.
(2) Estimators of these bounds from finite samples together with valid (asymptotic or finite-sample) confidence intervals that account for both sampling uncertainty and identification uncertainty.
(3) A protocol of realistic simulations (with known ground-truth structural models including hidden confounders) that calibrates the sensitivity parameters $\Gamma$ to plausible domain regimes and benchmarks the resulting fairness bounds.

The problem is to design such procedures, prove their soundness (i.e., $\Psi(P) \subseteq [\hat L, \hat U]$ with high probability) and sharpness (the bounds are attained by some $\mathcal{M}' \in \mathcal{F}$), and demonstrate that causal-fairness conclusions drawn from them remain reliable when the underlying counterfactual or interventional quantities are not point-identified.

(2023) propose a neural sensitivity framework for causal fairness under unobserved confounding, deriving bounds on causal fairness metrics. Kilbertus et al. Consider a wireless communication link assisted by a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS) consisting of N reconfigurable scattering elements. Let H ∈ ℂ^{N×M} denote the channel from an M-antenna transmitter to the RIS elements, and let G ∈ ℂ^{K×N} denote the channel from the RIS elements to a K-antenna receiver. In the standard (idealized) model, the end-to-end channel from transmitter to receiver is written in the factored form

  H_e2e = G Φ H,

where Φ ∈ ℂ^{N×N} is a diagonal matrix whose n-th diagonal entry encodes the reflection coefficient applied by the n-th RIS element, and is parameterized by tunable circuit parameters (e.g. varactor capacitances or PIN-diode states). This idealization ignores electromagnetic mutual impedances and mutual coupling among the densely packed RIS elements.

Let S ∈ ℂ^{N×N} denote the (frequency-dependent, geometry-determined) mutual scattering/impedance matrix of the RIS array, and let Γ(c) ∈ ℂ^{N×N} be a diagonal matrix of element loads parameterized by the vector c ∈ ℝ^N (or ℂ^N) of tunable circuit parameters. A physically consistent multiport-network model leads to an RIS response matrix

  Φ(c) = f(S, Γ(c)),

which in general is non-diagonal and depends jointly on S and on the circuit parameters c.

The problem has two parts:

(1) Derivation. Determine whether there exists a channel model that (a) retains the strictly factored form H_e2e = G Φ(c) H, with G and H independent of c and depending only on the propagation environment between the transmitter / receiver and the RIS, and (b) faithfully captures the mutual-impedance and mutual-coupling effects of the RIS array through a (possibly non-diagonal) matrix Φ(c) that is an explicit function of the circuit parameters c and of the coupling/impedance data of the array.

(2) Estimation. Assuming such a factored model exists, design a practical pilot-based channel-estimation procedure that, from observed input–output measurements taken under a set of training configurations {c_t}, recovers the parameters of G and H (and, if needed, of the coupling structure) with computational and pilot overhead that scales favorably in N, K, and M.

Several works (2023–2025) develop physics-consistent multiport-network and scattering-parameter models for RIS in which the RIS response matrix becomes non-diagonal due to mutual coupling, and propose mutual-coupling-aware channel-estimation algorithms (e.g., compressed-sensing formulations, two-stage MC-unaware/MC-aware estimation, and BD-RIS modeling). These results provide candidate factored or near-factored representations and practical estimators, but a fully general factored model G Φ(c) H that exactly captures arbitrary mutual coupling while admitting a scalable estimator is still under active investigation, so the problem is best regarded as partially solved.

Consider a wireless communication system equipped with a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS) consisting of N passive reflecting elements. Let the cascaded channel between a single-antenna transmitter and a single-antenna receiver via the RIS be modeled as

 y = (h_d + g^T diag(theta) f) x + n,

where h_d ∈ C is the direct (non-RIS) channel, f ∈ C^N is the transmitter-to-RIS channel, g ∈ C^N is the RIS-to-receiver channel, x is the transmitted pilot, n ~ CN(0, sigma^2) is additive Gaussian noise, and theta = (theta_1, ..., theta_N)^T ∈ C^N collects the reflection coefficients of the RIS elements. In an ideal model, each element n can be configured in one of three "deactivated" modes:
 (i) complete absorption: theta_n = 0,
 (ii) complete transmission (pass-through): the element forwards x with unit gain and no phase shift to the receiver via the direct path,
 (iii) complete removal of reflection: the element contributes nothing to g^T diag(theta) f.

Many channel-estimation schemes for f and g (or for the cascaded coefficients g_n f_n) rely on switching subsets of RIS elements into one of these idealized deactivated states during pilot transmissions in order to isolate or cancel contributions. In practice, however, an element configured to be "deactivated" still produces a residual reflection coefficient theta_n^res, which can be modeled as a random variable on C with |theta_n^res| ≤ epsilon for some leakage parameter epsilon > 0 (or, more generally, with a specified distribution centered near 0 but with nonzero mean and variance).

Problem. Develop a quantitative analysis of how this imperfect deactivation affects channel estimation of (h_d, f, g). Specifically:

(a) For a given estimator E (e.g., least squares, LMMSE, or compressed-sensing-based) that assumes ideal deactivation, derive the bias and mean-square error of the resulting estimates of h_d, f, and g as functions of the leakage statistics of {theta_n^res} and of N.

(b) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the leakage distribution (in terms of epsilon, mean, and covariance) under which the estimator E remains consistent as the pilot length and/or N tend to infinity.

(c) Design channel-estimation procedures that are provably robust to imperfect deactivation, in the sense that their worst-case MSE over all leakage distributions satisfying the assumed constraints is minimized, and characterize the optimal estimator and the corresponding fundamental performance limits (e.g., a Cramér–Rao-type bound) in the presence of imperfect deactivation.

Consider a wireless communication system aided by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS): a planar array of $N$ passive (or nearly passive) reflecting elements placed between a transmitter and a receiver, where the $n$-th element imposes a complex reflection coefficient $r_n = a_n e^{j\phi_n}$, with amplitude $a_n \in [0,1]$ and phase $\phi_n \in [0,2\pi)$, on the impinging electromagnetic wave. In most current designs the achievable pair $(a_n,\phi_n)$ is coupled: the amplitude is a (typically non-monotonic) function of the phase due to the physics of the underlying tunable element (e.g., varactor or PIN-diode loaded unit cell), which limits the achievable beamforming and channel-shaping performance.

Design and analyze a unit-cell hardware structure for an RIS such that:
1. Each element $n$ can be independently tuned to any pair $(a_n,\phi_n)$ in a prescribed two-dimensional region $\mathcal{R} \subseteq [0,1]\times[0,2\pi)$, with amplitude and phase essentially decoupled across $\mathcal{R}$.
2. The design operates over a bandwidth and at carrier frequencies relevant to wireless communication (e.g., sub-6 GHz or mm-wave bands), with insertion loss, response time, and power consumption compatible with real-time RIS-aided communication.

Design a unified evaluation framework for causal reinforcement learning (causal RL), with particular emphasis on model-based methods. Concretely, specify:

(a) A common collection of benchmark environments (Markov decision processes, partially observable MDPs, or contextual decision processes) endowed with explicit ground-truth causal structure — for example, structural causal models governing state transitions, latent confounders, interventional and counterfactual queries, distribution shifts across tasks, and observable/hidden variables — that exercise the distinctive capabilities claimed by causal RL methods (causal representation learning, counterfactual policy evaluation, off-policy/offline learning under unobserved confounding, transfer and generalization, and explainability).

(b) A unified evaluation protocol specifying training regimes (online interaction, offline datasets with documented behavior policies, mixed regimes), interventional/counterfactual test-time queries, metrics (sample efficiency, asymptotic return, robustness to distribution shift, accuracy of recovered causal structure, counterfactual prediction error, transfer performance), randomization and seeding, and reporting standards.

(c) A demonstration that the resulting suite enables meaningful head-to-head comparison of model-based causal RL algorithms drawn from disjoint prior literatures, by re-running representative algorithms from each family on the overlapping tasks and reporting their relative performance under the unified protocol.

The problem is to construct such an environment suite and protocol, and to validate it empirically as a common ground for comparing causal RL algorithms.

Consider a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) consisting of $N$ passive reflecting elements, each capable of imposing a (possibly frequency-dependent) reflection coefficient on impinging electromagnetic waves. Suppose the RIS assists a communication link operating over a wideband channel of carrier frequency $f_c$ and bandwidth $B$, where $B/f_c$ is not negligible (so that beam-squint phenomena are non-trivial).

In the reflectarray literature, two principal techniques have been proposed to widen the operating bandwidth of passive reflecting surfaces:
(a) coupling each radiating element to a true time-delay (TTD) line, so that the element imposes a frequency-linear phase response $\phi_n(f) = -2\pi f \tau_n$ for some controllable delay $\tau_n$; and
(b) coupling multiple resonance elements (e.g., stacked patches or multi-resonator unit cells), so that the element's phase response remains approximately linear, or at least controlled, across a broad band.

Formulate and resolve the following questions:

1. Under what assumptions on the RIS element architecture, the propagation geometry (far-field versus near-field, planar wave assumption), the channel model (line-of-sight, multipath, frequency selectivity), and the achievable delay/phase control resolution do the wideband remedies (a) and (b) from the reflectarray literature transfer to RIS-aided communication systems while preserving useful beamforming gain (e.g., array gain $\geq (1-\epsilon) N^2$ for prescribed $\epsilon>0$) uniformly across the band $[f_c - B/2,\, f_c + B/2]$?

2. Quantify, as a function of $N$, $B/f_c$, the steering angle, and the delay resolution, the worst-case beamforming loss and the residual beam-squint after application of (a) or (b), and identify operating regimes in which these techniques are provably effective for wideband RIS communication.

Recent works (2022–2024) have begun adapting reflectarray wideband remedies to RIS. In particular, time-delay-unit-based architectures coupled with element-grouping strategies have been shown to mitigate beam squint in RIS-aided communications, and hybrid TTD/phase-shifter schemes plus space–frequency-transform-based phase designs have been proposed for wideband and near-field RIS beamforming. The general question of when reflectarray-style wideband techniques transfer to RIS with provable uniform beamforming gain is therefore partially addressed but not fully resolved, especially for multi-resonance passive RIS elements and near-field/multipath regimes.

Consider the family of sequential decision-making formalisms that extend the standard Markov decision process (MDP) by incorporating one or more of the following features: (i) latent or hidden parameters governing transition and/or reward distributions (e.g. hidden-parameter MDPs, Bayes-adaptive MDPs, latent MDPs), (ii) unobserved confounders that simultaneously influence actions taken by a behavior policy and observed outcomes (e.g. confounded MDPs, MDPs with unobserved confounders), (iii) partial observability of the underlying state (e.g. partially observable MDPs, predictive state representations), and (iv) explicit causal structure on states, actions, rewards, and exogenous variables (e.g. structural causal MDPs, causal bandits, dynamic causal Bayesian networks for decision-making).

Each such formalism specifies: a (possibly latent) state space, an action space, an observation space, a family of transition kernels indexed by unobserved variables, a reward function, an observation model, and a class of admissible policies, together with an identifiability/learnability target (optimal policy, off-policy value, counterfactual value, intervention distribution, etc.).

Provide a rigorous mathematical framework that:

1. Defines a single class of decision processes — specified as a tuple of measurable spaces, kernels, and a causal directed acyclic graph (or structural causal model) over the relevant variables — that contains each of the above formalisms as a special case obtained by imposing explicit independence, observability, and identifiability constraints.

2. For every pair of formalisms F and F' in the list above, exhibits an explicit reduction (an injective, structure-preserving map of model instances together with a translation of policies and learning targets) from F to F' whenever one exists, and proves a formal non-reducibility result (e.g. an information-theoretic or identifiability obstruction) when none exists.

3. Within the unified framework, characterizes the identifiability of the optimal policy value and of counterfactual policy values in terms of graphical and observability conditions, recovering as corollaries the known identifiability results for each special case.

The problem is to construct such a unifying framework, or alternatively to prove a precise impossibility theorem showing that no single formalism with reasonable expressiveness and tractability can subsume all of the listed models simultaneously.

Consider a wireless communication system aided by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS): a planar array of N passive reflecting elements whose individual reflection coefficients (phase shifts, and possibly amplitudes) can be configured to shape the propagation environment between a transmitter and a receiver. When the RIS aperture is large relative to the wavelength and to the distances involved, a receiver or transmitter may lie within the Rayleigh (near-field) region of the surface. In this regime the standard far-field planar-wave assumption fails: the wavefronts impinging on the surface are curved (spherical), and the angles of arrival/departure, path lengths, and polarization states differ from one RIS element to another, so that the channel cannot be described by a single steering vector parametrized by a single direction.

Formalize the following research problem:

(a) Propose a tractable mathematical channel model for the cascaded transmitter–RIS–receiver link in the near field of a large RIS, accounting for (i) element-dependent spherical wavefront curvature (e.g., per-element distance and angle), (ii) element-dependent polarization mismatch, and (iii) possible mutual coupling, such that the model reduces to the standard far-field planar-wave RIS channel model in the appropriate asymptotic limit.

(b) Design and analyze a channel-estimation algorithm that, given pilot symbols transmitted under a chosen sequence of RIS configurations, recovers the parameters of the proposed near-field channel model with provable guarantees (e.g., identifiability, sample/pilot complexity, mean-squared-error scaling) that exploit the structure (such as spherical-domain sparsity) of the near-field channel.

Determine appropriate models and estimators meeting (a) and (b), and characterize the trade-offs between pilot overhead, RIS size, near-field/far-field regime, and estimation accuracy.

Let $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ denote the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ equipped with the supremum norm $\|f\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|f(x)|$. Let $L$ be the closed operator on $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ defined by $Lf=f''$ on its natural domain $D(L)=\{f\in UC_b(\mathbb{R}): f''\in UC_b(\mathbb{R})\}$. Then $L$ generates the heat semigroup $(e^{tL})_{t\ge 0}$ on $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$, given by
$$(e^{tL}f)(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi t}}\int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-(x-y)^2/(4t)}f(y)\,dy,\qquad t>0.$$

A strongly continuous family of bounded linear operators $(C(t))_{t\ge 0}$ on $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ with $C(0)=I$ is called a Chernoff function of order $k\ge 1$ tangent to $L$ if for every $f\in D(L^k)$,
$$C(t)f = f + tLf + \tfrac{t^2}{2!}L^2 f + \cdots + \tfrac{t^k}{k!}L^k f + o(t^k)\quad\text{as }t\to 0^+,$$
together with the standard Chernoff hypotheses ensuring $C(t/n)^n f\to e^{tL}f$ in $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ for every $f\in UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ as $n\to\infty$.

Known rate theorems guarantee, for fixed $t>0$ and $f\in D(L^k)$, that
$$\|C(t/n)^n f - e^{tL}f\|_\infty = O(n^{-k})\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.$$

Now consider $f\in UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ such that $f$ is once continuously differentiable with $f'\in UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ Hölder continuous of exponent $1/2$, but $f\notin D(L)$ (i.e.\ $f''$ does not exist as an element of $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$).

(a) Determine the asymptotic rate of convergence of $\|C(t/n)^n f - e^{tL}f\|_\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, for $t>0$ fixed, when $C$ has first-order Chernoff tangency to $L$.

(b) More generally, for $f\in UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ whose smoothness is described by a Hölder/Sobolev-type modulus weaker than membership in $D(L^k)$, determine how the asymptotic rate of $\|C(t/n)^n f - e^{tL}f\|_\infty$ depends jointly on the smoothness of $f$ and on the order of Chernoff tangency $k$ of $C$ to $L$.

representations.normalized:
Consider a reinforcement-learning setting in which an agent interacts with an environment modeled as a structural causal model (SCM) M = (U, V, F, P(U)), where U denotes exogenous noise variables with distribution P(U), V denotes endogenous variables (states, actions, rewards across time), and F is a collection of structural assignments determining each endogenous variable from its parents. At each time step t the agent observes a state S_t, selects an action A_t according to a policy π(A_t | history_t), receives a reward R_t, and transitions to S_{t+1}. The interventional distribution P(V | do(A_t = a)) and the counterfactual distribution P(V_{A_t = a'} | S_t = s, A_t = a, R_t = r, ...) are defined in the standard Pearl sense via abduction, action, and prediction on M.

Formulate and investigate the following problem:

(a) Define a principled framework specifying how an RL agent should incorporate counterfactual queries of the form "what reward / future trajectory would have been observed had a different action a' been taken in the past, given the actually observed history?" into (i) online action selection, (ii) policy search / policy gradient estimation, (iii) credit assignment for sequential decisions, and (iv) human-in-the-loop interaction where a human supplies counterfactual judgments.

(b) Establish formal conditions on the SCM M (e.g., identifiability assumptions on noise variables, monotonicity, invertibility of structural functions, partial knowledge of F) under which such counterfactual quantities are identifiable from data accessible to the agent (logged trajectories, on-policy samples, or expert demonstrations), and provide consistent estimators with finite-sample guarantees.

(c) Prove a separation theorem (or provide a concrete construction) exhibiting an environment class and learning objective for which any agent restricted to observational and interventional reasoning incurs strictly higher regret, sample complexity, or asymptotic suboptimality than an agent permitted to use counterfactual reasoning over M, thereby demonstrating that the benefits go beyond what observational/interventional reasoning alone can achieve.

(d) Instantiate the framework on at least one real-world decision-making domain and exhibit a counterfactual agent whose performance, robustness, or sample efficiency provably exceeds that of its non-counterfactual baseline.

Let $UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ denote the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous real-valued functions on $\mathbb{R}$, equipped with the supremum norm $\|\cdot\|$. Fix functions $a,b,c \in UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ with $\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}} a(x) > 0$. On the domain $C_b^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ of bounded smooth functions with bounded derivatives of all orders, define the second-order variable-coefficient differential operator
\[ (Lf)(x) = a(x)f''(x) + b(x)f'(x) + c(x)f(x). \]
Assume that the closure of $L$ generates a strongly continuous semigroup $(e^{tL})_{t\ge 0}$ on $UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$.

Recall that a family $(C(t))_{t\ge 0}$ of bounded linear operators on $UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ is called a Chernoff function for $L$ if $C(0)=I$, $\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|C(t)\|<\infty$ for every $T>0$, $C(t)f$ is continuous in $t$ for every $f$, and $\lim_{t\to 0^+}(C(t)f-f)/t = Lf$ for $f$ in a core of $L$; in this case Chernoff's theorem yields $e^{tL}f = \lim_{n\to\infty} C(t/n)^n f$.

Question. Do there exist a family $(C(t))_{t\ge 0}$ of bounded linear operators on $UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ and a dense linear subspace $D \subset UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ such that:

(i) $(C(t))_{t\ge 0}$ is a Chernoff function for $L$;

(ii) there is an explicit formula $(C(t)f)(x) = F(a,b,c,f,x;t)$ depending only on the coefficients $a,b,c$, on $f$, and on $x,t$, and in particular not involving the semigroup $e^{tL}$ (neither explicitly nor in any hidden way);

(iii) there exist constants $M>0$, $q>1$, and $n_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for every $f\in D$ and every $t$ in a fixed bounded interval,
\[ \|e^{tL}f - C(t/n)^n f\| \le \frac{M}{q^n} \quad \text{for all } n \ge n_0? \]

If no such "superfast" Chernoff approximation exists, exhibit an obstruction proving its impossibility.

Let $F = UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ denote the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with the sup norm $\|f\| = \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}} |f(x)|$. Consider the heat equation $u_t(t,x) = u_{xx}(t,x)$ on $\mathbb{R}$, whose solution defines the heat semigroup $(e^{tL})_{t\ge 0}$ in $F$ generated by $Lf = f''$.

Define the bounded linear operators on $F$
$$ (G(t)f)(x) = \tfrac{1}{2} f(x) + \tfrac{1}{4} f(x+2\sqrt{t}) + \tfrac{1}{4} f(x-2\sqrt{t}), $$
$$ (S(t)f)(x) = \tfrac{2}{3} f(x) + \tfrac{1}{6} f(x+\sqrt{6t}) + \tfrac{1}{6} f(x-\sqrt{6t}). $$
Then $G$ is Chernoff-tangent to $L$ of first order, and $S$ is Chernoff-tangent to $L$ of second order, so by Chernoff's theorem, for every $t>0$ and every $u_0\in F$,
$$ d_n^G := \|e^{tL}u_0 - G(t/n)^n u_0\| \to 0, \qquad d_n^S := \|e^{tL}u_0 - S(t/n)^n u_0\| \to 0 \quad (n\to\infty). $$
Fix $t = 1/2$. Empirically one observes a log-log linear relation $\ln d_n \approx \alpha \ln n + \beta$, where $\alpha$ is called the order of the decreasing error and $\beta$ the free term.

Numerical computation shows:
- For $u_0(x) = \sin x$ and $u_0(x) = \cos x$, the linear fit $\ln d_n$ vs $\ln n$ is essentially perfect.
- For the nonsmooth $u_0(x) = |\sin x|^{1/4}$, the linear fit is good.
- For the smooth $u_0(x) = \exp(-x^4)$, the linear fit is noticeably poorer, contrary to the naive expectation that higher regularity should improve the fit.

Provide a theoretical explanation: identify a mechanism (in terms of the structure of $G$, $S$, the heat semigroup, and the initial datum) that determines the quality of the log-log linear fit of $d_n^G$ and $d_n^S$ as functions of $n$, and that explains why the eigenfunctions $\sin x, \cos x$ produce a perfect fit, why $|\sin x|^{1/4}$ still produces a good fit, while $\exp(-x^4)$ produces a poorer one.

$$ d_n^G := \|e^{tL}u_0 - G(t/n)^n u_0\| \to 0, \qquad d_n^S := \|e^{tL}u_0 - S(t/n)^n u_0\| \to 0 $$

$$ \ln d_n^G \approx \alpha_G \ln n + \beta_G, \qquad \ln d_n^S \approx \alpha_S \ln n + \beta_S, $$
with $\alpha_G, \alpha_S < 0$ called the orders of decreasing error and $\beta_G, \beta_S$ the free terms.

Consider the heat equation u_t(t,x) = u_{xx}(t,x) for (t,x) ∈ [0,∞) × ℝ on the Banach space F = UC_b(ℝ) of bounded uniformly continuous real-valued functions on ℝ with the sup norm ‖f‖ = sup_{x∈ℝ}|f(x)|. The operator L f = f'' generates the heat C_0-semigroup (e^{tL})_{t≥0} on F.

Define two families of bounded linear operators on F by

  (G(t)f)(x) = (1/2) f(x) + (1/4) f(x + 2√t) + (1/4) f(x − 2√t),
  (S(t)f)(x) = (2/3) f(x) + (1/6) f(x + √(6t)) + (1/6) f(x − √(6t)),

so that G is Chernoff-tangent to L of first order and S is Chernoff-tangent to L of second order. By Chernoff's theorem, for every t > 0 and every u_0 ∈ F,

  d_n^G(t,u_0) := ‖e^{tL} u_0 − G(t/n)^n u_0‖ → 0,
  d_n^S(t,u_0) := ‖e^{tL} u_0 − S(t/n)^n u_0‖ → 0 as n → ∞.

Fix t = 1/2 and, for each parameter ξ ∈ (0,1), consider the two families of initial data

  u_0^{(sin)}(x) = |sin x|^ξ,    u_0^{(exp)}(x) = exp(−|x|^ξ),

both of which lie in F and belong to the Hölder class of exponent ξ. Empirically one finds a power-law decay

  log d_n^G ≈ α_G(ξ) log n + β_G(ξ),   log d_n^S ≈ α_S(ξ) log n + β_S(ξ),

and α_G(ξ) and α_S(ξ) each appear to be linear functions of ξ on (0,1) for both families.

Problem. Prove (or disprove) that for these two families of low-regularity initial conditions, the orders of decrease α_G(ξ) and α_S(ξ) of the Chernoff approximation error depend linearly on the Hölder/smoothness exponent ξ ∈ (0,1), and identify the slopes and intercepts of these linear dependences in terms of the structure of the Chernoff functions G and S and of the initial-data family (trigonometric |sin x|^ξ versus exponential exp(−|x|^ξ)). In particular, provide a theorem that predicts the observed linear dependence and explains why the slopes differ between the trigonometric and exponential families.

A neutron star is a compact stellar remnant endowed with a magnetic field whose surface strength B can be inferred from pulsar timing (via the spin period P and its derivative). Observations of neutron star populations across a wide range of ages (from young pulsars at ages ~10^3–10^6 yr to recycled millisecond pulsars and "black widow" systems with characteristic ages ≳10^9 yr) raise the following question about the long-term evolution of B(t):

Determine whether the magnetic field of an isolated or binary neutron star genuinely decays as a function of age on astrophysical timescales, and if so characterize the asymptotic behavior. Specifically, decide between the following competing scenarios and identify the physical mechanism responsible:

(a) B(t) decays almost completely on a timescale of order 10^6 years, so that very old neutron stars retain only negligible magnetic fields;

(b) B(t) decays only partially toward a finite, non-zero "bottom field" B_min > 0 that persists even in systems with evolution times ≳10^9 yr, as suggested by inferred field strengths of black-widow pulsars and other very old recycled systems.

Provide a quantitative model B(t) (including dependence on accretion history, crustal impurity, and thermal evolution) that is consistent with the observed distribution of magnetic field strengths in the full neutron-star population, and either establish the existence and value of B_min or rule it out.
