Consider the observed Galactic population of isolated neutron stars, which is empirically partitioned into several classes distinguished by their emission properties, spin periods, period derivatives, magnetic field strengths, surface temperatures, and ages. These classes include: (i) ordinary radio pulsars (rotation-powered neutron stars emitting coherent radio pulsations); (ii) central compact objects (CCOs), thermally emitting X-ray point sources located near the centers of supernova remnants, with no detected radio emission and inferred weak dipolar magnetic fields; (iii) X-ray Dim Isolated Neutron Stars (XDINSs, the "Magnificent Seven"), nearby isolated neutron stars showing purely thermal soft X-ray spectra, long spin periods (several seconds), and no radio counterparts; (iv) Rotating Radio Transients (RRATs), neutron stars detected only through sporadic single radio bursts rather than persistent pulsations; (v) magnetars (anomalous X-ray pulsars and soft gamma repeaters), neutron stars whose X-ray luminosity exceeds their rotational energy loss and which are powered by the decay of ultra-strong magnetic fields (B ≳ 10^14 G); and (vi) additional "hidden" classes of neutron stars that evade standard radio surveys.

Determine the evolutionary relationships connecting these subpopulations. Specifically, identify which of the above classes correspond to genuinely distinct populations of neutron stars with different formation channels or progenitor properties, and which instead represent transient evolutionary phases through which a single underlying type of neutron star passes during its lifetime. Provide a unified evolutionary scheme (for example, a directed graph of transitions among classes parameterized by age, magnetic field strength and its decay, spin period, and temperature) consistent with the observed number densities, kinematic ages, period and period-derivative distributions, magnetic field estimates, and thermal luminosities of each class, and consistent with the Galactic core-collapse supernova rate.

Consider isolated neutron stars exhibiting rotational periods far longer than those of the canonical magnetar population (periods of minutes to hours), referred to here as ultra-slow magnetars or ultra-long period transients, together with the class of Rotating Radio Transients (RRATs), which are neutron stars detected only via sporadic, short-duration radio bursts rather than persistent pulsations.

Standard magnetar evolution predicts that strongly magnetized neutron stars are born with periods of order 1 s and, through magnetic dipole braking enhanced by their ultra-strong fields (B ~ 10^14–10^15 G), spin down while their interiors cool over time.

Determine whether the following alternative is correct:

(a) The recently observed ultra-slow magnetars and other very-long-period neutron-star candidates are simply older, cooled and spun-down evolutionary descendants of ordinary magnetars; or

(b) They constitute a physically distinct population whose properties (e.g., quiescent X-ray luminosity, radio emission behavior, magnetothermal evolution) are more closely related to RRATs than to the standard magnetar evolutionary track.

Specifically, identify whether there exists a real physical distinction between RRATs and ultra-slow magnetars, and characterize the evolutionary channel(s) that produce neutron stars with periods of minutes to hours.

The question remains open as of 2025–2026. Recent theoretical work (e.g., "Late-blooming magnetars" model, May 2025) proposes that ultra-long period transients could be magnetars that remained dormant during an initial cooling epoch before crustal Hall-driven activity began, but the connection to RRATs and the precise evolutionary status of ultra-slow magnetars is still actively debated. Other modeling of magnetar spin evolution suggests magnetars are unlikely to evolve into RRATs, favoring an evolutionary link instead with X-ray dim isolated neutron stars. Consider the mass distribution of stellar-mass compact remnants (neutron stars and black holes) formed via stellar evolution and observed through electromagnetic and gravitational-wave channels. Empirically, neutron-star masses cluster below roughly 2.5 solar masses while observed stellar black holes are typically found at or above about 5 solar masses, suggesting a possible "lower mass gap" in the interval from approximately 2 to 5 solar masses (or, more conservatively, 2.5 to 5 solar masses).

Question: Does the underlying compact-object mass distribution contain a true gap in the interval [2, 5] solar masses (equivalently, is this interval essentially unpopulated), or is the interval only partially depleted, in the sense that there exist compact objects, formed through standard or alternative formation channels (such as core-collapse supernovae with different convective timescales, binary interactions, accretion-induced collapse, or hierarchical/dynamical processes), whose masses lie within the 2.5–5 solar-mass range with non-negligible probability? In particular, determine (i) whether a strict gap exists, (ii) if not, the lower edge above which any depletion begins, and (iii) the formation channels capable of populating the 2.5–5 solar-mass range.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The existence and structure of the lower black-hole mass gap (roughly 2–5 solar masses) remains an active and unresolved question. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a class of directed graphs (called demand patterns) that is closed under transitive equivalence (i.e., if $D \in \mathcal{D}$ and $D'$ has the same transitive closure as $D$, then $D' \in \mathcal{D}$) and closed under identifying vertices (i.e., contracting any subset of vertices into a single vertex, keeping the resulting digraph, possibly with parallel edges removed, in $\mathcal{D}$).

Define the problem $\mathcal{D}$-Steiner Network as follows:
- Input: a digraph $G$, a set $T \subseteq V(G)$ of $k$ terminals, and a demand digraph $D \in \mathcal{D}$ on vertex set $T$.
- Output: the minimum number of edges in a subgraph $H$ of $G$ such that for every $(u,v) \in E(D)$ there is a directed path from $u$ to $v$ in $H$.

Define Planar $\mathcal{D}$-Steiner Network to be the same problem restricted to inputs where $G$ is a planar digraph.

Question: Does there exist a class $\mathcal{D}$ (closed under transitive equivalence and identifying vertices) such that Planar $\mathcal{D}$-Steiner Network is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the number of terminals $k$, while $\mathcal{D}$-Steiner Network on general digraphs is W[1]-hard with the same parameter?

In the Standard Model of particle physics, the combined charge-conjugation and parity symmetry (CP) is violated in the quark sector through a single complex phase in the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa mixing matrix. The amount of CP violation predicted by this mechanism is known to be many orders of magnitude too small to account for the observed cosmological baryon asymmetry, i.e., the dominance of matter over antimatter in the present-day universe (with baryon-to-photon ratio of order 10^{-10}). Sakharov's conditions state that to dynamically generate such an asymmetry from a symmetric initial state one needs (i) baryon number violation, (ii) C and CP violation, and (iii) a departure from thermal equilibrium.

Problem: Propose and analyze a new mechanism of CP violation — beyond the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa phase of the Standard Model — that, together with appropriate baryon-number-violating interactions and out-of-equilibrium dynamics in the early universe, quantitatively reproduces the observed matter–antimatter asymmetry of the present universe. Specify the underlying field-theoretic model, identify the new CP-violating phases or operators, and compute the resulting baryon-to-entropy ratio, demonstrating that it agrees with the observed value while remaining consistent with current experimental bounds (electric dipole moments, flavor-changing neutral currents, collider searches, etc.).

representations.normalized:
Let D be a class of finite directed graphs (called demand patterns) that is closed under the following two operations: (i) transitive equivalence — replacing a graph by any other graph having the same transitive closure on the same vertex set, and (ii) identification of vertices — merging any subset of vertices into a single vertex (removing loops and parallel edges).

For a fixed class D, the Planar D-Steiner Network problem is defined as follows. An instance consists of:
- a directed planar graph G with nonnegative edge weights,
- a positive integer k, a set T = {t_1,…,t_k} ⊆ V(G) of terminals,
- a demand pattern H ∈ D on vertex set {1,…,k}.

The task is to find a minimum-weight subgraph N ⊆ G such that for every arc (i,j) ∈ E(H), the subgraph N contains a directed path from t_i to t_j.

Assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), give a combinatorial characterization, in terms of the structure of the graphs in D, that determines which of the following two regimes Planar D-Steiner Network (parameterized by the number k of terminals) falls into:

(A) solvable in time f(k) · n^{O(√k)} for some computable f, or

(B) not solvable in time f(k) · n^{o(k)} for any computable f, but solvable in time f(k) · n^{O(k)}.

That is, identify the precise structural property of the demand-pattern class D that separates the √k-exponent regime from the linear-k-exponent regime.

uho\sigma}$. Suppose one knows in detail the structure of these vacuum states as functionals of the backgrounds, and one computes the response (effective action) of the vacuum to small perturbations of $A_\mu^a$ and $e^a_\mu$.

Question: Can one derive, from a controlled calculation of this vacuum response using the detailed structure of the vacuum states, the Maxwell–Yang–Mills action
$$S_{m YM} \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{4}\int d^4x\,\sqrt{-g}\;F_{\mu\nu}^a F^{a\,\mu\nu},$$
and the Einstein–Hilbert action
$$S_{\rm EH} \;=\; \frac{1}{16\pi G}\int d^4x\,\sqrt{-g}\;R,$$
as the leading low-energy terms induced on the gauge and gravitational backgrounds? Equivalently, give a rigorous mechanism by which the kinetic terms for gauge fields and the Einstein–Hilbert term emerge as the response of the vacuum to gauge-field and vierbein curvature.

representations.normalized:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $\mathcal{P}(M)$ denote the space of Borel probability measures on $M$. A probability vector field (PVF) on $M$ is a Borel map $V:\mathcal{P}(M)\to \mathcal{P}(TM)$ such that for every $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(M)$ the pushforward of $V(\mu)$ by the canonical projection $\pi:TM\to M$ equals $\mu$. A measure differential equation (MDE) driven by a PVF $V$ is the evolution problem of finding a continuous curve $t\mapsto \mu_t\in\mathcal{P}(M)$ satisfying, in the sense of distributions,
$$\partial_t \mu_t + \mathrm{div}_x\!\big(\,\textstyle\int_{T_x M} v\, dV(\mu_t)(x,v)\,\big) = 0,$$
or more generally the generalized notion of solution in which $\mu_t$ is obtained as a limit of Euler-type discrete schemes built from $V$. Under composition of the associated time-$t$ flows on $\mathcal{P}(M)$, the family of PVFs carries only the algebraic structure of an abelian monoid (with composition of induced flows as the operation), and does not in general carry a Lie algebra structure analogous to the one available for smooth vector fields on $M$.

A controlled MDE is the data of a family $\{V_u\}_{u\in U}$ of PVFs parameterized by a control set $U$, together with admissible controls $u:[0,T]\to U$, generating flows $\Phi_t^{u(\cdot)}:\mathcal{P}(M)\to\mathcal{P}(M)$ on the space of measures.

Problem. Develop a mathematically substantive control theory for such controlled MDEs at the level of the induced flows $\Phi_t^{u(\cdot)}$ on $\mathcal{P}(M)$ (rather than at the level of individual solution curves), using geometric control techniques. Specifically:

(a) Define suitable notions of accessibility, controllability, and reachable sets for the semigroup of flows generated by a family of PVFs, in a setting where only an abelian monoid (and not a Lie algebra) structure is available.

(b) Establish analogues of the Chow–Rashevskii / orbit theorems and Krener-type accessibility results characterizing the reachable set $\mathcal{R}_T(\mu_0)=\{\Phi_T^{u(\cdot)}\mu_0 : u(\cdot)\text{ admissible}\}$ in terms of intrinsic geometric invariants of the family $\{V_u\}_{u\in U}$.

(c) Identify sufficient conditions on the family $\{V_u\}$ under which the flow-level control system is (approximately) controllable on $\mathcal{P}(M)$, and exhibit nontrivial examples in which these conditions can be verified.

Consider a multi-agent system whose state can be described at several scales and through several limiting procedures:

1. A microscopic description by a system of N coupled ordinary differential equations
   x_i'(t) = F(x_i(t), (x_j(t))_{j=1..N}, u_i(t)),  i = 1,...,N,
   where x_i(t) ∈ R^d is the state of agent i and u_i ∈ U_ad is a control taking values in a fixed admissible control set;

2. A mean-field description, in which as N → ∞ the empirical measure μ^N_t = (1/N) Σ δ_{x_i(t)} converges to a probability measure μ_t solving a continuity/Vlasov-type PDE
   ∂_t μ_t + div(V[μ_t, ν_t] μ_t) = 0,
   driven by a measure-valued control ν_t;

3. A graph-limit (graphon) description, in which the interaction weights w_{ij}^N converge to a graphon W: [0,1]^2 → R and the agent population converges to a continuum of agents indexed by α ∈ [0,1] whose state x(t,α) evolves according to an integro-differential equation involving W;

4. An embedding-based description, in which agents are represented as points/measures in a common Hilbert or Wasserstein space, and the dynamics and controls are formulated in this embedding.

Associated to each level is an optimal control problem of minimizing a cost functional J of the form
   J = ∫_0^T L(state, control) dt + Φ(state(T))
   subject to the corresponding dynamics, over admissible controls in U_ad.

Problem. Develop a rigorous theory of optimal control under these limiting procedures. Specifically:

(a) Identify conditions on F, L, Φ, the interaction kernels, and the admissible controls under which the value functions and optimal controls of the microscopic problems converge (e.g., in the sense of Γ-convergence) to those of the mean-field, graphon, and embedding-based control problems, and characterize the limit problems explicitly.

(b) Determine which structural properties of the control problem (existence of optimizers, Pontryagin-type optimality conditions, dynamic programming / Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations, controllability, stability of optimal trajectories, regularity of the value function) are preserved when passing between any two of these descriptions, and which are altered or lost.

(c) Establish the commutativity (or quantify the failure of commutativity) of the diagram whose vertices are the four control problems and whose edges are the mean-field limit, the graph limit, and the embedding maps.

Partial results exist: Γ-convergence of finite-agent optimal controls to mean-field optimal controls is established in several settings, and graphon mean-field control frameworks (including on sparse graphs) have been developed recently. Consider a multi-agent control system formulated in three equivalent ways:

1. (Lagrangian) A population of agents is described by trajectories $t\mapsto x_i(t)\in\mathbb{R}^d$, $i=1,\dots,N$, satisfying $\dot x_i(t)=v_F(t,x_i(t),\mu^N_t)+u_i(t)$, where $\mu^N_t=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{x_i(t)}$, $v_F:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)\to\mathbb{R}^d$ is a given interaction field, and $u_i\in L^2([0,T];\mathbb{R}^d)$ are controls.

2. (Eulerian) The mean-field limit is described by a curve $t\mapsto\mu_t\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ together with a Borel velocity field $w:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ that decomposes as $w(t,x)=v_F(t,x,\mu_t)+u(t,x)$, satisfying the continuity equation $\partial_t\mu_t+\mathrm{div}(w\,\mu_t)=0$ in the sense of distributions, with prescribed initial datum $\mu_0$.

3. (Kantorovich) Solutions are represented as probability measures $\eta\in\mathcal{P}(\Gamma)$ on the space $\Gamma=C([0,T];\mathbb{R}^d)$ of continuous curves, concentrated on absolutely continuous curves $\gamma$ that satisfy $\dot\gamma(t)=v_F(t,\gamma(t),(e_t)_\#\eta)+u_\eta(t,\gamma)$ for $\eta$-a.e. $\gamma$, where $e_t:\Gamma\to\mathbb{R}^d$ is the evaluation map $\gamma\mapsto\gamma(t)$, and $u_\eta$ is a control law that may depend on the curve.

Given a cost functional of the form
$$\mathcal{J}(\eta,u_\eta)=\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Gamma L(t,\gamma(t),(e_t)_\#\eta,u_\eta(t,\gamma))\,d\eta(\gamma)\,dt + \int_\Gamma\Psi(\gamma)\,d\eta(\gamma),$$
together with a sparsity-promoting term (for instance an $L^1$-type penalization of the control in a suitable sense), address the following:

(a) Provide a precise notion of "sparse" or "parsimonious" control within the Kantorovich formulation, namely a notion that captures the idea that only a small (in measure) portion of the population is actively controlled at any given time, and that is consistent under the equivalences with the Lagrangian and Eulerian formulations.

(b) Derive necessary optimality conditions (in the form of a Pontryagin-type maximum principle on $\mathcal{P}(\Gamma)$) for minimizers of $\mathcal{J}$ in the Kantorovich formulation, including the case with sparsity-promoting penalizations.

(c) Identify sufficient conditions (such as convexity/semiconcavity hypotheses on $L$, $\Psi$, and $v_F$) under which the necessary conditions in (b) are also sufficient for optimality.

A targeted search did not reveal a published treatment of sparsity, parsimonious controls, and necessary/sufficient optimality conditions specifically within the Kantorovich (measure-on-curves) formulation of multi-agent control. Consider a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), modeled as a planar array of N sub-wavelength scattering elements, each loaded with a tunable impedance that determines a complex reflection coefficient r_n ∈ ℂ. In a typical wireless communication setting, an RIS is placed in the propagation environment between a transmitter and a receiver, so that the receiver observes a superposition of (i) the direct (non-RIS) channel and (ii) the cascaded channel through the RIS, whose contribution depends linearly on the reflection coefficients {r_n}. For training and channel estimation, one often wishes to "deactivate" the RIS — meaning to choose impedance loads so that, when illuminated by an incident electromagnetic wave at the carrier frequency of interest, the RIS contributes no scattered field to the receiver, i.e. effectively r_n = 0 for every element n. Call this condition "perfect deactivation" of the RIS.

Formulate and resolve the following:

(a) Is perfect deactivation of every RIS element physically realizable, in the sense that there exist passive (or otherwise implementable) load impedances Z_n such that, accounting for mutual coupling between elements, the total scattered field produced by the RIS in response to an arbitrary incident plane wave at the operating frequency vanishes identically in the far field (or, more weakly, vanishes at the receiver location relevant to a communication link)?

(b) If perfect deactivation is feasible, specify the electromagnetic design conditions (load impedance values, element geometry, inter-element spacing, mutual-coupling constraints, bandwidth, polarization, angle-of-arrival dependence) and the implementation methods (e.g., open-circuit loads, matched loads, absorbing loads, switched terminations) under which it can be achieved in a conclusive and communication-relevant manner.

(c) If perfect deactivation is not feasible, quantify the minimum achievable residual reflected power and characterize the fundamental physical obstructions (e.g., structural scattering from the metallic backplane and element bodies, mutual coupling, finite-Q resonances) that prevent it.

A finite lattice $L$ is called semimodular if for all $a,b\in L$, whenever $a$ covers $a\wedge b$ then $a\vee b$ covers $b$. The lattice $L$ is called planar if it has a planar Hasse diagram, and slim if it contains no sublattice isomorphic to $M_3$ (the five-element modular nondistributive lattice with three atoms). An SPS lattice is a finite slim planar semimodular lattice.

Background and definitions:

- A finite lattice L is called rectangular if it is planar, semimodular, and has exactly two doubly irreducible elements on its boundary, called its left corner and right corner; these corners are complementary elements. A rectangular lattice L is a patch lattice if its left and right corners are both dual atoms of L (i.e., are covered by the top element 1_L).

- For lattices, the glued sum A ⊔ B of two bounded lattices A and B is the lattice obtained by identifying the top element of A with the bottom element of B. Let B_2 denote the four-element Boolean lattice.

- The congruence lattice Con L of a finite lattice L is a finite distributive lattice. It is known that a rectangular lattice L is a patch lattice if and only if Con L can be written as a glued sum Con L = Con^h L ⊔ B_2 for some finite distributive lattice Con^h L (intuitively, Con^h L is Con L with its "hat" B_2 removed).

Problem: Determine necessary and sufficient conditions, expressed purely in terms of intrinsic properties of a finite distributive lattice D^h, for the finite distributive lattice D = D^h ⊔ B_2 to be isomorphic to Con L for some patch lattice L. Equivalently, characterize the class of finite distributive lattices that arise as Con^h L when L ranges over all patch lattices.

Consider the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem with finitely many arms. A bandit instance $\mu = (\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_K)$ specifies the distribution of each arm; let $\mathcal{S}$ denote the class of instances admitting a unique best arm, i.e. a unique index $I^*(\mu) \in \{1,\ldots,K\}$ whose mean reward is strictly larger than that of every other arm.

In the fixed-budget best-arm identification problem, a total number of samples $n$ is fixed in advance. An algorithm consists of (i) a sampling rule that at each round $t = 1, \ldots, n$ chooses an arm $A_t$ as a (possibly randomized) function of past observations, and (ii) a decision rule that, after observing all $n$ samples, outputs a guess $\hat{I}_n \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ for the identity of the best arm. The error probability of the algorithm on instance $\mu$ with budget $n$ is
$$p_{\mu,n} := \mathbb{P}_\mu\bigl(\hat{I}_n \neq I^*(\mu)\bigr).$$

Question: Do there exist a class $\mathcal{A}$ of admissible algorithms and an instance-dependent function $\Gamma^*_{\mathrm{fb}} : \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item (lower bound) for every algorithm in $\mathcal{A}$ and every $\mu \in \mathcal{S}$,
$$\liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{n}{\log(1/p_{\mu,n})} \;\geq\; \Gamma^*_{\mathrm{fb}}(\mu),$$
\item (matching upper bound) there exists an algorithm in $\mathcal{A}$ such that for every $\mu \in \mathcal{S}$,
$$\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{n}{\log(1/p_{\mu,n})} \;\leq\; \Gamma^*_{\mathrm{fb}}(\mu),$$
\end{enumerate}
so that $\Gamma^*_{\mathrm{fb}}(\mu)$ exactly characterizes the asymptotic complexity of fixed-budget best-arm identification on $\mathcal{S}$?

The question is the well-known fixed-budget best-arm identification complexity problem posed by Qin (2022). Let S be a class of multi-armed bandit instances with K≥2 arms, where each instance μ=(μ_1,…,μ_K)∈S specifies the reward distribution of every arm and has a unique best arm a*(μ)=argmax_i μ_i. In the fixed-budget best-arm identification setting, an algorithm interacts with an instance μ for n rounds: at each round t=1,…,n it selects an arm A_t (possibly depending on past observations and internal randomness), observes a reward drawn from the corresponding distribution, and after round n outputs a guess â_n of the best arm. Let p_{μ,n} := P_μ(â_n ≠ a*(μ)) denote the probability of misidentification. Define the asymptotic error exponent of an algorithm on instance μ as

   E(μ) := limsup_{n→∞}  n / log(1/p_{μ,n}).

A smaller value of E(μ) corresponds to faster (better) asymptotic decay of the error probability. The "uniform sampling" algorithm draws each arm equally often (in round-robin or i.i.d. uniform fashion) and outputs the empirical best arm at time n; let E^{unif}(μ) be its error exponent on μ.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm π, different from uniform sampling, such that

   E^π(μ) ≤ E^{unif}(μ)   for every instance μ ∈ S,

i.e., an algorithm that performs uniformly no worse than the uniform-sampling benchmark on every bandit instance in the class S?

Subsequent work has addressed the problem in restricted settings. Degenne (COLT 2023, "On the existence of a complexity in fixed budget bandit identification") shows that for several classes (including two-armed Bernoulli bandits / A/B testing) no adaptive algorithm can strictly outperform uniform sampling on all instances, and more generally that any putative instance-uniform complexity must be attained by a static (non-adaptive) procedure. The strict version (no algorithm strictly beats uniform on every instance) is thus resolved negatively in some structured settings, but the general question of whether some non-uniform algorithm attains error exponent ≤ uniform on every instance of a general class S remains open in full generality.

Consider the fixed-budget best-arm identification problem for two-armed Bernoulli bandits. There are two arms with unknown means $\mu_1, \mu_2 \in (0,1)$, $\mu_1 \neq \mu_2$, and an algorithm is given a total budget of $T$ samples. At each round $t = 1, \dots, T$, the algorithm chooses an arm $A_t \in \{1,2\}$ (based on past observations) and observes an independent reward $X_t \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\mu_{A_t})$. After $T$ rounds, the algorithm outputs a recommended arm $\hat{a}_T$, and its error probability is $p_T(\mu_1,\mu_2) = \Pr(\hat{a}_T \neq \arg\max_i \mu_i)$.

It is known that, for each instance $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$, there exists an optimal (instance-dependent) sampling proportion $w^*(\mu_1,\mu_2) \in (0,1)$ characterizing the best achievable asymptotic exponential decay rate
$$\Gamma^*(\mu_1,\mu_2) = -\lim_{T\to\infty} \tfrac{1}{T}\log p_T(\mu_1,\mu_2),$$
but $w^*$ depends on the unknown means.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm, not having prior knowledge of $\mu_1,\mu_2$, that is asymptotically optimal in the sense that
$$-\liminf_{T\to\infty} \tfrac{1}{T}\log p_T(\mu_1,\mu_2) \geq \Gamma^*(\mu_1,\mu_2)$$
for every instance $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$?

Define the continuous-time critical beta-splitting random tree on $n$ leaves, denoted $\mathrm{CTCS}(n)$, as follows. Starting from a single clade containing all $n$ leaves, each clade of size $m\ge 2$ persists for an exponential holding time of rate $h_{m-1} = \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} 1/j$, after which it splits into two subclades of sizes $i$ and $m-i$ ($1\le i\le m-1$) with probability
\[
q(m,i) \;=\; \frac{1}{h_{m-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{i(m-i)}\cdot\frac{m}{2}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{1\le i\le m-1\}\cdot\tfrac{1}{?}\,,
\]
i.e. proportional to $1/(i(m-i))$ (with the appropriate symmetric normalization so that probabilities sum to one); subclades evolve independently in the same manner, and clades of size $1$ are leaves and do not split further. The time-height of a leaf is the sum of the holding times of the clades containing it (equivalently, the time at which that leaf is created).

Use the natural ``interval'' (or cyclic) representation in which the $n$ leaves are placed in a fixed linear order $1,2,\dots,n$ induced by the recursive splitting. For $1\le r\le n-1$, let $D_n^{(1)}$ and $D_n^{(2)}$ denote the time-heights of two leaves whose positions in this order are at distance $r_n$ apart, and let
\[
\rho(n,r_n) \;=\; \mathrm{Corr}\bigl(D_n^{(1)},\,D_n^{(2)}\bigr).
\]

Prove that whenever $r_n$ is a sequence of integers with $1\le r_n\le n-1$ and
\[
\frac{\log r_n}{\log n} \longrightarrow \alpha \in [0,1] \qquad (n\to\infty),
\]
one has
\[
\rho(n,r_n)\;\longrightarrow\;1-\alpha.
\]

Fix an integer $n\ge 2$ and consider the following interval-splitting construction of a random binary tree with $n$ leaves labelled $1,2,\dots,n$.

Discrete-time model DTCS(n). Start with the interval $[0,n]$, regarded as the root, containing the $n$ unit subintervals $[i-1,i]$, $i=1,\dots,n$, called "leaf-points." Recursively, any interval $[a,b]$ of integer length $m=b-a\ge 2$ that has not yet been split is split into two subintervals $[a,a+J]$ and $[a+J,b]$, where the split position $J\in\{1,2,\dots,m-1\}$ is chosen with the critical beta-splitting probabilities
$$q(m,j)=\frac{1}{h_{m-1}}\Big(\frac{1}{j}+\frac{1}{m-j}\Big)\cdot\frac{1}{2},\qquad j=1,\dots,m-1,$$
where $h_{k}=\sum_{r=1}^{k}1/r$ is the $k$-th harmonic number. (Equivalently, $q(m,j)=\frac{1}{h_{m-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{j(m-j)}\cdot\frac{m}{2}$ after symmetrisation.) Splits at distinct intervals are independent. The recursion stops when every remaining interval has length $1$; these unit intervals are the leaves and inherit the labels $1,\dots,n$ from their positions. The resulting rooted binary tree is DTCS(n), and the height of a leaf is the number of edges on the path from the root to that leaf.

Continuous-time model CTCS(n). Fix an integer $n\ge 2$ and consider the following interval-splitting construction of a random binary tree with $n$ leaves labelled $1,2,\dots,n$.

Discrete-time model DTCS(n). Start with the interval $[0,n]$, regarded as the root, containing the $n$ unit subintervals $[i-1,i]$, $i=1,\dots,n$, called "leaf-points." Recursively, any interval $[a,b]$ of integer length $m=b-a\ge 2$ that has not yet been split is split into two subintervals $[a,a+J]$ and $[a+J,b]$, where the split position $J\in\{1,2,\dots,m-1\}$ is chosen with the critical beta-splitting probabilities
$$q(m,j)=\frac{1}{h_{m-1}}\Big(\frac{1}{j}+\frac{1}{m-j}\Big)\cdot\frac{1}{2},\qquad j=1,\dots,m-1,$$
where $h_{k}=\sum_{r=1}^{k}1/r$ is the $k$-th harmonic number. (Equivalently, $q(m,j)=\frac{1}{h_{m-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{j(m-j)}\cdot\frac{m}{2}$ after symmetrisation.) Splits at distinct intervals are independent. The recursion stops when every remaining interval has length $1$; these unit intervals are the leaves and inherit the labels $1,\dots,n$ from their positions. The resulting rooted binary tree is DTCS(n), and the height of a leaf is the number of edges on the path from the root to that leaf.

Continuous-time model CTCS(n). The same recursive splitting is performed, but each unsplit interval of integer length $m\ge 2$ waits an independent $\mathrm{Exponential}(h_{m-1})$ time before splitting (with split position again distributed as $q(m,\cdot)$). The height of a leaf in CTCS(n) is the total continuous time elapsed from the root split down to that leaf.

For each $n\ge 2$, let $i(n)\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ be a prescribed (deterministic) leaf label; for instance $i(n)=1$, or more generally any sequence with $i(n)/n\to\alpha\in[0,1]$. Determine the distribution of the height of leaf $i(n)$ in DTCS(n) and the distribution of the height of leaf $i(n)$ in CTCS(n), and describe their asymptotic behaviour as $n\to\infty$.

Consider the discrete-time critical beta-splitting tree DTCS(n) on $n\ge 2$ leaves, defined recursively as follows: starting from the root clade of size $n$, a clade of size $m\ge 2$ is split into two child clades of sizes $i$ and $m-i$ (with $1\le i\le m-1$) with probability
$$q(m,i)=\frac{1}{h_{m-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{i}\cdot\frac{m-i+i}{?}\quad\text{i.e.}\quad q(m,i)=\frac{m}{2h_{m-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{i(m-i)},$$
where $h_{m-1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}1/j$, and the split is performed independently across clades until every clade has size 1 (a leaf). The resulting object is a rooted binary tree with $n$ labelled (or unlabelled) leaves.

A finite clade shape $\chi$ of size $i$ is an isomorphism class of such a tree on $i$ leaves. For each internal node $v$ of DTCS(n), the subtree rooted at $v$ (a "fringe clade") has some shape; let $N_n(\chi)$ denote the number of internal nodes of DTCS(n) whose fringe clade has shape $\chi$. It is known that there exists a constant $p(\chi)>0$ such that
$$n^{-1}\mathbb{E}[N_n(\chi)]\to p(\chi)/i\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.$$

Prove the following two assertions:
(a) The limit $\sigma^2(\chi):=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\mathrm{Var}(N_n(\chi))$ exists and is finite.
(b) The central limit theorem holds: as $n\to\infty$,
$$\frac{N_n(\chi)-\mathbb{E}[N_n(\chi)]}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(N_n(\chi))}}\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\mathcal{N}(0,1).$$

Consider the Markov chain on the integers $\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ called the harmonic descent chain, defined as follows. For $n\ge 2$, let $h_{n-1}=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}1/j$. From state $n\ge 2$, the chain jumps to state $i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n-1\}$ with probability
$$p(n,i)=\frac{1}{h_{n-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{n-i},\qquad 1\le i\le n-1,$$
and state $1$ is absorbing. For integers $n\ge m\ge 1$, define
$$a(n,m)=\Pr\big(\text{the chain started at } n \text{ ever visits state } m\big),$$
with the convention $a(n,n)=1$. It is known that the limit
$$a(m)=\lim_{n\to\infty} a(n,m)$$
exists for every $m\ge 1$.

(a) Find explicit (quantitative) bounds for $|a(n,m)-a(m)|$ as $n\to\infty$ with $m$ fixed (and, more generally, jointly in $n$ and $m$).

(b) Prove the following Ansatz. Let $f:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to[0,\infty)$ satisfy $f(j)=O(j^k)$ for some $k\ge 0$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] If $\sum_{j\ge 2} a(j)f(j)<\infty$, then
$$\sum_{j=2}^n a(n,j)f(j)\ \longrightarrow\ \sum_{j\ge 2} a(j)f(j)\quad\text{as } n\to\infty.$$
\item[(ii)] If $\sum_{j\ge 2} a(j)f(j)=\infty$, then
$$\sum_{j=2}^n a(n,j)f(j)\ \sim\ \sum_{j=2}^n a(j)f(j)\quad\text{as } n\to\infty.$$
\end{itemize}

Define the discrete-time critical beta-splitting tree DTCS(n) as the random rooted binary tree obtained by the following recursive construction. Start with the root labelled by the integer n. Whenever a node is labelled by an integer m ≥ 2, split it into two children labelled L and m − L, where L is an independent random variable on {1, 2, …, m − 1} with distribution

  P(L = i) = (1 / a(m)) · 1/(i (m − i)),  for i = 1, …, m − 1,

where a(m) = ∑_{i=1}^{m−1} 1/(i(m − i)) is the normalizing constant. Nodes labelled 1 are leaves. A clade of the tree is the set of leaves descended from any internal node, and the size of a clade is the integer label of that node. For each integer m with 2 ≤ m ≤ n, let N_m^{(n)} denote the number of clades of size m in DTCS(n).

It is known that E[N_m^{(n)}] = (n/m) · a(n, m) for an explicit kernel a(n, m). The problem is to determine the joint distribution of the random vector

  (N_m^{(n)} : 2 ≤ m ≤ n)

in sufficient detail to (i) compute the asymptotic covariances Cov(N_{m_1}^{(n)}, N_{m_2}^{(n)}) as n → ∞ for fixed or scaling indices m_1, m_2, and (ii) derive central limit theorems for linear (and more general) statistics built from the clade counts (N_m^{(n)}).

Define the critical beta-splitting random tree model DTCS(n) as follows. For each integer m ≥ 2, let q(m, i) for 1 ≤ i ≤ m−1 be the probability distribution
  q(m, i) = (1/h_{m-1}) · (1/(i(m−i))) · (m choose ... )
more precisely, the critical (β = −1) split distribution
  q(m, i) = (m / (2 h_{m-1})) · 1/(i (m − i)),   1 ≤ i ≤ m − 1,
where h_{m-1} = 1 + 1/2 + ⋯ + 1/(m−1). The random rooted binary tree DTCS(n) with n labeled leaves is constructed recursively: starting from the root labeled with the set [n] = {1,…,n}, a node labeled with a set S of size m ≥ 2 is split into two children labeled with a uniformly random partition of S into a part of size I and a part of size m − I, where I has distribution q(m, ·); the recursion stops at singleton leaves.

For a rooted binary tree T with n leaves, define the following balance indices:

(1) Colless index: C(T) = Σ_v |L(v) − R(v)|, summed over internal nodes v, where L(v), R(v) are the numbers of leaves in the two subtrees rooted at the children of v.
(2) Quadratic Colless index: C_q(T) = Σ_v (L(v) − R(v))².
(3) B1 index: B1(T) = Σ_{v internal, v ≠ root} 1/M(v), where M(v) is the maximum number of edges between v and any leaf descendant of v.
(4) B2 index: B2(T) = − Σ_{ℓ leaf} p_ℓ log p_ℓ, where p_ℓ = 2^{−d(ℓ)} with d(ℓ) the depth of leaf ℓ in the corresponding equiprobable random walk from the root.
(5) ŝ-shape index: ŝ(T) = Σ_v log(n(v) − 1), where n(v) is the number of leaves in the subtree rooted at v.
(6) Total cophenetic index: Φ(T) = Σ_{i < j} depth(lca(i, j)), summed over unordered pairs of leaves.
(7) Variance of leaf heights: σ²(T) = (1/n) Σ_ℓ d(ℓ)² − ((1/n) Σ_ℓ d(ℓ))².
(8) Rooted quartet index: the sum, over 4-element subsets {i,j,k,ℓ} of leaves, of weights assigned to the seven possible rooted quartet topologies induced on {i,j,k,ℓ}.

For each of these balance indices X = X_n evaluated on T = DTCS(n), determine the full asymptotic distributional behavior (beyond merely its expectation) as n → ∞: identify centering and scaling sequences a_n, b_n and a non-degenerate limit law L such that (X_n − a_n)/b_n ⇒ L, and characterize L (for example via its moments, Laplace transform, or as the fixed point of a distributional recursion). Carry out the analogous analysis for other natural balance indices defined on rooted trees applied to DTCS(n).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The critical beta-splitting (β = −1) DTCS model is the subject of recent work by Aldous and Pittel, who established expectations and Gaussian-type limits for some statistics (e.g. height of a uniform random leaf). However, full distributional limits for the listed balance indices (Colless, quadratic Colless, B1, B2, ŝ-shape, total cophenetic, leaf-height variance, rooted quartet index) on DTCS(n) have not been established in the literature found. Distributional results exist for Aldous's β ≥ 0 model (e.g. the quartet balance index), but not for the critical β = −1 case in the requested generality, so the problem appears open.

Consider the critical beta-splitting random tree model on n leaves, defined as follows. Starting from a root clade of size n, recursively split each clade of size m ≥ 2 into two sub-clades of sizes i and m − i (1 ≤ i ≤ m − 1) with probability

  q(m, i) = (1/Z_m) · 1/(i(m − i)),     Z_m = sum_{j=1}^{m-1} 1/(j(m − j)),

independently of all other splits, continuing until every clade has size 1. The resulting random binary rooted tree T_n has n leaves. From this model one can derive, as n → ∞, a limiting "fringe distribution" describing the law of the subtree rooted at the parent of a uniformly chosen leaf (and its iterates), as well as distributions of standard tree shape statistics (balance/imbalance indices such as Colless, Sackin, cherry counts, and other fringe-based or split-size functionals).

Carry out a large-scale empirical comparison between the critical beta-splitting model and large databases of real phylogenetic trees, addressing the following:

1. For a substantial corpus of empirical phylogenies (across many taxa and tree sizes), compute the empirical distribution of split sizes (the size of the smaller daughter clade as a function of parent clade size m) and compare with the law q(m, ·) of the critical beta-splitting model.

2. Compute empirical fringe-subtree frequencies (frequencies of small subtree shapes near random leaves) for these phylogenies and compare with the limiting fringe distribution of the critical beta-splitting model.

3. Extend the comparison to additional balance / shape / fringe-related indices beyond those already studied (e.g., Colless, Sackin, total cophenetic, cherry counts, generalized fringe statistics), and quantify the goodness-of-fit of the critical beta-splitting model relative to alternatives (such as the Yule–Harding model and the broader beta-splitting family with parameter β).

Provide statistically meaningful conclusions about for which indices, and on which scales of tree size, the critical beta-splitting model fits real phylogenetic data, and where systematic deviations occur.

Background and setup.

For each integer n ≥ 2, the discrete-time critical beta-splitting tree DTCS(n) is the random rooted combinatorial tree on n labeled leaves defined recursively as follows. Start from a root carrying the leaf-set {1,…,n}. A cluster of m ≥ 2 leaves is split into two child clusters of sizes i and m−i (1 ≤ i ≤ m−1) with probability
  q_m(i) = (1/h_{m−1}) · 1/(i(m−i)),  where h_{m−1} = Σ_{j=1}^{m−1} 1/j,
independently for distinct clusters, until every cluster has size 1 (a leaf). The resulting finite rooted tree, with its labeled leaves, is DTCS(n).

For a uniformly chosen leaf i ∈ {1,…,n}, let T_i^{(n)} denote the rooted plane tree obtained by re-rooting DTCS(n) at leaf i (so that T_i^{(n)} records the structure of DTCS(n) as viewed from leaf i). It is known that the local weak limit, as n → ∞, of the random sequence (T_i^{(n)}, i = 1, …, n) exists and is a stationary process (T_i, i ∈ ℤ) taking values in an appropriate space of rooted locally finite trees; call this the stationary fringe process.

Let Φ be a measurable real-valued functional on the tree-space such that Φ(T_i^{(n)}) and Φ(T_i) are well-defined.

Question.

Suppose that Φ satisfies a central limit theorem along the stationary fringe process, in the sense that there exist constants μ ∈ ℝ and σ > 0 such that
  (1/√m) · ( Σ_{i=0}^{m−1} Φ(T_i) − m μ )  ⇒  𝒩(0, σ^2)  as m → ∞.

Does it then follow that the analogous central limit theorem holds for DTCS(n), namely
  (1/√n) · ( Σ_{i=1}^{n} Φ(T_i^{(n)}) − n μ )  ⇒  𝒩(0, σ^2)  as n → ∞?

Determine whether this implication is true for every such functional Φ, or exhibit a Φ for which the fringe-process CLT holds but the DTCS(n) CLT fails.

Consider the following family of random rooted binary trees with edge lengths, denoted CTCS(n) for integers n ≥ 1. The model is determined by the following discrete recursive splitting rule together with continuous-time edge lengths: for m ≥ 2, a clade of m leaves is split into two sub-clades of sizes i and m−i (with 1 ≤ i ≤ m−1) with probability proportional to 1/(i(m−i)); each clade of m leaves is held for an Exponential(1/(m−1)) time before splitting (for m = 1 the leaf is held forever). The resulting random tree on n leaves with real edge lengths is CTCS(n).

The family (CTCS(n), n ≥ 1) admits an explicit inductive growth algorithm that constructs CTCS(n+1) from CTCS(n) as follows. Call each leaf of the current tree a "bud." Given CTCS(n):
 1. Pick a uniformly random bud and consider the path from the root to that bud.
 2. Move upward along this path; at each internal edge, with appropriate probability either:
    (a) insert a new side-bud (a new branch carrying a new leaf, attached at an interior point of the path with an Exponential(1)-length pendant edge), or
    (b) continue moving up; if the chosen bud is reached without insertion, extend the target bud by appending a new Exponential(1)-length branch terminating at a new leaf.
This procedure produces a sample of CTCS(n+1) and is consistent with the delete-a-random-leaf-and-prune dynamics on the family.

Question: Does there exist a nontrivial martingale (with respect to the natural filtration of this inductive growth process indexed by n) that can be used to derive quantitative information — for instance, fluctuation theorems or limit laws — about functionals of CTCS(n) (such as leaf heights, edge-length sums, or split statistics)?

independently for distinct clades, and this branching is iterated until all clades have size 1 (the leaves). This produces a random rooted binary tree with n leaves.

Draw DTCS(n) as a standard discrete cladogram in the plane: each internal node v of subtree size s(v) is placed at vertical height s(v) (with leaves at height 1), each internal node is connected by a horizontal segment to its two children's vertical lines, and each child c of v is joined to its own node position by a vertical line of length s(v) − s(c). Let

  L_n := ℓ̄(DTCS(n))

denote the total drawn length of this cladogram, i.e. the sum of the lengths of all vertical line segments in this drawing.

Prove that L_n grows on the order of n (log n)^4; more precisely, establish that there exist positive constants c, C such that

  c · n (log n)^4 ≤ E[L_n] ≤ C · n (log n)^4

for all sufficiently large n (and, if possible, identify the precise leading-order asymptotic).

Consider the discrete-time critical beta-splitting random tree on $n$ leaves, denoted $\mathrm{DTCS}(n)$, defined recursively as follows. Start with the set $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ at the root. At each internal node labelled by a set $S$ with $|S|=m\ge 2$, choose a split size $i\in\{1,2,\dots,m-1\}$ with probability
$$q(m,i)=\frac{1}{Z_m}\cdot\frac{1}{i(m-i)},\qquad Z_m=\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac{1}{j(m-j)},$$
partition $S$ uniformly at random into a subset of size $i$ (the "left child clade") and a subset of size $m-i$ (the "right child clade"), and recurse independently on each child. The recursion terminates at singletons (leaves).

A "clade" is the leaf-set associated with any node of the tree. Draw $\mathrm{DTCS}(n)$ as a standard cladogram in the plane as follows. Each clade $C$ is drawn as a horizontal line segment at integer height equal to its draw-height, defined recursively by: a singleton clade has draw-height $0$, and a clade arising as the parent of two child clades has draw-height $1+\max(h_L,h_R)$, where $h_L,h_R$ are the draw-heights of its two children. Each internal node (split) is drawn so that the parent clade's horizontal segment connects to its two children's segments by vertical line segments running between the parent's height and each child's height.

For an integer $h\ge 0$, define the drawn width profile
$$W(h)=\#\{\text{vertical line segments of the cladogram that cross the horizontal strip } \mathbb{R}\times(h,h+1)\},$$
equivalently the number of clades $C$ of $\mathrm{DTCS}(n)$ such that the draw-height of $C$ is at most $h$ while the draw-height of the parent clade of $C$ is at least $h+1$.

Study the process $(W(h):h\ge 0)$. In particular, determine its asymptotic distributional behavior as $n\to\infty$ (after any necessary rescaling of $h$ and of $W$), describe its mean, fluctuations, and any scaling limit as a stochastic process in $h$.

In this fringe process the ancestors of v form an infinite path on which "branchpoints" occur at certain integer heights, and at each branchpoint a sibling subtree is attached.

Represent the fringe process as a point process on ℝ_{≥0} (or on a suitable mark space) whose points are the heights of the branchpoints (decorated by the corresponding sibling subtree). Identify the appropriate rescaling of the height coordinate (and of the attached subtrees) under which this point process of branchpoint positions converges in distribution, and describe the resulting limit point process explicitly.

Setup. For each integer n ≥ 2, define the discrete critical beta-splitting random tree on n leaves recursively as follows. Take a root with n leaves below it; split the n leaves into a left subset of size L_n and a right subset of size n − L_n, where L_n ∈ {1,…,n−1} has the critical beta-splitting distribution

  P(L_n = i) = (1/h_{n−1}) · (1/i + 1/(n−i)) · (1/2),  with h_{n−1} = ∑_{j=1}^{n−1} 1/j,

i.e. P(L_n = i) ∝ 1/(i(n−i)) for 1 ≤ i ≤ n−1; recurse independently on each non-singleton side, with each internal split contributing one unit of edge length (continuous-time variant: assign exponential edge lengths). This produces a random binary tree CTCS(n) with n labeled leaves.

It is known that the family (CTCS(n))_{n≥2} is consistent under the "delete a uniformly random leaf and prune" operation, and admits a projective limit object CTCS(∞), which can be formalized as a continuous-time process (Π(t), t ≥ 0) of exchangeable partitions of ℕ.

Problem. Exhibit a discrete random tree model — defined by a construction superficially different from the critical beta-splitting recursion above (for instance, arising from a different combinatorial, branching, coalescent, or growth rule) — whose appropriately rescaled scaling limit, as the number of leaves tends to infinity, coincides in distribution with CTCS(∞). Equivalently, determine whether CTCS(∞) is a universal scaling limit shared by genuinely distinct discrete random tree models, or prove that no such alternative model exists.

Background and setup.

(a) Critical beta-splitting and CTCS(∞). For each integer n ≥ 2, define a random binary tree on n labeled leaves by the following recursive splitting rule: a clade containing m ≥ 2 leaves is partitioned into two sub-clades of sizes i and m − i with probability
  q(m, i) = (1/Z_m) · 1/(i(m − i)),  1 ≤ i ≤ m − 1,
where Z_m = ∑_{i=1}^{m−1} 1/(i(m − i)). Iterating until all clades are singletons yields the discrete critical beta-splitting tree. Endow each internal node v that splits a clade of size m with a real-valued "time" coordinate such that times along any root-to-leaf path are decreasing, with edge lengths chosen according to the natural continuous-time embedding (the clade of size m holds for an independent waiting time before splitting). Call the resulting random metric tree on n leaves CTCS(n). The family (CTCS(n))_{n≥2} is consistent under the operation "delete a uniformly chosen leaf and contract the resulting degree-2 vertex," and admits a projective limit CTCS(∞), an exchangeable random structure encoding the partitions of N obtained by removing all edges at times above a given threshold.

(b) The beta(2, 1) coalescent. Let Λ be the probability measure on [0, 1] with density f(x) = 2(1 − x) (the Beta(1, 2) density). The Λ-coalescent associated to Λ, in the case Λ = Beta(2, 1) (i.e. f(x) = 2(1 − x)), is the exchangeable coalescent process Π(t) on partitions of N whose rate of merging any specified k of the b current blocks into one is
  λ_{b,k} = ∫_0^1 x^{k−2}(1 − x)^{b−k} Λ(dx),  2 ≤ k ≤ b.
This coalescent comes-down-from-infinity and is associated with a stable-type subordinator.

Both CTCS(∞) and the beta(2, 1) coalescent are known to share the same underlying subordinator and to produce matching asymptotics for several functionals (e.g. collision counts and hop counts).

Problem. Determine the precise mathematical relationship between CTCS(∞) and the beta(2, 1) coalescent. Specifically, exhibit an explicit coupling, time-change, or functional transformation that maps one exchangeable structure to the other (or prove that no such coupling exists), and identify which joint distributional features of the two processes coincide and which differ.

The family {CTCS(n) : n ≥ 2} is consistent under the operation "delete a uniformly random leaf and contract the resulting degree-2 vertex," and therefore admits an inductive growth construction: CTCS(n+1) is obtained from CTCS(n) by inserting one new leaf according to a prescribed conditional distribution.

In this growth construction, classify the insertion of the new leaf into one of three local types:
 • branch extension: the new leaf is attached so that one bud of an existing terminal cherry is replaced by a new branch ending in a pair of buds;
 • side-bud addition: the new leaf is attached as a side-bud in the interior of an existing edge;
 • side-bud extension: an existing side-bud is replaced by a new branch with two terminal buds.

Let p↑, p→, and p↗ denote, respectively, the limiting (as n → ∞) probabilities of these three event types at the step from CTCS(n) to CTCS(n+1). It is observed that p↑ = p↗.

Determine whether the identity p↑ = p↗ can be derived as a consequence of some intrinsic symmetry of the random tree shape or of the growth dynamics, and if so exhibit such a symmetry.

Let $G = (V, E, \omega)$ be a finite weighted simple graph, where $\omega : E \to (0, \infty)$ assigns a positive weight to each edge. For $u, v \in V$, let $d_G(u, v)$ denote the geodesic distance, i.e., the minimum over all paths from $u$ to $v$ of the sum of the weights of the edges in the path (with $d_G(v, v) = 0$). Fix $\varepsilon > 0$. A subset $L \subseteq V$ is called an $\varepsilon$-net of $G$ if:
(i) ($\varepsilon$-sample) for every $v \in V$, there exists $u \in L$ with $d_G(v, u) \le \varepsilon$;
(ii) ($\varepsilon$-sparse) for every pair of distinct $u_i, u_j \in L$, $d_G(u_i, u_j) > \varepsilon$.

Determine optimal upper and lower bounds, in terms of $G$ and $\varepsilon$, for the cardinality $|L|$ of an $\varepsilon$-net of $G$. That is, find the tight worst-case maximum and minimum possible sizes of an $\varepsilon$-net for a weighted simple graph with given combinatorial/metric parameters.

Let G = (V, E, ω) be a weighted simple connected graph with edge-weight function ω : E → ℝ_{>0}, inducing the shortest-path (geodesic) metric d_G on V. For ε > 0, a subset L ⊆ V is called an ε-net of G if:
(a) for every v ∈ V there exists ℓ ∈ L with d_G(v, ℓ) ≤ ε (covering), and
(b) for any two distinct ℓ, ℓ' ∈ L one has d_G(ℓ, ℓ') > ε (packing/separation).
Elements of L are called landmarks.

Three known procedures for constructing such an ε-net are:
(i) a greedy algorithm that repeatedly selects a vertex at distance > ε from the current set of landmarks;
(ii) an iterative algorithm that updates landmarks via local exchanges;
(iii) an SPT-pruning algorithm based on pruning shortest-path trees.

Design an algorithm A that, given any input (G, ε), outputs an ε-net L ⊆ V of G and simultaneously satisfies both of the following:
(1) The cardinality |L| produced by A is, in the worst case (and/or on benchmark instances on which the three algorithms above have been compared), strictly smaller than the cardinality produced by each of the greedy, iterative, and SPT-pruning algorithms.
(2) The running time of A is strictly smaller than that of each of the greedy, iterative, and SPT-pruning algorithms.

Equivalently: provide an ε-net construction that strictly improves both the landmark count and the running time of all previously known ε-net algorithms for weighted simple graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists.

Let $G = (V, E, \omega)$ be a weighted simple graph with positive edge weights $\omega: E \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$, and let $d_G : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ denote the induced shortest-path (geodesic) distance on $V$. For $\varepsilon > 0$, an $\varepsilon$-net is a subset $L \subset V$ such that (i) for every $v \in V$ there exists $\ell \in L$ with $d_G(v,\ell) \le \varepsilon$, and (ii) $d_G(\ell, \ell') > \varepsilon$ for all distinct $\ell, \ell' \in L$.

For $\alpha \ge 0$, define the Vietoris–Rips complex $\operatorname{VR}_\alpha(G)$ as the abstract simplicial complex on vertex set $V$ whose simplices are the finite subsets $\sigma \subset V$ with $d_G(v,v') \le \alpha$ for all $v,v' \in \sigma$. Let $W = V$ (the "witness" set). Define the Dowker complex
$$\operatorname{Dow}_\alpha(W, L) = \{ \sigma \subset L : \exists\, w \in W \text{ with } d_G(w,\ell) \le \alpha \text{ for every } \ell \in \sigma \}.$$

As $\alpha$ varies, both $\{\operatorname{VR}_\alpha(G)\}_\alpha$ and $\{\operatorname{Dow}_\alpha(W,L)\}_\alpha$ form filtrations of simplicial complexes; let $\operatorname{PD}_1(\cdot)$ denote the resulting one-dimensional persistence diagram. Let $d_B$ denote the bottleneck distance between persistence diagrams, and let $g(G)$ denote the (orientable) genus of the graph $G$.

(i) Determine a rule prescribing a value $\varepsilon > 0$ and a procedure for selecting an $\varepsilon$-net $L \subset V$ such that, for all sufficiently large $\alpha$,
$$\#\,\operatorname{PD}_1(\operatorname{Dow}_\alpha(W, L)) \;=\; g(G).$$

(ii) Under the assumption that $L$ is an $\varepsilon$-net satisfying (i), establish an explicit upper bound for
$$d_B\bigl(\operatorname{PD}_1(\operatorname{VR}_\alpha(G)),\, \operatorname{PD}_1(\operatorname{Dow}_\alpha(W, L))\bigr)$$
expressed in terms of $\varepsilon$ and the lengths of cycles of $G$.

Let G = (V, E, ω) be a finite connected weighted graph, where ω : E → (0, ∞) assigns positive weights to edges. The weighted graph induces a shortest-path (pseudo)metric d_G on V. Fix two subsets L ⊂ V (landmarks) and W ⊂ V (witnesses). Letting α vary yields the Dowker filtration of (W, L) in G, whose persistent homology produces a persistence diagram Dgm(G; W, L).

A subset L ⊂ V is called an ε-net for G if for every v ∈ V there is some ℓ ∈ L with d_G(v, ℓ) ≤ ε, and any two distinct points of L are at distance more than ε. For two weight functions ω, ω' on the same edge set E, define the supremum distance ‖ω − ω'‖_∞ = max_{e ∈ E} |ω(e) − ω'(e)|.

(i) (Stability under reweighting.) Let G = (V, E, ω) and G' = (V, E, ω') be weighted graphs with the same vertex and edge sets, and fix L, W ⊂ V. Establish an explicit bound of the form
   d_B(Dgm(G; W, L), Dgm(G'; W, L)) ≤ C · ‖ω − ω'‖_∞,
where d_B denotes the bottleneck distance between persistence diagrams, and identify the optimal constant C (possibly depending on combinatorial features of G).

(ii) (Stability under change of landmarks.) Let L, L' ⊂ V both be ε-nets for G, and let W ⊂ V be a fixed witness set. Determine combinatorial or metric conditions on (L, L', W, G, α, ε) that guarantee Dow_α(W, L) and Dow_α(W, L') have the same homotopy type.

Fix positive integers $n$ and $t$, and an integer $k$ with $1 \le k \le n$. Let $A$ be the $n \times m$ binary matrix whose columns are exactly all distinct nonzero vectors of $\{0,1\}^n$ having Hamming weight at most $k$; here $m = \sum_{j=1}^{k}\binom{n}{j}$. Denote the columns of $A$ by $a_1,\dots,a_m \in \{0,1\}^n$.

For an $n \times t$ binary matrix $x$ with columns $x_1,\dots,x_t \in \{0,1\}^n$, define the $i$-th expressiveness indicator by
$$m_i^A(x) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{t} \langle a_i, x_j\rangle_{2},$$
where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ denotes the inner product in $\mathrm{GF}(2)$ (so each summand lies in $\{0,1\}$) and the outer sum is taken in $\mathbb{Z}$ (so $m_i^A(x) \in \{0,1,\dots,t\}$).

Let $x$ and $y$ be independent $n \times t$ binary matrices, each chosen uniformly at random from $\{0,1\}^{n\times t}$. Determine, as an explicit function of $n$, $t$, and $k$, the collision probability
$$P\!\left(\,m_i^A(x) = m_i^A(y)\ \text{for all } 1\le i\le m\,\right).$$

(a) Characterize (classify) all families $A$ of nonzero binary columns for which $P(A)$ can be computed exactly in closed form.

(b) Characterize (classify) all families $A$ for which $P(A)$ can be computed efficiently, i.e., by an algorithm running in time polynomial in $n$ and $k$.

Let H = (V, E) be a 4-uniform hypergraph (every hyperedge contains exactly four vertices) with two distinguished vertices s, t ∈ V. Given a bipartition (S, V \ S) with s ∈ S and t ∈ V \ S, each hyperedge e ∈ E is classified by how its four vertices split between S and V \ S as 4-vs-0, 3-vs-1, or 2-vs-2. Call the bipartition admissible if no hyperedge is split 2-vs-2 (i.e., every hyperedge has all four endpoints on the same side, or exactly one endpoint on one side and three on the other). The No-Even-Split 4-uniform s-t cut problem asks, among all admissible bipartitions separating s from t, for one minimizing the number of hyperedges that are split 1-vs-3.

Determine the computational complexity of this problem: is it polynomial-time solvable, NP-hard, or otherwise classified?

Let G=(V,E) be a directed acyclic graph in which each edge (i,j)∈E carries a numerical weight (the local partial derivative of the elementary operation at vertex j with respect to its predecessor i). For an edge (i,j)∈E, define two elimination operations:

- Front-elimination of (i,j): remove the edge (i,j); then, for every successor k of j (i.e., every k with (j,k)∈E at the current moment), add an edge (i,k) whose weight is incremented by the product of the weights of (i,j) and (j,k); if (i,k) already exists its weight is updated by summing. The cost of this operation is the number of successors of j.
- Back-elimination of (i,j): remove (i,j); then, for every predecessor h of i, add an edge (h,j) whose weight is incremented by the product of the weights of (h,i) and (i,j); if (h,j) already exists its weight is updated. The cost is the number of predecessors of i.

Call a sequence of front- and back-eliminations a complete edge elimination sequence if its application transforms G into the bipartite directed acyclic graph whose only edges go directly from minimal (input) vertices to maximal (output) vertices, with edge weights equal to the entries of the Jacobian of the function represented by G. The cost of such a sequence is the sum of the costs of its individual eliminations.

Decide the following problem: given a directed acyclic graph G as above and a non-negative integer k, does there exist a complete edge elimination sequence for G whose total cost is at most k? In particular, determine the computational complexity of this decision problem.

Let G = (V, E) be a directed acyclic graph with |V| = n vertices, modeling the data flow of a straight-line numerical program: each vertex represents an intermediate value, and an edge u → v indicates that the value at v depends directly on the value at u.

A "reversal" of G is a schedule that outputs the values associated with the vertices of G in reverse topological order, subject to the following rules:
- At any moment in time, a subset of vertex values is held in "persistent memory"; values not in persistent memory have been discarded and, if needed again, must be recomputed from currently stored values by following the edges of G.
- The "persistent memory" usage at any time is the number of values simultaneously stored.
- The "computational cost" of the schedule is the total number of (re)computations of vertex values performed during the reversal (each evaluation of a vertex from its predecessors counts as one unit of cost).

Given G together with two integers M ≥ n and O ≥ 0, decide whether there exists a reversal schedule of G that uses persistent memory of size at most M at all times and incurs total computational cost at most O.

Provide an algorithm (or a characterization) that decides this question, and analyze its complexity.

Let $M$ be an $n\times n$ real matrix with spectral radius $\rho(M)=\lambda<1$. Fix an integer $\ell\ge 1$ and partition $M$ into an $\ell\times\ell$ array of blocks $M_{ij}$ (with compatible row/column block sizes summing to $n$). For a delay matrix $\delta\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}^{\ell\times\ell}$ with zero diagonal entries, define the asynchronous update on block-vectors $\tilde x=(\tilde x_1,\dots,\tilde x_\ell)$ by
$$\tilde x_i(t+1)=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell} M_{ij}\,\tilde x_j(t-\delta_{ji}),\qquad i=1,\dots,\ell,$$
where $\tilde x_j(s)=0$ for $s<0$. This recurrence is a linear map on the extended state $(\tilde x(t),\tilde x(t-1),\dots,\tilde x(t-k))$; let $M^{(\delta)}$ denote the corresponding finite-dimensional linear operator and let $\rho(M^{(\delta)})$ be its spectral radius.

(a) Is it true that for every such $M$, every block partition, every $k\in\mathbb{N}$, and every $\delta\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}^{\ell\times\ell}$ with zero diagonal,
$$\rho(M^{(\delta)})\le \lambda^{1/(k+1)}\,?$$

(b) If (a) fails, does there exist a function $f:(0,1)\times\mathbb{N}\to(0,1)$ such that $\rho(M^{(\delta)})\le f(\lambda,k)$ holds for all choices of $M$, partition, $k$, and $\delta$ as above?

Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph on n = |V| vertices. The zero-forcing color-change rule is: starting from a subset Z ⊆ V whose vertices are colored blue (the others white), repeatedly apply the rule that if a blue vertex u has exactly one white neighbor w, then w becomes blue. A set Z ⊆ V is called a zero-forcing set for G if iteratively applying this rule starting from Z eventually colors all of V blue.

Fix an integer k ≥ 0. A set Z ⊆ V is an (n − k)-contingent zero-forcing set for G if, for every set of edges E₀ ⊆ E with |E₀| ≤ k, the set Z is a zero-forcing set for the edge-deleted graph G − E₀ = (V, E ∖ E₀). Let Z_{(n−k)}(G) denote the minimum cardinality of an (n − k)-contingent zero-forcing set of G.

Question: Does there exist an efficient (polynomial-time) algorithm that, given as input a graph G drawn from one of the following classes, computes Z_{(n−k)}(G) (or a minimum-size (n − k)-contingent zero-forcing set)?
(a) Graphs with few cycles (e.g., graphs G with |E| − |V| + c(G) bounded by a constant, where c(G) is the number of connected components).
(b) More generally, sparse graphs with large diameter.

Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph on n = |V| vertices. The standard zero-forcing process on G with initial set Z ⊆ V proceeds as follows: each vertex of Z is colored blue, all others white; repeatedly, if a blue vertex v has exactly one white neighbor u, then u is colored blue (the "color-change rule"). The set Z is a zero-forcing set if iterating this rule eventually colors every vertex of V blue.

For an integer k ≥ 0, call Z ⊆ V an (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set of G if, for every subset E₀ ⊆ E with |E₀| ≤ k, the set Z is a zero-forcing set of the edge-deleted graph G − E₀ = (V, E ∖ E₀). Let Z_{n−k}(G) denote the minimum cardinality of an (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set of G.

Consider random or deterministic families of graphs that model the structural properties characteristic of electrical power-grid networks (e.g., sparse graphs with heavy-tailed or bounded degree distributions, planar or near-planar embeddings, and small treewidth typical of transmission networks). Determine the typical (asymptotic) value of Z_{n−k}(G) for such graphs as a function of the number of vertices n and the number of edges m = |E| (and of k).

Let $k\ge 1$ be an integer, and for each $i=1,\dots,k$ let $V_i$ be a complex vector space of dimension $n_i+1\ge 2$, and let $d_i\ge 1$ be a positive integer. Consider the Segre–Veronese variety
$$V_{d_1,\dots,d_k}\;\subset\;\mathbb{P}\bigl(S^{d_1}V_1\otimes\cdots\otimes S^{d_k}V_k\bigr),$$
defined as the image of $\mathbb{P}(V_1)\times\cdots\times\mathbb{P}(V_k)$ under the embedding given by the line bundle $\mathcal{O}(d_1,\dots,d_k)$; equivalently, it parametrizes partially symmetric rank-one tensors $v_1^{\otimes d_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_k^{\otimes d_k}$ up to scalar. Let $N=\dim\mathbb{P}(S^{d_1}V_1\otimes\cdots\otimes S^{d_k}V_k)$ and let $n=\dim V_{d_1,\dots,d_k}=\sum_i n_i$. For an integer $r\ge 1$, the $r$-th secant variety $\sigma_r(V_{d_1,\dots,d_k})$ is the Zariski closure of the union of linear spans of $r$ points of $V_{d_1,\dots,d_k}$. Its expected dimension is
$$\operatorname{expdim}\sigma_r(V_{d_1,\dots,d_k})=\min\{\,r\,n+r-1,\;N\,\}.$$
The variety $V_{d_1,\dots,d_k}$ is called $r$-defective if $\dim\sigma_r(V_{d_1,\dots,d_k})$ is strictly smaller than this expected dimension.

Problem. Classify all tuples $(n_1,\dots,n_k;\,d_1,\dots,d_k;\,r)$ for which the Segre–Veronese variety $V_{d_1,\dots,d_k}$ is $r$-defective, and in each defective case determine the exact value of $\dim\sigma_r(V_{d_1,\dots,d_k})$.

Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $L$ be a line bundle on $X$. For a point $p \in X$, a "double point" at $p$ is the zero-dimensional subscheme defined by the square $\mathfrak{m}_p^2$ of the maximal ideal of $p$. Given $r \ge 1$ and generic points $p_1, \dots, p_r \in X$, let $Z_r \subset X$ be the disjoint union of the corresponding double points. One says that $r$ generic double points impose independent conditions on $L$ if the natural restriction map
$$H^0(X, L) \longrightarrow H^0(X, L \otimes \mathcal{O}_{Z_r})$$
is of maximal rank, i.e. surjective or injective (equivalently, $\dim H^0(X, L \otimes \mathcal{I}_{Z_r}) = \max\{0,\; h^0(X,L) - r(\dim X + 1)\}$). The line bundle $L$ is called special if there exists some $r \ge 1$ for which $r$ generic double points fail to impose independent conditions on $L$.

Problem: Classify all special line bundles on a product of projective spaces $\mathbb{P}^{n_1} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{P}^{n_k}$. More generally, give such a classification for other natural classes of smooth projective varieties.

The problem of classifying special line bundles (in the sense of generic double points failing to impose independent conditions, related to the classical polynomial interpolation / Alexander–Hirschowitz-type problems) is a long-standing open problem. While the Alexander–Hirschowitz theorem solves the case of $\mathbb{P}^n$ with the standard line bundles, the analogous classification for products of projective spaces and other varieties remains open in general; only partial results (e.g., for specific bidegrees on $\mathbb{P}^1 \times \mathbb{P}^1$, $\mathbb{P}^n \times \mathbb{P}^m$ in low dimensions, or specific Segre–Veronese settings) are known. Web search did not surface a complete classification.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $S = \mathrm{Sym}^\bullet V$ be the symmetric algebra on $V$, identified with a polynomial ring. For a homogeneous polynomial $f \in S^d V$ of degree $d$, recall the apolarity pairing: the dual ring $T = \mathrm{Sym}^\bullet V^*$ acts on $S$ by contraction (partial differentiation), and the apolar ideal of $f$ is
$$f^\perp = \{\,\partial \in T : \partial \circ f = 0\,\} \subset T.$$
A closed subscheme $X \subset \mathbb{P}(V^*) = \mathrm{Proj}(T)$ is called apolar to $f$ if its homogeneous (saturated) ideal $I_X$ is contained in $f^\perp$. The cactus rank $cR(f)$ of $f$ is the minimum of $\deg(X)$ over all zero-dimensional apolar schemes $X$, and a zero-dimensional apolar scheme $X$ achieving $\deg(X) = cR(f)$ is called a minimal apolar scheme for $f$.

Let $\mathrm{reg}(X)$ denote the Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity of $X$ (i.e., of its saturated homogeneous ideal, or equivalently of its structure sheaf).

Question: For every homogeneous polynomial $f \in S^d V$ and every minimal apolar scheme $X$ for $f$, does one have
$$\mathrm{reg}(X) \le d \, ?$$

Let $K$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, and let $S^{\bullet}V = \bigoplus_{d \ge 0} S^d V$ denote the symmetric algebra on $V$, whose elements of degree $d$ are identified with degree-$d$ homogeneous polynomials (forms). For a form $f \in S^d V$, a generalized additive decomposition (GAD) of $f$ is an expression
$$ f \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{r} \ell_i^{\,d - m_i}\, g_i, $$
where $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_r \in V$ are pairwise non-proportional linear forms, $1 \le m_i \le d$, and each $g_i \in S^{m_i}V$ is a form of degree $m_i$. To such a GAD one associates a $0$-dimensional subscheme $X \subset \mathbb{P}(V^*)$, supported at the points $[\ell_i]$, whose local component at $[\ell_i]$ is the scheme defined by the apolar ideal of $g_i$ (viewed after a change of coordinates centered at $[\ell_i]$). The length of the GAD is $\mathrm{length}(X) = \sum_i \dim_K (S^{\bullet}V / \mathrm{Ann}(g_i))$, and a GAD is said to be of minimal length if no GAD of $f$ has smaller length. The Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity of $X$ is denoted $\mathrm{reg}(X)$.

(a) For every $f \in S^d V$ and every $0$-dimensional scheme $X$ arising from a GAD of $f$ of minimal length, does the inequality $\mathrm{reg}(X) \le d$ hold?

(b) More generally, determine sufficient conditions on $f \in S^d V$ that guarantee the existence of a GAD of $f$ whose associated scheme $X$ has low Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity (e.g. $\mathrm{reg}(X) \le d$).

Let $X \subset \mathbb{P}^N$ be a non-degenerate irreducible projective variety over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. For each integer $s \geq 1$, the $s$-th secant variety of $X$ is defined as
$$\sigma_s(X) \;=\; \overline{\bigcup_{x_1,\dots,x_s \in X} \langle x_1,\dots,x_s \rangle} \;\subset\; \mathbb{P}^N,$$
i.e. the Zariski closure of the union of all linear spans of $s$ points of $X$. Assume that $\sigma_s(X)$ is a proper subvariety of $\mathbb{P}^N$ (equivalently, $X$ is not $s$-defective in the sense that $\sigma_s(X)$ fills the ambient space).

For $s = 2$, there is a known general lower bound for $\deg \sigma_2(X)$ expressed in terms of invariants of $X$ (such as $\dim X$, $\deg X$, and the codimension of $\sigma_2(X)$), obtained via a refinement of Terracini's lemma.

Problem: Develop, in the same spirit, general lower bounds for $\deg \sigma_s(X)$ for arbitrary $s \geq 2$, expressed in terms of intrinsic invariants of $X$ and of the embedding $X \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^N$, and which reduce (up to the appropriate specialization) to the known bound when $s = 2$.

Background. Work over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. For a non-degenerate irreducible projective variety X ⊂ P^N, the r-th secant variety σ_r(X) is the Zariski closure of the union of linear spans of r-tuples of points of X:
   σ_r(X) = closure of ⋃ ⟨x_1,...,x_r⟩, where x_1,...,x_r ∈ X.
When σ_r(X) is a hypersurface in P^N (i.e. has codimension one), one says it is of minimal degree if its degree attains the smallest value possible given the dimension and embedding data. (A variety Y ⊂ P^N of codimension c has minimal degree if deg(Y) = c + 1; this is the lower bound for non-degenerate varieties.)

Problem.
(a) Classify all non-degenerate irreducible projective varieties X of small dimension whose second secant variety σ_2(X) is a hypersurface of minimal degree, and analogously for the third secant variety σ_3(X).
(b) More generally, given an integer r ≥ 2, construct non-degenerate irreducible projective varieties X ⊂ P^N such that σ_r(X) is a hypersurface of the smallest possible degree.

Let $V = \mathbb{C}^{n+1}$ with coordinates $x_0,\dots,x_n$, and let $S^dV$ denote the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ in these variables. For $f \in S^dV$, the eigenscheme $X_f \subset \mathbb{P}V$ is the closed subscheme defined by the $2\times 2$ minors of the matrix
$$\begin{pmatrix} x_0 & x_1 & \cdots & x_n \\ \partial f/\partial x_0 & \partial f/\partial x_1 & \cdots & \partial f/\partial x_n \end{pmatrix},$$
i.e., the locus of points $v \in \mathbb{P}V$ such that $\nabla f(v)$ is proportional to $v$. For generic $f$, $X_f$ consists of a fixed number $D_{n,d}$ of reduced points (the generic eigenscheme cardinality, equal to $\sum_{i=0}^{n}(d-1)^i$).

Define the eigenconfiguration variety
$$E_{n,d} = \overline{\{(v_1,\dots,v_{D_{n,d}}) \in (\mathbb{P}V)^{(\cdot D_{n,d})} : X_f = \{v_1,\dots,v_{D_{n,d}}\} \text{ for some } f \in S^dV\}}$$
inside the symmetric product $(\mathbb{P}V)^{(\cdot D_{n,d})}$ (equivalently inside $\mathrm{Hilb}_{D_{n,d}}(\mathbb{P}V)$); this is a Zariski-closed subset.

Problem: Determine explicit defining equations (polynomial conditions cutting out the Zariski-closed locus) for $E_{n,d}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space of dimension $n+1$ and let $T \in \mathrm{Sym}^d(V^*) \otimes V$ (equivalently, a partially symmetric tensor, or a homogeneous polynomial map $\mathbb{C}^{n+1} \to \mathbb{C}^{n+1}$ of degree $d-1$ in each coordinate). An eigenvector of $T$ is a nonzero $v \in V$ such that $T(v,\ldots,v) = \lambda v$ for some scalar $\lambda$. The eigenscheme $X = X(T) \subset \mathbb{P}(V) = \mathbb{P}^n$ is the projective subscheme defined by the $2\times 2$ minors of the $(n+1)\times 2$ matrix whose columns are the coordinate vector and $T(v,\ldots,v)$; equivalently, the scheme cut out by the polynomials $v_i\, T(v,\ldots,v)_j - v_j\, T(v,\ldots,v)_i$ for all $i,j$.

(a) the possible degrees that an irreducible component of $X$ may have;
(b) which projective subschemes of $\mathbb{P}^n$ can occur as an irreducible component of such a non-reduced eigenscheme $X$.

Let $n_1,\dots,n_d\ge 2$ be integers and set $N=n_1n_2\cdots n_d$. Consider the Segre variety
$$S_{n_1,\dots,n_d}\subset\mathbb{P}^{N-1}$$
of rank-one tensors, parameterizing the classes of nonzero tensors of the form $v_1\otimes v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_d$ with $v_i\in\mathbb{C}^{n_i}$. The affine cone $\widehat{S}_{n_1,\dots,nd}\subset\mathbb{C}^N$ consists of all rank-one tensors (including zero).

The probability simplex of tensors is
$$\Delta=\Bigl\{\,u=(u_{i_1\dots i_d})\in\mathbb{R}^N\;:\;u_{i_1\dots i_d}\ge 0,\ \sum_{i_1,\dots,i_d}u_{i_1\dots i_d}=1\,\Bigr\}.$$
A tensor in $\Delta$ is called a probability tensor.

For a generic complex tensor $u\in\mathbb{C}^N$, the squared-distance function $T\mapsto \sum (T_{i_1\dots i_d}-u_{i_1\dots i_d})^2$ restricted to the smooth locus of $\widehat{S}_{n_1,\dots,n_d}$ has a finite number of complex critical points. This number is called the affine Euclidean distance degree $\mathrm{aEDdeg}(S_{n_1,\dots,n_d})$ and is independent of the generic choice of $u$.

Problem. For a generic probability tensor $u\in\Delta$, determine the set of possible numbers of real critical points among the $\mathrm{aEDdeg}(S_{n_1,\dots,n_d})$ complex critical points of the squared-distance function from $u$ to $\widehat{S}_{n_1,\dots,n_d}$, as $u$ ranges over $\Delta$.

Background. In algebraic complexity theory, polynomials over a field (taken here to be the complex numbers) are computed by various models, giving rise to complexity classes that consist of (sequences of) polynomials whose computational cost grows polynomially in the input parameters.

(a) The class VBP consists of (sequences of) polynomials computable by polynomial-size algebraic branching programs: directed acyclic graphs with a source s and a sink t whose edges are labeled by affine linear forms in the input variables, the polynomial computed being the sum over all s–t paths of the product of edge labels.

(b) The class VChow consists of polynomials of polynomial Chow rank, i.e. those degree-d homogeneous polynomials f(x_1,...,x_n) expressible as a sum f = ∏_{j=1}^{d} L_{1,j} + ∏_{j=1}^{d} L_{2,j} + ... + ∏_{j=1}^{d} L_{r,j} of r products of d linear forms, with r bounded polynomially in n and d.

(c) The class VWaring consists of polynomials of polynomial Waring rank, i.e. degree-d homogeneous polynomials expressible as a sum f = ∑_{i=1}^{r} L_i^d of r d-th powers of linear forms, with r polynomially bounded.

For each such class C, its border (or approximative) closure C̄ is defined as the class of polynomials f that can be written as a limit (in the Euclidean or Zariski topology, equivalently as the ε→0 limit of polynomials whose coefficients are Laurent polynomials in a formal parameter ε) of polynomials f_ε belonging to C, with the relevant complexity measure of f_ε remaining polynomially bounded uniformly in ε.

Problem. For each C ∈ {VWaring, VChow, VBP}, decide whether C = C̄; i.e., determine whether every polynomial in the border closure of C already lies in C.

Recent surveys and papers (2024–2025) on debordering describe the equality of these algebraic complexity classes with their border closures as an open central question. Progress has been made on quantitative debordering (e.g., improved upper bounds on Waring rank in terms of border Waring rank such as d·r^{O(√r)}, and fixed-parameter debordering of Waring rank), but no proof of equality (or separation) of VWaring, VChow, or VBP with their respective border analogues has been established.
