Let $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n_{\mathbb{Z}})$ denote the relative Hilbert scheme parametrizing length-$d$ zero-dimensional closed subschemes of affine $n$-space over $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})$. An irreducible component $C \subseteq \mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n_{\mathbb{Z}})$ is said to live entirely in characteristic $p$ (for a prime $p$) if the structural morphism $C \to \mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})$ factors through the closed point $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{F}_p) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})$; equivalently, every point of $C$ corresponds to a subscheme over a field of characteristic $p$.

Question: Do there exist a prime $p$, integers $n \geq 1$ and a small value of $d$ (say with $d$ as small as possible), and an irreducible component of $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n_{\mathbb{Z}})$ that lives entirely in characteristic $p$?

Jelisiejew (Inventiones 2020, "Pathologies on the Hilbert scheme of points") proved that for every prime $p$ there exist irreducible components of $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n_{\mathbb{Z}})$ living entirely in characteristic $p$, but only for relatively large $d$ (and large $n$). Consider non-central ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, in which the rapid relative motion of the spectator protons produces transient electromagnetic fields. Heavy charm quarks, created at very early times, can retain a kick from these fields. For neutral D mesons, define the charge-dependent directed flow with respect to the spectator plane as

Δv₁(y) = v₁(D⁰; y) − v₁(D̄⁰; y),

where v₁(y) = ⟨cos(φ − Ψ_SP)⟩ is the first Fourier coefficient of the azimuthal distribution as a function of rapidity y, measured relative to the spectator reaction plane Ψ_SP. The slope dΔv₁/dy near mid-rapidity is taken as a probe of the magnitude and lifetime of the early-time electromagnetic field experienced by charm quarks, where the Coulomb force from the long-lived electric field of receding spectators competes with the Lorentz force from the induced magnetic field.

Experimental measurements at top RHIC energies (√s_NN ≈ 200 GeV in Au+Au collisions) and at LHC energies (√s_NN ≈ 5.02 TeV in Pb+Pb collisions) report Δv₁ slopes that differ in both magnitude and sign, whereas state-of-the-art transport/electromagnetic-field model calculations predict an approximately flat, negative dependence on collision energy.

Problem. Provide a quantitative theoretical explanation, with statistical significance comparable to or exceeding the experimental uncertainties, for:

(a) the difference in magnitude of dΔv₁/dy between RHIC and LHC energies;
(b) the apparent opposite sign of the slope at the two energies;
(c) whether the observed sign reversal at the LHC, opposite to the model prediction, can be unambiguously attributed to the Lorentz force on charm quarks dominating over the Coulomb force, and if so, determine the corresponding constraint on the electrical conductivity and lifetime of the QGP electromagnetic field.

Recent works (2021–2026) on directed flow of D mesons at RHIC and LHC continue to debate the mechanism. Models with standard electromagnetic profiles can reproduce the STAR Δv₁ at √s_NN = 200 GeV but fail to reproduce the much larger, positive-slope Δv₁ at LHC energies. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field. A finite $k$-scheme is a scheme $\Gamma$ of the form $\operatorname{Spec}(A)$, where $A$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $k$-algebra. Such a scheme is called irreducible if $A$ is a local ring (so $\Gamma$ has a single point). Associated to $\Gamma$ is the tangent space to its deformation functor, denoted $T^1_\Gamma$; concretely, if $\Gamma = \operatorname{Spec}(A)$, then $T^1_\Gamma$ is the $A$-module of first-order deformations of $A$ as a $k$-algebra (equivalently, the module classifying isomorphism classes of flat deformations of $A$ over $k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$). A finite $k$-scheme $\Gamma$ is called rigid if $T^1_\Gamma = 0$.

Determine whether there exists an irreducible finite $k$-scheme $\Gamma$, other than $\Gamma = \operatorname{Spec}(k)$, such that $T^1_\Gamma = 0$. Equivalently, does there exist a finite-dimensional local commutative $k$-algebra $A \neq k$ that is rigid in the sense that every first-order infinitesimal deformation of $A$ is trivial?

Consider an expanding deconfined quark–gluon plasma (QGP) fireball produced in a high-energy heavy-ion collision. Inside this medium, charm quarks of mass m_c ≈ 1.27 GeV are produced via hard partonic scattering at early times and subsequently propagate through the plasma. Their interaction with the medium can be modeled as Brownian motion governed by a Fokker–Planck (or equivalent Langevin) equation, in which the spatial diffusion coefficient D_s(T), the momentum-space drag coefficient η_D(T), and the momentum diffusion coefficient κ(T) characterize the transport. Define:

(i) the kinetic-equilibration (or thermalization) time τ_th as the characteristic time on which the charm-quark phase-space distribution relaxes toward a local thermal distribution at the local fluid temperature T(τ);
(ii) the hydrodynamization time τ_n as the time after which the charm-quark stress–energy tensor is well approximated by its Navier–Stokes (first-order viscous hydrodynamic) form built from gradients of the local temperature and flow velocity;
(iii) the expansion (Hubble-like) time τ_exp = 1/(∂_μ u^μ) of the bulk medium, with u^μ the local fluid four-velocity.

Address the following:

(a) Quantify how closely charm quarks approach local kinetic equilibrium with the light partonic degrees of freedom during the lifetime of the QGP, as a function of T and of the transport coefficients (D_s(T), η_D(T), κ(T)), and determine the corresponding time scale τ_th relative to that of light quarks and gluons.

(b) Identify the range of values of the dimensionless diffusion coefficient 2π T D_s(T) (and equivalently of η_D and κ, related by Einstein relations) for which τ_n < τ_exp holds for a sizeable fraction of the deconfined fireball lifetime, so that a fluid-dynamic (viscous hydrodynamic) description of the charm component is internally consistent.

(c) Determine whether transport coefficients obtained from current phenomenological fits to heavy-flavor observables in heavy-ion collisions lie within this regime, and characterize the residual deviations from local equilibrium that should be expected.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent studies indicate that, using transport coefficients fit to data, the charm hydrodynamization time τ_n falls below the expansion time τ_exp for a substantial portion of the QGP lifetime, suggesting partial thermalization. However, the precise degree of charm kinetic equilibration, the temperature dependence of D_s(T), and the validity range of a fluid description for charm remain actively debated open questions in heavy-ion phenomenology.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The parity conjecture is now resolved in the negative: a counterexample has been produced, namely an explicit family of zero-dimensional subschemes of length 12 in $\mathbb{A}^3$ whose tangent space dimension has parity different from 12. The conjecture is known to hold in special cases (monomial ideals, by Maulik–Nekrasov–Okounkov–Pandharipande, and homogeneous ideals), but fails in general.

representations.normalized: In high-energy hadronic collisions, charm quarks hadronize into a variety of charm hadrons, including the meson D^0 and the baryon Λ_c^+. Define the pT-integrated production ratio Λ_c^+/D^0 as the ratio of the production cross sections (or yields) of Λ_c^+ baryons to D^0 mesons, integrated over transverse momentum at midrapidity. Existing measurements in proton–proton (pp), proton–lead (p–Pb), lead–lead (Pb–Pb), and gold–gold (Au–Au) collisions give a pT-integrated Λ_c^+/D^0 ratio of approximately 0.5, essentially independent of the charged-particle multiplicity at midrapidity within current uncertainties, while measurements in e^+e^- and ep collisions give a ratio of approximately 0.11. Current hadronic measurements do not extend to the regime of very low charged-particle multiplicity. Determine whether, in the limit of very low charged-particle multiplicity at midrapidity in pp collisions, the pT-integrated Λ_c^+/D^0 ratio converges back to the value ≈ 0.11 observed in e^+e^- and ep collisions, or whether the enhanced charm-baryon production (ratio ≈ 0.5) persists even when the hadronic activity is very small.

For a positive integer $d$, let $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^3)$ denote the Hilbert scheme parametrizing zero-dimensional subschemes of length $d$ in affine $3$-space $\mathbb{A}^3$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$. The smoothable component is the irreducible component containing the locus of $d$ distinct reduced points. At a closed point $[\Gamma]\in\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^3)$ corresponding to a subscheme $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{A}^3$ of length $d$, the Zariski tangent space has dimension $\dim_k\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{A}^3}}(I_\Gamma,\mathcal{O}_\Gamma)$. Two pointed schemes $(X,x)$ and $(Y,y)$ are called smoothly equivalent if there exist a pointed scheme $(Z,z)$ and smooth morphisms $Z\to X$, $Z\to Y$ sending $z$ to $x$ and $y$ respectively. Let $C(\mathrm{Gr}(2,6))$ denote the affine cone over the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(2,6)$ of $2$-planes in a $6$-dimensional vector space in its Plücker embedding, and let $0$ denote its cone point.

Question: Suppose $[\Gamma]$ lies on the smoothable component of $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^3)$ and the tangent space at $[\Gamma]$ has dimension exactly $3d+6$. Is $(\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^3),[\Gamma])$ always smoothly equivalent to $(C(\mathrm{Gr}(2,6)),0)$?

Consider high-energy hadronic collisions (e.g., pp, p–Pb, or Pb–Pb at LHC energies) in which a quark–gluon plasma is produced and subsequently hadronizes at chemical freeze-out, followed by a hadron-gas phase of typical duration 5–10 fm/c that ends at kinetic freeze-out, when all interactions cease. During the hadron-gas phase, hadronic resonances with proper lifetimes comparable to this duration may either decay inside the medium (so that their decay products undergo rescattering and the parent cannot be reconstructed) or regenerate via pseudoelastic interactions of their decay products, leading to a multiplicity-dependent modification of the reconstructable resonance yield.

Focus on the two open-charm-strange resonances D_{s1}(2536)^+ and D*_{s2}(2573)^+, and let their yields be normalized to the prompt D_s^+ meson yield in the same event class. Let dN_ch/dη denote the average charged-particle pseudorapidity density characterizing event multiplicity.

Establish the following:

(a) Determine whether the yield ratio D*_{s2}(2573)^+ / D_s^+ exhibits a statistically significant monotonically decreasing trend as a function of dN_ch/dη.

(b) Determine whether the yield ratio D_{s1}(2536)^+ / D_s^+ remains independent of dN_ch/dη within uncertainties.

(c) Quantitatively relate any observed multiplicity dependence of these ratios to the resonance proper lifetimes and to a model of hadronic rescattering and regeneration in the hadron-gas phase, thereby exposing how the interplay between resonance lifetime and hadronic-phase dynamics suppresses (or preserves) reconstructable resonance yields with increasing multiplicity.

Determine the low-energy scattering parameters (in particular the scattering length and effective range) characterizing the elastic interaction between charm hadrons (D, D*) and light-flavour hadrons (pions, kaons, and protons), namely the Dπ, DK, D*π, D*K, and D-p systems. In addition, decide whether the D-nucleon (ND) interaction is sufficiently attractive to support a bound state. Concretely:

1. Compute or measure the s-wave scattering length a and effective range r_eff appearing in the effective-range expansion
   k cot δ_0(k) = -1/a + (1/2) r_eff k^2 + O(k^4),
   for each of the channels Dπ, DK, D*π, D*K (in the relevant isospin channels) and for the D-p (ND) system.

2. For the ND interaction, determine whether the attractive strength is large enough to produce one or more bound states (poles of the s-wave scattering amplitude on the physical sheet below threshold), and if so compute their binding energies and quantum numbers.

3. Reconcile the observed pattern in which DK parameters agree with lattice-QCD and chiral-effective-field-theory predictions, while Dπ parameters appear significantly smaller than theoretical predictions, and D*π, D*K parameters are consistent with zero within current uncertainties.

Provide first-principles (lattice QCD and/or chiral effective field theory) determinations of these parameters with controlled uncertainties, and identify the precision required to discriminate between competing interaction models.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent femtoscopic measurements (notably by ALICE) and lattice-QCD studies have provided initial determinations of charm-light hadron scattering parameters: DK is consistent with lattice/χEFT predictions, Dπ is in tension with theory, and D*π/D*K are compatible with zero within uncertainties. The existence of ND bound states is suggested but not established. The problem remains open: precision is insufficient to discriminate between models or to confirm ND bound states, and improved Run 3/4 LHC data and lattice calculations are anticipated.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and let $n,d$ be positive integers. The punctual Hilbert scheme $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n,0)$ parametrizes ideals $I \subset k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ such that $\dim_k k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I = d$ and the only associated prime of $I$ is the maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m} = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$ (equivalently, $0$-dimensional subschemes of $\mathbb{A}^n$ of length $d$ set-theoretically supported at the origin). Inside $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n,0)$, let
$$\mathrm{Hilb}^{\mathrm{lci}}_d(\mathbb{A}^n,0) \subset \mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n,0)$$
denote the open locus consisting of those ideals $I$ for which the corresponding subscheme is a local complete intersection at the origin, i.e. $I$ can be generated by $n$ elements in the local ring $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]_{\mathfrak{m}}$.

Find a nontrivial upper bound, as a function of $n$ and $d$, for $\dim \mathrm{Hilb}^{\mathrm{lci}}_d(\mathbb{A}^n,0)$.

Let $\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ denote the unit circle equipped with normalized Lebesgue measure. For an integer $n \ge 0$, define the $n$-th Fejér kernel
$$K_n(t) = \sum_{k=-n}^{n}\Big(1 - \frac{|k|}{n+1}\Big)e^{ikt} = \frac{1}{n+1}\left(\frac{\sin\frac{(n+1)t}{2}}{\sin\frac{t}{2}}\right)^2,$$
and for $r \in [0,1)$ define the Poisson kernel
$$P_r(t) = \sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} r^{|k|} e^{ikt} = \frac{1-r^2}{1-2r\cos t + r^2}.$$
Let $K_n$ and $P_r$ denote the corresponding convolution operators $f \mapsto K_n * f$ and $f \mapsto P_r * f$, and let $I$ denote the identity operator.

For $1 \le p \le \infty$, let $L^p = L^p(\mathbb{T})$ be the usual Lebesgue space, and let $H^p \subset L^p$ denote the Hardy space of those $f \in L^p$ whose negative Fourier coefficients vanish (with $H^\infty$ defined as the corresponding weak-$*$ closed subspace of $L^\infty$).

Determine, in closed form, the exact operator norms
$$\|I - K_n\|_{\mathcal{B}(L^p)} \quad\text{and}\quad \|I - P_r\|_{\mathcal{B}(L^p)} \quad \text{for every } 1 < p < \infty,$$
and
$$\|I - K_n\|_{\mathcal{B}(H^p)} \quad\text{and}\quad \|I - P_r\|_{\mathcal{B}(H^p)} \quad \text{for every } 1 \le p \le \infty,$$
as functions of $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, $r \in [0,1)$, and $p$.

Inside $\mathrm{Hilb}_{H_r}$, the locus of saturated ideals of $d$ distinct (smooth) points of $X$ is an irreducible open subset; let $\mathrm{Slip}_{H_r} \subset \mathrm{Hilb}_{H_r}$ be its closure, the "scheme of limits of ideals of points."

Answer the following two questions:
(1) Is the multigraded Hilbert scheme $\mathrm{Hilb}_{H_r}$ connected?
(2) Does every irreducible component of $\mathrm{Hilb}_{H_r}$ intersect $\mathrm{Slip}_{H_r}$?

Work over an algebraically closed field. A finite subscheme $\Gamma \subseteq \mathbb{A}^n$ is called smoothable if it lies in the closure of the locus of reduced finite subschemes in the Hilbert scheme of points of $\mathbb{A}^n$; equivalently, $\Gamma$ is a flat limit of finite collections of distinct reduced points. For an arbitrary finite subscheme $\Gamma \subseteq \mathbb{A}^n$, define the smoothability defect
$$\delta(\Gamma) := \min\{\deg(\Gamma') - \deg(\Gamma) : \Gamma \subseteq \Gamma' \subseteq \mathbb{A}^n,\ \Gamma' \text{ finite and smoothable}\},$$
where $\deg$ denotes the $k$-vector space dimension of the structure ring. Investigate the behavior of the function $\delta(-)$ on finite subschemes of affine spaces. In particular, determine whether there exists a finite subscheme $\Gamma \subseteq \mathbb{A}^n$ (for some $n$) such that
$$\delta(\Gamma) > \deg(\Gamma).$$

Setup. Let $\mathbb{T}$ denote the unit circle with normalized Lebesgue measure. For $1<p<\infty$ and $1\le q<\infty$, the Lorentz space $L^{p,q}(\mathbb{T})$ consists of all measurable functions $f$ on $\mathbb{T}$ with
$$\|f\|_{L^{p,q}} = \left(\int_0^\infty \big(t^{1/p} f^{*}(t)\big)^q \frac{dt}{t}\right)^{1/q}<\infty,$$
where $f^{*}$ is the nonincreasing rearrangement of $|f|$. The Hardy–Lorentz space $H[L^{p,q}]$ is the closed subspace of $L^{p,q}(\mathbb{T})$ consisting of those $f$ whose Fourier coefficients $\hat{f}(n)$ vanish for all $n<0$.

A Banach space $X$ is said to have the bounded compact approximation property (BCAP) with constant $C\ge 1$ if there exists a net (or, when $X$ is separable, a sequence) $\{T_\alpha\}$ of compact operators on $X$ with $\sup_\alpha \|T_\alpha\|\le C$ such that $T_\alpha x\to x$ for every $x\in X$. The bounded compact approximation constant $M(X)$ is the infimum of all such $C$.

It is known that for $1\le q\le p<\infty$ one has $M(H[L^{p,q}])\le 2$.

Problem. For $1\le q\le p<\infty$:
(a) Establish a nontrivial lower bound $M(H[L^{p,q}])>1$ (or determine the exact value) for the bounded compact approximation constant of the Hardy–Lorentz space $H[L^{p,q}]$.
(b) Improve the upper bound $M(H[L^{p,q}])\le 2$, ideally to a sharp estimate analogous to the bound $M(H^p)\le 2^{|1-2/p|}$ known for the classical Hardy spaces $H^p$ with $1<p<\infty$.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, and let $A$ be a finite local $k$-algebra of $k$-vector-space dimension $d$, so that $\operatorname{Spec}(A)$ is a finite scheme of degree $d$ supported at a single point. Assume $A$ is smoothable, meaning that $\operatorname{Spec}(A)$ lies in the closure of the locus of $d$ reduced points inside the Hilbert scheme of $d$ points.

An abstract smoothing of $A$ over $k[[t]]$ is a flat $k[[t]]$-algebra $\mathcal{A}$, finite of rank $d$, such that $\mathcal{A}/(t)\cong A$ and $\mathcal{A}\otimes_{k[[t]]} k((t))$ is a product of separable field extensions of $k((t))$. The smoothing is called completely split if $\mathcal{A}\otimes_{k[[t]]} k((t))\cong k((t))^{d}$. The approximation degree of such a smoothing is the smallest integer $N\ge 0$ such that the isomorphism class of $\mathcal{A}$ (as a flat $k[[t]]$-algebra deformation of $A$) is determined by its reduction modulo $t^{N+1}$; equivalently, the smallest $N$ such that any flat deformation of $A$ over $k[t]/(t^{N+1})$ extending the given one lifts uniquely (up to isomorphism) to a flat deformation over $k[[t]]$ realizing $\mathcal{A}$.

Question (strong form): For every smoothable finite local $k$-algebra $A$ of degree $d$, does there exist a completely split abstract smoothing $\mathcal{A}$ of $A$ over $k[[t]]$ whose approximation degree is at most $d$?

Question (weak form): Does there exist a polynomial $P(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$, independent of $A$, such that for every smoothable finite local $k$-algebra $A$ of degree $d$ there exists a completely split abstract smoothing of $A$ over $k[[t]]$ with approximation degree at most $P(d)$?

Consider a Markov decision process (MDP) defined by a tuple (S, A, P, r, γ), where the state space S ⊆ R^{d_s} and/or action space A ⊆ R^{d_a} are high-dimensional and continuous, P(s' | s, a) is a transition kernel, r : S × A → R is a reward function, and γ ∈ (0,1) is a discount factor. Suppose, in addition, that one is given physical prior information about the environment in the form of (i) a (possibly partially known) governing dynamical system such as an ODE/PDE F(s, ṡ, a, t; θ_phys) = 0, (ii) conservation laws or symmetry groups G acting on S × A, and/or (iii) a set of measurable physical variables φ_phys : S → R^{m} (e.g., positions, momenta, energies) that are known to be relevant to the dynamics.

Design and analyze an encoder e_ψ : S → Z (with Z ⊆ R^{k}, k ≪ d_s) and an associated reinforcement-learning algorithm that jointly produces a policy π : Z → A such that the learned latent representation z = e_ψ(s) satisfies all of the following properties simultaneously:

1. Compression: the latent dimension k is much smaller than d_s.
2. Task-informativeness: the optimal value function V*(s) and an optimal policy π*(s) of the original MDP can be approximated to within a prescribed error ε using only z = e_ψ(s); equivalently, there exist π̃ : Z → A and Ṽ : Z → R with sup_s |V*(s) − Ṽ(e_ψ(s))| ≤ ε and a corresponding suboptimality bound on π̃ ∘ e_ψ.
3. Physical pertinence: the representation respects the given physical priors, in a sense to be made precise — for example, equivariance e_ψ(g · s) = ρ(g) · e_ψ(s) for all g ∈ G for some representation ρ, consistency with the governing equations (the latent dynamics ż = f_ψ(z, a) are derivable from or consistent with F), and/or recoverability of φ_phys(s) from z via a smooth decoder.

Provide a constructive procedure for learning (e_ψ, π) from interaction data together with provable guarantees on the trade-off between compression rate k, task-suboptimality ε, and the degree of physical consistency, in the regime where d_s is large and only limited environment interaction is available.

In ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions, real photons and dileptons (lepton-antilepton pairs from virtual photons) are emitted throughout every stage of the collision: from initial parton scatterings in the colliding nuclei, through the approach to thermal and chemical equilibrium, the expansion of the resulting quark-gluon plasma, hadronization, and the final hadronic rescattering and decays. The inclusive yield of these electromagnetic probes, as a function of transverse momentum, invariant mass, rapidity, centrality, and azimuthal angle (encoded for instance in the anisotropic-flow coefficients v_n obtained from the Fourier decomposition of the azimuthal distribution), therefore offers in principle a stringent constraint on models of the full space-time dynamics of the collision.

In practice, however, experimental measurements of photons and dileptons in heavy-ion collisions are subject to substantial backgrounds (notably from hadronic decays such as π0 → γγ, η → γγ, π0 → γ e+ e−, and conversion electrons) and have statistical and systematic uncertainties that are typically much larger than those of bulk hadronic observables such as charged-particle multiplicities dN/dη, mean transverse momenta ⟨p_T⟩, and anisotropic-flow coefficients v_n of identified hadrons.

Problem. Identify experimental strategies — including detector design, triggering, background subtraction, and analysis techniques — by which the precision of inclusive direct-photon and dilepton measurements (in transverse momentum, invariant mass, and azimuthal anisotropy) in ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions can be improved to a level comparable with that of bulk hadronic observables, so that the inclusive electromagnetic signal becomes a quantitatively stringent test of nuclear-collision dynamics across all stages of the collision.

Improving the precision of direct-photon and dilepton measurements in heavy-ion collisions is an actively pursued goal of the ongoing and upcoming experimental programs at RHIC (sPHENIX, STAR) and the LHC (ALICE 3, upgraded ALICE, CMS, ATLAS), as well as proposed facilities (NA60+, CBM at FAIR). Current measurements still have considerably larger uncertainties than bulk hadronic observables, and the question of how to achieve hadron-level precision is widely regarded as open in the field.

Consider a reinforcement learning setting in which an agent interacts with an environment whose dynamics are governed (at least in part) by known physical laws, expressible as differential equations, conservation laws, symmetries, or other structural priors. Let $\mathcal{T} = \{T_i\}$ denote a family of tasks (each specified by a reward function and possibly a time horizon) and let $\mathcal{E} = \{E_j\}$ denote a family of environments (each specified by a Markov decision process whose transition kernel obeys a common underlying class of physical constraints but may differ in parameters, geometry, or boundary conditions).

A physics-informed model learner is a procedure $\mathcal{L}$ that, given interaction data from one or more $(T_i, E_j)$ pairs together with physical priors $\Phi$ (e.g., PDE residuals, Lagrangian/Hamiltonian structure, invariances), produces an approximate dynamics model $\hat{f}_{\mathcal{L},\Phi}$ to be used for planning or policy optimization.

Consider high-energy nucleus–nucleus (A+A) collisions at collider energies, and the production of (i) high transverse-momentum prompt photons and (ii) high-invariant-mass Drell–Yan-type dileptons. The standard "binary collision scaling" hypothesis asserts that the inclusive cross section in A+A factorizes as

  dσ^{AA}/dX = N_bin · dσ^{NN}/dX,

where N_bin is the average number of inelastic binary nucleon–nucleon collisions in a given centrality class (computed from a Glauber model) and dσ^{NN}/dX is the inclusive elementary nucleon–nucleon cross section for the same observable X (e.g., photon p_T spectrum or dilepton invariant-mass spectrum). Equivalently, the nuclear modification factor R_AA(X) := (dσ^{AA}/dX)/(N_bin · dσ^{NN}/dX) is expected to equal 1.

Investigate the following question precisely:

(a) Under what kinematic regime (in p_T for prompt photons, and in invariant mass M and rapidity y for dileptons) and to what quantitative accuracy does the binary-scaling identity R_AA = 1 hold in QCD?

(b) Decompose any deviation R_AA(X) − 1 into the following four contributions and quantify each:
   (1) nuclear modifications of parton distribution functions (shadowing, anti-shadowing, EMC effect, Fermi motion), encoded in nPDFs f_i^{A}(x,Q^2) versus f_i^{p}(x,Q^2);
   (2) the isospin effect arising from the differing parton content of protons and neutrons (i.e., A consisting of Z protons and A−Z neutrons rather than A protons);
   (3) contributions of fragmentation photons (photons produced from the collinear fragmentation of a hard parton), which are sensitive to in-medium parton energy loss and therefore not expected to scale with N_bin;
   (4) any genuinely non-factorizing dynamical mechanism that makes the incoherent-superposition assumption inexact even after (1)–(3) are accounted for (e.g., coherent multi-nucleon scattering, initial-state energy loss, gluon saturation, Coulomb corrections, etc.).

Provide either rigorous bounds or controlled phenomenological estimates for each component, and determine whether, after subtracting (1)–(3), there is a residual deviation that signals a violation of exact binary scaling for these hard electromagnetic probes.

The validity of exact binary scaling for hard electromagnetic probes remains an active research topic. Consider the setting of physics-informed reinforcement learning (PIRL), in which a learning agent interacts with a Markov decision process (MDP) defined by a tuple (S, A, P, r, γ) — with state space S, action space A, transition kernel P, reward function r, and discount factor γ ∈ [0,1) — while additionally being supplied with prior physical knowledge such as governing ordinary or partial differential equations, conservation laws, symmetries, invariants, or other domain-specific constraints that the dynamics or the policy are assumed (or required) to satisfy. A PIRL algorithm uses this physical information to shape the state representation, the model, the reward, the action space, the loss function, or the exploration strategy.

Design a comprehensive, principled benchmarking and evaluation framework for PIRL that satisfies all of the following requirements:

1. Domain coverage: The framework specifies a finite collection of MDP environments {E_i} spanning multiple physical application domains (e.g., classical mechanics, fluid dynamics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, robotics, control of distributed-parameter systems), such that each environment exposes a precisely defined set of physical priors P_i (equations, invariants, symmetries) in a standardized machine-readable form.

2. Fair comparability: The framework defines a set of evaluation metrics M = {m_1, …, m_k} — including but not limited to cumulative reward, sample efficiency, constraint-violation magnitude, generalization error to out-of-distribution physical parameters, and robustness to perturbations — together with a fixed evaluation protocol (training budgets, random seeds, statistical tests) under which two PIRL algorithms A and B running on the same E_i with the same priors P_i can be compared in a way that is invariant to incidental implementation choices.

3. Assessment of physics-information quality and uniqueness: The framework provides a quantitative procedure to assess (a) how much performance improvement an algorithm derives specifically from the physical priors versus from non-physics components, and (b) the uniqueness of the physical-information mechanism used (e.g., a measure that distinguishes algorithms whose contributions reduce to one another from those that exploit physics in genuinely different ways).

4. Minimal domain-expertise burden: The framework includes abstractions and documentation such that a researcher without deep expertise in a given physical domain can run, interpret, and compare PIRL algorithms on environments from that domain.

The problem is to construct such a framework {(E_i, P_i)}, metric set M, evaluation protocol, and quality/uniqueness assessment procedure, and to prove (or empirically demonstrate to a stated standard) that it satisfies the four requirements above.

In the theoretical description of relativistic heavy-ion collisions, hard partons produced in initial hard scatterings traverse a hot and dense medium of quarks and gluons (the quark-gluon plasma) and lose energy through interactions with this lower-energy thermal bath. Schematically, the inclusive yield of a particle species X (X = hadron, photon, or lepton pair) takes the form of a convolution

    dN_X = (initial hard production) ⊗ (parton energy loss) ⊗ (fragmentation / hadronization or photon/dilepton emission),

where the energy-loss kernel must be evolved along the space-time trajectory of each hard parton through a hydrodynamically evolving medium, while the hard production and fragmentation pieces are most naturally formulated in momentum space.

For electromagnetic probes (real photons and dileptons), the energy-loss stage itself emits radiation: bremsstrahlung and medium-induced conversion processes produce so-called jet-medium photons and dileptons, and at the same time the fragmentation contribution to photon (and dilepton) production from the hard parton is suppressed or modified because the parton's momentum and color state have been altered by its passage through the medium.

Problem. Construct a single, theoretically consistent framework — for instance a Monte Carlo or transport scheme — that:

(i) implements parton energy loss as a space-time–dependent process along realistic medium evolution histories,
(ii) simultaneously generates the jet-medium photons and dileptons emitted during the energy-loss process,
(iii) yields the appropriately suppressed/modified fragmentation photon (and dilepton) spectra from the surviving hard partons,
(iv) preserves energy-momentum conservation, color coherence (LPM-type interference) and the correct interface with low-energy (thermal) parton and photon/dilepton production,

and quantitatively reproduces measured nuclear modification factors and direct-photon / dilepton spectra in heavy-ion collisions. Provide the formalism, demonstrate its internal consistency, and compare its predictions with data.

Consider a detached double-lined eclipsing binary system in which both components have precisely measured masses $M_1, M_2$, radii $R_1, R_2$, effective temperatures $T_{\mathrm{eff},1}, T_{\mathrm{eff},2}$, and a measured surface metallicity $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]_{\mathrm{surf}}$. Assume the more massive primary has already completed the first dredge-up (so its convective envelope has homogenized inner material with the surface), while the less massive secondary has not yet undergone first dredge-up. Stellar evolution models depend on, among other parameters, a common age $t$ for the two stars and a convective core overshooting parameter $\beta$ (which sets the extension $\ell_{\mathrm{ov}} = \beta H_p$ of mixing beyond the Schwarzschild boundary, where $H_p$ is the local pressure scale height). A calibration consists of finding $(t,\beta,\text{initial composition},\dots)$ for which a pair of stellar tracks simultaneously reproduces the measured $(M_i,R_i,T_{\mathrm{eff},i},[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]_{\mathrm{surf}})$.

Two physical scenarios are considered for the treatment of microscopic diffusion (gravitational settling and radiative levitation of metals) in the radiative envelopes of stars in the relevant mass range:
(A) microscopic diffusion is fully active and is allowed to modify the present-day surface $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ relative to the initial composition;
(B) microscopic diffusion is included in the interior, but its effect on the surface abundance is canceled by a competing mixing process (e.g., turbulent mixing or radiative levitation) so that the surface $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ effectively tracks the initial composition prior to first dredge-up.

Question: Given the same set of precise observational constraints $(M_i,R_i,T_{\mathrm{eff},i},[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]_{\mathrm{surf}})$, do calibrations performed under scenarios (A) and (B) yield statistically consistent inferred values of the system age $t$ and the overshooting parameter $\beta$, or do they produce materially different best-fit values and confidence regions? Quantify the robustness of the inferred $(t,\beta)$ to the assumed efficiency of microscopic diffusion at the surface in this mass regime.

Consider a relativistic heavy-ion collision modeled by a hydrodynamic stage of a quark-gluon plasma (QGP) with space-time temperature profile T(x,t), velocity field u^μ(x,t), and dissipative transport coefficients including the temperature-dependent shear viscosity η(T), bulk viscosity ζ(T), and possible second- (or higher-)order transport coefficients. Suppose the plasma may also exhibit incomplete chemical equilibration (parameterized e.g. by a quark fugacity λ_q(T,t) ≤ 1), incomplete thermal equilibration (parameterized e.g. by a non-equilibrium momentum-anisotropy parameter ξ(x,t) characterizing the ratio of longitudinal to transverse momentum scales of partons), and a freeze-out hypersurface Σ_f below which hadronic degrees of freedom govern the dynamics.

Thermal photons are produced from the QGP with a Lorentz-invariant emission rate
  E dN_γ/d^4x d^3k = - (1/(2π)^3) f_B(k·u/T) Im Π^μ_μ^R(k; T, λ_q, ξ, …),
and thermal dileptons of invariant mass M and four-momentum q with rate
  dN_{ℓ^+ℓ^-}/d^4x d^4q = - (α^2/(π^3 M^2)) f_B(q·u/T) Im Π^μ_μ^R(q; T, λ_q, ξ, …),
where Π^μ_μ^R is the retarded electromagnetic current-current correlator of the QGP medium, including viscous corrections to both the distribution functions and the rate.

Assume that hadronic observables (identified-particle spectra, anisotropic flow harmonics v_n, HBT radii, etc.) already strongly constrain the low-temperature portion (T ≲ T_pc, the pseudo-critical temperature) of the hydrodynamic evolution, including η(T) and ζ(T) for T ≲ T_pc.

Problem. Develop a quantitative inference framework that uses measured momentum (k_T) and invariant-mass (M) differential spectra and anisotropic flow coefficients v_n(k_T) and v_n(M) of thermal photons and dileptons—after subtraction of identified hadronic decay contributions and selection of kinematic windows dominated by the QGP stage—to constrain, simultaneously and with quantified uncertainties:
  (i) the QGP space-time temperature profile T(x,t) (in particular the early-time, high-T regions inaccessible to hadrons);
  (ii) the chemical equilibration history λ_q(T,t) and the thermal/momentum-anisotropy history ξ(x,t);
  (iii) the temperature dependence of the shear viscosity η(T)/s(T) and bulk viscosity ζ(T)/s(T) for T > T_pc;
  (iv) at least one second-order transport coefficient (e.g. the shear relaxation time τ_π(T)).

Specifically, determine which combinations of photon and dilepton observables (k_T-bins, M-bins, v_n harmonics) provide independent constraints on each of (i)–(iv), prove or argue under what assumptions these combinations identify the underlying functions uniquely, and quantify the precision with which each quantity can be extracted given current and projected experimental uncertainties.

Consider detached eclipsing binary stellar systems in which both components have masses in the range 1.2 M⊙ ≲ M ≲ 1.5 M⊙, with very precisely measured masses, radii, and effective temperatures. Stellar evolution codes used to model such systems contain free or weakly constrained parameters (e.g., the convective core overshooting efficiency, the efficiency of microscopic diffusion at the surface, mixing length, initial helium abundance, and initial chemical composition), and standard fitting pipelines determine these parameters together with the system age by matching computed stellar tracks to observations.

(a) Determine whether, in this mass range, binary-system observations of the above quality suffice to yield calibrations of the free model parameters (in particular the core overshooting efficiency) that are robust against the modelling choice for the evolution of the surface iron-to-hydrogen ratio [Fe/H] — specifically, against the choice between (i) a scenario in which microscopic diffusion is allowed to modify the surface [Fe/H] and (ii) a scenario in which competing mixing processes cancel out this surface depletion so that the surface [Fe/H] tracks the initial value.

(b) For the specific detached eclipsing binary Ai Phoenicis (Ai Phe), with its currently available precise mass and radius measurements for the two components, decide which of the two surface-metallicity scenarios (i)–(ii) above gives the more reliable description of the system, and determine whether a precise spectroscopic measurement of the individual surface [Fe/H] values of the two components is sufficient to discriminate between these scenarios.

representations.normalized:
In a numerical simulation of a relativistic heavy-ion collision, the hot QCD matter is modeled in successive stages. In an intermediate stage the medium is described by relativistic viscous hydrodynamics, characterized at each spacetime point by local temperature T(x), flow velocity u^μ(x), and dissipative corrections (shear stress, bulk pressure, baryon diffusion). In this stage, the spectrum of electromagnetic probes (real photons and dileptons of invariant mass M) is obtained from a macroscopic formula of the schematic form

  E dN_γ/d^3p = ∫ d^4x  Γ_γ(E·u(x), T(x); δf)  ,
  d^4N_ℓℓ / d^4q  = ∫ d^4x  Γ_ℓℓ(q·u(x), M, T(x); δf)  ,

where Γ_γ and Γ_ℓℓ are thermal emission rates (per unit four-volume) computed from the in-medium electromagnetic spectral function and δf denotes off-equilibrium corrections. In a later stage, once the medium becomes sufficiently dilute, the dynamics is described by a microscopic hadronic transport (Boltzmann-type) cascade evolving discrete hadrons through binary scatterings and resonance decays; in this stage electromagnetic emission can be obtained microscopically by summing 2→2+γ, 2→2+ℓℓ, and resonance decay contributions along the simulated hadronic trajectories.

Let τ_relax(x) denote the local microscopic relaxation time of the hadronic medium and τ_evolution(x) the local macroscopic expansion time scale (e.g. 1/(∂·u)). Address the following:

(a) Formulate a quantitatively justified prescription, valid throughout the transition region where τ_relax(x) and τ_evolution(x) become comparable, for computing the photon spectrum E dN_γ/d^3p and the dilepton spectrum d^4N_ℓℓ/d^4q so that the result smoothly interpolates between the hydrodynamic emission-rate formula above and the microscopic transport-based emission, avoiding both double counting and omission.

(b) Identify a criterion (in terms of T(x), τ_relax(x)/τ_evolution(x), or other locally computable quantities) that determines, at each spacetime point, whether the macroscopic hydrodynamic emission-rate treatment should be replaced or supplemented by the microscopic hadronic-transport calculation, and demonstrate that the resulting unified description for electromagnetic probes is consistent with the transport description already used for the hadronic sector (i.e. the same particle content, cross sections, and off-equilibrium distributions).

representations.normalized:
Setup. Consider a self-gravitating collisionless ensemble of identical particles described by a phase-space distribution function f(x,v) on R^3 × R^3. In the (Newtonian) Vlasov–Poisson setting one looks for time-independent solutions of the system

    v·∂_x f − ∂_x U·∂_v f = 0,    ΔU = 4π ρ,    ρ(x) = ∫_{R^3} f(x,v) dv,

with U(x) → 0 as |x| → ∞. Fix a prescribed total mass M > 0, and a prescribed "particle ansatz" Φ : R × [0,∞) → [0,∞) that is to be evaluated on the particle energy E = (1/2)|v|^2 + U(x) and the modulus of angular momentum L = |x×v|. Let D be the set of admissible nonnegative, integrable spatial densities ρ on R^3 with ∫ρ = M and suitable decay.

Define the iteration map T : D → D as follows. Given ρ ∈ D:
(i) solve ΔU_ρ = 4π ρ with U_ρ(x) → 0 at infinity, obtaining the induced gravitational potential U_ρ;
(ii) form the candidate density

    ρ̃(x) := ∫_{R^3} Φ( (1/2)|v|^2 + U_ρ(x), |x×v| ) dv;

(iii) define the amplitude K(ρ̃) := M ( ∫_{R^3} ρ̃(y) dy )^{−1}, and set

    T(ρ) := K(ρ̃) ρ̃.

Problem. Prove that, for a suitable class of ansatz functions Φ and an appropriately chosen domain D, the map T admits a fixed point ρ_* ∈ D (which then yields a stationary solution of the corresponding Vlasov-type system with total mass M).

Pose and solve the analogous fixed-point existence problem for:
(a) the Newtonian Vlasov–Poisson system, as described above;
(b) the spherically symmetric Einstein–Vlasov system, in which U_ρ is replaced by the metric functions determined from ρ (and its associated momentum/pressure components) via the spherically symmetric Einstein equations, and Φ depends on the corresponding relativistic conserved quantities (particle energy and angular momentum);
(c) the axially symmetric stationary Einstein–Vlasov system, in which the metric is determined from the matter via the axisymmetric stationary Einstein equations and Φ depends on the corresponding conserved quantities (energy and the axial angular momentum).

In each case, establish existence of a fixed point of the corresponding map T.

Let $M$ be a complete $d$-dimensional Riemannian manifold whose sectional curvatures all lie in the interval $[-K, K]$ for some constant $K \ge 0$. Equip $M$ with its Riemannian distance and the usual exponential and logarithm maps. A subset $D \subseteq M$ is called geodesically convex (g-convex) if for every pair of points $x, y \in D$ there is a unique minimizing geodesic segment $\gamma$ in $M$ joining $x$ and $y$, and this segment is entirely contained in $D$. A function $f: D \to \mathbb{R}$ is g-convex on $D$ if $f \circ \gamma$ is a convex function (in the usual sense on an interval of $\mathbb{R}$) for every geodesic segment $\gamma \subseteq D$.

Fix a reference point $x_{\mathrm{ref}} \in M$ and a radius $r > 0$ such that the closed geodesic ball $\overline{B}(x_{\mathrm{ref}}, r)$ is g-convex. Let $f: \overline{B}(x_{\mathrm{ref}}, r) \to \mathbb{R}$ be g-convex on $\overline{B}(x_{\mathrm{ref}}, r)$ and $M_{\mathrm{Lip}}$-Lipschitz with respect to the Riemannian distance. Let
$$ f^* = \min_{x \in \overline{B}(x_{\mathrm{ref}}, r)} f(x), \qquad \zeta_{r\sqrt{K}} = \frac{r\sqrt{K}}{\tanh(r\sqrt{K})}. $$

Work in the black-box first-order oracle model: an algorithm issues queries $x_k \in M$ and in response receives $f(x_k)$ and a subgradient $g_k$ of $f$ at $x_k$.

Question: Does there exist a deterministic first-order algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ with the following two properties?

(a) For every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, $\mathcal{A}$ produces a point $x \in \overline{B}(x_{\mathrm{ref}}, r)$ satisfying $f(x) - f^* \le \varepsilon M_{\mathrm{Lip}} r$ using at most $O(\mathrm{poly}(\zeta_{r\sqrt{K}}, d) \cdot \log(1/\varepsilon))$ oracle queries.

(b) Between oracle queries, $\mathcal{A}$ performs at most $\mathrm{poly}(\zeta_{r\sqrt{K}}, d)$ arithmetic operations to compute the next query point.

Consider the spherically symmetric Vlasov–Poisson system and the spherically symmetric Einstein–Vlasov system, describing self-gravitating collisionless matter in Newtonian gravity and in general relativity, respectively. A standard procedure to construct static/stationary solutions of these systems is the following mass-preserving fixed-point iteration: starting from an initial gravitational potential (resp. metric), one defines a distribution function f as a prescribed (decreasing) function of the local particle energy (and possibly angular momentum), rescaled to keep the total ADM/Newtonian mass fixed; one then recomputes the potential (resp. metric) from f via Poisson's equation (resp. the Einstein constraints), and iterates. Numerical experiments indicate that this iteration converges to a steady state on a certain subset of microscopic equations of state, and that the steady states so obtained appear to be precisely those which are dynamically stable under the full nonlinear time evolution of the corresponding Vlasov system.

Problem: Establish a rigorous mathematical link between nonlinear dynamical stability of stationary solutions and the convergence of this iterative fixed-point algorithm. Specifically, prove (or disprove) that, for the spherically symmetric Vlasov–Poisson system and for the spherically symmetric Einstein–Vlasov system, a stationary solution arising as a fixed point to which the iteration converges is nonlinearly dynamically stable, and conversely that nonlinearly stable steady states lie in the convergence set of this algorithm.

Consider ultra-relativistic Pb–Pb collisions at a nucleon–nucleon center-of-mass energy √s_NN = 5.02 TeV, in which a quark–gluon plasma (QGP) is produced together with strong, short-lived electromagnetic fields and a large fluid vorticity associated with the angular momentum of the non-central collision. For an inclusive sample of J/ψ mesons reconstructed at forward rapidity, define the polarization with respect to an axis perpendicular to the reaction (event) plane via the angular distribution of the positive-charge decay lepton in the J/ψ rest frame,

  dN/d cos θ ∝ 1 + λ_θ cos² θ,

equivalently parametrized by the spin-density-matrix element ρ_{00} = (1 − λ_θ)/(3 + λ_θ). In the kinematic window 2 < p_T < 4 GeV/c and centrality class 30–50%, a small but statistically significant positive value λ_θ > 0 is observed.

(a) Construct a quantitative theoretical framework that connects this measured λ_θ(p_T, centrality) to the underlying QGP properties—specifically, to the magnitude and time evolution of the early-stage electromagnetic field, to the local fluid vorticity field ω^μ(x), and to the modification of the cc̄ bound-state dynamics in the deconfined medium—and that reproduces the observed sign, magnitude, and p_T-/centrality-dependence of λ_θ.

(b) Determine, within such a framework, the predicted polarization (λ_θ or ρ_{00}) of the D*+ vector meson in the same collision system, accounting for the spin alignment of the charm quark generated at the earliest stages of the collision by the produced magnetic field and for the spin transfer through hadronization to the D*+ final state. Specify whether the predicted D*+ polarization signal is large enough to be experimentally distinguishable from zero and from charmonium polarization, and identify the observables that would isolate the early-time charm-spin-alignment contribution from later medium effects.

The ALICE measurement of inclusive J/ψ polarization with respect to the event plane in Pb–Pb at √s_NN = 5.02 TeV established a small but significant λ_θ > 0 effect, but a fully quantitative theoretical description connecting it to QGP electromagnetic fields and vorticity is not yet established. Consider the axially symmetric, stationary Einstein–Vlasov system in asymptotic flatness, describing a collisionless ensemble of particles whose phase-space density f on the cotangent bundle is conserved along the geodesic flow and which sources the Einstein equations via its stress-energy tensor. Assume the metric admits two commuting Killing vectors (a timelike ∂_t and an axial ∂_φ), and write f as a function of the conserved energy E and angular momentum L_z along orbits. Restrict attention to ansatzes of the form f = Φ(E_0 − E)·Ψ(L_z − L_0), supported in {E ≤ E_0, L_z ≥ L_0}, that yield regular toroidal matter configurations (the spatial support is a torus topologically encircling the symmetry axis) with finite total mass M and net angular momentum J. Define the compactness Γ = 2M/R, where R is an invariantly defined areal radius of the configuration, so that Γ → 1 corresponds approaching the extremal Kerr horizon ratio J = M^2.

Question: Does there exist a one-parameter family of such regular stationary rotating toroidal Einstein–Vlasov solutions, obtained by decreasing the cutoff energy E_0 and simultaneously tuning the cutoff angular momentum L_0, along which the compactness Γ tends to 1 and the asymptotic Komar quantities (M, J) approach those of an extremal Kerr black hole (J/M^2 → 1)? Equivalently, can a quasistationary transition from regular toroidal Vlasov configurations to an extremal Kerr black hole be realized? Or is every such sequence forced either to satisfy a strict upper bound Γ < Γ_max < 1 or to degenerate into a thin-ring (singular) limit before reaching extremality? Provide either a construction of such an extremalizing sequence or an analytic obstruction ruling it out.

The question of whether a quasistationary transition from regular stationary axisymmetric Einstein–Vlasov solutions to an extremal Kerr black hole is possible is explicitly identified as a central open problem. Consider beauty quarks (b-quarks, mass ≈ 4.18 GeV) produced in heavy-ion collisions and propagating through a deconfined quark–gluon plasma (QGP). Model their interaction with the medium as a stochastic process characterized by a spatial diffusion coefficient D_s (or equivalently a momentum diffusion coefficient κ), so that the thermalization/hydrodynamization time scale is τ_Q ∼ (M/T) · D_s, where M is the heavy-quark mass and T the medium temperature. Because M_b ≫ T, simple Brownian-motion estimates suggest τ_Q for beauty is comparable to the typical QGP lifetime (∼ 5–10 fm/c), while recent nonperturbative (lattice-QCD) determinations of κ at temperatures relevant to the QGP yield smaller D_s, suggesting at least partial hydrodynamization is possible within the medium lifetime.

(a) Determine quantitatively to what extent beauty quarks participate in the collective dynamics of the QGP — in particular, characterize, as a function of transverse momentum p_T (with emphasis on the low-p_T region p_T ≲ M_b), the magnitude of the nuclear modification factor
   R_AA(p_T) = (1/⟨N_coll⟩) · (dN_AA/dp_T)/(dN_pp/dp_T)
for non-prompt (beauty-decay) D and J/ψ mesons and B mesons, and of the anisotropic-flow Fourier coefficients
   v_n(p_T) = ⟨cos[n(φ − Ψ_n)]⟩, n = 2, 3,
of the same beauty-hadron observables.

(b) Given a set of such measurements (with the statistical and systematic precision expected from LHC Run 3 Pb–Pb data sets), determine the precision with which one can extract the temperature-dependent spatial diffusion coefficient 2πT·D_s(T) of beauty quarks in the QGP, and assess whether the data can discriminate between models in which beauty quarks fully hydrodynamize, partially hydrodynamize, or remain out of equilibrium throughout the medium evolution.

Consider the Einstein–Vlasov system in general relativity, which couples Einstein's field equations to the collisionless Vlasov (kinetic) equation for a phase-space distribution function f = f(x,p) ≥ 0 on the tangent bundle of a 4-dimensional Lorentzian spacetime (M,g). The matter is described by the energy-momentum tensor

  T_{μν}(x) = ∫ f(x,p) p_μ p_ν (−det g)^{−1/2} d^4 p,

restricted to the mass shell g^{μν} p_μ p_ν = −m^2, and f is constant along the geodesic flow. A stationary solution is a triple (M, g, f) admitting a timelike Killing vector field, with g asymptotically flat and the spatial matter density

  ρ(x) = T_{μν} n^μ n^ν

(where n is the unit normal to a stationary spacelike slice) compactly supported in the slice.

Question: Does there exist a stationary, asymptotically flat, axially symmetric solution (M, g, f) of the Einstein–Vlasov system whose three-dimensional spatial density ρ has a core that is highly flattened toward an equatorial plane — quantitatively, with the ratio of the vertical extent of the support of ρ (perpendicular to the symmetry axis) to its radial extent arbitrarily small, while ρ is not supported entirely in a two-dimensional plane — so as to resemble the morphology of an observed disk galaxy? Equivalently, can the family of stationary three-dimensional Einstein–Vlasov solutions include configurations whose density profile is as planar and as extremely oblate as observed disk galaxies, going beyond the mildly oblate spheroidal and rotating configurations currently known to exist?

The literature on stationary solutions of the Einstein–Vlasov system reports spherically symmetric static solutions, axially symmetric oblate spheroidal and rotating solutions, and (in 2022) axisymmetric bifurcations from Kerr. No construction of three-dimensional stationary Einstein–Vlasov solutions whose density core matches the extreme flattening of realistic disk galaxies has been reported; the question is identified as a central open problem and no resolution has been found in available sources.

Consider the axially symmetric, stationary Einstein-Vlasov system in general relativity, in which a collisionless ensemble of particles is described by a non-negative phase-space density f(x,p) on the cotangent bundle of a four-dimensional Lorentzian spacetime admitting a timelike Killing vector field ∂_t and an axial Killing vector field ∂_φ. Along geodesics, the particle energy E = -p_t and the axial angular momentum L_z = p_φ are conserved. Restrict attention to ansätze of the form

   f(x,p) = K · Φ(E, L_z),

where K > 0 is a normalization constant and Φ : ℝ × ℝ → [0,∞) is a measurable function (the "ansatz function"). The induced spatial mass density ρ is obtained by integrating f over the momentum fiber, and the metric is determined self-consistently from the Einstein field equations sourced by the resulting energy-momentum tensor.

Problems:

(a) Determine which classes of ansatz functions Φ(E, L_z), and which (nontrivial) linear or non-linear combinations of such functions, yield convergent stationary axisymmetric solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov system whose spatial density ρ has one of the following morphologies:
   (i) a prolate "spindle" concentrated along the axis of symmetry;
   (ii) a "toroidal" support encircling the axis with a central hole;
   (iii) a composite morphology combining the above with disk-like or bulge-like components, including ring-shaped supports and halo-type extended supports.

(b) For the convergent solutions in (a), characterize quantitatively the resulting density profiles (e.g., aspect ratios, equatorial-to-polar extent, hole sizes, mass concentrations) and decide whether they reproduce the morphological features attributed to physical configurations such as prolate spindle-like galaxies, active-galactic-nucleus tori, disk galaxies with central bulges, dark-matter halos, or ring galaxies.

(c) Provide a mathematical criterion explaining why arbitrary nontrivial linear combinations of individually admissible ansatz functions need not yield convergent stationary solutions, and identify sufficient conditions on Φ ensuring existence and convergence.

The question is posed as part of a survey of open problems on stationary solutions of the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system. No subsequent work appears to give a general classification of ansatz functions Φ(E,L_z) producing convergent spindle, toroidal, or composite morphologies; existing studies (Andréasson, Ames, Logg and collaborators) provide numerical examples but no systematic existence/classification result. The problem appears to remain open.

Consider the exotic charm hadrons D*_{s0}(2317), X(3872), and T_{cc}^+, observed as narrow resonances containing one or more charm quarks whose masses lie close to two-meson thresholds (DK for D*_{s0}(2317), D D̄* for X(3872), and DD* for T_{cc}^+) and which do not fit naturally into the predictions of the conventional constituent quark model for q\bar q or qqq states. Several competing internal-structure hypotheses have been proposed for such states: (i) hadronic molecular states bound by meson exchange between two ordinary mesons, (ii) conventional but orbitally excited q\bar q resonances, (iii) compact tetraquark configurations of the form (qq)(\bar q\bar q) bound by colour forces between diquark and antidiquark clusters, (iv) pentaquark-type configurations, or (v) mixtures of such components with possible q\bar q cores.

Determine the actual internal structure of each of D*_{s0}(2317), X(3872), and T_{cc}^+ within QCD, and identify the set of experimental observables of charm-hadron strong interactions (for example, charm-meson scattering lengths and effective ranges with light hadrons, line shapes near thresholds, production yields and momentum correlations of charm-hadron pairs in heavy-ion or pp collisions) that are sufficient to discriminate decisively between the molecular, conventional excited q\bar q, compact tetraquark, pentaquark, and mixed interpretations.

while f satisfies the Vlasov (collisionless transport) equation along the geodesic flow on the mass shell.

Seek stationary, axially symmetric solutions (g, f) admitting two commuting Killing vector fields, one timelike at infinity and one spacelike with closed orbits, such that the spacetime is asymptotically flat and contains a central black hole, i.e. there is a non-trivial event horizon H whose induced geometry one prescribes as an inner boundary, and such that f is supported in the domain of outer communications and is not required to be small (in particular, not a perturbation of a vacuum Kerr solution).

Question: Do there exist such stationary axially symmetric self-gravitating Einstein–Vlasov solutions with a central black hole in a genuinely non-perturbative regime (the Vlasov matter not assumed close to vacuum)? Equivalently, can one construct such solutions—analytically or numerically (e.g. by imposing inner boundary conditions at the horizon in an iterative scheme)—beyond the known perturbative existence near Kerr with small matter content?

Consider the charmed baryon Λc+ (a hadron consisting of an up, down, and charm quark with electric charge +1) interacting with a proton p. Two classes of Λc+–p interaction potentials are commonly proposed: (i) potentials derived from lattice QCD calculations, which tend to be moderately attractive, and (ii) phenomenological meson-exchange potentials, which tend to be more strongly attractive and in some cases admit a two-body Λc+–p bound state surviving the repulsive Coulomb interaction between the two positively charged baryons.

(a) Determine whether charm hypernuclei — nuclei containing at least one bound Λc+ baryon together with ordinary nucleons — exist as quantum-mechanically bound systems, and characterize the Λc+–nucleon potential that would bind a Λc+ to ordinary nuclear matter.

(b) For the two-body system specifically, decide whether the Λc+–p system supports a bound state once the attractive strong interaction and the repulsive Coulomb interaction are both included.

(c) Show whether femtoscopic two-particle correlation functions C(k*) of Λc+–p pairs, measured in high-energy pp and heavy-ion collisions as a function of the relative momentum k* and the emitting source radius, can quantitatively calibrate the Λc+–p interaction potential and discriminate between lattice-QCD-based and phenomenological potentials, in particular by exploiting the predicted source-radius dependence induced by the interplay of Coulomb repulsion and strong attraction.

Consider the Einstein-Vlasov system in general relativity, in which a collisionless ensemble of particles is described by a non-negative distribution function f on the cotangent bundle of a four-dimensional Lorentzian spacetime (M,g), satisfying the Vlasov equation along the geodesic flow of g, while the metric g satisfies the Einstein field equations with stress-energy tensor T_{μν} obtained as the momentum-space moment of f. Restrict attention to axially symmetric spacetimes, i.e. those admitting a spacelike Killing vector field with closed orbits, and consider stationary solutions of this system (admitting in addition a timelike Killing vector field) that are highly compact, meaning that the ratio 2M/R of twice the ADM mass to a suitable areal radius approaches the Buchdahl-type limit, and which have been constructed numerically only at very high spatial resolution.

(a) Determine whether such highly compact stationary axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov configurations are dynamically stable under perturbations evolved by the full nonlinear axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov evolution equations, or whether they instead undergo gravitational collapse or dispersion.

(b) Devise a numerical evolution scheme (or analytic framework) capable of inheriting the very high spatial resolution required to resolve such stationary solutions, so that simulations of their evolution—and in particular their stability or collapse—are computationally feasible.

Let $\mathbb{T} = \{e^{i\theta} : \theta \in [0, 2\pi)\}$ denote the unit circle, and for $1 \le p < \infty$ let $H^p$ denote the Hardy space of analytic functions on the open unit disk whose boundary values lie in $L^p(\mathbb{T})$, equipped with the norm
$$\|f\|_{H^p} = \left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} |f(e^{i\theta})|^p\, d\theta\right)^{1/p}.$$
For $f \in H^p$ with Fourier series $f(e^{i\theta}) \sim \sum_{n\ge 0} \hat f(n) e^{in\theta}$, define the backward shift operator $B : H^p \to H^p$ by
$$(Bf)(e^{i\theta}) = e^{-i\theta}\bigl(f(e^{i\theta}) - \hat f(0)\bigr).$$
Equivalently, if $K_0 f = \hat f(0)$ denotes the rank-one projection onto the constants, then $|Bf| = |(I-K_0)f|$ on $\mathbb{T}$, so $\|B\|_{B(H^p)} = \|I - K_0\|_{B(H^p)}$.

Determine, for each $1 \le p < \infty$, the exact value of the operator norm $\|B\|_{B(H^p)}$.

Determine whether the following statement holds: for every integer $k \geq 1$, there exists an integer $m \geq 1$ (possibly depending on $k$, $n$, and $p$) such that whenever $A, B \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}_p)$ satisfy
$$AB \equiv BA \pmod{p^m},$$
there exist $A', B' \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}_p)$ with

Let $\mathbb{H}^3$ denote three-dimensional hyperbolic space and let $\mathrm{Isom}(\mathbb{H}^3)$ be its group of isometries. For a discrete subgroup $H \leq \mathrm{Isom}(\mathbb{H}^3)$, define the critical exponent
$$\delta(H) = \inf\Big\{ s \geq 0 \;:\; \sum_{h \in H} e^{-s\, d_{\mathbb{H}^3}(o,\, h\cdot o)} < \infty \Big\},$$
where $o \in \mathbb{H}^3$ is a fixed basepoint (the value is independent of the choice of $o$). It is known that for any lattice $\Gamma \leq \mathrm{Isom}(\mathbb{H}^3)$ one has $\delta(\Gamma) = 2$, and for every infinite normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq \Gamma$ one has $\delta(N)/\delta(\Gamma) > 1/2$.

Question: Does there exist a lattice $\Gamma \leq \mathrm{Isom}(\mathbb{H}^3)$ and a sequence $\{N_i\}_{i\geq 1}$ of (infinite) normal subgroups $N_i \trianglelefteq \Gamma$ such that
$$\lim_{i \to \infty} \frac{\delta(N_i)}{\delta(\Gamma)} = \frac{1}{2}\,?$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The strict inequality $\delta(N)/\delta(\Gamma) > 1/2$ is established for normal subgroups of groups acting on hyperbolic / negatively curved spaces with strongly contracting elements (e.g., Jaerisch–Matsuzaki–Yabuki; Coulon–Dougall–Schapira–Tapie; Gekhtman–Levit; Arzhantseva–Cashen et al.). Whether the value $1/2$ is achieved as a limit for sequences of normal subgroups in a lattice of $\mathrm{Isom}(\mathbb{H}^3)$ does not appear to be settled in the available literature, and recent works treat $1/2$ as a sharp lower bound whose attainability (as a limit) remains unresolved.

Let G be a finitely generated group and fix a finite symmetric generating set S. For an action of G on a set X and a point x ∈ X, let Vol_{G,X}(n) denote the maximum, over x ∈ X, of the cardinality of the orbit {g·x : g ∈ B_S(n)}, where B_S(n) is the ball of radius n in the word metric on G associated to S. For functions f,g: ℕ → ℝ_{≥0}, write f ≼ g if there exist constants C, k > 0 with f(n) ≤ C·g(kn) for all n.

Say that G has Schreier growth gap f if, for every faithful action of G on a set X, one has f(n) ≼ Vol_{G,X}(n). The gap is called nontrivial if f is superlinear (i.e. f(n)/n → ∞), and exponential if f(n) = exp(cn) for some c > 0.

Question: Does there exist a Gromov hyperbolic group G that admits a nontrivial Schreier growth gap but does not admit an exponential Schreier growth gap?

Define an $\ell_p$ complex (for $p\in[1,\infty]$) to be a simplicial complex equipped with a length metric such that each closed cell is isometric to a Euclidean simplex in $(\mathbb{R}^n,\ell_p)$ for some $n$, with isometric face identifications.

Recall that a (conical, convex) bicombing on a metric space $(X,d)$ is a map $\sigma:X\times X\times[0,1]\to X$ such that for every $x,y\in X$, $t\mapsto\sigma(x,y,t)$ is a constant-speed geodesic from $x$ to $y$, and such that for all $x,y,x',y'\in X$ the function $t\mapsto d(\sigma(x,y,t),\sigma(x',y',t))$ is convex on $[0,1]$. A geodesic metric space $(X,d)$ is called Busemann convex if for any two constant-speed geodesics $\gamma,\gamma':[0,1]\to X$, the function $t\mapsto d(\gamma(t),\gamma'(t))$ is convex.

A group $G$ acts geometrically on a metric space $X$ if the action is by isometries, properly discontinuous, and cocompact.

Question: Let $G$ be a Gromov-hyperbolic group. Does there exist a number $p\in[2,\infty)$ and an $\ell_p$ complex $X$ on which $G$ acts geometrically such that
(i) $X$ admits a convex bicombing, or
(ii) $X$ is Busemann convex?

The question appears in a recent (2023) problem list on $\ell_p$ models for hyperbolic groups and is stated as an open problem. While it is known that every hyperbolic group acts geometrically on a proper finite-dimensional space with a unique convex bicombing (Lang and collaborators), realizing such an action on an $\ell_p$ simplicial complex with $p\in[2,\infty)$ remains open. Related recent work on link conditions for piecewise $\ell_p$ cell complexes and CUB spaces does not resolve the question.

Inside an intact eukaryotic cell, the genome is spatially organized in three dimensions and can be partitioned, on the basis of chromatin conformation capture data, into two broad classes of regions called the A compartment (associated with transcriptionally active, open chromatin) and the B compartment (associated with transcriptionally inactive, closed chromatin). Investigate the following:

(a) Characterize, in a spatially resolved manner within intact cells, how the three-dimensional arrangement of chromatin influences transcriptional activity. In particular, describe quantitatively what happens to nascent transcription, RNA localization, and chromatin state at the interfaces (borders) between A and B compartments.

(b) Determine whether there exist additional, finer spatial or structural features—beyond the binary A/B partition—that further distinguish distinct genomic compartments from one another (for example, sub-compartments, contact-frequency signatures, radial positioning, or association with nuclear bodies), and provide criteria that rigorously identify such features.

Provide a framework (experimental, computational, or mathematical) capable of answering (a) and (b) and validate it on genome-wide data from intact cells.

representations.normalized: In stellar evolution modeling, the boundary of a star's convective core is conventionally located where the Schwarzschild (or Ledoux) criterion is marginally satisfied. To account for inertial penetration of fluid elements beyond this formal boundary, one introduces a convective-core overshooting parameter β ≥ 0, which prescribes that the mixed region extends a distance β·H_p beyond the formal core edge, where H_p is the local pressure scale height (with appropriate modification for very small cores). The value of β controls the size of the mixed core during the main sequence and thus strongly influences a star's evolutionary track, lifetime, and observable properties.\n\nConsider main-sequence and post-main-sequence stars with masses M in a range (roughly 1.1 M_⊙ ≲ M ≲ 10 M_⊙) for which a convective core is present and overshooting is dynamically relevant. Determine whether there exists a well-defined, physically meaningful function β = β(M) (possibly depending also on metallicity and evolutionary phase) such that stellar evolution models using β(M) simultaneously reproduce the observed properties (masses, radii, effective temperatures, luminosities, and ages) of independent calibrators, in particular detached eclipsing binary systems with precisely measured component masses. Equivalently: prove or disprove that the calibrations of β derived from different binary systems (and from other observational constraints such as cluster isochrones and asteroseismology) at comparable stellar masses are mutually consistent, or exhibit them as incompatible and characterize the source of the discrepancy.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Multiple independent studies of detached eclipsing binaries, open clusters, and asteroseismic targets have proposed mass–β relations, but they disagree in both the functional form and the calibrated values of β at fixed mass. Recent works (Claret & Torres; Constantino & Baraffe; Tkachenko et al.; Higl et al.) report mutually inconsistent calibrations, and the issue remains an active and unresolved area of stellar astrophysics.

Consider a living cell modeled as a dynamical system characterized by two coupled state descriptors: (i) a high-dimensional gene-expression / cell-state profile e(t) ∈ R^n (e.g. transcript abundances across n genes, together with discrete or continuous cell-type labels), and (ii) a morphological/behavioral descriptor m(t) (e.g. cell shape parameters, membrane geometry, polarity, and instantaneous velocity / migratory behavior). Biologically, membrane composition — largely lipids and proteins whose abundances are controlled by gene expression — strongly constrains m(t), while changes in m(t) (shape deformation, motion, mechanical environment) feed back to alter e(t).

Formulate and characterize the bidirectional coupling between e(t) and m(t). Specifically:

1. Identify which components of the gene-expression profile e(t) causally determine which features of cellular morphology, membrane dynamics, and motile behavior m(t), and quantify the corresponding forward map e ↦ m.

2. Identify how perturbations to morphology and motion (changes in m(t), including mechanical stresses, shape changes, and migration through different environments) feed back to alter gene expression, and quantify the corresponding reverse map m ↦ e.

3. Combine (1) and (2) into a coupled model (e.g. of the form de/dt = F(e,m), dm/dt = G(e,m)) whose predictions agree with experimental observations across diverse cell types and conditions.

Provide a complete mechanistic and predictive account of this bidirectional interaction.

Consider a detached eclipsing binary system whose two stellar components have masses, radii, effective temperatures, and surface metallicities determined to high precision by photometric and spectroscopic observations. A stellar evolution pipeline takes such observational constraints as input and returns estimates of two calibration parameters: (i) the common age t of the system, and (ii) the convective core overshooting efficiency β (parametrized, e.g., as the fraction of the local pressure scale height by which the convective core boundary is extended). Such a pipeline depends on choices including the stellar evolution code, the prescription and efficiency of microscopic diffusion of heavy elements, the inclusion or omission of additional extra-mixing processes (e.g., rotational mixing, thermohaline mixing, turbulent mixing), the adopted nuclear reaction rates and opacities, the input grid of evolutionary tracks, and the statistical estimation algorithm used to match models to observations.

Formulate and answer the following questions:

(a) Given a fixed set of observational constraints for such a binary, do two different pipelines that differ only in their assumptions about microscopic diffusion efficiency and the presence of extra-mixing mechanisms generically produce statistically distinguishable estimates of (t, β)?

(b) Quantify the spread in the inferred (t, β) induced by varying (i) the stellar evolution code, (ii) the diffusion/extra-mixing prescriptions, and (iii) the estimation algorithm, while keeping the observational data fixed.

(c) Determine to what extent the resulting calibration values (t, β) reflect intrinsic properties of the binary system, as opposed to systematic artifacts of the modeller's chosen input physics and inference procedure, and identify conditions (if any) under which the inferred parameters can be regarded as code-independent properties of the stars.

While there is an active literature on neutral drift, biased clonal competition, and lattice/Voronoi models of clonal dynamics (e.g. work by Klein, Simons, and collaborators), no single result has resolved how local neighborhoods, tissue geometry, and niches jointly shape clone size, composition, and dispersion. Let a tissue be modeled as a finite set of cells $C$ together with a spatial adjacency graph $G=(C,E)$ and a gene-expression map $x:C\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$. Suppose each cell carries a heritable lineage barcode that partitions $C$ into clones, and that a lineage tree $T$ is reconstructed so that every internal node corresponds to a generation (division event). For a clone $Y\subseteq C$ that forms a connected component of a subgraph $Q\subseteq G$, let $|Y|$ denote its cardinality (clonal size) and let $g(Y)$ denote the set of generations at which the rate of expansion of $Y$ along $T$ falls below a fixed threshold (i.e.\ slows or halts).

Address the following:

Consider the Vlasov–Poisson system in three spatial dimensions modeling a self-gravitating collisionless gas. Let f = f(t,x,v) ≥ 0 denote the phase-space density on R^3 × R^3, satisfying

  ∂_t f + v · ∇_x f − ∇_x U · ∇_v f = 0,
  ΔU = 4π ρ,  ρ(t,x) = ∫_{R^3} f(t,x,v) dv,  U(t,x) → 0 as |x| → ∞.

A "flat" steady state is a time-independent solution f = f_0(x,v) whose spatial support is concentrated on a two-dimensional disk {x_3 = 0} ⊂ R^3, with a corresponding axially symmetric induced potential U; such configurations serve as Newtonian models of disk galaxies. A general framework for producing steady states is the following fixed-point iteration: given an ansatz f = φ(E, L) where E = |v|^2/2 + U(x) is the particle energy and L is the angular momentum about the symmetry axis, define the operator T that sends a candidate potential U to the potential U' generated (via the Poisson equation) by the spatial density associated with φ(E_U, L); a steady state corresponds to a fixed point U = T(U).

Problem. Develop a rigorous fixed-point iteration scheme of this type that produces flat (disk-supported) axially symmetric steady states of the Vlasov–Poisson system. In particular, identify a function space and a class of microscopic ansatz functions φ for which T admits a fixed point yielding genuine flat steady states, including configurations relevant as Newtonian disk-galaxy models (e.g., those exhibiting flat rotation curves).

Recent work (2024) establishes a mass-preserving fixed-point algorithm and proves existence of fixed points in the spherically symmetric Vlasov–Poisson case, with the authors stating belief that the result extends to the flat axially symmetric case but without a full proof yet. Numerical construction of flat steady states with flat rotation curves has been carried out, while a complete rigorous existence theorem covering the disk-galaxy-relevant flat solutions via the fixed-point method remains open. Some related variational (Energy-Casimir) existence and stability results for flat Vlasov–Poisson steady states exist but do not cover the same class.

Let $Q_n = \{0,1\}^n$ denote the $n$-dimensional hypercube. A $k$-dimensional subcube of $Q_n$ is a subset obtained by fixing $n-k$ of the coordinates to values in $\{0,1\}$ and letting the remaining $k$ coordinates range freely over $\{0,1\}$. Write $Q_n^k$ for the set of all $k$-dimensional subcubes of $Q_n$, so $|Q_n^k| = \binom{n}{k}2^{n-k}$.

For integers $0 \le k \le d \le n$, say that a family $\mathcal{F} \subseteq Q_n^k$ is $Q_n^d$-free if every $d$-dimensional subcube of $Q_n$ contains at least one $k$-dimensional subcube that does not lie in $\mathcal{F}$. Define
$$\mathrm{ex}_k(n,d) = \max\{|\mathcal{F}| : \mathcal{F} \subseteq Q_n^k \text{ is } Q_n^d\text{-free}\},$$
and define the Turán density
$$\pi_k(d) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\mathrm{ex}_k(n,d)}{|Q_n^k|}.$$

(This limit is known to exist for $0 \le k < d$.)

Prove or disprove: for $d = 3$ the three nontrivial densities all coincide, namely
$$\pi_0(3) = \pi_1(3) = \pi_2(3) = \tfrac{3}{4}.$$
